textfield_comment_value:
Although I have never owned Catan, I have played enough to feel as though I’ve gotten my moneys worth.

I have a mixed relationship with Catan. On one hand, this game has introduced an entire new generation of players to actual board games (not just party or card games). It has usurped the monolithic Monopoly as the go-to board game. It has achieved great things and its contribution to the board game scene as a whole is unparalleled. 

I, however, dislike Catan. Catan sucks. It is not fun. It is like someone once ate hotdog buns (Monopoly), and upon discovering you could throw a hotdog (Catan) in there, your experience is increased tenfold and you feel as though you are enlightened. But you are missing all the ketchup, mustard, and relish that exist for games much better than Catan.

My main problem with Catan is that the board setup sucks. Oftentimes, there are 1-3 optimal spots which are gobbled up first, and the other players place for some middling positions. Catan mitigated this as best as possible with a snake draft, but it is unarguable that games are won and lost at placement. Sure, tiles are balanced as fairly as possible with a 2d6 distribution, but even then the resource swing is too great. 

Catan is an engine-building game. The player first to place a second settlement is often the winner, because they can bankroll their engine even faster. There is little counterplay (the most important element of a competitive game) for the sucker trying to hit 11s and 12s to build a road or settlement. In tandem, there is extremely limited flexibility: you have to plan out where you want to go long before you get there. With the minimal counterplay there is, it is usually racing to secure a spot via road/settlement before the next player. And what happens if the other player gets there first? All your resources and investments is a total sunken cost. Ports follow a similar vein - they are somewhat useful, but their fixed position can make them entirely useless or too expensive of a sink to even bother.

This game is relatively straightforward. Players can generally figure out the best course of action. Whether or not they are able to accomplish it is totally up to the whims of the dice gods. If you’re second to a resource or intersection, it is almost better if you had never tried in the first place. This leads to players often realizing their demise long before the game is over, similar to Monopoly and Risk’s greatest pitfalls. 

To improve this game, there needs to be better counterplay and more flexibility. And unfortunately, by design, Catan offers very limited options. It’s an engine building lite game where you get slim resources by weighted chance; it’s a resource management game where you can lose half your resources on a 7 roll, or blow four turns of resources by someone beating you somewhere first.

I don’t hate chance in games, I am not a skill-purist like some, but man when you lose to dice, and not to other players, it isn’t only unsatisfying, it is frustrating. I like games that are satisfying and rewarding, not games that are frustrating.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value: There's a reason Settlers of Catan is so popular. It still stands up to time. Interesting game choices. Some area of control aspects. Some machine building. Some pushing your luck. Some trading. Some bluffing. Some take that and bitter revenge. It really balances a lot well. That being said, the choice of your starting settlements is hugely important. I do love that it's hugely important, but it does set the tone for the rest of your game. Trading may help balance some of that, but it's not guaranteed. My favorite part of the game is the setup. It's so important to choose good locations for your starting two towns. And the snaking order that those starting towns are placed is great too. First player to place the first town is the last player to place the second town. Last player to place the first town gets to place their second right after. And you earn starting resources based on your second placement. It's such an interesting choice. The rest of the game is interesting too, but that starting setup is just fantastic and so important to the rest of the game. Each turn the dice are rolled & summed and each town adjacent to a region with that sum produces the a resource of that type. You collect and trade resources to pay for different actions like building roads, building towns, upgrading towns to cities (which produce twice as much as towns), and buying development cards (which have various effects). You can make trades with other players, or trade 4 of a good type for any 1 good, or trade with ports at better rates once you build a town or city next to them. When a 7 is rolled, instead of producing goods, the player who rolled the 7 can move the robber to a region, preventing it from producing goods, and allowing the player to steal a random resource from a player with a town or city adjacent to the region. But if you have more than 7 goods when anyone rolls the robber, you lose half of them rounded down (your choice which). So you are both trying to save up goods, but also avoid hoarding too many. The first to 10 points wins. Each town is worth 1 point. Each city is worth 2 points. There's points for having the largest road. The development cards can also give points (either straight up points or for having the biggest army).  Now I will warn that while I love the game, it is certainly a rich get richer kind of game. Once you are on a roll, you could leave other players in the dust and it could still take a while to end the game. There is also luck in what die rolls come up, though I still feel like the choices are so strong in this game that they make up for it. And it's funny when a weak number keeps getting rolled. Often players won't want to trade unless they are getting something really good. While weaker players might form an unofficial alliance to help each other, it's more likely they will take any advantage they can get, even if it screws over other weak players. But generally when I don't do well in the game, I still feel responsible. The choices are still more interesting to me than most games.

textfield_comment_value:
This was a completely new gaming experience when I first played this. There's a lot of luck with the resource generation, but it is really a matter of "covering all the numbers", or making sure you can generate/trade resources whenever you can. Easy to play, but filled with a wide range of strategies, and just the right amount of luck. I've used this as a gateway game to convert several Scrabble die-hards into enthusiastic Settlers fans! The Cities & Knights expansion adds another layer of complexity, and more tension. The 5-6 player expansions add yet another dimension to the game, with the addition of the "special build" reactionary phase. Seafarers seems to be suited for scenario play, but not much else. Initial rating: "8". Peaked at "9", briefly with the 5-6 player expansion.

Update (05/28/2009): 6 F2F plays. This is turning out to be a frustrating game, in terms of the trends in dice rolling. Some games are simply dominated by an preponderance of 5's, 9's, 10's... any number that I happen to NOT be on. Or it could go the other way; there have been games where several people sit around and cannot do anything, simply because the rolls are not coming up in the frequency that they should be based on statistics. Either the dice are funky (which mean don't play with the dice that came with the game), or this is just one of those things. The Law of Large Numbers indicates that eventually, EVENTUALLY, the dice will start rolling favorably. But this trough of bad luck could last most of the entire game, making play extremely frustrating. It may be time to start using the "number cards", because this is starting to break the game for me, as well as others. This is evidenced by the fact that most meetup members refuse to play this game because of its excessive randomness. Dropping to a "7".

Update (08/17/2010): Lately, it hasn't gotten the love it once engendered. Downgrading to a "6".

Update (12/21/2013): It has been 4.5 years since last play. It is a significant achievement in the world of board gaming, truly a "classic" in every meaning of the word right up there with Monopoly--a game that is even "better" than Monopoly. It was a great game for the period, but the group has moved on to greener pastures. It looks like the game doesn't have the legs we thought it had; since there is too much unmitigated randomness, it has alienated most of the veteran gamers I know. But, the design is a perfect blend of competition, negotiation/trading, randomness, and skill, with a very accessible rule set and game mechanics, I am sure it will continue to bring in and endear many new generations of board gamers to come. Still holding at a "6".

Update (03/13/2015): 7 F2F plays. Finally! After nearly six years, we played a 4-player, base Catan game! It's like a homecoming. We forgot some of the basic rules, but the fun was back. Nice, quick romp, just like Dominion--a classic that you never forget. Still a "6".

so I finally played the granddaddy of them all, and all I can say is: the jury is still out for me on this game. The random set up and production rolls can lock a player out from contention early on. i don't like having to play a game for 30 more minutes with no chance of winning. Some resources seem more useful than others--why would anybody trade brick with you? seems to suffer from a rich get richer problem. those who can build roads can build settlements, can gain more resources, etc. maybe some of the problems were due to a very weird random board set up--like resources were all lumped together and a we had a full compliment of 6 players, which seemed to add to the length and randomness. I would like to play this again with just four.  

o.k. i've played this again this time with 3 players and i enjoyed it a little more. i can see where the appeal of this game with people who aren't game enthusiasts lies. very easy rules to teach and learn. the modular board is attractive and so different from what most people who don't play games as a hobby are used to seeing in a game, that the game can draw in uninitiated players  right in. 

i like how the trading stimulates player interaction, which is an element of the game that is much different for people only familiar with mass market US games. though, in my opinion,  the trading mechanism doesn't quite work 100% well, or is mostly uninteresting. 

there are some commodities in some games that will be more valuable than others because of the random production roles. players in the lead will at some point in the mid to late game find themselves never lacking. when they do need a trade, however, its in order to put them close to the win or to just win outright. this puts players who are behind, in a kingmaker position. sometimes to be able to do anything useful you will be forced to trade somebody something that's infinitely more useful to them because of their position in the game. your only other choice is to not make trades to these players and languish, or put another player in a position to win. if you don't trade, it becomes a matter of sitting there and waiting for the players in the lead to get lucky and have their production numbers come up, so that one of them can build whatever it is they need to win. how fun.

i enjoy the game up into the mid to late game where it gets boring, and it's obvious who is going to win, but the game nevertheless continues. 

i just don't really feel that a player's decisions amount to much in this game. production roles: luck. stealing resources with the robber: luck. drawing cards from the development deck: luck. 

still i'm happy to have this game on hand, despite my negative comments, because it something to play with people who aren't big on games due to the reasons i listed above.

CRITIQUE OF SETTLERS OF CATAN
Settlers of Catan is a mixed bag for me. I appreciate many aspects of the game: the variable setup of the board, the trading (a Euro game with interaction!), the different paths to victory, the short playing time. But on the other hand there are many things the game could do better.

The trading in Settlers has none of the fun of the trading in a game like Bohnanza, where you actually have to trade in order to do what you want. In Settlers, trading is entirely optional, and very often frustrating with less experienced players. It's annoying to watch the player in last place trade freely with the leader, giving them exactly what they need to win. In my opinion, the most important use of trading is as a catch-up mechanic, but everyone has to be on board, understand what's going on, and trade strategically for the purpose of keeping the game close. Unfortunately, this sours the game's main interactive element, making it feel very much like "bash the leader" style play.

The Robber is the same, and the use of the robber also increases the boredom factor by slowing the flow of resources in the game.

I do like the conversion of resources into roads, settlements, or cards, but the flow of these resources is based on a roll of the dice, which make it all too easy in Settlers to have a turn in which you can do nothing. For me, this is a BIG negative, because doing nothing is not fun. Furthermore, the imbalance in the relative value of the resources undermines the "multiple paths to victory" aspect of the game.

The decisions in Settlers are fairly interesting, and give the game another way for players to interact (by means of the area control aspect of the game). Unfortunately, every interaction is just a variation on the theme of "blocking." And the fact that your network of roads and settlements is developed so slowly means that there is little recourse for a blocked player. Unlike worker placement games, in which blocking only works for a single turn, blocking in Settlers is often permanent.

None of this prevents the game from being fun, but it does make it less fun than other games I own. Finally, there is the production value of the game: Settlers has sub-par components. Mayfair should be embarrassed to put out a groundbreaking game like this with such shoddy bits. I could list all the defects, but honestly only the rulebook seems like a quality product. Aesthetically the game could have been much better done.

I ended up giving away my copy of Settlers, which I had never had the urge to get to the table. I've played the game several times, with experienced players, but just never enjoyed it as much as I enjoy other games.

Finally got a chance to play a real game of Settlers and I enjoyed it. textfield_comment_value:
I've been in the gaming scene long enough to know that this title is not the end all be all of gaming.  If anyone were to tell me that this was their favorite board game, I would have to ask them if they had played any other euro games.  I can't but think that anyone who had tried several titles would have to know that the genre has evolved since Catan.

Still, Catan is not completely obsolete.  It occupies a unique position in that it is light years ahead of Parker Brothers in terms of depth, but still accessible enough to be interesting to new players who are not immersed in board gaming.  This makes it valuable as a gateway game.  I still use this to introduce friends to serious board gaming.

The gameplay itself is perhaps better than people give it credit for.  The negotiations for resources are always interesting.

The biggest problem with the game comes down to how much the dice can deny unlucky players a chance to enter the game.  Good placement and smart trading can only take you so far, but I've played numerous games in which for the first several turns only three numbers were rolled.  There are house rules and expansions that help smooth out the distribution of resources, but ultimately a pig-headed group can ruin your game.

That is not an unforgivable feature of a game.  Most games are more fun with better players, but some games just do a better job of making sure the players have to really work to hold their lead.

Ultimately, I think this a title that is well worth owning.  Even though I don't really play it with my regular game group any more, I still enjoy introducing it to new players or taking it for a spin for old time's sake.  Gaming has moved on from Settlers, which may make it seem like it's gotten worse, but it's still as strong of title as it ever was.  If you don't have it, you may not need to buy it, but if you do have it, you probably shouldn't sell it.  You'll eventually be glad you still have it.

It is worth mentioning that Catan now has approximately one million expansions and more seem to come out all the time.  Perhaps they've found a way to reproduce?  At any rate, these expansions do make the game better.  However, I think this is more worthwhile as a means of extending the life of your current copy of the game than as a reason for buying the base game.

Right now, Catan with two expansions costs around $80 ($100 for a six player board).  With three you're looking at $120 ($140 for six players).  I have had fun playing with the expansions, but I don't think the experience was worth that much, especially when Archipelago is only $60 and doesn't need expansions to be awesome.

textfield_comment_value:
CATAN’s box, with its ketchup and mustard color palette and lifeless illustrations, acts as a deterrent to people unfamiliar with modern board games.  Somehow it has managed to sell millions of copies, so I guess it operates under the “if it ain’t broke, don’t fix it” principle.  I was initially smitten, but my enthusiasm quickly abated.  Its vintage status partially excuses the fact that you need three or more people to play, but it doesn’t cut the mustard by today’s standards (just one more mustard reference and I’ll hit the trifecta).  The ability to play these types of games with just one other person is what has really brought me and so many others into this hobby, and I have also begun to devour solo modes.  But the bigger problem is game length.  My last two four-player games of CATAN went on for two to three hours.  That’s too long for something that really amounts to dice rolling and card trading.  The “distance rule” seems to be the sticky wicket here, since it repeatedly foils opportunities for expansion and scoring.  It’s annoying, and I think I prefer the game without it.  Then there’s the trading mechanism, which is a chore.  There’s no real point to it since people tend not to trade unless it is mutually beneficial, so there’s no actual creative wheeling and dealing.  Is anyone willing to trade a brick?  No?  Okay.  Your turn.  Finally, there’s the robber, who stops being amusing pretty quickly.  I try to keep my hand lean to avoid his wrath, but sometimes I get lucky on a couple of dice rolls between turns.  I scheme up my best options as I wait for my turn, and once it comes I immediately roll a seven and lose half my bounty.  Poof.  No more options.  Does anyone want to trade a brick?  No?  Okay.  Your turn.  I can still laugh about it, but they’re tears of a clown at this point.  CATAN remains a great gateway game, especially for demonstrating how there can be a lot of fun inside the blandest of boxes.  Monopoly is French’s yellow, CATAN is Grey Poupon, and now there’s an entire aisle full of stone ground, hand-crafted in small batches artisan mustards from which to choose.  Trifecta.

Update: Sold on February 4, 2025.  For me, there are two major problems with CATAN: each game’s outcome is almost entirely luck-based, and my significant other refuses to play - and those are just the major problems.  The luck aspect wouldn’t be so bad if this were a short, light experience; problem is, games always seem to move quickly until they inevitably stall out, and the lengthy deadlock that follows is all grind and no gratification.  It’s also very ugly.

textfield_comment_value:
Reglas básicas de *Catan* en 15 puntos:

1. **Objetivo**: Ser el primero en alcanzar 10 puntos de victoria, que se obtienen mediante construcción de asentamientos, ciudades y cartas de desarrollo.

2. **Preparación**: El tablero es modular, compuesto por hexágonos que representan diferentes tipos de recursos (madera, ladrillo, lana, grano y mineral). Cada hexágono tiene un número asignado.

3. **Turno del jugador**:
   - **Lanzar los dados**: El jugador lanza dos dados, y los hexágonos cuya suma coincida con el resultado producen recursos para los jugadores que tienen asentamientos o ciudades adyacentes.
   - **Intercambios**: Los jugadores pueden comerciar recursos entre sí o con el banco.
   - **Construcción**: El jugador puede construir asentamientos, ciudades o carreteras, si tiene los recursos necesarios.

4. **Construir asentamientos**: Requiere 1 madera, 1 ladrillo, 1 lana y 1 grano, y debe colocarse en una intersección vacía, alejada al menos de dos asentamientos rivales.

5. **Construir ciudades**: Requiere 3 grano y 2 mineral. Una ciudad reemplaza un asentamiento y otorga más recursos al producirse.

6. **Construir carreteras**: Requiere 1 madera y 1 ladrillo, y deben conectarse a un asentamiento o ciudad propia.

7. **Cartas de desarrollo**: Se compran con 1 grano, 1 mineral y 1 lana. Estas cartas pueden ser de caballeros, avance, progreso o puntos de victoria.

8. **Ladrones**: Si sale un 7 en los dados, los jugadores deben descartar la mitad de sus cartas si tienen más de 7. Luego, el jugador que tiró el dado mueve el ladrón a un hexágono, bloqueando su producción y robando una carta a un jugador cercano.

9. **Puntos de victoria**: Los asentamientos valen 1 punto y las ciudades 2 puntos. Las cartas de desarrollo pueden dar puntos adicionales.

10. **Carretera más larga**: El jugador con la mayor cadena continua de carreteras obtiene 2 puntos adicionales.

11. **Ejército más grande**: El jugador que tenga al menos 3 cartas de caballero y haya jugado más caballeros que otros, obtiene 2 puntos adicionales.

12. **Intercambios con el banco**: El jugador puede intercambiar 4 cartas del mismo tipo por 1 de cualquier recurso en el banco, o en puertos, con tasas más favorables.

13. **Puertos**: Los puertos permiten intercambiar recursos a una tasa favorable. Hay puertos de 2:1 y 3:1.

14. **Turno final**: El juego termina cuando un jugador alcanza 10 puntos de victoria, incluso si es en el turno de otro jugador.

15. **Estrategia**: La clave del juego es gestionar bien los recursos, comerciar y posicionarse estratégicamente en el tablero.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
I like that this game got a lot of non-gamers into real boardgames.  I consider this the first "real" boardgame I ever played (meaning, Monopoly and Checkers and such aren't real).  I like that it's innovative and original.  But now I don't play it anymore and I'll tell you why.

The biggest thing is that it's too random, luck-based, for how long it is.  I'm fine with randomness in a short game, but once you start adding expansions (and the game is too boring without them), the games can take 3-5 hours if you include setup and teardown.  That's way too much of a time investment considering how swingy the dice can be.

Now I will play this game occasionally with the cards that replace the dice (they come in the Traders and Barbarians expansion).  That system is absolutely great.  It keeps the same probabilities of rolls coming up, but it ensures that each die roll (5's, for instance) will actually come up a certain number of times, but without guaranteeing exactly how many times it will come up.  Brilliant.

But those cards have events on them which only exacerbate another problem the game has: the catch-up mechanisms.  There are waaaaay too many of them when you play with the cards and you have the fish (which involves the boot) and you're playing Cities and Knights (the 3 stacks of development cards).  These are my family's favorite things because without them the game doesn't seem meaty enough.  But these 3 elements all have catch-up mechanisms and basically, the best strategy is to not be in first place, be in second, and then as the first place player gets beat down, take his place towards the end of the game.

And like with luck, it's no fun to have a game have a lot of catch-up mechanisms if it's also very long.

In summary, Catan isn't elegant at all.  To play a fun game you need expansions and expansions add complexity and it's not elegant how they interact.  Other games are more meaty to begin with, or have expansions that are more elegant.  

This isn't a great game.  I know some people will say, "well it's a great way to get non-gamers into boardgames.  It's a gateway game."  Again it's too long for how random it is.  If you want the luck and light strategy, get them into Machi Koro, which is a third the timespan so you can play multiple times.  If you want something with better expansions get Alhambra, the Big Box.  Or if you want something that's already well-rounded and can handle large player counts while being very strategic, get 7 Wonders (has expansions) or Between Two Cities (shorter).

We don't need Catan any more.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
I came to Settlers maybe a year or two into my gaming career, and as such, I think I have a very different view of the game whose first great gaming love was Settlers.

I've just never really enjoyed playing it. But I think I understand the game's popularity. It meshes together several different mechanics (one of which, importantly, is trading) in a simple and clean package, with enough luck that even new players can win. I can see how coming from a lifetime of Parker Bros. games this feels like the pinnacle of gaming.

As I said above, I think one of the reasons this game is so beloved is that it incorporates trading. There are plenty of trading games out there, but often that's ALL they are. Settlers, to this day, is one of the few games that is a hybrid board manipulation/building and trading game. I wish there were more games like this - I really believe trading being a part of a bigger whole is what has made this game so irreplaceable for many, many people.

That said, trading is one of the reasons I don't enjoy Settlers. Trading feels incredibly limited here - most of the time, people don't have anything to trade you, and if they do, they might have one of it and you just make very straightforward trades. You almost never have the opportunity to feel like you've got the upper hand on someone, like you're sneakily making a really excellent trade for yourself, or like you're making a bad trade for you because you're desperate for something (this really only happens if people have been denying you because you're in the lead). It's just too cut and dry for my tastes. Hell, Bohnanza has more variable and exciting deals.

I do like that resources always feel scarce and valuable. In my experience, you never tend to stockpile resources like you do in other games so losing a resource always feels like it's doing real harm.

But to me, it's always felt like the most interesting choice you make is made at the beginning when you place your initial settlements, and after that you're at the mercy of the dice (your rolls and other people's). It really feels like the die is the determining factor all too often (and the game runs too long for me to be okay with that). It's pretty easy for one player to get locked out of winning the game early on due to some bad rolls, and then just have to sit there watching everyone else expand. Blech.

And then there's the games that run some three hours for no good reason. Ughhhh.

I can be talked into playing this, but really, I'd be happy to never play again.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
02/08/2013: This game has been around a while and seems to have brought a lot of people into the hobby.  I started with Carcassonne but soon picked this up because of the sheer amount of "press" it gets around here...good and bad.  I think a lot of negativity has arose just because so many gamers have played it too much.

I think it's a very solid game that can have stretches of poor luck thrust upon you from the dice rolls.  Players are trying to build roads, settlements, and cities on the island of Catan, earning VP along the way.  The first to 10 VP is the winner.  Two things come to mind when I think of Catan - trading and those dice.  You collect resources based on the number rolled with the dice.  Usually, you'll get something, but there can be seemingly endless stretches where you get diddly.  One thing we just tried out was too use some coins (from the Settlers of America game) when someone receives zero resources on any turn.  They can then trade in two coins for any one resource.  That really helped a lot with the flow of the game and randomness of the dice.  However, it did seem to affect the other main mechanism of the game.

Trading is a big part of this game.  You must be willing to trade with any and all players throughout most of the game.  Someone is always needing resources and if you can find a trade that will help both players, you'll be successful.  However, when we played with the coins, that did seem to stymie the trading just a bit.  If you're asking for an Ore and you've got two or more coins in front of you, that made the other players hesitate regarding the trade.

Anyway, I'm really going on too long about this stuff.  The game is very good.  Very fun.  It runs a little long with my family though.  Our last play (with coins) was a solid hour and a half...and that was quick for us.  The components looks nice and are mostly good.  However, right from the get go, the framing tiles (the water) that goes around the main island were warped and unusable.  That wasn't a big deal; just set up the island and use the harbor tiles instead.  But when we played recently, I noticed that several of the tiles are staring to warp as well.  That's not cool.  I store my games in my bedroom closet so there shouldn't be an issue with "weather conditions."  And considering we've only played this half a dozen times, the game should be in pristine condition.  I'm a little upset about that.  Otherwise, the cards and dice, and wooden pieces are all standard, good quality.

textfield_comment_value:
"VERY GOOD"

I have a Jubiläum Edition (25 Jahre Catan - base Catan + Seafarers) that has been waiting about 2 years for the kids to get "old enough" to play, and we finally tried the first game (3P): I and my two sons, 9 and 7 y.o.  (he turned 7 the day before !). 
Actually, they have been playing a lot with the components as toys, but the first game we played was yesterday.
Don´t listen to some disparaging comments about Catan ("old-fashioned", "outdated", "didnt´age well", "too luck-driven", etc.). As happens when the subject is wine, fashion, etc., some people end up being pedantic ...

This game is unique in many ways, and really fun!

We used the suggested board configuration for beginners, and can´t wait to try the random setups.
As game length is a sensible matter among us (30 - 45 minutes is our sweet spot; 45 - 60 minutes, a threshold), we used some ways to accelerate the beginning and shorten the playtime, which served also to apply handicaps, adjusting the difficulty for the kids: 

- they both started with a village and a city, instead of 2 villages (I started with 2 villages); 
- the robber was only allowed to show up from the 3rd round on (any "seven" rolled in the first and second rounds would be re-rolled);
- they could place the robber only on tiles that affected ME, but not one another;
- whenever I rolled a seven (or played a knight), I would place the robber on tiles that affected them in an alternating fashion, starting with the elder;
- I suggested we finish at 8 points, but as the game went on, we agreed to go for 10 points.

Our dining room turned into a street market !  :-D

The younger got the longest road AND the largest army tiles (!), and reached 9 points. The elder managed to grab the largest army tile from him but, as everybody was tired, we opted to leave the game undecided.

Well, I was stomped bad, so we will have to reassess those tweaks !  >:-/

No doubt the playing time will shorten with further plays (60+ minutes duration was the only downside so far).

And to diminish the luck factor (if it ever becomes an issue), many options are available for testing, among which:

- re-rolling when a number comes up twice in a row - which at least prevents that the same resources be produced twice in a row (or the robber being moved so);
- using a deck of dice (which "forces", to varying degrees, the statistics of the 2 dice).
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
One of the games that brought my sister and me beyond the borders of the known boardgame world. When we were kids, my mom used to play the Catan computer game, and when she found a copy of the boardgame at a local toy store, she bought it and taught it to us during our weekly summer holiday in the Austrian Alps. From then on, for about ten years, we would be playing Catan all week long while on holiday - but not during the year. This changed in the last few years, when I got more involved in boardgaming, and we've played Catan during a weekend now and then.

Even though this game could be considered old, I think it still holds up against its competitors nowadays. Catan has become a well-known game in the mass-market, and I think that's a good thing.

I like the game. Even if you're losing, you can still set your own small goals, achievements to be reached in your own personal struggle. I also like that the level of 'viciousness' is completely adaptable to the group's desires, while still staying within the framework of the rules: I once had a player who allowed another player to decide where he'd put the robber, as long as that other player promised to make a certain trade with him during that turn - on the other hand, I've also had games where the robber got parked out of harm's way because the player decided everyone had been punished enough by having to discard half of their cards.

There's an interesting variety of strategies available to players: will you invest in long road networks to grab and hold the longest trading route, or buy develoment cards in search of victory points (and the biggest army), work towards building up your infrastructure with many villages (preferable on tile numbers that already grant you resources) or upgrade your villages into large cities?

This may sound weird, but Catan leaves me room to develop a story. An epic tale about how the different civilizations on the island flourish or wither away. One remarkable thing about our copy, by the way, is that the red - statistically most likely to be rolled - numbers often get rolled less than the weird numbers with low oddes, like 2's, 11's or 12's.

N.B.: I also prefer the wooden bits from my old copy over the ones from the wooden 15 year anniversary edition (though the wooden resource and number tiles are cooler) and especially over the plastic ones from newer editions.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Before I even got into board games, I hated Catan. No particular reason- I had never played it, but it disgusted me. Now, a year or so after adopting the hobby, I've had a chance to try it, the patient zero of euro games' western journey, and... It turns out my gut was right. "Patient Zero" turns out to be an apt metaphor, as this game needs to be quarantined and carefully examined, so we can all see exactly what's wrong with it and never, ever again make those mistakes. 
Catan is unbelievably frustrating, boring, and random. The complete incompetence in which each of its mechanics are implemented is nothing short of incredible. Rolling for resources is okay in a lighter game like Machi Koro, but Catan wants to be a Game For Big Boys(tm) with its modular board and hex tiles and wooden houses and 2-hour play time that feels like 8. Open resource trading is okay in... Well, nothing I've ever played, but it's at its worst and most painfully pointless in Catan. Take-that mechanics are okay in plenty of games, but in Catan you don't want to use them because your fellow players are already suffering enough. A friendly game of Catan is mechanically equivalent to a group of starving POWs playing Craps for their last few pieces of moldy gruel for the week occasionally giving each other unprompted cigarette burns while listening to their captors having a rollicking good time eating steaks and playing King of Tokyo or something on the other side of the cell door. Maybe one of them steps in from time to time and gleefully pistol-whips somebody. 
Some say Catan deserves respect for its role in paving the way for better games, but I say the benefit of experiencing time in a linear fashion is that we now have access to all those better games, and your copy of Catan can be safely discarded in whatever manner you choose without any fear of games like Space Base getting sucked out of existence via time paradox.
So yes, Catan is bad. Some of the awfulness can be alleviated by house rules, variants, or maybe expansions, so I won't give it a 1, but wouldn't it be easier to just play something else?
Conclusion: 2/10, At least it's better than Munchkin.

Version Notes: Overall, I think the 2005-ish re-issue of Die Siedler von Catan from Kosmos - featuering plastic pieces - is the most attractive, funcational version of the game. It has bright, pleasing graphics, the smaller resource cards are easy to manage, and the plastic inserts are the most functional inserts ever for a game. It is in German, though. But every version has its charms, even going back to the borderline-ugly Mayfair 1st and 2nd printings (the ones that used photos - I don't actually own either of those printings, but I'd like to just to add to my collection). The 2007 Mayfair edition (the bigger box) is probably the nicest version that Mayfair has done, and is comparable and even superior in some ways to the 2005 Kosmos edition, the first time Mayfair has gone their own way  and done something at least as good as Kosmos. It also has the advantage of being in English. I generally like Mayfair's 3rd printing better than most players - I think it's a nice, distinct set with its own flavor apart from the other versions - but I'd also agree that it's overall not as graphically effective as the other versions, being a little dark.

textfield_comment_value:
[i]7/10 for the base game, 8/10 with Seafarers, 9/10 with the added Fishermen, Harbor Master and Event modules from Traders & Barbarians[/i]

Catan receives way too much hate these days. On the surface there's loads of luck involved in gathering resources, but this is part of risk management in this game. Without randomness and unequal distribution of resources players would have no incentive to negotiate and trade. That player interaction and convesations around the table are the very things that make playing Catan an enjoyable experience.  You just need to play with an easy-going group of friends who are willing to actively participate in negotiations. I had fun playing this game and would gladly revisit it some time in the future. 

[b]/update, May 2024[/b]: I have revisited after 8 years and I think Catan still holds up and has the type of player interaction very few other euros have. There are better trading games, better resource management games and better games with map expansion out there, but I still haven't found anything else that would combine those three elements in such a way.

I can't wait to try some of the expansions (especially the event deck, the Harbormaster and the Fishermen module from T&B).

/update: Traders & Barbarians is wonderful, get this expansion! You know what? I've grown to LOVE this game. especially with some easy to implement expansion content. There is really something special about it that no other game really does in the same way. And I never feel downtime in Catan, there's always something to count on or analyse during other players' turns. This is an absolute classic and it's a real shame it doesn't have the appeal among "serious gamers". 

/update: I have to try Seafarers with the abovementioned modules from T&B, I think this would be a very fun way of experiencing Catan! I really liked what ships bring to the game, but I still think the event deck is my favourite module. I'm extremely pleased with all this additional content and I'm honestly keen on playing Catan regularly! Can't wait for the reprint of The Helpers.

textfield_comment_value:
Well, I've played this classic enough times now to give it a firm rating. I have to choose giving it a 3 because I really don't want to play it again. For starters, it's actually a rather long game given its very narrow decision tree. In Settlers, you roll the dice, and players with wooden blocks bordering tiles receive goods if the numbers on the tiles match the number on the dice. You also get opportunities to trade five different types of good, and an opportunity to build things. Building things gets you victory points, and the first player to ten victory points wins. Once your initial little houses or villages or whatever have been placed, it's in your best interests to focus on upgrading them to cities (which give you double goods on the correct dice rolls), build the longest road (which gives you a couple bonus points), and build more villages. But the game offers little in the way of long term strategy. You simply hope the rolls are good, try to get others to trade you what you need, and grind on. Of course, this simplicity is also what makes Settlers easy to teach, and has been a contributor to its success as a gateway game.

Settlers is an impressive game in some ways, foremost in that it's accessible. It also introduces gamers to trading, odds, and the concept of victory points. But it suffers from too many liabilities compared to the games it inspired. For me, it's kind of brain dead. I would much rather play one of Teuber's other games. There aren't many interesting decisions. Assuming a table of reasonably intelligent players, way too much of the outcome rests on initial village placement. So much so, that I now have no interest in playing. This isn't sour grapes on my part, but last game I played I had to watch my wife and one other player twiddle their thumbs for an hour because although they were still "playing" Settlers, they had no chance to win. None. Zip. It was like playing Monopoly when one player is clearly dominating, and everyone's just going through the motions until the end game condition has been met. This is a massive strike against Settlers, even more damning than the anemic play.

textfield_comment_value:
Components: Beautiful, durable, functional components in a shoddy box. The most recent addition improves on the original design with an interlocking sea border and distinct art on each tile.

Experience: Update: Played a variant whereby the robber is a fountain, that allows everyone on the fountain to get a resource when that hex produces (if not already on that hex), rather than stopping production on that hex. Makes the game much more enjoyable.

Update: This game hasn't aged well. The very beginning of the game, during initial placement, is the most interesting part. The rest of the game is too capricious. The dice rolls are too random, and even when they give me resources, it might not be at the right time or in the right order. The robber punishes players for being unlucky enough to not build on their own turn; and players use it to target not only the person in the lead, but whoever has built beside them. The Monopoly card is just mean. I dislike that each game has the same goals (get to ten points). Games feel very similar to each other. Too random; too mean; too long.

Previous:
Excellent. The modular board gives each game a distinct flavor, and I find the dice rolling to be a thrill, with players always hoping for the big payoff. There are several different ways to climb to the top; it's very satisfying to finally get an engine going.

It's interesting even during the initial placement, as I scour the board looking for the sweet spots, scarce resources, likely paths, etc.

This game has aged well. Except for one thing that now bothers me greatly (after losing in my most recent game). Like in a game of Risk, when a player starts to lose, that player might have to endure losing for a long time. And during that time, the player will have very few meaningful or interesting decisions. There are so many ways to get hosed in the game; if a player is not in a good position already, with a safety net, then that player can be in for a long, miserable ride.

textfield_comment_value:
I want to make sure that I note that this rating reflects the board/houserules with which my group plays the game.  This includes:
-a larger board (it may be the 5-6 player board, but we play that board with 4 players)
-No "hand size".  I know everyone is saying 'There is no hand size'.  What I mean by this is that on a 7, we re-roll.  There is no robber, you don't lose half your resources, etc.  This means someone can have a crazy big hand and ergo crazy big turns.
-If the same number comes up 3 times in a row (including a 7), we don't collect our normal resources, but instead each player may take one of any resource. This then starts our count for that number (i.e. if that number came up a fourth time, it would be the first time towards the next 3 in a row).  
-Play to 15 (start with 6 settlements, 5 cities, and 26 roads)
-Play with the Fishermen of Catan variant/expansion.  Can't recall which expansion it's in.  Basically replaces the desert with a pond that produces fish on a 2,3,11,12 (same odds of rolling a 7) and the coastal spots between the ports with fish that come up on numbers between 4 and 10.  Fish can be traded to steal a card(3), for any one resource (4), to build a road (5), or for a development card (7).  
-We can build "Metropolises".  We think this is an actual variant from an expansion, but again don't remember which.  A city can be turned into a metropolis for 5 rock and 3 grain.  This adds a second city on the same spot.  It produces 3 of an adjacent resource when it comes up, is worth 4 points at the end of the game, and you can build settlements one spot away from a metropolis (anyone can, so I could build a settlement next to yours).  
-The monopoly card we nerf to half of everything someone is holding rounded up.

This clearly won't be for everyone, but our group really enjoys these changes.  We don't like the tightness of the original board/hand size and it makes for very competitive games.  If I had to rate "Catan" with no changes, it would probably be in the 6-7 range, but most people I know play with some form of house rules so I feel comfortable rating my group's version.

textfield_comment_value:
I HATE Settlers.  Is it a bad game?  No, anything but.  Why then?  Becuase we played nothing else for *months* when our group first moved from MtG to board games.  Once every 6 months is fine for me.

So why do I dislike it so much?  In an ideal game everyone would have equal luck with the resources at an equal time during the game.  However, the game can be skewed so badly by one player getting their share of the luck early on in the game. Once that player or even those players are ahead it is very difficult to rein them in simply because if they have not been stupid with their expansion plans they will be getting resources more often than everyone else. 
A good starting position while essential to win, in no way guarantees it.  How many 5 'n' 9's games have you had when you have been able to get a 6 and 8 for your starting villages.  Some randomness in games is a good thing, perfect information and grand strategy has it's place but for me the spice and seasoning is the little random events that make you re-think, re-evaluate and plan on the fly.  Settlers has far too much of that good thing. 
It is a frustrating game for that reason with a lack of control to go with it.  Sure over time the skillful player will win more games in the same way that an expert backgammon player will beat the novice every time over a set of games. 
Oh and heaven forbid that you as the unlucky one be adjacent to the "leader" in which case the robbers directed at them will happily sit on your resources as well.  
Yes it is a great game that can simply bring new and innovative mechanics to an audience raised on the gaming hind teat that is monopoly and Clue(do).  Yes it has been hugely influential in the expansion of this hobby and yes I hve probably played this more than any other game that I own.  
But there are better games.  Better games for gamers with more control ahd deeper thought; better gateway games for non-gamers with simpler rules and a more forgiving start. 

Settlers will always have a place in my collection the trouble is twce a year is more than enough for it to hit the table.

textfield_comment_value:
Bought the game and 4-6 player expansion for $50-$70 (I forget) MANY years ago. After many games, I started to keep a Hall Of Fame paper where we recorded: Game Length, # of Players, Who won and what position did they place, and Least and Most common Dice Roll #. We have 91 games that we kept record of on the HOF (I won 41 of them :) ). I have played over 100 games of Catan. This has been one of the best game purchases I've ever made. 

BUT, that was years ago. Back then, this game was a 10 easy. Now, with the way games are changing and new mechanics being created, I'd say it's a 7. We still play it, but it doesn't get chosen many times (perhaps because we've played it so many times).

Couple notes:
My gaming group and family aren't big fans of chance, luck/lack of luck, or ganging up on. Therefore, most of the time we played without trading. This was mainly to stop bad players from giving the person winning what they needed to win... Too many times I'd be winning and I'd convince a silly player to trade me a terrible trade and game over. It's not much fun when that happens.

Another variant we did was, we played a lot of game (maybe 50%) without the thief. If you rolled a 7, you just picked someone to steal from. 

Another variant we ALWAYS played with, and I think this helps the game, is that you could negotiate. If you're about to be stolen from, you can ask the thief "what do you want?" He says "wood", you hand him a wood and thus protect your other precious resources. OR he says "wood" and you need wood, so you say "good luck" and then he picks randomly. This addition was always nice to have. 

When we played with the thief, you could negotiate with the thief and say, "I'll give you what you want IF you block my 12 and not my 6" etc... this rule is also great. Everyone is happy. Of course sometimes the thief says, "nice try" and just smacks the thief down on your 6 that has 3 cities on it. BOOM.

So, if you haven't played the game before. Get it. Play it. You'll enjoy it. I don't think you'll get 100 games out of it like I did, but you'll get some good mileage on it.

textfield_comment_value:
Immernoch eines der beliebtesten Spiele in der Familie, allerdings nur modifiziert!
Im Folgenden unser persönliches Standard-Setup, das aus dem zu glückslastigen und oft eintönigen Catan ein entscheidungs- und abwechslungsreiches Kennerspiel macht, bei dem auch der Letztplatzierte noch bis zum Schluss um den Sieg mitspielen kann, welches aber vollumfänglich den Charme des nostalgischen Grundspiels beibehält:

- Szenario 9: Neue Welt (Catan – Seefahrer Erweiterung, vgl. Regelheft S. 18-19), aber mit einem Wüstenfeld (ersetzt ein Wasserfeld) und Räuber und Seeräuber

- Zusätzlich Sondersiegpunktkarte „Hafenmeister“ (aus Catan – Händler & Barbaren Erweiterung, vgl. Regelheft S. 4)

- Zusätzlich ein schwarzer Würfel: wird bei den Würfen mitgewürfelt. Zeigen die regulären Würfel eine Augenzahl von 7, gilt diese als geworfen. Anderenfalls darf sich der aktive Spieler für zwei der drei Würfel frei entscheiden.

- Robin Hood-Regel: Sobald ein Spieler 7 oder mehr Siegpunkte (mehr als die Hälfte der erforderlichen Gewinnsiegpunkte - wir spielen bis 12) erreicht, können Sechseckfelder, an denen der Spieler mit den zu dem Zeitpunkt wenigsten Siegpunkten gesiedelt hat, nicht Ziel eines durch Würfel erzeugten Räubers oder Seeräubers sein (gilt nicht für das Ausspielen einer Ritterkarte). Außerdem gilt für diesen Spieler die „mehr als 7 Rohstoffkarten“-Regelung nicht (dieser Spieler kann sämtliche Rohstoffkarten behalten). Gibt es aufgrund eines Punktegleichstandes nicht genau einen Spieler mit den wenigsten Siegpunkten, ist diese Regelung nicht aktiv.

- Hafenblockade durch den Seeräuber: Über Häfen, die an ein Meeresfeld grenzen, auf dem der Seeräuber sitzt, kann solange der Seeräuber dort sitzt, kein vergünstigter Seehandel betrieben werden. Falls der betroffene Spieler keine weiteren Häfen besiedelt hat, kann sodann nur auf den 4:1 Handel zurückgegriffen werden. Eine Hafenblockade hat keine Auswirkungen auf den Raub einer Rohstoffkarte durch den Seeräuber (ist weiterhin nur möglich, wenn ein anderer Spieler mindestens ein Schiff an einer Kante des Meeresfeldes stehen hat).

textfield_comment_value:
The perennial game - a classic. My game group played countless games over the years, before we even heard of BGG. We've had marathon gaming nights lasting until dawn. We even keep a game log (complete with questions/answers to complex game situations and a list of winners).

Even though SoC is a dice game with a med-high luck factor, my group believes that you can effectively strategize and change tactics depending on what's rolled and what resources people have. Why build a settlement on the 8 or 9 when the 10 or 11 is hot? What do you do when 3 is rolled 3 times in a row and the 6 hasn't been rolled all game? Where's the best place to put the robber, on a hot number or a more likely number? 

The player interaction level is fairly high too. Screw someone too early in the game, you have an enemy working against you. If you take the lead too early, you're a marked player. We love to talk during trades too (look, my sheep is better!). And perish the thought of trading someone with 7+ points, you'll be heckled for the rest of the game. Oh look, so-and-so has all those development cards, must be victory points, they are in the lead! Hours of fun!

I rate plain SoC higher than the expansions because it's fast-paced and easy, and we can get in multiple games in a night. Also, SoC games are typically close games where everyone has an active role. Even if it's a blowout, it's usually quick and painless. 

Played SoC dozens of times before I started tracking my games played (approx. 50-100 games).

UPDATE: Finally played this again after a long hiatus. We started with the sample board and starting positions to even out the board for the 2 new players. Turned out, the sample board was awful - poor settlement and road placements that didn't make sense (for example, some second round choices settlement and road placements would have been better in other places). 

New version: Flimsy board pieces, ports are permanently set on border pieces, but they don't sit well to frame the hexagonal board. 

Tracked on family list (grooven)!

textfield_comment_value:
This was my gateway game a few years ago. I knew there was so much more now than just Hasbro, Milton, and Parker, but I didn't know all that much. I did know of Catan though, and so I bought it for my family and younger sisters. We loved it...and played it quite a bit. Once I learned more and picked up some new games we found it hard to pick this one up again. It's far more choices than any previously known game, but most of them are made at the beginning in the first 5 minutes, deciding where to put your houses and roads. The other choices are the robber and building, but not too much. It feels just like the roll of the dice, and seeing what comes out of it. The development cards aren't really good enough to justify purchasing (most of the time), it's almost always better to go for more houses and cities to get more resources. But it just feels like a long haul. The fact is if your resources aren't drawn there's nothing else you can do. Not "hampered" but literally no actions you can take on your turn.

There's a social element, if you like that. Trading with others really helps, as the exchange rate with the bank is terrible. But finding a good match is harder than you might think, and definitely harder than other games. After many months of this I was getting really tired of playing it, but luckily I found and started going to a gaming group, and learned of far more.

It's not something I'll be picking up again soon. There's too many more fun options available. Of course, I know there's quite a few expansions, and several people love several of them for the choices they give. I don't doubt them, it probably does make it better. But the main gameplay mechanic just isn't that fun.

5/10 looking back and comparing it to all the games I now have tried. But I'll boost it up one more to 6/10, as it technically did bring us many hours of entertainment. I would have brought it up to 7/10, but I rolled for it and the dice just didn't turn out that way.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
This was my gateway game into the world of Eurogames. The first time I played it I was blown away. There is, indeed, a lot to like in this game: trading, route building, player interaction, blocking, long term strategy, short term tactics, etc... However, the more I played it, the less I enjoyed it. Especially after I became a more experienced Eurogamer. It took me a while to figure out what I didn't like, and I think what it comes down to is the simple fact that- when everything is boiled down- the key to winning the game is simply getting more of the correct resources than other players in order to build quicker than them. How do you get resources? They are randomly dealt out through dice rolls. Sure you can play the probabilities, but that doesn't always help. I've played most of a game without an 8 being rolled. It's in the "Monopoly" mold of distributing currency randomly. I didn't like it in that game and I don't like it here either. You can plan and carefully line up your pieces, but it doesn't matter if the dice don't roll your number. You are at the mercy of the dice for nearly everything in this game. The simple fact is that some people get more resources through sheer luck and not due to good or smart play. I really don't mind randomness in games, but having your entire economy run by random dice results is ludicrous. Looking at the game now, it looks to me like the whole trading aspect was simply added on to try and fix the inherently broken economy of the game and isn't entirely successful.

Then there is the fact that this game is just much too long. After I came to the realization that it was the dice that bothered me, I bought the dice deck of cards which evens out the luck. After playing it with those cards, I found my experience with the game didn't really improve much. Perhaps I'm simply burned out on the game, but for me Catan is a trial to get through. It drags on and the fun is over long before the game is.

textfield_comment_value:
Igazi klasszikus.
A Catan esetében a szabályok elsajátítására, tanulmányozására nem kell napokat áldozni az életünkből. De még órákat sem. Ez nem jelenti, hogy nem lehetnek vitás kérdések. :D Elég könnyen átlátható akár már első próbálkozásra. Lássuk be, rendkívül nagy a szerencse szerepe ebben a játékban is. Hiába próbálunk úgy helyezkedni, hogy a könnyebben kidobható számokat tartalmazó mezőkkel érintkezzen a településünk, városunk, ha utána mégis ritkán jönnek elő azok a számok. Szerencsére azért ez nem egy felturbózott szerencsejáték csupán. A kereskedéssel meg kell próbálni a céljaink eléréséhez nélkülözhetetlen nyersanyagok beszerzését. Ez jó kis interakciót biztosít a játékostársak között. A győzelemhez szükséges 10 pontot meg egyáltalán nem olyan könnyű elérni.
Az tetszik a Catanban, hogy ha egy család úgy dönt, hogy csak az alapjátékot veszi meg, akkor is rengetegszer újra játszható a társas, mert a területlapkák elhelyezése szabadon variálható, meg persze az azokon szereplő számok is. Ez is olyan játék, ahol több úton is el lehet jutni a győzelemhez. Van, aki csak a települések, városok építésére áll rá, van aki a fejlesztési kártyákat gyűjti, van, aki mindenféleképpen birtokolni szeretné a leghosszabb út címét, stb. Ráadásul nagyon hangulatosak az illusztrációk. Nekünk már a műanyag figurás változat van meg, de nem érzem gagyinak ezt sem. Biztosan más érzés fabábukkal játszani, de nekem ezzel sincs gondom, itt legalább részletesebb egy-egy elem kidolgozása.
Azért 4 fővel ez sem a legrövidebb játék, mind a két menet kb. másfél óra volt.
Egyébként az, hogy minden egyes dobásnál figyelsz, hogy kapsz-e nyersanyagot, minimálisra csökkenti az üresjáratot két köröd között. Persze előfordulnak olyan szerencsétlen szériák, hogy akár két teljes kör is végig megy, te meg csak ülsz és szomorúan nézed az egy szál erőforrásodat a kezedben, ami sehogyan sem képes az osztódással szaporodásra.

textfield_comment_value:
This is a game about collecting resources to construct buildings and buy development cards.  The first player to reach 10 points will win.  Each player begins with 2 settlements and a road segment.  On your turn, you roll 2 dice and add the values.  Every terrain on the board is associated with a number and terrains matching the rolled number will produce resources for every player with a settlement or city next to that terrain.  The robber figure will block resource production and can be moved when a 7 is rolled.  No one will get resources when a 7 is rolled and any player with 8 resources or more will have to discard half of them.  Then the active player will move the robber to a new terrain tile and steal 1 random resource from a player of their choice who has a settlement or city next to the blocked terrain.  Players can also trade with the other players or with the bank and build roads, settlements, or cities or buy development cards with their resources.  Development cards can be played at any time during a players turn, but must be from an earlier turn.  Settlements are worth 1 pt and cities worth 2.  Some development cards are worth victory points.  Then there are vp cards worth 2 points awarded for largest army (knight cards) and longest road.  A player having 10+ points will trigger the end of the game.

This is a good game to introduce someone to board games.  It is easy to learn without overwhelming a new player with concepts, and it is fast to play.  It is very easy to mess up with your initial settlement placement which can lead to a slow, painful game as you will not recover.  Other players are unlikely to trade with you just so you can get back into the game.  I enjoyed it very much years ago when it was one of the first board games I purchased.  I don’t enjoy it as much anymore, but I respect how many people it has brought to board gaming.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Catan! This is a classic title, one that I came too very late when my sister bought the game a few years back. In the game you roll dice and collect resources based on the result and where you have buildings. These resources allow you to build more settlements which increase the chances of collecting more goods when the dice are rolled and you can build roads to expand in order to build the settlements. You can also commit your resources for powerful cards. To win the game you need a certain amount of victory points and you get them from the settlements you have, objectives and cards. During the game if a number 7 is ever rolled the person who rolled it can move the robber piece to a location adjacent to another players settlement and they can steal resources from them. Its an evil and harsh mechanic but works well. The board is made up of tiles with numbered tokens placed across them and you build along the edges and the corners of the tiles. There is more to the game but the above is a simple overview.

Pros - The game is simplistic and a perfect introductory point for someone into gaming. Combines a good deal of strategy and planning with a little luck. Ideal balance in my opinion. Plenty of expansions so lots of extra content. Its a good length game too.

Cons - Not the most advanced title, collecting the resources is linked to die roll so depending on the number you need it could be a long time before reaping rewards hence the luck factor.

Overall its a great introductory game. Its simple to introduce new players too with a good level of strategy to be challenging. I enjoy it as an occasional game to go too, even though I don't think its very popular from what I hear.
