textfield_comment_value:
I grew up with this game. Settlers replaced Skat(!) in our local pub as the game you could play every evening – there were always players coming to the pub wanting to play Settlers and the pub soon purchased a game so nobody had to bring his own. I was still a little kid accompanying my parents, later it was the favourite boardgame to play with friends for many years.

Two aspects of the game that stand out for me: random drawing of the whole island and the trading aspect. The trading is the core of the game – you roll the dice to earn resources that you can trade. And you can trade everything: three corn make one beer, three sheep to drive me home tonight. Again, this is meant to be a social/pub game as the players do not play just for themselves against each other. As for the random aspect, this game is so customizable. You could use the 6 player expansion or just a second base game to build a bigger map and/or play up to 15 or even 20 points. You can also make one or two resources very scarce or even non-existent. Endless variations.

One bad thing about the game is that it can be boring or frustrating if there are players of different levels as the random aspect is not as big as in, say, Monopoly. Settlers is quite easy to learn (as for the rules of the game) but better players play much faster and know what things to do in certain situations. Peacefully developing your stuff turns into hecticly buying basically everything you can get. So this may be one aspect Settlers share with Skat – you might play it with players at the same level as you are slowly getting better at it. In my opinion, this game is mainly made for three players. So again – sort of a Skat replacing board game... Just be sure to get the old edition with wooden parts and cleaner artwork or even the anniversary wooden box. The newer edition with plastic parts is just ugly.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
I only own the digital edition of the game on the Xbox 360. 
I have three(+) issues with this game:
1) I hate that there is hidden victory points, because I might be the perceived leader because of my visible points, so nobody will trade with me...but it turns out another player has 3 points hidden from everyone, but keeps getting all sorts of good deals, and then he ends the game out of the blue. I HATE that people have hidden victory points. 
2) I hate the random chance of the game, and how much it can kill your game...your numbers don't come up, you don't get resources, if you don't get resources you can't trade, you could watch three rounds go by and accomplish NOTHING. That is NO FUN, and it has nothing to do with how you play, it's just random, totally random, with no way to mitigate it. Even worse, you have only a couple of resources in your hand on your turn, then in the next two players' turns, you get a bunch; then on the next player's or your turn, they or you roll the thief and you now have too many resources and have to discard down, just in time for your turn where you can't do anything...again...hate it.
3) I hate that you are plugging along, making your roads, building up, drawing cards and making deals, building up your little corner of the map, then another player lays down a bunch of hidden points (see 1 above) and wins the game out of nowhere. I HATE how the game end is so sudden, it's not like there is a set number of turns to build toward, if one player hits all the right numbers or has the perfect card draws, it's over, and you're just getting into the game. I hate that. 
4) On a lesser note, the whole bartering with other players for resources is just a hectic minefield...do you ever feel like you got the best deal? I always feel like the other player got the better of any exchange I make...maybe that's just me though.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
tl;dr: still a solid game

This game is now 27 years old. I first played it when it was already 10 years old. By that time, it had build up a reputation for being the poster child for the euro game phenomenon and one of the prime examples of a gateway game. It was not my gateway game, but I had only been playing games for a few months when I was first introduced to this. It had been on top of my "want to play" list ever since I heard of it.
From the start I quite liked this. I still think it's a good game. I am no longer interested in playing it.
The thing is: in the last 17 years, I have had plenty of time to figure out what I like and what I dislike in games.
Things I am not fond of:
- Competing for position on a map, though I don't mind this too much depending on how it is implemented
- Trading. Usually it is too time consuming. I'll tolerate it in [thing=11][/thing]
- Stealing things from other players.
- Playing cards to hurt other people.
This game has all of those things to differing degrees. It can be very in your face and, depending on the other players, mildly to very aggressive. And that's not for me.
I don't mind competing for resources, competing for action spaces, competing for access to things... But in this game, to do well, you have to, regularly, do things that might not help you (steal a resource card that might be of little use) to possibly hurt the other player a lot. Again: not for me. Not in this day and age where I have so many really good games to choose from that suit my tastes better.
So yeah, if you're just getting into gaming, make sure to give this classic a try (but don't use the 5-6 player expansions!) to see what all the fuss is about. But I personally don't need to play this again.

Rating: 7.2/10
BGG scale: 3/10 (willingness to play)
BGG scale: 7/10 (quality of game design)
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value: Here we have the "Monopoly" of the Modern Age of board games - roll the dice, possibly collect some resources, negotiate with the other players, perhaps build a house or two, and move along to the next player.  I hesitate to speak negatively about a game that is of such importance to the world of board games, and that is indeed my wife's personal favourite board game.  After all, it's probably not an exaggeration to state that Settlers was largely responsible for the rapid rise in popularity of German games, as well as for introducing, or at least re-introducing, many of us to the hobby of gaming.  But that being said, I was never very impressed with the game.  Sure, it has some fun elements of gathering resources and spending them to expand your settlements, but the fact that you are so much at the mercy of rolls of the dice really takes away the fun of it (unless you have the "Event Card" expansion).  Add to that the fact that a player can get blocked in right from the beginning of the game (I've played a few games where I sat and did very little all game, watching helplessly as other players expanded across the board), and you can end up with a pretty frustrating playing experience.  (For proof that it is not the fact that I often do poorly at this game that influences my decision to give it a poor rating, see my reviews of "Cleopatra and the Society of Architects", and "Fury of Dracula".)  When played with the "Seafarers" and "Cities and Knights" expansions my rating goes up to a 6/10, even though the already tedious set-up and play time becomes painfully long.  However, you can save yourself the trouble and expense of purchasing all the expansions and just get "The Settlers of the Stone Age", which in my mind is a much more fun stand-alone version.  Game design: 3/5  Personal enjoyment: 2/5  Total: 5/10
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
CATAN - an old milestone 

This game influenced our modern boardgame world - which I get considering it was released in 1998. But I wouldn't suggest it to anybody anymore. 

PART 1: Randomness and how it leaves someone sad at the table

Base Catan lacks on too many aspects for me me and the biggest one I think once was one of the two things that made this game so popular: its accesability. 
But don't get me wrong - it's not accessability in games I don't like (I quite like accessible games if they offer enough depth) - it's the reason what makes Catan so accessible: the dice.
And those are a big flaw nowdays in my oppinion as they make the game extremly random eventhough Catan still is often presented as highly strategic. 
Randomness in games can be fun if its used correctly. Two examples would be Challengers! and Dorfromantik - The Boardgame. Both play with the element of randomness in a certain way which don't make the games feel lacking depth.
In Dorfromantik you cooperatively build a landscape through tiles which a randomly drawn from a deck of tiles. What balances the randomness out is the cooperative aspect of the game. It makes the randomness a problem to deal with and to make the best out of.
Carcasonne on the opposite (to stay with the topic of randomness) has in its core the same element of tiledrawing from a random stack of tiles and it lacks something for me. Sometimes you just are unlucky all the time but compared to Catan it's relatively short and leaves you with something to do eventhough the luck isn't with you.
Catan often leaves you with nothing when you don't roll your numbers.
And which numbers you chose at the beginning just aren't important if you don't roll them. You can have only 6 and 8 spaces but only roll anything but them. Sometimes it's the other way around.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
I've come to accept that this game is best at 4 played on the 5-6 expansion board. It's a little too long with more players. I appreciate that 4 players on the base board is a tighter, more cutthroat experience, but there are better cutthroat games than Catan. I find Catan more fun as a light-hearted game with more trading than less.

Citites & Knights is the more interesting of the expansions, insofar as it's not simply more of the same. Players engage in a mild form of cooperation against the barbarians while also competing for contributing the most protection. It's a longer game, however.

Little expansions like Frenemies, Helpers of Catan, and the Harbormaster from Traders & Barbarians freshen the base game experience without adding much overhead.

• 5-6 player expansion (base)
• Cities & Knights
• Cities & Knights: Legend of the Conquerors
• Frenemies
• Helpers of Catan
• Dice cards from Traders & Barbarians
• Harbormaster card from Traders & Barbarians
• Catan: New York map (kept in Daytona 500 box)

• Catan: Starfarers
Starfarers is essentially a space-themed variant on the original. Roads are replaced by a ship movement mechanism (shake the mothership to randomize multicolored balls within, then the colors of the two balls that appear in the ship's propulsion nozzle determine the rate of movement). The components are excellent. When you upgrade your ship, you attach a corresponding plastic piece. Some say these components are overproduced and cheaper pieces would have sufficed. A fair point. However, the components fit the theme so well, the game would lose some of its charm without them. Encounters add a slight "choose your path" element, but I wish it was somehow deeper. Game says 3-4 players, but BGG has 2-player variants posted that change little of the core gameplay.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Settlers, Settlers, where to start.

In the late 90's I was looking for a board game that was better than, or at least equal to but different from, Talisman.  People kept telling about Settlers of Catan and I eventually found a copy at a local game store.  After playing it turned out to be a big dud.  I eventually got a copy of Robo Rally and that turned out to be the next best thing to Talisman at the time.

Back to Settlers, I had a copy of the game, didn't like it much, bought all the expansions (the local game store only had Warhammer, CCGs and Settlers so what else was there to buy?) to see if they would add that little spark to the game.  I became somewhat fond of the six player all expansions way of playing.  All my friends liked it so I ended up playing it quite a bit (my copy of the game is quite beat up).

Why didn't it work for me?  Because Catan is a negotiation game.  And when you play with people (myself included) that love to argue about the minutest detail even vanilla Catan can become a two hour slog.

The game is just not designed for the purpose of fierce competition.  It's a family game where people get to build cool houses and cities.  These things increase a player's ability to produce.  So you feel like you are doing something as the game progresses even if you lose...except for when you get a sequence of bad die rolls that allow your opponents to cut you off at the beginning of the game.

The game is quite simple: roll dice, produce goods, trade with your opponents, build.  It's thrilling as any dice game is.  Everyone is invested in every die roll so the game can provide a fun party-like atmosphere.  It's not the greatest game, nor is it particularly revolutionary, but it is fun, interactive, popular and allows players to build cool things.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Good trading and gateway game. Some replay value, but gets boring if you play it too much. I burned out on this when I took it to Australia. I took a bit of a break from this game in 2005/2006 academic year, but since Autumn 06 I got back into it, then burned out again, and doubt I'll be keen to play it again since I realised how high the randomness really is. Also it is slightly too long. The game can get boring if your numbers aren't coming up.

Settlers is best with 4. 3 or 5 means it's too easy to expand, 5-6 is too slow. I think the expansions all make the game worse.

It was my first Euro. I also now realise that there is too much luck - early luck gets compounded, and players can be out of contention after 10 minutes (or 0 minutes if they put their 2 settlements in stupid places). Also it is kind of the same every time - there's only a few ways to get points so you end up doing the same things every game. Or every few games I suppose: you might get longest road one game, and largest army + VP cards the next, but there's not much strategy space to explore. Funny I'm saying this now, when I first played it I was impressed by all those multiple paths to victory.

Another issue I have is that 50% of the skill/important decisions in the game are the setup initial placement. After that the dice tell you what you should be building. The trading phase keeps me engaged because you have to pay attention and negotiate with the other players (that's the best part of the game), the robber and competition for longest road are good aspects.

These days when I see a bunch of Settlers-ers setting up, I like to watch the initial placement and then predict who will win based on resource access. More often than not I am right.

Bought Spring 2004, Sold 2009/10 via BGG
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
I used to like this game a lot, I even can say it was a "gateway drug" for me, into more interesting sorts of games.  However, I've outgrown it.  The game is initially very fun to play, at least most of the time, and it has a nice element of balance built into the strategy, in that players usually refrain from trading with whatever player is in the lead, and this tends to give the weaker players a fighting chance.

The reason I have come to dislike this game is that it doesn't seem particularly balanced in the sense of chance playing far too big a role in who wins.  A series of good or bad rolls early on in the game can give a player a boost (or hinder their development severely) early on.  It's easy to get boxed in or cut off...and many games are decided early on by which player wins a competition for a key expansion site.

In the end, this is a game that can be excellent and engaging, but too many games have been spoiled for me by luck.  I've also had a number of games where either I or another player gets out of the running very quickly and then ends up having a crappy time for the rest of the game, and doesn't want to play again.  Several of my friends have played once or twice only to get alienated from the game after a bad experience.  It's common for the game to end and one player only has 5 or fewer victory points, by the time another player got to 10.  This is not the case with most of the top-100 strategy games, games that are more balanced.

I'd rather play these other games both because I find they more consistently satisfy newer players and lead to a better gaming experience for all, and because they have a richer strategy in the long-run.  This game was fun from the start, but it didn't grow on me.  Instead, I grew apart from it.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value: When it was made, Catan was a groundbreaking, interesting, beautiful, and unique game. There are some parts of the game I appreciate. I like the artwork, the trading, the cover and the font. However, I almost never enjoy playing this game. Catan is a grueling game that just makes people frustrated and angry at one another. In addition, the game is largely decided on starting position and dice rolls. I also feel as though there aren't many strategic in-game decisions. You mostly just build what you can given the resources you were lucky enough to get. The game is not deeply strategic at all. Once you know how to play this game (having played at least 5 times), your not at a big disadvantage to someone who considers them self a Catan master. And that wouldn't bother me except that so many people think that this game is so deeply strategic. Another aspect that frustrates me is depending on the board, sometimes you are screwed from the very start of the game, which then makes it hard to put on a happy face and finish. I will say this game is very satisfying to win, because of all the built up emotions throughout the game. "Oh c'mon I've been screwed by the robber all game!", "that's a horrible trade, you realize she is going to win the game now!", "Wow, you've gotten so lucky with those 10s, I wonder if we are ever going to roll a fricken 5!" . Klaus is an evil genius. No matter how frustrating this game is, he got people addicted to playing it even if it risks the health of important friendships. No matter how much Catan frustrates me, I can't hate this game, because this is the board game that got me in to board games, and for that I am forever thankful. And this game has paved the way for all the awesome new games we see today.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
My first German game, the allure died off only after two months of regular full day (read noon to the wee hours, we had sessions ending at 5 AM for a while there) play sessions with everyone I know and I have easily logged over 100 games of this. I still enjoy dragging this out every once in a while. Siedler mainly has a niche for the very casual atmosphere it creates, plenty of time for table talk, banter, and such during the game, one of the reasons it has such broad cross-over appeal methinks. I made the mistake of playing this with a deck of dice for a period of time, essentially trying to turn this into something that it shouldn't be, I'm back to the dice again, and the game has been getting some more play.

This game is interesting in that unlike most modern gateway games, it is actually very prone to position-destroying mistakes when you first set up the board and stake your initial claim. Most people who like it tend to play it a fair bit, especially when they first get it, and in that setting the random boards and initial set-up are a good deal of the allure, but it does tend to make the game a bit dicey when you mix "serious" gamers with newer players, as it is very easy to sink yourself with a poor initial placement and end up sitting around for the game doing a lot of nothing because of that. I would go so far as to say that the initial placement is at least half of the game, with another 1/4 being trading skills and board play and the final 1/4 being luck of the roll and development draw. Take it for what it's worth. I probably wouldn't like it as much as I do if I played it for the first time today, but I do have fond memories of this one and still enjoy pulling it out on occasion with the right group.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
The game that reinvented the board gaming  hobby, opening the eyes of the masses to the possibility there was more to board games than Risk and Monopoly.

Settlers' popularity actually makes complete sense. The game is quite easy for new players to grasp giving it wide reach in terms of its potential audience. But what makes it really unique is that the game play appeals on so many different levels. Whether you like building stuff, or managing resources, or trading and negotiating, or rolling dice, or collecting sets, or building an economic engine... there really is something there for everyone to enjoy.

One of the real highlights for me is the free-trade mechanic, which I haven't seen much elsewhere. The economy self-regulates based on the availability of resources and stage of the game. Someone might pay you three resources for that brick now, but two minutes later its worthless! It's fun to figure out what kind of deals you can pull together each turn and it also keeps everyone constantly engaged.

Obviously the variability of the game is a huge plus. The hexes are laid out in a random order each game, the numbers which determine resource frequency will also change. You can try out different strategies by using development cards or ports. And there are some neat organic catch-up mechanics like the robber and negotiation, which mix things up and lead to many very close games.

I have played probably 200+ actual person to person games of Settlers and I still really enjoy it. These days I play it most often with the family or with newbies as there are better games for a truly strategic head to head. But nevertheless this is a versatile, elegant and highly repayable game - a must have for any collection.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
2005-2006-ban a Carcassone mellett ez volt a másik játék, amit az "újabbak" közt volt szerencsém kipróbálni (új alatt azt értem, hogy nem activity és társai). Rám a kettő közül ez volt nagyobb hatással. Számomra addig ismeretlen elemek (pl. az alkudozás, a nyersanyagszerzési mód, stb.) nagyon színessé és vonzóvá tették a játékot, annak ellenére, hogy nem igazán voltam benne jó. Mára kicsit megkopott a varázsa, sok jobbat láttam már, de most is szívesen játszanék fele, főleg hogy van egy kiegem, amit még nem próbáltam!
---
Kipróbáltam a kieggel is. Nos nem rossz játék ez a Catan, de így hogy több mint 400 féle játékot ismerek, azt mondom, hogy vannak abból az időszakból olyanok, amik sokkal jobban kiállták az idő próbáját (El Grande, Tigris, Hannibál), bár a felsoroltak mindegyike eleve komolyabb játék, mint ez. Ma már csak nosztalgikus okokból ülök le a Catanhoz.
---
Újra előkerült, ebből is látszik, hogy még ennyi játék ismeretében sem zárkózom el tőle, de azért már nem az a megkerülhetetlen játék, ami 10 éve volt. Tegnap 2 partit játszottunk, és 10-8-4 ill. 10-4-4 lett az eredmény kb. azonos képességű játékosok közt (nem mindkétszer ugyanaz nyert, és nem is pont ugyanaz volt a játékosok összetétele). Ha az induló 2-2-2 pontokat nem számoljuk, akkor 8-6-2 illetve 8-2-2 a végeredmény. Az első parti másfél óra volt, a második 1 óra. Több játékossal simán lehet 2 óra feletti a játék, ehhez képest nevetségesen nagy a végeredményben mutatkozó különbség. A második partiban fél óra elteltével látszott, hogy ki lesz a győztes, és nem lehetett ellene mit tenni. Szerintem többek közt ezért áldozott le egy kicsit a Catan csillaga. De nosztalgiának továbbra is jöhet, csak fenntartásokkal fogom kezelni.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Finally got to play this classic, Prototype of the eurogames, and all the other honorifics it is known for... and having done so, I can say understand both sides: those who praise it, and those who praised it but now claim it's done.

It is simple enough that it can be called a gateway game and yet I can see why so many say it has durability. It is a cute resourse gathering and trading game; however it is soooo far from perfect. Its greatness comes from what it's done for boardgaming, but evaluating as it is now (and that's how it should be done), it's nowhere near a 10 or a 9. 

It does play fast, I don't see any serious issues with scalation and it can play from 3 to 6 (although you need the expansion, or you're stuck with 4), nice art and components, set up is no big deal... but the resourse gathering...

It is both why it can be a gateway game, and the reason a good deal of gamers (especially eurogamers) might have a problem: depends on dice roling. You can play the odds and search for the most likely numbers to come up during the placing of your cities at the beginning, but is still luck and you can have a hard time if it's not your day. 

In theory, the trading aspect it's there to make up for that, but if you're playing with people really trying to win (and while I understand not being a S.O.B. is good, I don't think I could blame someone for trying to win), they can really twist your arm in those trades, so you can probably get that much needed wood or brick, but at such a cost, you might as well not have.

It is fun and I want to play more, but in general, if I'm going to play an euro, I'd rather play those where your resources don't depend solely on rolling dice, but on strategy.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Since re-discovering boardgames about a year ago, after a gap of 25 or so years, I've encountered many superb games, some that are so-so, and a few stinkers. This is easily the worst. All it takes is a string of unlucky dice rolls at the start and you're knackered for the whole game. Other players will move ahead and their success breeds more success. I wouldn't say that the winner is determined in the first few rounds, but the loser usually is. It is much like Monopoly in that respect.
I simply do not think this works as a four player game, the board is too small and one player, the one who is unlucky with the early dice, will inevitably find that they're boxed in, unable to expand. The game is slightly better with three players but the in-built problem caused by being at the mercy of the dice remains. I've played Settlers of Catan a dozen or so times and in almost every game there has been one player who sits there turn after turn unable to do anything useful, forced to continue the game knowing they have no chance of winning. In that respect it is unlike Monopoly, which at least eliminates the players in the worst positions. 
It is wrong to consider this a gateway game. Yes, it is simple, but for at least one player sitting round the table it is likely to be the most tediously frustrating game imaginable. The experience, I would have thought, would be capable of putting newcomers to boardgames off for life. 
And don't even get me started on that chuffing robber.
Update. OK, I've given this a load more tries. My rating of 2 remains if this is played with 4 people, but I'd increase it to 5 if playing with 3.
Further update. Seafarers of Catan rescues this. Rating with this expansion: 6.5.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Excellent introduction to german games for a number of reasons:       The number of brain parts stimulated in the game is large, though stimulation is fairly gentle.  This is not your hitachi magic wand vibrator that focuses on one organ and wiggles the hell out of it. no.  it's more like a vibrating tub of warm, soft jello that you jump into hairless and naked, all nerve endings exposed. there's cajoling, laughter, tension, secrets and bluffing, memory, press your luck, arms races, strategic thinking, tactical considerations, the joy of building.     there's just a *little* viciousness, enough to make the game juicy, but not enough to provoke any real hurt feelings (for most people).    virtually zero downtime for anybody, as everyone is interested in everything that happens at all times.   the game has been designed to give every person playing the hope of winning at all times, even if it's the smallest glimmer.  the person that is waay too far in the lead can be effectively slowed down by other players, leading to close, tense finishes.  Some here have argued that this aspect makes it an inferior game, as skill is constantly being stymied by luck and group-lynching, but I believe that a game for non-gamers should allow everyone the possibility of winning.    

 On the minus side, the start-up is intimidating (to a non-gamer), as rules are moderately complicated, and the board looks geeky, with the hexagons and #s and pips.  But most non-gamers with whom I've played have warmed to the game after playing just two rounds, and are extremely enthusiastic (and exhausted) by the end.  Complexity is an issue, however, for grandma or grandpa who have trouble with all the rules.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
[Original comment] This is currently the favorite game in our family (April 2005). It has most of the features we enjoy about gaming. There is a lot of interaction and negotiation with other players; the gameboard is different every time; there are enough important factors to consider that no single strategy will win every time; there is just enough randomness to make it interesting (and sometimes frustrating); the rules are not complicated; the game time is just right (we can now play a 5-player game in about an hour); and players have a number of options almost every turn, to require some decision-making. It's an excellent family game.

Update February 2006 -- We usually play with 6 players now, and it is still a family favorite.

(December 2006) And now, we're playing with 7 players, and it's still a favorite, although we've had to modify some rules to play with that many.

May 2009 -- This is still a family favorite, and we play it often.

October 2011 -- This long-time family favorite continues to be at or near the top of our selection lists for game days. We always play with at least 5 players, which makes for a crowded map. The negotiations, blocking, the moans over the dice rolls, and the surprises (like stealing the Longest Road to win the game) keep it high on our list of favorites. I doubt we will ever tire of this game, which is about as high a compliment as can be made.

November 2012 -- We may play this game forever. Our daughter and son-in-law purchased the fancy version with wood tiles, which makes the game much more attractive. It continues to be a family favorite.

2013-November:  We haven't changed our minds about this game -- it's still a family favorite.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
This was the first considerable board game I had played since I was a child playing Monopoly.

And I must say, I love it.  The game seems simple on the surface, and is relatively easy to pick up, but strategy permeates the entire game.  From placement, to building strategies, and trading for resources, every action has consequences and there are always multiple options to choose from.  Often, a single card can change your entire strategy; I often see players about to build a development card, make a good trade, and shift gears into building a city or a settlement.  With so many ways to gain points, and so many ways to build up, there are always different strategies to try.  Combined with the interaction between players and the random board designs, there is no perfect strategy, requiring players to constantly be aware and plan their next moves accordingly.

My only complaint is the fact that dice rolls determine what resources you get.  While a little randomness keeps things changing and unpredictable, resources are so important that an unlucky streak can break even the best strategy.  Combined with the exponential productivity growth, a slow start due to unlucky rolls can quickly separate the winners from the losers.  This sometimes results in people giving up mid-game, complaining that they've already lost and making unreasonable trades to break everybody else's strategy.  There's a lack of sportsmanship apparent here, but the fact that players can get into an unstoppable losing or winning position can make the rest of the game less fun.

Still, this is an excellent game that I have played dozens of times over the last couple of years and I still enjoy playing to this day.

I know why some of you love it. The game offers great tension and plenty of choices. Part of it strength is also the reason why I can't rate it higher is that in the dutch rules you have to throw the dice at the start of your turn.
I started by saying that I won 2/3 games. The game I lost I had won if I didn't throw a 7... I had all the resources to upgrade. Stil had a chance if I drew the right card but didn't do so.
Obviously that adds to the fun . It's fine if I can play the game in 60 minutes. I will upgrade the rating to an 8 then.
By the looks of it my group will take close to two hours to finish the game. To be able to lose a game when you are five  to one favourite before YOU yourself roll the dice, anything but a seven, well that can be tough.

This probably won't ever be a personal favourite of mine but i have to say that I wouldn't have thought that a game with such a small ruleset  has so much replay potential.

If one player doesn't understand the trades and  or trades favorable towards on player the game is broken. 
If everyone plays it right and quick this is definately fun. I've played games I liked much more but this one is for the masses and I liked it.

Update : Essen thursday 2010 RATING 7=>5
Played it with the group at Karl's place. Karl,alain, gust. All were new to it and they didn't think much of the game. General feeling was that if the rolls are in your favour you do well. and if you are the first person to take the lead it will be hard to win.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Would like to give this game an even lower rating, but I recognize that it is actually a great game so I don't really feel like it deserves it.  It just allows one specific behavior that I absolutely hate in games, and therefore will not play it with many people.

This game lends itself to the really annoying problem of: "some player who doesn't really care about winning (or doesn't understand the game yet) can really help a different player win."  This in and of itself isn't generally a problem in other games where people can do it, but in Catan there is no way for someone (or a group of people) to stop the just one person from ruining a game.  I can't play this game with certain groups of people anymore because almost every game becomes: "person X isn't playing competitively and ends up giving the game to person Y because they're upset about something person Z did that's just a normal part of the game".

Instead of a climb to the lead and punch the leader as expected, you get person X got mad and decided to give the win to person Y for no reason other than to spite the other player(s).  Most king of the hill games do not suffer from this problem because the mechanics don't really allow it to be done easily by one person.

I eventually decided to sell the game because I had no situations with groups of family or friends anymore who I had any desire to play it with.

Component Quality:  The game I bought had hexes that never really fit into the core part of the map (in between the water edges) like it should have.  Very poor component production (though apparently this wasn't a really common problem with the game overall, maybe just the printing I bought)
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
After placing first towns, almost no more major decisions. You cannot but do only action you can do with resources which dice rolls gave to you. Moreover, with bad rolls, you have nothing to do.

Not enough thematic feel.

UPDATE July 2007--------------------
SoC has a potential of being fun. Random map, resource production and management, some nastiness(monopoly, robber, etc.), luck and strategy... but the problem is that strategy often doesn't work.

To do any, you need resources. To get resources, you need good roll. To increase probability of getting resources, you need more settlements. But to build new settlement you need resources! So in the beginning of game, everyone has only two settlements and only three resources, getting good rolls can be crucial. Someone who gets enough resources first and build another settlement get huge advantage - she or he gets increased probability of getting resources, can take good place, and can block other players' expansion. In the middle of play after building four or five settlement there can be some ways of dealing with bad rolls, but in the beginning there is none.

Secondly, it is hard to save cards for future, you often have to do unwanted trade or build unwanted building. It is very bitter when you oards many cards only because you couldn't manage to get NEEDED resources and then robber comes out.

At last, I don't like the "sudden end." When having 8 or 9 VP and struggling for a couple of points, someone suddenly declares the end of game - it is not so pleasant. (Of course dice luck can be crucial here again) I wish there were end game.

Now I think SoC as a well-organized dice-race game...
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
A classic. Albeit slow, and heavily luck based. But...

A few changes and house rules, change the game for the better.

1. Use the better settlers app for set up
2. Combine #'s (2&3) and (11&12) on the respective hexes. (Make your own token of you must and put 3 dots for probability)
3. Robber doesn't get activated for 2 turns.
4. When a 7 is rolled (or drawn[see#7 on this list]) that player gets to roll or draw again, if another 7, then ignore it and then next persons turn. So the person rolling a 7 gets another production roll, in order to get the game moving.
5. Victory point cards have to be automatically revealed. Or remove victory point cards all together (preferred) and decrease points to 8 or 9. (Last few rounds become a drag when more players involved, and victory point cards cause a very unclimactic win).
6. Print the harbor master card (2 points for the most harbor settlements, and you need 3 harbor points to attain it [a city counts as two and a settlement counts as 1]) and use it like the longest road card. 
And additionally a player can't have all 3 of the cards (longest road, largest army, and harbor master) if a player at any point does acquire all 3 they have to choose which 2 to keep.
6. 20 second timer on trades.
7. Get rid of the dice and build a deck of cards using 2 deck of playing cards. Shuffle and draw each turn. When five 7's are drawn, reshuffle. (Build the deck: Put in six-7's, five-6&8 each, four-5&9 each, three-4&10 each, two-11&3 each and one-2&12 each ( 3 if you combine 2&3 and 11&12).
8. On a 5 or more player game, get rid of the special build phase and increase robber threshold fo 8 for 5 players, 9 for 6 players.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value: Does a lot of things well, in particular the fairly open trading rules, but there are two major issues I can't get past. First, there's enough strategy that you have to play well to win, but the dice add just enough randomness that the best strategy often will lose to a decent one. I've lost games I should have won due to dice, and worse still, I've won games I had no right winning because of them. In some ways, this is almost more irritating to me than games that are mostly luck, because it gives you the illusion that your strategy matters. As of this writing, the most recent game I played is a good example of this. I was on two 9 hexes of the same resource, which I had a 2:1 harbor for. Another player was on several of the 6s and 8s, and had high probabilities for all resources - but no 9s. We proceeded to roll something like 7 9s in 10 turns, allowing me to rally and take the lead to win. Some might call that risk/reward; for me, that was a hollow victory. My bigger problem with the game is that the structure makes it so that some players may face a fate worse than elimination: being mathematically eliminated from victory but forced to sit through until the end of the game anyway. Some have argued that a shrewd trader can still come back, but it's very apparent when someone cannot do it themselves, so only a pity trade could help them, and nobody likes a pity trade. This probably sounds overly negative, and it's probably a testament to the rest of the design that I still give it a 6 after all that complaining. Those two points are pretty much the only faults I have with the game itself. (Mayfair's pricing practices are another matter...)
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Like a lot of gamers out there, I owe a great debt to Catan. It is one of the reasons I got into boardgaming in the first place.

And that's probably the best thing about Catan: its simple rules, attractive components, short play time, fun trading mechanic, and rather friendly atmosphere mean that Catan is a superb introduction to the wonderful world of boardgaming. There's also relatively little down time in Catan, as you can potentially collect resources on anyone's turn (and turns don't take very long, anyway.) It can hold people's attention.

For the veteran board gamer, however, Catan falls short. Everything is really chance-dependent. That's not necessarily a deal-breaker (I love Eldritch Horror, after all!) but the problem is that there is a paucity of interesting decisions to be made. After you've picked where your first two settlements are, there's basically nothing you can do to tilt the odds further in your favor. The opening setup is interesting and requires a lot of thought, but after that you more or less sit back and let the dice happen. 

There's also a bad snowball effect--the player who is able to grab additional early settlements and cities (i.e., the player who had lucky early die rolls) stands the best chance of getting even more resources, and so forth. This can somewhat be rectified by all the other players refusing to trade with the leading player--but then a core mechanic of the game is destroyed if the players aren't trading. 

All in all, Catan will always have a soft spot in my heart as an excellent introduction to boardgaming. But once that introduction has been made, Catan itself can be left behind.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Very good strategy board game, not that difficult to learn, yet more challenging and interesting than Monopoly, and with multiple ways of trying to win.  Great player involvement even when it's not your turn.  "[url=http://www.boardgamegeek.com/thread/150443]Welfare variant[/url]" (= Foodstamps) [[filepage=22173]PDF[/filepage]] is a must to minimize the frustration of randomness and too much dependence on luck, plus speed up the game and prevent runaway leaders (closely related is the [thread=1184279]Poverty is No Shame variant[/thread], which feels more like regular Settlers but just gives players some control over what numbers are rolled - see my thoughts on both [url=http://www.boardgamegeek.com/article/15951421#15951421]here[/url]).  Another option is to [thread=134095]roll three dice[/thread] and pick two.  Game play can also be improved and made more even with the Event cards.  I also suggest using a [url=http://boardgamegeek.com/article/15950941#15950941]score track[/url].  

Here's a website that creates `balanced maps' for starting resources, and is even used in some tournaments: [url=http://bettersettlers.com/]bettersettlers.com[/url].

Also owned: 
[gameid=2807] - Base game add-on for playing with five to six players.  As much fun as the base game with three to four players.
[gameid=20038] - Potential to improve Settlers by eliminating some randomness and adding some strategy and events.  The Earthquake event can be a bit harsh early in the game though, so we've ignored that.  Overall, it seems to improve the game and make it more balanced.  This along with the Foodstamp variant are must-plays for Settlers of Catan.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
There are 3 major flaws in the design of Catan:

1. Initial placement of settlements.
The thrill of selecting your initial settlements (this part is fun, I'll admit) can be very short-lived once the player realizes that they picked poor locations for their initial settlements and then are stuck playing from behind for the rest of the game. Few games can seal one's fate as quickly as Catan-- in fact I am hard-pressed to think of another game where one realizes about 10 minutes into the game that there is no longer a viable path to victory and yet you must slug through the next miserable hour of Catan so as not to be labeled a quitter. This mechanic may be the biggest flaw in Catan.

2. The Robber.
The other problem is the robber-- having a catch up mechanism to reign in a runaway leader is one thing but trust me when I say that it makes for an absolutely miserable ~60 minutes when you are singled out throughout the game as the target of the robber (yes, I know other games have similar ways of ganging up on another player, but in Catan the robber not only doles out damage when first played but often continues to inflict pain for a number of rounds as you are denied resources from the hex blocked by the robber).

3. "The dice hate me!"
And of course there's a large element of luck in the game with the roll of dice playing a very prominent roll in who wins or loses.


For these reasons Catan is one of the few modern board games I refuse to play any longer and I would not recommend it as an introductory game to those new to the hobby, especially now that there are so many newer and better designed gateway games.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
50 plays:

Such elegant design! So few choices, but ones that matter! Such good use of randomness! Such simple compensation for being behind! Such pressure and reason to negotiate! So many ways to win! Just a perfect game, satisfying nearly every time I've ever played. 

OK, here is where I acknowledge the many things that some gamers don't like about this game. It's true that you can get stuck for many turns without enough income to take action -- I can only say that for me, the luck element and strategy elements combine in a very satisfying way, and I find it equally satisfying if my gambit doesn't pay off and there is a "drought" for many turns. I love seeing the market turn, seeing brick go from saturated to rare, and back again. 

But when I tried to play this with eight-year-olds, the drought was just crushing for them. My daughter actually burst into tears at one point because she was getting so many sheep, and nothing but sheep!

The game is nearly immune to analysis paralysis, because you can't foresee rolls, and so few options are open each turn. However, it can get a bit stuck in complex negotiation proposals; players may need to be coached into how to quickly propose a variety of trades.

Another parent suggested playing with kids using two rules adjustments:
1. settlements and cities can be placed 1 space from each other (not just 2)
2. on the first turn, you earn resources from both your initial settlements

I'd add a third:
3. the robber only forces players with more than 7 cards to discard one card (to avoid the heartbreak of discarding half your hand)

Lightness (1)-Heaviness (5) rating: 3
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
This game basically got me into modern board gaming.  Once I started playing, I couldn't stop.  It's simple and addictive.  However, after having gotten into board games and having played many others, Catan doesn't quite hold up.  First off, there's too much luck involved.  This can overcome with good building placement, but there are some games where 6 or 8 (the numbers that should come up more often when rolling 2 die) just never come up but 3s or 10s come up over and over again, rewarding the lucky player who just happened to chose those resource hexes with an easy victory.  Bottom line is: if your numbers aren't rolled, you lose.  And the game gets very frustrating and/or boring when you're hopelessly losing since the better you're doing, the easier it is to do even better.

I recommend new gamers give this a try.  It's fun and will get you into gaming.  Then, to add some complexity and replay value, get some of the expansions.  The Cities & Knights expansion makes the game great by adding the needed complexity.  Explorers & Pirates is also really fun, though it basically makes it into a different game. I've never been a big fan of Seafarers, it doesn't really add a whole lot in my opinion like the other expansions do.  Traders & Barbarians, in my opinion, is the best at fixing the original game without changing too much.  Some of the additions (especially fish and the cards instead of dice additions) really make the game less about luck and more about strategy.  

Catan is not my favorite game, but I keep comping back to it.  It holds a special place in my heart I guess.  It's worth playing for sure.

textfield_comment_value:
Overall I think this is a terrific game and a fun way to kill some time by engaging in some friendly back-stabbing. There are a few tiny flaws that occasionally get in the way of the game for me, but in general I think the design allows for a nice balance between luck and strategy. And I think luck is as important a part of gameplay as strategy, so I appreciate the attention to balance in games like this. 

The highlights of the game for me are the player interaction (through trading and "unholy alliances") and the resource management. Thinks like the "Longest Road" and "Largest Army" also provide some flexibility to strategy, and reward players for doing more than just building up settlements and cities. Building roads and buying soldiers are an important part of the game, but I think those added bonuses give the game some extra punch. All in all I think the point system is very flexible and allows for players to pursue a variety of strategies, most of which will remain viable for the entire game. 

The only thing I don't like about the game is the way that resource tiles are assigned fixed numbers for dice rolling. I can't tell you how many games have become once sided slaughterfests because the dice refuse to roll anything other than five or ten (and it's always five or ten, never six or eight). In most games I've played one resource will remain scare due to the number system, which is fine and indeed a part of the game, but occasionally a "sheep tyrant" will emerge and destroy us all. When the game takes on a sense of inevitability it becomes a lot less entertaining and rewarding.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
A new-era modern classic board game and in that sense heir to [b]Monopoly[/b], considering [b]Catan's[/b] [i][b]huge[/b][/i] worldwide impact (which also lead to an insane amount of spin-offs, expansions and re-themes).

Still a good gateway game for absolute newcomers, although like [b]Monopoly[/b], it did not age very well: [b]Settlers of Catan[/b] is from 1995 and it simply can not compete with more modern games.

Back in 1995, this was a 10/10 for most people (including myself) and as it marked a turning point for the board game hobby -- or a new dawn, if you will, considering the game's cover ... It will always rightfully be considered a milestone in the history of board games.

The first expansion ([b][thing=325][/thing][/b]) is great (and in my opinion even essential), while the other expansions did not do so well for me, as it always felt to me that the designers forcefully tried to transform the game into something more complex, which this game simply is not meant to be -- but I see that it made sense back then to keep the fans busy and make [i]a few[/i] $$.

It's often "cool to hate" [b]Catan[/b] among avid board gamers nowadays, but what they often actually mean is that they burnt out on it and/or that it did not age well.

I also practically lived on that island with my family and friends for years on every weekend, and I'm happy that I managed to escape one day, having never looked back.

If you are reading this as a complete newcomer to the board game hobby: Go ahead and give it a try, but make sure it's not the only game you will be playing.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
This was my gateway game as an adult back into the boardgaming world.

People complain of randomness but I don't mind it at all.  To me it's part of the game. Like in Monopoly if you don't get your rolls you're not going to get Park Place and Boardwalk.

However, there is so much more here in terms of strategy and different paths to victory.

It's a great gateway game and a very fun game which is the most important point above all other criteria when evaluating a game for yourself, whether you're into strictly highly strategic games with no luck or a newbie who loves high change light games.

For me, this is a great family fun game in the Medium to Light category, played in about an hour and we always have fun playing it. There's a bit of player interaction with the robber (you can choose to gang up on the leading player to an extent), and trading cards with others, creating longest road or largest army and stealing the points from the current leader, or blocking opponents paths with your roads.

Haven't had a chance to add the expansions which I think would allow one to tailor the game and make it even better for them and longer.

As you can tell from the way it exploded in North America as a gateway game it appeals to a higher percentage of the population and non-gaming people than most other games. Some people just don't want or can't handle too complicated and strategic a game.  They want it medium/light for a reason - to relax and have fun and Catan hits the spot extremely well!

I'll always remember it as the game that got me back in...and Love It!
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value: One of the most famous (and infamous) Euro-type games. However, as a Euro fan you are much better off playing Concordia, or Power Grid, or Agricola, because those are objectively much better and deeper games. But, this game is more popular than those because it does something your average none-gamer friends really wanted from family game night: player interaction. The trading of resources basically turns this into a mild role-playing experience, probably in an overly dramatic way that the clean Euro design and rule-book never intended. The game underestimates and thus leaves room for, the sheer mess of human political scheming and ravenous desire to enact another role by the greedy standards of the Stanford experiment. So, it makes for good stories you will rarely tell in any other Euro: embargoes, truces broken, alliances/coalitions formed and wrecked. Monopolies on certain resources, non-aggression packs, backstabbing, promises, wheeling and dealing multiple successive trades in a labyrinth of human made rules and changing political feelings about the board state, will be all too common. The skill of this game comes from your deception, your gift of gab, your cunning political mind. You still probably won't win; the game isn't that good and a random spike in points will probably just send someone to victory from out of nowhere. But if you like Catan, you never played it to win this silly game did you. All it's world is a stage, and you were merely a player. It is what non-gamers wanted from board game night, even if it pains some to admit that.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
First impression: 6.5

A good game with a nice load of player interaction, but in my short experience it seems to be too long in playing time for what it is.

It have a respectable amount of luck involved, but as a light family game it can be a choice, maybe not my first choice, but neither my last. Definitely I'll be playing it in the future wit my family.

On the side of components production, I have to say that my Devir edition is just gorgeous with it's nicely detailed plastic models of towns, cities and roads, and the amazing illustration work of Michael Menzel.

I hope to find some expansions at a good price to see if the gameplay can be enhaced.

---------------------------------------------------------

Update: 7.5

After some more games I'm begining to think that Catan is as good gateway game as Ticket To Ride. In the first few games we didn't understand the role of the area control element of the game, but now is more clear and a lot more enjoyable. I'm seeking to buy the 5-6 players expasion as usually there is one more willing to play.

---------------------------------------------------------

Update after 18 Plays: 6.0

Maybe there is to much luck involved (or my dice are seriously adverse to the statistic normal distribution), and a 5 or 6 player game (with the expansion) can get too long or too chaotic. Some times I'll be willing to play it but maybe a slightly more common choice will be to play other game.

Still I hope some day I'll buy an expansion that will make the game shine again, because deep down I know I like the game...

Times played: 20+

Strategy: 25/35 (C-)
Speed: 23/25 (A-)
Freshness: 18/20 (A-)
Ease of learning: 8/10 (B-)
Theme: 5/10 (F)

Overall: 79/100

Strategy: a lower rating means the game is shallow in depth, or heavy luck is involved to win. A higher rating means the game is rich in depth, has a good skill/luck balance, and is almost always won through better skill.
Speed: a lower rating means the game drags on, or not much happens when it’s not your turn. A higher rating means time flies when playing this game, or that things continue happening even when it’s not your turn. (The overall length of a game is not what is being rated, though this may contribute to the rating.)
Freshness: a lower rating means the game usually feels the same and stagnant. A higher rating means the game constantly feels different and new.
Ease of learning: a lower rating means the rules are complex or cumbersome for most people. A higher rating means the rules can be grasped by most without a huge time input.
Theme: a lower rating means the vibe isn’t the most compelling, or that the mechanics don’t thematically relate to the game’s world. A higher rating means the vibe is beautiful and fascinating, or that the mechanics thematically relate to the game’s world.

Each category is weighted differently based on how much it matters to me for the overall rating. For example, I believe the level of skill and luck involved and the speed of the game contributes more to the overall enjoyment of a game than the theme of a game or its initial ease of learning, but others may disagree.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Of course I've known about this game for years, but after finally playing it (Feb. 2009), I found it intriguing, even though prior to playing I had a hard time understanding how a game of this sort could be interesting. There is much to think about, it's more competitive (and even a bit more cutthroat) than I imagined, and it's well balanced and can be tense. 

I'd agree with those who say this game has earned a place on department store shelves next to stuff like "Clue," "Monopoly," and "Sorry." In that regard, I'm happy to see games like "Heroscape" "Axis & Allies" and "Blokus" on such shelves. Too bad other new standards like "Scotland Yard," "Carcassonne" and "Ticket to Ride" aren't also there regularly. [Note: As of 2012 I'm seeing more of these new standards on shelves in stores like Target.] 

I bought "Settlers of Catan" for a friend and his 14-year-old son: he couldn't figure it out, so I took it back home with me (they live way out of town) and taught myself. Then, when my friend next visited (June 2009), I taught him and he took it back. That's one way to do it! As to whether I might buy my own copy of this, to date (April 2010) I haven't yet, and I'm guessing I won't, simply because there are many other games more interesting to me. But to repeat, this is a seminal game and definitely has its place in the pantheon of outstanding games. 

[Since of my sons got into gaming after going to college and learned how to play "Settlers..." I figured my family would play it so I traded for a copy of the 4th Edition, December 2014.]
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
IIRC, I first played Settlers in 2006. Played 2-3 times, tops. There was some curiosity about modern boardgaming, so I thought I'd get a companion game to Settlers for the group, which ultimately ended up being Carcassonne. In other words, I pulled a standard Gateway maneuver many years after these two games were released, but I left Settlers behind so quickly it never made an impression on me. I played a lot of Carc (about 20 sessions), but half of that was at the request of more casual, non-gamer friends. So they responded to the "gateway game" while I was off and running. 

I say all of this because I came back to Settlers recently (10/28/09) for one session just to see how it would strike me as a died-in-the-wool, hardcore gamer. I don't have any nostalgia for this game. I never experienced it as the only game in town or as the forerunner of a whole movement. 

So to me, in 2009, Settlers is a distinctive but fairly unengaging game. In essence, the game is built around a random distribution of goods that is, in theory, corrected by manipulation of the odds and player negotiation. In practice neither of these things really do enough for the game. It does play quickly and simply. I've also read that 4-player Settlers is inevitably "an exercise in futility for one player, an exercise in false hope for another, and a real contest between the other two." That's been my experience as well. 

As gateway games go: TtR < Settlers < Carc < Pandemic. Althought as a cooperative, Pandemic doesn't really introduce people to the mainstream.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
For myself and many others, Catan was the 'gateway drug' that got me immersed into the hobby of strategic board games after previously only being exposed to overplayed 'Classics' like Monopoly or Risk, party games like Cranium and Trivial Pursuit, or a couple of complicated war games that took an entire day to play if you were lucky.

Catan (or Settlers of Catan when I first played it) hits a lot of key areas for a great board game - easy to understand and teach rules, excellent replayability with the board being different for each game, relatively short time period with games averaging 45-60 minutes, a variety of potential strategies and paths to victory, a lot of player interaction with trading, and gameplay that typically keeps all players with a shot at victory up to the very end. The only real knock against Catan may be it's theme - which can be a little vague (I guess it's early Medieval settlers on a newly discovered island??) and not necessarily the most appealing - and can feel a little tacked on (there's a reason why there are so many alternative versions of Catan - like Star Trek Catan).  But overall, this is an excellent game board game that is easily accessible to casual board-gamers and is definitely an essential part of any collection.

Adding to its value, there are also a variety of expansions that layer additional elements on top of the basic set.  By far the best expansion is Cities and Knights, which practically transforms Catan to a different game - while maintaining the same core mechanics.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
One of my "gateway" games. When I first played, I was sucked into an experience that I had never seen in board games before. First game I was confused, next 5-6 games I was amazed. After that I realized that the luck factor and the low amount of depth really wasn't what I was looking for, and looked to branch out. However, I am unsure on this being the "go-to" gateway game as players are often at a huge disadvantage the first time playing, its difficulty to teach compared to other gateways, and its relatively long play time (which feels longer when you're losing! haha.) 

Anyways, lots of props to this game for sucking me in and others into the hobby. Still using it today to help people get into boardgaming. It's pretty darn player independent, and has relatively wide appeal. However, I find it annoying when people ask to play it AGAIN and AGAIN, when there's other games that these people are capable of and enjoy as well.

I feel like this game has really low strategy, and is often determined on who rolls the best. This can be solved with a deck mechanic that I have yet to try, but I would just save my time for other games. Components are nice, theme is good, and execution for what it is is spot on. 

The interaction with 5-6 players is a lot more enjoyable though, and I would be willing to play Catan with friends if its with that expansion (comments on that should be somewhere around here). It bugs me when people pride themselves in winning Catan though, as I feel like it is very luck-based. Just my 0.02 ;)
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value: Fabulous game that probably cemented my interest in Eurogames.  Probably more luck than you think, but a really nice game.    "We shall not cease from exploration, and the end of all our exploring will be to arrive where we started and know the place for the first time". T S. Eliot.  This quote reminds me of Settlers.  You buy it as a gateway game, go mad buying so many other games that you take it a bit for granted, but when you come back to Settlers after a break, you are reminded again that is it simply a brilliant piece of boardgaming (18/12/08 - Rating 9). UPDATE: Push to ten in that it is the cornerstone game for me (5/4/10 - Rating 10). UPDATE: This is still a very enjoyable game (and still a 10) (24/11/12). UPDATE: My new rating system is to 3 decimal places, so that when I eventually rate every game, I can do a top 100.  This is still a brilliant game, which for me is still an enjoyable experience.  So, the 3 decimal places, I rate is a 9.728 (Dec 2015). UPDATE: Maybe familiarity does breed contempt for my views now on Catan?  I still really like the game / series, but there are now for me better board gaming experiences I would rather go to.  Still rightly a classic, but I think I have reach a point where nothing is left to surprise or further delight me with this game (Rating 8.741, Feb 17).  UPDATE:  The occasional play just reminds me still what a good design this classic game presents.  Although I will still continue to call it Settlers .... Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Catan is a classic. When introducing people to more complex board games beyond monopoly, Catan is often one of my first choices. The rules and ideas are similar to light-weight board games people are familiar with, while asking them to do a little more than role dice. 

Gameplay - Catan is rather simple game and very accessible for almost any age. That same simplicity that makes it accessible, is often the thing that turns it off for me. I've played grindy games, where multiple turns will roll by (literally), with no one rolling any numbers that matter and no one will acquire resources. The bandit is a fun piece, but often causes tension and if you aren't playing with seasoned board gamers, can feel mean and be a turn off for them. Once someone gets a little ahead and builds a city, they can often run away with the game. All this to say, I still love the game. It has its flaws, but there is a reason it is a classic, it is simply a fun game. 

Pieces - My biggest complaint of Catan is always the board. It never sits flush together, in fact I've purchased another board to hold the board itself together. Even putting everything in the box is fine? You have a general idea of where to put things, but sometimes they do not always fit right. 

Final thoughts - This review has been very critical, but that's mainly because it is easy to see the faults of Catan. Despite those faults and the things I do not like, the game speaks for itself. A wonderful game, easy to access, and will always have a place on my shelf.

textfield_comment_value:
[b]Spiel des Jahres 1995[/b]
[b]Deutscher Spiele Preis 1995[/b]

[i]Posted: 10/2/04, Rated: 9[/i]

[i]The Settlers of Catan[/i] focuses on colony building and trading. There is no combat element to be found anywhere in this game, although a player can be a bit ruthless with the placement of the "bandit" piece. This lack of simulated armed conflict makes [i]Settlers[/i] an easy game to recommend for children.
 
The game board can be randomly created, which definitely adds to the game's replayability. Interaction between players is essential to winning this game -- another plus. Lastly, the resources are represented by cards, so there aren't any complex money transactions that would require a calculator to compute. 

[i]The Settlers of Catan[/i] offers innovative gameplay, is easy to understand, does not attempt to model violent conflicts, and above all is fun to play. I am looking forward to introducing many of my friends to this great game.

[i]Updated: 4/22/06, Rated: 8[/i]

[i]The Settlers of Catan[/i] was one of the first "Eurogames" that I played.  Since that time, I've developed a bit more perspective.  I still really like it, but it has lost some of its luster.  On your turn, a bad roll can benefit your opponents more than yourself.  Enough of those rolls, and the other players can prevent you from developing (with 3 or four players).  Trading in desperation just makes matters worse.  If this scenario happens to you, you're effectively removed from contention, sometimes very early in the game.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
I've gotten into the hobby for a little more than a year as of this writing. I realize this game is now generally thought to be past its time, and its merits as a "gateway game" are questioned, but it was the gateway game for me and my game group, and we do go back to this game regularly.

I've found it useful as a parent, my kids have learned the basics of setting up a game, taking turns, rolling dice, gathering resources, building, etc. They don't like the robber much at all (who does), and I found it interesting and funny when they banish the robber to a part of the board that isn't inhabited, so it doesn't hurt anybody. 

When this game goes bad for a particular player, it definitely is frustrating eg. when the rolls aren't going your way or the robber is on you constantly as the rest of the table gangs up on you. And the 5-6 player expansion is not as enjoyable. Nevertheless the controlled but open negotiation of trades generally keeps people engaged throughout the game.

Our favourite "base game" is to add in the fish from Traders and Barbarians (takes away the desert, and gives the table another resource), and to also play with the Harbor Master to go along with the Longest Road and the Largest Army. 

The 10 rating is in part given to historical context of my own personal journey into this hobby, as it is far and away the game I've played the most, that I continue to enjoy. It's also boosted up by our "base game" add-ins from the expansions. "Vanilla" Catan I would rate around 8 out of 10.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
We finally found our own copy of Settlers of Catan after first playing it in WI years ago (circa 2004).  We used to have our own copy, but my sibling "borrowed" the game and never returned it.  You know the type, they keep games they borrow from you long enough that they believe they are actually "their" games.  Anyway, we found a bargain copy in the USED games section at Black & Read and we were lucky enough to discover it had the 5&6 player expansion in it.  Having local game stores that take in used games for store credit, and that sell bargain priced used games is amazing to have in our local community.  

Introduced our 7 & 9 year old to it and they really liked it.  At one point our older son needed a resource and our youngest traded him 1:1 for what he needed.  We asked why he did it, "he's my brother and I love him," was the answer.  A turn or so later the older boy returned the favor by using the Robber on his generous little brother.  The little guy said, "but I traded with you."  When the older boy insisted he was going to rob him anyway...the little guy said, "No snuggles for you tonight!"

The boys both love this game and play with different strategies.  Our youngest likes to try to win with just two settlements, a port, and development cards and longest road and biggest army.  Mom loves building cities early.  Dad thinks he can trade his way to victory.  The oldest boy tries a different strategy every play, and is aways there a turn away from winning.   A family favorite for a reason.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
We had an extremely old and worn 4th edition of this. They changed the board so the newer expansions won't work with it. In any case, the number tiles had been lost and replaced by little bits of paper . . . so my sons bought me a new edition with the 5/6 expansion for Christmas. The 5/6 player expansion is necessary since our family grew, thus we always have 5/6 players, but it's ridiculously expensive. These should be sold in one box as a 6 player game. I'm not sure how they get away with charging so much for separate boxes, especially re. the expansions!  That's my biggest grump about the game--seems way overpriced for a few pieces of cardboard and bits of wood. We haven't bought any expansions yet. I'm waiting for pre-xmas sales. Adding another element or two to the game would probably make it more fun . . . 

I've always enjoyed Catan but sometimes find it frustrating. Seems like every time we play there are certain numbers that get rolled over and over (not just six and eight, it seems different per game), and if you aren't one one of them you're out of luck, or you need someone soft-hearted to be willing to trade constantly. It feels too "luck based" to qualify as a true favorite for me. I also hate the robber and would prefer to play without it, but I get outvoted on that. I still like the game however. I'm a bit of a sucker for tiles that can be laid different ways with nice art, and I like the action of collecting resources and building. Play time for us is usually around an hour.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
The historically quintessential German gateway game, and also the one game I find in the hands of people who have heard of little more than Monopoly.  It was the first game I bought when I decided to get serious about collecting German-style games, but I'm getting a bit worn out on it as I get deeper into the territory. 
 
9-2-08: Have to move this down to a 6.  I appreciate what this game has accomplished, but I've thought about trading my copy and would, were it not for the sake of respect, nostalgia, and some degree of hope that I'll find some resurgence in interest through one of the expansions, or the right group, or what have you.  As it is, can't think of a time when I wanted to pull it out even for old time's sake, and I'll even try to avoid playing it.  That probably means I should rate it a 4.  I'm not one to rag on a game just because it's popular, so that's not "it."  I think, at the risk of being inconsistent, it's ultimately the dice that do me in on this one.  I generally don't mind games which rely so heavily on dice rolling, but this is one that can really make me look at my watch if lady luck is canoodling with one of my rivals--there seems to be too little I can do in too long of a game.  

12-24-07: Played the game again recently on Xbox Live.  Maybe it's the extra options, the built-in session report, the detailed statistics tracking, or the sense of playing with an  animated version of the collector's edition, but I give it an extra point over the base board game.

textfield_comment_value:
10/11/99 Bought. I own the English third edition from Mayfair. 

11/17/09 I finally played using the fourth edition. And... I think the graphics are terrible. Especially the port icons being so tiny. One third the size of the ones in the 3rd edition, and hard to tell apart from across the table. Some of the hill hexes were throwing us old hands off. They had so much green in them we weren't sure whether they were hills (producing brick) or meadows (producing wool). It seems the graphics guy decided to make every hex unique. Well, that's all fine and good if you're creating art. But a game must be functional above all else. And its very difficult to sweep the 4th ed. board with your eye and get a grasp of what is what without a lot of pausing to squint at stuff. Could Mayfair leave well enough alone? Nooooo.  02/21/17 Gamed with the 4th edition again plus its 5/6 player expansion. Same comments. 

I'll let my initial rating stand, as its for my 3rd edition. But if I owned the 4th edition I'd rate Settlers a 5 for the ridiculous graphics. 

03/05/16 A three-player game with the English 5th edition. The graphics were *much* better than the 4th edition. I'm not a fan of the rule changes concerning VP card play after the game is over and mixed trading & building. I feel its "dumbs down" the game. I also think taking "The Settlers of" off the box is arrogant and stupid. If I owned this version I'd rate it a 7.5.

03/19/22 And.. I'm still playing die Siedler von Catan on a semi-regular basis!
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
THE classic gateway game for me, which brought me into the hobby. What I love about Catan, is that it provides players a wide variety of different mechanisms - everybody gets something to enjoy - without adding bloat and a lot of rules. Also it's a very social game, encouraging players to talk and interact in a casual, but still competitive way.

Some people reduce Catan to its random luck component, which doesn't do the game justice, as there is much more going on. Also the game should not be treated as the highly strategic title some want it to be, instead it's just a simple, easygoing game and if I want to play something more complex, I play something else. 

More annoyingly is that Catan games not rarely suffer from a runaway leader issue. The rich get richer and the poor players, whose numbers never get rolled, are left behind. Allying against the leader only works out in cases, when there is one clear leader and all players realize the necessity to consequently do so. Which can be difficult for newcomers, wanting to innocently trade with each other and never putting the robber onto their best mate's hexes.

Overall I had many fun and fantastic rounds as well as some rather boring and tedious ones with Catan. While I've gotten tired of it quite a bit by today, I can't help but still admire this fabulous design, which I will always have a soft spot for. It remains my reference games must allow themselves to be measured against and not rarely Catan gets away with the cake.
