textfield_comment_value:
Civilization:City building:Resource Management:Trading:Negoiation

100  plays (most were computer version or online): Very addicting game in the discovery stage even though it is mostly luck dependant, especially when playing with equally skilled players. This is a classic example of how luck and dice do not automatically mean the game will be bad or broken, it is one of the main reasons the game is so fun but it can also get occasionally frustrating when the dice work against you. Expansions add a few more choices/decisions but the C&K is the only one worth the money and sometimes regular Settlers is really all you want. Rating this fairly high due to high fun factor and that "let's play again feeling", also this has high replay value and a few paths to Victory. My theory is the "greed" aspect of it is why it's so fun as well as "take that" when cutting off your opponet's road.

[u]UPDATE[/u]: After 100 plays this fell a little from a 9 but only a classic could see 100 plays and my rating won't ever fall below 8.5 even though it doesn't see much play now. It also gains extra points for it's "uncanny" ability to win over non-gamers to the hobby and we found some ways to play with 2 players as well. 

[u]UPDATE[/u]:8.5 => 7.5 What can I say, after playing a lot more other games I now don't like playing this much (mostly due to the high luck factor), it especially becomes too long for what it is with 4 people. If you are new(ish) to the hobby this is still a great choice.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
I feel the need to explain this one.

Why I think I love this game more than most is because of the competitive nature. It's the game that feels the most like a sport to me. There are very clear and replicable actions available to you, and yet there is a lot of nuance.

People who don't study the game often don't realize how many ways you can influence it and twist situations in your favor. A good player can "create magic" and seemingly always find a way to claw their way back into the game.

Positive:
- Very competitive/sports-like
- No downtime. You can always do things on other players' turns and it's highly relevant what others are getting/doing/planning.
- Social interaction. Personalities and what you say/how you speak matters a lot.
- Resource collection. Piecing together the cards you (and others) have, and might get in the future, to build your engine and form plans is a fun puzzle.
- Multiple different ways/strategies to reach 10 points
- Very high skill expression (balanced by the social aspect)
- Interesting and impactful drafting phase at the start
- High tension both in the beginning and end of the game. Consistently has a pretty climactic ending, which is rare for a euro.
- Easy overview. You can tell the state of the game with a single glance at the board

Negative:
- Possible to be completely shut out of the game early
- Randomness; can be very swingy
- Kingmaking
- Breaks if anyone plays for "second place"
- Only playable at exactly 4 (!)

textfield_comment_value:
This game introduced me to Euro gaming and the entire genre. For that, I suppose I owe Klaus Teuber a debt (which I repaid by buying 4-5 expansions, Das Book, and the $400 "chest" version, plus 2 years on online play, and the Xbox version).

Played perhaps more than any game but Chess and Risk, hundreds of times online and on PC as well. I enjoyed this game, for a long time. Frustrated by poor setups, and bad runs of the dice, my solution was to play it more.

12/11/05 - after over 100 plays on MS site, 20-30 on BSW, and 30+ f-t-f, I am tiring of this game. It has it's place, but I wonder about it's affect now on some folks I've introduced it to. Is it better to get them hooked on PR, or PG? or PoF? I am winning 40+% of my online games, but what does this mean? I am clearly losing some games purely to chance, driving me to play more to counter-act this effect. But when I am winning, are others losing because of chance? How many decisions that I make really are decisions at all?

1/08 Dropping to a 6, but with no disrespect.
1/12 Dropping to a 5. Every year new stuff comes out that improves upon Settlers concepts. I do very much thank Klaus T. for designing this game and bringing me back into the hobby.

9/2014: My rating of 5 is simply my current desire to play. It in no way reflects how important this game was to me and my family. It literally brought me back in to hobby gaming, and had a strong hold on me for 10 straight years. Thanks again Klaus.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
An all-time classic and the game that got me into modern games. I loved games as a kid and played plenty of Risk, Monopoly, Clue, chess, poker, hearts, Phase 10, Sorry, and Stratego. Catan was a breath of fresh air at the time from cutthroat slogs like Risk and Monopoly and offered so much more strategy and fun decisions than Sorry, Clue or Stratego. (Phase 10 is garbage/firestarter, the others are classics.) 

Catan is easy to teach and has a satisfying build up and visible progression on the board. Multiple paths to victory award repeated plays and varying strategies. A nice level of player interaction via trading, blocking paths and the robber. Literally anyone can play and enjoy this game.

Catan is very luck dependent, dice rolls *can* lead to runaway winners or (much worse) players that can never get anything going. Trading is necessary to an effective strategy, so you have to have a little charisma or at least interact with other players frequently to succeed (this is not a game for players who just want to build their own tableau and rack up VPs).

There is a reason this game is so highly regarded and at times I think I should rate it higher. Playing with other people who are into it makes it amazing. It is new gamer friendly and available everywhere with a gajillion expansions. Catan gets a lot of hate, but most people (myself included) that have anything negative to say actually played the game a ton and just want to play other things.

textfield_comment_value:
Played 22 times.
Last play was May 3, 2008.

This was fun.  It was enough different from Settlers of Cannan that I don't mind having both in my collection even though the primary reason we got this was to play with the 5-6 player expansion.

The close quarters and more evenly distibuted numbers really makes this game harder, and seems to suffer from a run-away leader problem that I didn't notice in Settlers of Cannan.

The last game we played was the first really close game - but that was because my husband didn't choose to win when he had the opportuntity and then gave me the exact trade I needed to get three points at once.

Just played the game with 3 players and it was a much closer game than when we play with 4.

I've decided I just don't like this game with 4 players.  There just isn't enough realestate and tempers get raised when one player out races another player to that critical corner.  There always seems to be one player that just doesn't have a chance.  Next time we play with 4 we are going to try and use the map for the 5-6 player expansion and see how that works. (This was just confirmed again in last nights game of cities and knights - and I was the player with NO chance.)

We just played a 4 player game of Cities and Knights and used the expansion tiles and it was a much more even game.  We didn't have as much running out of space issues and there wasn't ever a run-away leader.  But ther was still penty of tension.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
The more you play this game, the more you begin to notice the flaws which reduce the replayability. For one, there is plenty of luck involved. It honestly doesn't matter much on where you put your settlement, because sometimes you'll see the same rare combination roll again and again. At some point, the top player will be shut down by everyone, making it near impossible for him or her to win. Players will refuse to trade with them and cut them off any chance they can.

This almost always results in the 2nd place player to win, because everyone has overlooked them. Aside from that, because you can trade with everyone without many limits, there are heavy biases. Couples will do unfair trades with one another, players who dislike each other will deny each other's trades, and so on. Players will have also grudges against one another, from previous matches and the early stages in the game. Players will also get involved in these feuds and there is very little a player can do to stop everyone from ganging up on them.

To summarize, this game is more about luck than strategy and while luck may be in your favor, other players will demolish you because of it. There is not much you can do to combat any of this, except not being noticed and/or being in good favor with all other players. If people notice that you're winning, you're significant other isn't playing, or you're generally not liked in the group, you won't have much fun.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value: Catan (Klaus Teuber) – oder: Zweimal verkauft… Catan hat drei grundlegende Schwächen, die als solche benannt werden müssen. Erstens: die Würfel. In der Unendlichkeit kommt zwar jede Zahl gleich oft vor beim Werfen. In der Endlichkeit einer Inselbesiedlung kann einem das Würfelglück aber derart abhold sein, dass man auswandern möchte. Zweitens: Das Spiel vor dem Spiel. Es macht zwar Freude, die Insel zu screenen, um den jeweils bestmöglichen Ort zu finden. Aber eine falsche Wahl und man ist praktisch aus dem Spiel raus. Da hilft auch der Handel nicht, denn drittens: Der Handel. Im Gegensatz zu Civilization, wo der Handel durch Expansion und Entwicklung an Sinn und Bedeutung gewinnt, ist er bei Catan praktisch am falschen Ende angesetzt. Je größer die Expansion vorangeschritten ist, desto stärker nimmt die Bedeutung des Handelns ab, weil es kein übergeordnetes Ziel gibt außer Expansion. Bei Civilization geht es um Siegpunkte, die durch Handel erworben werden. Bei Catan liegen die Punkte schon in der Expansion. Zweimal haben wir versucht, den Zauber in Catan zu entdecken. Zweimal haben wir das Spiel nun verkauft. Die spielhistorische Bedeutung ist ihm nicht abzusprechen. Im Kern ist es dennoch stark fehlerbehaftet, da die drei Kernelemente würfeln, handeln und bauen so aufeinander abgestimmt sind, dass ohne unendliche Wiederholung einfach zu viel Frust aufkommt. Nur ist es bis zur Unendlichkeit noch zu lange hin…
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Like many, this was my introduction to modern board games.  I was immediately captivated by this fascinating creation.  It's strategic, but it has random dice rolling!  It's competitive but there's no player elimination!  You'll likely get stomped your first game, but once you have the basics down, most games come down to a close finish.  

My wife and I soon bought our own copy and played and played, and introduced it to new people.  After a while, and a lot of plays, the game started to irk me more and more.  I disliked getting screwed over by a string of streaky dice rolls.  I disliked everyone ganging up on one player with the robber.  I disliked that the five resources were not evenly balanced.  I disliked other players making suboptimal trades with each other.  I started to discover other, newer (clearly better! lol) games, and began to turn up my nose at lowly Catan.

I've since come back around.  There are other better gateway games that have come along (e.g. Ticket to Ride, Splendor, Dominion).  There are other games I'd rather play on most any given game night.  But I enjoy it for what it is:  a solid light-middleweight euro that's fun to dust off every once in a while.  It's not the be all end all of strategy games.  But even in spite of its unprecedented success, it has a unique mix of mechanics, strategy and interaction that has never been duplicated.

approximate number of plays (pre-2017):  50+
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
I'm not saying anything new when I call this game a classic. I like to play with a random hex and number setup. The game is easy to setup and play, and offers quite a bit of strategic depth. Dice adds a little luck to the mix, but only over the short term. How do I maximize my resources? Should I compete for the biggest army or biggest road bonuses? UPDATE: Dropping my rating from 10 to 8.5, since there are so many other games I'd rather bring to the table before this. Still a great game.

UPDATE Jul-12-2010: Dropping it solidly to an 8, since this game fails the "always want to play it" test. Also, I think I was mad to say the game has only a "little luck." The game often never gets to the "long term" for the resources to even out -- it's only played to 10 points.

I really need to get a newer edition of this game. The '96 Mayfair edition has some visual design issues that make it difficult for new players to tell the resources apart. Specifically, A. the hexes and cards are all photographs (and dark, at that) and B. there are different images for the terrain (e.g., forest hex) and the resource (e.g., timber). The resource is illustrated as a circle. The player aid shows the resource circles only, and of course the hexes just show the terrain, but the resource cards have both. I was aiming for a conversion of an older player into a gamer, but instead I turned him off to "complicated" games such as this. :(

La primera vez que jugué este juego lo encontré entrenido, aunque cabe recalcar que fue de los primeros juegos "modernos" que probé, por lo cual mis referencias eran uno, monopoly y ludo, luego con el paso del tiempo se volvía cada vez más tedioso, pasando de tener discusiones entretenidas sobre los intercambios, como el "te cambio una paja por X material" que nunca fallaba con mi grupo de amigos, a tener a un mismo tipo preguntando por enésima vez por un material y que nadie quiera, extendiendo ese trade por más tiempo de lo necesario, como cuando con tu grupo de rol tienen una sesión de ir a comprar, y un wn pasa 3 horas tratando de bajarle el precio a las cosas, entiendan ambos grupos, tanto cataneros como roleros, ESO NO ES ENTRETENIDO (un shout out pa mi amigo pistacho QEPD).

Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
I love this game because it is modular & extensible.  One can easily add expansions or parts of expansions as well as adding additional tiles to scale the game to as large as desired.  The modularity & flexibility also give this game a fantastic re-playability factor.

My wife and I regularly play Catan, and for our standard games we use Seafarers, Cities & Knights, Frenemies, and both the Fishermen and the Harbormaster (from Traders & Barbarians).  Additionally, we use the Mayday "Yucatan" wooden tokens.  We have the Helpers of Catan mini-expansion, but rarely use it.

We play using mostly vanilla rules from base/expansions with the following exceptions:
  1) We play as a two player game using the Seafarers' Fog Islands 5-6 layout
  2) Our end game trigger is when one of us has built two complete catan sets (10 settlement & 8 cities).  With the awards & such, the winner is usually around 45-50 VP.  The games last about 3 hours.
  3) We include the following award cards for 2 VP each:
     - Largest Army Card - applies to C&K Knights
     - Largest Fleet Card - The pirates card from E&P
     - Most Island Cities/Settlements - The spice card from E&P
     - Most Cities/Settlements on a fish hex or fish shoal - The fish card from E&P

Every once in a while, we will play a Mega-Catan game on a board of approximately 300 hexes (8 feet x 3.5 feet).  These games usually last all day.  See photo in Gallery
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
I don't mind luck in games. I do mind luck/randomness in games if it solely determines if I can do anything at all during the game. Settlers unfortunately is such a game. The one and only mechanic that decides what resources you get during a turn, if any at all, is throwing dice. If the dice roll badly, you will get nothing during your turn. That is not just a bit of bad luck which can be mitigated through proper risk management - that is putting you out of the game for the turn, while other more fortunate players run away with the win.
This also results in a huge runaway leader problem, because whoever is the most lucky in the beginning of the game cannot be reeled in, as he will be the first to build all his stuff, get more resources, and further capitalize on his initial string of luck. Catch-up does not happen in Settlers.
Other than this, Settlers could have been quite a nice game with all its then-innovative elements. However, if the game decides whether or not I get to do anything on my turn, I'll pass. It's no better than a roll-and-move mechanic were certain locations you end up say "skip your next turn".

Finally, Settlers has been caught up by time - newer releases do what Settlers is trying to do much better anyway, so why bother? If somebody suggests playing this I will reluctantly accept if and only if nobody wants to play one of my suggestions instead. Fortunately I usually succeed.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
To be clear, my 8 stars is trying to be objective... if I'm being honest, I'd love to never play this game and you'd need to brow-beat me to get me to at this point... But that because I've played it SO many times because it is just SO good. It's a genre-breaker and a classic for a reason, it's a brilliantly designed game fit for causals or hardcore tacticians, total nerds or family game night with grandparents and nieces; it's simple, quick, and bland enough to not intimidate anyone, while complex enough to please real gamers. It's only redundancy and the fact recent games have filled the niche better that have this collecting dust on the shelf at this point... it definitely covered it's price tag in the day.
My one big piece of advice? Avoid the exapnsions. Like the plague. It's like how various "Battle chess" rules alterations to the namesake can't every live up to the original... the game is already in a good place tactically... Adding elements is supurfluous, and it makes it so you aren't getting better at Catan, you're getting better at screwy fake Catan. Being a grand-master chess player is impressive, nobody cares how you'd rank nationally in like Fantasy Chess or whatever... just get good at the game itself (or better yet, branch out to its successors... I suggest Machi Koro if you want something else outsider approachable, or Valeria Card Kingdoms if you want something deeper and nerdier.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
This game falls into the "okay" category for me. I'm happy to have played it and that a friend owns it so we can take it out every once in a while, but I wouldn't want to own it myself.

With experienced players who know where to place their settlements and aren't prone to nerd rage if things go wrong, it's a fun little game with the potential to be addictive.

BUT... Due to the randomness inherent to getting resources in the game, players can--through no fault of their own--be left with NOTHING to do on their turn. This can sour the whole experience, with some of my friends justifiably insisting it is poor game design, and it can become even worse if you have a slow start and other players box you in. To some degree, comebacks are possible depending on how lucky you get later on, but there are cases when such a thing is impossible. These negatives have made some I know ABSOLUTELY REFUSE to play Catan.

Also, if you are playing with newer players, turns can take forever due to trading. How persistent someone is in trying to get an exchange of goods done is also something that has to be taken into account and--if need be--restricted through house rules.

Still, the rules are easy to learn and, in a less competitive environment, it's an alright game to get people started on their board game journey. Even with all the criticisms I have of the game, it sees regular play due to the addiction factor.

textfield_comment_value:
So done with this game, see comments for star trek catan. there are some great things this game did, but a number of bad design choices ruin this. Really if the game took about 30-45 min. it would be really good, I cant devote 2 hrs plus to this. Last game took 2.5 hrs; 2.9.17 (andrews place)

Let me also add to the star trek comments: the Longest Road and most military are stoopid, and obviously tacked on mechanics that dont add anything to the theme. Drawing cards hoping for an army is about as unimaginative and as far from developing an army as anything. And when was building a long road a strategy? OK maybe the Burma road, but modern thinking even questions that strategy. So dumb.

The tedious trading mechanic is one of several irksome features. It's actually a very good mechanic of generating production with a randon iterative proces (rolling dice), so it's worth checking out. But it takes too long for what it is and that is perhaps the only reason I rate it this low, if this could play in 45 minutes, it would probably be at least a 6 or 7.  Too many scoring systems detract from any pretence of "classic" feel. Monopoly with proper house rules, that rein in the time, is better. ALso dont like the placement strategy of roads and cities as this seems too simplistic. The new version of settling america looks more sophisticated and better. (original comments 4.20.13; rated 6 in june '14))
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value: F&%k all the elitist, snotnose backlash this game gets from people who think they've "moved on" to supposedly superior fare like PUERTO RICO- SETTLERS is the definitive Eurogame and the absolute best in its class, a truly transcendant title that encompasses the best that gaming has to offer.  Direct and meaningful player interaction, luck and strategy, long term planning and situational flexibility, competition, and a sense of narrative development serve to ensure that SETTLERS will long outlive the 5000 or so inferior European designs that have followed in its wake.  This is truly one of the watershed titles in the hobby on par with DUNGEONS AND DRAGONS and MAGIC: THE GATHERING in terms of industry impact, accessibility, and paradigm shifting.  It saddens me to see folks say how they've somehow burned out on SETTLERS when this is one of the rare games that has virtually unlimited replayability and is almost always a unique and fun experience.  You don't like the dice?  Go do Sudoku puzzles and cram your statistics textbook up your ass.  The dice make the game dramatic, variable, and it forces players to adapt and adjust throughout the game.  With trading, you are _never_ screwed unless you're one of those shrewish gamers who's afraid to speak up at the table to get what you want.  Without a doubt, one of the greatest games ever published and a timeless classic.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
The first Eurogame I ever played is still one of my favorites. There is a slight problem in the game with The Robber remaining in one place for too long (if a seven isn't rolled, it's difficult - though not impossible to move him) which can take away from the fun of the game for whoever is unlucky enough to have a settlement near him. Overall, the game is a fascinating and exciting tile-based game.

Update: Lowered my rating from 7 to 6. This was my first Euro and I have many fond memories of it, but I've found many other far superior games since and I can't say I've wanted to play Catan very often recently. I actually enjoy the two player card game much more than the original.

Update: Lowered my rating from 6 to 4 after a recent play. This game relies far too much on dice which can present the unfortunate situation of sitting around turn after turn with nothing to do. And while many people have commented on the luck of the dice, might I just add that working your ass off to collect three ore and then getting a worthless soldier card from the random-draw resource deck doesn't help the game. I have a hard time imagining myself wanting to pull this off the shelf again anytime soon. I'll always be thankful to this game for introducing me to the wider world of board games, but there are much better games out there and I can't see myself wanting to play this again.

textfield_comment_value:
Número de Jogadores: 3 a 4
Dificuldade: 2,0/5,0
Indicado para Iniciante: Sim
Contras: Número muito limitado de jogadores; o fator sorte pode atrapalhar a experiência; o jogo pode se estender mais do que o necessário.
Prós: Clássico; boa interação.
 
Comentário: Esse jogo é a entrada de muita gente para jogos modernos. Regras bem simples e partidas que viciam rapidamente.
Hoje em dia existem jogos bem melhores, mas até hoje Catan tem o meu respeito. Ele é o verdadeiro clássico dos jogos modernos.
No jogo estamos colonizando a ilha de Catan, tentando aumentar as nossas rotas de mercadoria. E para fazer novas construções precisamos dos recursos necessários, mas temos que cuidar dos ataques dos ladrões e dos vizinhos para não tomar o terreno que queremos. O objetivo é fazer 10 pontos primeiro que seus adversários, seja por construções, cartas, cavalaria ou estrada.
O bacana do jogo é que mesmo não sendo a sua vez, você interage o tempo todo com o jogo, seja ganhando recursos ou negociando.
Ideal para quem quer começar a jogar jogos modernos.
O jogo tem um pouco de dependência de sorte que pode atrapalhar muito um jogador e acabar deixando ele frustrado com o jogo; outro ponto negativo é o limite de jogadores que às vezes atrapalha a formação de mesa; bem como o tempo do jogo que pode se prolongar demais.
Mesmo assim, um bom jogo, recomendo!
 
Modo Solo: Não existe.

textfield_comment_value:
I think game is a important landmark of the modernization of the new boards we have today, and thank the creators for that. This game is very fun, and I like the non-war theme in the game. This is technically a "euro" game, however... one of the important factor of this game is based on a dice rolls. The best probability of these dice rolls can be curve to be closest to "7 result", however it a strong mechanic of American games are known for. I enjoy american games but I think a dice rolls are the worst part of american games, and this game isn't the worst example of that (many games have multiple dice). 

Funny enough I see this game as evolution or "spiritual" sequel to Monopoly franchise of board games because both games deal with capitalization with controlling the market and both deal with the educational values of economy that most people should learn that world isn't fair and sometimes it can be very greedy. I have to say that Catan has a very major upgrades over Monopoly (rightfully so), and the dice rolling problematic effects are reduce compared to Monopoly. Another important factor in this game is milestone in current board games is that it introduce "victory points" and that it a few alternatives of getting "victory points" that unique compare to other board games that came out before Catan (usually only had 1 major path to winning to the game)

textfield_comment_value:
[i][u]Disclaimer:[/u][/i] This is a [color=#000099][b]standalone game[/b][/color]. Its rating is based on [color=#000099][b]desire to play[/b][/color].

An immense classic of our genre, [b]Catan[/b] hasn't aged too well in my opinion.

While I like randomness in games, I don't like it when there isn't much you can do to adapt to it. And getting robbed over and over ranks among the worst experiences I've ever had in gaming.

I also dislike the trading aspect of [b]Catan[/b] which isn't limited in time and leads to endless sequences of negociation.

Finally I'm not a big fan of the "kingmaker" aspect that the game can sometimes include : there are times when a player will have to screw over somebody with a road placement or a robber decision. Let's call him player A, and his opponents B and C. And let's say A decides to punish B. When there isn't a clear leader at the table, everybody will feel bad : A for having to screw a person for no reason, B for being punished for no reason, and C for an undeserved lead.

In the end I thank [b]Catan[/b] for its contribution to the renaissance of the boardgame industry. I'm happy to keep my box as a tribute to a classic, and it's a decent gateway game for new players, but outside of this particular use I have no desire to play it anymore.

[u]2023 update:[/u] I have since sold it, and I'm very happy I did.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Catan is a game on which my opinion has changed overtime. I didn't like it on my first play, I didn't like after a dozen plays and I still don't like it now. However I have a better understanding of why people like it. 

For me Catan's biggest failing was how it was presented. When I first started playing board games it was presented as this great "gateway game" for getting into the hobby. It wasn't my first game, but I did get around to it eventually and I was disappointed. I spent half the game doing virtually nothing while another player skyrocketed to victory. I first blamed it on bad dice rolls on my part so I tried again and again and still lost. After a time I realised that it was in the strategy, and since dice rolls were random, it must be around the initial settlement placements at the start of the game.

As time went on, I realised that there was a huge element of skill to Catan, however it was more subtle than I realised. Even though I do appreciate that now, and understand why some people like it. I think the greatest problem Catan has is the image of a gateway game ingrained into the community's mind when in reality it has more in common with Chess than the other light board games that are considered gateways (TTR, Pandemic, Carcassone, etc). While Catan is an easy game to understand the basic rules, the learning curve is huge.

textfield_comment_value:
It's not a perfect game, it's theme doesn't exactly match the mechanics and it does have that random element that probably drives some people nuts, but judging by the amount of time spent on the table it's still our gaming group's favorite game.  

I have bought the Seafarers expansion and played a game of that, but I personally prefer the original.  Settlers is an "island" generated by laying hexes of various resources (+ one desert), and then surrounding it by sea hexes.  Numbers (reflecting die rolls, which also includes probabilities in a simple dot system) are placed on each of resources, and the black piece -called The Robber- is placed in the desert.  The mechanic of placing settlements over corners of hexes and then a road segment adjacent to it seems at first blush to favor the player who places two settlements in a row, but that is not the case as smart roadbuilding and sticking to a sound strategy will win out in general.

The rolling of the dice to get resources makes a statistician want to play the resources with the best chance of coming up (6 and 8, because 7 moves the Robber), but if those resources are mainly wood and brick, then in the late game that doesn't help you very much.  You have to balance out the early game (building roads and settlements) with the late game (cities, soldier cards, and development cards).

Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Random resource generation? Eh, not really. You take control of nodes as a gambled investment on gaining resources. You always know the odds something will be rolled, so it's a very economic bidding game in this way. 

That's why it's balanced - it's for repeated plays. Play this with the same group and it won't matter if you go 2 games in a row not getting many resources, because the next 2 games may play out much different. And the routes to victory (especially in expansions) becomes so fleshed out that maximum resource generation isn't as required.


---


Has so many mechanics within. Games that have better mechanics also sacrifice elements that Catan weaves together. A strong game. You can play it if you're in the mood for trading, building things from resources, area control, and so on. Not many games can give you that.

The variety of gameplay in settlers makes it a game most gaming groups won't be too worried to play, because whatever gaming mood they are in, it's likely Catan will give them what they want. And if their gaming mood changes next week, Catan may still have what they want. At least a little bit of it. 

That makes this game continually hit the table. It's one we usually are cool with playing no matter what mood we're in, because it has a little bit of something for every mood. Not many games can do that.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Summary at bottom. Note that this review does not include the extensions for Catan!

Classic and a fair buy. Good for kids and casual players in terms of pace and content, as it's not too complicated yet you don't feel insulted by the weight of the game.

That being said, the game is relatively linear with little strategy required. One simply follows the sequence of collecting resources, trading with players and building settlement after settlement. It's not excruciatingly boring, but once you've played the game a couple times one may get stale of the predictable, slow-paced grind.

That being said, the game does include a sort of disruption mechanic to hinder other players, but it's completely based off of luck so not much thought required there either.

TLDR: Decent relaxing game. Great family game considering it runs along at a tolerable pace and is easy enough to grasp for the young and old. However, it requires little strategy and becomes rather stale after a couple of sessions.

It is extremely important to remember that this review is purely based off of the base game. There are several add-ons available that add a mountain of content and different play styles, that likely make the game a lot more compelling. However, I have played few sessions with them, so I suggest you take a look at the reviews for those as well.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
I play Settlers every week (that means every time we play, since our meeting is once a week). After all these times I have played it I lowered my rating from 8 to 6. I just hate (more and more every time) that one decision at the start of the game (initial placing of settlements/roads) can decide the winner, together with the luck of dice. Even if you play with a standard initial placement (booooooooriiiiiiiiiiiiing) you are screwed if the other players leave you out of the negotiations.

A 6 only for how often it hits the table.

EDIT JUNE 7TH, 2020

OK, I admit I don't care what other people think about it and how good it is and I decided that I really hate everything in this "game":
1. Zero decisions in the game. Just throw the dice and watch the others earn the resources and win.
2. Even if you were alone around 6s and 8s you are still screwed if your group leave you out of the negotiations.
3. Oh, you found these resources to finally realise your big turn and screw your opponent? Well, screw you; the player before you just rolled a 7. You lose half of your cards and he steals an additional card from you. Isn't it FUN-NY?

I have one expansion (I think it's barbarians) and will honestly try to play the game again with the expansion, but so far EVERY play left me with only 2 feelings: FRUSTRATION & ABSOLUT BOREDOM.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
A well designed game. The idea were you roll your dice then collect resources is different than most games I've played. Not to mentioned that the goal is just ten points... Which is just enough time for you to get your fair share of fun from the game, but at the same time not to over kill the amount of glory the game deserves. 
This game is also quite simple, meaning this game could be refered to as a gateway game. A gateway game is a game that leads people who pretty much only knows how to play checkers to play more games. Like "Power Grid", ""Ticket to Ride", "The Resistance", and many more.
However I would not give this a ten because... Well, the game really doesn't give you that much options to do things, in other words you can only do what the game itself gives you. 
So if you are a person who likes to kinda sit back and watch the show, or game so to speak (I know I do sometimes) then this is probably the game for you. I know I like to actually legit participate in a game when I play it and this game doesn't really allow it. But I find my own ways to strategise in this which is one of the reasons I gave it such a high rating. This game also deserves a high rating because it is a very, VERY good family game. So if you want to spend more time with your family, this would be a good game for you.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
I think it interesting and totally appropriate that the community rating for Catan rests around 7/10. It is of course, a staple of board gaming history... it changed the presence of board games in the household in ways that only Monopoly could have dreamed of at the time, but there are a few things about Catan that always irked me. At first, in the early plays, I thought that Catan was essentially the perfect game: it was relatively short and sweet, it had concrete basic rules with dynamic strategy, and it was always an interesting time. But, as I got more and more familiar with the game, there has always been an aspect that I never loved: That the game inherently feels lopsided toward one player right away from the setup phase of the game. While this isn't always a bad thing, the games that can go on for hours always feel drab when you don't start with a decent position, and also, winning with a conquering position feels drab in the same context. 

All in all, I love it, it is without a doubt part of how I became involved in the board gaming community... but I can't convince myself to call it a 10/10 game now that I have had all the years between its release and right now to study other game mechanics and see what else is out there. - That being said... does anyone have wheat for bricks? ^_^*
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
[b]RO:[/b] [i]12/17/2015[/i]

What is there to say about Catan? Well, a lot actually. Of course, there is it's prestigious (and hardly arguable in my opinion) claim to bringing "German-style" board gaming to the world. For most of us, Catan was probably the first non-American classic you played, or at least heard of. 

My group and me mispronounce the name, at first ignorantly, and now out of habit as "Kay-ten", of course the correct pronunciation is "Cuh-tahn" but we've grown so used to it, that the simple misnomer "Kay-ten", or occasionally, "Settlers", is almost always how we refer to it.

There is a lot of luck here, resource generation is dice based but player investment is constant because resources can flow into your [-]sweaty hands[/-] warehouses even when it isn't your turn, and trades are flying this way and that on a regular basis. It can drag, if luck isn't on your side or you placed your settlements poorly, but overall it is leagues beyond your normal Monopoly, Risk, or Life game in terms of interaction, interest, and ability to influence the outcome through clever play. It is always fun, even if it occasionally overstays it's welcome. Many "better" games have come along, but there is something about the nostalgia and brilliant design that will keep most coming back.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value: This game does not get enough love. People compare this to games like Risk or Monopoly but I think that is unfair. This game is what got me into the hobby of boardgames and I still go back to it often. This game is very strategic without being complicated. If you know how to play well you can even pull off a win after being placed in terrible starting locations. I also really like how you can trade with your opponents. Sometimes you really don't want to trade because you know it's going to really help out your opponent possibly even more than you but you still really need the resource so you don't have much of a choice. I also love how the robber can really stop someone from running way ahead of everyone else and the threat can sometimes force you to make a purchase you didn't really want to. My mom and dad surprisingly love to play this game even though they aren't big on strategy and sometimes they can even pull off a win. If you are unsure if this game is still relevant in 2024 I would say so. Look at games like cosmic encounter, it's been out since 1977 and it's ranked 190 and it's many peoples favorite. Obviously there is a reason to that but still, I think Catan can stand up there with some of the greats if you are looking for a more simple strategy negotiation game.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
*Generally in most game designs players will know well before their last turn where they stand (unless vps are kept secret such as in E & T) so robs most of the players of the excitement.I think one main reason why Settlers does it for me is that there are a few elements which makes the game less likely to be anti-climatic than any game design I have played before or since. 

Resource holdings are secret, so there is tense uncertainty (unless you have memorised the transactions) whether other players will overtake you in the vp race, which incidently is kept at a simple and visual level.

But the clincher is the dice which in their nature provides hopeful swings in fortune or devasting schaudenfreude. The use of the commonly rolled "7" has been used to great effect to put risk filled fear in the leader from hoarding and also the robber as another mechanic to try and level the playing field, in a thematic way. 

So the tension of declaring the 10th vp is often in doubt until the right resource is secured in a trade, the vp development card is drawn or worse you have accummalated more than 7 resources and fingers crossed no-one even yourself that a 7 is rolled. The development costs menu means that an internalised narrative of needs is established cranking up the climax.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
I hate how the most complex decision is at the very beginning of the game, when you place your first settlement. After that, it is often close to autopilot (trading is pretty easy, despite what anyone says) and very luck based. This makes the flow of the game pretty anticlimactic. People go into huge AP as they place their first settlements, and then just sort of sit there while the dice determine the winner. This can be immensely frustrating, since after agonizing over the correct play and finally placing the settlement perfectly, you often just lose to variance anyway. For how difficult placing your settlement tends to be, it's often not worth the mental effort.

The game is also MEAN. Placed your road the wrong way? Too bad, player 3 cuts you off in the settlement placement and you're screwed for the entire game. Are you winning? OK, expect the robber baron to land on your settlements every time a 7 is rolled. This is just NOT ok for a casual, luck-based game - I want my casual games to feel casual, not like some cutthroat brawl.

The game gets better if you play with only 3-4 players on the 6-player expansion. There, there's enough room so that people get randomly screwed less, and placing settlements is also easier due to the large availability of "good" places.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Like most other people, Settlers was one of the first Euros I played and it helped start me on the hobby. I can't add anything to the praise it has received. The design is inspired and clever all at the same time.

That said, I find myself not really wanting to play much any more, especially with four players. Part of this is due to luck as some games the rolls just don't go your way. Another part is the downtime. I find myself spacing off during other players turns. Most players I know are unwilling to trade because they are worried about helping you too much. Further, I try to not plan ahead too much as things can change a lot before the dice come back to you (roads block you, solider/robber steals cards, etc.). 

A biggest part, however, is the endgame. Just when it looks like someone will win, another player bashes them and further delays the game. I usually don't mind "beat up on the leader" as this is an important strategy for winning. For Settlers, however, it makes what should be a 30 minute game into one that is 60 hour or longer.

As such, it is the best game that I rarely have any desire to play. 

Note: online play against AI helps as it speeds things up considerably. I recommend, http://games.asobrain.com

Kept for nostalgia value and as a gateway game.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
I own Catan with almost every expansion out there at the moment.
It was the board game that got me into board games.

The design is nice and simple, the gameplay is easy to learn and simple enough to teach anyone. It's pretty fun.

My problems with it might be patched up by some of the expansions but none of them makes the game any shorter, in fact most of them makes the game much longer, which can be nice but can be tiring.

While playing you would build settlements on the map which can block other player's directions of building. - this is most of the hostile interaction you will experience in this game, the only other interaction is trading resources.

The fact that you can block someone from going a certain path is a concept that fits well but when the rest of the map is pretty dry it's gonna make the game pretty dry.
Without the expansions people who are behind don't have any way to make up for having weaker areas on the map, or being completely blocked off.

My favorite expansion is Traders & Barbarians which adds more interests on the map, it forces different players to play in a different way than the other making strategy less linear.

with this expansion I'd give it 7/10
But that's about it.
To be frank, I don't recommend it too much even with this score.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
It seems it has become fashionable to knock Catan these days. Yes, if you're a 'serious' gamer of a certain age then you've probably played this to death, but that's only because it was (is) so good.

This is still a phenomenal game and it will still blow the mind of new gamers who have only ever played the mass market games. The 'temporary victory points' for longest road or largest army, the trading element, it's just great and we're always happy to play it. Seafarers adds some more choices without changing the game too much.

Don't get me wrong though, there are plenty of reasons why this game can be frustrating. Firstly, it's a dice game so whilst proper selection can improve your chances you can still get completely screwed over by poor dice rolls. Secondly there's the robber which, if you've been struggling to produce for a while and then the robber forces you to discard half of what you have, can be very frustrating. Then there's the politics of a player ganging up on another player with robber attacks or monopolies, or the fact that people can block your production, steal your largest army or longest road - this game can be a pretty miserable experience if you get pummled into a corner!

That said - it's an ever-green for me.

But i'm doen with it now.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
A classic barter-heavy eurogame. My opinion on Catan has fluctuated over the years, from being bad at it to getting slightly burned out on it to experiencing it again with a more casual crowd and going from hating it to enjoying the laid-back experience.

As a hardcore player, I find Catan a little too random -- I hear the best online Catan players win something like 60% of the time, which strikes me as still a little bit low. It also feels you aren't given a lot of wholly different options. And as far as feelings go, I find that the island feels a little cramped in four player games. And the 5-6 player expansions for your expansions are a little greedy. And to cap it off, it's a bit too long for its level of complexity.

But when it comes down to it, everyone knows how to play Catan, and it's a lot better than Monopoly. The expansions (probably) help with the claustrophobic island and limited decisions, and the real highlight is the casual bartering that Catan brings to the table. Nothing has really made Catan obsolete for me, or even really bridged the gap between this and Terra Mystica, because those games tend to have less player interaction.

====================
Personal notes, rules and rulings:
1) Knights can be played on your turn before the dice roll
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Ah, the literal gateway game. Nobody needs my opinion, because everyone's heard of and played Catan. 

Honestly, I played approximately 300 games in high school and early college to great success, back when I didn't know much about board games, but now you'd have to really convince me (or butter me up with some great snacks) to get me back to the table for this one. This game is a combination of infuriating bad luck, backstabbing "friends", and someone being a poor sport by the end, which is really not my cup of tea. I did recently play with a bunch of expansions and houserules a friend had mashed up, which made the game more interesting and complicated, but also incredibly long and needlessly complex, so I'm not sure that was actually a net win. 

I will fully admit that this game singlehandedly created a generation of board gamers (including myself), who would never have moved on from Scrabble and Monopoly if it weren't for Catan, and it's honestly not a bad game, it just really doesn't live up to the hype now that I have games in my collection much better suited for my personality and life. It should be noted, however, that I am just not a fan of competitive games by and large, so that's a major reason this game hasn't withstood the test of time for me.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
I figured I just had a bad first play, and gave this game a chance for the second time last night.  This has been a staple gateway game for many starting to get into the board game community.   It seems to me there are a million games in existence now that have taken any positive traits from this game and improved upon them.  The game mechanics of this game seem very outdated and poor.  

The thing that bugs me the most about this game is how reliant it is on luck and initial placement.  Better games allow the user to do something to better their position every turn regardless of how bad that person is at the game or how far that individual is behind.  For this game, you can easily waste countless turns waiting for the dice to roll in your favor.  My first time playing it, I spent half the game unable to do anything due to bad rolls.  For me, this game is very boring and very frustrating, with the potential to go way too long.  What's even worse, is this game has the potential to prevent newcomers to the community from giving better designed games a chance.  Had this been more widely adopted, I think this game deserves more of a negative stigma than Monopoly or Candy Land since the actual player involvement has the capability to be so low with bad rolls.

= 2012-05-21

The game that started it all. Some friends introduced us to this game in January of 2012 and now I have a BGG account, two shelves of board games and a wishlist that grows by three for every one I remove.

I won't say we've "moved on" from this game, but it hasn't had much play since being used as a gateway game. I blame this on us mostly wanting to play two player games and there are just so many better two player games out there than any two player variant of Catan.

= 2014-02-14 - R:6.99

Happy Valentine's Day. In sticking with the theme for the day, I'd like to share some love for this game. I gave it a 6 because, on the official BGG scale, it's a game I admire but would only play when in a certain mood. That mood is more situational than anything. There are many times when my wife and I want to play a game together and we'd like that game to have the feel of Catan, but so far we haven't been able to capture that feel in a two player game. When we do have enough people over to be able to play a four player game, I rarely want to play board games. So poor Catan never makes it to our table even though I think I want to play it. In honor of how much Catan influences our search for other games, I'm bumping the rating from 6 to 6.99.

textfield_comment_value:
(5/2011) I've played a couple of times in recent weeks. The experience has cemented my matured opinion of the game. Blah. Manila crushes it for fun and gateway value while still being an interesting game. So many other games are just plain better. The negotiation is limp. The decisions are almost false. The playtime can drag.
(2/2/10) This and San Juan make me question how I do my rankings. On the one hand, I want to rate games on a scale of how interesting I find them. On the other, I find that I want to rate them according how good they are at being what they are. Settlers is THE 'family' Euro. Luck, social interaction, a little screwage without player elimination, and tons of fun, all in an hour. I'll play it with newbies any day of the week. But will I bring it to game night? Unlikely.

Original comment: Great game. I love the interaction. The components are beautiful (although the tiles could be thicker and fit better in the frame on the new edition). A rich game without insanely complicated rules. I'm new to eurogames, so this one was a big eye-opener for me (pretty trite story I know). While I can imagine tiring of it ever so slightly, I think I will alway enjoy playing it with first-timers who still think monopoly is a good boardgame.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Game in a Nutshell: Players compete to settle and secure the best spots on a modular island. Roll dice to collect goods, trade with other players and spend to expand.

Played as: 3,4 player

Played with: Seafarers, Cities and Knights, 5-6 Player Expansion, and Plain

Pros: Good mix of luck, area control, player interaction and replayability make for an excellent, addictive game. Serves as an excellent gateway because of enough familiar mechanics combined with some fresh innovative ideas. 

Cons: It can be luck driven for players of equal experience. It's not unusual to see a person who benefits from some lucky roles early on have a sizable advantage as the game progresses.

Other: If you're reading this and haven't yet played it yourself, do yourself a favor and change that. It got me hooked to euros and more then a few people have gone out and bought it after just one game of me introducing it to them. However, having played this so much, I'd almost prefer playing any other game over this one given the choice. That still doesn't stop me from giving it big props for what this game has meant to the gaming community at large.

Best Use: One of the first gateway games people should be thinking of introducing the 'is it like monopoly?' crowd to.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
2-21-10
Lowered my rating from an 8 to a 6 now that I've played both ways (randomizing the board and playing the 'beginner' setup). I realize this game isn't as much fun as I once hoped.  It's too random as to who is getting which resources, you can't really get any type of momentum going unless the dice are in your favor.  You can trade, sure, but if you have the same junk everyone else wants, you're out of luck.

You can get built in if other people are able to expand faster than you, and it can get to the point in a 4-player game where one or two people get 'eliminated' by the halfway mark of the game.

It takes too long for the level of depth.  Two hours for this game is absurd!  There needs to be more points in the deck as otherwise it's just not a wise investment.  Too many knight cards.

The social aspect of the game is fun but the game itself doesn't feel much more fun than games like Monopoly, because really, if you don't get the dice rolls and don't have the right stuff to trade, you lose - just like Monopoly.  At least in Monopoly when you get to the point where you know you can't win, you can just trade away your money and properties and go do something fun.  Here you get stuck being useless until somebody finally gets 10 points.

textfield_comment_value:
I've played this on various computer games, and it's always bored the living whiz out of me.  ALWAYS.

But, hundreds of thousands of copies sold can't be wrong, right?

EDIT:  Played this and had a great time.  It did run a little long even for as reasonably streamlined as our turns were, but that was nothing that couldn't be solved by say, playing to 8 rather than 10.

What I really liked about it, is if I had to come up with one game that encompassed all that it meant to be a game, with negotiation, strategy, and luck in all equal parts...  this would be that game.

08-15-11:  This game always takes just a hair longer than it aught to.  It's probably me that causes it, too.  In the end though, I'd rather play almost anything else.

Oh, and grind the development stack.  You can't go wrong.

SOLD.

09-18-11:  I think one of the things about this game going too long, is that it's a bit of a fractal representation of everyone on the board.  That is, the story doesn't really ever arc even as a winner is emerging.  People still trade, because it's helping their individual positions anyway.  The guy on the board who is getting the most shit, will find a way to get even more shit just as well getting his 10th point as he is getting his 7th point.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Pre-Catan, I used to like Board Games, but wouldn't have really been that into them.
Post-Catan, I realised that what I knew of board games was very out-dated. 

I'd say that my experience of playing Catan is similar to so many people. Our friends introduce us to Catan and it serves to bridge the gap in our appreciation for board games. We realise that Monopoly, Cluedo and Game of Life are not really "good" games at all. We realise that player elimination is a bad thing. We learn that the mechanics of the new wave of board games are so much more of an experience than what we had as kids. Most of all, we learn that board games are now really fun!

The mechanics of the game are very simple, but can bring out great strategy. Luck can be a factor, as in any game with dice, but dice go both ways in games. Of course, good strategy and luck with dice can be overcame by players scheming and grouping up against one player - so it's always unlikely that one player will always win!

While I don't get to play Catan as often anymore, I'm still usually happy to join a game when it's suggested. And for a new gamer, it is still part of my armory to try and get them hooked. 

Catan will now and forever occupy a favorable place in my memories of gaming!
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
[b]Like:[/b]
-Simplicity for what it achieves
-Trading
-Building stuff and receiving more stuff for it
-Many people know this game

[b]Dislike:[/b]
-Robber
-Having multiple turns without anything to do because your numbers didn't get rolled

The game I played the most before I really got into board gaming. I mean, what other game lets you build towns and cities, and gain increasingly more resources when you do so while also allowing you to negotiate with others; am i r8?! No wonder I considered this a masterpiece at the time.

If Dead of Winter has the meanest dice of all time, Catan probably has the meanest gaming piece of all time: the Robber. This little sh*t used to make the people I played with literally cry. Luckily, we all kinda realised this and only put it in someones place if that guy was far ahead.

Also, going through multiple rounds without getting anything just sucks, especially if all the others get huge amounts.

Catan: Cities & Knights is absolutely required for me to enjoy this game though.

While I'd rather play other games now, it still's got the advantage of being the simplest build, receive more and trade game I know of. Be careful not scare the new-lings away from the hobby with the robber though!
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Good gateway game, but definitely not for me.

Pros: 
- Easy to learn
- interesting mechanic for new table top gamers
- Trading aspect can bring out good social interactions

Cons:
- Too many dead turns. Most games have it bad enough waiting for other people's turns. Having nothing to do on your own turn due to RNG/robber makes for unpleasant play.
- Frontloaded decision making. A good chunk of the strategic play is frontloaded. The setup is (or at least feels) extremely important and starting a game from behind feels bad. Large Hate aspect here too.
- Poor scaling. Game plays extremely differently with different number of players. The board size remains the same, but players increase. With 4 players the board is very cramped, with 2, you have much more 

Overall, the biggest Con is the number and prevalence of hate mechanics which leads to feeling bad (even on your own turn!). There are explicit hate mechanics (using robber. stealing away the longest road. knight cards, monopoly cards) as well as un-escapable ones that are just a core part of the game (blocking people off during setup/expanding, esp at larger player counts).

The main draw then becomes enjoying RNG and dice rolling or trading, which is not enough for me.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
The game that got me into board gaming, and is still a favorite. Even though there is a significant luck factor to this game [i](which will likely turn off hardcore gamers)[/i], Catan should be in every board game collection.

The Epic Win ... Why I still love Catan:
Nothing quite compares to being pathetically down-and-out ... written off as the player who has no chance ... wanting to blame the dice, but knowing you made some poor choices ... but then ... though a series of unpredictable events ... combined with reluctant alliances ... followed by a few key placements ... coupled with the correct physiological warfare pitting opponents against each other ... having the stars align just right .... like a flash in the night, you manage to pull 180 with a point shifting victory that nobody saw coming ... and all they can do is sit there - jaw dropped - wondering what just happened. That excited/nervous/poker-faced feeling for 15 rounds or so when you see how you might possibly win ... but know you probably won't ... and then somehow pulling it off ... priceless.

[b]Expansions[/b]: [thing=325]Seafarers[/thing] & [thing=2807]5-6 player[/thing], [thing=20038]Event Cards[/thing]

textfield_comment_value:
un juego equilibrado y muy entretenido si los jugadores conocen la mecánica. teniendo en cuenta esto último, la evolución de cada jugador durante el juego se desarrollará muy pareja, si alguno se ve en problemas, podrá optar por opciones que le permitirán avanzar. la interacción entre jugadores es primordial para avanzar rápido, si no, la partida será eterna, por lo que si un jugador no sabe jugar bien, o es desconfiado en las transacciones, el juego podría tornarse lento por ratos. es muy posible que si un jugador avanza mucho durante la partida, el resto se ponga de acuerdo para anular los intercambios, o bloquear sus recursos con el ladrón, sin embargo, esta situación podría llegar a ser momentánea, pues están los intercambios con la mesa, entonces el juego no deja a merced del resto de jugadores para poder ganar.
un juego totalmente recomendable. las primeras partidas pueden ser lentas (¿pero que juego de este tipo no es asi?), pero una vez que se aprenden las reglas, los juegos fluyen rápidamente. con la ampliación el equilibrio se mantiene, insisto, si todos los jugadores saben lo que hacen, pero aumentan las posibilidades de intercambio, y la interacción entre jugadores, que para mi lo hacen mas entretenido.

Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
This game is why I don't like, at least my understanding of, libertarianism. My friends that are winning love this game because they think they're the best traders. But my friends that are losing this game know it's because they can't participate in any trades because their numbers were never being rolled. We can all acknowledge and appreciate a good meritocracy, but as is the case in real life, only those who have get to play the game, while the have nots sit back and watch-- and the starting line that divides the two is determined by luck.

It does mean two things about this game. First, the most important decision (and only real hard one) you'll make is the very starting decision of your settlement, since that is what matters the most. From there on out, may the odds be ever in your favor.

Second, my favorite variant of Catan is ironically called the "Welfare Variant", where each time you do not get a resource off a roll, you receive a welfare token. You may then exchange welfare tokens for a resource of your choice at an exchange rate equal to your current number of points (so those in the lead require more tokens for a resource than those who have fallen behind).

Thanks for coming to my Ted Talk.

textfield_comment_value:
Previously played Catan online many years back a lot (a LOT!), and decided to buy a physical copy for my playing group which consists of my partner, my family and/or her family, and my friend (who is a gamer) for the following reasons:

1. Good components - components are excellent, and the hexagonal map is modular allowing for different set-ups each time [variability]

2. Mechanics - well thought out and put together, which work really well with the theme, and more importantly has a fair degree of player interaction even during other players turns

3. Simple and logical rules - concise and build upon the theme and mechanics. Very cohesive

4. Interaction - fair degree of player interaction through trading, blocking roads, and moving the robber

It may be fashionable in some quarters to bash Settlers for its success and market penetration, it still holds up as a worthwhile game (unless you detest any form of luck in games), is still relevant, worthwhile, and fun to play now. 

Catan is no longer an automatic shoe-in as the default gateway game (testament to the vast range of excellent games available), however it is a worthwhile choice as a gateway game. One that I still enjoy playing on occasion.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
I liked the game when I played it a long time ago, but the fact that I played a lot better games made this one stop here. I don't have too much nostalgia about it since I ALWAYS, SINCE THE FIRST GAME disliked a feature that is not only prominent here, but also something other games LOVE doing, and in its essence is what I dislike in Scythe, Kemet, GoT and here (there are other games I played in this list with a similar sudden endgame condition that EITHER give players at least a "salvage round" to cushion the disaster for the players not ending the game or make this a ): sudden endgame conditions. It can be tied to a score of sorts (8VP in Kemet's case, 10VP in Catan's case, 6th star in Scythe's case) and doesn't give the rest of the players a chance to do anything, resulting in a frustrating endgame condition.

I never liked those. I think they are a cheap (while easy) design feature made in lazy manner. I tend to like games giving the "consolation round" WAY more, since, at the very least they give the player some agency in what to do in their last round (it usually doesn't change spectacularly the endgame placement, but at least gives the player that last chance of achieving something).
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
I first played this game as an adult so I don't have fond memories of it.  It does not occupy a 'warm-spot' in my heart.  My rating, based entirely on gameplay, is a -2 (negative two).  Without Catan, however, I may never have played a modern board game and for that it scores a 3.  That's how it gets a 1.  

If I owned a copy, I would burn it and put it on YT.  

Update 2022 - Had a chance to play it again and be reminded just how horrible this thing is.  I prefer Monopoly, at least you can be the banker when you're out.  Lower from 3 to 1.

Update 2017 -- Enough with the badmouthing of this classic.  My previous comments can be summarized,  "I'd rather play checkers with my cat." 

Actually this game is very much like Monopoly.  I think that's why it's such a great gateway.  It has the horror of the "dead-money" player -- just like Monopoly.  It allows senseless, reckless, free trading -- just like Monopoly.  And also, like Monopoly, you pretty much know who is going to win forty minutes before the game is over.  Yawn, Daddy-O, yawn!  It manages to paint the mean, pointlessness of Monopoly onto a resource gathering area control game.  It's a bridge to escape the very type of game it is.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
This was so good game 15 years ago, but now I think that this is quite last season for me. 

There are couple of issues with this game. Winning the game depends too much on player order when placing the first two settlements. The first player gets the worst starting position for their second settlement in 4-player game and player who places their first and second settlements one after another has too good advantage. Usually even more if you lay tiles randomly. Bad starting positions can ruin your game and it's quite impossible to fix your game then.

Also, I must mention, that I'm not fond of the robber mechanic in the game. It often causes that the game drags on too much, as if there is a shortage of some resources in the game and you are trying to save similar cards for exchanging them 4:1 (or for some more favorable exchange rate), then comes the robber and you need to discard your hand cards to half rounded down. Then someone even steals one card. And oh, then your game is set backwards by some rounds. 

Let alone bad dice rolls, that happen again and again in this game.

I don't have been very interested to play this during the past like 5 years, so I decided to sell the game away.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
THIS GAME HAS BECOME OBSOLETE!

Pros:
1. Revolutionized the gaming industry

Cons:
1. Success is dependent on other players. It is counter-intuitive to help out other players when they are competing against you. This is not a mechanic you see often anymore (you see this in older games like Cosmic Encounter). Early in the game, it works "okay." But once a leader has been established, players typically choose to not trade with that player. This can even out the game, but it also makes it disadvantageous to have an early lead. Small World suffers from the same problem. If a game is dependent on negotiation, there need to be alliances. Fief is a game that works in this way. Settlers, on the other hand, falls flat if players aren't willing to work together. 
2. Takes too long for what it is (think Monopoly)
3. BORING! This game has absolutely no theme, the board is hard to read, and the choices just aren't interesting. 
4. Stale components
5. Perhaps most importantly, so many games have replaced this one. Every mechanic has been replicated and improved.

I'm glad I played it, but only to know that I never want to play again. Plain and simple, this game has no soul. I'd rather play Monopoly.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Like so many others, for me Catan was the "gateway game" that brought me into the wider world of table tops past risk and monopoly.  

It rates a solid 7 for 

1) having an accessible shallow learning curve that's easy to pick up in less than 10 minutes
2) for being balanced enough to have multiple different paths to victory
3)for often forcing cooperating and trading between the players. 
4) and of course, for having a ton of map and number variation so you're never playing the same game twice.

As a downside, the game falls on the side of a little too random in my book.  There will be some play sessions where you swear your numbers will never come up.  The person who wins probably had a good strategy, but also wins with a fair amount of luck.  Yes this makes the game more accessible for some novice players, but it also makes it the kind of game that I'm more reluctant to walk into.  

I've found that the "Oh I just got screwed by bad rolls" mindset is mitigated when you:

A) make the map bigger with expansion sets
B) increase the number of victory points required to win

However, this can greatly extend the length of the game depending on how efficient your opponents end their turn
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
I can only think of 3 games I've played hundreds of times and this is one of them. It has relatively simple rules and a randomness associated with setup and resource production which leads some people to believe that this game is more luck than skill. They are wrong. A combination of strategy , trading, and diplomacy can overcome bad initial setups and bad rolls of the dice.

The only thing that stops very experienced players from winning the vast majority of games against less experienced players is that the less experienced players learn after a few games that their only chance is to gang up on the more experienced/skilled player if it looks like they're in the lead. And that leads to more experienced players adopting strategies that make it appear as if they're behind in the first half of the game even though they're setting themselves up for a sprint at the end . . .

One thing I particularly love about this game are the slow-the-leader mechanisms (robber, trading embargoes, development cards) that makes it possible for people to come back from behind and win, which keeps everyone engaged, and makes this game fun to play even when player age and/or skill level is a wide range.
