textfield_comment_value:
I used to like this game alot. However now it is just mediocre. 

I have recently taken board games up again in the last months, and this is by far one of the most dissapointing. Its not neccesarily bad, it just lacks strategy in it. The whole game revolves around dice, and whoever wins is 90% based on what the dice give. There is little strategy element to it, and its easily repetitive. Even the expansions give this game little justice, and being expensive aswell, it is not one i am likely to pick up. The expansions are like £35 each, and they do not give much to the game either. 

This game is trying so hard to be a "proper" board game but just reminds me of a sort of ancient monopoly. Not to mention they change the graphics every year. so the resources in the base and the expansion look so different you cant tell them from others.

If someone offers me a game, then i will accept, but it is not one i play often. That being said, it is a sort of a bridge between the basic games and the slightly advanced ones.

Also to mention, they no longer give out spare parts anymore, so i have had to play with an incomplete set, as i am not willing to splash out for a game i play rarely
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value: My wife and one of our gaming friends both absolutely love Settlers (which I find strange - both are experienced gamers), so there was quite a long period where I was forced to play it on an approximately weekly basis (that has thankfully stopped, the game now only gets played when they have someone else to play it with). As you can probably guess, I've never been a fan. To be fair, it's not that bad as a game, what is there works reasonably well - but there's nothing particularly good or interesting about it, and any individual game is too dependent on the dice rolls (or other luck like which cards get stolen). And it throws up incredibly frustrating moments, like finally getting that brick when a 5 was rolled for the first time all game, only for an opponent to play a monopoly card for it before you can use it. Or getting picked on even when you're already doing terribly, just because the opponent who just rolled 7 knows that one of your 2 cards is that precious wheat. And many many more. I can understand why this game became popular 20 years ago, but really, even for a gateway game there are dozens (at a very conservative estimate) of better and more fun ones around now.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Catan used to be a ton of fun back when I got started in the hobby. While it's not a terrible experience, it's not that great either. I dislike the randomness of the game and the fact that the value of resources tends to stale - the negotiation part is almost never satisfactory. 

Getting turns and turns in a row where you don't get anything because dice don't roll your way isn't a good mechanic. Getting tons of resources every turn simply because you get lucky with the dice isn't fun either. No player agency.

Would rather play almost any other euro at this point - but I will not turn down a game if it is for introducing other players or for a family/kids game night.

I've played with two or three expansions, and while they add new stuff to take care of, doesn't make me any more interested or disinterested.

Catan is a great gateway game and it's still fun - it's just been replaced for me, but it remains a great family game and classic

I find the variant of "socialist Catan" very funny though - when you roll a 7, after having placed the thief, everyone gives up their cards to a common pile, which is shuffled and then distributed equally among all players. Brilliant!
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value: Settlers of Catan is the first board game outside of the usual few like Monopoly or Risk that I purchased. I purchased it to have something to do with a group of friends of mine and figured it was worth a shot. We had a blast and I quickly got the 5-6 player expansion so the whole group could play. That was back in 2013. Since then I have explored more of what the world of board games has to offer and found a lot of games that are better in a lot of aspects. I figured all these games with their better mechanics and more interesting themes would be just as much fun to play with my friends. They did not think so. Some games were fun to play but just a bit too tedious like Suburbia, or we can't take 100% serious like Carcassonne. We try our best at Hanabi, but the coop challenge is not the same as attempting to out roll each other for resources and embargo each other for rolling hot. So, while it would never be my first choice for a game night outside of my circle of friends, as I have tried to play it with others and found it an alright experience, this remains as the game to play with my group and I'm not sure there is anything out there that will replace it.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
I want to hate this game, I really do.

But I gave it 4 stars because of how many friends I have that really enjoy this game for some reason. I'll play with them, I can manage, and even have a small amount of fun, but I usually hate this game.

Why?

It's nothing but luck with a dash of strategy.

Most games that are out now a day have a way to mitigate bad dice luck, take a look at Dead of Winter for instance.

This game however, it doesn't matter if you have settlements in good locations, bad dice rolls in a row, top with players who are specifically targeting you make this game terrible.

So why 4 stars?

It's such a basic and easy game to get into that you could teach this to a stick and it would be able to play. The simplicity and small learning curve allows for players of all ages and all types to have fun while engaging in this game.

I don't reccomend it.

Play something else, I'll even recommend Pandemic (A game I don't particularly enjoy) over this. There are so many better games out there that are casual, involve strategy, and are better executed.

This review is based off of the core set, it may be subject to change if expansions change my opinion.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Got this, then gave it away in frustration. I think everything about this game is so smart, but there is just too much luck involved for how long it takes. I can take some luck in a short game, but when you're over the hour mark and YOU CAN'T EVER GET A DICE ROLL TO GO YOUR WAY... I rarely get frustrated playing games, but one time I was covering every number except 2, 3 & 11, and the ONLY numbers that would appear were these three or the number where the thief was hanging out on my land. Which was right after a game where a similar scenario had occurred. Late in this game, I rolled the number where the thief was hanging out - which happened to be the sixth straight turn where I received NOTHING - so picked up the board, dumped everything on it into the box and handed it to one of the other players, telling them to never bring it into my house again. 

Trading is also a game mechanic I'm rarely in love with, especially when it can go on and on AND ON. And it does here. Even with limiting the number of trades a person can ask for, this game can still drag out. I have no idea why this game is so popular. Friends are not even allowed to mention it in my presence!
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
https://anchor.fm/board-game-doctors/episodes/Brass-Lancashire-after-10-plays--Trailblazers--Sunshine-City--Trek-12--and-more--August-2022-Wrap-up-e1n6bqm

I played it again after 10 years since my inaugural play and, after playing so many modern board games, I think this was still fun! 
- I like the interaction between players through trading, playing for spots on the shared board, and even the robber, although we played a version where you would just get a good of your choice for free.
- I like the randomness of getting goods. Even though it's probably a little too lucky for "Euro" gamers nowadays, I can see the forward thinking needed to set yourself up to get as many chances of rolling well for goods in the future.
- The shared board reminds me of Gaia Project, where you can variably change the landscape every time you play, making the settlement draft tense at the beginning of the game.

I can see the mass appeal of this game and I can see how players can get heavily invested into strategy of this game. It may be a little bit too lucky for my tastes as far as competitive gaming is concerned, but I'm willing to keep playing and see how my taste evolves.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Don't own anymore; sold it together with the 5-6 player extension and Seafarers (both of which were never played).

Catan is a decent game that occupies an important spot in board gaming history, and is still a lot of people's gateway to the wider board gaming hobby. I played it quite a lot with modified rules for two players, and a few times with three and four.

However, it has a couple of pitfalls which hold it back for me personally. It's possible to choose very suboptimal starting locations that put you at a large disadvantage. To counter this, it's centered around trading resources between players, which means it works best at four. But with four players, it's relatively easy to get blocked in and be forced to either devote large quantities of resources trying to get out or try and make do with what you have. Finally, because it's focused on trading, the game depends more heavily on the group you play with. Other players can significantly set you back by refusing to trade, leaving you at the mercy of die rolls. Overall, it's not a bad game and you'll most likely have a good time, but it's an older design less focused on constant player enjoyment.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Catan is a classic, that ages far better than Bang for instance, but not well enough for me to play much of it lately.

Lets get through the bad parts: Catan has a very bad runaway winner problem and a lot of luck in it.

The initial placements matter a lot, and you can definitely feel trapped if that placement isn't good enough, and there is only so much you can do even with a lot of skill and experience. Over the course of the game, if you get a little ahead, you can often keep that lead and make the gap even greater.

Every player stats their turn with a dice roll, which determines each players income. That is a lot of luck, but I'm willing to give Catan a little slack, its 2 decades old, and the feeling of income is just awesome.

This is not todays strategy game, but I don't take it as such. The components (I own the wooden version) are awesome even by todays standards. Its not even that long!... if you don't take ages taking turns and pursuing trades that are never going to happen. Sadly, this happens often enough because I usually play Catan with non-gamers that tend to do that more.

I wouldn't buy Catan today, but I sure as hell won't sell it.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
This was my gateway game that brought me into the hobby in the early 2000's. I played this probably close up 50 times with many different groups, expansions, and player counts, and have (for the most part) thoroughly enjoyed it.

I've since moved on, but will still play if I'm amongst an enthusiastic crowd clamoring for it. The game gets, in my humble opinion, a lot of underserved flack from board game enthusiasts. In particular, I find the criticisms that "it's all luck" and "it just comes down to your starting locations" to be way overstated. The game presents options to mitigate bad luck, and strong negotiation skills can help compensate for a bad situation.

Speaking of which, I think the one reason that this game hasn't truly been dethroned from its place after all these years is because it provides a rare mix of things that are not usually found together: high interactivity (via trading and area control) laid on top of a euro with simple rules and multiple paths to victory.

I'm making it sound like I adore the game when, in fact, I do not. But it still holds up well after all these years and is still a great way to bring people into the hobby.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
The seemingly peaceful cover illustration belies the fury and frustration this game can stir. Or maybe that's the top of a mushroom cloud on the horizon.

It's odd to me that a game with the potential for so much disappointment ever became quite so popular, never mind that it's regarded as a family game. I wonder if it would achieve anything like the same success if it were released today. Would a publisher release it new, as-is, today? I doubt it.

Not getting a single resource after rolling the dice on your turn (and/or every other player's turn) is just a crappy experience, especially for new gamers. People have such bad dice luck that they want to quit. And the game state changes so much, your plans are frequently dashed, making for long turns. The tightness and starting position in the four-player game can soon make victory hopeless: once you're blocked from expanding by aggressive players, it's game over. And the Robber and Knight are sadistic. How on earth is this a gateway game?

Unless the kids are grown, this isn't a family game. And there are much better gateway games. This is the first game in my collection that I actually want to sell.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
The gateway game.... This stupid thing is exactly why I probably don't own a Ferrari because I've put SO MUCH MONEY into boardgames. It's still fun, it's still a game I'll play if there's nothing else to do, or someone brings it along and I forgot to bring a game, etc. This is and should be the game every family owns instead of Monopoly. That said, the game is good, but not great. The setup is kind of lengthy (including settting the first two settlements), and the components are meh. Someone once told me that seafarer's was supposed to be part of the game as well so the sheep are just as valuable as the rest and I can see it. IF that's the case, then OG Catan would score at least an 8, if not 9 because I always wind up with enough sheep at the end of every game I'm praying for a 7 just to bring my hand down in size.

I'm being hyper-critical. If you've never played Catan, throw a rock into a crowd of people you know, odds are someone has a copy nowadays. It's a good time and will break your mind out of the Matrix of what a "board game" is compared to the junk that is out there... looking at you Clue, Monopoly, Sorry, Life, Scrabble and Connect 4.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
[UPDATE 3.2022]

Context is everything.

Catan was first published in 1995.
I was introduced in 1999-2000 and had been out of gaming for a while.  

Up until this point my Top 5 games consisted of Samurai Swords, Axis and Allies, Risk, Monopoly, Various card games (and Backgammon as an honorable mention).

Catan was new and offered probability mitigation, resource management, hand management, trading, and racing to 10 Victory Points!!

For its time:
Analytical.
Social.
Highly Competitive (so many loud loud arguments/negotiations/politicking).

Catan was Dorothy Gale stepping out of her drab Kansas Farmhouse into Oz.

***

This is the game that got helped me rediscover my love for boardgames.  Up until I played Catan (circa 2005) the games I mainly played were Risk!, Samurai Swords (Ikusa), and Strat-o-matic Bball.  Catan served its purpose well of a gateway game.  I played this game (usually 1-3 in one sitting) and its variants once a week with a gaming group (usually 4-6 players) for about 2 years.  Catan led me to playing other games from other publishers and is no longer played much at all.  Nonetheless, Catan is in my hall of fame.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Once you've played this enough, it gets a little boring in my opinion, partially because you have a solid strategy and can win most of the time against less experienced, so you're just going through the motions. Against equally skill opponents, it depends who was targeted more by the robber and who got better rolls.

The dice roles can also affect a bit, and between 2 equal players, the dice will determine the game. Its a decent starting/gateway game I suppose but some level of gaming maturity is needed. Negotiation and trading makes it low/no downtime which I really love, but even so, there's just not enough control/variety for me to rate this higher. TBH, I haven't found a game that does the negotiation/trading so well in tandem while maintaining gameplay, but it must exist somewhere, so I really hope to find something better/more fulfilling than this game (if you know such a game, please tell me!). I also kind of think that the original game should just be 3-6P default and not have to need an expansion. And yes, I do like this at 5/6P counts since its more trading and more dynamic, even if the game stalls a bit more.

Plays: Many, 10+
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Rating based off of first game that I played and taught my 8 year-old twin daughters. They learned it pretty easily, though the game took a while because of one of the girls not keeping her hand in order, especially later when we all started getting more cards. I won with 11 points after I played a Knight to take the Biggest Army card from one of my girls (who ended up with 7 points down from 9 and could have won the next turn otherwise) and my other daughter finished with 9 points. So it was a really close game and we were all in it to the end. Trading went well and they picked up on that quickly and were good sports about it. 

My one complaint so early in my experience with the game is the components, and that was reflecting in my rating. They aren't the greatest. The perimeter puzzle pieces are kind of flimsy and bend easily with humidity. Considering the game came out so long ago, perhaps they just didn't make component's as thick back then? 

My rating will likely go up with more plays. I like the simplicity of it and I love that my kids really like it, so that means it will get more play and that's always part of ratings for me.

textfield_comment_value:
This will always hold a special place. It's a timeless classic that has its share of flaws, but it really has helped bring a lot of people into modern board gaming. It's fun to play once in a blue moon, especially as a gateway for non-gamers and new gamers. It's tense with hoping for certain resource numbers to appear, racing to take space before your opponents, and pushing your luck with hand size limits and the robber. It's interactive through negotiating trade with your opponents and through the building race.

To help mitigate the overly swingy luck factor that I find to be the biggest flaw, I like to use a stack of cards with perfect probability distribution instead of dice, and also a board setup calculated for fairness by the Better Settlers website. (Side note:  I had a friend who was opposed to this deliberate balancing saying it was out of the spirit of the game, but then the game we played ended up with final scores of 9-9-9-10. I have never seen a 4 player game so close! Everyone was one turn away from victory.) The kingmaking aspect can get a little mean, so hopefully players don't take it personally.

textfield_comment_value:
+1.5 strategy outweighs rule-book (Beginners seem to take to this game wonderfully)

+1 good balance of "just doing my thing over here" and "take that!" mechanics which appeal to a broad range of players

-1 (up from .5 - more I play, the more playtime seems to lag) not the lightest game, with a little setup and a few minutes teaching time and an hour or  so to play

Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
*It's a modern classic for reason: It is easy to get people into, and it introduces them to a whole new world of Euro games.

*Trading resources is a great mechanic that people love.

*Catan can be a bit mean. The dice rolls can be frustrating, and the robber is often oppressive. I think people forget that part of the game is mitigating these chance elements or employing diplomacy and careful planning to avoid getting punished too badly. This is a trading game much more than it is an economic game.

*I have certainly had games that *seem* unwinnable, but in most cases, I have been able to mount a comeback and make a run. A lot of the tension in the game comes from having to adjust your plans based on the shifting game state, so these down-and-out situations are part of what makes it interesting.

*In many ways, I think sorting the BGG Board Game Rank by Number of Voters (and maybe excluding games with a rating of less than 7.0) is a better indicator of what games are all-time greats or the games that everyone needs to play. This puts Catan at #3, which I think is maybe a more appropriate place for this classic.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
The game that got me into modern board gaming. I've easily played Catan 200+ times--mostly over the span of 2 years when Settlers and Carcassonne were somehow enough to satiate my desire for tabletop gaming. These days, I just never really want to play it. Maybe to try out an expansion or two, but not much beyond that.

There are still things I appreciate about Settlers--the modular board setup, negotiation, intuitive set of resources to manage in order to race to 10 victory points, spatial elements that involve indirect conflict in settlement planning, and so on.

Certain things that have gotten old include unpleasantly high degree of luck in resource rolls; Constructing buildings doesn't really *do* anything other than help get you more resource cards (want more gameplay function!); And the game can really break down if people aren't willing to make good, interesting trades (see: luck). It's really a pretty simple game when it gets down to it. And there is a significant runaway leader problem, or at least a runaway loser problem. Resources, dice, Settlers.

(Own base + 5-6p + Traders & Barbarians)

textfield_comment_value:
This game deserves the accolades it gets; it probably opened the North American doors to German/Eurogames and I'm very thankful for that. I like a lot about the game - it's essentially a multiplayer solitaire (which I tend to like), has an interesting theme, and most people I've played it with really enjoy it. It's also quick to learn - the basegame seems to play best with 3.

The trading portion of a player's turn, however, is poorly designed; it greatly increases gametime and creates some confusion for the very small price of increasing interaction. This tone, indeed, has created some spillover problems for games of Settlers I've played - I've played with players who have used their knowledge of what other players want to affect drawing cards from other players during the Robber phase.

Also, be wary if you plan on buying this: there's about 20 different expansions for it (5-6 player expansion, Seafarers of Catan, Seafarers of Catan 5-6 player expansion, which is different, Knights of Catan, Knights of Catan 5-6 players ... )  so you could really be dropping a lot of money before you're done.

textfield_comment_value:
Catan earned its reputation. It was the (literal) game changer by popularizing euro-style games here in the U.S. and inspiring countless designers. While I welcome a game of Catan, other games have crowded it out of the higher tiers, so it is no longer my first box to pull from the shelf, even when we have the players for it.

The gameplay remains simple and engaging: roll two dice, give resources to people with towns and cities at vertices adjacent to hex tiles with the rolled number of the island map (or move the robber on the roll of a 7). Trade for resources, spend resources, and get more Victory Points than your opponents. That's it. The trading mechanism allows for engagement on other players' turns, and it usually does fairly well at keeping people from being sidelined during play.

Setup and re-boxing are moderate for a game of this complexity (or, as it now stands, relative simplicity), and that is one of the other reasons I have started to seek it out less. Nonetheless, if you are looking for an engaging competitive game for 3-4 players and want something pretty simple, this is it.

The one major gripe is that an initially poor position could end the game right there and then for you. Being fourth to speak on an unfavourable layout means you'll be playing catch-up all the time.

textfield_comment_value:
I always find this game exciting.  Catan, more than almost any other game I play, makes me feel like I'm building a little civilization. I feel such pride when I build a road, or when I put up a new settlement.  It's also quite exhilarating to roll the exact number needed to get the resource that you need just as it's devestating to roll a seven when you've got a hand full of cards.  With as many times as I've played this game (I got it before I started keep close numbers on my play stats), I still enjoy it a lot.

The only thing that I find frustrating is the dice rolling.  If Catan had no dice, and instead had some other way of allocating resources, it would possible be in my top ten.  Instead, it's a game that I play sometimes because it's a classic and because it's a game that I discovered fairly early on in my development from game enjoyer to game enthusiast.  

***Update***

I haven't played Catan in months because I'm just not that interested in it now that I've passed the gateway stage.  The dice just bother me so much that I never take it out and play it.  Rating lowered to a six.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
I have been on a bit of a rollercoaster ride with Settlers.  Like many others, this was the first Euro-style board game that I played, and it opened my eyes to a whole new way to game and a whole new type of game to play.  For that alone, it holds a special place in my heart.  I played this game almost exclusively for a year or more, and then became burned out on it.  There was a point when I didn't want to play it anymore.  But now that I play it with much more moderation, my opinion of it has increased again.  It has some great strategic decisions when it comes to placing your initial pieces, and the player interaction and replayability are fantastic.

You are certainly at the mercy of the dice in this game, and it is also possible that a player who is not winning can suffer when the other players jump on the leader, merely by sharing a space or two with the leader.  The game is not perfect, and sometimes a particular session just falls flat.  But the fact is that this is a great gateway game with a lot of strategy and a good dose of fun.  In reasonable amounts, it is quite enjoyable.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
The original is still very good at what it does. This is the board game that you introduce to someone who thinks Monopoly and Clue are the sum total of what board games represent. Sit this one down in front of them, get them to try it out a few times, and then slowly introduce them to actual GAMES! 
I mean, there's a renaissance out there people!

There are games on the market that create experiences you could only have if you had an actual working TARDIS: WWII battles, pursuing Jack the Ripper down a twisted branching alleyway, or defending King Arthur from a betraying errant knight.
I marvel at the current artistry of the Golden Age of game design. We truly live in interesting times.

You know what? Don't play this game with people who've only ever played YHATZEE and BUNKO. Screw 'em!  If they've limited their experience of game mechanics to the intricacies of Chutes and Ladders, then this game is too good for 'em! They're in the Dark ages (which is a great expansion for Dominion, by the way).
Let those people go. You can't save them. They're weighing you down. Cut the rope. 
Move on.

This is simply a classic.  No other game changed board gaming more than Catan.  Without this game most of us would never have gotten into modern board gaming.

This is also the most deceptively cut throat euro out there.  For a game with "no conflict", I have seen more arguments and hurt feelings during this game than any other I've played.  And it's awesome.  I may not be able to attack you directly, but when I cut you off with my roads and then refuse to trade you that wheat you need after I played the "Monopoly" card and took all of yours...classic.

This game gets a lot of hate, but there is a reason so many people have played it.  The most common criticism is that initial placement is the most important aspect and then it's all luck and dice rolls.  I disagree.  This is a negotiation game.  All other game mechanics revolve around the trade mechanic.  Victory or defeat is all based on how well you can trade and convince other players to give you the resources you need to win.  If you play thinking that you can ignore this and win through mechanics alone, you are playing wrong.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
It is only fitting that my very first post to this board be towards the first game that opened my eyes to a different level of board games -- and BoardGameGeek.

I would actually have given The Settlers of Catan a "10", if it were not for the expansions -- which are even better than the base game, in my opinion.

In any case, this was my first experience with a game of this type.  I grew up in a world of Monopoly, Life, Sorry!, Yahtzee, etc. -- all okay games in themselves, especially when playing with friends and family.  This, however, was the first non video game that really involved some strategy and thought -- and officially blew all of those previous family games out of the water.  It was an instant hit for this family of three!

We rarely play it these days due to our enjoyment of the expansions, but I would still look forward to playing it, if I did not have the expansions at my fingertips.

Overall, a wonderful game that involves thought and strategy, but is not overly deep to frighten gamers new to this realm.  I can definitely see why this is used as a "gateway game".
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
The trading and resource gathering is interesting -- and it was a trailblazer -- but for many people, there are more interesting games out there.

Look, Catan got me into gaming. I can't deny that I've loved and played it a lot. But Catan (especially with no expansions) just isn't interesting anymore. I have played it upwards of thirty times online against AIs, and as such I'm pretty much played out on the game. Diversify your hexes, go for largest army or longest road (whichever has less competition), and trade only as much as necessary. Spread out and diversify your resources early, then bulk up on cities mid-game. I don't know, strategies vary, but I just feel like I'm always playing Catan on rails. It feels solved. 

So yes, Catan is a great gateway game. It's exciting for new players who've never played a German-style game before. But I don't need to buy the game, or its expansions -- there's no need to. I've got plenty of other games that scratch that itch, and while I'm happy to recommend it, there's no need for me to personally own it.

textfield_comment_value:
A lot to like here, but a few nits as well: too much hinges on too few die rolls (not enough to smooth out distribution), usual runaway loser, occasional runaway leader. The robber can be a feelsbad, but worse, it can slow the early game way down. I think the pauper variant (or whatever it's called) is great: if you get no resources on a roll you get one marker; you can trade X markers for a resource of your choice (where X = your current VP).

Baffled as to why they keep meddling with the English art, as the German/original is still the best, hasn't changed, and they don't monkey with the rest of the Kosmos line. Weird.

Setup and takedown is rough if expansions are involved. I'm less and less certain they should be, though sometimes the base game feels a little too vanilla.

Overall, it keeps everyone involved, it has some direct (but mostly positive) interaction (if you have resources), and it's generally a good experience. It didn't hit my family/group as hard as some groups, where it was apparently revolutionary, but I still respect it, and it's still a great gateway game.

The in-laws said they really like the game and with a 1 hour playing time, I suspect that it could make the rounds more when we get together.

As geek user Glamorous Mucus says, "I actively avoid this game. textfield_comment_value:
Dull.  I have played too many games where one person ends up with a hand full of nothing or resources nobody wants and then proceeds to sit there miserably for the majority of the game.  Often, I have been that person.  Even though I know how to play the odds, it sometimes happens that an 8 never rolls in a game while an 11 will roll 5 times in a row.  You can't control that and half the time you can't even mitigate it.

I don't really think Settlers is necessarily a bad game, but the dice mechanic makes it so.  I have always contended that trying a new mechanic, such as card drafting or something else would make the game quite fun.  Hell, I rather enjoy Settlers of America: Trails to Rails in spite of the dice rolling because the gold coin mechanic and the sheer number of ways you can DO things with your resources really helps to avoid the rut that Settlers can induce.

EDIT: my opinion of Settlers has improved. I now consistently do well and can appreciate the game despite the age of the design. I've still played it too much to enjoy it more than a 7, though.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
I enjoy Catan because it is a good all-round game for beginners and advanced players, however I wouldn't play it any time or with any crowd because sometimes the difference in skill can make the game less enjoyable for me, as I'm not super competitive.

My favorite part of the game is building and negotiating, and some games result in a lot of players-helping-each-other making deals, but other times I just sit around doing nothing and before realizing, another player is far ahead and I have no chance of winning, as well as not much else to do during the game.

It is an inspiration in many ways, both for things done right (balance of the map, resources, dice mechanic with the cool math trick for the distribution of resources, etc.), accessibility for beginners, critical success, but also things that I would do differently (finding ways to allow inactive/underdog players to still participate in the game, finding more ways of interaction and trade). Possibly those things might be addressed in the expansions, but it is a huge space to explore and a bit intimidating.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
This is one of my favorites to bring out when there are 3 or 4 players at my house.  An excellent game that involves a touch of strategy, a forward-thinking perspective, and a lot of player interaction.

I only use the Event Cards for this - I think it speeds the game up by quite a bit, as there is the possibility with a few of the cards to reward EVERYONE playing with a resource card - which is usually a good thing.

This is one of the few games out there that can be played "AS IS".  What I mean by that is that there is no need for any house rules or other variants.  It is a very well balanced and finely designed game that does not need tweaking or modifications to make it play "better".  Not saying that is bad, but if you don't like to have to keep track of a bunch of house rules (Monopoly, Descent, etc.), then this game is perfect for you.

This game is also single-handedly responsible for the worst one-line cliche in all of gamedom - "I have wood for your sheep."  Although it is still funny to say, even if you aren't a Beavis and Butthead type fan.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
With a "difficult" starting position and a few unlucky rolls of the dice you may practically be out of the game after a few minutes, and the rest of the game is an exercise in enduring an hour of pointless boredom to wait for someone else to win the game. Avoid.

Yeah, yeah, yeah - the bad luck evens out over several games, but why play this poorly designed game several times when there are hundreds of much better games, today.

Luck in games is perfectly fine to change your odds or to determine your available options etc. - but not to determine if you are in or out of the game from the beginning or after a few rounds.

Buy it and put it on your personal "boardgame museum" shelf, next to Monopoly, of classic, but bad and never to be played again, boardgames, if you must, but there are many, much better games to buy and play.

Would only ever play this game again to try the "Welfare variant" (http://www.boardgamegeek.com/thread/150443), or the "Event cards variant" (http://www.boardgamegeek.com/boardgame/20038) which may solve/reduce the luck problems.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Copycat purchase.  played many times prior to joining BGG.  of course, this was the game that got us into boardgaming, just like so many others.  PROS:  variable board set up, initial placement of settlements is the highlight for me, collection of resources for road/settlement/city building/development cards, relatively short playing time.  CONS:  dice(when rolled unfavorably, there is NOTHING you can do to gather more resources), in our group the negotiation/trading does NOT work, therefore we tend to have more downtime than other groups.  OVERALL:  after our honeymoon period, the dice were the killer of our love for catan.  the excitement of the initial placement of settlements could not overcome the droughts of bad rolls or the constant 7's that plague us.  i will always remember catan fondly for introducing us to the boardgame hobby, i may play with a newbie at their insistence but i will probably never ask to play it again.  
4/18/17:  gave it to another family that will give it some love.  thank you catan for lighting the boardgaming bug in us.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
It's common for gamers to sour on Settlers but its ability to get new people into the hobby can't be underrated. I think the reason it's proven so enduringly popular is its familiarity to non-gamers. Like Monopoly, you roll two dice at the start of your turn and do what they say. Like Monopoly you try to build houses to enable you to gather more resources. Like Monopoly you haggle and trade with other players to try and make up sets. And compared to Monopoly, the commonly-made gamer complaint that you can be hosed by unlucky placement and dice rolls pales into insigificance - at least you can't be eliminated! 

When I first played Settlers, I was blown away by how many clever things it does compared to the 'classic' games I knew: properly makes use of probability; continuously moves towards a conclusion; keeps everyone involved when it's not their turn. Sure I can see some of its weaknesses now, and it's a game that I don't really play with gamers. But I'll happily pull it out any time with my family - my non-gamer sister and her husband adore it.

textfield_comment_value:
Juego entretenido y correcto. Muy adecuado para jugar con niños y con “no-jugones”. Duración del juego apropiada (1 hora 30 min). Si esto es lo que buscas, este juego cumple de sobra tus expectativas. Más complejo que los típicos juegos infantiles (Parchís, Conecta 4, La Oca, etc.), pero todavía en el campo de los juegos sencillos.

El problema que le veo al Catan es que se puede quedar corto para jugadores experimentados. Las partidas son bastante similares con la caja básica. Hay poca variedad entre unas y otras.

Por otra parte, resulta cansino tener que convencer a algunos jugadores para que comercien. A lo largo de los años he detectado que algunos jugadores no experimentados son bastante propensos a tomar posturas aislacionistas que entorpecen la dinámica del juego por miedo a perder.

Eso sí, tiene una ventaja: se puede jugar con familia/amigos extranjeros (o gente que no hable el idioma en el que están las reglas). Solo un puñado de cartas tienen texto.

No he jugado expansiones y no puedo valorar si mejora con ellas.

Le doy un 6,5 al juego.

textfield_comment_value: Una gran alternativa para reemplazar al TEG todo viejo y hecho mierda que heredaste de tu bisabuelo. Rated after 23 confirmed games with different opponents. In first games there was lots of interaction between players, but later the interaction level drops down when players don't try to propose every possible trade. In the end, when players have more or less experience, the interaction between players is quite scarce. A good game in good company, but the benefit of experience means this is not a game I would like to introduce to new players.

Randomness in the setup means that this game is very playable for long time. Unfortunately my latest games have used the beginners' setup.

Updated after 24th and 25th plays, introducing the game to new beginners despite the comment above. After all, this is a classic game everyone should know. Let's say, I won't introduce this one to non-players very easily. :) Updated the rating from 7 to 8. Now three plays of Catan on three consecutive Tuesdays, but still without expansions...

Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
I didn't play Catan at the height of its popularity. I played much later and it did not do its reputation justice. I found this game very dry and not terribly exciting. The key mechanism is on getting resources through die rolls and if your numbers just so happen to never come up - you're out of luck. It could be argued that you're supposed to plan around this by spreading your towns to the most likely places, or trying to cover a wide spread, etc, but in the early game you have no real say in this.

The trading is okay, but since this is a 'gateway' game, most new players take the 'Monopoly Method' to trading: they just won't. This can be mitigated somewhat with the sea trading spaces, but then once again you're beholden to the mercy of the dice to get the resources you need for those spaces.

Overall, this game just has not stood the test of time. The over-reliance on dice rolls is a complete turn off for the SO and I since there's little you can do to mitigate them. The other aspects of the game did not make up for this failure either.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value: There is so much in this game that impresses. The theme and feeling of the game is comfortable. The uniqueness of each game thanks to the random game board keeps the game new. The changing boards and the changing order of setup gives players an opportunity to pursue very different strategies each game. The play time feels about right, at least for three players. There is a balanced amount of interaction between players through board interference, trading, certain development cards, and of course moving the robber. I might say the robber sometimes adds a little too much take-that between players. The overseas trading option provides a reasonable solution to balancing the roll of the dice for resources, though even with that, sometimes the randomness is significant. One negative in the game is that a player can make bad choices in setup or early on to the point that there is no coming back. Because scores are clear all the time, a player that falls behind can become frustrated with the rest of the game. The rules are easy to learn and teach.

Ho giocato al gioco base senza espansioni. Un classico che non avevo mai provato. La produzione delle risorse dipende da dove piazzi la tua colonia iniziale, quindi c’è della strategia ma la fortuna incide molto col lancio dei dadi e la potenziale sottrazione di carte da parte degli altri giocatori. Sono rimasto senza carte, non potevo costruire nulla e i dadi mi erano sfavorevoli. Non divertente come prima esperienza.

The production of resources depends on where you place your initial colony, so there is some strategy but luck affects a lot with the roll of the dice and the potential subtraction of cards by the other players. Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Quite simply, the best game I have ever played.

This was my first Eurogame and I am truthfully not sure if I would have become as hooked as I am now playing any other game.  I believe that this remains the best game to introduce nongamers to when trying to convert them to Eurogames.  Further, if the nongamer has a dice game background, such as Monopoly, it makes my argument stronger as they will be comfortable with the dice roll.  The rules are quite simple and after a ten minute quick explanation and quick couple of rounds, most newbies will have things down pat.

Settlers has some randomness to the game as resource production is determined through the roll of dice, but more often then not I find that the person who manages their resources best wins the game.  Trading plays a very important roll in this as people who are able to complete more trades improve their position more often then not.  This game is a lot of fun and very addicting!  A must have for every gamer and a great way to send you down the path of gaming for nongamers.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value: Light resource/civilisation game let down by a few too many flaws. Players place settlements adjoining different types of resource, which contain numbers. If the number is rolled, the players gain resources, which in turn allows them to develop their civilisation (upgrade settlements to cities, build roads, acquire development cards etc), which will often gain them victory points, the first to 10 winning the game. The game is simple and seems to strike a chord with players new to gaming but beyond that there are too many flaws that will keep seasoned players away. The main problem arises from there being far too much luck involved with the rolling of dice for resource production, an element you have absolutely no control over and which drives the game. It can become quite galling to place a settlement next to a hex containing a number with a high probability of being rolled only for it never to appear (or only when the robber has been placed on it). For me, this game can become far too frustrating on too many occasions to be enjoyable.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:

+ Good and simple game to play

+ Decent mechanics ( Ex. Robbers to keep hoarders/monopoly of a single resource in check)
+ Good for competitive people

Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
It's popular at the moment to put down Catan, but I honestly don't find that deserved! Have their been many better games published since 1995? Absolutely. But I think this one still holds up and deserves its popularity.

The most unique and interesting part of the game is the trading aspect, which allows a great degree of player interaction. It's simple but effective and increases the enjoyment of the players during the game, especially when it's just played casually with a few friends. I do understand the critique of just not being on good production spots or not getting good rolls... or at least I used to moreso. If you watch people playing it online, it gives you a deeper appreciation for how to choose your starting spots and when and with who to trade with and the amount of considerations that go into those decisions. 

It's certainly not my favourite game by any means, but I think this is a fun game (whether you play it casually or more competitively) and serves as a good starting point into the hobby - I should know, it was mine!

Additionally, I think it plays better with 4 than with 3, because there are more people involved, more numbers being rolled, and more trading going on.  In short, it has more possibilities.  It's still a fun concept, and still a great game!
