textfield_comment_value:
The Settlers of Catan (as it should still be called) is an absolute classic. But whilst everyone knows its a historically important game, and was also the gateway into Euros for so many players (including me), I think what is under-discussed is that it's also just a really good game.

It's not a surprise that it was this game that vaulted Euro/German family games to a new prominence in the Anglosphere: gameplay is a wonderful mix of trading, resource management, and tension-filled races on the hexagonal map. Every rule makes logical sense in the narrative of the game as presented, making things easy to learn, and whilst there are some nuances to learn in the composition of the development card deck, the game as a whole is accessible right from your first play.

It's inevitable when a game is this popular and sells so many copies that lots of expansions to the game follow. Personally I can take or leave Seafarers and would rather avoid all of the others. The base game is the best way to play, and is an enduring classic for a reason.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value: I am surprised Catan has not been awarded a Nobel Prize yet. Not for being a good game, but for finally proving that statistics and probabilities are fake, and in fact, just wanting a number, will influence the dice against it. If you don't go with the standard board setup, and allow some tile/number randomness, then this game is often won or lost at the initial town placement. Simply blocking a resources for the entire game, allows you to become the oil-baron you always wanted to be, by starving everyone of a single resource. For this reason, I suggest only playing with first time players, who does not understand the initial town placement. They will enjoy the game enough to not have a bad experience, and you will enjoy getting more cards per round, than an angry soccer player. Finally I don't feel the scoring quite reflect how reality works. Building towns near the ocean should be worth more points in the future. Realisticly speaking, is a town in a desert worth th same as a town near the ocean - just saying, property value.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
A classic game that got me into board games. There are issues with it though.

Pros:
- Simple rules most people can pick up easily.
- There is a very satisfying feeling of building up and scaling due to the need to build up your infrastructure to acquire more resources.

Cons: 
- The game is highly influenced by your starting setup, which feels highly punishing for a game that's considered to be a 'gateway' game.
- The game can take a long time. This is a particularly big con for a game like Catan, where the early game influences so much of your success later on. If you didn't choose great starting locations, the game might feel like a drag as you get further and further behind. 
- Early game is highly RNG, because it's mostly dependant on dice rolls. 

Considerations:
- The trading aspect of this game blurs the line between casual and competitive. This is usually not a good thing for people looking for something serious to play, but for casual gamers looking to get into the hobby, it can lead to some fun social bargaining.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
This is a controversial one for obvious reasons. For me the game just doesn't click. I like games that lets you do things on your turn. Even losing at such games feels like an accomplishment because, hey, maybe I wasn't able to accomplish as much as the winner, but I was still able to build these and these things. Such games leave me with a sense of accomplishment, a sense of having done something. 


On the other hand Catan leaves me frustrated irrespective of whether I am winning or losing. It is so restricting. It's not fun when you don't get to do stuff on your turn. I need resources to build, but the only way I can get resources if the dice tells me I get resources. There is nothing I can do. "anyone wanna give me brick? No? Okay. So I guess just sit this turn out." No, I wanna build things.I don't want to be dependent on the dice to be able to build. If that wasn't bad enough, the robber just makes things absolutely horrendous. 

Anyway, I don't mean to go on a rant. Just that, I don't wanna play this game ever again.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Catan was truly my gateway game at the early years of the XXI century (i never get to knew Carcassone at the time and, anyway, it won´t qualify) so, it sets another standard point at my rating list.
Englobing just a few more mechanics and set up work than a vintage, Catan has already most of the features of a modern eurogame, though at small level. 
Easy to grasp, with fast playing turns in a suitable short overall playing time and keeping pure chance at low level, it was perhaps the first non abstract game that could provide the feeling of really taking your destiny into your hands while building something.
Nice to go along with family, friends or even maybe light gamers (who knows), Catan still remains a quality product and enjoyable, if one is by now not tired of playing it again and again.

Edit: In spite of all what is written above, after almost 4 years of new games experiments, it is quiet unfair to other modern games to rate Catan so high (7.5), so i am forced to drop it a bit, in order to keep things balanced.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Catan, another classic board game out of the great starters. It has since got a card game version (which i also have) and even a Roll-and-Write dice game (which you can also play alone!). To win the game, you just BUILD, but finding resources can be taking time and it is not easy for those who pretend to easily place settlements in where they want to.

What i find annoying in this game is that most of the turns can be done without spending anything (road, settlements, often even buying a card), resulting the fact if you wrongly position your settlements, you'll end up being unable to surpass any other player. I've played a two player game with dad using a 2-player variant i found on the internet (i don't remember the name), and for the most of the time i had only built a settlement through almost the end of the game while my dad already built all the cities he needed to win the game, but this game has done well punishing you for placing into terrains that can't produce often. Might probably want to be careful next time.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
A good solid game. I'm probably the 15th million person to say it... but it definitely is a very good "gateway" style game. There is the good old VP chase common to hundreds of other Euro games but there's also multiple paths to victory, trading, frustration and elation in the dice rolls, road/city building and a variable modular board which makes for a slightly different game each time. All in all a very good game... not quite great because it's still a bit too easy to be hosed by the dice no matter how hard you try to trade and negotiate your way out of the hole you are in when that damn robber is sitting on your production hex.

Above everything else this game produces fun sessions with a lot of chatter and banter. Lot's of "Why are you picking on me?" and "Move the robber there to stop him from getting the sheep he needs" type of conversations. Just for the level of interaction the game provides its worthy of its status as a good solid family game that can be played for fun without much concern who wins or loses.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
This is hailed as the new Monopoly, not because of its gameplay, but because of its incredible mass adoption by big retail chain stores.  It is the poster child for bringing a new generation into the world of board games.  It in large part represents a renaissance of the market, and for that reason this game has transcended the significance of its own gameplay.  

If you play the game with all of that cultural importance aside, I think that is best.  You play the role of a settler, building settlements, cities, and roads across the landscape. The twist and main meat of the game is that you can strike deals with other players to get vital resources for your colonies to expand.  Since I have played the heck out of this game, I'm not too keen on playing it anymore.  I think the game is excellent, but at this point I think it has largely been outclassed by newer and more interesting games.  There's too much out there to choose from for this to be THE game you play first as an introduction to the world of board games.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value: Interesting game which I played for the first time recently as many non-casual gamers fear it like the vampire fears the cross, I am not sure why. The game and the fun you have while playing it depends on who you are playing it with, some people enjoy the fierce competition and trying to blockade each other, refuse trading etc., others may find it too vicious. The random element is a nice idea, also experienced players have a big advantage. Another flaw in my opinion is the accumulative nature of successes, the more resources you have, the more you can build and the more you build the more resources you have, which can be a pain in the ass should the starting conditions be unbalanced because that will be hard to flatten out later in the game. Still, a neat little game which could have done with some better artwork and theme instead of the plaster-on. I reckon that the expansions add a lot to it but I am not sure whether Ill ever be able to give those a go, considering the general reluctance of geeks to play it.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Easy enough to learn.  It's not necessary for each player to study the rules before playing as its simple enough to explain along the way. Rules can be summarized pretty quickly. 
Luck-dependent but not completely. There definitely are strategic decisions to be made in where you place your pieces but ultimately what results from them is luck dependent.
Strong theming. Trading mechanics, artwork, and piece construction brings the game together cohesively.
Lots of player interaction. Good social game to hang out and talk to people. There may be longer periods of time where it is not your turn, but during that time you're still actively playing.
Game length can vary quite a bit, sometimes you're scrapping down to the last card and sometimes one person gets quite a bit ahead and wins early. In 4 player games I've had some just over 30 minutes but none have gone over 2 hours. 
Overall its an simple but enjoyable social and luck based game for a group of friends, new or old, as long as you've got the time for it.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
The game that started me down the Euro path... I like it a little less each time I play it, though. I've pretty much decided that, with a few exceptions (Twilight Struggle, Backgammon), if there's dice in the box, I'm not all that interested.

The trouble with this one is that there really is no way to mitigate the dice results. In just about any game, there will be one person (usually me, if I'm playing) who grabs up a nice couple of towns next to (say) 5's and 6's only to see 8's and 9's come up every turn. Then when the dice do finally decide to smile on the right lands, look who's here! The Robber. There's no alternate strategy, no way to work around it: I'm just screwed. After a few turns with nothing to build and nothing to trade, I start looking forward to playing a different game. 

There's a lot to love about Settlers, and I do enjoy it still. It can be exciting, and the dice cards do help to even things out some. But I'll usually reach for something else when I'm looking for a good gateway game.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value: [Dice rolling, Resource Management, Building, Trading] [3P:3, 4P:3] A question: how is this better than Monopoly? The random resources are the worst aspect of the game. It's got the same basic problem as any game that uses a random mechanism to bestow resources - if luck is against you, you don't get anything. Zilch. Zip. There's no workaround. There are no alternative paths to victory. You NEED your numbers to be rolled. Yes, it will statistically even out, over several *games*, not the same game. Since Settlers takes up to two hours (or even more, aka "The Settlers Game from Hell" which I've been stuck in), that just doesn't cut it. In addition, the theme is remarkably uninspiring. Why are the resources random? We don't know. Somehow the sheep in this game don't grow wool on a regular basis. The trading is boring, consisting of people asking for the same things over and over - if brick is never rolled, *no one has it*. Gah. I don't see how this hooked so many people. This is "The New Monopoly". Avoid.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
1st Euro - or at least Gateway Game to bringing Euro's to US en masse.

Although I am painfully bored of this game having played updwards of 500 games, I can find no room in my heart to give this classic any less than a perfect 10.  I think, for me at least, this was the game that helped bring games from overseas to America and continues to help bring about the mainstream board game revolution that we all hope and pray continues to grow. 

Update: Victorious!  That's right, my countless hours of Catan-ing finally paid dividends...literally.  I took down the Settlers of Catan Mega-Tourney at the Strategicon last week and got 100 bucks to spend on more games.  Yay sheep!!

Update 2: Victorious again! Won the US Settlers Championship at GenCon and got an all expenses paid trip from Mayfair to Germany to represent the good ol' US of A.  I was the highest English speaking finisher coming in at 8th in the world out of 56 competitors from 28 countries.   Awesome experience.  Wouldn't trade it for anything.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
I understand the significance this has had for our hobby, but for me, the runaway leader problem kills this one. Someone can get boxed in with no decent expansion possibilities and have no hope of winning literally over an hour before the game ends. I understand this only happens when someone makes mistakes during the early turns, but if we're using this as an introductory game, it is very possible that someone's first experience with European-style board gaming involves putting down some starting settlements and then getting surrounded and feeling powerless for the rest of the game. That is board gaming at its worst; is that really what we want our first impression to be?

Historical rating: 10
Gameplay rating: 6

EDIT: After reading several interviews with designer Klaus Teuber, I can say that his presence in the games industry is an absolutely wonderful thing, and I admire his attitude and actions. I wish I liked his game more, but I have no trouble liking the man himself.

Klaus Teuber rating: 10/10
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Sorry, hard-core gamers.  I continue to like this game a lot & I am not tired of it.  If I could find more interested players I would purchase all the variants.  

The luck of the dice certainly dominates the game.  I recently went 12 rounds without getting any resources or if I did, my opponents stole my lonely resource before I could use it.  So I had nothing to trade, nothing to use.  After that experience, I lowered the rating on the game.  I prefer games with less dependency on the dice rolls.

Having the longest road helps VP's but I have noticed I win more often if I concentrate on upgrading settlements to cities as quickly as possible, especially surrounding one product numbered a 6 or 8, and connecting to a port that gives an exchange advantage.  I buy cards when I fail to have enough to upgrade settlements (otherwise my products always get stolen)--potentially 9 products & 3 turns might get you the largest army whereas it takes a minimum of 10 products & 5 turns to maybe get the longest road.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
The selling point of Settlers of Catan is the combination of strategy, engine-building, luck and trading. Also, much is emerging from the variable board configuration. The rules are easy to teach and playing the game works on an intuitive level. It's versatile in terms of adjusting risk and goals. The flow of the game can produce a relaxed, layed back atmosphere, but also serious and tense situations. 

It's one of those low commitment and high impact games with a lot of freedom in how you play. Most common points of criticism seem to be randomness, dependancy on starting locations and runaways  as a consequence, but I find the game to feel rewarding because of them.

All in all, Catan has everything I enjoy about classic Euro-games. It has a nice mixture of strategy, luck, and negotiation, it oscillates between cooperation and competition, it plays quickly and easily, it's flavorful, it's professionally produced, and, as a bonus, expansions can be used to customize in both directions of complexity.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value: This is a great game for all those people out there who think Risk and Monopoly are good games. It will show them the error of their ways and open their eyes to the beauty of the non-department store games. Settlers is colorful, easy to learn, and most importantly; random. The pieces are layed down in random fashion, then the number tiles and ports are randomly applied. Players then choose their starting positions and begin rolling the dice. The game has some minor balance issues, but the only great fault I have found, is that if a player has a run of bad luck early in the game it can leave them hopelessly behind, and trod upon by their fellow gamers. Less mature gamers often want to give up part way through when it is clear they are not going to win. The Seafarers expansion was weak, but the Cities and Knights expansion, while a bit complex, is a nice addition once the original has lost some luster. Not my favorite game, but it will have a place near the top of my game stack for many years to come.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Settlers of Catan is a tough one for me. It very much introduced me to the modern world of board gaming and for that I owe it a debt of gratitude. It's pretty simple to teach and play. The game board setup is a bit awkward at first but once the pieces are in place it's fine.

But...it's a bit of an old beast now and while I detest the "cult of the new" approach to modern board 
gaming, it's undeniable that the game hasn't aged as well as it could have. It can be a bit too luck dependent with the dice rolls and can get annoying when you've picked settlement start points on statistically more likely numbers, only to have them barely come up for the whole game! 

It can also last a bit long sometimes which isn't fun, especially if you are losing. I can be persuaded to play this on occasion but it's likely to find its way off of my board game shelf pretty soon as I am trying to adopt a one-in-one-out rule and Catan just doesn't see the light of day much anymore.

Neil and Kristoffer own this. 

*Sold*
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Unlike many others, I started my tabletop with wargaming and Warhammer, and met Catan far later. I really enjoyed my first few games, and later my brother bought it, and left it with me.

This is where I fell out of love with it, and decided it is not the game for me. After one two many games where I was left with several turns with nothing to do, I just realised that it very quickly can become a not fun game to play.

The reliance of luck is not only related to whether you win or lose the game, but even worse, bad luck can leave you for several turns of NOTHING to do. That for me breaks this game. When for 2 or 3 turns I can't do anything, this is not fun. I like games where a bit of good or bad luck can decide, but let me take risks, let me try to affect the outcome!

Pro:
- Easy to learn
- Nice feeling of 'building a little empire'
- Trading is nice when people let you

Con:
- Luck that decides whether you can even play.
- Each game very 'samey'
- Not very interesting after the first few games
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
What on earth did the designers do to get you all rating this game so highly? Did they come round to each of your houses with a ham, tell you you're beautiful and touch you on the leg?!

This game is a lesson in self flagellation. Rolling dice and waiting for your number to come up so you can actually do something whilst your opponents get resources from rolling double 1 nine times in a row and shoot to victory is boring and not fun - a bad combo for any game.

Yeah so there's some strategy with road/settlement placement and trading, but that is also SO dependant on you having resources from those dice rolls that there's very little to do but watch if you haven't received what you need.

There clearly lies its mainstream popularity; anyone can win this game regardless of experience or skill, as at the end of the day its just down to dice.

Maybe the reason it slammed me so hard is because I expected it to be deeper with more strategic depth- this is really just a dice game disguised as a Euro.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Sometimes in reviews, instead of impressions of the game itself, I describe the sensations that arise in certain situations. At the same time, such reflections allow me to evaluate my perception of games, such as dice. It's hard to say at what point I became afraid of dice, but mechanics with probabilities, such as those with a random set of resources, cause unfairness to the values rolled out.

The dice are unpredictable in that you hope for them and get mad at them, depending on the values dropped out. And when you play again, there is this feeling that makes you not want to finish the game. Once I understood the reason, I had to rethink and get used to the probabilities. 

The game itself I only like the ability to create cities, building chains between roads to get more resources. Even though trading resources creates activity between players, it's up to them to make belief checks look good. Development cards (like dice) can sometimes create unfair probabilities for someone to gain more.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
El primer juego tras los clásicos (monopolio, risk, Stratego) que jugué. Lo compré el año 1997 y por flojera lo aprendí recién el 2004.
Muy entretenido pero puede cansar un poco la etapa de negociación para adquirir materias, cuando se transforma en un diálogo de sordos. No da respiro ni permite distracción, porque de lo contrario otro ha logrado un mejor acuerdo.
Tal vez el factor suerte (los dados) hacen que cuando a uno le va mal, pese a toda lógica, uno se desanime y quiera jugar algo más controlable.
UPDATE: en mi último juego, junto a Seafarers, en dos horas logré hacer dos caminos; es decir, me quedé con los dos puntos iniciales. Mala suerte total; aburrimiento total. Prefiero dedicarme a juegos con factor suerte menos importante o que se pueda revertir con un buen juego. En este caso, es practicamente irrevesible remontar la mala suerte con los dados. Y lo peor, se traduce en un juego interminable...a la media hora ya quieres que termine (y a esas alturas falta una hora y media)
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
The Emperor's new clothes?  Well, I reckon it feels like that.  

To me, this is the gaming equivalent of Morrisey's music.  Many friends are telling you that it's wonderful, but it just grates, feels like the dirge that the old cow died of, and bores the pants off of you.  

There's really only one so called "Classic Euro" on this Forum that I just don't like and this is it.  What on earth is all the fuss about!  I just found it dull and too luck based.  I can understand why some would say it was a good introduction to German Games, but it has been surpassed by many others.  Lost Cities is much easier and more elegant, Ticket to Ride is vastly superior, easier, better made and more fun.  If you want to place things, then there are much better games.  If you want depth you've got games like Wallenstein.  Then there's the quality of the components (mediocre at best).  So what gives?  It's palpably not the worst game in the world, but, for the above reasons,  it's not for me I'm afraid.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
This is a game that too often then not revolves around the dice/luck element and not enough about tactics. Every game I've played of this has involved someone losing badly through no fault of their own (8's being rolled when they needed 6's)

Played again and once again someone had a load of early luck and easily won the game with it's snowball affect. 3's and 11's being rolled more than 8's. Also only about three times was a 4 rolled in the entire game.

Latest play confirms all that I've said above and more, this time I had 10's and they only appeared 3 times in the entire game, the 4's must have been closer to 20 times. Needless to say the player who only gained resources on a 3,4,5 or 11 original and never throughout the game gained off a 6 or 8 won easily 12pts to 4pts to 4pts. His win was of course purely down to the phenomenal dice rolls.

A total luck fest, a game seriously flawed that allows players to sit there doing nothing for 15 minutes at a time through no fault of their own
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
The game that started it all for me.  Found this on Xbox Live and ended up playing it all the time.  My other 60 dollar games collected dust. That game led me to this site, which led to my new boardgame obsession, which led to the Dark Side..and so on and so on.  I hesitate to give a game a 10 but according to the info on ratings: "Outstanding.  Always want to play and expect that will never change."  This is true for me with this game.  Unfortunately most of my gaming is 2 player, and the 2 player variants aren't nearly as enjoyable to me.  Fortunately the Xbox AI on hard is a good challenge, plus there's always live opponents..so when I need my fix I can get it.

Edited three years later from original comments above:  The game is no longer a 10 for me.  When I first got it it was really my only exposure to this type of board game.  Now that I've acquired and played many more games poor old Catan has kind of been left behind.  Still, for sheer nostalgia alone I still give this game an 8.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Probably not much more can be said about this game, but it's historically probably one of the most played games in my collection with a variety of groups. Nowadays I play games mostly with family, and this is one of our standards. I probably would not choose it as often as we play it, but it has stood the test of time and is still an entertaining enough game that I don't mind playing it when other people make the request. 

The variable game board and luck of the dice rolls make each game different enough to avoid to much same-ness from game to game. Good for just about everyone, but probably less enjoyed by those who dislike lucky swings in games as it relies heavily on the aforementioned dice rolls. There is some room for strategy in what spaces you choose at the start and where you decide to build, but really the success of those choices is relegated to the dice. That doesn't bother me as I like a little luck shakedown in my games (probably because pure strategy isn't my strong point!)
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
[b]Positive points[/b]:
• A classic; good introduction to modern Euro board games (if you play with the recommended setup), chock-full of innovative mechanisms for those new to the hobby
• Out-of-turn player interaction allows for more involved gameplay

[b]Negative points[/b]:
• Unmitigatable randomness, in particular resource gathering, can severely hold back player agency, occasionally even completely invalidating your entire turn

[b]To note[/b]:
• The initial board set up is crucial as it can balance or unbalance the game; consider using the [url=https://www.catanstudio.com/events/catan-world-championship/official-map-library/]official tournament maps[/url]; full-on random can only set someone up for a miserable experience
• Player trading is sometimes superfluous depending on group or game stage (mid onward)
• Your starting settlement placement can be crucial, helping or hindering you
• Can be prone to "bash the leader" and there really isn't much the leader can do to mitigate that
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Settlers of Catan

IMNSHO, this is the best multiplayer negotiation game ever to hit the market!  It has an incredible depth to its strategy that gets overlooked by “gamers” because they dislike the amount of luck in the game.  I used to despise the luck factor because I wanted to win if I was the best player at the table.  Now I'm just as interested in who I get to play with.  and the great amount of luck in Settlers makes the outcome of each game unpredictable even when I am playing with non-gamer friends.  At the same time, I am never bored during these games because the optimal strategy is in continual flux.  I am always amazed by how difficult it is to determine the value of each resource as the game proceeds.  Learning how to negotiate with different types of players is another aspect that never gets boring.  I have played this game well over 50 times and I still enjoy it.  This is unusual for me as I normally get tired of games that I can play with non-gamers after 1 - 3 tries.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
For many players this is the introduction game to the hobby, but not for me as I learn to enjoy euros through other games. That is maybe why I don’t have the same nostalgia associated with this game as many other gamers. The game is fairly straightforward to explain, where the phases are distinct and simple. During the game there is usually not much thinking about how to use your resources, but there is definitely an amount of resource management.

What it comes down to in most game in my experience is two things, die rolling and initial set up. If you get your machine going in the beginning of the game you are hard to stop. The robber is simply not enough to stop and by not trading with him you might lose out on that too. That is also my main complaints about the game; there is too much luck and circumstances. 

I like to play this game with either 3 or 4 players. With 4 players the board is a little tighter, so players can be shut-in, but that is generally in the end game anyway.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
My criterion for rating games



http://boardgamegeek.com/geeklist/147053/item/2300390#item2300390


1) Sense of wonder: Game changes each time with different strategies and initial placement of colonies and roads.

2) Meaningful/fun decisions. Lots of resource and card management. Throughout the game there are a lot of lucky dice rolls, but how you deal with the resources you have and trading will determine how well you do.

3) Player interaction:  Lots of player interaction with the dice rolls and trading as well as blocking on the board.

4) Components/artwork: Great components and the board if very cool.

5) Game length/complexity: Good game length. It can drag on at times and dice rolls will not go your way can be frustrating. However you can lower vp total if you want a quicker game. 


Bottom Line: FUN way to spend an evening. You can easily teach it to new players and there is some strategy and tough decisions as well as great fun as you roll dice and keep getting a "12" :)
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value: A decent game for its time, but suffers from a few flaws which will likely keep me away.  First, while it seems that the luck factor is low, luck actually ends up having much too large an impact on the game.  The fact that there really aren't THAT many die rolls means that being on the losing end of too many of them pretty much kills you no matter how good your strategy.  Also, it is far too easy to stifle a player using the robber, and luck plays in to this, too.  If you don't like this type of screw-your neighbor, you will really dislike Settlers, because it can be nasty.  The robber is really the only mechanism to haul in a runaway leader, other than a "stay close" strategy, so it suffers badly for that as well.  Negotiation plays a big role, except that negotiation is often worthless, as everyone can very plainly see what you are after.  Could maybe use a little hidden information.  Just doesn't quite do it for me, but might play on occasion if it is strongly desired by others.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
I still have my childhood copy. The main rulebook is missing, the almanac is water damaged, stuff isn't in bags. I added an old Mage Knight figure to replace the robber, and a d12 "just to see how the game changes".

I played a lot of Catan in my life. I don't regret most of my time with it, as it was one of those games that introduced me to the type of games called "Not Magic, but it'll do".

But I will be happy if I never play Catan ever again. And I'll be even happier to introduce Catan players to newer, sharper games, and get them out of their comfort zone. 

Honestly, Catan just feels dated. Dealmaking is boring and low stakes. Initial map placement is massively consequential. Many turns result in you just doing nothing, because dice still control the speed of the game.

And to cap it all off, my brother and I still use the same Heavy Development Card strategy that we have defaulted to for over 15 years now, and still have not found convincing arguments to do something else.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Közel 20 évvel a megjelenését követően játszottam vele először, a pontszám ezt is tükrözi. Lehet, hogy a kilencvenes évek végén még bejött volna.

Android appja van csak meg, a dobozos táblást nem vállaltam be, mert ahhoz elég gyengécske szegény, hogy még a helyet is foglalja (az appot meg egy bundle akcióban vettem, kb egy gombóc fagyi áráért). Először a táblással játszottam, aztán adva neki egy újabb esélyt, megnéztem az appot is. Kár volt.

Maga a játék nem lenne rossz, ha nincs az a rettenetesen idegesítő dobókockás mechanizmus a termelésre, ami miatt körökig várnod kell, hogy megkapd az utolsó fádat az építkezéshez, mert senki sem hajlandó cserélni veled.

Szóval a mechanika így 20 évvel a kiadását követően már elég köhögős, és dühítő is olykor, tényleg csak megszállottaknak, dobókocka fetisisztáknak és azoknak ajánlom, akik még csak a Ki nevet a végén? - Gazdálkodj okosan! játékokig jutottak el a társasjátékok izgalmas világában.

A többiek ezt nyugodtan ki is hagyhatják...
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
The only reason I hate Catan is because I know there are better things out there. That doesn't mean the game itself is terrible. I just feel like there's a disappointed parent hovering over my shoulder whenever I play, sadly whispering "I know you can do so much better, if only you tried."

There is a lot going for Catan, though, as an introductory game for non-gamers to the Wonderful World of the Euro. Unfortunately, the game feels like it's actually about 10 minutes long (initial placement + the first few rolls), since most of the game is decided then.

It also incorporates freeform trading, which I strongly dislike due to the fact that it creates a ton of kingmaking or blacklisting ("I don't like you, so I won't trade with you even though you're behind and it's beneficial to me to do so") opportunities.

I have a standing rule for myself that I limit playing games of Catan to about once every 2 months. Any more than that and I'd probably rather just do something else instead.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
The gateway game, Catan is a modern classic. Trading resources keeps everyone involved and offers high enough interaction between players. It looks simple but under surface it offer surprisingly deep gaming experience. Only reason why I usually wouldn't suggest Settlers in a gaming night is the fact there are games I haven't played as much and want to try them instead. Best with 4 players, I'd rather play something else with 3.

Update (15.5.2009) : My rating for Catan has shifted between 6-9 during my time on BGG. (Rating of 6 was when I had overplayed). Right now it feels that because of intense gaming experiences (when played with 4 players) it offers every time when you play it, it deserves at _least_ a rating of 9. 

Update (28.6.2018) : That is if everyone play cuthroath enough. Even one player making too loose trades (that benefit too much one party breaks game a bit. When played with players of similar skill it is tense, good game even after 20 years. A modern classic.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Good game for an active and talkative group. Some strategy mixed with a healthy dose of luck, but usually not so much that it seems based on it. The dice rolls typically pan out near averages over the course of a game due to the number of rolls. 

Not a lot of depth and once you have played this game a few times it will get stale as an experience. It is a very strong "gateway" game, but for people who are familiar with board games and mechanics, it will not be a very strong overall experience.

This game is definitely family friendly as well, but due to the complexity of the rules and of negotiation, it's not recommended for young children (10 and up are fine, 8-10 if they are advanced intellectually). 

Games don't take too long either, although they can drag if negotiations are too frequent. 

Overall, a 7, with the main faults being the level of luck and the fact that you really need an active group of players to have fun, since trading is such an integral part of the game.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
We have not yet played this with three or four players yet, so I can't give it a fair rating.  We tried many of the two player variants found here, but none of them really worked for us.  Probably the most fun part, the trading, was virtually non-existent.  As a result, the game became a basic resource/building game without too many frills.  However, there was a significant runaway leader "rich gets richer" problem---the first person to get a city saw their resources start to take off well beyond the other player.  There were few ways for the second player to come back.  There were a few games where the robber was parked solely on the losing player's side for most of the game.  As a result, this left a bad taste and drove us away from all things Catan for a long time (which we regretted since there [i]are[/i] some quite good two player Catan games).

To be fair, [GAMEID=13] looks like it would be a lot of fun with more people, but with just two there are much better games.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
I was really surprised by how little I liked this game - I had really been looking forward to playing it. I've only played once, so perhaps I haven't seen enough of the depth of the game yet.

I found the general theme to be kind of boring - I just couldn't get excited about building the little cities. The downtime was painful - there really wasn't anything to think about when the other players were taking their turns. Mostly, however, the thing I didn't like about the game was how I kept losing cards. Everytime someone rolled a 7, there was a good chance that I would lose 1/2 my cards. In addition, I really don't like games where others can steal my cards, something that follows the rolling of a 7. Finally, I just don't enjoy trading games. I'm not really interested in trying to keep track of everyone's hands so that I can make "shrewd" trades. As a result, I usually come up on the losing side of any trade.

I can see why folks like this game, It's just not a hit with me.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Esse jogo é uma excelente maneira de introduzir novos jogadores brasileiros ao mundo do jogos modernos. Ele é rápido, cada partida dura em média 50 minutos. As regras são fáceis de explicar (10 minutos). A jogabilidade é fantástica pois permite uma série de possibilidades e o peso dos dados (sorte) é pequeno em comparação aos jogos tradicionais do Brasil. Na realidade a sorte no CATAN "é para todos" já que o valor dos dados pode prejudicar ou beneficiar vários jogadores ao mesmo tempo. Outro fator importantíssimo é que todos os jogadores sempre crescem, uns mais que outros, mas sempre crescem. O tabuleiro formado de peças hexagonais, fato novo para o brasileiro, o que gera sempre um jogo diferente do outro devido a disponibilidade e organização dos recursos. Recomendo.
-------------
Esta versão européia tem as peças plásticas que são um pouco mais difíceis de visualizar. As cartas são pequenas e também dificultam um pouco manuseio mas nada disso tiram a proeza da partida.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
I first played at Gen Con when I was substantially younger.

I like that you have to pay attention during other turns, and that it's not a hurry up and wait mechanic.  I like the balance of the different construction options, and the different ways to score points.  However, I've always won the same way- build the longest road, use it to spread out your villages and harness needed resources ports, and once you're out of villages and have your empire in the right position, build it up to cities.  The only exceptions are when you need a city for more wood or brick to build more roads or villages.

I don't like the kingmaker aspect, and that poor strategic decisions by losing players can hand victories to other players (When 'don't give him a brick, that's all he needs to win' is ignored).  I've benefited from this before, but I don't know that deceit belongs here.  

 Maybe next time I play I'll gun for 'largest army' and VP cards, even though I've never seen it work.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Usually categorised as a popular gateway game, which now surprises me as this game is way too long for what it is. I introduce a lot of people to new games as I love reading rulebooks and teaching, personally, this wouldn't be a game I would introduce a new player to, as it can easily turn into a frustrating experience.

Because I've found that Catan is prone to players getting the board game version of 'soft locked', wherein you are entirely stuck for multiple turns without being able to take a single action. 

In terms of it being a strategy game, the payoff for your planning and the actions you take don't feel as satisfying as in Agricola or in Gaia Project. This could be chalked up to the limited variety of actions you can take, which becomes rather repetitive, especially noticeable because the game runs long.

Perhaps this game works best if everyone around the table is of the same skill level and have the same amount of comfort and familiarity with the game.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
[Mayfair third edition w/ pre-2007 adapter kit] {Catan, Civilization, gateway; trading, modular-board, development, dice-rolling, resource management; optimal 3p} Settlers of Catan is a decent family game with a strong development theme. It is fun and exciting. The game flow is very smooth and has less down time. It's not a heavy strategy game but it provides many tactical options. It is of good player interaction from the trading, robber and the competition of roads. The dice rolling, though luck-driven, adds excitement to the game.

It has several novel mechanics - dynamic board, rolls for production, etc, which have been re-used in many other games.

Beginners' setup should be used when introducing this game to your friends. No matter how you remind them, they will easily overlook the importance of initial placement of settlements and priority of resources at different stages of the game. They will then feel desperate that they are blocked from the game.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
The game that opened mine, and alot of others' eyes to a world beyond monopoly.  A classic.  I find I never tire of playing, and I don't mind the dependability on probability.  Not a deep. or heavy game in any sense, but it's hard to say if there are many better light, or gateway games.

UPDATE:  Although Settlers is a true classic, that would find it near impossible to ever leave my collection, I have to sadly say my rating has fallen to 7.  I still believe Settlers can offer a wonderful gateway experience, but with Elasund taking charge in the house of Catan, it rarely finds table time.  This great Teuber game I will always have a debt to for opening my eyes, but now, with the apple bitten I no longer find paradise in this garden.

Downgraded further to a 4.   Played a game recently, maybe an anomaly, but after two hours with seasoned gamers we were no where near an end.  Trading breakdown early in the midge as no one wants to king make. Shows its age.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
This is a 10 if played with dice decks instead. It has the bell curve for planning, trading/robber for interaction, and some blocking for cut throat play. Just a magnificent package, except for the dice! 

Update: 4-16-2007
This is the game that got me into this hobby.  I loved it and even played this 2 player and still loved it.  I thought it was the greatest game ever in the world.  I don't know if it is a good or bad thing, but the aforementioned sentiments has passed.  I find the gameplay/strategies in this game to be elementary and dull.  Really, the only exciting thing going on the game is seeing where the dice will fall.  Those two bones greatly affect how you are going to do in the game.  Of course there are somethings you can do to help you out, but the luck in this game is significant.  This game is hard to rate as I respect it and have nostalgic baggage that comes with it but I just don't want to play it more than I have to.
Update: 9 -> 6
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value: Klaus Teuber; In Settlers of Catan, players try to be the dominant force on the island of Catan by building settlements, cities, and roads. On each turn dice are rolled to determine the current production on the island. Players collect raw materials to build up their civilizations to gain enough victory points to win the game. This game is a Spiel des Jahres (German game of the year, 1995) winner, primarily because of its amazing ability to appeal to non-gamers and gamers alike. Die Siedler von Catan was originally published by Kosmos and has gone through multiple editions. It was licensed by Mayfair and has undergone at least 4 editions as Settlers of Catan. It has also been re-published in a travel edition by Kosmos and in yet a different edition for Japan/Asia, Settlers of Catan : Rockman Edition. Settlers of Catan is the original game in the Catan Series. Expanded by: The Seafarers of Catan, The Cities and Knights of Catan, 5-6 Player Expansion.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
I had a very bad experience playing this board game. It is extremely luck intensive and unfair. It suffers from a snowball effect, some players get to have all the luck in the game, which sets them up for a win no matter what you try to do. Choices do impact, but most of the time is just luck. Playing with toxic players does not help.

One of the new players to our table was very vengeful because "I did not explain the rules well enough". That player did not ask for clarification of rules and prefered to be vengeful with me (I was the most experienced player) through the whole game even though I was helping them the whole time to make moves or transactions. The player started making bad trades to help the winning player consolidate the win and make me lose. It was very frustrating, I did not get the good rolls to get me out of that lousy situation. I hate it, it is just not worth it, won't play Catan again, please play Concordia or El Dorado instead.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
This may actually be a 6.5 for me, but it is difficult to distill my feelings on the actuall game play and design from the warm feelings it gives me as my first eurogame. It really is an excellent game in many ways, but two unfortunate parts plague it. For one, the luck factor screws it up for me. You roll two dice each turn, and these rolls give you your resources, which ultimately determine your success in the game. Of course, you place yourself on the map to best take advantage of the probabilities, but anyone who plays this game will tell you, dice sometimes have a mind of their own, and will often disregregard the probabilities. The other part that bothers me is how completely malicious the robber mechanic is - amazingly brutal for a gateway type game. 

Having said all that, I'll also say that the Traders and Barbarians expansion neatly wipes out both of these issues for me, so get the expansion if my issues with the game seem sound to you.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
You know why people think this game is "not very good"? Because it's so old that even if you played just five new euro style games, this one lacks a lot of features and theme. All hat made this a classic game was released was revolutionary for a board game for families, today are the basics of every euro style game with weird themes you could throw a bunch of sheeps and wheat to.

It's ancient by today's standards, but still is pretty tight. If still today is many people's first game into the hobby aspect of boardgames, is because it teaches a lot of ground breaking rules and mechanics as their basic and most understandable form without overwhelming curious players.

Its apparent simpleness shows how well designed is, that you could have a life without needing expansions. Sometimes, the feeling of something classic and simple is just what you need, like a hot beverage at a cottage during a cold gray afternoon. Catan is that hot beverage even today.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value: Settlers - as has been well chronicled by many other people - was a bridge game for me - that took me from the world of 'board games' as I knew them (think Monopoly, Scrabble, etc) to the world of modern/Euro type board games as I know them now (think bgg.com). At the time, I was blown away by this game and it made me catch the modern board game bug. I thought the mechanics and strategy were great.  Now, however that I've been exposed to many more (imo better) games, I'm actually not a fan of Settlers.  What I don't like about the game is that you are reliant on the trading aspect of the game for success.  Meaning if your opponents decide not to play nice and trade with you, you are sunk. I also don't love how the robber can freeze your progress of the game, and if others gang up on you your sunk. I don't typically mind the 'screw you' aspect of games, but in this case the robber combined with the trading dependencies make this game flawed for me.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value: The more I play Settlers, the less I enjoy it. The game is simple and good at drawing in new gamers, but the longer the game goes, the more the design frustrates me. The dice mechanic for getting resources just feels so very, very wrong and disappointing. I like dice and do not have an aversion to their use in a game. However, in a game you should always have the power and option to do something on your turn with your die rolls; Settlers denies you this. You could have a Settlers game where nearly all your rolls give you nothing and your opponents are rewarded - leaving you with nothing to do but end you turn. Meanwhile, games like Alien Frontiers and Kingsburg use your die rolls as a mechanic to gain resources, but in those games you always have options for using your dice even if the roll is bad. If I wanted a game with resource management and trading that makes all players active on each others turn, I think I could find a more enjoyable game.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
What stands out first about Catan is its simplicity and accessibility. The rules are easy to learn, allowing novice players to quickly dive into the action. However, the strategic depth the game offers ensures that more experienced players always have an interesting challenge ahead.

The gameplay mechanics revolve around resource management, trade, and the construction of roads and settlements on the island of Catan. The random element of the dice adds excitement to each turn as players compete to obtain the resources needed to expand their colonies. Furthermore, trade is a crucial part of the game as players actively negotiate to get the resources they need and build their paths to victory.

The socialization component is another highlight of Catan, as player interactions are critical for trade and negotiation. This dynamic makes the game perfect for gatherings of friends and family as it encourages communication and strategic decision-making.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
The Settlers of Catan may well be the single greatest board game ever designed. Like many other German games, it combines simple rules and a short playing time with the potential for intricate strategy and battles of wits. But Catan is arguably the best example of bringing all these elements into perfect balance.

Catan satisfies a wide range of people, even those who normally hate board games, since it is the players themselves that choose the character of each game. It can be as cutthroat or as amiable as you want (or both!). It also excels at keeping every player actively involved at all times, both through the ingenious system of resource production and the constant opportunities for trading and deal-making. I could go on, but others already have.

I have no hesitation in recommending Settlers of Catan to pretty much anyone. From there, you may choose to explore more complex or more simple-structure games, but Catan is good for all!
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Very popular light-weight gateway goods collection and conversion (trading) game based on rolling 2 dice (2xd6). Modular board with hexagonal tiles where players expand via houses and streets to generate more resources / points. 

+ Artwork (colorful, bright)
+ Trading goods
+ Network building (streets)
+ Expanding with buildings (adjacent tiles generate resources)
+ Modular map (hexagon tiles)
+ Quick playing time
+ Family-friendly / most kids love it
+ Easy to teach
+ A lot of expansions and variants
# Robber figure is very mean and can be placed on a tile so that it does not generate goods). It can be placed when rolling a 7.
- Luck of the dice roll

Thoughts:
All in all, too much dice randomness for may taste.

See also:
* Space Base (similar mechanic for "gamers", engine builder, no downtime because usually all player get resource on each turn, space theme, no hexagonal world, no route building)
* Ad Astra (space theme, more mechanics)
Title: CATAN

Mata los carretes más rápido que alguien con guitarra.

El más amado y más odiado, en mi caso me gusta porque puedes jugarlo mientras conversas, tiene una cantidad limitada de estrategias: o te dedicas a las cartas de desarrollo o a construir caminos como loco, pero igual el gil estúpido que construyó alrededor del 3 gana porque sale su número a cada rato por alguna razón. Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
For me, the game that started it all!  Like many, the first real board game I was introduced to, compared to the clue/monopoly/sorry garbage games of childhood. 

A lot of nostalgia factor here, since I remember weekly game sessions playing epic double-random, double-blind, 6 player boards while shouting "nobody wants your sheep" at each other into the morning.  (And blasting Starship over the speakers any time someone built a city.)

But again, like many folks, as I discovered a whole world of other games out there, Catan spends much more time on the shelf than on the table anymore.  

While still a good game, compared to more modern games, it feels a little slow. Games when that number just won't hit for a particular resource are brutal, and we've gotten in the habit of just keeping the robber in the desert as it really just slows EVERYONE down.

I'd still play if someone else wanted to, especially with the Cities and Knights expansion.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
This was my introduction to german style games.  At the time, it was amazing.  It'll probably always have a bit of a soft spot in my heart.  

But now that I have more experience with the hobby, I just don't find the game that entertaining.  The "gateway" nature of the game means I usually only play with non-gamers.  That in turn means that the game is usually filled with frustrating distractions, confusion, and interminable trading phases.  Although I have no issue with the die rolling (even though I'm not usually a die-rolling person), I don't like the table-talk and kingmaking that the Robber induces on frequent sevens.  It's essentially a decent light Eurogame with some of my least favorite aspects of Monopoly and Risk tacked on.

With beginners, I'd rather play Ticket to Ride.  With gamers, I'd rather play something with more strategy and depth.  

Also, this game has been know to start nasty fights if played while intoxicated.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
The first eurogamer we purchased and a great starter game to try for new boardgamers.
Our go to game with friends for a regular weeknight session. Conceptually great and very replayable. Randomising the hexes and number chits provides for so many different scenarios that it is a group favourite.
Set up is pretty fast, and it is easy to teach to new players.
The game can become a bit of a grind if you get constantly stuck with the robber, or several bad dice rolls creates a runaway leader. Occaisionally it can feel like you are bit of a seat warmer when bad luck (and poor decisions) puts you out of the game early on.
Although the base game is great, we sometimes add Seafarers to provide some variety (as play is still very close to the base game). Have tried several of the expansions and keen to give Cities & Knights a bit more of a go.
Chits have been put in protective cases and the cards all sleeved to slow the inevitable wear and tear.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value: Was OK at first, but became tiresome for me after a few plays; fun depends on the group and its willingness to trade.  Good potential for interactivity, but my group tended to not trade since we didnt want to help other players too much.  If an essential commodity is scarce due to randomness, a player who has the scarce commodity is even less willing to trade (since they want to use it themselves), and so a bottleneck emerges to strangle trading. But at least the game can move along quickly. The main flaw is that the extent you participate in the game is dependent chiefly on luck, and (to make things worse) is exponentially tied to having luck in the initial few turns.  The result: deadly boring games for those players not initially producing many commodities (esp longer 5-6 player games are terrible)-- there simply isnt enough for these players to do.  Sure, the game is short, so it can have its place, esp. with non- or casual gamers.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
(Not)* Gaming nirvana.  And it gets even better with Cities and Knights!

This game really shines with random hex and chit distribution.  I really love thinking about how to best exploit the limited resources on the map; and throwing down my roads, settlements, and cities in various winding and twisting configurations.  There's no need to worry if an opponent takes a spot I want as long as I set myself up in a good trade position, and not get tempted by the deceptive chits that whisper odds that may never play out.  It's a wheeling and dealing puzzly game where every move is a calculated gamble.  It's a pirate in a merchant's clothing, and I'm always up for a game.

2017 Update after owning the game for ten years: I hate the way you can trap people early in this game and they'll just sit there with nothing to do.  I also get kind of bored waiting for my resources to roll. It feels too slow, even when it goes fast.

*Ten'ish year update

textfield_comment_value:
I was quite late to the Settlers party, and it's hard for me to have much historical appreciation for the old warhorse.  I get that it opened a lot of eyes to the Euro possibilities here in the States, but I just wasn't blown away.  I got my Gateway on playing Carcassone H&G and Ticket to Ride Europe, and that was enough to send me on my way.  By the time I got to Settlers, I was all, "Oh.  That was...nice."

The best part of this game is that it can be very social and very tense.  The worst part is when it's neither social nor tense.  The VERY WORST THING about Settlers is that you can go several rounds (or half the game) without doing anything on your turn.  Roll the dice, pass the dice.  Yuck.  Basically, I think that the set collection and building mechanics were improved upon quite a bit with the Ticket to Ride franchise.  

I'll play this when my just-getting-into-gaming friends suggest it, but I'll never offer to play it again.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
One of my favorite games partly because it is the reason I entered the wonderful world of board gaming, and partly because it is a pretty darned good game. 

I really enjoy the trading part of the game that gives a lot of interaction even without direct conflict. Multiple ways of scoring. 

This was my go to game for introducing players to board gaming. They never really understood how to win the first game but almost everyone wanted to play again. 
Now maybe ticket to ride would be better but that is a bit to easy\limited for me. 

It doesn't get very much play anymore but when we do I always enjoy it. 

Cons
If you are tied down early it can be a boring stretch until finished. 

Prefered robber rule: (Note I've read two different rules regarding the robber and I believe this is the intended way to play, otherwise make it so). If you roll a seven You move the robber. Makes it a lot more fun and do not double punish you for the roll.
Title: CATAN
