Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
There's something I don't like about Catan and I can't put my finger on what it is.  If I know in advance that my group will be playing Settlers, I'll probably skip game night.

I don't mind the dice.  I haven't played it enough to burn out on it.  I'm not one of those people that dislikes things just because they're popular.  It tends to drag a bit by the endgame, but I don't think that's the problem either.

In fact, it's a decent game, that I mostly enjoy while I'm playing it.  But I never, ever, ever want to play it, and I would rather play almost any other game instead of it.  Oftentimes, I'd rather not play any game at all.  I just don't know why.

UPDATE: I figured it out--if I'm playing Settlers than I'm not playing Keythedral, which is a somewhat similar game but ten times better.  Imagine wanting to play Race for the Galaxy but having someone say "Let's play Crazy Eights instead!"  That's what playing Settlers is like.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Classic, and still is pretty good. The game has a lovely arc of development and building things up while offering fun trading opportunities. I don't love the lucky/variable nature of it, even though it's not as big a factor in determining a winner as many would seem to think it is. (What I'm saying is that Catan still is largely won by being a better player and playing the odds well). 

It plays fast and is very accessible. I have fun playing this here and there even though I've grown to enjoy resource management/development games like Terra Mystica much more. 

Update Apr 2019: I've played this a bit more in the past few months and upping this to a 7. It's a very good game and it does so many things better than many newer designs. It actually has some really solid player interaction, it has a good amount of depth and skill despite those who would proclaim it be about luck, and a nice little arc of engine building development.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Catan is not a game where you are trying to solve an efficiency puzzle like in a modern euro. If you try to play it that way you are going to have a bad time. Catan is a game of diplomacy and negotiation at its heart. What is happening outside of the game is where the real game is. You need to appear weak when you are strong, interfere with other players trades, bash the leader, and any number of unsavory things modern hobbyists look down upon all in an effort to try and trick everyone else into letting you win. You don't win by playing optimally, you win by playing deviously.

The reason why the game gets a bad rap from hobbyists is that they don't expect to find these kind of antics in their strategy games, that sort of behavior is normally reserved for social deduction and dudes on a map type games.

And that is why the game is uniquely positioned to stay forever revelant in the hobby, there is just no other game like it.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value: This being a very popular game, often referred to as a gateway game, I had high expectations for my first play. I was a little disappointed, although it is clear this is a good game. The most disappointing element is that this game is essentially Monopoly, as the rich get richer and the poor fade away. When someone isn't producing, they have no opportunity to trade and are essentially out of the game. There's little balancing there, as the only thing such players can hope for is pity. (There's no pity in this sort of game. Altruism is almost never a factor in a game unless no one is actually playing to win.) I imagine the German expansion with the helper cards (somewhat recreated in the Star Trek variant) and/or the cards that replace the dice would be a bit of an improvement, but at that point you almost have a different game. Regardless, I'll be willing to play. There's something absurdly fun about people begging for sheep.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
It's a classic for sure, one of the first board games I've owned. There is a nice amount of strategy involved, but it's very hard to ignore the flaws. 
There aren't enough ways to mitigate bad luck: if your numbers simply aren't rolled, you won't have as much cards to work with, and there's no alternative to that. Not even trading helps, since you need cards to trade away in the first place.
Some resources are objectively better than others, which puts too much emphasis on the turn order and the starting positions (which makes it that much more difficult for new players to enjoy).
The robber makes the game too slow, especially since it is tied to the most likely number to be rolled. It just slows down everyone's building progress, and the blocking only makes the aforementioned bad luck sting that much more.
The game has a runaway leader problem; whoever builds a new settlement first is much more likely to pull ahead and win.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
This is a game that strikes a nice balance of strategy and luck, and its pleasures and nuances become greater with every play. The luck factor needs to be absorbed since a long run of bad rolls can beat you down and create some very cranky players, but most bad luck balances out over several plays. I think this game deserves every accolade it has received and even writing about it now makes me want to play. This is a great game.

Update: After a couple of years of playing this seminal game, I stand by my original assessment. There are other games that have come after which I would often prefer to play now, but the fact is it remains the most requested and often-played game in my family. It also remains the most contentious, as the luck factor seems to make everyone rather edgy at least once during any given game. Still, it is often the go-to game on a night when everyone just wants to sit down and play something quickly.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
One of the most influential board games ever, Die Siedler is unfortunately becoming dated - other games have used the nifty ideas that made this such a blast (modular board, all players benefitting from one player's actions, combination of several ways to gain resources with building and negotiating) without incurring the same mistakes (a poor initial layout spells doom no matter how hard you try, winning players getting so much advantage after the start that the last half hour is just waiting for the kill). The replayability of the game can be raised if you add on some of its multiple expansions (choosing which one can be quite fastidious for non-hardcore fans of the game, though).

Overall, Die Siedler is another one of the classics everyone should have played at least once -being as popular as it is, it shouldn't be difficult to find it at a friend's-, but it's actually bigger for its influence than for the game itself.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
if i played this first before any other modern board game then I would think its not bad.

However after experiencing this for the first time after playing dozens of modern board games. This is complete trash. I have to agree with a review I read before playing this game, decision making can be as limited as monopoly where dice determine everything. If the dice don't even give you a single resource, what do you do all game?

I had maybe 4 or 5 turns in a row from the start of the game where I couldn't do anything because I never had any resources and as soon as I finally got resources before I could spend them, Robber.

You might say I placed my settlements poorly however, I used the first time default set up where both starting settlements were near high probability roll results.

I will NEVER suggest to play this game but will be dragged into it if everyone else wants to.

got rid of it at the first possible opportunity
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value: It's a decent gateway game with trading and building and resource management, but runs for way too long for what it is, and I played this a bit later in my board gaming hobby so it no longer really had the same impact as it probably did for a lot of folks who started out with Catan. It's just way too luck-heavy since you absolutely can get completely shafted just because of terrible dice rolls. The decision space is very small as the best choices to make are usually really obvious (ie. the game just gives you an illusion of choice), and the trading and negotiation part just always seems to eventually lead into hate-trading and unnecessary haggling. The robber is also annoying since "steal a card at random from another player" is a stupid and outdated mechanic. It does improve a lot with the seafarers expansion since sheep becomes an actually a somewhat more useful resource plus you can create bigger funky looking maps.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Collect and trade resources to be the first to expand your settlement to 10 points.

Plays: More than a dozen?
Type: VP engine = a game where you build an engine to collect victory points most efficiently.
Complexity: Family game = a game that is easy to teach and play.
# of players: 4.
Playing time: 90 mins.
Player interaction: Trading. Competition for scarce resources - settlement locations. Targeting - placing the robber.
Randomness: Medium - dice, but you can prepare for rolls to some extent.

Replayability: Medium. This is always a good experience and most people are fine to play again, but maybe not right away? There is some depth to explore.
Fun: Good fun. Trading makes it highly interactive. It's fun when your numbers come up, less fun when they don't.
Memorabiity: Not so high, it's still a VP engine that doesn't create stories.

Thematic integration: Weak.
Components: Nice.

Who will like this: Family gamers.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
I'm playing my first game with some friends, some have played, others haven't.
The game dragged terribly (over two hours for a 4 player basic game, after setting up and going over the rules - but it seemed like three or four hours of play), especially when players asked again and again (and again and again) about the same trades that no one wanted to take them up on.
One player spent the last hour of the game involved in another conversation entirely, and not paying attention at all, but then got the "Monopoly" card, and was able to win the game.
I can't believe that the game has such a broken card that a player who isn't even trying can luck into it and gain 6 victory points in one turn to win.

Yes, I could be persuaded to play again, because I have friends who love this game, and I enjoy playing games with them.
I will also keep my travel edition for classroom use (although I may have to "lose" the monopoly card).
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Como muchísimos de aquí, fue de mis primeros juegos y mi primera experiencia con un juego extenso... Hace poco quise intentar una regla casera para arreglar esos momentos frustrantes en los que no te sale una buena tirada, Y AÚN ASÍ se las arregló el juego para extenderse bastante... No me desagradan los juegos tardados, pero la mecánica de tirar dados, obtener ese recurso e intercambiar se vuelve rápidamente repetitiva; incluso cuando el juego te ofrece algunas maneras alternativas de puntuar, al final todo eso lo obtendrás con las mismas acciones: tirar y cruzar los dedos... La estrategia es muy escasa, aunque te hagan creer lo contrario; pero, con la gente correcta, puede ser un momento agradable con muchas risas y discusiones por los intercambios, en especial con jugadores poco experimentados.

Luego probaré la expansión de Ciudades y Caballeros, y tengo esperanzas de que eso le dé una nueva vida a este juego.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Catan (or Settlers of Catan as I will always remember it), is a good game. It holds up by having a very timeless quality to it. People can approach the game having never played anything like it, and they will quickly be able to understand and embrace its gameplay because it has a combination of elements that are at once familiar, but also unique in how the game presents them. 

Nowadays, I find that the game doesn't fit any sort of niche that satisfies what I look for a in a game. It's too random for when I'm wanting a satisfying strategic experience; it's too casual for when I'm wanting to get engrossed in a game; and yet it usually takes too long for a game I would like to play casually. 

I think Catan is the archetypal "gateway game", in that, I would only ever play it when using it as such (and know it would thrive being played in that capacity), but I have no real desire to ever play it of my own volition.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
This was my "gateway game" that introduced me to the broader aspects of boardgaming.  It doesn't get played much now that I have a 200+ collection, but I pulled it out recently and it still held.  I find the dice a bit frustrating, but not so much that I would use cards, because that aspect of it is part of the appeal to the game I think.  Having played this probably 50+ times, I do find myself always going for similar types of strategies, etc. but it's still a fun game.

I really like the totally open trading aspect of this game, which is something that other games still don's seem to replicate all that well.  Other games with trading tend to have restrictions on them, whereas in settlers you can trade things like port use, robber placement, intentions on where you are building, etc.  (I know these aren't all strictly following the rules, but we allow pretty much anything in trades in the games I play).
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Catan continues to be one of the perennial favorites for our family. Everyone knows the game so it is easy to pull out and start, especially for family members who don't play games too often. 

There are a few house rules that we put in place. We choose to not even use the robber sometimes, b/c that can really make people mad when you block their resources. We also tend to not use 2 and 12 on resources, since those numbers don't get rolled very often... instead, we put in an extra 3 and 11 to make those numbers more enticing (a player just re-rolls if they roll a 2 or 12). 

For some extra interest, it's great to use the Seafarers expansion, really adds to the game, with ships, islands and "gold" tiles which yield any resource you want. 

We also have the 5/6 player expansion, which is an awesome way to play, because anyone can build in-between turns, which I find actually makes the game feel faster.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
The Classic! Nearly 30 years ago, the late Klaus Teuber single-handedly changed boardgame culture in Germany. A whole generation grew up with long "Siedler"-evenings.
After several revisions still very nice to play. A very good tactical and extremely interactive family game with two big unsolved crucial problems: 1. The problem of turn order from the start, i.e. who can build the first / has to build the last settlement. We prefer to play with the Seafarers-Expansion and the additional hexagons of the 5-6 Players Extension (more interesting building sites per player). 2. The dice implements a huge luck dependency. To find a remedy, omit dices and use the Event Cards from "Traders & Barbarians" instead. Another houserule: Each round, players missed-out with resources get a wild resource. With that, it´s great.
Very nice artwork by Michael Menzel, very good rulebook. And there are so many expansions...
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Wow. Game boxes used to be so ... drab!  It's brown with some brown on it. Yawn. The game is still the same though.

After not playing Settlers for ten years or so, and playing it 4 times in a month, I think I'm a bit Settler'd out. It's a good game, but it's definitely been surpassed (for me) in complexity and fun by later games.

UPDATE: I think I've identified what "gets me" about Settlers. If you are the player that falls behind -- and there's almost always a player that falls behind -- there is very little you can do to dig your way out of the hole you're in. In the rare game that doesn't have this happen -- like the game I played tonight, which ended with 9-8-7 points -- the game is a fun contest all the way through, but boy does it suck to be the pre-destined loser.

4/2012: Updated rating to be more realistic. Settlers is still quite a good game, even if it's not one I want to play a lot of.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Perfect blend of strategy and chance. While I can sympathize with those who say there is too much randomness here, I have consistently seen strong players win by positioning themselves to take advantage of probability. Mitigating the risks of chance is a big part of this game. Brilliant in its accessibility and broad appeal.

EDIT: After playing a few more times with casual gamers, I'm reducing the grade to an 8. The set up and site selection, unless you use a pre-set configuration, really does set some at a severe disadvantage. While I don't mind at all the randomness of the dice roll, it is never fun when you don't feel you have much of a chance from turn one, which can happen in this game. Also, I find that getting to that last victory point or two can be painfully slow. I usually target a number a point or two lower than recommended.

If I pick up exansions, keep in mind I have the 2012 version.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
As with many other gamers, Catan introduced me to the world of designer board games. It was a huge hit with my friends, my roommates, my family, and even me. I say this because I rarely desire to play it.

I've become Cataned out, most likely because I've moved on to greener pastures (with other sheep). My tastes in games have become more clear and I've developed a palate that is more defined, making Catan slip in my regards. Add to that the fact that my brother always wants to play Catan and I've become a little burned out on it.

However, it's a classic, both in the history books and in my mind. I've played enough games to realize that Catan is still one of my favorites, despite my hesitance to play it sometimes. I'm more willing to try new things and introduce a friend or family member to a game that is perhaps a little more thrilling or deep or thematic. All that said, Catan is a splendid game.

textfield_comment_value: Jeu très fun, très accessible et original. On se prend facilement aux mécaniques, à essayer d'augmenter nos chances de faire de beaux tours. On lance les dés et quand le numéro qu'on espérait tombe, c'est super amusant (et ça arrive plusieurs fois par partie en général). Par contre soyons sérieux, la chance entre beaucoup en jeu pour gagner, entre 4 joueurs ayant l'habitude des jeux de société modernes qui ont déjà joué au jeu, seule la chance les départagera, sauf exception. Le jeu peut vous faire passer votre tour 5 fois d'affilé (littéralement) sans que vous ne puissiez faire aucune action. Un joueur qui a moins de chance d'obtenir ses ressources peut les obtenir 3 fois d'affilé sans que personne d'autres n'en obtienne. BEAUCOUP DE VARIANCE susceptible de casser le rythme de la partie. C'est parfois très frustrant. Amusant donc, mais ne jouez pas pour gagner, vous seriez souvent déçu du jeu.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
At one time I used to think this was one of the greatest games ever made.  Now I know better.  Still, though, it can be fantastic, but it really is prone to certain circumstances.  If the dice get screwy it can make for a long and arduous game. When playing with 4 there is enough opportunity to yield resources so that when your turn comes around you have something to do, but of course one player gets the bone usually and gets pinched out (although there are enough other things that they can still do to win if they don't get too worked early on in the game).  With 3 even more dependent on dice rolls to yield for you to be able to do anything that turn.  I would never give up my copy, as it still hits the table fairly often.

UPDATE: You know, the rating on this has gone all over the place depending on how jaded I am, but in reality, this is a damn fine game.  Really one of the best of its kind.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value: Pretty much tied with Boggle for my favorite game. Settlers has so much room for change with the unique board for every game, and the complete arbitrariness of luck on the dice roles that I almost never get tired of playing. The game is great both for 3 or 4 players, with each situation providing for a very different kind of game. It's also possible to combine two sets of the game to play with 5-7 players (though I wouldn't recommend going over 6), and without needing to buy any of the expensive expansions. Every time I introduce a friend to this game, they get hooked by about half-way through the first game. Settlers is a great strategy game which doesn't rely solely on brute force and has no military based. Rather, one relies on trading resources as well as timely and intelligent use of them buy, barter and build one's way to victory. Highly addicting, but you'll never regret getting hooked!
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
My gateway game and probably yours, too.  Though I've arguably "moved on" from this game, I'll never pass up a chance to play it.  My wife enjoys playing vanilla, but I like adding the River (you might hate it, but I like it), Fisherman, Catan event cards, and Cities and Knights.  Looking to add Seafarers but I need an older copy.

A lot of people hate on Settlers after they graduate to other gaming mechanics, but I think this is wrong.  Settlers is what it is - a VERY well-thought out game that offers much replayability (tiles, resource markers).  

Combining Settlers with its expansions--I like to play with The Great River, Fisherman, Event Cards (for the events only), Harbormaster, and Cities and Knights--makes for a long, but enjoyable, experience.

I would recommend this game to anyone trying to get into board gaming, and I'd gladly play Settlers with anyone, even after all these years.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
This is a wonderful game; or at least it was for a couple hundred plays. I picked this up on a whim at a comic store down the street to play with my friends before we'd go out drinking. Except we had a hard time leaving the table. Soon we were scheduling Settlers evenings and playing repeatedly till the wee hours. Ah, those competitive nights of playing Settlers when somebody always wanted "one more game."

It seems unfair to rate this game against today's games, but I revere it as the landmark game it is and all the enjoyment it gave me, so I'll bump it up a notch. I'd be hard pressed to sit through a play of it now, however. At least give me Elasund which has a lot more going on. For expansions, I recall Seafarers and Cities & Knights as both being worth it.

This game brought me back into the hobby and, by association, to BGG, so it will always have a place of reverence in my heart.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
After playing on and off for years on various phone/tablets, I broke down and bought the board game to play with my kids.  It's too heady for my 5-year-old, but both my 7 and 10 year old daughters enjoyed it.  The game, which runs a little longer than some of our favorites (Forbidden Island, Ticket To Ride) was perfect for myself and the 10-year-old.  The 7-year-old had a good time but was a bit jacked up during play.  I'm not sure if it was because she was losing interest or just being 7.  Either way, we completed the first game and I got a thumb's up from both kids.  

Update, in future game plays, both the 7 and 10 year old had a good time.  Once they fully understood the game, what it takes to win, and could estimate how much time was left (because the youngest gets a bit bored), it became more enjoyable.  Since they like this game, I'm thinking Stone Age will be our next purchase.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
22 years. It took 22 years for me to finally get a chance to play this game. Despite its age, The Settlers Of Catan still holds up. Yeah, I could see having too many of the same resource being clumped together during setup cause balance issues, but that is a minor quibble. Trading, points for victory, a minor screw-your-opponent ability, and an innovative dice roll payout mechanics; its no wonder that tSoC took the world by storm and ushered in an era of interest in Euro board gaming.

There are so many versions of Settlers and expansions for the game, but were I ever to buy it, I would probably stick to the vanilla version as 3-4 players is probably the best for game length and a theme change doesn't interest me.

Oh, and despite the official shortening of the game to just 'Catan', I will probably always refer to it by as 
'Settlers' as that was how we referred to it, back in the day.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value: This game is most definitely overhated. I personally like the trading and building of this game. However, there are 2 big downsides that make me not want to play it over other games. The first is how long it is. Some long games (For instance... food chain magnate) Are long, but keep people engaged the whole time. With this game, however, I don't feel that engaged. This adds on to #2 which is... as everyone says... the dice rolling. This makes some people's turns just naturally worse than others. This makes turns kind of dull, especially if the dice are not in your favor. To make the game more exciting, we use the following house rules: we go to 7 points instead of 10, and link the numbers to the tiles in a way, where the 4 top numbers would always be diverse among different resources, preventing the dice from taking over. Overall, it's a good game that is a few steps away from perfect.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
A solid game, but not one I really go out of my way to play. I completely understand the game's popularity and its historical significance. Without Settlers, board games would still be relegated to the toy aisle. I also realize that many people cut their Eurogame teeth on Catan and most of those who did are still absolutely loyal to it. I get it, but I still would rather play something else.

As one of the first Euro's to cross the pond, it often gets a free pass for the parts that don't always work. I'm not usually one to bitch about randomness, but I have had more than a couple of experiences where I've had to sit around for half an hour doing nothing because my territories simply would not produce. Again, I know that's just a dice thing and it's not likely to happen ALL of the time. It just seems to really irritate me when it does happen...and it always seems to ruin my experience.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value: I think Settlers illustrates well how not to implement randomness in a game.  Random battles work well as risk management.  After all, the players in, say, Nexus Ops, get to build up troops and at least see the satisfaction of something happening that they caused, even if it's the hot laser death of their own strike force.  Random income, on the other hand, means a highly frustrating experience for the players whose numbers don't come up, since for them nothing happens at all.  It just isn't fun to sit and watch other people grabbing goods.  For all the game's virtues, and there are many, there are too many turns where the only thing to do is roll the dice and pass building.  (Trading is great in theory, but if you don't get any resources anyone else wants due to crappy dice rolls, you're not trading anything, no matter how much of a social butterfly and great negotiator you may be.)
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
I came late to the world of Catan, but after having the game's merits described to me, I took a chance and brought the box home from the game shop. 

I have never once been disappointed by this game. It's a perfect mix of strategy and simplicity. Everyone gamer I know loves this game, and there's good reason for it. The game mechanics are simple to learn and understand, but the strategy and luck elements keep it interesting (or frustrating) every time.

Setup time is relatively quick after the first few plays, and average game time has been around an hour depending on how chatty people get during trading and making up elaborate stories about why they're attempting to dominate sheep production.

I've never had this much fun simply playing a game and not caring whether I'm winning or losing. My experience with Settlers of Catan is becoming the standard by which I judge all other games.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
This game was my first encounter with modern board games. The basic idea is great which grant you a ton of theme. We used to play it a lot, and im still happy to get it on the desk. It has easy rules, which means it is easy to teach. The robber is also a great addition to stop someone who is in front of you in terms of points.

Pros / Cons:
-Every game is different because of the constantly changing map and due to this always different opportunities.
-I love the trading mechanics that completly kills the downtime in the game.
-You roll a 7 and immediatelly start laughing while you are looking into the victim eyes is a fantastic feeling.

-I absolutely hate to be tricked by luck, so these dices are killing me sometimes (even if im on 8 and we always roll just 4-5-6 for example).
-You can be blocked right after the first few turns, and after this you don't have chance to overcome it.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value: Catan, such a classic game. This is the definitive board gamer's game. It is expandable, full of strategy and is truly the definition of next level of board game beyond the Monopolys and Sorrys of this world. I have had a great deal of game nights in which the only game we played was Catan, and while I cannot say it is my all time favourite board game, I can say it is in the top 10. The only issues Catan struggles with is how brutal bad luck can be. Running low on luck (especially in the 4 or 6 player games) can make the game painfully slow and impossible to win if you get locked in.to a corner. This doesn't happen often to skilled players, but when it does it can just make the game drag on. I also added Harbor Master to the game and kept it at 10 points to win to keep things moving smoothly towards the end of the game. Overall, Catan is a classic everyone who is a gamer should own.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Catan is Catan. This feels like the foundation of so many games that have come since, and it nailed so much right. 

Playing again after 10 years, I still love a lot of what this game has to offer. The concept is iffy but is generalized so much it doesn't matter so much as the map and the rewards you're trying to uncover for yourself. One thing that stood out on replaying it is the bartering sessions -- that one piece of everyone's turn seems to be the odd bit left out of all the games that have come since. I'm not really sure why because it's *so fun*!

My main complaint comes around victory -- it doesn't seem well thought out or aligned with the rest of the package. Everyone's taking their turns and then the game will just abruptly end because someone hit an arbitrary threshold with their cards and pieces. There's no sense of a build up.

Currently in storage @ my pops' in the US.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
I'm sure this was a relatively good game 20 years ago, but now that there are dozens of games I'd rather play, I find it annoying it still sees so much play.

Its flaws have been discussed at length by others, but just to state the biggest ones:

1. The dice rolls are quite overwhelming in this game, especially considering the economic snowballing in this game. Players who get good dice rolls early are at a disproportionate advantage, and similarly players who get bad rolls early are at a huge disadvantage.

2. The solution the game uses for this problem is to incorporate a bash-the-leader/take that mechanism via the robber. Unfortunately, this just uses one bad mechanic (i.e. bash-the-leader) to cover up another (i.e. randomness/runaway leader).

3. There are literally turns where you get to make no choices. It's not even that unlikely for that to happen multiple turns in a row.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
i mean, it's (settlers of) catan. like many, it was my "gateway" game that pulled me away from monopoly, clue and the other 1990s "standards." i may have overplayed it a bit, and some games are frustrating due to land placement, rolling luck and extortionist players. but ultimately, as long as my wife isn't around (she refuses to play), i don't mind a game now and then.

ios app: own - i have the "classic hd" version of the app and i rage quit a number of times. every time i said to myself, what are the chances the ai will "roll a 7 now to put the robber on me and happen to steal the wheat they keep offering me crap for," or "what are the odds theyll finally roll the 12 and get 4 bricks to build 4 roads and take longest road from me," etc...and the ai always got exactly the thing that would win the game. strongly dislike the game (especially without house rules) and hate the app.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Ezzel kerültem kapcsolatba újra a társasjátékok világával. A maga idejében jól ki volt használva. Akkoriban rendkívül izgalmasnak találtam. A nyersanyagok kockával kidobása viszont egyre jobban idegesített. Nem mintha zavarna, ha egy játékban sok múlik a szerencsén, de bosszantó ha a nyavalyás sorsvetőn ilyen sok múlik. És a többi játékos kínlódását is alig tudom kivárni. És az se tetszik, hogy kialakulhat egy olyan helyzet, hogy még azért is küzdeni kell ,hogy élvezzem a játékot, mert alig maradt lehetőségem a játékban a terjeszkedésre és/vagy a kereskedésre. Szóval most ott pihen a szekrényben, mert minek üljek le olyan játékhoz ami csak felidegesít. Végül a sírját az újdonság utáni vágyam ásta meg.

textfield_comment_value:
I've played a lot of catan with family and enjoyed it but I have come to the conclusion that the game has many fundamental problems.

 There seems to always be a player who will do horrible and a player who will only do mediocre because of the design of the game.  It is not fun to not be doing well in catan because you don't get to really play the game.

The Trading is a highlight, especially if you play with a group that encourages creative trades.  Although I ruined this game with my group by coming up with the idea of tribute, in which player's could give me free resources or favorable trades so that I wouldn't place the robber near them.  Everybody in my family now does this and the robber mechanic is fundamentally broken for us  

Most of the expansions are bogged down by a flawed base, but are still interesting experiences.  Some of the standalone versions are pretty neat
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value: The father of modern board games remains quite solid in an era of highly thematic, ambitious. and complex new releases. While of course it has its own flaws, it did not have the luxury of 25 years of board game evolution to behind it that games nowadays have. In an era of when board games were thought to be an indoor pastime for children until they go outside again or decrepit monstrosities only the most dedicated wargamers would touch, Settlers of Catan opened many to the fact that board games could be simple enough that all members of the family could enjoy, complex enough so that players can dedicate time to understand it, and random enough for replayability. For its time it was probably the best boardgame that could have existed, and even today while it might not have aged well, it still holds the title as one of the best games to introduce newcomers to the boardgame hobby.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value: If you are only considering the game design and the ratio of luck to strategy, there are definitely better games than this. However, I have more memories of awesome times I have had playing this game than with any other game. It is very much dependent on the people playing, as I had played games that were not much fun because the players played too seriously or one player accepted pretty much any trade offer. I have won this game by only building on two hexagons before (I had four cities and believe it or not, Longest Road.) I have played a game where we combined two base sets and played to 25 VPs. It lasted three hours, but it was awesome and one of the most fun times I have had playing a board game. I love the intellectual challenge and brain burn of other games, but with the right players, Settlers is a blast, and still has enough strategy and tactics to keep me interested.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
The modular map is nice. It and the variety of uses (and non-uses) for different materials allow for the structure of the board to create meaningful difference in the city-rush and the sprawling-settlement styles of strategy.
The way the game seems to tend towards trading with the board rather than other players is frustrating, since that player interaction is otherwise cool. Trading gets frustrating in some groups of players, though.
The game absolutely flags in a big way once any player gets to about 8 points, and cinching the win becomes a meaningful but laborious affair.  This slowdown is especially troublesome because one or even two players will long since lose contention for first.


House Rule: I like to randomize the distribution of resource hexes, so the Friendly Robber is no longer sufficient. Instead, nothing happens on 7s until someone has gained a visible point.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value: Uno dei pochi boardgame tedeschi che vendono nei supermercati, e in italiano: gli va quindi reso merito per essere una delle teste di ponte nella diffusione dei german game in Italia. Il gioco ha regole semplicissime, e c'è moltissima interazione tra i giocatori: oltre alla possibilità di sgambetto (col brigante e con la semplice occupazione territoriale) c'è lo scambio di materiali, indispensabile perché all'inizio è difficile essere indipendenti. Il gioco è enormemente influenzato dal fattore-culo (anche se la distribuzione normale dei tiri di dado aiuta chi non si distraeva alle lezioni di statistica), ma rimane godibile e leggero. Da giocare quando si ha fretta - anche se allo scopo ci sono in giro titoli migliori - o per catturare nella spirale dei giochi da tavolo gli amici non praticanti. Nota negativa: nella versione italiana la spiegazione delle regole è demenziale.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value: I have played this game with all of its expansions more times than I can possibly count.  Early on it was great fun because it was my first venture into strategic gaming.  My friends and I played multiple evenings every week.  However, as we progressed we realized the fatal flaw of this game--the heavy weight of the dice rolls.  You can have great strategy and still lose horribly if there is a string of rolls that don't go your way.  This is especially maddening when you choose the numbers that should be rolled more frequently like sixes or eights and someone else wins because they set up shop on threes and they got rolled a ridiculous amount.  I still play this game occasionally, usually when we are hanging out with people that aren't as used to strategic games.  It is a good game to use to cut your teeth on, but it has little value to grow with the player over the years.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value: This is the game that got me into the hobby, as seems to be the case for a lot of people on BGG. It also appears that many have abandoned the game as too "random." I've toyed with posting a defense of Catan in the forums, but I think there are several threads already discussing that. In short, the strategy is certainly obscured somewhat by the dice rolling mechanic, but to argue the game is random or luck based is far from the truth. After countless plays both in person and on XBox Live, I argue that the number of games that are severely tainted by absurd dice rolling statistics are fairly rare. Much more often, mistakes in judgement, or strokes of genius drive the outcome. Most importantly, getting the final 1-3 points often feels like a rewarding puzzle. Throw in that there is usually at least one other person vying for those points, and you have a quite satisfying climax.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Qué puedo decir del Catan... juego clásico entre los clásicos, sencillo pero profundo y divertido, eso sí satisfactorio o frustrante dependiendo de la partida.
Quizás la fase más importante sea la de elección de dónde ponemos los poblados al principio del juego y luego nos limitamos a ser espectadores con pocas deciciones.
También te das cuenta muchas veces que pese a que hayas planteado el mejor escenario posible con las losetas que probabilísticamente más van a salir al final el factor suerte hace lo que le da la gana y te quedas con todas las ganas.
El juego tiene lo justo para llamar la atención, y no es peyorativo al contrario, lo que tiene lo tiene muy bien. Recoleccion de recursos, puntos por construcciones, azar y estrategia y también la parte de comercio que comienzas tan alegremente y luego hace florecer lo peor de cada uno.
Juegazo en su día y juegazo años despues

textfield_comment_value:
The game that got me back in to the world of board gaming.  It will most likely retain the most played in my collection crown; not playing it in the past decade, I would welcome to get this to the table again with my family and a group of friends.

I enjoy the simultaneous mechanic of gathering resources on another player's turn.  I have been enjoying Space Base for this reason.  I am indifferent to the negotiating and trading aspect of the game; you need the right people to enjoy this mechanic and have no hurt feelings over it.  This is the reason why Catan, Compounded, and Chinatown doesn't get played.

I've always preferred 3 or 5 players simply due to the size of the game board.  It's never fun worrying about how your big move will impact another player and if you get blocked out, spending the rest of the game going through the motions.  It is rare, but it does happen.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Good:
-Trading
-Lots of player interaction
-Borderline gateway game
-Easy to understand and execute strategies
-Cheering for die rolls

Bad:
-Waiting on rolls
-Balance issues (city strategies are too good)
-Encourages mean-spirited play
-A little long for what it is
-Starting villages typically determines who will win

Overall:
The player interaction that comes from trading adds a lot of interaction and seems to be the main selling point.  But trading slows the game down and gives savy players an even bigger advantage.  This was one of the best gateway games when it came out and holds a special place in my heart but I now struggle to find a reason to play it.  It's not deep enough for play with hobbyists, not a top-tier family weight game, and not ideal for introducing the hobby.  While I definitely got my moneys worth, it will be collecting dust for the foreseable future.

textfield_comment_value: I rate this game 9 because it is a great game but also considering the following...  We never play it anymore without Seafarers and almost never without Cities and Knights as well.  But Settlers is a terrific game even without the expansions.  The masterful balance of strategy and luck is just right.  You have to be able to adjust your strategy frequently. You can achieve a sense of accomplishment in obtaining one goal and then refocusing your effort to the next development in your game plan. It is exciting to disguise your agenda by building many things at once at the risk of someone (or yourself) rolling a 7 or the risk of an opponent building in your way.  One of my favorite things about this game, however, is to see the blank stare of quite clever people as the game is explained to them for the first time and then seeing how quickly they pick it up when we play.

This is the game that introduced me to modern board gaming.  I have played this game many times over the past 20 years and it has special place in my heart for that reason. The game itself however is broken.  
Very high on luck with dice rolls, I try to mitigate this with getting a variety of numbers, but that does not always work. I have spent 5-6 turns in a row passing because all that was rolled were 4s 3s 11s and 7s and even with a lot of number options, get no resources.
Very easy to block a player with huge impact. If one player lucks out with numbers and blocks your road with one of his and beats you to a spot on the board, very early on you can tell that you have already lost.  The next 1.5 hours you go through the motions of playing for someone else to win.
Many flaws, I will likely not play this many more times in the future if I can help it.

textfield_comment_value: Catan always feels like there's a lot more strategy involved than what is really going on. Still very enjoyable but can easily be frustrating when the most likely dice roll, doesn't get rolled and loses you the game. The best part about this game though, is the trading aspect. Trading with people is awesome because it allows you to interact with the other players and feels amazing to get a 2:1 deal that just gives you exactly which resources you need to build a settlement/city. textfield_comment_value:
I own a copy at the insistence of friends that I was trying to lure into the hobby. They definitely think a lot higher of it than I do and marvel at the fact this isn't included in "Best of" articles about board games... 

Quality of components are good, ruleset is nice and fairly clear, and the early to mid-game has a nice feeling of building and possibility. The theme is very so-so but the finite resource collection and trading is intuitive to learn.

Criticisms of the game design are well-documented and valid, my main being the anti-climactic end, runaway winner(s) and luck of the dice + hex-placement concentration. Some of these can be countered by house rules such as drawing for resource production rather than rolling.

Anyway, all-in-all I find the game enjoyable with the right crowd who are having fun, but the game in itself doesn't push my buttons.

textfield_comment_value: A game for statisticians: Catan cannot be won if the right numbers do not come. Nevertheless it is not a gambling game, because the different probabilities of two dice should be known. Those who are surprised that 2 and 12 are rarely rolled miss the appeal of the game. It's not about playing chess and it's not about gambling either, it's about improving your chances in a calculated way. Moreover, the game does not follow a more or less sophisticated game mechanics, but leaves the players room to make each other's lives difficult. This build-up game also appeals to children and it is a pleasure to see them grow into the mechanisms of trading and tactics.

These slight tweaks allow the game experience to work well enough.  The game takes a little while to "set up" - that might be my only slight critique. textfield_comment_value: The ultimate starter board game. Would recommend for anyone getting into the more advanced board game scene or trying to introduce their friends to it. One of the best aspects of this game is that every dice roll matters to every player. This provides incentive to pay attention to every roll, and prevents long waiting periods. If you get the 5-6 player expansion they also add intermittent building, which does wonders for player engagement. The worst part of playing many board games with a large group is waiting forever for it to come back around to your turn. This game solves many of the problems that keep people away from the hobby in an easy to learn, hard to master, must have addition to every board game collection.

textfield_comment_value:
I changed my January 2011 rating of 7.9 down to 6.75 on 5/4/16, to reflect what I have been telling people for years - this is an excellent "gateway drug" game for getting people into the board gaming hobby, but it just isn't that much fun to me any longer.

A combination of expansionism and rolling dice, with a rudimentary card system on the side, this game is lean and mean.  Expand your abstract cities and roads based on the accrual of 4 resources; and do so in a way that makes life harder for the other folks on the board.  Many fundamental Euro game principles at play here, and thus many prospective gamers find it to be delightful.

textfield_comment_value:
A classic for a reason.  Easy to pick up and play, Settlers is guaranteed to provide an hour or two of fun as you collect resources and expand your town.

If you're looking for an in-depth and full-featured experience, though, look elsewhere.  The frequent dice-rolling means players will start complaining about being unlucky (and rightfully so).  Be wary of the expansion packs; while they add some much-needed complexity to the game, some are worth your time more than others.

All in all, Settlers is a casual German-style board game that can be enjoyed with family and friends.

textfield_comment_value:
Frustrating and slow to get moving if the dice abhor you from the start. The game gets better once more towns are built and there is an economy for real trading to occur. 

Regardless, there is no mechanism to affect dice rolls. If you have nothing worthwhile to trade and roll badly then you sit idle while your opponent's roads/towns corral you to a steady cancerous death. Unforgiving for a gateway game. This game will make you hate bad dice more than Monopoly. How did this game start a revolution?
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value: It's not a perfect game, but it's what got me into boardgames and after all these years I still enjoy it. Another great thing about it are all the expansions, some of which change the experience, atmosphere and challenges of the game so much that it's always fresh. Be careful about the player count though - it's pointless at two players, and drags at more than three. Also, there's lots of luck involved because the dice influence it's main mechanisms, but still, it's a beautiful presence on the table,  very enjoyable in almost all aspects

textfield_comment_value: Settlers of Catan fits the definition of gateway game quite well.  There is a good balance of luck and strategy.  The game can be easily taught in ~7 minutes and anyway, a new player can learn 90% of the game by just being the last player (i.e. watch the others play).  Negatives include the initial setup time and difficulty in recovering when behind (i.e. generally 1 or 2 players do really well while the rest aren't even close).

NEW COPY FOR TRADE...

I like this game, but I hardly play it any more.  My main beef with it is how limiting a starting position can be when playing at the max player limit (4/6).  Add that to the randomness of dice rolls, and the first several turns can reveal your end 30-45 minutes before it happens. Attention to probability mitigates only a portion of this, because there are always going to be placements that are more advantageous than others, especially with a random setup.  Moreover, the dice are what they are--random.

I accidentally traded this for Jambo in a math trade.  I can't say that I regret that trade one bit.  I think I'm just over Catan.

I've been noticing this oddly Monopoly-esque backlash against Catan recently. Popular things tend to get picked on, I guess.

Which is a shame, because Catan was and still is a great introductory board game, and a great game in its own right. Yes, it relies a little bit too much on luck, and yes, you can get screwed over by bad starting placement, but you can overcome this with clever negotiations against people and judicial use of the robber. It tends to run a little long, especially with 4 players, but it's not a big deal.

~

I am not going to go into a lot of detail explaining Carcassonne.  By now everyone knows what the game is and how to play.

I believe it is enough to say that Carcassonne is one of the grandfathers of the gaming hobby and is clearly the frontrunner of tile-laying games.

This game is easy to teach and the learn.  Even learning by reading directly from the rules is simply.  That makes it a great game for beginners.  Yet even well seasoned gamers find the game enjoyable.

That is because everything just sort of fits with Carcassonne.  

The components are very nice.  Thick cardboard was used.  The artwork is likewise.  Not flashy, but it fits well.

The theme is interesting and fits the game wonderfully.

The mechanics are completely solid and fit the theme well.

This an all-around excellent game.


Pros - 
- Fun
- Great mechanic
- Simply to learn and play
- Innovative for its time


Cons - 
- Many of the expansions are out of print and hard to get



Overall Playability = 8.0

Design = 9
Strategy = 8
Luck = 8

Fun = 9

[b]------------------------------------------------------[/b]


Here I will discuss the [thing=2993][/thing] expansion as played during the Carcassonne Project.


[b]New Components[/b] - 
- 6th player pieces.
- Big meeple worth two normal meeples.
- 18 Tiles.  Most are either new city tiles or Inns on road tiles.  One Cloister. 


[b]New Mechanics[/b] - 
- The Bigger Meeple offers new strategy for control of structures.
- Inns on roads and the Cathedrals in cities offer more points for finished structures respectively.  But offer zero points for unfinished structures at end of game.


[b]Thoughts[/b] - 
- This is a great expansion.  Easy to learn and play.  No complicated rules.  And it blends into the base game easily.
- The Big Meeple is great for take-overs and you can really start playing the game on the attack.
- The bonus points on finished structures is really nice, but it makes you plan ahead a lot more.  Unfinished structures will not score at End Game any more and many times the points for unfinished structures makes the difference.


[b]------------------------------------------------------[/b]


Here I will discuss the [thing=5405][/thing] expansion as played during the Carcassonne Project.


[b]New Components[/b] - 
- 24 tiles with all but two containing city parts.  
- 20 Goods Tokens
- Pig Meeples for each color
- Builder Meeples for each color


[b]New Mechanics[/b] - 
- The new city tiles have Goods on them.  The player that finishes a city collects those Goods present in that city.  End game offers a new scoring mechanic for majority control for each of the three Goods at 10 points each.
- Pig Meeple can be added to a Farmer to increase the value of Farms at End Game.
- Builder Meeple is added to a structure a player already has a Meeple in/on.  In later turns if that player adds to that structure the Builder allows the player to take a single extra turn.


[b]Thoughts[/b] - 
- Fantastic expansion.  
- Maximizing the Builder get nasty quick.  It is wonderful and adds a layer to the game where other players want to finish your structures to limit your extra turns.  Turns the game so players often play tiles defensively.
- The Goods add a cool new scoring feature that can alter the End Game just enough to tip the scales.  Also adds to the defensive play of the Builder as players will want the Goods.


[b]------------------------------------------------------[/b]


Here I will discuss the [thing=2591][/thing] expansion as played during the Carcassonne Project.


[b]New Components[/b] - 
- 12 tiles with sections of River on them, include a Spring to start the River and a Lake to end it.  Some tiles also have structures on them.


[b]New Mechanics[/b] - 
- This is a new way to begin the game.  Players first build the River and can place Meeples on the River tile structures.  This sort of seeds the game.  Then the game is played as normal.

[b]Thoughts[/b] - 
- This is a great new way to begin the game.  Much better than the single start tile.


[b]------------------------------------------------------[/b]


Here I will discuss the [thing=7707][/thing] expansion as played during the Carcassonne Project.


[b]New Components[/b] - 
- 7 new tiles.  5 Structure tiles with one King tile and one Scout tile.


[b]New Mechanics[/b] - 
- This expansion offers a new scoring mechanic.  The King and the Scout each score bonus end game points.  The King is awarded to the player that built the largest city and grants 1 point per completed city at game end.  The Scout is the same but with Roads.


[b]Thoughts[/b] - 
- A simple expansion that offers a fun new scoring mechanic.


[b]------------------------------------------------------[/b]



Here I will discuss the [thing=12903][/thing] expansion as played during the Carcassonne Project.


[b]New Components[/b] - 
- 12 new tiles that make up the City of Carcassonne and a new Count of Carcassonne meeple.


[b]New Mechanics[/b] - 
- The City of Carcassonne is a new way to begin the game.  The game starts with the City of Carcassonne already in play.  The city is comprised of four sections; Cathedral for Cloisters, Blacksmith for roads, Castle for Cities, and Market for farms.
- Each time a player finishes a structure for another player and scores no points for themselves, that player can add one of their meeples to the City of Carcassonne into one of the sections of the city.  That player may also move the Count of Carcassonne to another city section.
- On later turns when a structure is scored a player may remove his meeple from the corresponding part of the city to score that same amount of points or add to his majority/minority control of that structure.
- The section of city the Count of Carcassonne occupies is closed and may not be used.


[b]Thoughts[/b] - 
- This can be a rather nasty addition to the game and can make for brutal games as everyone fights for control and points of structures.  But it is fun addition to the game as well.
- This expansion takes more long term strategic planning.  Players need to account for meeples leaving the city and stealing points and plan to do so themselves.  Furthermore you must be more careful with your meeples.  You will find yourself very short on available meeples if they are all in the city.


[b]------------------------------------------------------[/b]


Here I will discuss the [thing=15158][/thing] expansion.


[b]New Components[/b] - 
- 30 tiles all containing either a Volcano, a Dragon, a Magic Portal or Princess symbol
- Dragon meeple
- Fairy meeple


[b]New Mechanics[/b] - 
- The Volcano brings the Dragon into play and the Dragon flies to each Volcano as it enters play.
- The Dragon moves whenever a tile with the Dragon symbol enters play.  Each player moves the Dragon one tile orthogonally until it moves 6 total spaces.  The Dragon eats any player meeples on a tiles it is on.  The Dragon will not enter a tile with the Fairy meeple.
- The Magic Portal allows the player to place a meeple on any previously played tile obeying all normal tile laying rules.
- The Princess when played to a city containing any player meeple must remove a meeple from the city.
- The Fairy scores the controlling player 1 point at the beginning of his turn.  If a structure is scored and it contains the Fairy that structure scores an additional 3 points.  The Fairy protects against the Dragon.  When a player lays a tile, but does not play one of his own meeples, he may instead take control of the Fairy placing it on any tiles containing one of his meeples.


[b]Thoughts[/b] - 
- This expansion offers many new changes to the rules including new scoring mechanics and new attack mechanics.  Keeping all the new rules straight is difficult the first few plays.
- The Dragon can get really nasty and clear the board if the Volcano tiles are place well.
- The Magic Portal is meant to allow players to claim structures the Dragon or Princess has cleared of meeples.  But many times it is useless as there are no valid, nor any good, previously played but yet unscored and unclaimed tiles remaining.
- The Fairy often gets forgotten to score each turn given its nature of constantly moving around.
- The Princess can get nasty.  Don't accidentally place her in a city with only one of your meeples present because the Princess must remove a meeple.
- Overall I am not impressed with this expansion.  It is primarily about attacking the other players.  The attacks will either be vicious or completely useless.  The additional scoring mechanics are not really powerful enough to make a difference.


[b]------------------------------------------------------[/b]


Here I will discuss the [thing=18836][/thing] expansion.


[b]New Components[/b] - 
- 12 tiles with sections of River on them, include a Spring to start the River, a River fork and two Lakes to end it.  Some tiles also have structures on them.
- Some tiles contain additional components from prior expansions like an Inn or a Pig Farmer.


[b]New Mechanics[/b] - 
- This is a new way to begin the game.  Players first build the River and can place Meeples on the River tile structures.  This sort of seeds the game.  Then the game is played as normal.

[b]Thoughts[/b] - 
- This is a great new way to begin the game.  Much better than the single start tile.


[b]------------------------------------------------------[/b]


Here I will discuss the [thing=21385][/thing] expansion.


[b]New Components[/b] - 
- 18 Tiles each holding a Tower building place
- 30 Tower pieces
- 1 Tower that holds the tiles


[b]New Mechanics[/b] - 
- A large Tower now holds all the tiles.
- After a player lays a tile he may place a Tower piece instead of a follower.  It must go on an open Tower building place or on top of an existing Tower to further heighten that Tower.
- A meeples may be placed on top of a Tower to cap the Tower so it may not be further built and extended.
- Each Tower has an orthogonal area of influence equal to its height in Tower pieces.  Any opposing meeple within that area of influence may be taken Prisoner after adding a Tower piece.  The player takes that Prisoner meeple off the board and puts it with his meeple supply.  It is no longer in play and no longer adds its influence toward control.
- Prisoner meeples are given back to their controlling player once two players have taken each others meeples as Prisoners.  Or a player can pay 3 points to have a Prisoner meeple returned.


[b]Thoughts[/b] - 
- The Tower is silly.  I did fine without it holding the tiles.
- The Tower rule for taking Prisoners is extremely powerful.  Over powered in my opinion.  With 18 Tower tiles finding them is not difficult.  And with smart placing, you can easily put a Tower in a place to remove many meeples.  The overall effect is that is makes the game center around attacking your opponents.  
- Overall, I do not like this expansion much so it won't get played much.


[b]------------------------------------------------------[/b]


Here I will discuss the [thing=26615][/thing] expansion.


[b]New Components[/b] - 
- 12 Tiles.  Two of the new tiles are used with the two River expansions and are a new Spring and new Lake.  The remaining 10 tiles are new structure tiles.  1 tile has a pig farmer to boost Farmer scoring.


[b]New Mechanics[/b] - 
- No new mechanics.  This expansion uses the rules from the base game and a few other expansions.


[b]Thoughts[/b] - 
- This is a fun little expansion.  A few of the new structure tiles are interesting and not previously seen. 
- Always a good addition to any game.


[b]------------------------------------------------------[/b]
