textfield_comment_value:
Número de Jogadores: 2 a 5
Dificuldade: 2,0/5,0
Indicado para Iniciante: Sim
Contras: Não possui.
Prós: Clássico; jogo lindo na mesa; rejogabilidade bem alta; fácil e rápido de jogar.
 
Comentário: Jogo fácil e rápido de jogar, mas que pede uma estratégia muito grande dos jogadores, o que chama a atenção de jogadores mais experientes.
Clássico dos jogos modernos, pai da nomenclatura "meeple".
No jogo estamos montando a cidade de Carcassonne, onde na sua vez de jogar você compra uma peça e encaixa de acordo com as iconografias devidas, depois você decide se vai descer um meeple nesta peça, podendo virar um ladrão, cavaleiro, fazendeiro ou monge de acordo com o local posto. Cada personagem pontua de uma forma diferente. O jogo termina quando acabarem todas as peças.
O jogo funciona de uma forma muito simples, mas os iniciantes terão um pouco de dificuldade em aprender como conseguir roubar pasto, estrada ou cidade, e até mesmo em ver como funciona a pontuação, principalmente a do fazendeiro. Mesmo assim, indico ele para pessoas iniciantes por ter virado um clássico entre os jogos modernos.
Como você pode montar as peças de várias formas, dificilmente você vai conseguir repetir o mesmo jogo, fazendo com que o jogo tenha uma rejogabilidade absurda.
A arte do jogo vai ficando cada vez mais linda à medida que mais peças entram em jogo.
Jogo para toda família e fica muito lindo na mesa. Indispensável para quem está conhecendo o hobby!
 
Modo Solo: Existe uma variante que me surpreendeu muito! Muito gostosa de jogar e te ajuda a administrar muito bem seus meeples, além de aumentar sua visão na hora de jogar com outros jogadores. É possível encontrar a variante aqui mesmo no site, e digo que é uma das melhores variantes que já joguei!
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
OK, quick fun game.  I much prefer it as a two player affair for many reasons, mostly because it becomes a more strategically taxing game.  With multiple players it's ok to get a little lazy with meeple placement as opponents often complete features and return your meeple for you - two player mode is much more unforgiving and much much more of a game.  Having said that, Dr. Knizia must also have recognised this which is why Carc the Castle is geared so heavily for two player confrontation and results in a far superior game.

I've always seen the tile drawing as making the best use out of what you pull and keeping options open on the board so that you can make good use of as many tiles as possible, playing the odds if you like. If you find yourself relying on getting specific tiles out of the bag then I'd argue you've boxed youself in to poor positions, either that or you are playing with an aggressive wanker like me who will deliberately try to box you in to keep your meeple out of scoring cycles. I guess in that respect I see it as a way of introducing a respect for fluid strategy and putting direct pressure into your opponent's play area, neither of which are admittedly a big thing in the average Euro. I would say that each tile has a subjective value dependent on the current game state, which is why I would pitch it as being a more suitable intro into games where having a fluid and reactive strategy is important.

Even then there is always value in every tile - I may not be able to score anything on a road right now, but you absolutely don't want me to run a road directly into the open end of the city you are building, doubly so if you have the builder in there. The tile can have it's 'value' assessed in different ways.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
If you enjoy this game and want to inject a little extra strategy, try this rule mod my group came up with:

    start the game as normal, but at the end of your turn, draw 3 tiles and place them face up in front of you such that they are visible to all players.
    at the start of each subsequent turn, instead of drawing from the tile pool, choose one of your three tiles and play it as normal.
    at the end of your turn, refresh your hand by returning the tiles you didn't play to the tile pool and drawing three more.
    in the final rounds of the game the tile pool will be too small to maintain this for the group, and unfortunately we have yet to find an ideal solution for this. you may choose to revert to standard tile drawing rules (if you do this I would recommend reverting a round or two before tile circulation becomes impossible, as to avoid full player knowledge of what tiles remain), or to keep what tiles remain in your hand, or to simply end the game at that point.

    possible [and perhaps more strategic], but untested variants of this could be to choose which of your unused tiles get exchanged for new ones if any, and then draw back to 3 tiles. or you could make keeping your tiles for the next turn a trade-off by only drawing fresh tiles when your hand is depleted.

     one last caveat is the builders expansion. when playing a second tile in a single turn your group will have to decide whether it is more balanced to use one of the two tiles remaining in your hand, to draw a random tile from the pool for the builder's turn, to refresh your hand mid-turn for the builder's action, or some other method of resolving the problem. (if you come up with something good, please do tell me about it).
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
The rules are fantastically simple to pick up or explain. Laying down the tiles is an aesthetic joy as the map is created. Though the randomness is inherent to the game, skill will prevail as the 'cheat-sheet' makes it relatively easy to calculate the probabilities of drawing a particular card - weighing up the likelihood of your farmer being connected to a contested field or of your ability to successfully block an opponent's city makes for some interesting decisions.

Ultimately about balancing immediate and eventual rewards, whilst trying to connect cities or farms in your favour, this seems like the ultimate family game - simple enough to explain, enough randomness to give everyone a chance, enough skill to reward playing well and fairly universal instant appeal.

Played with Joel 4x, since we both enjoyed it so much and it seemed a quick game.

-----------------------------------
2008-04-05
Against Dave and Barry, the game dragged on a lot more. I don't know if this was because of the over-analysis or because of the 3-player nature. 

Maybe just a case of improper game/group matching?

Still, I'm now a bit more cautious about how it'll perform with the family.

-------------------------
2010-01-03

Finally played with Family. Played 3x (5p,5p,7p). First 2 times, played without famers or crests. 3rd time, introduced the farmer rule.

Afs took long enough to get a complaint from everyone else. He also (correctly) decreed that only the farm mattered. Indeed, most of the map was a single farm and I won by having 4 farmers. 

Not sure if the single-big-farm was because we didn't play with the river tiles or because of chance.

Still a great game. Works fine with 7. (We used Go stones for dad/I).
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
tl;dr: still solid

This is like the quintessential tile laying game. Players take turns playing tiles with different features in a shared tableau. The only real rules are: tiles have to be adjacent and match any previously played tiles on all ends. Players can place a follower on the newly placed tile in the hopes of getting points. Thanks to some simple rules this creates interesting choices because you can not go on a feature that already has another meeple on it it, so you have to weasel your way in and hope you at least share the majority by the time it scores.
Always play the strategic variant. Firstly, that includes the farmers which have been removed from the base rules to make the game easier for beginners. Shame, it's not that complex, is it? Secondly: players have two tiles, play one and draw a replacement on their turn. This mitigates the luck of the draw somewhat but in our last game I had multiple turns where I had the exact same tile twice. Two bends, two straight roads, two one side cities, two three side cities...
Which brings us to the luck factor: it is there and can play a significant role. If you get almost exclusively road tiles, you are probably not going to win as cities are very important for scoring and road tiles by themselves usually don't offer many opportunities to weasel your way into high scoring farming spaces.
Still, I think this game holds up excellently and is still worth playing. I think I'd probably prefer to play with some of those first expansions thrown in (I have not played any of them after [thing=21385][/thing]) but I'd have to replay them to be sure.

Rating: 7.2/10
BGG scale: 7/10
Components: 8/10 (at least for the original editions)

Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Uno de los euro-juegos más clásicos y el primero que tuve en mi colección.
Su simplicidad es francamente genial, se trata de una especie de una especie de híbrido entre un rompecabezas y un dominó moderno: se amontonan al principio del juego, y al azar, todas las piezas con las que se juega, cuadrados de cartón que contienen dibujos de pequeños trozos de un paisaje compuesto de dos o más de los cuatro elementos que conforman el juego (segmentos de ciudades, segmentos de caminos, segmentos de campos o conventos). 
Se coloca una pieza inicial en la mesa y luego, turno tras turno, cada jugador roba una pieza adicional, al azar, del montón y la coloca en la mesa de tal manera que empalme perfectamente con todas las piezas con las que colinde (segmentos de ciudad deben empalmar con segmentos de ciudad, segmentos de camino con segmentos de camino y segmentos de campo con segmento de campo) hasta que las piezas del montón se terminen.
Cuando un jugador coloca una pieza, tiene la posibilidad de colocar a uno de sus seguidores (fichas de madera, cada jugador empieza con 7) sobre alguno de los elementos presentes en ella (camino, ciudad, campo o convento), bajo ciertas reglas, y así reclamar el elemento como propio.
Las reglas definen los mecanismos para definir como se finaliza la construcción de cada elemento y como se obtienen puntos cuando eso suceda y lo más interesante, como lograr que los jugadores invadan territorios de sus oponentes y tomen posesión de ellos.
Es un juego muy divertido, dinámico y fácil de aprender, ideal para jugar con personas no habituadas a euro-juegos o para personas que quieran empezar en este mundo.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
This is a staple classic I had to add to my collection. I have only played it once so far and we just played the bare minimum so we will be adding in the rivers the next time. I think so far it is a good gateway game or a filler game. There isn't a lot of depth to it or strategy. Sharing something someone else has started building almost seems really cheap but it gets you those points you need. 

It doesn't take up a lot of room on the table which is always nice for a gateway game. It doesn't seem as overwhelming that way. I feel like expansions or variants of this game are definitely needed for me to enjoy it but it is a simple enough game to teach and for people to understand so it will be hitting the table again soon.

EDIT: 
After 5 physical plays and countless plays online I have found that I really enjoy this game. It has a lot more complexity than it might seem at first. The placement restrictions can stop people from taking over your city but other times, someone can jump onto your city or road really easily and you can't do anything to stop them other than hope you have the perfect tile. This can be really annoying but also a big reward if you're the one able to hop onto what someone else is building. 

I have played almost exclusively with the river and it isn't as confusing as I first thought it would be. I would suggest playing with that expansion whenever you can. However, I have just now started to understand the field mechanic. It can be difficult to visualize the area that they will score and it can change really suddenly over the course of the game. Definitely a great addition to the base game though.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Everyone loves this game for some reason, but the lustre has dimmed for me lately. Now when I play, I almost always use some variant to bring down the time of the expanded game (leaving one third of the tiles in the box seems to work well, or you can use Richard Garfield's variant of adding the 50/100 tiles to the tile bag and stopping when three have been drawn).

Carc is the most successful gateway game in my collection, but it has a big problem in that it scales poorly. It's best with 2 players, good with 3 and okay with 4, but with 5 or 6 (as you often see in a gateway gaming situation), it's too random and too long. I've been playing a lot of 4, 5 and 6 player games lately, so I'm a bit burned out on it. Definitely best with 2P, but still too lucky to have staying power as anything other than a gateway / family game.

I would recommend keeping the expansions to a minimum: Inns & Cathedrals plus the tiles (but not the rules) from King & Scout. If you add too many expansions the game becomes fiddly and way too long, and you have to shorten it using one of the above variants. We usually play that after a tile has been placed, the player can draw a fresh tile to study during downtime. This is helpful also.

If you're uncertain whether to get a copy, I say go for it. It's relatively cheap and as a gateway game it's amazing. And meeples come in handy for other games: as player markers in Traders of Genoa, role selection markers in San Juan, etc.

Update: Hating this more. It has well and truly outstayed its welcome.

Update: The iPhone version is much better -- not so much downtime.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value: Brilliant as a first choice Eurogame when introducing a newbie; but probably a bit too too much luck over tactics to regularly sustain playing.  When 4 or 5 players, game starts to become too chaotic to be tactical. More a game for those who enjoy the journey rather than the destination (and hence for 5 players, would -1 from rating if not with newbies).  River expansion a mild diversion if you were a regular player, and you may need to clarify which edition rules you are using at the start of play, otherwise there will be argument over scoring of farmers (13/12/08).  UPDATE: the iPhone application has resulted in my rediscovery of how wonderful this game is, especially after I introduced it at work and with friends.  It really is an enjoyable classic, and I update the rating from 7 to 9, especially as the 4-5 player game starts introduction the concept of mini-alliances which can negate some of the luck of the cards (26/12/10).  UPDATE: To clarify rating, I have given vanilla Carc a rating of 7, but Inns & Cathedrals as a 9; hard to imagine not playing this with the expansion except when introducing the game to newbies - clearly an active game and a definite classic of Eurogaming (17/9/11). UPDATE: Vanilla Carc is still a great game (8.274; May 15).  UPDATE: The older I get, the more I think this is a classic game not just for newbies but to revisit.  Scales well from 2 to 5, with the Inns & Cathedrals expansion making this perfect (any other expansion is superfluous). Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Somehow, I managed to make it to 2014 (that's something like 12 years of being active in the hobby) without playing Carcassonne.

I understand why this game has such a lasting appeal. It's a REALLY good weight - it's deep enough to be interesting for gamers and simple enough that I could see explaining it to a non-gamer easily, and actually having them get something out of it. I really like the curve of the game where you start out with very limited options and gradually as the game progresses you wind up with more and more to think about - feels perfect for a gateway game. The choices themselves are sufficiently juicy, and the not-insignificant amount of luck ties neatly into a fun risk-reward system and the game's profoundly interesting social landscape.

The game has this really fun semi-coop element (especially at larger player counts where you really have to rely on other players) that really promotes tabletalk and keeps people engaged. I've never seen such a simple dry Euro get people talking so much before - each tile draw sees players crowding around the active player, discussing the pros and cons of potential placements, and how they affect other players.

The only things that truly bug me is the farmer scoring and the road tiles. Farmers feel overly complicated and it's just hard to judge whose farmers are doing well at any given point. And roads just feel underpowered.

Note: Always play this where you redraw at the END of your turn so you have a full round to consider your next move. This should really just be the official rule.

textfield_comment_value:
I had heard so many good things about this, but every time I looked at pictures or reviews I thought "this is so bland." How in the world could you have an enjoyable game by placing a tile, and then claiming it by deciding to put a little man on it or not? I got into modern board games to get away from chess-like abstract things like this.

Someone at work was having a moving sale, and had this up for grabs for $10 or so. I figured what the heck, for $10 I can at least say I've tried a classic. And man was I wrong.

This game IS an absolute classic and deserves all the praise its had heaped upon it over the years. It's charming in its simplicity - to me, it's the perfect "play on a lazy summer afternoon, drinking iced tea on a patio with the sound of droning lawnmowers in the background" game, but it also has a deceptively deep level of strategy that may not be apparent your first play or two. I've heard that the earlier big box expansions are pretty good, but honestly? I don't want to try them just yet. Carcassonne in its base form has a purity that I don't want to risk tarnishing with needless additions.

If there's one thing I could ding it for, it's that it might be too lightweight for me to play over and over again in a short period of time, but it's a minor complaint. What a great way to have my expectations broken.

~

After a bunch of plays, I find that my complaint of it being a bit too light for me definitely works to its detriment. I still enjoy it but it doesn't really satisfy me as much as a heavier game would.

textfield_comment_value:
I'd bought this game about 3-4 years ago, and we'd played it once in that intervening time (I got stomped, and I wasn't so thrilled about bringing it back out to play).

In 10/2006, I dragged the game out and we (a friend, my wife and I) decided to give it a try again.  I learned two things:  this game is really rather good, and don't annoy my wife.

The game is the classic tile laying game, so it really needs no introduction.  If everyone knows how to play it (and can get past the rules, which constantly change the name of the figures you have and so make it hard at first to understand), the game is rather fun.  Unfortunately, we were a little hazy on the farm part, and so when my friend put down a farmer, my wife got really annoyed that she'd now pretty much lost the game before it started.  In spite of me trying to point out that there were plenty of opportunities to get back in the game, my wife remained annoyed at me until we played a game of Settlers (in which she stomped all over us).

What I've been tempted to do with the rules is to cross out the terms "thief", "farmer", "knight", and "abbot/monk" and replace them with "meeple" to make for easier reading.

Since that day in October 2006, my wife and I have played many times, and now that we have some strategy down, the game is really rather fun.

(EDIT: Aug 22, 2007): We don't get this game out to play that much these days, and when we do, it's usually a fallback filler type of game.  I'm bumping the number down to 6 accordingly.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Carcassone is a light, relaxing game. In Carc, players take turns placing a single tile which might depict a farm and a road, a city, or a cloister - or a combination of these. Then you have the option of placing a meeple on your tile (as a knight, bandit, monk, or farmer - depending upon whether you put him on a city, road, cloister, or farm); and then there's some scoring business. There is something very pleasurable about slowly building the French countryside with others, and the scoring mechanism is ingenious. Learning when to deploy farmers takes a bit of strategizing. Now don't get me wrong, there is real strategy at work here - Carc just "feels" kind of light to me. This makes it an ideal game for social play. Skill matters (some anyway), but you don't feel that you have to watch the play like a hawk to perform well. My rating for this game includes a slight variant we use: we add the river tiles in with the rest (as opposed to playing them all at the beginning or leaving them out) and then use them to "screw your neighbor." Try it! It adds a little bit of ruthlessness to the bucolic setting.

There was a time when I rated Carc higher, and I do think it is a great game. But I've now played it sooooo many times, it's become a little stale. For a strategic game, I find myself desiring something a lot meatier, with greater control.

CHILDREN'S RATING: 8

This is fun to play with even very small kids too - just remove/simplify the scoring and play it primarily as an edge-matching game.

textfield_comment_value:
TL;DR: Genius.  Perhaps the best family board game in the "real board game" category.

We've all had that "first date" moment when we've got some new friends over and you get vulnerable and admit to liking board games, at this point one of two things happens, either they say "Oh, I love Sorry!" and you know it's just not going to work, or they say: "Oh you mean like Catan?"  And you're like "I can tell that we are gonna be friends!"

This is the prime example of a game to be used if there is anything in between those two situations.  It is, like Catan, the gateway drug of what my wife and I call "real board games".  It is perhaps not as rich as the "harder stuff", to continue the metaphor, but a great staple for any board game shelf.

The farming mechanic is the one difficulty with getting "Sorry players" into it.  But it is also the one mechanic that you must master in order to be a truly accomplished veteran of this game.  It is the part of the game the is actually a challenge to master and it becomes a key part of veteran strategies.

Even great for littles if they know how puzzles work, and you're willing to let them play with the components.  My 4 year-old could join us for a "real" game.  Good-bye snakes and ladders/candy land!  Granted, her strategy isn't great most of the time, but just putting down meeples in random places resulted in a strong win.

Pros:
- Simple mechanics
- Good amount of randomization
- Nice artwork
- Fun to replay

Cons:
- Farming is a bit difficult for beginners
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value: Most of this game is a fine, if a little basic town building euro game, but it hs a few flaws that completely ruin it for me. The game is very random since every card is shared in the same pile, you can't really plan ahead, the only form of skill or strategy can be done in the moment, or planning aroudn which pieces EXIST not what is likely to find, spending half the game hoping you're the lucky player to find the one card in the deck that fits in a certain space based on how the board hs developed. Then it also hs the mechanic I despise more than almost anything else, town joining. By being able to start a city next to someone else's and join into theirs, you can share it for both getting the points and basically leeching off their effort to score a lot of points, and joining in extra to take control fully. The purpose of this is to allow interaction and counterplay, but due to the way the deck is designed, there is very little you can do against this, so a lucky/malicious player can just leech off of the town that was all you've been able to build up all game, causing everything to feel pointless because you can't build a point lead. Maybe if there were a lot more tiles that could block out joining attempts maybe it'd be better but as is it just makes the game a frustrating mess of hoping nobody joins into your hard work and made all of that time wasted. Additionally, this is one of the only games my dad will want to play, so I am sick of him doing this all the time I hate it so much.

textfield_comment_value:
The beauty of Carcassonne is in its plug and play expandability. There are piles of interesting expansions for this game, almost all of which can be added or removed without negatively impacting gameplay. In fact, using different combinations of expansions drastically alters gameplay strategies (and almost always in a good way). The game has never really gotten old, mainly because we are always trying new things with it. Every time Carcassonne hits the table, it is with a different combination of expansions. As such, every play is a whole new experience.

I also enjoy the fact that the game can be played as a relaxing social experience or a brutal gamer showdown. There is a surprising amount of screwage that can be passed around the table for such an unassuming little game, yet you can just as easily play nice and make pretty pictures. For me (and my group, for the most part), this is one of those rare games that has gotten better after every play. I remember being lost my first play and confused my second, then loathing even sitting down for my third game. After the scoring mechanisms had finally sunk in, I found myself compulsively wanting another play. It's a hit with my wife, my kids, and most of my gamer buds, What more could you ask for?

Recommended Variants: Always play with a starting hand of two or three tiles instead of simply drawing and playing off the top of the stack. This adds even more strategy and planning to what is already a deceptively deep game.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
“If you build it, he will come.” - Shoeless Joe Jackson

GAMEPLAY
Player take turns laying connecting city, road and abbey tiles to build the city of Carcassonne. A player turn consists of laying a tile and deciding wether to place a meeple. As the city grows, the meeples claim cities(as knights), roads(as thieves), cloisters (as friars), and farms(as farmers). Completing each will give points during the game and return the meeple to the player’s hand. Unfinished areas are scored at the end of the game. Points are totaled and a winner declared.
COMPONENTS
The whole game consists of 72 tiles, 40 meeples, and the scoring track. All of the pieces are of high quality. The tiles are thick and hard which is important because they are handled so much. The meeples are painted wood and feel good in your hand.
THEME
Carcasonne is one of the important games of modern board gaming. Meeples have become an icon of gaming. The meeples and the art style work well together but this game could be re-themed to suit many eras.
WHO IS IT FOR?
This is a great game for families and is familiar to so many that its a good way to start your gaming session. Because there is little to keep track of, its fun for younger players from 8 and up. Games last from 30 to 45 minutes.

There is a wonderfully implemented ios version of Carcassone. Play locally or online. Also there is a solos version of the game with a set stack of tiles. Scores are based on how few tiles necessary to complete cities and roads.

textfield_comment_value:
[i]Soylent Green is Meeples![/i]

Quickly a favorite at our house.. And since my wife loves it, Carcassonne gets more play in the house. Fantastic as a gateway game for our non-gamer friends, but usually requires a second play before they fully "get it." Carc gets the most play out of any of the games we own and is the most requested among friends, both gamers and non-gamers. It works well as a group game and exceedingly well as a very confrontational 2-player game. 

[b]We play only third edition rules.[/b] :) We play with Basic, both River sets, King & Scout, Inns & Cathedrals, Traders & Builders and Die Katharer. We are very skeptical about what The Count, Princess & Dragon and The Tower have to offer, so we haven't bothered. 

[i]House Rules[/i] - Game starts using the river (using River 1 & 2), we start with the river fork and set three river ends aside for after the other river pieces are played.. expanding the river in three directions at once. We use colored glass markers (similar to Go pieces) as scoring markers instead of sacrificing a meeple to the scoreboard. We also use these glass markers to mark who built the biggest city & road during play and to assist in counting completed cities and roads at the end of the game for King & Scout scoring. 

[i]Note[/i] that this rating I've given Carc is for playing with the above mentioned expansions and 3rd edition rules. Playing Carc with just the basic set and 1st ed rules would be a rating of 8.

textfield_comment_value:
Update: Gave to Bryan.

Over time I have realized this game has two features I have increasingly come to dislike in Eurogames: 

First, while at first appearing to be a light building game, it often features moves to either share, or worse, snatch, the points from an area that someone else worked over time to build.  This tends to sour the mood. A game I got rid of for similar reasons is Tikal, and Serenissimma also has this problem with capturing ships full of cargo. Note this is different than area control, since the values of areas in area-control games pre-exist, you don't create their value with your turns only to have them snatched away. These days I vastly prefer games where stuff you build or collect can't be messed with. 

Second, I have realized some card-counters are tracking the types of tiles left in the bag, essentially playing what should be a light game at far too competitive a level.  Hidden-but-trackable information spoils the soup for me because I always wonder if one of these people is at the table with a hidden advantage.  Tigris & Euphrates also has this problem but you can at least solve it there (albeit by slowing down the game) by playing the points openly.

-----

Lots of fun, light, lots of luck (which bothers some people), better with some expansions - in the original game it was often too hard to finish cities, leaving ugly gaps all over the map.

Includes Inns and Cathedrals, and Traders and Builders.

textfield_comment_value:
Pienso que Carcassonne es uno de los mejores juegos de mesa para aquellos que empiezan a adentrarse en el mundillo (como yo, básicamente jajajajaj). Tiene unas mecánicas muy sencillas pero que ofrecen partidas infinitas. Hasta el momento, no he tenido ninguna partida similar a otra, en todas ocurren cosas que no esperas. Además, la proporción entre suerte y estrategia es más equilibrada, que, por dar un ejemplo, Catan. La naturaleza minimalista del juego base es suficiente para ofrecer mucho contenido. 

Lo único que le echo en falta a la versión original es que le falta choque entre los jugadores (me gusta mucho el puteo, lo siento), pero esto se puede paliar con la expansión de La Princesa y El Dragón. Sé que no es la expansión preferida de muchos jugadores, pero pienso que le da mucha chicha al juego base y les fuerza a planear las estructuras con mayor antelación. El hecho de poder perder toda una ciudad o perder un Meeple a punto de conseguir un monasterio, hace que la tensión sea mayor, y la estrategia, también. 

También hay más expansiones con otros propósitos, todo depende de lo que cada jugador busque. Lo que tengo claro es que, una vez juegas con una expansión, es complicado volver al juego base, en especial cuando buscas una mayor complejidad en las partidas. Por último, me gustaría comentar cómo cada vez el artwork ha ido empeorando más y más con los años... Una auténtica pena. Sigue siendo recomendable.

textfield_comment_value:
Buy the full game. The pieces in this travel edition are only slightly smaller than the original set. This means two things, ultimately - it isn't all that much more portable and it will never be compatible with the normal expansions. This version has none of the other common travel-related features, such as magnetic tiles/meeples to reduce sliding. (Magnetic Meeples! oh my.)

That said, I'd like to comment that our normal play set consists of the original game, Inns & Cathedrals, Traders & Builders, King & Scout, River 1 & 2, die Cartherer, and the mini-expansion from Games Quarterly magazine #11. All of these pieces from all of the sets fit into the original box with the original insert (without hiding pieces underneath.) The trick is to carefully lay the meeples flat in a ziplock sandwich baggie on top of the scoreboard. We almost always take it with us when traveling and have never had an issue with room.. although it could be further collapsed into a smaller package by removing the box from the equation.

The only thing I do like (and feel a bit envious of) is the scoreboard bag included in the travel set... We normally prefer to pull tiles from a bag, but this would not be possible if using the bag as a scoreboard. I can, however, see the advantage of having a cloth scoreboard, since it would be easier to pack. I may have to design such a thing from an old shirt and printer-friendly iron-on paper.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
I struggle to rate this higher since it has such a niche place in my collection. I've almost exclusively played it two player, and almost every play has been with my wife. I truly enjoy our games together as much as almost any other game experience I have, but I don't know how much of that is the game.

Carcassonne is beautiful, and it's a delightful experience to see the board slowly come together over the course of a match. The expansions are a lot of fun, and add some interesting wrinkles to the base game strategy.

Carcassonne can be annoyingly cutthroat. Optimal play can seem pretty brutal at times, and someone stealing a castle you worked on for many turns can feel pretty crappy. There is also a potential for large blowouts in cases of dissimilar skill. Thankfully not an issue I have much anymore, since my wife has learned the game well enough to routinely thump me.

All in all, I really enjoy Carcassonne, but I have such a narrow use for it that I'm not sure it deserves a higher grade. In the specific situation of two player games, with my wife, it's an 8 or a 9, but outside of that, I can't see it reaching that high.

No sleeves required.

Update April 3, 2019:
6->7
Credit where credit is due, I play this a reasonable amount with my wife's family, and it's a good time. Point awarded for being so accessible and pleasant that I can recruit three other people to play without much difficulty.

textfield_comment_value: I don't like giving Carcassonne just a Five. Building the board as you play, and placing your peeps on it feels cool. It is simple, easy to play, and really fun to watch the board expand into a beautifully confusing medieval landscape as you progress. I really do appreciate this game. BUT for me, its just not that exciting to play. I'm a competitive person and when I play, I find myself just placing tiles in a spot where they look the prettiest, not really focusing on winning. It's just not invigorating enough. Once you've placed one of your people on the board, you're kind of just waiting till you get the right pieces so that you can take them off and score points. The only part that can get exciting is the end of game farm warfare. Trying to steal your opponents farms can get pretty intense. It also feels good to magically find the perfect piece you've been waiting for all game. I wonder if the expansions add much spice to this game? Oh and I HATE the river tiles, they always ends up messing with the aesthetics of the board because it will leave holes where you couldn't find a piece with a river, road, and city in it. But the river tiles are a great tool for screwing over your opponent(s). I would be interested to see what rating this game would get if it were released today. All in all, I get a little bored playing this game, but it's still solid and I love that it exists.

textfield_comment_value:
Where this game obviously shines is that it's very easy to learn, and can be a great gateway game. A lot of people also like to for nostalgic reasons. I however have not played it back in the day and had the chance a while ago.

I've moved past the gateway game phase a couple years ago and this just isn't very interesting. The only thing you're really doing is flipping a tile and hoping it is one you can place on your territory. Aside from the fact that it's purely luck pased, there's also a lot of downtime. With 2 players it's allright but the more players participating, the more the downtime because. And then the game can really drag on for what it is. So for me it just isn't interesting at all. There are no interesting decisions. Someone can also really fuck up your city by randomly drawing a tile and deciding to place it in your area, causing your chances of picking a tile that fits to decrease drastically.

This being said the end product (when it finally comes) is satisfying. Every time you play you build an entire landscape which really looks cool. The strength of this game is introducing people to boardgaming and it does that fairly well. Because of the high luck factor new players also have a good chance at winning. For a seasoned boardgamer who isn't nostalgic however, it's just uninteresting because of the high luck factor and long playtime.

textfield_comment_value:
Liked it with experienced players who helped me. Still can't visualize the farmer's fields well enough or know when to place them. I do like the graphics better than Hunters and Gatherers but like its scoring better. Just venturing in to expansions now.

Almost twenty years later: use two tile hand variant?

Enders Game says:
An excellent tile-laying game, children also enjoy the game play and medieval theme immensely. 2001 SDJ winner. Best with just two players. House-rule of having three tiles in hand is worth considering when playing with more than two players, to make the game more strategic and less dependent on luck-of-the-draw. At the very least, draw your tile after your turn, so that players can plan their move and avoid downtime.

Recommended: play with third edition rules, where scoring is more consistent:
- 2 tile cities are worth 4 points (i.e. all cities and pennants score 2 points per tile)
- farmers scoring works by scoring each field, not each city (i.e. calculate which farmers control a field, and then that field scores 3 points per completed city touching that field)
These 3rd Edition rules score fields just like all other features: (a) points go to the players with the most followers in the feature; (b) remove followers, score next.
See here for discussion on 1st vs 3rd edition rules. (See Geekbuddy comments)

2/17/2023
With expansion 1 and 2 and the mini expansion (which has the old art).

My wife really dislikes the farmers. So we stopped playing with them and haven't missed them at all. I teach this without them (or the related pigs) and there's enough content with the expansions that I have never wanted to add them back in. I think I've also decided I don't like them either and the game plays faster without them.

The river: We always use this. I like it. It gives a shape to things. We don't use the farming mechanism, so I use a combo of old and new river tiles so that they all have a scoring option.

Expansion 1: We always use the Big meeples. Cathedrals are in the bag, but sometimes we skip them when they are pulled. Inns are also sometimes yes and sometimes no, but I like having more tiles, whether we score the inns or not.

Expansion 2: We sometimes use the Traders, I like it, but when this gets played, people usually like to keep it simpler. We never use Builders, and, of course, we never use the Pigs. So, why purchase this one? The cloth bag is nice, but it also just adds a bunch more tiles.

This is a really good game that I feel has aged very well. You can certainly mix and match to desired complexity, but, with the exception of the big meeples that we always use, I am fine with playing base rules minus the farmers.

[i]Posted: 10/2/04, Rated: 8[/i]

[i]Carcassonne[/i] is a fun game, with easy mechanics.  My five year-old (at the time of this writing) is able to play effectively.  I do have a couple of small complaints, though. The first has to do with tile memorization: when it is my turn, how I place a certain tile should be affected by my knowledge of the remaining pieces.  I feel that my understanding of the game is limited by not memorizing all of the different tile configurations with respect to roads, cities, fields, etc.  

The other complaint that I have is how overwhelmingly strong a well-placed farmer can be. In some games, I have found myself eschewing the completion of cities or monasteries, just so I could extend the reach of a single farmer. The farming score at the end of these games was obscenely large, and resulted in what appeared to be a huge come from behind win.

[i]Carcassonne[/i] can be taught to new players very quickly, and is a good introduction for those who have never played a European game before.

[i]Updated: 8/29/10, Rated: 7[/i]

[i]Carcassonne[/i] is still a good game, but it's not a "go to" title for which I would go out of my way to find a game.  Perhaps with the right blend of expansions it can still be an "8," but not on its own.

textfield_comment_value:
Carcassonne is great, a solid design that has stood the test of time, but man I have just played it so much over the years that I'm kind of starting to be done with it - or at least with the vanilla base Carcassonne. I would always want to play with at least the first two expansions, the problem of course being that the more expansions you add the longer the game goes on for, often to a point that it starts to outstay it's welcome a little bit. I also only really like it at two (or a maximum of three) players since both the downtime and the luck of the draw increase as you add more players, and with lower player counts it's really quick and fun head-to-head.

It is a very good and beautifully simple classic though, since at it's very core it's just "draw a tile, place a tile, and (optionally) put a meeple on the tile". It feels like no other game to come out since Carcassonne has managed to really hone in on the pure tile-laying experience like this. Remains as one of the best casual gateway games (though the farmers always seem to be super confusing for new people), but can still be played and enjoyed by experienced gamers in a more competitive way. It's also just really enthralling seeing the map of the landscape sprawl and develop during the game, even though I do wish the tiles were hexagons instead of squares...
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value: Getting Carcassonne marked the beginnings of the boardgame hobby for me. This was before I was even aware of the plethora of categories of games and before I knew of Euro or AT mast to pin my colors on. I can't remember what attracted me in Carc, or whether it came recommended by someone, but I can remember that initially I really enjoyed the game. I introduced it to just about anyone we had over, and it seemed to fit any group, any time and every mood. We played this with all counts, but most games, around half I'd wager, have been just the wife and I, and we played really cuththroat. No matter how I've changed and how what I value in games has shifted, one thing has clearly remained: I play for fun. In our 2P Carc, winning mattered, but having fun mattered more. And what was fun was contesting castles, nevermind how effective it was pointswise, and imagining what was happening, teasing each other and, sometimes, outsmarting the other and being outsmarted. Sadly, we've come to a point where I can't approach Carc with that same, open let's-have-fun-with-this -attitude I used to.  For better and for worse, I acquired a taste, and am unable to enjoy anything and everything. It's not with a heavy heart that I gave up Carc, or with teary nostalgia or anything soft like that, but it does remind me of a simpler time.

textfield_comment_value:
This is many people's gateway game for good reason. It is simple to learn, satisfying to lay tiles, and can be played either mindlessly or quite confrontationally.  I play this with my 9 year old, and I also play with the other game night dads (this is one game that we can all agree on).

Gameplay at low player count is more about building smaller things and cycling through meeples, whereas at higher player counts there is a lot of stealing farms and cities or placing tiles to screw people over.

I have played with Inns and Cathedrals, and I am not sure if it adds much.  This tends to devolve into trying to ruin someone's city with the cathedral.  The rare time the cathedral city is completed, it results in a runaway, so it kind of takes the fun out of the game.

To increase complexity, you can add an auction mechanic ala Kingdomino. Start players at 5 points and play in rounds by flipping tiles equal to number of players at start of a round. Then have players bid points for each tile. Winner places tile first. 

Pros:  Simple to learn. Wide appeal. Good level of player interaction. 

Con: Less long range planning/depth and can sometimes feel like next move is too obvious, Favors those who know the distribution of the different tiles, otherwise can be dependent on luck of draw.

textfield_comment_value:
Do you remember your friends from kindergarten? Remember how you couldn't wait to leave the house in the morning because you were still working on that airplane to fly to the moon, or to see that invisible squirrel again, or to finally convince Ms. Miller that beans actually can grow out of children's ears? Do you remember how you were entirely convinced that life will always stay that way and you will always be friends, solving the worlds mysteries together?

And do you still see your friends from kindergarten? Well, to be honest, I don't. My kindergarten friends were great, while I was at kindergarten age. Life was simple. Planes that were made of cardboard were able to fly you to the moon (and back). But by now, life is more complicated, and suddenly cardboard airplanes are ... well ... basically just the cardboard wrapping that came with new fridge. 
It is the same with Carcassonne (and Settlers of Catan, really, I don't see a difference). It was great starting with those games, they defined a whole new world while that world was new. But by now, so many other great games are out there, and Carcassonne and Settlers are ... just cardboard. Nice, lovely cardboard full of good old memories, but basically just cardboard.

Oh, screw it. I admit I do miss that squirrel.

Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
This is another early game that I taught my girlfriend and one that remains as one of her favorites to this day. 

I went through a period where I was cool to this game. It seemed a little too random to be really interesting, and I was busy with investigating other games. Since then, my opinion of the game has improved quite a bit. 

At its core Carcassonne is an investment game. It isn't about investing in stocks, or countries, or railroads but about investing in particular landscape developments. Now, these investments may not pay off. You may end up failing to get the tiles you need to get the really high dividends. You must also manage your resources (actions and meepless both) in order to take true advantage of your existing investments without ignoring emergent possibilities. You have to watch out for hostile take-overs from other individuals who have decided they liked what you have built up and want to take it over.

So now I am quite fond of it, particularly with the various expansions both big (Traders & Builder plus Inns & Cathedral) and small (The River II; King & Scout; Cults, Creativity, Siege). It will never be a Top 10 game for me, but it is a game that has earned a definite place in my collection. 

Best with 2>3>Anything else

JUEGO DE COLOCACIÓN DE LOSETAS Y COLOCACION DE TRABAJADORES

Carcassonne es un juego de colocación de fichas en el que los jugadores dibujan y colocan una ficha con un trozo de paisaje del sur de Francia. La ficha puede incluir una ciudad, una carretera, un claustro, un prado o alguna combinación de los mismos, y debe colocarse junto a las fichas que ya se han jugado, de manera que las ciudades estén conectadas con ciudades, caminos con caminos, etcétera. Después de colocar una loseta, el jugador puede decidir colocar uno de sus meeples en una de las áreas de la misma: en la ciudad como un caballero, en el camino como un ladrón, en un claustro como un monje o en el césped como un granjero. Cuando esa área está completa, ese meeple anota puntos para su propietario.

Durante un partido de Carcassonne, los jugadores se enfrentan a decisiones como: "¿Realmente vale la pena poner mi último meeple allí?" o "¿Debo usar esta loseta para expandir mi ciudad, o debo colocarla cerca de mi oponente, lo que le dificulta completar su proyecto y sumar puntos?" Dado que los jugadores colocan solo una ficha y tienen la opción de colocar una sola pieza sobre ella, los turnos se desarrollan rápidamente incluso si se trata de un juego lleno de opciones y posibilidades.

Carcassonne was my 'gateway' into the world of proper board games.

I guess for the same reason that not many people know about "that little Italian place outside of town that serves the most unbelievably authentic pizza", and instead frequent the more obvious and dominant restaurants, such as Dominoes, Pizza Hut, or Pizza Express*, one can never really know the true depth of scope when it comes to board games, if all you know is Toys'R'Us.

* don't get me wrong, I will happily trample over my own grandmother for a Pizza Express.

I had not scratched the surface of this world, but I was eager to claw my way into its depths. In purchasing Carcassonne, I had effectively discovered the Italian place, and tentatively ordered a margarita.

This game is great for kids (I have a 12 year old who can verify this), but just as good for a wine-fueled evening for two. Games are quick enough to not feel too hard done by if you lose, because before you know it, you're playing the next one.

As with all games, play this one enough and you'll eventually get that "played to death" feeling, but don't let that put you off. Carcassonne is a great game and I would wholeheartedly recommend it to anyone... especially if they're not really gamers.

textfield_comment_value:
I like games where the board is never the same and this is one of Carcassonne's biggest perks.  You create the board as you play.  I like it far more than Catan simply because there is less luck involved (anyone who tells you Carcassonne involves mostly luck simply doesn't know how to play it well - make good plays and it's rare you'll draw a tile that is not useful to you in some manner).

In a nutshell you are building a landscape with Roads, Cities, Fields, Abbeys, etc.  You 'claim' one of those things (if someone has not already) with a game piece (a 'meeple') of which you have seven.  Once someone has claimed the start of one of the individual structures building on to it and completing it will provide you points.  When you complete one you get the 'meeple' back that was on it in order to play it on a new construction.

The base game is very simple and easy to learn, but mastering it will make you really pay attention to the board.  There are many expansions to this game, so I would suggest buying the base game and the "River II" to start with, then read up on the expansions and add in the ones that look appealing to you.  I've added a couple expansions, but I find trying to use them all gets to be too much.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
GAMEPLAY: A tile-placement and area-control eurogame. Players take turns drawing and placing a tile. The player who placed a tile decides whether to place one of her limited supply of meeples on one of the features on the tile, hoping to score victory points later on when the feature is completed by the placement of other tile(s) or at the end of the game. The game ends after the last tile is placed. The game is improved by some of the expansions. I recommend Traders & Builders and Inns & Cathedrals in particular. I prefer to play with no more than two expansions at a time.

WEIGHT: Medium-light. The rules are not complex.

PLAYER INTERACTION/CONFLICT: High. If there are not struggles for control of large features in your game, you aren’t playing it right.

PLAYER COUNT: Scales fine from two to five players but luck increases with higher player counts. A good high-conflict two-player game.

LUCK: Moderate. Lucky tile draws can certainly determine the outcome of games. As the player count increases and each individual player necessarily draws fewer tiles throughout the game, the luck factor also increases and more games will be won by whomever happened to draw the right tile at just the right moment.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
The classic game that popularized tile-laying.  There are a lot of factors involved in winning the game: there is the luck of drawing the right tile you need, there is strategy of seeing the best option amongst many on the board; there is also a push-your-luck aspect when you decide if you should finish off a castle or keep going.  Very experienced players may often have an advantage as they’ve already seen all the possible tiles that exist and can even judge the probability of drawing the one they need.  However luck is still a mitigating factor to keep new players involved and usually scores are always very close amongst all players.  
The only cons I can think of is that the scoring session at the end is can be a bit involved, and scoring for the farmers in particular can be a bit of a pain.  There can also be a bit of downtime between turns when playing with five or six players (expansion for sixth player sold separately) especially with players prone to Analysis Paralysis.   The popular house-rule of drawing a tile for your next turn at the end of your current turn is recommended for faster play.   
Overall, this game holds up very well over the years and makes an excellent gateway game.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value: Meh.  I play mostly 2 player games with my boyfriend, and we played this when we were relatively new to gaming.  This game shows up on all of the lists recommending games for newbie players/couples to start out with, but I'm really glad this wasn't the first game we got because I don't know if we would have continued.  It was "fine" but decidedly underwhelming.  We got the Inns & Cathedrals expansion and also tried some house rules (drawing more tiles for example) -- that helped, but the game just had no tension.  Maybe if we knew the tiles better and could predict which tiles would come up and then try to plan out our moves... but if we were going to do that, I'd rather play a heavier game with more to it.  I can say that I enjoy the iPad version much more -- moves way quicker and it's helpful to see where you can/can't move.  Also, we didn't find the scoring that complicated as some people did, so that didn't scare us off.  I get that the board is nice looking, but there's no sense of having accomplished anything at the end -- you have no idea looking at the board at the end which of the cities/roads are yours, and which are your opponents.  Really just quite boring.  We traded it away.

這款美術與農家樂一樣!簡單的線條外加淺色調的彩繪，美術看起來十分有童趣，說真的這一類有強烈主題的歐式遊戲，若改搭美式漫畫風格或寫實風格就真的就格格不入了，我喜歡這一款的美術!至於米寶工人，我不知道起源在那一款遊戲!但我接觸到的桌遊!好像卡卡頌的米寶最具知名度，令人印象深刻!

規則:0.9
抽圖板、擺放圖板(拼圖)、放置工人、換對手，就是這麼簡單的流程，除了要將最後的農夫計分講解清楚外!其他工人的計分方式都十分直覺，教學上也十分容易，除了擴充有一大堆不同規則要消化外，基本上款這遊戲的規則讓遊戲流程十分順暢!

設置:1
這是一款設置容易的遊戲!我喜歡攻城塔的擴充配件，把圖板全部放置攻城塔上，圖板抽完遊戲結束，十分實用的小配件!(尤其是一大堆擴充圖板不知要如何取捨時)

路線:0.4
基本上就是看你抽到板塊的運氣，來選擇要用那種工人取分，得分路線不多(擴充增加部分得分路線，但相對的也給遊戲增加複雜度，造成遊戲規則太多特例影響遊戲流暢度)，有時抽牌運氣不是很好的時候，你會發現你會被卡很久!

互動:0.8
基本上我覺得卡卡頌是兩人遊戲，雖然遊戲可以2-6人(加擴充)但人越多玩家閒置發呆的情形就更明顯，尤其要在一大片拼圖中，找出可以放置手上這片板塊的位置，有時真的要找好久!加上多人遊戲中，大家互相卡來卡去，越多人就越卡，真的變成卡卡不爽的遊戲了!所以我推薦本款兩人玩最佳人數!不過三人局也可以試試，玩起來會更有合眾連橫的政治角力感覺!

個人:0.8
我是很推薦這款遊戲，想等小朋友長大點就教他玩這款遊戲，可以訓練觀察力、也好過單人玩需要大量時間又無代入感的拼圖遊戲!(這句話得罪很多拼圖愛好者)

朋友:0.8
我跟我老婆玩兩人場，老婆說十分有趣，跟同事玩五人場，大家只想草草結束，我想這款還是兩人專用就好!雖然同事並無惡評，但我想大家會更想玩別的。(挑人數開很重要)最近跟5歲的女兒玩兩人局，小朋友愛的反應出乎我意料之外，女兒常說要開卡卡頌，而且要玩不同的擴充。學校桌遊社教學，大部分的小朋友也很喜歡。

想玩:0.8
玩了很多重度策略類型的遊戲，偶爾會想試試這款輕度桌遊，享受你卡我我卡你的樂趣!

收藏:1
擴充很多，每款都替這遊戲帶來不同的變化，說實在的這款遊戲不容易玩膩，我會想好好收藏!

總分:8.4
講評:兩人互卡、三人眾橫、四人等等、五人等等等、六人等等等等等!好遊戲?我會說是經典遊戲!
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
This was our gateway game.  The tile placement mechanism is very conceptual and understandable---you just have to match up the edges.  Using meeples for controlling different areas elevates the strategy above simple tile matching.  

We were also able to still have fun playing with only two players.  For the first couple of months, we would play several times each night.  We would play over and over again.  The best part of the game, and something that I think is underrated, is that the gameplay scales very well with your experience level.  In the beginning, we would play nicely and it became more of a "race" game to finish features.  But as we played it more, we began to get a lot more aggressive and cut-throat as we'd hone in and try to steal each other's cities, roads, and farms.  You can fine tune the amount of interactivity in the game to the comfort of each player.  

Even after several years, we still have [url=http://www.boardgamegeek.com/geeklist/39484/item/862918#item862918]tense, nerve-wracking games[/url].  I have to give it a well-deserved  10 rating.

Session Reports:  [url=http://www.boardgamegeek.com/thread/297568]A Farewell Carcassonne Match[/url]

Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
PROS:
- The decision space has a lot of room for experienced gamers whilst being simple enough ruleset for a gateway game
- There's a underlying push your luck element which isn't easily solved
- No 2 games are ever the same as the map evolves differently game-to-game
- Game is very interactive as you can snipe points off other players given the right plays

CONS:
- The game is still so luck based depending on the tiles you draw (a community rule to draw 2 tiles instead of 1 helps mitigate this)
- You need at least 1-2 expansions for the game to be replayable, otherwise the game will feel quite rinse and repeat
- There's some downtime as you can't really plan out your turn until you draw the next tile (a community rule to pre-draw your next tile after you take your turn helps a lot with this)
- Sometimes, it can feel quite solitary if you're building on a lesser contested side of the map

FINAL THOUGHTS:
My favourite gateway board game, as it is highly interactive and highly engaging. I haven't yet met a person who didn't enjoy this game.

Replayability: 4/5
Player Interaction: 5/5
Downtime: 3/5 (4/5 with community rule)
Strategy vs Luck: 3/5 (4/5 with community rule)

textfield_comment_value:
This one comes out with the family a lot. Lot's of people think of it as a gateway game, but I have trouble teaching it. I have had success teaching the first game without farms, then adding farms the second game.

It also makes a great lunchtime game.
-----------------------------
[Update] This will probably continue to be the family's most played game for a while. It has enough elements for my wife, who likes an asthetically pleasing result, and finds that more important than a win. It has enough tactically to satisfy my son and I, who are a little more cutthroat. Actually, we have a friend who wins regularly by playing a low key, opportunistic game while the sharks are out eating each other, so there are lots of routes to success.

The basic game plays quickly, particularly if you take the next tile at the end of your turn, giving you a "hand" of one tile. That gives everyone a chance to think a little before their turn arrives. The end result is a game with strategically solid game played in roughly an hour.

Carefull with expansions.  I think it would be pretty easy to have a pretty chaotic experience if one tried to play too many expansions at once.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value: Ah, Carc!  You were one of The Originals that started my wife and I gaming together.  It's hard to remember any more what the original game without the expansions was like, although it was certainly a fine little game in its own right.  I have carefully chosen which expansions I have purchased [edit: I have thrown caution to the wind and now own most of the expansions, which has pretty much destroyed the game by drastically increasing the amount of time required to play] and every one of those expansions has added an interesting element to the game.  When playing with all the expansions I own (The River, The River II, Inns and Cathedrals, Traders and Builders, King and Scout, The Princess and The Dragon), and with about half the tiles in the bag to decrease the play time, I would rank this game 7.5/10.  With my wife as my most frequent gaming partner, this has been one of the most played games we own (although it was one of the first games we owned!).  [Edit: Well, we finally killed poor Carc - http://www.boardgamegeek.com/geeklist/27391 - so we traded it away and purchased "Carcassonne: The City".  Game design: 3/5  Personal enjoyment: 2/5  Total: 5/10
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
This game on its own is alright. Just alright. Definite potential. But the game REALLY comes to life with the expansion 'Inns and Cathedrals'. As many say, it should have been part of the original game. After adding that expansion and 'Traders and Builders' it feels more rounded and robust in strategies.

Lots of people mention the luck factor in the game, but I think it's all about making the tiles you draw work for you. You have to be flexible and go with the flow in this game. There is limited planning ahead BECAUSE of the luck of the draw, but it doesn't dampen the strategy too much. Even so, you can make a slight rule modification that you can hold 2 or 3 tiles in your hand.

But all in all, I often wonder why this game is always in the top 15. I mean, it's not THAT good. It's an OK time passer, but not something I would consider spectacular enough to be among the top rated and most popular games. And when introducing this game to new players, it's hit or miss. Many don't seem to like it at all. So just keep that in mind.


For trade. In like new condition, also have the expansions Inns & Cathedrals, Traders & Builders, and The River II
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
I don't like the farmer rule. with gamers, it's ok but it seems inelegant compared to the other rules. And I hate teaching that rule to beginners. And so I don't. And people still have a good time. I like how the game caters to different levels of players and of meanness in a short timeframe. That said, I feel like you don't have much agency with more players (because the number of pieces doesn't scale). Also, it is a bit of an odd phenomenon that the maps don't end up looking good. Unfinished towns, deadend roads - signs of some quality gameplaying, but ugly nonetheless. I'd have to research some of the other versions and see if any of them fixed the aesthetic part of it. 

Anyhow, I would never have bought it but i received it as a gift. And I do occasionally play it. My spouse really enjoyed how short it was and asks to play occasionally with guests.

2024-12-06 - recently I've introduced to people who didn't like it. And my girlfriend and mother are not so keen on it anymore. Go figure. The whole point of this game for me is that it is accessible fun for people I want to play with. If that fades, then so does the game. Lowered 0.5

textfield_comment_value: I first played Carcassonne in 2007 with three people who regularly played and I got absolutely crushed. I didn't think much of it at the time, probably due to the horrendous loss I had suffered. Although this was my first exposure to modern board games, it didn't really influence me then and I mostly stuck to things like Magic: the Gathering, Risk, and Munchkin. In 2014, I bought a Humble Bundle of mobile games that included Carcassonne and that sent me down the path I'm currently on. I was obsessed with it, playing it at home, on the bus, and when I should have been doing homework. After Carcassonne, I bought Catan, was gifted Ticket to Ride and Pandemic and dove down the rabbit hole. But Carcassonne was where it all started, even if it took a while to get there. I used to go to game stores looking solely for Magic and scoffed at the price of board games - especially seeing a display of lots of mini expansions for Carcassonne, but now I regret not purchasing those and wish I would have dove in earlier. Carcassonne will always have a special place in my heart as the game that got me into gaming and will always be my favorite game.

Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value: An excellent game, at least for two players. Everyone loves the building aspects of the game and they hardly notice the genius inherent in the mechanics, which is genius in and of itself. Anyone who has played dominoes can learn how to play, but better, more experienced players always have an edge. I really like this one in two player because you don't have to worry about two other people sharing large cities or something, but even with 5 (or 6 with expansions) the strategies are very similar. Farming very often wins games, but the more you farm, the more you limit your options since you never get farmers back until the end of the game. And a single enormous completed city can net you many more points than one or even two farmers. Farming, unfortunately, is a bit too complicated and not visually intuitive, not to mention the 3 different sets of scoring rules based on the edition of the game. Lately, I have been less and less interested in playing this one though. It seems to really only shine in two-player as the more people you add, the more chaotic it gets. And there are just mechanics I like better than tile-laying.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
A classic for a reason. Very light and easy-going, but you can still mess with other players with some sneaky moves. But it does sit somewhat uncomfortably between a “gateway game” and a “gamer’s game”. For me the base game is a bit too light without the first two expansions, but I would probably leave them out with new players. 

Some of the rules are rather convoluted and hard to explain - even in the (new) base game. The abbot’s special rules seem totally unnecessary to me, and new players always seem to struggle with the farmer rules. The farmers can win you the game, and still they feel somewhat detached from the rest. Which is why new players always forget about them and typically lose the game as a result.

Isle of Skye obviously owes a lot to Carcassonne. And while Isle of Skye doesn’t exactly replace Carcassonne, I definitely consider it to be a superior design. It is a bit more complex, but the rules are elegant and streamlined. Because of the brilliant tile auction mechanic the feeling of randomness is replaced with a sense of agonizing agency.

Expansions owned:
- Inns and Cathedrals
- Traders and Builders
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value: Personally, I find this game shares the same syndrome as Lost Cities in that the game play is enjoyable, but determining player status requires maths gymnastics and the climax of scoring is an overlong, dull chore.  My other experience niggles are that: A) the pace of the game tends to become inverse (from quick to slow) as the options to place a tile increases (a limiting border as in TaYu/Entdecker would help), neither does playing with more than two players or the original rule of picking a tile at the start of your turn speed up pace. B) to help in making an informed decision you have to speculate on the remaining distribution of tile types and configurations which isn't uniform and so difficult to commit to memory.But these objections contradict the popular experience of the game. What's the universal appeal? I guess it is the several mini scoring advancements and the satisfaction of completing a desired castle, road etc to get a scoring opportunity back. The other elements could be the creative expression and continually different designs the plays make. Could the greeness of the board be pleasantly calming?

[Original comment] Great family game -- especially for folks who like a challenge, but who don't care for war games or themes of violence or mayhem. Can be played friendly or very competitive.

Update February 2006 -- We always play with three expansions: The River, Inns and Cathedrals, and Traders and Builders. The latter two add lots of scoring variables, which makes the game more challenging. Great for 5 or 6 players.

(December 2006) We've added some components, to allow for 7 players, and it works fine. This is a very popular game in our family group.

May 2009 -- This is still a favorite game for us, and we play it occasionally.

October 2011 -- We continue to play with the same expansions and thoroughly enjoy this game. It is one of my favorites.

November 2012 -- This game never grows old, and remains a family favorite. Recently, in a 3-player game, it appeared my son and I had tied (with over 300 points, each), until I noticed and told him that he had a few more points coming, with his pig in one of the fields he scored. Great game!

2013-November: Another year, and we still like this game very much.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value: [b]Update 11.26.07 :[/b] I raised this game from an 8 to a 9. I still haven't played it with any expansions except River 1 and the Mini-Expansion from one of my gaming mags (which introduced the much needed new river start tile). I have now played it quite a few times with 2, 3 and 4 players. For me I prefer it with 2 or 3 players, although with 4 it still ranks around an 8. Normally I'm not a big fan of luck, but this game shares similar traits with [gameid=24508] which I also enjoy quite a bit too. [b]Original:[/b] I found this game to be pretty fun. You randomly draw a tile (luck) and place it to where it helps you the most (luck again). The luck in the game though is balanced by the strategic placement of your meeples which you can only place on the tile you just placed. Do you hold off or do you place a knight, thief, or bishop to help score some points so you can reuse them later, or invest a few farmers that are stuck in the fields the entire game but might bring home the bacon (and the win) at the end of the game? Easy to learn and teach, the few rules offer quite a bit of depth in terms of game play.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
While very simple to play, this game can be very difficult to master.  You are essentially building a puzzle, where you can create castles, roads, churches, and farms.  Place your marker to gain points of those areas, get them back if completed.

It is so simple just about everyone I know figured it out in about 3 minutes (including a 5 year old) and enjoyed it.

Unfortunately this game suffers the same flaw as card games; card/tile counting.  To actually compete in this game you need to remember how many of each tile exists, build yourself structures that are likely to get finished, and disrupt the building of opponents structures.  It is a real bummer to "walk yourself" into a "dead end" in this game.  

The other downside of this game is that luck takes a large part in the game play.  Each player pulls cards at random to complete their structures.  It is possible that you will simply pull the right tile and never get to finish your building/road/farm.  Now over an infinite number of trials this probability drops to zero, but that doesn't mean that you will ever get to finish your castle this game. :)
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Still a classic. Best played in a pub with a crowd of bemused but intrigued onlookers or on a pool table by merging a couple of dozen boxes together. Lacks depth after a while, but an expansion or two will perk that up, no problem. We prefer this with three - the heads-up waiting game for downing one's farmers palls very quickly, and a third player adds just a little screwage to the to-ing and fro-ing of the two-player game.

textfield_comment_value:
My wife and I truly love this game.  It works best as a 2 player, but doesn't suffer much in a 3 player game.  More than that and it weakens a bit because each player has fewer turns.

We often use this as one of our intro games to get non-gamers interested in playing board games with us.  The mechanics are super simple.  I've been able to teach my 5 year old niece and my in-laws to play.  

Simple mechanics, easy to grasp, very enjoyable.

UPDATE: after not playing it for almost a year, we got it out on a night we didn't have the energy for a longer / heavier game.  It's still refreshingly great.  It's light enough that we can have an interesting conversation while playing and it doesn't interfere with figuring out our moves, but it's not so light that it's boring.  I removed Traders & Builders and the River II, leaving only Inns & Cathedrals and it plays smoother and more elegantly.  What a great way to spend time together.  This game probably more than any other turned my wife and I into board gamers.

Wrote a review about it here: [b]https://yourturndad.com/2017/09/20/crazy-for-carcassonne/[/b]
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Wow... just wow.  I played this for the first time today.  Honestly, just from hearing what the game would be about, I wasn't too keen on it.  Building cities? Connecting roads?  Gah, boring!  But now that I've played it, I don't even remember what I thought of it before... it has been erased with the awesome that is the game.

Sure, I didn't win, it was only my first time playing, but it is exactly the type of quick game I like to play - the laying of the map tiles is very much like a puzzle, and I was able to screw-up my husband, not once, but twice with a single river placement.  That alone made the game for me.  Well, that and messing up another one of his cities later in the game...

I really like games that have a visual matching aspect - probably because that is my strong suit.  Anyway, long story short, I now need this game, so that I may thwart others in the building of their cities and cloisters!
