Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
[i][Rating for Carcassonne with River and Inns and Cathedrals expansions][/i]

Easy to learn, charming components, and elegant simplicity all in a casual (or more cut-throat, if you so desire) game for two to six (though I prefer to play with four players or fewer). The game can sometimes come down to a few critical tile draws, so chance can play a reasonably large role. Despite this, player decisions certainly contribute much more to final scores than chance, and the game [i]is[/i] intended to be a fairly lightweight family game, so I think the level of chance is appropriate. The River is a nice expansion, but Inns and Cathedrals is absolutely critical for the large follower and inns. Once I&C has been added, Carcassonne is a very nice game indeed.

Recommended 'variant': Each player has a 'hand' of one tile. The turn order is (i) Play tile; (ii) Draw new tile. This way players get to think about what their next placement is during other players' turns, reducing downtime during the active player's turn and giving each player something to think about while waiting. (2009-03; revised 2014-02)
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
[size=8][b]Succumbed to input randomness[/b], where success is highly correlated to luck rather than skill. Admittedly, there are ways to 'block' opponents to reduce their Knights and Farmers into unfavorable positions, but the ability to execute these blocks are still gated by input randomness - if you do not receive the right tiles, you would basically be a passive observer as the game unfolds. Worker management is key in Carcassonne, where players have to constantly retrieve workers so that they may be assigned to other duties. However, you may fail to retrieve workers through no fault of your own other than input randomness (you could literally have no workers for 10+ turns), or you may be blocked forever from retrieving by your opponents - but remember, your opponents likely had lucked into the opportunity to block you through no merit of their own other than the dumb luck of drawing the right tile at the right time (again, their input randomness). While some input randomness is required for most games, Carcassonne has overdone it, thereby leading to unidimensional gameplay 
[/size]
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
This is one of the newer most hyped games I have tried that fell completely flat. No strategy due to one tile at a time and very little tactical choices and did not find it fun at all. 

Very dry and boring, strictly tile-laying. Still would get played over some other low-level games but it won't be suggested. Reminds me of "waterworks" from what I remember only I think I enjoyed that more, at least you could throw a wrench in the guy's plumbing...

To be fair I'm sure this is somewhat better with the expansions and maybe a house rule letting you hold 2 or 3 tiles and maybe even picking from an open pool like El Cab but El Cab is far better (although EC is NOT a gateway game so they are pretty different in that respect).

I'm waiting to try "The City" or "The Castle" which looks better and more involved as straight tile-laying doesn't excite me a whole bunch (at least in this form where as in T&E it is masterfully beautiful). 

I can see why people like it for its simplicity and as a Gateway, for me a little too simple but with some tweaks it would be another good gateway tool.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Carcassone is a fine game, but it's not really my thing. I tend to prefer games that allow for and reward long term planning. Carc however is a game mostly about tactics. 

That maximizing the turn in front of you thing is something many enjoy and this game is great at letting anyone just jump in and play. Overall I will play, but there's almost always some other option I'd prefer to be playing. 

Update November 2022: I still feel mostly the same way. Carc is a very well designed game that is heavily tactical, and I mostly am good and enjoy games that reward more long term planning. 

I know there is more skill here in leaving yourself open so that any draw is good, but all too often I just feel my opponents are getting easier path to points while I draw my 10ths giant city portion in a row that is leaving me limited in how I can score.

I also think the farmer scoring is just a tad confusing, but more annoyingly I think the farmer scoring is too big of a shift, as players can jockey for who has the most farmers and have to do it in weird ways to try and connect things in sometimes.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
This review is for the base game, and for the “Inns & Cathedrals”, “Traders & Builders”, “The Princess & The Dragon”, “The River”, “The Abbot”, and “Winter Edition” expansions.

It is an immersive experience to build your world through this game, at least at first. The tile art is beautiful, the worker placement is straight forward and purposeful. On most turns, unless you draw unhelpful tiles, you have interesting decisions to make to advance your strategy and/or thwart your opponents. This is very much an interactive experience between the players, and not simply each player building their own world separately.  The expansions add interest, and I particularly liked how “The River” created a nice structure to the landscaping, while the others just added new things to think about for your score maximizing strategy.

I say it is only an immersive experience “at first” because the more I played, the more it became a mathematical score maximizing puzzle, and less a town building experience.  I suppose that is true of most games, if you play them too long, you play the fun out of them.

textfield_comment_value:
[RGG Carcassonne Big box 2006 edition] {City building, gateway; tile-laying; optimal 3-4p} Carcassonne is a very good family game. It's easy to learn and interactive. Scoring happens all the time, which allows player to visual scores more easily, although it slightly disrupts the game flow. In addition, it's fun to play Carcassonne. Highly recommended as a gateway game in any collection.

It's more forgiving than Hunters & Gatherers, where incomplete roads and cities can still score.  It has good player interaction with mild confrontation. In addition, it is dynamic because tiles can be merged together and there are bonus tiles so that the situation may change abruptly.  

The Big Box edition is real good. It saves space and has a good insert for all tiles. In addition, it has a reference sheet for the distribution of tiles in the basic game and all expansions.

[Rulebook] The annotated rulebook in BGG shall be used with RGG Big Box edition. This rulebook provides the latest rules and FAQs, which makes the rules it much clearer.  I prefer the scoring rule of 3rd edition.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
It grows on you like mold.  Slow, fuzzy, and not too offensive smelling.  In fact, for some reason, you keep coming back to smell it.  It actually smells pretty good.  Wait, did I say mold?  I meant moss.  Moss!

The awesome part about this game is that it lets you think with your eyes.  With most Euros I'm crunching numbers in my head and trying to figure out what the other players want to do.  With Carcassonne, I'm visualizing what shape the board can potentially take, and the position of your opponents' pieces flat out tell you what they're thinking.  There's no hidden information here, the board is easy to look at, the scoring options are very straight forward, and they're nicely tied to the layout of the board.  Looking at the board tells you everything you need to know in order to make good decisions.  

This game is really about visualizing what shape you want the board to take and working your darndest to make it happen.  The catch is that everyone else at the table has a vision for the board as well and their visions probably don't match yours.  Fantastic game!
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
One of my first 'modern' games. I remember hunting around for a copy with the SO for several months trying to find a copy at a retail store (this was before we knew of the plethora of online shops).

Carcassone is a wonderfully simple tile-laying game. It can be as leisurely or as cutthroat as your group wants it to be. The rules are easy to teach and it's fun to watch the countryside unfold before you. The plethora of expansions available also kept the game fresh for a long time.

My only gripe with the game is that your decisions can sometimes feel a bit pre-destined since you only draw one tile. If that tile doesn't help any of your ongoing projects, it feels a bit like a wasted turn. Luckily, playing with a hand of 3 (or more) tiles fixes this problem for us and creates a larger decision space.

Carcasonne doesn't see a lot of table time anymore as we've moved on to more complex games (and we've played it to death), but it still holds a special place in my heart and it's one of the first things I'll pull out if anyone ever says "Boardgames? You mean like Monopoly?".

textfield_comment_value:
Carcassonne is a simple tile placing game to learn, but has some decent strategic depth at the same time (think Chess in this regard).  While there is certainly some luck involved regarding the tile you draw, it really comes down to what you *do* with that tile and how you use your followers that makes the difference.

Now that I have many of the expansions, I could never return to play this by itself, but at the same time, I do remember initially enjoying the game when we were first playing this by itself.

Note:  My wife normally plays all games with my son and I, but she was not into this one.  In fairness to the game, she did not give it a fair shake, as she only played one game (and we were learning as we went).  Still, this was one game that was not her cup of tea.  Therefore, I have only played this as a 2-player game, and very much enjoy it as 2-player (although I would think adding another player or two would make it that much more interesting).

In any case, overall, it is a game enjoyed by my son and I, but we now have included many of the expansions.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Carcassonne is a tile laying, and worker placement game.  On your turn you place a tile down into the play area.  The tiles depict various terrain such as cities, roads, fields, and cloisters.  To properly place the tile one of the four edges must touch, and match terrain with a tile already played.  Then you may place a worker on the tile you just placed to claim it.  Once cities, roads, and cloisters are completed, they score.   Farmer's fields score at the end.  The players with the most points at the end wins.

Carcassonne, is light.  It's usually referred to as a gateway game.  Meaning it works well introducing people to the board game hobby.  As such, I really liked it a lot when I began playing designer games.  After awhile though I found it very repetitive.  It's possible that this could be mitigated by the large number of expansions, but I never got into them.

I would recommend Carcassonne to new gamers for sure.  I'd still play it from time to time, but for the most part I've moved on to games with either more interesting mechanics, themes, or both.

Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Scenic, fun gateway game.
-Explanation is about 5-10 minutes for the base game, and an extra 5 minutes if you add the first or second expansion.
-This game is great for newcomers (though the "big box" makes it look intimidating). The game can be aggressive or sedate, depending on how you play. 
-Laying tiles feels fun -- it feels like you're building an interactive jigsaw puzzle.
-The game makes it difficult and risky, but potentially quite rewarding, to "raid" other peoples roads, farms, and cities. This encourages interaction, and can lead to many fun rivalries.
-Only minor dislikes. The base game can feel a bit unexciting, especially if you leave out the farmer (which can be tricky to explain to complete non-gamers). Adding the cathedrals, inns, and possible the builders and resources make drawing the tiles feel a bit more exciting and encourages player interaction -- however these additions also makes the game lose some of it's elegance and ease, and adds some luck.
-Even with the minor dislikes, this is fantastic, highly replayable game.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Not quite my gateway game, but my first rabbit hole. Can be played for relaxation or with serious competitive intent - higher player counts lend themselves to the former, lower to the latter. In both contexts it is way better than its straightforward mechanics and passe reputation suggest.

This reputation is its main problem - too many gamers consider themselves above it. Yes, it is a light medium game, yes the artwork shouts "family friendly" at the top of its lungs and yes tile draw is random. [b]But[/b] it's remarkably replayable - the decisions continue to be challenging and interesting [i]and[/i] there's genuine tension and competition.

The realisation that expansions and mini expansions are best enjoyed selectively - individually or perhaps in twos or threes - rather than via a more-is-always-better approach solidified my appreciation and enjoyment. And saved me from extending my burrow beyond what can be contained in the base box.

(First [b]logged[/b] play January 2020. Estimated 5 unlogged plays pre 2020, in the preceding month.)
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Very easy to pick up and play, rules are simple enough to explain even to my family and relatives who don't speak English.  The game is good with any number of players.  While the gameplay itself is fairly straight forward, with your ability to score largely depending on the tiles you draw, I think the most strategic element of the game is the farmer, which often give an amazing amount of points at the end of the game, without the player's realization.  Carcassonne is also great because of the amount of socializing it illicits, everyone gets to participate during anyone's turn.

Update #1: Game seems to take longer and longer after each successive plays, rather than the other way around (even with only one additional expansion).  Too much metagaming during other people turn for my taste, I try very hard to just keep my mouth shut and let them do what they want, but sometimes it is maddeningly frustrating when they take forever.  Especially annoying when someone goes I'll help you out if you do this for me.  This isn't a negotiation game!
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
I used to think this game was too simple and (mostly) luck-based. Then I played a few game on Carcassonne iPad app. Boy, was I wrong... 
This game is a strategic masterpiece hidden behind a cute, relaxing theme. It's also much more evil than most people can imagine, at least when played optimally. There is LOTS of skill in basic (no expansions) 2-player game, obviously with more players the luck factor increases.
Have you ever tried to get into the someone's big city, or even a road? Have you ever placed your tile(s) in such a way so as to minimize opponent's chances of filling in a big city or road? Do you know how and when to place your farmers? (bad farmer placement can easily lose you the game) Do you know the distribution of the tiles and take it into consideration when deciding on your move?
Guess what - strong players CONSISTENTLY do all of the above and are able to post very impressive win rates. Even if you know some (or all) of these concepts you'll still get trashed (in the long run) by someone who employs them better than you.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
This game is very simple, both to teach and to play. Players take turns and draw a tile and connect it to the existing map then may place a “meeple” to try and determine control of certain key positions for points. The player with the most points after the last tile is played is the winner! Slight complications arise with scoring rules but it’s nothing terribly complex. That said there could be very deep strategies involved playing this game and choices where to place tiles and Meeples become crucial. There’s not a lot of player interaction and it’s usually light in confrontation but can be played more aggressively as players vie for control over certain types of structures and areas on the map. A great, flexible game that can be taken as seriously as you wish. 

Some of the expansions add some interesting wrenches into the mix and spice things up! Always a good “go to” game and I have had very successful sessions of using Carcassonne as a “gate way” game to other, more complex offerings. Very highly recommended! Truly, a must have!
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
[q="Past me"]Given to me by my sister for Christmas 2012.

Maps. Mmmmmmmm... MAKING maps. [i]Oh yeah...[/i]

I could play this game forever. No expansions necessary. Although [thing=2993][/thing] adds just the right amount of spice.[/q]

The thing that makes this game stand out (as long as you're playing it with more than two) is the highly dynamic temporary alliances. At any given time, you will naturally create alliances with other players, potentially in several areas of the board at once, which will be fruitful for each of you - but can just as easily be betrayed for personal gain. The rules don't force any of this, it happens organically. For my money, no other game achieves this as effectively with such straightforward rules, except maybe [thing=483][/thing], but you get to keep your friends with Carcassonne.

[b]PROS:[/b]
- Works well with a broad player count.
- Has a million expansions and variants.

[b]CONS:[/b]
- Feels "vanilla" - more exciting games often get picked over this.
- Has a million expansions and variants.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
I just don't get it.  I've only played the base game without any expansions but it's just boring to me.  The drawing of tiles is completely random and I get that there is strategy involved in shaping your roads and cities and meeple placement against this but that's not enough to keep me interested.

After playing this game several more times in an attempt to give it a fair shake I think I like it even less.  I really don't get the love for this game!

2 players is the maximum you can play this with any semblance of strategy and still sometimes you will never see the tiles you need while your opponent gets the perfect one every turn.  With more than 2 it is just nonsense.  The chances of you getting usable tiles that fit your strategy is diluted even further with every additional player and the number of tiles placed that screw with your whole plan is increased.  Every tile you place you have no idea if it is going to help you or just end up being a waste of a turn.  I'm ultimately convinced this is not a very good game.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Carcassonne is a good addition to any board game collection because it's easy to learn, quick to play, and can be played with only two players. It fills a nice niche as something you can play on a whim when you've got some time to kill.

Unfortunately, I don't find the game itself to be that wonderful. The game is a mix of luck and strategy, but I find it's too far on the luck side. I also find that the game has balancing issues. I've played over ten times now and I still don't see any compelling reason to play robbers as a significant part of your strategy. The lack of penalty for not completing a road or cloister doesn't help the balancing issue in my opinion. 

I think the funnest part of the game for me is the cat-and-mouse game of trying to secure farm lands, but it's a strategy that more often than not does not pay off (even if you manage to secure them), so it's hard to justify engaging in it.

All in all the fact that the game fills a nice niche means that I'm rating it higher than I would just for the gameplay.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value: Always fun to play, simple to learn, but lacks a little bit of cutting edge.  It's a tile laying game where you match the borders of each tile to ones already played and score points by investing a worker in ownership or attempted ownership over some feature of the map you're creating.  The strategy is to score as many points as you can, while making it difficult on your opponent(s) to score points on whatever they have invested or are trying to invest their small finite source of workers on. It's a high luck based game where it's difficult for anyone to be truly out of it.  Experience is important, but two people of equal experience will generally always have a competitive game due to the high amount of luck involved.  The best moments in the game are in completing massive cities, sneaking in and taking over someone else's massive city, getting massive points off of farms, and blocking off opponents from completing construction of something and thus taking away their workers from helping them to score points for them.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Rating dropped to an 8 after playing Carc: The Discovery, which is a better game and also highlights some of the problems with this one.

This was my gateway game, and it's still one of my favorites (and one of the only games my wife and I both enjoy). I find the base game to be very relaxing and a nice balance of skill and luck. Another huge plus is that it can be played very cutthroat or nearly cooperatively depending on the preferences of the players, which gives it a lot of flexibility. About the only downside is that I've found one player drawing more than about 75% of the monasteries virtually guarantees victory, but that doesn't happen often. This may be the only game that I think all gamers should own, because it's such a wonderful introduction to the hobby; out of literally dozens of people I've introduced the game to, only 2 did not like it (and they both have admitted to disliking any game where it takes more than one sentence to explain the rules, so I don't think anything would've been a hit with them).

textfield_comment_value:
A classic credited with starting a Eurogame craze - the test of time has shown that the game is a bona fide classic, still standing up amazingly well today (2019). 

I've played the game in a range of formats including physical tabletop with friends and randoms, Microsoft Store, Android and PC (Asmodee/Steam), the latter of which is a great rendition second only to tabletop.

Lovely components, nice thematic art, and beautiful game design where simplicity belies real depth, particularly farmer placement and meeple conservation. There is an element of chance on the tile draw but strangely it rarely feels unfair to get a streak of bad tiles - possibly because you are drawing from a pile rather than a stack, possibly because there are so many draws in the game it evens out, and possibly due to schadenfreude of seeing your opponents get just the tile they DIDN'T need. Good game length which doesn't scale too long with increased player counts owing to the finite number of tiles. 

One of my all-time favourites.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value: Another modern classic found in most decent board game collections. Simple tile laying game with minimum set-up. It seems a bit simple at first, but there's actually a good bit of strategy to be had in Carcasonne once it 'clicks'. It's all about the Where and When of where you place your Meeple (Farmers... or something). You're working collaboratively with the other players to build roads, cities, abbeys and farms. But you need to be the one to claim them at the right time. Too early and you might not finish them alone. Too late and another player could shut you out by claiming it first. I think the main negative for Klaus Wrede's Carcassone is the artwork. I read it once described as 'Dusty', and for some reason that word sticks. It's quite uninspiring. Where are the rolling plains? The sprawling metropolises? The awe-inspiring cathedrals? Nope. None of that. It's a long brown line leading up to a town that looks like the digestive that dropped in the bottom of your mug of tea. Sort it out, Klaus.

textfield_comment_value:
I'm not sure how to review this when the original game was released over 2 decades ago. I can see how this was credibly innovated for the time, but by today's standards I find it forgettable. In this game you are placing tiles to create a shared map. When you place your tile, you can place a meeple on one of the features on the tile. The meeple will later count towards the scoring of the length of road, size of the city, completed monastery, or size of the field (number of cities within). In comparison to today's games, the art is rather bland, but functional. I find the scoring of the farmers a bit confusing and also rather annoying especially given the length/depth of the game.

If I had to pick a Carcassonne game, I would recommend South Sea as the farmer equivalent (fisherman) is easier to understand. 

I am grateful for this game as it has helped pave the way for so many other games. I wish I could have tried this back when it came out, I think I would have been more enthusiastic.

textfield_comment_value: The more I've played this the more I like it... so subtle and beautiful and really unlike anything else I own. Those that complain it is too simple, too abstract, or too uninteresting are themselves too simple and too uninteresting. With the right ruthless opponent (like my wife) this game becomes an excruciating competition of area control, and essentially gambling as you weigh the benefits of placing a meeple for scoring much later against the possibility you will not draw the tile you need, or have your opponent place a tile in a position to prevent you from completing your plans. Best with 2 only, since it becomes pure competition. Also, it doesn't really become a pure game until both players are familiar enough with all the pieces (the way one becomes familiar with the 52 cards in a standard playing card deck) that each decision of placement (tile and meeple) becomes educated based on knowledge of future potential. Not worth playing without the Inns & Cathedrals expansion.

textfield_comment_value:
Has become one of my favorite games.

~

1) Build and develop the city of Carcassonne and the surrounding countryside via tile-laying.
2) Draw tile, place tile, (maybe) place meeple, (maybe) score. Simple tile-laying, area-enclosure/control. The decisions come from using your tiles to achieve multiple things - expanding your areas, starting new areas, and making the completion of opponents’ areas more difficult.
3) I loved: How fast-flowing and easy to learn the game is, how pretty the table looks at the end, and that with 2 players the luck diminishes and the strategy and tactics shine through.
4) Can be improved: The more players, the worse this game gets, and that is problematic for a quintessential gateway game.
5) My enjoyment of this has waxed and waned. I’m now in a position where I enjoy playing it with 2 or 3 players, and in some situations would suggest it, but would avoid it at higher counts. Great for non-gamers while being a nice light filler for gamers.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
We play this a LOT. It's a near perfect level of strategy for winding down after work. We play it with the river expansion which greatly accelerates the initial part of the game which can be slow when you start from a single tile as in the base-set. The river expansion should just be considered an essential part of the base game as it perfectly solves the one downfall of the base set which is the slow start.

But the river is the only expansion we use. I've found some of them fun - but some, like the Tower, radically alter the nature of the game (turns it into a mean-spirited "gotcha" game) Trying to stuff too much into a beautifully crafted smooth-as-silk-playing light strategy game sort of defeats the point. Carcassone, Patchwork, Morels, Tramhahn, Splendor, these are so perfect in balance and weight and fun. I can't see trying to bulk-up Carcassone into a midweight game. It isn't - and that's part of its charm. It's a near perfect lightweight strategy 2p game.

textfield_comment_value:
We often use this game to introduce new players to gaming -- especially kids -- and the premise of building the board out piece by piece is an easy one to grasp. Deeper strategy lurks beneath the surface, however. 

If you play without blocking and passively interfering with your neighbors, the game plays out as a pleasant luck-of-the-draw game, where the player who draws the most appealing tiles will win. Like I said, it's not hard to optimize placement of your particular tile for most points. What gives the game wings is the threat of blocking and disturbing others.

Unfortunately, I lack an opponent (or opponents) who care to play the game in this way. Thus, Carcassonne sits on my shelf with a bit of unrealized potential. But even for introducing new players, it continued to be a smooth-playing game with a lot going for it.  What it does, it does well.

I have yet to play this one with expansions, but people often say that expansions make it way better. It is already a very good game, so that would be amazing!
I like the theme, the artwork (simple as it is), the tile laying gameplay. You can be ambitions and go for massive, risky structures or play it safe and score many small amounts of points. There is exactly the amount of components to it that there needs to be; no more, no less.
I rate it less than perfect because: (1) Maybe it is true that expansion will make it better so I need to try that for myself. (2) I'm still new enough to board games that I prefer to leave some head room for future favourites, score wise.

https://wikicarpedia.com/car/Main_Page#carcassonne_editions 

Fun tile-laying game -- the one that made the genre popular! But it's been around a while, and rating has fallen slightly - prefer the variants to the original, now. 

Tiles show some combination of land/city/road +/- cloister. Place starting tile in center. In turn order, draw then play a tile adjacent to one already on the board, until last tile placed. When placing, features on edges must match adjacent tile. MAY place a meeple on a feature of the tile you placed, but only if no other meeple is already present on that type of feature on another tile, where the features are contiguous. If your tile placement completes the feature, score it immediately (city: 2 per tile; shields count as extra tile; road: 1 per tile; cloister: 9 when completely surrounded). At end of game, each farm (contiguous cluster of land) scores 3VP/city to the player with meeple majority in the farm. Most VP wins.

own ios version. I think it shows it’s age: pretty random for a euro, poor theme, etc. In the early 00’s, this was the game I argued against a pair of recently converted board gamers to say that boardgaming was stagnant since the early 90’s. Boy was I wrong as it was about to explode due to explosion from Germany that this game presaged.

Haven’t played with expansions though. Not too sure they could overcome the theme or be fun to play without turning it into a fundamentally different game.

If you like tile laying as a mechanic, there are more modern games that have both better components, mechanic, and theme. Unfortunately, I don’t feel this is innovative enough or old enough to be considered a classic (for example: chess, Diplomacy, Cosmic Encounter, Axis & Allies, Agricola), though it’s historical importance should not be overlooked.

This and Settlers of Catan became staples in any tech hipster den I visited in the second boom (2006-2012).
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
My first Euro.  Ironically, despite the seemingly benign geographic theme, this is one of the most cutthroat games that we have.  Stealing control of farms, making cities more difficult to complete, piggybacking on opponent's cities are all great ways of saying "take that."  

Downgraded my rating from 7 because I'd much rather play some of my higher rated games.

My 21 month old daughter loves to "play" this.  She asks for "Cahcahsonne" very frequently.  Typical turn consists of me asking her whose turn it is, then that person picking up one tile ("Just one tile, ok?").  If it's me, I play it somewhere.  If it's her, I give her a suggestion.  If it's Pooh Bear (a frequent Carcassonne partner around here), see previous.  She doesn't quite understand that tiles need to match on all side.  Game is over when she loses interest and stomps on the pieces (we play on the floor).  That's another positive...pieces are durable and setup/cleanup is quick!
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
After enjoying Settlers of Catan for many years, this was the second modern board game I bought, and I was surprised to find there was a game that I liked even better than Settlers.  I no longer enjoy the base game of Carcassonne on its own very much because I've become so used to playing with the Inns & Cathedrals and Traders & Builders expansions, which I consider essential at this point.  I have tried a few of the other standalone versions (e.g., Hunters & Gatherers, Castle, City), but have not been very impressed by any of them, and don't feel the need to own any of them, I even traded away the Castle despite high expectations with Knizia at the helm.  Finally, I think the naysayers of this game fail to play it as aggresively as it should be played, trying to steal opponent's cities/roads, and trap opponent's large meeple/builder.

See my review to read more at:
http://www.boardgamegeek.com/thread/133252

Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
[category: family]. The game is simple, but it is not particularly interesting for children, because there is nothing nice or interesting enough to attract their attention (unless you don't have any other games). A good family game, pleasant with a slight negative interaction, you can think a little here, the game is simple in its rules, but not brainless. Despite the years, it's still in my collection, I always take it out when I don't feel like doing anything special and would like to play something quick. This is not a game for gamers, because there are no unique mechanics, and, contrary to appearances, the game has a lot of randomness and too few complicated decisions.
I don't see the need to buy add-ons for this game. This game ranks so high in my book just because it's simple and yet very satisfying. The level of complexity increases with additions, but the game is still simple in principle, so the satisfaction does not increase.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
For such a simple game, carcassonne has a nice balance of cooperation/competition, 
conservative/aggressive use of resources (meeples), attack and defense, utilizing different functions of each tile's features.  As a result, even though the game is about taking and putting down a single tile and a single wooden piece each turn, it's got a lot to think about.  All this would probably induce analysis paralysis if it weren't for the fact that you get to show your situation to your opponents, who then can offer 'helpful' suggestions (sometimes really helpful if they're nice, sometimes some sort of 'let's help each-other' kind of move).  This makes the game a bit social.  Not as social as a trading game like Settlers of Catan, but nice, tea-time manners, social.  I personally like rowdier games or more thought-provoking games, but still i enjoy it when i'm in the right mood--a bit sedate and polite, like with a church group or something.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Light and simple, it's good as a gateway game and with the right mood (no deep thinking, just easy going tile placement) can be a pleasant filler once in a while. Quite simply, it never really caught my heart, wearing down quickly. The luck factor can be a problem, further exalted by a high number of players, but most of all its limited depth simply doesn't appeal my inner meeple, I suppose. And, of course, my overall feeling about this game is not even remotely biased by the fact that, the last time I played, a pretty lady heavily kicked my rear end twice in a row. 

RGG edition w/ River included. Tiles are sturdy and with a simple yet nice artwork, same goes for the scoreboard (large but going only to 50, not enough for a typical Carcassone game but also not a big problem, anyway). And then there are the meeples! Cute, highly symbolic for modern eurogaming, absolutely needed (and great) to keep yourself occupied during downtime.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
No game is perfect, however Carcassonne is pretty close.

It is a game for anyone and everyone. It works at all player counts, can be played as friendly or as cutthroat depending on the group, has minimal setup and tear down, as well having an impressive table presence.

Something of note worth mentioning, is that many Tile laying games reduce your options the longer a game goes on as the gameboard fills up. But in Carcassonne since you are collectively building up the game board as you go, you options increase the further the games on.

I think this is the key to the games success, as at the start of the game you have few options to place your tiles so players aren't overwhelmed by choice like in other tile layers, and simultaneously allowing players to make impressive and inventive plays in later stages of the game, instead of the usual predictable plays you see in the later stages of other Tile layers. 

Certified Masterpiece.

Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
A classic for a reason, but difficult to articulate exactly why it is one of my favourite games - and so prevalent throughout the hobby. There is certainly satisfaction to be had in watching the world develop as it is built by the players throughout the game. Mechanically, the game is incredibly smooth and intuitive but remains deeply engaging - and each tile that is flipped offers the player with unexpectedly numerous choices. 

A huge portion of my enjoyment of the game stems from how different each play feels as well; sometimes it's a real cut-throat affair as people are consistently building into one another's farms and cities and other times it's a serene affair, as I can calmly build roads and abbeys undisturbed by the players elsewhere in the world we are building. Furthermore, despite the game so often being very interactive and very "thinky" it never feels mean-spirited, slow-paced or frustrating. Highly enjoyable game.

Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
I have found that games with up to 4P are quite enjoyable, while 5P games tend to be a bit crowded and hectic, which can be mildly frustrating. I've found that 2P games are a blast and enable you to carry out much more of a cohesive overall strategy than is possible in games with higher player counts. Because it scales so well for two AND offers a 30-45 minute play time, I find that it makes a perfect game for after dinner with the wife. 

Carc is an excellent gateway game, yet still manages to offer plenty of strategic depth. The concept of farmer scoring can be a bit difficult for those new to the game to understand, but it is usually quickly absorbed after the first game or two. Replayability is of course quite high due to the ever-changing nature of the "board", much less the myriad expansions available. This is a well-rounded game which possesses very high appeal, and it is one of my favorites, all things considered.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Carcassonne is the epitome of a gateway experience.  You simply draw a tile and choose a legal location to place it.  After that you can lay a meeple on one of the tiles features for scoring possibilities.  Opponents may try to force there way into your scoring opportunities and then points are given based on majority.  The game works and is alright but I think I would rather play other gateway games like Pandemic or some easy card games with non-gamers.

Edit: This game has been replaced for me by Isle of Skye.

Digital Alert:

I've recently started playing this through iOS and played that way I would rate it an 7 as the benefit of a digital format is the enforced rules, it has a nice tutorial, and the randomization of tiles is done by the computer.  In addition the game is played much faster.  I think playing the physical copy of the game would result in a 5 rating.  So my 6 rating is an average of digital and physical.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value: Carcassonne is a tile-placement game where you must build up a shared landscape with roads, castles, and other features and score points by completing features with your meeple on them, while trying not to help your opponents in the process. Playing without farmers (as I always have), the game isn't too complicated, and it's definitely a great gateway game. There is a limited decision space, since you don't choose which tiles you get and often there's an obvious space or two to go, or a number of basically identical choices making it an arbitrary choice. Since you don't get to choose the tiles, players are quite strongly in the hands of randomness, as getting that tile you need to finish a castle or not, or the number of monastery tiles you get over the course of the game, can greatly affect your score. Still, Carcassone manages to keep you engaged and has a lasting charm that makes you want to play it despite its flaws.

textfield_comment_value:
This game is the reason I am back into board games.  While my GF (now wife) and I were traveling in Wales, we stopped by a game store to see if there was something we could play at night in the youth hostel we were staying at.  The store owner suggested Carcassonne and what a great suggestion it was.  We played it a lot for a couple of years until we started playing other games.  We don't play it very much at all any more, but I think we both would play it if asked.  I think I also killed it when for Christmas, I bought 4 different expansions all at once.  Now, when we do play, we generally only use one or two of them.

I prefer to reduce the farm scoring just because that to me is where analysis/paralysis comes into play.  It can get downright nasty and dreadful trying to work out the best way to take over the fields.  When introducing it to new players, I don't even do the farm scoring at all in the first game.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Easy to teach and fun to play. My gf loves it as it involves building up stuff amd has just about enough confrontation. Personally I like it more with less players: it makes for a more strategic and cutthroat experience.

Update (Aug 2012): after few dozens of plays with the base set I can safely support who says this is a classic. Games play smoothly one after another, and no game feels repetitive or boring. To me it's an experience like a good ole trustworthy card game (like Spades perhaps), but more fun thanks to the bits and flavor of the game. I'm starting to include expansions right now, so my current 8.5 could potentially grow.

Update (Dec 2012): still a good game, but a combination of factors has made me decrease substantially my desire to play it. I can still appreciate the elegance and smoothness of gameplay, although some gamble-aggressive players can make the game annoying with more than 2 people.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value: 50+ plays. Given how fast we play, this is mostly a filler/closer now rather than the light Euro it started life as. Too many expansions add more weight than the mechanic (draw a tile, play a tile) can bear so we just use our favourites – the doubler meeple, and traders and builders, as they provide more dynamic, less stagnant board positions. It’s very elegant in its simplicity. Pick up a tile, play a tile, score if you've completed an element you started earlier, place a meeple on one of the elements you've just placed to potentially score later. The key to its success is the claim now, score later feature - in most tile-laying games you score with the playing of the tile itself. Combine that with offering people different elements to claim on each tile to offer choice, and fast turns to boot, and the game has broad appeal. While it doesn't come out as often as it used to, it's still a quality game I enjoy.

Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
A lot of people started with Settlers of Catan, but I started with Carcassonne after reading about it on a friend's blog. After reading him gush about this game that had no board that he and his wife were playing together, I was intrigued. That was October of 2009, which was my entry to this whole world of modern games. 

As for the actual gameplay: I think this game scales well in a number of ways. It plays well 2p all the way to 4p, and it also plays well whether you want to play cutthroat or casually. You can modify it by having a hand of tiles, if you want, but we've played it where you draw a tile at the end of your turn so you can think about your move. 

Regardless, it's satisfying to grow a countryside, and the use of meeples is a great (and light) way to balance Now against Later. It's a very clever game, even this far after its release date. There really is something special about Carcassonne.

Played 10+ Scoring is contrived and the Meeple placement is often fiddly. I enjoy this game now I am familiar with the mechanics. A novice or even an intermediary player can be left feeling like a spectator when playing with experts, this is not a criticism, it is a joy to watch the pros at work, locking your meeples into unfinishable cities and worming into lucrative farms. I prefer Hunters & Gatherers but hats off to the original. *UPDATE* I am playing this game a lot at the moment with my gamer friends. The clean graphics and a better knowledge of the tile set have increased my rating. Sept 05

textfield_comment_value:
Generally the people I have introduced to Carcassonne have enjoyed it, but after I introduce them to other games, it tends to fall by the wayside.  One problem I have is that I can never remember what the 'right way' to score cities is, there's so many various 'official' ways of doing so that I get them all jumbled.  I highly recommend playing where each player draws their next tile immediately upon placing their current one - this tends to cut down on analysis paralysis as people can decide where to place it while everyone else is playing their turns, and get stuck only if another player's placement changes the strategy on the board.

Revised January 2010 from 6.5 to 5.5 - I haven't played this in almost two years, and even the people I've introduced it to that liked it never even think of it.  It's like one of those games from days gone by that was once a shining star and is now pedestrian.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
[u]Key Words:[/u] Tile Placement - Area Control - Gateway - 2-5 Players - 45mins

[u]Summarized Opinion:[/u] Good, simple game. The lukewarm rating is primarily because it's lost its interest for me and nowadays I only play if I'm not up to something heavier (which happens only rarely). As a gateway, this game is easily a 9.

[u]My Rating Explained:[/u] Ok game, will play sporadically if in the right mood.

[u]Verbose Assessment:[/u]

This light tile placement game is great for beginning or casual gamers. It offers manageable options each turn and is easy to explain, while still interesting enough even for more experienced gamers. The game takes under an hour to play and down-time is minimal.

Expansions can be added to add a little more options to the game if so desired. Just be careful which you choose, they're not all good.

Fantastic as a gateway. Only ok if you're into heavier fare.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Carcassonne was the game that brought me into the modern gaming hobby. I've played it so much in person and online that I've cooled on it since 2000 and now don't really play it anymore. Most of that cooling has come from significant expansion fatigue and bloat which this game particularly suffers from since you play until you use all of the tiles you've set out.
The thing I love most about Carcassonne is the way the simple tiles build a clean looking map that is easy to read and tells the story of the game. The myriad combinations means that a new challenge is presented every time so even though the strategies are the same the implementation and the tension to figure out what is the perfect tile and then hoping that you can pull it is always present.
I'm glad that the game got a face lift without overhauling the mechanics because that just illustrates how elegant it was from the start.

textfield_comment_value:
My first "serious" game. It´s a very solid design and I really like this game. The fact that my wife never turns down a game of Carcassonne makes me like it even more. 

I like the multiple paths to points, the puzzle aspect, the simple rules, the short-medium time to play, the high replayability and the meaningful decisions. 

One thing that I specially like is the end scoring. Even if you score a lot of points during the game, you have to wait until the end scoring to confirm the victory. This keeps the tension until the very end.

I think it´s an excellent game for 2 players and a very good game for 3 players. With 4, 5 and 6 players, each player looses control and the game is just OK.

Despite being my first modern game, Carcassonne still reaches the table when we are in the right mood.

Unfortunetly, I had no success introducing this game to my non-gamer friends, I don´t know why!

textfield_comment_value:
Even as players place with the intent of making placement harder for each other player or of stealing features from each other, the game remains surprisingly serene.
The tile distribution is pretty good: While it is easy to focus on the tiles one isn't getting, there is very rarely nothing useful to do with a piece if one gives more thought to a it.
Unfortunately, a lot of the 2-player game is centered around stealing particularly valuable farms which is basically luck based in effectiveness.  Multiplayer games break down to sharing valuable features, but since you get so fewer turns the game feels miserable.
-
One thing that has immensely soured me on Carcassonne is the overall feeling that players who draw city closing pieces have so much more power than those who don't.  I'd like the poll a database of games and see the correlation to score and number of city-closing tiles drawn.

textfield_comment_value:
Base game is enjoyable, and quick.

Rating goes down exponentially if more than 4 players are involved. I think it's optimal with 2, and still very good with 3. I would opt out with 4 although I can see it being [i]decent[/i] with that many as long as turns go quickly.

I used to always play with I&C and T&B mixed in, but lately have picked only one major expansion to play with since tactics, tiles, and game length all seem to stay more fresh. Although we do include the K&S (excluding bonus mechanic) and Mini Expansion tiles in every game.

textfield_comment_value:
I must have logged over 100 plays in this game. Everytime when I'm introducing board games to anybody, this is a must. Even my 3 year old daughter plays it with us. The scaling of difficulty (I.e. include rivers for beginners/novice, abbotts for intermediate difficulties, and farmers for the experienced). You can even house rule it (one less meeple per additional player count) to make it a tighter game.

This game tests your creativity (tile laying), strategizing point optimizations (deciding which feature to complete), resource management (finite amount of meeples to use), and fosters take that amongst  players (wrestling control over Castles and Farms). While it scales very well from 2 to 5 players, it also provides a different enjoyable layers of gameplay at various player counts (the game plays very differently with two and with five). 

So much fun in such a small little box.

Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Carcassonne is perfect if you are looking for a strategy game that you can explain to friends in less than 5 minutes.  Very simple to understand, but still a lot of strategy involved.  

The big trade-offs in Carcassonne involve investing for the short-term vs the long-term.  Thieves have an easy short-term payoff.  Cities can involve short-term, mid-term, or long-term planning, depending on your preferences.  Farmers are the the definite long-term strategy, and if played well, players can rack up significant points with them. 

In most cases, it's unwise to play all short-term or all long-term; it's a game where you have to find a balance.  If you go all long-turn, you'll miss huge opportunities that come along.  If you go all short-term, you can get burned at the end. 

And yet in spite of all that strategy, it's fairly simple to explain and understand.  One of my favorites.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value: Cuando se habla de "juegos de iniciación" siempre se menciona la triada Aventureros al tren, Catan y Carcassonne. En contra de lo que pudiera parecer en un primer contacto, Carcassonne me parece el juego más completo y complejo de esa triada, y además es el juego que atesora la mayor cantidad de mala baba de todos ellos. Es un juego que se presta a jugarse de forma amable y distendida, pero que oculta en su oscuro corazón un sin fin de posibilidades de incordio y fastidio cuando se te pone delante un malnacido que, con malas artes, viene a quitarte esos puntitos que afanosamente te esforzabas en coger. Es ese momento, en el que te das cuenta de que no sólo esperas que el suministro sea compasivo, sino en el que además ves que tienes que apañártelas para desmontar la envolvente que te están haciendo, cuando descubres y valoras la esencia destilada e implacable de Carcassonne.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
1-3-09
Lowered from a 7 to a 5.  This change is mostly in light of finding Drakon.  Drakon has a similar feel - laying down tiles to make a modular board and using your player (meeple) to get coins (VPs) from said tiles.  Yes, this is only a fundamental similarity but it's a very strong one in my mind.  Drakon also lacks the stupid amount of randomness that Carcassone has - draw one tile and play it makes it difficult to formulate any plan.  Drakon's hands of 4 tiles that can do a variety of different things gives you a lot of room for planning/scheming.  I also hate the strategy of 'backdoor farming'.

Basically I suppose if I were offered the choice between Carcassone and Drakon, I'd pick Drakon hands down, every single time.  Also when talking gateway-level games, Ticket to Ride and Pandemic are far superior, really giving this game no place of particular interest for me.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Fantastic family game.  Not the most strategic or complex but there's no one who flat out doesn't like it, and it's a good game to include children. I like the art and the act of laying tiles. We got the new big box which has better art than our older version and includes several expansions. I'm not a huge fan of the expansions as this is an essentially simple game which I enjoy best as-is--it's nice to have a game that feels so straightforward without complicated rules. Adding more complexity doesn't really add enjoyment for me, but certain members of our family like them. I let them do the adding up and scoring at the end.

The game be played cooperatively, working on cities together, or in a more competitive way--cutting other people out or cutting off other people's cities.  It's a game that can enjoyed on different levels in different ways and by different age groups.

textfield_comment_value:
Solid with or without expansions. Doesn't always see a lot of play, as it is often passed over for more "exciting" games. But every time it comes to the table, I love it. 
 Multiple paths to victory (always key). Don't listen to the naysayers - play with the farmers. It totally switches up your strategy, encouraging small cities and piggybacking off your opponents' success. While this is clearly a tile placement game, and that is its key mechanic, I would not consider this an "area control" game - to me it's worker placement! Hello, meeples! Limited number available, use them wisely! You could make the argument for area control with the farmers and the cities, but it's not aggressive (removing someone else's pieces) as much as it is subtle, edging in until you outnumber them. While nothing exciting might jump out about this game, its still a fantastic, strategic choice.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
As cut-throat and tense as the group wants to play it. Sure, you can be screwed by the draw and your opponents can have everything fall in their laps, but that's true for most games I play - and on the whole, you have more influence on the outcome than not.

I'm eager to try the expansions Inns & Cathedrals, and Traders & Builders, as they seem to add some interesting dynamics to the game while not pushing the complexity too far from the original.

Easy game to play with anyone, but it still has enough to consider for people who enjoy more complex games. Works great with the whole range of players as well (though preferably not more than 4 I'd say) - so that's also a plus. 

A great game!

UPDATE: Played with Inns & Cathedrals, Traders & Builders and the River. Unsure about the River but otherwise these two take the game up a couple of notches, absolutely recommended!
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
[BGCOLOR=#99FFFF] [b]7 [/BGCOLOR] March 2021 - 19 plays[/b]
A quintessential gateway game that also doubles for an enjoyably casual time for experienced gamers. With the first two expansions, you can really scale this to suit the players at the table. If it is mostly new players, consider removing farmers from the game so that they'll have a better chance. I find it fun to go for high stakes city steals where I may or may not draw just the right tile. I get the most use out of the expansions when playing with only my wife. If I've got a group of 3 or more experienced gamers, there are more cognitively rewarding games to choose.

[BGCOLOR=#33CC99] [b]9 [/BGCOLOR] Oct 2022 - 20 plays[/b]
I should give Carcassonne more credit. It holds up to a lot. Party game with a high player count, cutthroat couples' game, or just a casual anytime game. It plays breezy and satisfying.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Ein toller Klassiker, mit einfachen Regeln und dennoch Tiefgang. Es ist damit Einsteigerfreundlich und trotzdem auch für Vielspieler interessant. Schön ist es obendrein.
Aufgrund des " Alters" ist es vielleicht etwas ausgenudelt (in der Form, das es von sehr Vielen, schon sehr oft gespielt wurde) . Abgesehen davon, ist es kaum gealtert und könnte ohne weiteres auch heutzutage rausgekommen sein.
Carcassonne wird (neben Catan) von vielen als der Vater/Mutter aller modernen Brettspiele gesehen. Und der Meinung bin ich auch.

Abschließend ist es erwähnens- & lobenswert, das in den neueren Versionen die Erweiterungen "Fluss I" und "Abt" direkt dabei sind.
Kurzer Nachtrag zum Abt: Es ist eine weitere Figur, die aus Gärten die selbe Funktion wie Klöster macht. (Gärten wurden mit der 2. Auflage 2014 auf einege Plättchen gedruckt). Bringt etwas mehr Varianz ins Grundspiel.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
+1 light. easy setup, short teaching time. 
+1 Initially strategy seems extremely shallow, but a little more meta strategy reveals itself with a few of plays. 

-1 Huge amount of random chance. 
-1 lots of my turns involve no meaningful choices or actions ('oh boy, another straight road piece...spare merson? yup... goes here then...')
-.5 what deeper strategy there is only comes with meta knowledge (how many of this tile is there, etc) or random chance
-1 Scoreboard is often meaningless, as final tally can feel almost random ('oh, I  won?') or meaningless if folks are paying attention. 

Takes too long to be a filler-game, but fills time with atable of very new/attention-scarce players. Bores me to tears if played more than once in a blue moon. 

I suspect a few expansions, or min-maxing with some very competitive players might make this a little more enjoyable.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Simple tile laying game that is interactive allowing you to place figures, called meeples, on graphical features such as cities, roads, farms, monasteries, etc. Everything is medieval themed. A great family game, that is also excellent for a small party willing to learn a few simple rules and play something that has potential to be as advanced as you want to make it. Short gameplay with just the base game. Many expansions are available that will increase the strategy and length of play.

The best aspects of Carcassonne are the variability where no two games are exactly alike, the simplicity, yet depth of strategy involved in outmaneuvering an opponent and maximizing your scoring with a limited, random tile selection. Perfect intro game for inexperienced gamers. Young children are better off exploring a simpler version of Carcassonne called 'My First Carcassonne.'
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
01/17/02 Bought the 2000 edition. Love it. A great gateway game. You can either "play nice" with newbies, showing them where they can help themselves the most. Or the screwage factor can be very high if you want to try to hinder as many of your experienced opponent's structures as possible, or glom on to them when the opportunity arises. 
As of 03/23/24 I've played 142 games, the majority with an expansion (or two).

08/15/17 Played using the new edition, and its Abbot expansion. The abbot was a nice addition.  Though I have no idea what fields have to do with being an abbot.  I did find a lot of the incidental artwork on the new edition tiles distracting as it was 2-3 times the size of the old version's minor artwork (pig pens, sheep corrals, and the most annoying, buildings around road intersections). Also, a few of the roads were yellow instead of white. Huh?

(From Big Box 2009.)

2010-04-14 (rating 8):

The game is great! The rules are simple (not counting some bizarre expansions interactions) and yet the game is challenging and fun.

It can be played aggressively or calmly so should fit many needs. Due to large number of expansions a lot of options is available and the game scales well with used time (just a base game is short, all the expansions are long - it is easy to choose a combination which fits needs and available time very well).

However playing just the base game especially in more than 3 players may become somewhat boring and a bit too random after some time. But again the expansions are there so no problem!


Currently I prefer to use [gameid=45748] as the base game. Also I am testing a variant where one draws 3 tiles selects one and discards the rest back to the pool. This way the game is less random.

textfield_comment_value:
My all time, go to game for 'modern' games.  It was one of my first modern games, and i STILL play this game a lot.  My copy is so well loved, the box is falling to pieces.

I have accumulated many xpacs along the way, but to be honest in recent years me and my group always play vanilla.

Vanilla Carc is one of the best games out there.  Love the tile laying aspect, love the simple premise of 'help yourself or screw an opponent - ideally both'  per turn.

An excellent game for noobs in 'modern' games.  The tile laying and worker placement is often so different to what they have played, that they find it really intriguing.

the ONLY (tiny tiny ) thing i dont super love is that Carc is a game where it is hard to keep pace with the scores...  in some games so much of the final result is counted up post game, that you lose that 'race/keep up/overtake' excitement.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
One of the first wave of great Euro-strategy games, this is a game that has a very simple gameplay and easy setup and execution, but which also has endless replay value.  There's a huge number of expansions and versions available, but the original set alone is enough to keep you occupied forever.  It can be taught in just a few minutes, but with the degree of variation, it never gets stale.  You can play offensively or defensively, the strategy can get quite deep, and it's not too random.

As perhaps the very definition of a tile-laying game, it works great -- the pieces are solid with attractive artwork, and the theme is simple enough to lend itself to a lot of variations.  It takes up a decent amount of space, but there's not too many pieces or too much complexity.  This game is a classic for a reason, combining simplicity and elegance for tons of play value.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Carcassonne accomplishes exactly what it sets out to accomplish - it is, like it says on the back of the box, a "simple tactical game". I think this is what people who complain about the randomness of the draw involved miss entirely - it's not intended to be Ora et Labora. I rate it so highly because it accomplishes this very, very well. 

The beauty of it is how the level of competitiveness scales to your playgroup. It can be played in a laid-back way with casual gamers and relatives, a sort of semi-collaborative puzzle where much of the enjoyment is derived from observing the gradual growth of your bucolic French countryside. It can also be a cutthroat battle to the death for 30 point cities and farms. It doesn't force either of these split-personalities on you - it is what you make of it. 

It is simple, elegant, and can be played with practically anyone.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
I realize Carcassonne is popular.  I try to grade games on what they bring to the table, not what they aren't.  No doubt Carcassonne has brought a lot of people into the hobby.  

That said, I just think there are far too many tile games that are more interesting.  I would recommend Alhambra over this game times ten.  I'm certain that the Alhambra Big Box would be more played and more enjoyed by most average people than Carcassone and its best expansions.  

Carcassonne almost drove me away from all tile laying games.  I tried several times to like it, but it just never felt that interesting.  I only reluctantly tried games like Alhambra and Fjords . . . and realized I didn't have a problem with tile games, I had a problem with just Carcassonne!

Carcassonne, like Catan, deserves its place in history. But just like Settlers, better games have come along.

textfield_comment_value:
Place map tiles and meeples to complete map features for most points.

Plays: More than a dozen?
Type: VP race = a game where you race to collect victory points (fastest/most).
Complexity: Family game = A game that is easy to teach and play.
# of players: 2-5.
Playing time: 30 mins.
Player interaction: Can be played without interaction. Competitive play will involve competition for scarce resources and opportunity prevention. These become more pronounced with 2 players, making the game less family and more strategy.
Randomness: Medium - tile draw.

Replayability: Not so high, usually this serves as a starter or a filler.
Fun: A bit of fun to complete your map features.
Memorability: Not really.

Thematic integration: Workable, with broad appeal.
Components: Iconic. The original Meeple.

Who will like this: Everyone. A must have in every game collection.

textfield_comment_value: 6.5 - I generally did not enjoy playing this game but it haunted my memories years and years later with questions about would I still hate it?  I decided to give it a second chance and so went out and purchased a new copy thinking that my tastes may have mellowed a bit.  When I first played this game I was barely into the board gaming hobby and I didn't like all the points and didn't like that it was just flipping tiles over.  Now that I have a better understanding of the mechanics I see a deeper strategy, blocking some areas while being a total sneak and jumping into someone else's town through clever placements.  Learning the tile pools helps a great deal as well so you aren't blindly hoping that a tile that doesn't exist comes up.  The game is definitely more fun and I occasionally feel an itch to play so I think it will be sticking around this time.

textfield_comment_value:
Carcassonne was a blind buy after Settlers of Catan was becoming the staple game at my house. I wanted something new and refreshing that had the replay value of Settlers. I had not heard about Board Game Geek at the time of this purchase and my confidence in this title came from reading customer reviews of Settlers on Amazon.com and other vendor sites.

Carcassonne has since become my favorite "gateway game". Much like Alhambra, I love this game with four or less. Two is obviously this best, three is good. Four is manageable and anymore than that is purely when I am playing with non-gamers. Carcassonne has won over so many people into acknowledging that boardgames are a great way to pass the time.

Add to that the game has numerous GREAT expansions which make it completely customizable and you have the makings of a top 10 game for me. I love this game.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
[b]Includes expansion 1 Inns and Cathedrals[/b]
[b]Includes expansion 2 Traders and Builders[/b]

Carcassonne was the second "gateway" game that I bought in Jan. 2009 (after Ticket to Ride). Consequently, it has been a mainstay in my collection from the beginning.

Carcassonne is an excellent gateway game for a couple of reasons--the rules are simple and straightforward, and a turn consists of simply placing a tile, and optionally sticking a meeple on it. It can be played very politely, or incredibly cutthroat. It's a great two player game, but plays well up to four as well. And finally, the result of the game is a very attractive map that everyone has worked on together--there's something rewarding about that.

If you plan on playing this with any regularity and with any desire to add some strategy, then the Inns and Cathedrals expansion is essential.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
In collection: 2018 August
Why did I buy it: Gift from a friend for my birthday.

Kid age sweet spot: 5+ (started with simplified rules at 4)

One of my most played games. Love teaching it to new players because there is no text and nothing hidden. I explain how to lay the tiles and the point system in 3 minutes and then we start a game! I can help new players make decisions at first and then let them do their thing. 

Started playing with farms and it gets more interesting because I feel every tile counts, where before when I got a road tile it would sometimes feel like a wasted turn.

Also tried the official solo variant from April 2020 once and it was a difficult and fun puzzle with tough decisions.

Started playing with my 4 year old son and he is slowly getting better and needs less and less help with strategic tile placement and counting points.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Non è solo il nome di una città della Francia meridionale. È diventato il simbolo della lotta all'eresia condotta dalla chiesa medievale. La cittadella fortificata, unica nel suo genere, è circondata da un paesaggio molto bello e intricato. I giocatori piazzano le tessere che contengono gli elementi del paesaggio (città, monasteri, strade e campi) ampliandolo ad ogni turno. Con i propri seguaci (cavalieri, monaci, ladri e contadini) i giocatori cercano di estendere definitivamente la propria influenza sulle singole aree e in questo modo ottengono punti vittoria. Bravo il giocatore che riesce a conservare i propri seguaci per le fasi più calde della partita... 
CARCASSONNE - Un gioco di strategia semplice e duraturo, assicura sfide nuove ad ogni partita.

Contenuti:
72 Tessere Paesaggio
40 Seguaci in legno
1 Segnapunti
1 Libretto delle regole

textfield_comment_value:
Carcassone (Devir/Esp) (7/10)

Uno de los primeros juegos de mesa que compre de la editorial devir.

Pros:
Reglas sencillas: Muy pocas reglas y fáciles de entender.

-Introductorio: Al tener sencillas reglas es perfecto para introducir personas en este mundo de los juegos de mesa.

-Variedad de expansiones: Muchas expansiones para darle más emoción a este juego, además de nuevas dinámicas.

Contra:

-Monótono: Después de jugar varias partidas, las estrategias se repiten y no existe mucha variedad (Al menos con el juego base) por lo que si jugase 3 partidas seguidas seguramente me aburriría.

-Tamaño: La caja es demasiado grande para la poca cantidad de componentes que trae, por lo que quizás podrían haber achicado un poco más la caja.

Resumen:
Lindo juego para comenzar en este mundo, lamentablemente lo tengo juntando polvo y no sale mucho a mesa.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Finally got around to getting/playing this game and I can only say that it is absolutely wonderful. Watching the countryside take shape and adjusting strategy and approach as it does is mesmerizing for me, like a fluid jigsaw puzzle where the outcome is created as you go. Only have the base game as of yet, but I can see where I'll want to add expansions quite soon. Easy to learn, but with many different approaches available for strategy, and the right sprinkling of luck of the draw, this is a keeper for me and my family. Truly deserves to be called a classic.

Update: after over 40 plays and the addition of Inns and Cathedrals, this has become one a favorite. We always play with the expansion now and it managed to make a great game better. My daughter and I play this whenever we get the opportunity now and I simply can't get enough. Great game.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Our other go-to gateway game. Rarely gets played when it's a group of 'gamers', as there always seem to be other games which are more attractive at the time. But when put in a social situation with people who haven't played many games beyond Monopoly, it still manages to please. Simple but still strategic in gameplay, scoring somehow manages to bewilder those new to the game; to the point that we essentially ignore the farmers unless we're playing with those who have played the game before.

Despite the fact that we rarely bring it out on its own, the plethora of expansions keep extending Carcassonne's life - breathing fresh air each time. As of this writing, we've only scratched the surface with one expansion. But it's nice to know that as time goes by, we can quickly and easily (and cheaply) keep the Carcassonne love going for a while to come.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
I love this game.  It's fast moving, simple in its concept yet very strategic, and doesn't take too long.

I bought it when my daughters were 5 and 7.  They both understood the basics of the game, so I was able to play with them but they didn't understand the strategy (understandably).  My 5 year old (now 7) didn't like it after the novelty wore off.  My 7 year old (now 9) still likes it. My wife doesn't like this game because of the "screwage" factor, but enjoys it if I promise to play nicely.

Some notes:
~ The water expansion that came with my version is pretty good
~ The Farms element of the game is something I haven't introduced to my kids...it's a bit too advanced for them I think.  The game plays fine without playing Farms.
~ The quality of the tiles is fantastic, have held up 100% after about 20 plays
~ I like it best with 2 players.

textfield_comment_value:
This was the game that sucked me into boardgaming.  It got to the point where we were playing mega-Carcassonne, using several hundred tiles, letting the tension build throughout the game as farms get connected to each other in convoluted and unexpected ways.  In some games, we end up with 7 or 8 meeples competing for a single massive farm.  The L-shaped road piece is the greatest single tile in the game.  So much damage can be done using this unassuming tile.

Personally, I don't like the rules in the expansions that allow a player to eventually free meeples from the board.  It's fun to trap your opponent's meeples and force them to look for a specific tile, watching them squirm the longer and longer they wait for that elusive tile.  You can really get an edge over your opponent if you make them squirm and lose focus on what they need to do.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
The best part of this game is that it's ready to play within seconds. No setup necessary. Most strategic game takes around 5 minutes to setup and is boring to do so but not this. This is because the board is built during the game. This also adds high replay value. 

So far only played with two players and it works great. It's very interactive in a very subtle way, something few games manage. 

So one could say it's very luck driven because you draw what tile to play. But I think it's one of those play with what you got games. 

The most negative part of this game is the incredible boring theme. Although very pleasant artwork the boring theme (or lack thereof) gives this game a lower score. With the mechanics in this game it could have been in space, monsters or anything really but instead it consists of villages, road, cloisters and farms.
