Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
How can a game so simple amaze me every time I play it? The main mechanic, take a tile, place a tile is simple, yet open to so many tactic and strategic moves. I still love, as much as the first day, that you end up having created a unique ‘city’ of your own at the end of every game.
I also love how you can adjust the level of evilness between players. Want to stay in your neighbourhood? Certainly possible. Want to be aggressive? Also doable. You can even modulate this with the expansions. The firstone is great, now you can be more aggresive. Second expansion, specially for larger groups, allows positive interaction between players, which I adore.
I’ve played other tile-laying games, but Carcassone is still the king. It defines the genre,  and shows how much can you achieve with so few rules, just sticking to tile laying and area control.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Good game to pass the time. a bit boring, to be honest. There isn't much going on the board.

!!UPDATE!!

The more I play this game, the more I enjoy it and 3 years later and my opinion totally changed. I used to rate it at 6, but now I give it an 8. Why?

a) It's extremely simple to setup and teach.
b) It has an element of puzzle solving with endless variation. Every game is never the same. Different player offer different challenge.
c) It has good interactivity among players to guarantee any session will always be lively and lighthearted.
d) It has the perfect length. It's not too fast that you feel you haven't done anything, but not too long that the game overstay its welcome.

I'm one of those guy who rotates his collection a lot. Of all the light/medium game that I bought, Carcassonne is the only one I keep and will never be sold.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Update:  This will always be a good game to introduce to new gamers, but I don't seem to reach for it too often otherwise.

Update:  We did finally play the uber-game with all the expansions at once, it was huge and took over 2 hours!

This was our first real 'Geek Game' that I found via BGG.  There's a very good reason that it's so highly considered.  This is just a terrific classic that is accessible yet always challenging.  There are too many permutations to get jaded with it.  We liked the base game so much, that after one week with it, we ordered the "Big Box II" so that we could have all the best expansions and we passed the base game along to my in-laws.  We've never played all the expansions at once, and yet, it's fun to try to pick ones that will work well together.  This is one we will keep coming back to time and time again.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
This, Catan, and Ticket to Ride were my gateway games back into the hobby. I played them a ton on Xbox Live Arcade, and then eventually got physical copies and played a bunch with friends, and then eventually branched out to other games.

I also used to work for a small video game publisher, an we used to play a game of this every single morning to determine who would have to go out to get coffee (person in last place went). I didn't have to get coffee very often :) On Xbox, a game only took about 10-15 minutes for the three of us.

So because of that, this may be the single board game I've played the most, probably at least 200 games. And I still enjoy playing it (playing it again on BGA right now, as a matter of fact).

I hope someday I'll design a game as timeless and well played as this is, even 22+ years after its first release.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Carcassonne is a classic Euro game of tile laying, meeple placing (and is in fact the original source of the word, which of course is a portmanteau of "my people"). You place tiles, claim regions (in the most basic game, roads, cities, and monasteries). Closing off regions score them, roads can be shared in ties, cities are not, and cloisters score for being surrounded, and it's all very straightforward. 

I'd only played this game once before, with a copy I'd bought when I was in Germany, and that was before I really delved into Hobby gaming. I can understand why this game has a dozens of variants, expansions, mods, and other ephemera, and at the same time I can grasp why this game has a sorta odd place in the hobby games canon. It's fairly light, fairly strategic, super low conflict, and just right to bring people into the fold.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Carcassonne is easy to learn, simple to play, and challenging to master against good competition.  I can see it making for a good gateway game for those who think of rolling a die and moving spaces when they think of board games.  This clearly isn't that and I think it'd be a good experience to break people out of that mentality.

But it's not a game I'd stick with for too long afterwards.  Would I play it if others were?  Sure.  But I'm not going to be picking it out of my cabinet on a regular basis.  It just sort of grew stale for me.  I don't think there's anything wrong with it per se, but there are only so many times I can build the world in Carcassonne before I start losing interest.

That's not to say it doesn't have a well-deserved place in one's collection.  But it is to say that it doesn't see daylight very often in mine.

Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value: Carcassonne went through a "dark age" for me after intially being very interested in it as a two player game...it got a little old, mainly because I played it a lot.  Then the newbie flux of 2002-onward started happening and it seemed like it's all anyone wanted to play.  Some bad experiences with 4-6 player games put me off.  Lately, I've been playing the game again and I realize that it's a genuine classic- a game that will truly stand the test of time.  It's one of the best casual games and one of the rare games where accessibility and ease of play don't foreclose on fun.  It's essentially abstract, but the sense of building and "project management" makes up for that.  With all expansions (the Carcassonne Big Box), it's a 9 all the way...without expansions, it's more like a 7 so I'll split the difference and give it an 8.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Note: I play with 3rd ed/HiG rules, not the 1st ed/RGG rules that came with the Big Box. 

Carsossonne is a tile-laying game, allowing you to build roads, cities, or fields, all interconnected. You only scores points by claiming a tile when you play it, using a limited supply of "meeples."

In my experience, Carcassonne is very dependent on who you are playing with. Playing a tile that makes a city or road difficult for your opponents to complete is one thing but this game can turn aggressive with some players. There is aggressive yet still fun, and then aggressive and ugly. 

However, it is by nature a variable game, different each time. And with the right crowd, is lots of fun. 

This game also travels well. Throw the tiles and figures in a couple Zip-lock bags and (with paper/pen to keep score) you are good to go.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
I've played Carcassonne close to 20 times.  It plays very quickly, and I don't think there is quite as much luck as some think there is.  It's more about managing your farmers than hoping to draw that perfect piece which will complete an over-sized city.  There are many shrewd tactical choices to be made.  When you draw a tile which doesn't directly benefit you, think about using that piece to hinder your nearest competitor to the greatest effect.  Doing so will make the game seem far less luck-driven.  

I've never lost at Carcassonne.  I've tied for first twice.  Generally my play group with it has been the same two people.  They beat me their fair share in other games.  So, either I'm extremely lucky, or this game is indeed deep in its strategy and tactics, and the luck is minimal.  I believe the latter is true.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
A classic children's game in which cities, buildings and roads rain from the sky, and you take turns trying to FOR GOD'S SAKE MAKE IT MAKE SENSE, PLEASE!

If I were to describe this as the perfect poster child for the "meh" that is the modern Eurogame, that would be terribly unfair. There are literally hundreds of suitable candidates.

But it is entirely fair to describe it as a children's game with an elaborate scoring system, like so many of its Euro brethren.

If for some reason I play this with you--yes, you there, with the scowly face--please do not be alarmed by my apparent incompetence at such a simple game. It's just that I am imagining hordes of zombies emerging from the monastery to fight a swarm of cybernetic spiders with laser-beam eyes at the Battle of There's a Crossroads Here for No Particular Reason.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
3 plays. 

I can definitely see the appeal: clear, elegant, in some ways free-flowing, in other ways back-stabbing.

So why am I not eager to play Carcassonne again? It's a matter of taste, I guess, and this game simply isn't for me. If I'm making tricky investment decisions, I think I need a fairly straightforward way to evaluate my possibilities; I'm thinking, for example, of Lost Cities, which I love, or Battle Line. 

In Carcassonne, I just don't feel like the map everyone builds together gives me satisfying agency. I founded a city! I'm going to make it big! Oh no, you decided to make it tiny. Why are we doing this again?

I dislike doing so much scoring tabulation, and relying on scoring for victory. Wish there was a bit more direct player interaction surrounding victory.

Lightness (1)-Heaviness (5) rating: 2
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
I like a lot about this game - competitive, probabilistic thinking, and interesting tension between short term, medium term, and long term point gains. My son started playing this when he was 4 (no farmers), and full rules by the age of 5 and he continues to like it.

However, my wife SO doesn't like the end-of-game importance of farmers (where everything you've worked towards all game can be undone by 1 or 2 skillful and/or lucky farmer placements) that it's hard to get her to play. The result is that we play this far less than comparable gateway games. That's what brings down the score for me - if it's hard to get my favorite game partner to play, then what good is it?

We tried the expansion Traders and Builders and that made it even more fun for me but less for my wife. Haven't used any of the other expansions.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
I personally don't care for it a ton. I'll play rarely and I'm willing to give expansions a try to attempt to spice it up, but if I never play Carcassonne ever again, I'll be fine with that. 

One of my biggest complaints is the spiky cities that develop, and the way farms are scored/formed. Neither of those things are truly terrible, but they bug me enough to lower my enjoyment of the game overall. I've also had personal issues understanding some cases where spike edges of cities touch or come close to each other, and whether it forms a connected farm. Again, not a gamebreaker but it did affect my enjoyment. 

For a new/novice gamer, I think there are better light games out there like Ticket to Ride or King of Tokyo. For an experienced gamer, there are way better and prettier tile laying games that have come out.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Much better game than people give it credit for. No output randomness, satisfying tile laying, can be explained to beginners in two minutes and has a non overwhelming yet very interesting amount of player interaction. Beginners may not ignore the other players a bit more, and see less interaction, but anyone with a couple games under their belt will discover more and more depth, for example with "hostile takeovers" or blocking other players' structures. It's always exhilarating when two players are trying to attacg more and more meeples to a giant game-winning field, especially when they gamble away so many meeples that neither of them win.

Game plays best with 2 players as you really get to flesh out the board. Good up to 4 players. With 5, you don't get enough tiles to feel like you can affect the board enough.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
I really like this game.

CONS: not very confrontational with 2 players. The scoring track sucks - it only goes up to 50 by which time you flip your meeple on its back to signify 50+ and keep going around. Probably not a big deal with more than 2 players- thus less scoring but we find ourselves loosing track if we score big as then you gotta flip your meeple a different way...sigh.

PROS: well the pros far out weigh the cons.  EASY! game play, fun tile laying, opportunity to steal points (I like this :) Fast for those need to fill between games moments.  Good all rounder! Great for first timers!

UPDATE: if you find Carcassonne a bit unchallenging or a tad bit boring you HAVE TO get Traders and Builders extension- best buy ever. It turned my Carcassonne game hating partner into a believer (or is it follower?) :)
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
When I was first introduced to this game a year or two back, I put the following brief review on my website:

"If you%u2019re into tabletop games, you could do far worse than give Carcassonne a look. Having played it (till my head hurt) quite a bit over recent weeks, I%u2019m blown away by how perfect a game it is. The rules are staggeringly simple, the strategy simple enough for a beginner to pick up (yet subtle enough to reward experience), and the games themselves last less than an hour. In my book, that ticks all of the boxes perfectly. Highly recommended."

I still stand by it. Carcassonne is, in my eyes, the perfect board game and ideal for opening your friends' eyes to the joys of gaming. Granted, many of the expansion packs can detract from the game, but the plain vanilla original is bang on the money.

Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Beautiful game, unusual in that it's a lot of fun for anywhere from 2 to 6 players. Great for all ages 4+ (though scoring needs to be done for the littlies). The brilliance is the lovely board, a unique version of which you create in the course of playing... so set-up time is very short. More strategy than you might think; my mother-in-law LOVES this game but has never beaten me, despite many dozens of plays (we play Carcassonne rather than talk!). In fairness, she does suck really badly at it - my (then) 5 year old daughter was a good match for her. Interestingly, the style of game changes dramatically as the skill of the players increases, and also with the number of players.
Has an excellent iOS app with strong AI that play very aggressively - "evil" is quite beatable, but it will require some thought.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value: Players draw and lay a tile each turn, incrementally building structures that score the builder points upon completion. Players vie to disrupt others' plans or to annoyingly assist and thereby share in others' reward points. There's a small challenge in deciding where to place each tile, but there's nothing especially deep to the game. I've only played a few times and should probably play more and with some of the many expansions before forming a final judgement, but I think the game will only ever be a pleasant diversion rather than something exciting to seek out, which is why I've played so little. The basic theme does lift it above comparable abstract games. But abstract gamers are going to like it more than those who like theme. It is quick to teach and would be good to play with kids. A gateway game.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
I enjoy all Carcs as ideal two-player games: Relaxing pastime, accessible play, and I'm not normally bummed when I lose because watching the countryside develop is just enjoyable. And what's not good about a game you can play with your grandmother. There was a while when I was swayed into the slightly superior elegance of H&G and the other Carc expansions, but I've come to appreciate the big swings of original Carc. I really only play this as a 2-player. (It just doesn't do it for me with more)

I understand why so many gamers think there are very little decisions to actually make. But, really, I just enjoy this game as an activity to go with conversation and a good friend. I get why you think there isn't much game here, but I wouldn't feel right without the time I've spent playing this. It is a joy.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Simple rules, interesting and interactive game play.  Plus, you create lovely "map" on the table.  Multiple expansions to keep it fresh. Excellent stuff.  Winning a "field war" or completing a hostile takeover of a city is wickedly pleasing.  (Fortunately the highs of succeeding at those things are higher than the lows of failing at those things, if you know what I mean...) Best with 2-3 players in my judgment (I think I most prefer 3p but it’s a very close call).  It can stretch to 4p but personally I wouldn’t play with more than 4.

What's interesting to me is how varied the range of games is that results from a simple rule set and the same set of tiles. Some games are cutthroat wars for the 1 or 2 huge farms; in other games, the farms are splintered and farms are secondary in importance as a result.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value: I have many mixed feelings on this game. On one hand, it’s not a favorite. But it seems to scratch a joy that few other can especially for those new to gaming. I think, you know, there’s gotta be some elegant game that this inspired, something heavier or more interesting. But somehow, it always ends up feeling flatter than the original (though I hear the official spin offs are good, I’ve yet to try them). I do miss the old softer and more serene art. The new art just looks busy to me and lacks that calming quality I so enjoyed in the original. But oh well. Things move on. I sold this game. Then bought it again. Now I regret buying it but I’m afraid to sell it again for fear I’ll want to buy it again. Gateway games are dime a dozen but few manage to come anywhere near the classics, no matter how flawed.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Game that got me into all this (thanks methsdrinker!) - great stuff - easy to learn, and easy to get others involved, inc. non-gamers. 

With slightly modded rules, have even played with my 3-year old, and not a single meeple casualty (so far).

Often use "The River II" (for an uber-river - by the way, Meeples can't swim...though they do float) & 12 central tiles from "The Count of Carc" (but not the count himself) to add starting set-up variety - Inns & Cathedrals are pretty much always in there too, except when playing with the wee one - too long otherwise!

Interesting solo variant described on the geek too.

EDIT: Comments from Jan 2010 above; now 3 years later I'm still enjoying this, particularly on the ipod and with Emma, including Inns and Cathedrals, but not counting fields, and she's good!
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value: Mixed feelings on this one. It is a light and pretty game, but there is not much control to it and the choices are hardly tense or deep. Not a great favourite when playing with adults, hence my pretty low rating. I would, however, give this a nine as a family title. My kids (five and seven) love it and can compete on equal terms, both with each other and with their parents. The fact that it is part of the game to have discussions about the tile placement helps a lot in this regard while the scoring is of just the right complexity to introduce the feel for Germanic titles. Also, the potential for high scoring farmers at the end of the game and the potential for some nice bits of screwage (a plus in our family!) adds a level of strategy that they can grow into as they become more familiar with it.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Ingenious and very well done. Easy to learn and teach. It involves varied strategies and tactics. The counting is easy but a bit annoying. The game is quite balanced. All matches ended with a minimal difference in points between players. Good for both two and three players. It also worked in five, but it is difficult to sustain the strategies. -1 due to luck that still determines the victory.

This game fits as a metaphor for life. You get the pieces chance offers you and try to fit them in the right way. You have the workers representing your attention and investment labor, decisions based on prudence, prevision and consideration capacity.
Would like to see a metaphor for life not so based on Ego though...
Maybe a co-op spin-off objecting the building of a better or more beautiful common board.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Very good game. Takes only a five minutes to explain the rules and one or two play throughs to adopt the them. With maximum number of six players and with one or two add ons this game still takes only about one and half hour. About 30-45 minutes with two to three players.

The game board is made up placing square tiles one at a time by each player so the game board will always different. I liked the art work very much, it's simple, beautiful and functional. Basic rules are simple and each add on adds an extra set of rules, which will all fit together with the basic game or with any other add on. Although, playing for example with six add ons youd better move the game from table onto the floor to make sure there is enough space and playing with six sets of rules can make a game a bit complicated.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
The other game that got me into modern board gaming.

Pros:
A great starter game for people new to the hobby.
Easy to teach, easy to scale the difficulty by turning mechanics on or off (we only play cities, roads, and monasteries with kids and newbies).
Fun to watch the landscape develop as the game goes on
A lot of different ways to play
Usually good and masking who is winning until close to the end (unless it's a clear blow out but that's rare).

Cons:
Table hog
Most of the expansions aren't really worth it except to get more tiles (which makes the game longer).
Games can become really heated if you're playing in a cutthroat manner - just go over expectations beforehand
Can create decision paralysis if someone doesn't like having lots of options
Mechanics can be broken down into points per turn

textfield_comment_value:
Nice, relaxing, fun game. Of course we quickly became cutthroat with it by trying to steal and ruin other people's cities.

We include the tiles for the first two expansions, but typically play base rules except for cathedrals. Reading the full rule books for those expansions gives me the impression that they add needless complexity.

Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value: Definitely worthy of its reputation and its popularity.  Carcassonne is one of those rare games that appeals to hobby gamers, families, and even non-gamers.  It has surpassed Bohnanza, Settlers of Catan, Daytona 500, Union Pacific, and Showmanager as my #1 game to pull out with non-gamers. [Edit: it has since been usurped in this capacity by Ticket to Ride.]  And among seasoned gamers, the game reveals a surprising level of depth.  By all means, use the original farmer scoring rules (4 points awarded per city to whomever has the most farmers touching the city).  It is better balanced, more intuitive, and easier to explain than the later revisions.  Carcassonne in its basic configuration rates at least an 8 with me, and judicious use of expansions knocks it to a solid 9 or even approaching 10.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value: Considering we have more than 150 recorded plays of this game (when you add in every mini-expansion and variant) you'd rightfully assume it to be among our favorite games of all time. . . you wouldn't be wrong. Carcassonne has all the hallmarks we look for: easy to play, learn and teach gateway tile laying mechanic with more strategic depth than at first glance, great art and theme, plays quickly with evident scoring and above all it's fun! Whenever we tire of the base game it's so easy to refresh by adding in a full expansion, or mini-expansion or two or three. When we want a more novel tile laying experience we get out one of the superb variants like H & G or South Seas or Gold Rush. We feel this pioneering game should be the cornerstone of any great gaming collection. Long live the meeple!
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
What a delightful game!  This is my favorite light Euro.  It is easily accessible to newcomers yet varied and strategic enough for frequent gamers.  Each expansion also seems to add and enrich the game.

To be fair though, the base game all alone has a few shortcomings for me: the lack of a 6th player, the incomplete feel of a total package, and too short.  Inns & Cathedrals make up the first two points while Traders and Builders takes care of the last 2 points.  I rarely play the game without at least these two expansions.  Even if I don't use all the rules, I keep all the tiles in the game.

So basic vanilla Carc probably deserves a score of an 8 for me.  Hunters & Gatherers and Ark of the Covenant are the better basic games.  But with the expansions, Carcassonne is impossible to beat.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Combined base game, Big Box and expansion to make huge game.

+ Great gateway game. A good way to introduce new gamers, and slowly up the depth and difficulty with expansions.
+ Fun with 2
+ Expansions offer a lot of variability and difficulty settings

o The farmers, although seemingly simple, offer a lot of depth. (even more when adding Barns) Which is great for experienced players (I'd rather not play without) but might be difficult for beginners, or those who have trouble 'seeing' how they can expand their farmland.

- We hardly play this anymore, because with the amount of tiles we have, it takes hours to complete. We'd rather spend our time on a heavy euro. Whenever we want to have a quick 1:1 Carcassonne experience, we turn to Carcassone: Star Wars, which add a bit of direct conflict.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
The famous game that I really never cared for. I played only 2-3 times with some expansions (river expansions and something else that I don't remember). I thought I would play if I buy the game. So I bought it. I never opened it. I found Die Burg and I liked Die Burg. I only played Die burg. I sold the game unopened. Now I love Die Burg and think about this original Carcassonne. Do I want to play? Not really. 

It is so interesting to find out that these two games (Carcassone and Carcassone - Die Burg) are a lot more different than I thought.

Carcassonne - flip a tile. Find where it is playable. Later flip a tile and hope it is the one that matches the other tile that benefit you.

Die Burg - flip a tile. Now it can be played almost anywhere. Wow. So many decisions. Decisions Decisions....
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Despite loving this series of games, I don't actually love the balance of base Carcassonne. 

Players have a larger set of meeples than I prefer, but it's kind of needed because trapping pieces on the board is easy due to a limited tile mix. Scoring doesn't feel very balanced with roads being quite bad and farming clearly the strongest option.

But add in an expansion or two (preferably Inns & Cathedrals together with Traders & Builders) and original Carc turns into a lot of fun! Unfortunately adding two expansions extends game length as well, and you end up with so many meeples that deciding whether or not to place a piece each round often becomes an obvious "yes"... but neither of those complaints is that bad.

Still a classic game, even if I think some of the stand-alone sets are better.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
:star: simple, straightforward rules make it very approachable for new players
:star: plays quickly, especially with 2
:star: offers plenty of decisions and player interaction

2012-04-12

Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
My wife and I love playing this game!  Good strategy game and a great stepping stone for people getting into board games.  Also the games are fast enough that you can play a few back to back or a quick game before bed.  

Game play is only three steps and is super simple, but the options are nearly limitless for how the game could play out.  Building a small city?  Four edged city piece placed by an adversary ruins everything.  Control a huge section of farmland?  Suddenly your opponent connects a field with a standalone church and takes control of the entire map.  The blend of unpredictability, luck, and strategy makes for a great game.  Plus the indirect form of competition makes you feel less like you're playing against your opponents and more so as if you are playing alongside them.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value: My girlfriend, whom I introduced the fun of board gaming to, will not leave me alone about carcassonne! I love the game but every night shes begging to play it. She texts me during our work days talking smack or asking to play at 8pm when the kids hit the hay. We have just about every expansion for it. except for the catapult. She wants to make an extra large bag (bag included in the builders and traders exp) so we can hold all the tiles from org + expansions+ wheel of fortune all at once..good lord. So anyway its a great game. Any friends we have introduced have liked it first play. And oh we don't play with the dragon/fairy cause I tend to get neglected or vise versa for a day or more do to temper flares! (we do use the tiles that came with the set though) Get it. its easy to learn
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Played with 4. 
Used Rivers Expansion.

One of the easiest games to introduce new players to.  I would explain the basics of scoring but not get too long in explaining as the games end fairly quickly.  After a game or two most people will understand the scoring and city mechanics.  The game is played by laying down tiles and placing meeples on different parts of said tile to create roads, cities, monasteries and other scoring areas on the board.  

I enjoy this game a lot more than Settlers of Catan if only because you do not have the resource trading that can agitate players, nor do you have the streak of really bad rolls or unlucky pick order.  I would score it an 8 if you are playing with the "competition" rule of drawing 3 tiles initially and redrawing one after each tile played.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Fast pace game with almost no down time if everyone plays in normal speed. Very easy to learn with only a few minutes to learn to scoring system. Though the game is heavily lucky based to see what tile you draw, your token placement is very important and affect your point greatly. Very well balance game with a little leaning toward the luck side. Very new player friendly.

Who would enjoy: Light and fast game play.

Easy to learn: 8/10
Replayability: 6/10
Theme: 5/10
Tactic: normal
Personal Fun Scale: 9/10
Luck balance*: 3/10
Abstract reading**: 1.5/5

* score of 10 would mean no luck is required, while 0 means luck based completely

** critical thinking and reading in comparison to classic board game such as shogi, chess, and go since I personally like simple yet delicate problem.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
[With River, River II, Inns & Cathedrals, Traders & Builders, Count, King & Scout, the Phantom]

It's a fine game, we sure have played plenty.  Hunters and Gatherers may be a bit more elegant, though.

So, the base game + Traders & Builders or Inns & Cathedrals is LONG, too long for what it is.  The base alone has too few city tiles, making luck of the draw too important, even for this.

BUT, for two players, base + King (from King & Scout) gives a light, fun game -- less thinky and deep than Hunters & Gatherers, but more relaxing, perhaps.  Thanks to sister-in-law for leading us to figure that out.

Hrm, update:  K&S is too luckish once you both are playing well (yeah, took me a while).  So, what to do?  Carc is good, but maybe not so good as we thought, once you are used to it.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value: My appreciation for this game has gone up and down, very first times to try this game did not spark the interest too much (and it was well before playing Settlers of Catan - the game that really got me hooked). After getting more into board gaming I started to play Carcassonne again and few first times were good. Then again it felt boring after 10 or so plays, especially as some of the games were with 5 players (not recommended at all). Then I discovered how competitevly this can be played and especially with 2 players. And now I think it is a very good game for 2-3 players with really great replay value - every game evolves differently. Traders & Builders Expansion also sparked new life into this game and is now the preferred way to play the game for me (base Carcassonne + T&B)
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
The game is brilliantly competetive in 2 player, is with 3 players still roughly predictable. It is great fun all around, played it a million times. But it is very much reliant on memorization of the tile set and that gives a definite advantage over other players. Add the tile sets from the first two expansions and it dilutes that to a good degree.

Main issue is the publisher's policy to churn out expansions detrimental to the gameplay. From the first two expansion I prefer to play only with tokens, the big meeple and abbot. The cathedral rule staying. I play without the river, because it makes the map too static and the builder double turns are gruesomely bad with unconquerable roads to nowhere.

I very much prefer the old artstyle and it is a shame there is no choice given.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
My foray away from my roots and into more Euro games has finally led me here.  And I have to say... I like it.  Quite a lot actually.  It can be played in so many different ways and is open to different strategies, yet its simple tile drawing/laying mechanic allows even non-gamers to quickly grasps the concepts involved.  I have read a lot of comments about how confusing the farmers are but that has not been the case for my group.  I have also read that this game can be very cutthroat... ahem... that HAS proven to be true with my group.  And thats what I love about it.

Update - Still a staple and no sign of fading.  We now play without the river and with a hand of three tiles.  This combined with the abbey opens the door for a lot of combinations and pre-planned plays.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Such a classic game. Some pros:

1) Pleasing aesthetically
2) You feel that you are always playing, even in others' turns in order to find the best possible move
3) Expansion to try out
4) Huge replayability

There are some cons though, that's why I subtracted some points

1) Luck plays a decent role. Since I started playing on BGG, I got stomped by a lot of people and I can assure people that despite the luck factor, you have to be good in order to score good points. However, luck, indeed plays its role, leading you to master the "get the most out of a bad situation/tile".

2) Some concepts of the game (I am looking at you farmers) are kinda difficult for some people to grasp.

Game is classic for a reason, its pure tile placement madness and fun. IMO it's worth every penny.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value: This game isn't nearly as good as I expected from the hype.  If you or your opponent/s don't understand how to steal points away or to prevent point scoring, the game becomes just a very simple game of placing your drawn tile where it fits.  I've yet to lose a game of carcassonne simple because no one I've played has caught on to the deeper strategies involved in scoring.  Kids love it though.  The expansion does help to make it more interesting and balanced. Update:  After a year of playing other great games, this just doesn't seem to compare.  There is so much luck involved that it isn't fun.  I bought the Traders and Builders expansion to hopefully make the game less luck dependent but it makes the game much more difficult to teach.  I'll pass and play something else.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
(01/08) It is a classic for a reason. It continues to engage with people I play it with. It usually gets to be played more than once in one sitting, even without any expansions games tend to vary a lot from game to game. It can accomodate experienced players and new players.

It is as simple as pick a tile, place a tile and decide if you want to put a meeple on it to try and get points according to the tile you placed it into, yet it can generate really interesting interactions and risky moves that can almost become a meta-narrative on the game. (A player built a castle that just keep on growing, will he be able to close it before the game ends?)

Quick, fun, simple. It has influenced other games to use this mecanism as part of a bigger machine (Isle of Skye, for example)
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Meh.  As far as gateway games go, I'd take Ticket to Ride, Pandemic, or Catan over Carc any day.  Maybe more plays and some more cutthroat opponents would help out, but I think the expansions will be the only thing that encourages me to bring this to the table with anyone except complete board game novices.
---
Just tried this with my fiancee's family, so 5 of us, and it was great.  I mean, it wasn't the deepest gaming experience, but it was great to introduce this to people and get such a great reaction from them.  Gateway game FTW.
---
I now see why this game is so tremendously popular.  It's a great gateway game, but plays very well as a richly competitive 2 player game as well.  The expansions just add more seasoning to the mix, if and when you want it.
Rating 7->8
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Maybe I'm still stuck in my board-gaming infancy, but I love this game.  It's probably the most enjoyable game my fiance and I play together, I love it for 2 people as it's much easier to set up your strategies and block the other player.  With the addition of the big meeple from an expansion, you really have some strategic choices to strong-arm the other player and try to steal their buildings.

I really enjoy the fast-pace, quick-turns, and satisfaction of looking at the unique board you created each game.

The reason it stays highly rated with me is that it's just so easy to jump into and play.  Want to play? Okay, grab the bag and pull out a tile.

Have to admit, it's starting to slowly drift down in rating though, as I get more games that I'm more anxious to play.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
One of my favorite games of all times.  Scales WONDERFULLY from 2 to 6 players it's the same fun.  People who say they don't like this game make me wonder if they are playing passively becuase the game is not a passive game.  Even without expansions like Princess & Dragon and Tower it's a very aggressive game if played correctly.  Don't believe me, give it a go on BSW.

After a lot of agonizing over this I am going to move Carc. up to the coveted 10 rating.  After all this time of playing this simple little tile laying game I still get juiced up playing it. Any game that can do that deserves a 10.

UPDATE: Yes definitely made the right choice moving this to a 10. Fits all the criteria and after literal years of playing I'm still loving Carcassonne.

Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Quite a simple tile laying game but can be very strategic for the more experienced players. The idea is to lay tiles to form the board. Each time you lay a tile you have the option to put one of your pieces (Meeples) on that tile to try and get points later in the game. They can be on roads, cities, cloisters or farms. Even though you may have more points early in the game the main part of the scoring happens right at the end when some big scores can start happening.

I would recommend this for kids with autism as I see it a structured game. I would 1st teach it using only the tiles without the meeples to just get the idea of correct tile placement. I would then add just one type of meeple at a time in subsequent games (no farmers) until this concept was understood.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
I'd say it was great but didn't age well.

The mechanic is awesome.  Simple & efficient
...but after having played it quite a bit, it feels way too random to me
How can you note hate it when you draw like 5 or more road tiles in a row ? (My personnal best must be 6 straight ones, in duel)

Also, I only tried the most common extensions, but the game felt better without them.
More tiles makes for unnecessarly a longer games
River/abbot => awful.  River tends to make one huge field, and abbot is a too powerful (&random) meeple.
Merchs&builders => Builder is OP, balance-wise, resources on fortresses would probably better have been put on routes, which, again, s*ck !

Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value: Carcassonne recently shot up to become one of my favorite games after a bunch of one-on-one plays with my partner.  This is a simply fantastic game; simple and fairly easy to teach, friendly-looking and colorful, but rewarding of a lot of thought and downright cut-throat when it comes down to it.  My partner even introduced it to my parents-in-law, and now they have their own copy that they play regularly, too!  A beautiful and elegant game.  I enjoy it most two-player, since it tends to take a bit longer with more players (only because people think harder about their turns and aren't able to plan ahead as much), but fun no matter what.  I honestly don't see getting too many expansions, I think they'd ruin the nice simple-but-difficult feel the game currently has.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
I owned Carcassonne several years ago. It was played a bit, but I never got into it. I lost the game while I was in the Army and I really did not have the desire to replace it. 

Recently I have been gaming quite a bit more though and one of the things that we have been looking for are good language independent games. We picked up the Carcassonne Big box because it just seemed like a good fit.

I have not been dissapointed. The game fits the bill for what we need. It has been enjoyable and I am looking forward to trying out some of the expansions.

Update: Added a few of the expansions in last night and suprisingly enjoyed the result. This game is getting played a lot due to the language independence and the ease of setup. I am glad I am trying this again.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Carcassonne does deserve it's place as a so called 'gateway game'. It's relatively simple and works well at all player counts. The game falls flat for me though in that it lacks replayability. Yes each game does play a little differently but I find the games lacking after repeating plays.

On a smaller side note this game is a worker placement and my personal preference with these sorts of games is that the theme really needs to stand out (more so than other games) and Carcassonne really falls flat on this. It's closer to an abstract game than a themed one (as seen by other versions of Carcassonne).

Edit: I am pushing this up to a 6.5 after playing this with two people. Much better game and less downtime between rounds. Most of my criticisms still stand though.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value: I'm starting to come around a bit on this game. I still am not a huge fan, but I can at least see it's appeal to the right crowd. For the serious gamer, this is still a game you won't be suggesting much, but if you have smart, non-gaming friends this can be a solid entry for doing somthing casual with them that will engage them without being threatening. For the fan of El Grande or Modern Art or Settlers of Catan, though, this doesn't have a whole lot to recommend it. If you do play, the first two expansions (the River, now included in the basic set, and The Expansion) are recommended in the strongest possible terms. Better yet, go direct to the more entertaining and visually appealing Hunters & Gatherers. Certainly later expansions should probably be avoided.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value: Was for a while my favorite game (with the expansions). I understand the criticisms, but the randomness is not an issue with me. And I know from beatings I endured on BSW that there is skill to this game, and tile draws will not mitigate against a difference in skill levels. Tis game has been a hit with every family member and friend we have taught it, and it is one my wife and I can play again and again. I prefer it for only 2-3 players. When it is just my wife and I, we play non-aggressively (limited blocking of each other in, etc.), and as a comfort game, it works just as well as when played in a more confrontational style. There are people whose opinion I value who really, really don't like this game, but the objections they raise don't seem to bother me.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value: Everyone seems to love this game, and I don't get it.  The appeal is that it's light, easy to understand, and good for new gamers who aren't that serious about getting into games.  But I am a serious gamer, and this game just has way too much luck involved.  It takes skill and strategy too, but because tiles are drawn randomly from the box each round, and that not every tile is of equal value, chance has a lot to do with who comes out on top.  And with the score board keeping track of who's in what place, it can be very very frustrating for the person in last place who keeps drawing "roads" while another player keeps drawing the one very specific tile she needs to complete her huge castle.  I don't have fun playing this game, I just find myself getting angry.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value: We play Carcassonne like an overweight man at a buffet, piling our plate with expansion after expansion, and engorging ourselves with an outrageous amount of different levers we're able to pull provided by the plethora of tile types. The game never feels overwhelming or like its over bloated with expansions (looking at you Arkham Horror). Quite the contrary. Without all the expansions, this game would be a nice 6. This game encourages and tempts players to compete for prizes all over the board, such as farms, cities, and large roads. The expansions just add onto that with even bigger cities and circuses to name a few. Sure you could play a peaceful carcassone game where everyone sticks to their own corner...but its a big shared procedural board for a reason!
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
I don't know why, but I always find this game incredibly relaxing for some reason. As with all games based on a blind draw, you're restricted to using judgement to determine the best play. It helps to be thoroughly familiar with the tiles and winning a valuable feature is all about combining nearby tiles such that your men form the majority. Be sure to use the 3rd Edition rules as these balance the farmer scoring much better. In all, a pleasant light game that's undemanding enough to appeal to just about anyone. 
Be warned though, Carcassonne has been much diminished by over-expansion. One large or a couple of the smaller expansions are all that you need, anything more and what should be a pleasantly light diversion turns into an analysis-paralysis monster.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
I have been having this game for years. I still like to play it occasionally. The game itself is awesome — true work of a genius, a design that happens once in century. Due to numerous expansions, and endless tweaks of the rules the game is a bit rough in some aspects and with too many expansions tend to drag, so the more the tiles, the lower the rating. But I'm adjusting rating for basic game and raising it, because core set is excellent. I think I'd like to see only some rules from expansion sets, pawns and tiles in a single Designer’s Cut Set… ;)

Edit: After a few years of hiatus I returned to the game. Now the feeling is a bit different. Bigger drag, less excitement, rating goes down. I still think this is very interesting design but it has some flaws.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value: Very enjoyable, simple game.  I get turned off by the sudden scoring swings that can occur when someone draws the perfect tile...  it makes the game *seem* more luck-based than perhaps it is.*** Updated (2008-05-28) - After playing a few hundred ranked games on XBox Live Arcade, I don't think I can fairly rate this anything lower than a 10, which is a significant jump from the 7 I had previously rated it.  There is a fair amount of strategic and tactical depth here that may not be apparent until you've played it several dozen times against some very good players.  I can't stress enough that this is my rating FOR 2 PLAYERS ONLY.  With three or more players my rating is significantly lower, starting at about a 7 and sliding downward as more players are added.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value: As the main game studier, buyer, player, etc. in my group of family and friends, I like games that other people like.  They just make it so much easier for me to get to play games.  I have found that most of my non-gamer friends and family take to Carcassonne easily, so I like Carcassonne.  There's more to it than that, however.  Even though it is a fairly light game, there is enough depth to keep me interested and having fun as well.  There are a lot of defensive moves that are not obvious at first glance, ever-shifting alliences are key, and blending a farmer into an important field always gets a bit of adrenaline flowing.  After having said all that crap about being the main game studier, let it be known that my wife almost always wins at Carcassonne.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Carcassonne is easy to teach, easy to play and quick. It's a good "gateway" game to get non-gamers interested in the hobby.

The things I enjoy most about the game:
- The board is different every time.
- Scoring is easy and tactics can be simple or complicated depending on your play group.
- There is good player interaction, but it's not a make or break element of the game.
- The components are simple and the tiles are easy to read.

The only thing that keeps me from giving this game a 10 is the fact that a player can get lucky and draw a bunch of favorable tiles that gives them a decent advantage. On the same token, drawing nothing but roads can be a major frustration. However, luck plays an integral part of the game, but it sometimes can feel a bit much.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Carcassonne: The Castle kept

6/19

The base game makes it hard at times to find a specific tile that one is looking for given the relatively tight placement requirements. The Castle loosens these requirements while constraining the area players play within, making the choices of where to place more consequential and tense. The fixed fun nature of the game results in players getting to take more actions when there are fewer players.
The design enables players to build a city or landscape. We prefer the more constricted and challenging Carcassonne: The Castle.

Earlier

I've enjoyed trying to sneak my followers into other peoples' castles, as well as maximize the rest of them.

As Paul Dean says, Carcassonne has a good turn simplicity to game impact ratio.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Carcassonne is a classic that I played a LOT in the first ten years I had it. We introduced house rules and played it in many different ways. 

It had been 8 years or so since my last play of this game, and recently played it again with straight out-of-the-box rules... and realized how much it is showing its age. There is a reason we created house rules for this- the luck factor is incredibly high. I actually hoped that perhaps there was an advanced ruleset that let you have a hand of 2-3 tiles, or drafting, or Smallworld-style card selection. 

The simple draw and play base mechanic is just... out of date. It's frustrating to draw straight road after straight road after straight road, while your opponent is building cities, completing monasteries, etc.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
So, I've been thinking - I really ought to play this more. In the time between turns, I could finish my thesis. And with all the expansions, a game could take several weeks.

Most viable for two because of this, and  while I recognize that there is a backgammon-like element of trying to make sure that you have a good move no matter what the next tile is, in general I don't have a lot of patience for the passivity of the draw-one-tile-then-play-it games. Of course, the Carcasonnes are prettier than backgammon, which helps a little.

Vanilla Carc though is just well, vanilla. Almost no tension, and I tire of it. I don't play games just to kill time. Hunters and Gatherers is a significant improvement, but even that I don't want to play with more than two.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value: One of the first games that i picked up to get my girlfriend to play more boardgames with me, and i can say that it has worked much better than expected. A very simple game that you can teach anyone but still with enough tactic to make it interesting for more hardcore boardgamers. I must say that this is a little gem and because om the short playtime it comes to the table quite often. At first my girlfriend was a bit sceptical of my pretty hard gaming style, screwing up her castles and such, but with time she grew fond of that style of play and now we have a real hard showdown every time we play. I can also add that this review is seen out of a 2 player perspective altough ive also played a few 3 player and 4 player games and really liked those aswell.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value: Carcassonne is such a fun unique classic. The create your board as you go mechanism is charming and I love how every map looks different at the end of each game. The farmers mechanism is a little tough for brand new gamers to grasp, but playing a game without the farmers is a good intro to work into the full game. This game can be a fun relaxing, chill but competitive experience, but it can also be downright nasty and mean if you set your priority to screw up your opponents' plans over your own scoring. Definitely group dependent on the tone of game you'll get out of this one, but I've not really found the fun to be anywhere near as fickle and dependent. It's almost always a great time and one that I love to use to introduce new players to the hobby.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value: [Tile-laying] [2P:4, 3P:3, 4P:3] How in the world did Carcassonne win the DSP? It's so fluffy and random, makes Puerto Rico a computational monster. It's still a decent gateway game to introduce the non-gamers to German-style boardgames, but more than three players increases the downtime (and the already-limited pleasure of putting tiles down) too much. The expansions don't do anything to improve this simple, rather boring game. Carc is most suited for children and non-gamer family and friends. *** UPDATE: Revisited the game to give it another chance, and it fell flat on its face with two newbies. It also bored me three-quarters to death. I really do not understand the appeal, but I'm not playing this or any of its non-Knizia derivatives ever again.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Been playing the base game for a while.  A 5-year-old can actually play this game and totally understand the rules--and do well!  (Assuming others in the game concentrate on trying to hurt each other and leave the little one alone.)

The base game is fun for the whole family.  There is both strategy and luck involved.  It plays maybe 30 minutes if your group is good at making decisions--and hour if they aren't.  There's enough interaction that it feels like you are playing together.

The one drawback is that the game really isn't deep as a base game, and next to Kingdomino, which packs roughly the same level of strategy into a cheaper game with a faster play time, it seems a teensy bit plodding.  Still, a game that it pretty, fun, and interesting.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
I've come to appreciate this game over time, but it's been a long road. These days I prefer it with four players and I think the odd lucky tile is outweighed by clever play and the fun of taking the odd risk. The basic game is fine.

I bought the very first German edition - where the rules for farmers were rather obtuse. Since then various rules about points scoring have been modified, so now I don't know what I'm playing until we run through the rules before a game and agree on them - usually depending upon what edition game we're playing. I'd suggest to the publishers that they start printing rules titles like "Big Box Carcassonne using fifth edition rules" on the cover, so we gamers could just start referring to the ruleset by edition numbers.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value: I picked this up after I read so many good things about it.  I was very disappointed.  This isn't a gateway game, it's just a children's tile-laying game.  The strategy is overly simple, and eventually comes down to memorizing the tile distribution -- Blech!  I've tried using it as a light gateway, but have had very limited success.  Most people I know just kinda look at me funny at the end and say "That's it?"  And god help you if you decide to play with more than three players, as the game drags on with no end in sight.  The rules are minimal and pretty easy to grasp, and the feel is familiar, which is the only explanation I can find for its popularity.  As someone who is entrenched pretty firmly in the hobby, though, it doesn't get me.  Pass.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Carcassonne habe ich mit 13 Jahren kennen und lieben gelernt. Ich hatte gleich inklusive der ersten Erweiterung angefangen und dann jährlich um eine Erweiterung ergänzt. Es ist ein Brettspiel, das sich für mich nach "zu Hause" anfühlt.
Mittlerweile habe ich über 20 große und kleine Erweiterungen und das daraus resultierende [i](eigentlich fast unüberschaubare)[/i] Regelwerk finde ich durch sein Facettenreichtum sehr spannend.

Vor ein paar Jahre habe ich dann zum ersten Mal das Grundspiel gespielt und gemerkt, dass ich diese Variante öde finde.

The tougher rule to explain might be the farmers, as I find quite some people who would rather skip that rule, I think the different crossings, bridges, small gaps, etc. Make it difficult for new players to really get it the first few times.

If you feel like a long game, have many extensions, and don't want to explain too much you can always skip any 'non standard' rules that are added by the extensions (I.E. Ignore the tower bases, vulkans, etc). That way you might cover your whole table with carcassonne tiles! :D

Nice relaxing game. I actually prefer it as a 2 player over anything else - a 2 player game allows some strategy to be worked in - it is more difficult to work any kind of strategy in higher player counts since your probability of drawing the tiles you need is drastically reduced. I prefer to play with Builders & Traders, Inns & Cathedrals, the abbot and the farmer. The other expansions add too much randomness for me.

Downgraded the rating: I like this game, for 2-players. At higher player counts there's too much grudge matching, king making and no hope for a strategy. The upside is that my non-gamer friends can handle it, but I would prefer to play something that doesn't give you 10 roads in a row after placing your builder in a city -_-
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
I think I enjoyed Carcassonne the first time I played it, but for some reason it always feels like a game which is slightly less than the sum of its parts.

I think it is surprisingly hard to have a good game - players can have wildly differing expectations of how aggressively it should be played, and enthusiasts can often insist on one of the dozens of variants and expansions being used when the base game is probably the best way to play. I also personally find the farmers difficult to visualise which detracts from the experience as they can be absolutely crucial (and/or cause an argument as to which of the scoring rules for them is being used).

Whilst an OK game if I'm in the mood, I find there's almost always something I'd rather play.

textfield_comment_value:
Simple to teach, which makes it great for newbies, but it has enough strategy to keep it interesting for experienced board gamers.  The games aren't overly long, and there's plenty of opportunities to screw over your opponents.  Works very well as a two-player game, but scales really well too.  It's also a small box, which makes it a great option as a portable game to bring along on trips.  

Good quality durable components, and neat to look at as you gradually build the towns and roads.

It's somewhat luck based and not overly strategic, but there's enough features to keep it interesting, competing for farming space means you can get back into the game even if you fell behind, and the short game time keeps it light and non-frustrating.

textfield_comment_value: Este juego es prácticamente perfecto y, ahora que lo pienso, tiene todo lo que suelo buscar en un juego: es fácil de enseñar y de aprender, compacto y fácil de transportar, competitivo, adictivo y, además, es engañosamente simple porque puede volverse muy complejo según con quién y con qué seriedad lo juegues. Los únicos dos puntos malos de este juego son el precio (excesivo para el tipo de piezas que trae) y el sistema de conteo de puntos, que puede ser muy confuso para quienes juegan por primera vez. Pero si no le pongo un 10 es simplemente porque no lo jugué lo suficiente ya que lo jugué principalmente de prestado en un viaje (y es perfecto para viajes). Algún día podré ponerlo en un estante propio y ese 9 se metamorfoseará en un 10.

textfield_comment_value: This is a good game overall, especially for your younger ones learning basic strategy and how to plan out routes to maximize points. I think this game could be greatly improved with a few added features such as castles you could take over, more strategic pieces, or perhaps simple battlefields you could use to compete against opponents.

textfield_comment_value:
Player interaction is so limited that Carcassonne feels almost like a solitaire game. The interaction that does exist is almost entirely with the intention of screwing your opponents over and yet the game remains very relaxing: Draw a tile, play that tile, and maybe put a meeple on it somewhere. A deep, off-topic conversation would disrupt the flow of most other games, Carcassonne is the exact opposite: You can have a deep conversation, forgetting you are playing the game, and when your turn arrives it won't even interrupt your train of thought.

The appeal of the game is actually in watching the layout of the Carcassonne countryside gradually unfold. 

In both gameplay and atmosphere, Carcassonne is this generation's Dominoes.

textfield_comment_value:
A real classic, and it's portable too! I must've played hundreds of games against the AI using the Inns & Cathedrals and Traders & Builders expansions.

What I find interesting about Carcassonne is how the nature of the game changes depending on the player count. With 2P it is more calculative, especially when playing with those who have memorised the tile compositions (not something I'd plan to do again any time soon, but it is an enlightening experience). With more players added, it becomes more like a party game, since players are prone to negotiate the sharing of certain features.

I've had a lot of success using Carcassonne as non-gamer's game because it's simple and the gameplay is as gentle as the players want it to be.

textfield_comment_value: An excellent game that just misses being considered a superb gateway game for me. Carcassone doesn't quite have the same caliber in game play as many of the typical gateway games. Overall, it tends to do better in raking in non-gamers, but it's not deep or complicated enough to push them over the edge into "real" gaming. The game is always fun to play, and the torrent of expansions do nothing but improve the game. I agree with most that there are way too many Carcassone expansions coming out way too frequently, but this can easily be eliminated by Not Buying All Of Them. Probably my favorite aspect of this game is that it is very playable with any age, from adult to teens, younger children down to two-year-olds. Fantastic.

textfield_comment_value:
There's little that can be said that hasn't been said a thousand times already, but in any case: 

Carcassonne is a simple, elegant, preeminent example of a German family game. It can be played friendly, or incredibly cutthroat. The game rewards skill to a great degree; there's no need for a hand of tiles. Such a variant is for people who haven't realized the power of blocking and stealing.

The game also works surprisingly well with 2 and greater player counts. The ability to share features becomes something to watch out for and help with or hurt.

The expansions add interest, too. There's certainly enough there to interest both a new and experienced player. Carcassonne is well worth your time, if you haven't yet played it.

textfield_comment_value: I fundamentally love Carcassonne; it's as placid or as cut-throat as you want it to be, one of the few games I've known which fits that bill. As an added bonus, it's a tile laying game (which I love for some irrational reason, maybe the building aspect, dunno). Best played with around 2, maybe 3 expansions at a time and that's it. (Almost always I&C, T&B, and one other that gets changed out periodically). One requirement is having a hand though, if I can have a hand of 3 or 5 tiles to choose from and draw at the end of my turn, it's great. As the rules are, the order of draw and place saps the game for me too much.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value: Played with 6 players and some basic expansions. I have to admit that the rules are rather easy to explain and understand, but the game is just too random and imbalanced. The player that won simply rolled a ton of cathedrals, which were much easier to score with than e.g. castles. I didn't feel like players had much strategic choice, and any sort of planning fell flat by the time it was their turn again. I could see how the game would be better with less players or some minor adjustments to limit the randomness aspect, but it's not something I'd like to play with a larger group of people.

En cuanto a la cantidad de personas me entretiene más jugarlo de a 2 o 3, ya que uno coloca más losetas y el bloquear lugares del oponente se hace más importante que cuando se juega de 4 o 5, ya que uno tiene que colocar menos losetas y no siempre se puede dar ese lujo.
Recomiendo sí o sí tener este juego en cualquier colección, es fácil de jugar y no dura mucho.

textfield_comment_value:
Draw and place a tile. Place a meeple on a city or a road to gain VP. Area control
The advantage is that it is easy to learn and to explain even to younger players (match road with road, grass with grass or a city with a city)
Your play depends on the tile you draw so AP should be limited overall though kingmaking could also happen, at least the way our friends play.
But this is a quick game even at a higher player count. We play it every now and then and still have a good time.
Not a bad game to play with people who don't want to have to remember too many rules. This works well overall.
