2004 jeu de l'année

Les Aventuriers du Rail

J’attendais les Aventuriers du Rail, que beaucoup décrivaient comme étant « le jeu que Trans America aurait dû être » avec d’autant plus d’impatience que j’avais déjà beaucoup apprécié le trop souvent décrié Trans-America. Je n’ai pas été déçu. Ce jeu magnifique de simplicité et d’élégance, bénéficiant en outre d’une édition de grande qualité, est sans nul doute appelé à devenir rapidement un grand classique. Les Aventuriers du Rail est un jeu dans lequel les joueurs construisent des réseaux ferrés concurrents sur une carte des Etats-Unis, ce qui est à peu près aussi original qu’un jeu d’affrontement entre civilisations antiques sur une carte de la Méditerranée. Un genre convenu et balisé, qui a déjà ses classiques comme l’excellent mais ardu Age of Steam, ses sujets de controverse comme le très agréable Trans America, ses perles méconnues, comme le magnifique Santa Fe Rails, dont l’auteur n’était autre, déjà, qu’Alan Moon.

Durant le jeu, les joueurs collectent des cartes wagons, qui leur permettront de prendre le contrôle de liaisons ferroviaires entre les grandes cités des Etats-Unis, tentant de réaliser des objectifs secrets qui rapporteront en fin de partie des points supplémentaires. Les règles d’une rare simplicité – chacun à son tour fait l’une des trois actions possibles, piocher des cartes wagons, piocher des cartes objectifs, prendre le contrôle d’une liaison en jouant des cartes wagon – permettent néanmoins des stratégies variées. Faut-il choisir d’abord des objectifs cohérents et ambitieux, puis construire ensuite son réseau, ou au contraire contrôler rapidement le plus de liaisons possibles et choisir ses objectifs ensuite ? Faut-il stocker les cartes wagon pour faire de grandes liaisons, celles qui rapportent des points, ou les jouer rapidement pour ne pas se faire doubler et bloquer ses adversaires ? Trois personnes m’ont déjà affirmé qu’il n’y avait qu’une stratégie gagnante à ce jeu, mais chacune préconisait une technique différente, et c’est sans doute là la marque d’un grand, d’un très grand, jeu.

À peine plus complexe que Trans America, Les Aventuriers du Rail est un jeu tout public, dont la légèreté et la simplicité enchanteront les joueurs occasionnels, tandis que la tension permanente, les possibilités de coups en traître et la multiplicité des choix séduiront les joueurs acharnés. Cela en fait sans doute, avec les Colons de Catan, le jeu idéal pour convertir vos amis aux jeux de société d’aujourd’hui.

S’il fallait faire une critique, une seule, à ce jeu conçu avec soin et publié avec l’élégance baroque coutumière de Days of Wonder, elle concernerait le petit texte introductif des règles, avec cette histoire absurde de personnages de Jules Verne se retrouvant vingt ans plus tard. Pourquoi ne pas avoir donné à ce jeu son thème naturel, celui des railway tycoons, de ces magnats du rail qui un demi siècle durant, de 1850 à 1900, ont été au cœur de l’économie, de la politique et de l’imaginaire américain.

Les Aventuriers du Rail – Europe

(Un an plus tard)
Les Aventuriers du Rail ont été un grand succès, vendu à quelques centaines de milliers d'exemplaires, et l'éditeur a fort logiquement demandé à Alan Moon de dessiner quelques autres cartes pour renouveler quelque peu le jeu et entretenir son succès. Les Aventuriers du Rail - Europe est la première de ces nouvelles boites, mais sans doute pas la dernière. La nouvelle carte, au dessin un peu méchant permettant un jeu plus agressif, séduira sans doute plus les joueurs acharnés. Quelques nouvelles règles viennent en outre enrichir le jeu, sans véritablement le complexifier. Si je reste un peu mitigé sur l'intérêt des gares et des ferries, j'ai trouvé très agréable la règle des tunnels, qui introduit un amusant facteur de prise de risque, et la nouvelle méthode de distribution des objectifs, qui produit un jeu plus équilibré. J'envisage d'ailleurs de dessiner quelques tunnels à travers les Rocheuses ou les Appalaches sur ma carte des États-Unis, et déjà nous y distribuons les objectifs initiaux comme avec le jeu européen.
Les nouvelles règles étant surtout intéressantes pour ceux qui connaissent déjà le jeu, je conseille à ceux qui souhaitent découvrir les Aventuriers du Rail d'acheter d'abord la boite originale, celle avec la carte des États-Unis, et de ne passer ensuite à la boite européenne que quand ils ressentiront le besoin de se changer les idées. Si vous êtes déjà fan de l'original, en revanche, précipitez-vous sur la nouvelle version, elle en vaut la peine.

Les Aventuriers du Rail – Märklin

(Encore un an plus tard)
La troisième boite des Aventuriers du rail, qui a pour cadre la très exotique Allemagne, surprend d'abord par ses graphismes, d'un tout autre style que ceux des deux premières éditions. La boite "Allemagne" de Zug um Zug a en effet été réalisée en collaboration avec Marklin, un fabricant allemand de trains électriques, dont Days of Wonder a dû respecter la charte graphique. Et comme la charte graphique de Marklin c'est "moche, avec un beaucoup de noir ", il a fallu faire moche avec beaucoup de noir, mettre de pâlichonnes photos de modèles réduits à la place des jolis dessins de Julien Delval, et dessiner une carte d'Allemagne sans décor ni relief. Cela suffira sans doute à faire préférer l'une ou l'autre des versions précédentes à tous ceux qui ne sont pas suffisamment accros pour acheter les trois boites.
C'est un peu doute dommage car du point de vue du jeu lui-même, cette version, sans doute la plus sophistiquée, apporte des innovations intéressantes, qui devraient séduire les "hardcore gamers" et même, peut-être, une partie du public plus "familial" qui, après quelques centaines de traversées de l'Europe et des États Unis, se sent prêt à aller plus loin. C’est ainsi qu’apparaît une troisième manière de marquer des points, avec des passagers qui se déplacent de gare en gare, enlevant au passage les jetons de score placés en début de partie. Cela complexifie bien sûr le jeu, mais crée des choix tactiques intéressants et rend certaines décisions plus difficiles encore – le choix n’est plus entre piocher des cartes ou poser des wagons avant qu’il ne soit trop tard, il est désormais entre piocher des cartes, poser des wagons avant qu’il ne soit trop tard, et déplacer un passager avant qu’il ne soit trop tard.

USA 1910

L'extension USA 1910 consiste essentiellement en un deck de cartes wagon, pour ceux qui auraient trop usé les leurs, et surtout un volumineux deck de cartes objectifs, plus nombreuses et plus équilibrées, pour le jeu de base. Son grand avantage est qu'il n'est désormais plus besoin de se demander quelle est la meilleure version du jeu - c'est le jeu de base, avec sa simplicité et son évidence, plus l'extension, qui lui amène équilibre et variété.

Extension Suisse

Sans pions ni cartes wagon, la boite Suisse n'est jouable que si l'on possède déjà une édition des Aventuriers du Rail. La carte, assez resserrée, est conçue spécifiquement pour deux ou trois joueurs.

Les Aventuriers du Rail - Scandinavie

Cette fois, il s'agit d'une boite complète, elle aussi conçue pour deux ou trois joueurs. Je la trouve plus amusante et plus intéressantq eu la carte de Suisse. Je signale aussi que deux des couleurs de pion, blanc et violet, ne sont pas dans la boite de base, ce qui permet de jouer à six joueurs sur la carte des USA.

Les Aventuriers du Rail - extension dés

L'idée est de remplacer les cartes wagon par des dés. Cela accélère certes le jeu, mais lui enlève beaucoup de tension et d'intérêt. C'est la seule version du jeu à ne pas m'avoir du tout convaincu.

Réglages et variantes

Les Aventuriers du rail sont sans doute le jeu auquel j’ai le plus joué ces dernières années, et nous avons procédé à quelques menus réglages que je vous livre ici, libre à vous d’y prendre ce qui vous sied.

Score
Quelle que soit la version du jeu utilisée, noter tout au long de la partie les points marqués lorsque l’on pose des wagons tend à ralentir le jeu, et à le rendre un peu plus calculatoire. En outre, comme les oublis sont fréquents, il est de toute façon nécessaire de tout recompter à l’issue de la partie. C’est pourquoi nous décomptons désormais les points pour les lignes construites à la fin de la partie, en même temps que ceux pour les objectifs.

Distribution des objectifs dans la version Amérique
Le système initial, celui de la version américaine, conduit à des déséquilibres, celui qui a la chance de piocher deux gros objectifs étant à peu près certain de la victoire. C’est pourquoi nous procédons désormais avec les objectifs américains comme avec ceux de la version européenne, en donnant à chacun un objectif parmi les sept de 17 points ou plus, et trois objectifs plus modestes. Les objectifs restants, et ceux rejetés par les joueurs, sont ensuite mélangés en une pioche commune (on fait ça aussi avec l’Europe).

Version Märklin simplifiée
Les règles sur les passagers enrichissent indubitablement le jeu, mais elles le complexifient et allongent sa durée. Rien n’empêche, avec des plus jeunes ou pour aller vite, de jouer sur la carte d’Allemagne en ignorant entièrement tout ce qui concerne les passagers. L’inverse est aussi vrai, et rien n’empêche de placer jetons marchandises et passagers sur la carte d’Amérique pour compliquer un peu les choses.

Jouer à 6
Les couleurs des joueurs dans les versions Marklin et Scandinavie ne sont pas les mêmes que celles des autres éditions. Il est possible, en combinant les pions de la version Europe et de ces versions Märklin, de jouer à 6 sur la carte d’Amérique ou, sans les passagers, sur la carte d’Allemagne.

D’autres cartes
De très nombreux joueurs ont imaginé de nouveaux objectifs et plateaux de jeu pour les Aventuriers du Rail. Parmi les nombreuses cartes en téléchargement sur le web, que je n’ai pas essayées, j’ai entendu dire beaucoup de bien de celles de France, d’Égypte ou de Belgique. Vous trouverez des liens vers toutes ces cartes sur le site officiel du jeu, dans la rubrique « règles et téléchargements ».

Plus qu’une nouvelle version du jeu avec de nouvelles règles, l’extension dont je rèverai aujourd’hui serait une belle boite avec deux plateaux de jeu recto-verso, soit quatre cartes, et les cartes objectifs correspondantes nécessaires. Je précise que je n’ai aucune information quant à ce qui se prépare et que, si Alan Moon et les gens de Days of Wonder sont des amis, ils ne me disent rien de leurs projets en ce qui concerne les Aventuriers du Rail. Ceci n’est donc pas un teaser soigneusement étudié, mais juste un souhait dont j’espère qu’il sera entendu.
	
Ticket to Ride

I’ve been eagerly for Ticket to Ride, a game that some of the lucky playtesters used to describe as “what Trans America should have been”. Since I already liked Trans America, I was sure I’ll love Ticket to Ride – and I do. This game is a masterpiece of evidence and elegance, and the edition is gorgeous. I have no doubt it will become a classic.

Ticket to Ride is a game about building rail networks on a map of the United States – this is almost as original as a game about rival civilizations played on a map of the Mediterranean sea. This well established genre already has its great classics, like the excellent but complex Age of Steam, its controversial topics, like the light Trans America, and its overlooked gems, like Santa Fe Rails, a game by Alan Moon, who is also the author of Ticket to Ride.

During the game, players draw rail car cards, that they will use to take control of railway line between American cities, trying to fulfill secret goals that will give them extra points at the end of the game. The rules are incredibly short and simple – each player on turn can make one of the three possible actions : draw rail car cards, draw goal cards, play rail car cards to take control of a railway line between two towns. Sounds basic, but this makes for varied and interesting strategies. Is it better to draw goal cards first, choosing ambitious and coherent lines, and then build ones network, or is it better to take control of the main lines as soon as possible and then choose goals ? Is it better to draw and stock rail car cards and play all of them later on long lines, worth more points, or to play them as soon as possible on short lines, thus blocking opponents ? Three players have already told me there was a killer strategy in this game, but each one has a different strategy in mind – this is the sign of a great game.

Ticket to Ride is only slightly more complex than Trans America, but has much more depth. Its light and evidence will charm occasional gamers, while hardcore gamers will enjoy the tension, the backstabbing opportunities and the various strategies. This means that Ticket to Ride is probably, along with Settlers of Catan, one of the very best games to lure your non gaming friends into these games of ours.

The game is wonderfully produced – as usual – by days of Wonder, and I have only one small concern with it. The background story on the first page of rules, with Jules Verne characters meeting again twenty years later, is absurd and doesn’t fit with the game. Why not give to this game its true natural theme, the railway tycoons who, half a century long, from 1850 to 1900, were the center of American economics, politics and collective imagination.

Ticket to Ride – Europe

(One year later)
Ticket to Ride was a hit, and sold a few hundred thousand copies. Logically, the publisher asked Alan Moon to design a few new cards to keep the sales going and revitalize the game. Ticket to Ride - Europe is the first new box to hit the shelves, and is more than just a new map. The new map is more nasty and makes for more aggressive play, which may please the hardcore gamers. A few new features have been added, but they don't make the game complex. Though I'm skeptical about railways stations and ferries, which don't add much to the gameplay, I think the "turning the flop" rule for tunnels is a really fun and nice additions. It adds some risk taking in the game, and make it more fun to play. I'll probably take a black pen and add some tunnels through the Rockies and the Appalachians. The new rules for starting destination tickets also makes for a more balanced game, and we now use it also with the American game.
The new rules were designed to renew the game and were designed mostly for players who already know the basic game. If you've never played Ticket to Ride so far, I suggest you first buy the original game, with the American map, and move further to Europe after a few months, when you'll need something new. On the other hand, if you already like the original game, you can buy the new box without the slightest hesitation, since it really brings a new dimension to the game.

Ticket to Ride – Märklin

(One more year later)
The third Ticket to Ride box has a fun, sexy and exotic setting - Germany. The graphics are surprising for those used to the two first versions of the game. The “Zug um Zug” German box has been published in collaboration with Märklin, the main German train model company, and Day of Wonder had to respect the Märklin graphic chart, and since the Märklin graphic chart is “ugly with much black”, it is ugly with much black, the nice train car paintings by Julien Delval have been replaced with faded pictures of train models, and the map of Germany has neither scenery nor relief. If you want to buy only one box, this will probably be enough to make you prefer one of the other two versions of the game.
It’s a pity, because the game itself is really good, with some very interesting new features that will appeal for hardcore gamers who thought the original game was too childish, and can also be of interest for more casual gamers who have already explored the two first editions and are ready to go a bit further and deeper. The main new feature is a third way of scoring points, with passengers pawns that move from town to town, removing score tokens that were placed there at the beginning of the game. This makes the game more complex, and makes for even more agonizing choices. Now it’s not only either draw cards, either place trains before it’s too late, it’s either draw cards, either place trains before it’s too late, either move passengers before it’s too late.

USA 1910

The USA 1910 expansion is made of a replacement deck of train cards and, more important, a new deck of ticket cards for the basic USA game, with more and better balanced destinations. This means you don't have to hesitate anymore if you don't know which version of the game to buy - the best version is the original USA game, for its simplicity and directness, with the expansion, for a better balanced and more varied game.

The Switzerland map

The Switzerland box has no train cards and pawns, only board and ticket cards, meaning it can only be played with cards and pawns from another box. It is specifically designed for two or three players.

Ticket to Ride - Nordic Countries

Like the Switzerland map, the Scandinavian one is designed specifically for two or three players, but it's sold as a whole game. I find it more interesting and challenging than the Switzerland map. The colours of the trains being differnt than those in the basic set, you can use them to play six players game on the USA map.

Ticket to Ride - the dice game

The idea is to replace the train cards with dice. It works, it makes the game a bit faster, but it also removes most of its tension and interest. It's the only version of Ticket to Ride I don't like.

Tuning and variants

Ticket to Ride is probably the game I’ve played most these two last years, and we have made some minor tunings and imagined some variants. Here they are, take what you want from them.

Score
No matter what version of the game we play, we don’t score the train points when the train cards are placed. This slows the game, and experience proves that there are always one or two errors during the game, and it’s always necessary to check all scores again at the end of the game. So we now score everything in the end, which makes for faster paced game.

Dealing Destination ticket cards in the original game
The destination tickets dealing rule in the American version is unbalanced, and that’s why Alan Moon has used more sophisticated systems with the Europe and the Germany maps. We play with the American map like with Europe, dealing to each player one of the seven tickets worth 17 or more, and three shorter ones. The remaining tickets, and those discarded by the players, are all shuffled together in a single drawing deck for the rest of the game (we also play this way with Europe tickets).

Märklin lite
The passenger rules make the game more challenging, but they also make it longer and more complex. With young players, or for more casual gaming, you can ignore the passenger rules. Of course, the reverse is also true, and you can add goods and passengers on the American map.

6 players game
A nice twist of the Märklin box is that two player colours are different from those in the two former ones. This means that, with combining pieces from two sets, you can play with six players on the USA or the Germany map. Of course, this makes for a tense game and a really congested map, so better use also the railway station from the Europe set.

Other maps
Many gamers have designed original maps for Ticket to Ride. I’ve not had the time to print and playtest them, but I’ve heard much good of the Belgium, France and Egypt maps. You’ll find links to all those unofficial maps on official Ticket to Ride website, under “rules and downloads>

The new box I would ike to see somday for this wonderful game is not a new version of the game with new rules, but an expansion box with four new maps – two doubles sided boards – and the corresponding tickets. Even when Alan R. Moon and the Days of Wonder guys are friends of mine, I don’t know anything about their projects about Ticket to Ride. This means that this is not a discreet teaser, just a wish.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Ticket to Ride is a huge commercial success and also well-beloved by niche gamers and the general public Nothing much to say beyond my amazement that the game transcends so many levels of player experience. While the base game is probably enough for most casual gamers, all the unique maps for Ticket to Ride are designed to cater the lifestyle gamers. Each map and expansion will tweak the base game in subtle ways, allowing players to extend their experience of the base game. For me, I enjoy the base game just fine, but having played it so many times, I no longer really crave it and rarely bring it out to the table. That said, I still play it with my six year old. Playing with her has made me realize that Ticket to Ride is not only a good gateway game, it is also an excellent game to expose kids to Euro-y mechanisms that might be missing from other kids games.

Much like My Little Orchard being the first game for many toddlers, Ticket to Ride can function as a turning point for 5-7 year olds to steer them toward light-mid weight Euros. I observed that many games targeted at kids will feature perhaps 1 or 2 mechanisms that drive the game and the decision-space tends to be more explicit and direct. There is not much metagaming going on in these games and the risk-reward are clear and easy for kids to comprehend. Ticket to Ride takes it to another level. To play well requires more in depth analysis and players must be able to project the decision space beyond just the next move. Importantly, these subtle gaming skills aren’t cloaked by a heavy and complicated rule set because Ticket to Ride remains one of the simplest games out there. The underlying mechanisms in Ticket to Ride can serve as a foundation for playing other more complex Euros. It is actually as much a gateway game for the general public, as it is for a kid, ready to take the next step.

Rather than reviewing the game in the traditional way, which at this point, really has no value given the mountains of glowing reviews, I think I much rather evaluate the game from the perspective of an emerging gamer.

Kids Corner

From 5 years to 6 years and 6 months: My kid and I started playing Ticket to Ride at the age of 5. We played intermittently for about a few months, then stopped and moved on to other games. She wasn’t completely ready. At that stage, she could put down train tracks and was happy to just score points. That was that. I wasn’t expecting much anyways and the game wasn’t all that fun for either of us. A competitive game of Ticket to Ride was still beyond her skills. Fast forward a year and multiple games later, she has matured as a gamer. Certainly, laying tracks is no longer an issue as is completing destination tickets. The fundamentals are there, but I was curious about her competitive drive to win and how she executes her vision. While she is much better at the game, there are still some areas that still feel….”lacking”. For example, even though I pointed out the relationship between track length and points scored, it did not seem to ring a bell. Her focus was solely on completing destination tickets and I think she takes great pride and satisfaction in completing the connection. I wonder if route building overrides any decision to make random six-car placements for 15 points, which in some cases, is more optimal. I would at times risk a slightly longer routes to include building connections that score more points.

I fell she is still unable to evaluate the trade offs between scoring points from laying down long tracks versus completing tickets. It’s clear that she did not seem to care as much about scoring immediate points, perhaps not fully comprehending the competition for track space. I could tell this by her choice to pick up the locomotive wild card at the expense of set collection. This means she still cannot project her decision space beyond one or two steps ahead. So, its likely that multi-tasking and future projections is something that she is still waiting to acquire.

There is very little aggression in her decision space right now and she does care for blocking other routes. If she does end up blocking other routes, they are all unintentional. She is however, very capable of circumventing blocked routes and not at all bothered by being blocked. I have at times intentionally built disjointed connections which opens up blocking maneuvers, but she has not really capitalize on that and seem to shy away from aggressive plays. It will be interesting to see if that attitude changes over time and whether there is a specific trigger for that transition. I have pointed out a few times on those opportunities, but she seems to just shrug it off.

As a parent, it’s tempting to remind her of strategy or pointing out certain logical actions to take. I have resisted the temptation to guide her decisions and to let her have a light bulb moment. She does get annoyed with “parental guidance” during games and I have defintely made a conscious effort to zip my mouth. Believe me when I say it is harder than it looks to hold back since my overriding desire is to “teach”. But I see value in letting her explore the decision space, however frustrating it is for both of us.

My partner and I don’t really believe in playing sub-optimally to let her win. Most of our games are competitive and consequently, she has learned to lose gracefully and it no longer bothers her unless she is exhausted. In which case, she can get cranky. Honestly, that happens to adult gamers too. Prompting her about losing and winning gracefully help. In Ticket to Ride, it feels like she cares even less about victory. Perhaps there is something inherent about route building that makes her feel happy just laying down tracks. Still, there is a noticeable gap between her skill set and ours in Ticket to Ride. In letting her explore the decision space with parental intrusion, a certain balance must be struck between maintaining a competitive balance and the frustration of losing constantly. Overall, she is great at losing gracefully but still gets understandably frustrated at times for being constantly steamrolled. Rather than playing sub-optimally, we have been playing with handicaps.That evens out the odds a little. For example, we are halving the positive points from destination tickets. It works.

Ticket to Ride is not a far leap from other games she has played complexity wise, but it does represent a jump in critical thinking skills. In most of her other games, this secondary processing is not nearly as evident and perhaps not as intertwined as Ticket to Ride. For example in Carcassonne, you can kinda tell where the optimal tile placement is (we play without farmers) and you don’t really have that many choices; in Ubongo, you either have the pattern recognition skills or you don’t, same is true for Rummikub; in Memoaar!, it’s all about memory; in Straw, you learn how to push your luck and keep specific cards at hand to avoid going bust. Each of these games and others in her collection focus on one angle or one specific skill to win. She can excel in these games. Ticket to Ride will push her toward developing multiple skills relevant to the modern Euro gaming. For example, TTR promotes risk-reward assessment (drawing tickets), aggressive play making (route blocking), forward planning (set collection), calculating odds (picking up additional tickets or anticipating end game scenarios), etc. These skills have to be combined and processed simultaneously to play well.

I have resisted getting TTR: First Journey because I think she is ready for regular Ticket to Ride. I highly recommend the regular game as a bridge between the HABAs and Gamewright and the light weight Euros that appeal to adults. There are several other games that could serve as a gateway game for kids along with Ticket to Ride. Many of the simpler Knizia games like Through the Desert, Sumatra, Whale Riders, etc. can fall into this category. There might be some elements within each game that needs to be progressively introduced for it to work. For example, the enclosure of territories in Through the Desert to score a massive chunk of points. But I will have to explore these variants.

Overall, I really enjoy seeing her develop into a mature board gamer and also look forward to the day I get whalloped by her in TTR.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
There was a time when I thought Ticket to Ride was too much about accidental player interaction and ticket memorisation. And I was clearly wrong, possibly because of the groups I've played it with, possibly because even player counts allow the peaceful-minded to mostly avoid frustrating each other. Different environments (online and offline) showed me that paying attention to the train cards drawn gives already plenty of relevant information as early as your very first session; and if nothing else, control over choke points is pretty darn important. You just build up knowledge from there in future games. So, I'm reevaluating my former dismissal: as a game system, Ticket to Ride is a strong recommendation, and possibly the most universally liked introduction to modern board games. If you want a stepping stone towards TTR expansion maps (and don't mind the tiny train cards), the original box is a worthwhile acquisition: it has the most legible - if boring - geography (thanks the USA being a large potato not burdened by old historic cities) and the lowest amount of rules amongst every mainline game.

As a self-contained product, however, vanilla USA is a bit meh; mainly due to tickets being the randomisation of annoying constraints, rather than of an enticing game plan: you mostly attempt to fulfil those that you have to keep at the beginning of the game, but would rather be allowed to keep none and won't draw any further ones, as the real source of points is the 5-6 length routes (and the longest road bonus card while we're at it). The game sort of knows this, as if each of 5 players took the "draw additional tickets" action once, the ticket deck would already run out. This wouldn't necessarily be a problem in a hypothetical further iteration that de-emphasizes tickets in favour of some gimmick of the day; but had Ticket to Ride been a one-and-done box, I wouldn't have blamed anyone for missing the point of the board and deeming the whole thing nothing more than a weird Rummy variant. The 1910 expansion is pretty much required if you intend on playing the USA map long term (or dislike the tiny train cards), and I'm sure Days of Wonder is making a sweet amount of money by still offering it as a separate purchase almost 20 years later.

Side rambling: I don't understand the insistence of the publisher in pretending that Ticket to Ride is about some Phileas Foggesque travelling competition (rather than the building of train lines): the "claiming" of routes disconnected from the rest of the network makes even sense less under that narrative, the deployment of plastic trains onto the board isn't conducive to that narrative, 100% distinct line segments per player don't make sense under that narrative, asymmetric objectives don't make sense under that narrative (where company building contracts do), a large amount of expansions' gimmicks don't make sense under that narrative, and everyone I've ever seen teach and play TTR operates under the idea that you're building a railroad network. Even the mini-descriptions in BGG's attempt at neutrality of a database have forgotten about the official plot. My only conclusion is that Days of Wonder is misguidedly afraid that the reputation of inaccessibility and dryness surrounding the hex-map shareholding kind of game that hobbyists refer to as "train games" has transpired onto the mainstream. Well, no. In the meantime, you've become the mainstream understanding of a train game, and nobody's fooled by your "cross-country adventure game" intro blurb anyway. You can abandon it. It's fine.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Ticket to Ride is an interesting one to track on BGG.  I never know whether to track plays under the expansions or the base game, since you basically ignore everything except the trains and a deck of cards from the original.  I've leaned toward logging under expansions, but have not been consistent with it.

There's not a lot left to be said about Ticket to Ride that hasn't already been said.  It's a classic family game for a reason, and the elitists can pooh-pooh it all they want, but I still think it's a fantastic game that has stood the test of time very well.  The expansions add some neat twists, and the game is easy to teach.  Perhaps the best praise I can give to Ticket to Ride is to say that it's been a gateway game for family who really aren't gamers, and that is just wonderful.  I once organized a big family gathering at a rented house on the beach, and brought along some games to pass time in the evenings.  Two different people who were visiting went out and bought TTR within a week or two of the trip's end.  That's high praise coming from folks who hadn't played a board game in years.

My current ranking of the expansions / alt versions I've played:

1.) UK / Pennsylvania.  Both maps in this recent expansion are excellent.  The tech tree in UK is a lot of fun and gives you the opportunity to follow what other players are able to do and race to get access to the regions / routes that you want and need.  The set collection of the stocks in PA helps give alternatives to pulling tickets and makes end-game much more tense as you try to balance route size and chasing stock majorities.

2.) India / Switzerland.  I like that both of these maps are tighter, more heavily branched, so there's lots of competition, but less "oh, you took the one five train route going where I need to go, so now I have to come up with 15 different cards to work around it", because the links are typically closer together and shorter with more options.

3.) Original TTR.  Really solid, good ole USA map.  Fun with 1910 or the original rules.

4.) Africa.  I didn't really care for the way colors tended to cluster together.  If you are trying to get to a particular city, and it has two red routes facing the direction you're coming from, and you can't find any red, you're pretty well boned.  The terrain doubling mechanism was novel, but seemed to make for huge point swings that made it difficult to gauge who was the best target for blocking.  I wouldn't be in a hurry to play this map, given how many better choices there are.

5.) Rails and Sails.  Bad.  Bad bad bad.  The worst Ticket to Ride map by a huge margin.  The new depots combined with the two-card market made the game waaaayyyyyy more random.  The bigger board and higher piece count made the game wayyyyyyy longer than it should be.  This isn't just my least favorite of a game a like a lot.  This is a game I actively dislike.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Sem palavras!

Jogo rápido na duração, dinâmico, regras robustas, downtime e AP praticamente nulos (pisca o olho e já é sua vez novamente!), bela arte, ótimo acabamento, cartas muito pequenas.

Dica: como a quantidade de vagões é uma informação pública e ao mesmo tempo condição única para o gatilho de final de jogo, é extremamente importante que os jogadores mantenham os vagões de plástico bem visíveis em cima da mesa e que todos prestem muita atenção nesta condição, pois qualquer equívoco aqui pode alterar drasticamente a pontuação e também o vencedor da partida. E provavelmente o erro será percebido tarde demais para tentar voltar atrás desfazendo jogadas, o que arruinará a partida e frustrará todos na mesa (sei que é ridículo, mas já vi inclusive jogador ocultar os carros de propósito só porque queria usar os dois últimos trens que ainda tinha).

Existem duas coisas que prejudicam o design do jogo, mas que em toda partida tem alguém querendo fazer achando que vai agilizar:
1. Embaralhar o descarte de Cartas de Vagão e colocá-las de volta no monte antes da última Carta de Vagão fechada sair: o problema com isso é que depois que as cartas foram recolocadas no monte, muitas cartas podem ainda continuar sendo descartadas pelos jogadores. Assim, a menos que o monte fosse sendo embaralhado de novo com as últimas cartas descartadas (o que seria uma perda de tempo), o novo monte embaralhado ficaria com cartas faltantes até o próximo embaralhamento. O que prejudicaria algum jogador que estivesse em busca de uma cor específica. Não façam isso.
2. Continuar o jogo enquanto um jogador está analisando os novos bilhetes que resolveu comprar: a ação de comprar bilhetes realmente é a que mais demora no TtR e esse procedimento realmente traria mais agilidade para o jogo, se não fosse pela possibilidade do tabuleiro mudar consideravelmente enquanto o jogador está ainda escolhendo seus bilhetes. Só é possível fazer isso sem impactos negativos para a partida se o jogador seguinte ao que optou por comprar bilhetes também for comprar bilhetes ou Cartas de Vagão, pois isso não mudará o tabuleiro. Caso o jogador seguinte opte por construir rotas, ele terá então que esperar o anterior finalizar sua compra de bilhetes.

textfield_comment_value:
This is a classic gateway game that works well with most families or non-gamers.  If you are new to gaming or need something to introduce others to this hobby this is a great choice.  However, my favorite of the series is the Europe version, so after reading these comments go check out my Europe comments.

In ticket to ride players are fighting to build train connections between cities.  Also enough of these connections will make a destination route from one city to another that isn't next to it.  Whoever can do the best will score the most points and win.

To start the game each player is dealt 3 destination routes.  These have point values on them where longer routes are worth more points than shorter routes.  So going from El Paso to Denver isn't worth as many points as going from San Francisco to Atlanta.  Before starting you may give up one of your routes if it just doesn't seem to fit well with the others, because it is advantageous to work on multiple routes all at once.

Now play will continue around the table with each player getting to choose one action from three options.  The first, and probably most commonly used, is to take train cards.  Five of them will be face up, with the rest face down.  These are a bunch of different colors that match the colors on the map which are required to get a certain connection between to cities.  You can either take a face up wild card, or you can take any two other cards, either face up or face down.  The other option is to use these train cards to actually build on the map.  One key here is once you take a connection nobody else can use it, so getting blocked and having to go around is common.  Each of these connections will score you points as you go.  The last option is to draw additional destination routes.  You draw 3, but you only have to keep 1 of them.  You can keep all 3 if you want, but this isn't common.

The game ends when somebody uses up almost all their trains (until they have less than 3) and each player then gets one last turn.  Then you add on to your points for each destination ticket you completed, and take away points for each one you don't.

This is very simple, for new gamers it can be very addictive.  This is a must have for any collection, although as I said before, I prefer the Europe version to this one.

textfield_comment_value:
Without a doubt, THE definitive gateway game to modern boardgames for non-gamers.  This was really the first Euro-game that got me into Euro Games.  Prior to this I played Chess a lot as a kid, and played the old Milton Bradley “GameMaster” series games “Axis & Allies” and “Conquest of the Empire” along with “Risk” and “Diplomacy”.  In fact it was at a Diplomacy meet that I played Ticket to Ride for the first time.  We had finished a five hour game and one participant pointed out this game to us and recommend we give it a try.  None of us had really played anything outside our usual strategy war games before.  I had played “Settlers of Catan” before, but that game never really grabbed me.  After we finished Ticket to Ride we all looked at each other wide-eyed like we had just found the map to El Dorado.  I myself could never go back to playing those old strategy war games again and began my journey into Eurogame land.  Fast forward many many years later and I STILL enjoy playing the original Ticket to Ride (although you really do need the 1910 expansion).  
I’ve introduced so many people to modern boardgaming through this game and it always go over so well with non-gamers.  Although the game is something of a litmus test as I can count three instances where this game showed that some people really can’t handle anything beyond Sorry, Uno and Monopoly.  
I think the reason this game makes a better gateway game than Settler of Catan is that the tickets give players some very SPECIFIC goals that they can zero-in and focus on.  With very simple streamlined rules (for about 99% of the human population) and a set of starting individual goals that players can zero-in on, players can really get a hold of game after just a few rounds.  Yet there is strategy required here and players are focusing on multiple objectives and stay intrigued with gameplay even when its not their turn, breathlessly hopping no one blocks their route before they can play their hand.  
One thing you really do need to hammer in with new players is that there is no correlation between the color of your trains and the color of your routes/cards.  I’m not sure why, but it can be troubling for some people; for example, they want to claim a route that needs five green cards but then look at their (red) train supply and say, “oh, I can’t do that, I only have red trains” even though I’ve gone over the rules several times (and even laid down some routes myself).  They then realize that and say, “Oh, that’s right, I knew that!” but honestly, its just something they can’t get past mentally and I’ve seen it happen a few times while teaching the game.  Although once they are able to get past that, its bye bye to Sorry, Uno and Monopoly.  
Overall, Ticket to Ride is THE PERFECT GAME.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
A modern classic!  Ticket to Ride is a straightforward, family-friendly game that simulates the construction of the railway system in North America.  Players represents different railway companies (more simply, a color of trains) that are competing to dominate the railways by maximizing victory points.  These can be earned by claiming particular routes (longer ones are worth more points), by connecting particular cities together through an uninterrupted chain of routes (as describe by a particular "ticket"), or by creating the longest chain of routes.  Usually, players have to find the right combination of these to win the game.

The gameplay is fairly straightforward.  On their turn, a player collects cards representing colored train cars, or when the player has enough cards of a particular color, the player may claim a route by discarding the exact number of cards matching the length of the route and color of the route.  Some of the cards act as wild cards, and some of the routes don't require a particular color, which adds variety to gameplay.

The real drama of the game stems from the fact that there are a limited number of routes.  So, the player has incentive to be the first to claim a desirable route.  However, playing a route too early leaves the player with less cards, which means less options in the short-term.  Because the claimed routes are visible to everybody, other players can take advantage of your lack of options by claiming routes near your claimed routes, which may ruin your long-term plans!  

Players may alternatively feel the need to keep collecting and hoarding cards, giving them more options to play later in the game; but if players wait too long, other players may claim critical routes!

Many other tabletop games struggle to balance mechanics by either favoring players who are aggressive (first to make big move) or players who "wait-and-see" (react and counter other players).  But Ticket to Ride strikes the right balance!  The variability in the tickets, card drafting, and players means that there is no dominant strategy, and players will need to adapt to the conditions of the current game.

Ticket to Ride works best when you approach the game with a casual attitude.  Intense gamers may find the random elements (card drafting, routes, etc.) frustrating and may find the card hunting tedious.  Additionally, the game can lose its charm when playing with spiteful opponents (i.e. players who deliberately block or disrupt others players despite any discernible strategic advantage).

Considered a gateway game for many, this game is increasing each year in it's mainstream appeal, and will eventually be considered a tabletop staple in the vein of Monopoly (although Ticket to Ride is vastly superior).
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
My opinion of this game keeps going down each time I play it. The theme/game disconnect is just too wide. Ticket to Ride is really just a melding game with complicated and misleading scoring; the rewards for completing routes (via the ticket cards) are not sensibly given out.
---
I am wierdly conflicted on Ticket to Ride.

To me, this seems to be a game that is clearly in the American style. That is to say, it's winning converts based on being a) familiar through its melding-game heritage, b) modestly engaging, and c) pretty much non-threatening. That's cool, but leaves it a bit in the margins for the gamer who is a fan of much more sophisticated German games like Beowulf, Settlers, Modern Art, etc. You can tell this is not a Knizia because of the impressive imbalances between the various activities - tickets are a sucker play, you want to just put down large routes. This is at least partly because the value of each ticket is just the number of trains required to complete it, without any regard to difficulty whatsoever - a route that contains many short links in a central, contested area is going to be vastly more difficult and more expensive to complete than one containing a few long links on the periperies. Thus, getting a ticket for the long northern or southern routes is a ticket to victory, and drawing tickets is a very risky sucker play. This is a double-whammy because it kills the theme - anyone who mistakes this for a route-building game instead of a point-scoring game is screwed.

Where does that leave me on Ticket to Ride? If I was going to play an "experience" game with a large chaos element, I'd rather do a game with a fun factor, like Liar's Dice or Pitchcar or Nuclear War. I've never been clear where the fun factor is with Ticket to Ride, which is why I never recommend it, even as a "gateway" game. In fairness, there is more to engage the intellect in Ticket to Ride than in many low-brainpower games, but in this class I'd definitely prefer the less-fiddly, less time-consuming Reibach (Get the Goods) or High Society or For Sale, or at the very least something with a minimally functioning theme. Ticket to Ride also has a problem with limited replayability, rapidly becoming pretty samey - much moreso than similar weight class games like Carcassonne: Hunters & Gatherers or Through the Desert.

All this is not to say that Ticket to Ride is a bad game; it's not. It's a decent game, it works, it's attractive, it's easy to play, and so on. But for me personally, it's just too bland. Too long to make a virtue of brevity or simplicity, yet too light to be really engaging. Even after all these years, give me Settlers any day.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Each player must complete a series of rail lines spanning cities based upon destination cards drawn at the beginning (and throughout) the game. Each destination carries points related to the length of the line, so a New York to Los Angeles line would score more points than Chicago to Boston. Incomplete destinations count against players at the end of the game, so completing them, even through circuitous routes is a must. The exciting part of the game comes from not knowing who is completing his or her lines, plus the ability to overlap lines, stymieing other players.

Game play takes between 30 and 90 minutes depending on the number of players and the speed at which they make decisions.

GAME PIECES

High quality throughout, the game includes:

- A fold-out board of the United States and southern Canada, plus a scoring track around the edge. The cities on the board connect through colored track lines, each line between one and six units in length.

- A set of destination cards showing lines that must be completed.

- Five sets of forty-five train pieces. Each player takes one same-color set of trains.

- A set of colored train cards that correspond to the colored lines that connect cities.

- Scoring markers that correspond to a player's train color.


Each player is dealt three destination cards in the beginning and must keep at least two. These form the basis for their lines. They also receive four train cards. To claim a line, players must create sets of the same color and number of train cards as the line connecting two cities. (The color of the lines has nothing to do with the player's train color, but the cards they have in hand.)

Each player, in turn, can perform one of three actions:

1. Draw two train cards per turn from either the set of five placed up for all players to see, or blind from the train card deck. (One card if one of the showing wild cards is chosen.)

2. Play a set of matching train card colors to claim a line between two cities.

3. Get dealt a new set of three destination cards, keeping at least one.

Players score points when they claim a line of track connecting two cities, the length of the track yielding proportionately higher scores. Scoring markers are moved around the 100-point scoring guide on the board perimeter.

When one player has laid all his or her train pieces, the other players get one last turn. Players then reveal their destination cards and add (or subtract, for incomplete lines) to their total. The longest continuous length of claimed track scores additional points, too. Highest point total wins.

Overall its a really fun game that can last a good amount of time.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Visual Appeal: (4)
The game board looks very nice. The routes are easy to read and have colorblind assistance. Box art looks like every other train game, but a little less serious. It almost hints at having characters although the game itself features none. 

Components: (4)
The original game comes with tiny cards which is really the only thing that I hate. There's no reason for it since there's plenty of room in the box for full size cards. I use the 1910 expansion cards now. The trains are nice and durable. At least one has been stepped on with no noticeable damage caused. I had to replace a few of the mini-bags they come in though. Even with light handling they can tear at the seams.

Theme: (3)
I didn't really expect a theme. I think there is some story along the lines of: some rich people are racing to build a rail network. If that's true then there's a problem. What are they buying it with colored train cards? I think this is one of the few games that is more enjoyable if you ignore the theme and just have fun with screwing people over.

Learning: (4)
The rules are really easy. I've taught this game to first timers more than any other game except maybe Pandemic. The most common issues that arise are wanting to do two different things on the same turn, and wanting to play a partial route between two cities. So, now I make it a point to repeat those points a few times before we start. The rulebook is perfectly succinct and problem free.

Gameplay: (5)
This game can get really heated. My favorites are 3 and 5 players. With 3, the double routes are still locked, so certain areas like around the Mississippi River corridor get really competitive. With 5, you have the max number of players allowed and everyone is just getting up in other peoples' business. There's no limitation to where you are allowed to put trains so if someone blocks you, the great thing is you can block them right back. Just make sure that you are still able to complete some tickets. I tried playing a game once where I didn't focus on tickets, but instead on blocking everyone I could. It didn't go well, so you need those tickets!

Overall Fun: (4)
This is always a reliable game that I can bring out at any time and have a good time. There are some games where I have great feelings and not so great feelings coming out of a play. With this game, I always feel good about it. It doesn't do anything special or complicated. It's just a box o' fun.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
I had played a couple of Euro-style games before my first game of Ticket to Ride, but this was the game that really set me down the path of the Serious Boardgamer (TM). 

First, the bad: I now mostly play the game online, where it is substantially faster than in real life. In person, I find things move pretty slowly, especially when playing with less experienced players. Sometimes you have lots of three-wild boards and need to shuffle the deck a bunch, which means even more sitting around waiting for things to happen. Sometimes people will stare at the board wondering what to do for a bit too long, and you don't want to push them along because it's a pretty casual and newbie-friendly game, but come...on...already...

In terms of actual mechanical lackings, the most readily apparent one is the randomness of the opening ticket draw. You will sometimes get three terrible routes that go North-South along short routes that eat up valuable resources, and then you will sometimes get Los Angeles-New York and Los Angeles-Miami or some other busted start and have to actively work to lose the game. It's not fun knowing that you've got so much riding (no pun intended) on something that happens at the beginning of a potentially hourlong game. Obviously a skilled player can overcome this (and I'm far from a high-skilled player), but it's still frustrating. I don't know how to improve it, though.

On the other hand, this game is just very fun for something so simple and so easy to teach. You can take someone with no gaming experience beyond Monopoly and have them putting up a fight in TtR within five minutes of the board hitting the table. There's a sort of push-your-luck element where you grip your cards hoping that nobody else takes that valuable 6 car route before you can get it without using your wilds, but unless you have exceptionally bad luck off the top of the deck you will rarely be completely out of the game. The theme is obviously well-implemented, if a bit straightforward (you're not gonna see 18xx mechanics here, and that's fine), and I love trying to make a really cool route or a really powerful route with lots of long journeys.

Ultimately, the game rewards longtime players and still offers plenty for a beginner. It's by no means perfect, but it's an excellent gateway that still held up for me even as I moved to heavier games.

26-Jan-2014:  Still my favorite "gateway" game.  It's a great option for family gaming or a lighter option for hobby gamers.  With the absolute must-buy USA 1910 expansion, the replay value of this one is very high.  The rules are simple.  The components are great.  This is my first recommendation to any new gamer or family interested in the hobby.

08-Feb-2013: This is easily my favorite family friendly hobby game (or "gateway" game, if you will).  If you boil it down, it's basically a rummy style, set collection card game.  Players collect cards of various colors and when you have enough of one color to make a link between two cities on the map, you turn the cards in and place your trains marking track you own on the map.  You get points for reaching destinations based on other cards you choose at the beginning of the game as well as ones you add during gameplay.

This is a simple, fun, easy to learn/teach game for almost anyone.  Some gamers may find it too light and lacking in strategy for their taste, but for the right audience, this is an easy win in my book.

The components are great with a large, thick map board.  There are colorful, plastic trains to place on the map.  The one negative I have is the size of the cards that come with the base game.  Unless you have hands the size of a 6 year old, they can be pretty annoying.  I highly recommend buying the 1910 Expansion immediately upon purchase of the base set.  It's so worth it.  You get full size cards to replace the ones in the base game.  And you get additional destination cards, one additional end bonus card, and three additional ways to play the game.

We play this game with unintentional conflict, for the most part.  As a family, we are all generally working on our own set collections and destinations.  Eventually, as the map fills up more and more, you'll get in each others' way, but it's not malicious.  However, you can also just play it cutthroat and grab those hard to get, smaller connections right from the start and look to purposely block your opponents once you have a good idea where they are headed.  It depends on your group.

Either way, this is one of the best games I own for almost any situation where I want others to get a feel for our hobby.  It's not the deepest game around, but I think it's one of the best.

[u]Sold on August 16, 2019.[/u]

***
Update 11/6/2017 - Upped my rating. Sometimes, you just want to lay trains with family and friends. TtR does it best.

***

To date, I've played Ticket to Ride multiple times, across four TtR maps: USA, Europe, Nordic Countries, and the updated Marklin map now Germany. TtR is pleasant enough fare for family gaming, and it certainly elevates itself in those scenarios, but the natural competitor in me just turns my nose up at the randomness sometimes. It is married to every aspect of the game, and when it burns you, it burns bad. When games that I spend time with retain this amount of unmitigated randomness, I want them to be quicker, leaner, or else possess means to address it. The Nordic Countries map allows for that, thankfully. 

At the end of the day, I recognize and respect that this is Alan Moon's intent in his design, and he has, without question, succeeded marvelously. While I am not clamoring to play it, in most situations, I will not turn down a game. It is a fine diversion when not taken too seriously.

If I had to pick a favorite map, it would be Nordic Countries, by a long shot. The overall aesthetics and the map layout of that one is, I think, superior to the others, as it creates more moments of head-to-head route competition. However, the other maps are similar enough (and in the case of the USA map, less interesting enough) that I think it is fine to rate the games similarly, as an average of my ratings, for what is essentially the same type of gameplay across all maps.

(+) Truly a classic example of elegant, accessible game design
(+) Modular mechanism lends itself to various scenarios with potential for more interesting gameplay (new maps, new expansions, slight adjustments in rules)
(+) Plays quickly, and smoothly.

(-) Gameplay can be uninteresting and repetitive.
(-) Depending on the route distribution and/or number of players, the amount of player interaction can be less than I like.
(-) Randomness abounds with no way to mitigate it (TtR Europe 1910 expansion has station cards that are a neat idea towards addressing this issue)
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
One of the perennial questions that people ask once they get deep into the board gaming hobby is "what's a good game to play with non-gamers?" with non-gamers including people who play the odd hand of Cribbage or game of Yahtzee once or twice a month. Right now, my best generic answer is Ticket to Ride.

Among Ticket to Ride's virtues, I would count the way it is built from a collection of straightforward mechanics (Carcassonne suffers from the opacity of farmers) that revolve around the fundamental act of building a network of connections on the map; turns go quickly, and many plays are obvious or straightforward – so not too stressful – but you have an underlying plan that keeps them meaningful; meaningful but non-malicious interaction (yes, deliberate blocking is possible, but you can avoid it without being obvious about it, a la the Robber in Settlers of Catan) and a nice sense of narrative produced organically by the fulfillment of tickets and how decisions feel different as the board fills up.

Not everything is sunshine and roses, of course. Arguably, the game would be better if it could keep the narrative arc while shaving fifteen minutes off the play time. For gamers, at least, I think you can argue that the game goes on a bit when it clocks in at 45 minutes. While the luck of the ticket draw is mitigated, it's not trivial, and I'm not sure the push your luck element of drawing more tickets evens it out. Because of the longest route bonus, a collection of tickets that naturally trace out a long route have a distinct advantage over a collection that are easier to fulfill when you branch your network.

I've only played one of the expansions (Switzerland) and that only once so far, so I'm not prepared to pontificate on that topic. Instead, I would say the general guidelines for good extensions would be: keep new systems strongly attached to TtR's network-building heart; extra randomness is deliberately push your luck, not getting randomly hosed with little option and don't make the game noticeably longer.

Not the second coming of Princes of Florence, but well-crafted light fun.

textfield_comment_value: I know a lot of people love Ticket to Ride, but it's way down on my list. The fact that you are trying to connect specific locations but other players can easily take a segment of the shortest path and make it more work for you is annoying. Or they can block you from connecting it entirely, and then what would have been positive points is then negative points, not just zero. In a 3 player game, each segment can only be owned by one player. With 4 or more players, some segments can be owned by 2 players though you are still going to but heads plenty with that many players. But you don't 100% know what they are trying to connect to either since destinations are kept secret. You might just waste your turn trying to block them. Or someone might block someone else completely unintentionally. You could just ignore the destination cards and just build large segments for a lot of points without as much risk. Yes, your unfinished destinations become negatives, but you don't have to take more than 2 destination cards, and they might be small point values at that. There's a lot of luck in which destination paths you draw. You might still win by connecting destinations, but you might draw destination cards that have nothing to do with each other or require you to cross the whole map. They try to mitigate that by having you draw 3 destination cards and choosing which to keep, but if someone draws 3 good ones and someone only draws 1 good one, that doesn't even it enough. There's also points for building the longest road, but if you are focusing on connecting destinations with shared roads, you're less likely to get longest road. It's a way to help even the points. But scores can be quite swingy anyway. That's not to say the rules aren't elegant. I understand why its such a popular game. Very easy to teach and get playing. I just don't like how take-that it can be, both intentionally and unintentionally.

textfield_comment_value:
It nails the lack of direct conflict pretty damn well, since the only interactions with other players are via blocking routes or hoarding colors. And the game is structured so that destination tickets are always hidden information and colors in hand are usually partially hidden. Thus there is rarely enough information to deduce other player's objectives, and next to no strategic basis for ever trying to deny them those objectives in place of pursuing your own. There might be an interesting game of bluff and tells and reading opponents if not for the fundamental flaw that the game calls a point system. Not only is this so fiddly that the typical game will have most players with moves scoring as low as 1 point while the game end totals are usually in the triple digits, but that mere fiddliness was not enough needless complexity for the sake of avoiding the very conflict that makes a game interesting. No sirree bob, Ticket To Ride avoids the low-burn kingblocking of typical Euros like Settlers by making one hundred and ten percent sure that it is impossible to deduce the currently leading player at any point in the game. Destinations are usually the biggest component of a player's endgame score, and they are kept secret until the endgame, and everyone has several all the time. And if you don't complete them, they count negative. So not only is there no way to know any other players' actual score at any point where you could make a choice based on that knowledge, but there's not even a usual approximation based on averages from that hidden information -- you can't assume that the player with more Destination tickets in hand has a higher hidden component of their score, because they are just as likely to have additional negative points as positive points. 

This is not a train game, this is a train wreck of a game.

A lovely game that has the advantage that a lot of people know it. It has so many small details that I'll mention in the following paragraphs that together make it sooo good!

The moment someone first starts placing their trains and everyone is like "Oh God, I better hurry up" and also start placing their trains like a chain reaction. Sooo funny!

The wild trains make this game amazing! "Should I place this route now that I can with the wild train or should I wait till I get the right color so I still have it left for later?" Mostly I choose the later and just end up with lots of unused wild trains.

Lastly, the moment you think "I kinda want a pink train, but there is none in the pool. I do have literally every other train though so I have nothing to lose drawing 2 blindly right? Oh God, I didn't have a green train yet! WHAT?! BROWN IS IN THE GAME TOO?!"

I normally don't like blocking but TtR is one of the exceptions, since you always could've prevented it. You don't feel bad because your opponent did something you could do nothing about, you feel "bad" because you were an idiot.

The only problem I find though is that it's hard to sell the game to someone with just the theme. Also, counting points is a bit tedious compared to other games but at least you don't know (exactly) how far you are behind.

I think I like Ethnos more cause it plays so much more faster, but this is still the more known game, which is a big advantage. It also feels very satisfying finishing a route, and has more funny moments than Ethnos. IDK, I'll keep them on the same score for now.

textfield_comment_value:
I liked this on my first play, back when I was new to this board game thing, but time and repeated plays have knocked it from its generous perch of a "7" rating. And it hit every branch.

I would almost go so far as to say this is the "illusion of a game".  You're basically playing an open-draw variant of rummy.  Scoring happens by placing trains on a map of the States, but this is where the game falls apart.  

You're secretly trying to connect certain cities to fulfill "Destination Tickets", but the winner is almost always decided by whomever happens to draw the Destination Tickets that work best together.  If you've got "Chicago - Boston" and also "New York - Santa Fe", all you've got to do is tack a few extra routes  to either end of the smaller one and you've got an extra 10 points free and clear.  Stupid.

Also, blocking other people is a negligible strategy, and I almost never saw it happen.  Sure, if you've got a Destination Ticket that directly competes with another person's, both of you are screwed.  As for claiming routes to purposely block someone else's path, are you really gonna waste the cards and a turn just to slow someone else down?  You're likely hurting yourself as much as her.

Lastly, the worst thing I can say about the game is that the best strategy I ever played with was to completely ignore the Destinations and just claim the longest routes on the board.  Completely contrary to the theme and spirit of the game, and so we arrive back at TtR's real predecessor:  RUMMY.

The only nice things I can say about this are (a) at least it's simple to teach and (b) the train theme is fun.  It's a shame they are selling so many of these, though, because all it's likely to do is make people think these "designer games" are almost as bad as Monopoly.

:arrowE: [u]Synopsis[/u]:
Rummy played with a board and fancy trains. Draw train cards and play them in sets to construct routes between cities. Use destination cards to allow for scoring completed routes across the continent. Draw two cards of your choice, or draw from the pile blind, or take a single wild train. Once a player gets down to two or fewer available trains, the last round is triggered. It's basic, but compelling.

:arrowE: [u]What I like most[/u]:
The base game is bland, even for a gateway game. TTR: Europe adds just enough complexity to make the system more interesting, but it's really TTR: Team Asia that provides the evergreen rating I ascribe to Ticket to Ride. Team Asia adds a sort of blind, mostly-cooperative aspect to scoring for a pair of players, wherein a single tray of train cards are shared between both and can be used by either player, but the individual hands of train cards and destination cards are still hidden from each other. This creates a great sense of industrialist cooperation in a time period where neither company has complete access to each other's planning. I love it. It's fun. It's hilarious. It makes for a lot of "YES! I hoped you would do that!" and "GAH, I needed those! No!" moments. If you can read the actions of your teammate, you can do very, very well.

:arrowE: [u]What I like least[/u]:
Overall, I find Ticket to Ride can be boring for some new players who might do better with "deeper" entry points, and  I need to get a good gauge on what I should expect from beginners. Should we start with the base or Europe? Should we add Asia? Should we just play a different game? I see TTR as a tool more than a game I want to go out of my way to play.

textfield_comment_value:
“You choo choo choose me?" - Ralph Wiggum

GAMEPLAY
One of the most well-known designer board games out there it has recently seen a huge influx of players with a very well done ios version of the game. The game turn consists of three simple choices. Pick up cards, play a train route by playing cards, or get more route cards. It's great because rounds go very quickly and no one feels left out. There is no direct interaction between players, but it is possible to block others from connecting routes.

COMPONENTS
The board is a good quality card stock and the cards are smaller than playing cards so small hands won’t have a problem. Days of wonder includes some extra trains of each color in case you lose some. Make sure to count out your trains before each game. The art throughout is wonderful, The trains themselves leave something to be desired, I would like to see wooden trains but that's nitpicking.

THEME
The base game uses a map of America which has about 40 cities on it. Connecting routes throughout the country is simple and resonates with most people as a traveling adventure. The small disconnect is that the players don’t have to connect the routes in sequence. This abstraction doesn’t distract from the enjoyment.

WHO IS IT FOR?
This game is for everybody. Really. I entertained three nephews ages 15, 16, and 18 recently. None of them gamers and they all had a great time. Families with children as young as 8 will have a great time with games lasting about 45 minutes. Even power gamers will enjoy it once in a while; there is light strategy based on your route cards and blocking the other players. For established gamers use it as a gateway for your friends you would like to engage in your hobby.

textfield_comment_value:
The hype train, excuse the pun, was so strong on this game for so long that I deliberately passed on playing for many years... However, having finally bit the bullet I'm pleased to say the praise is very well-deserved, it is truly a great game design. 

The base USA map is lots of fun, looks great, and the "dual carriageway" rules for higher player counts is a good balancing mechanic. The USA map definitely makes TtR casual in the sense that if you miss a single critical one-train link for your route(s) you can end up with a large point swing due to the ruling that if you don't complete your routes you end up having points deducted instead of added. Also, the strategy whereby you ignore routes altogether to aim for the higher-scoring long-train sections is a little bit too strong vs playing traditionally. My other criticism would be that route draw randomness has a bit too much of an effect on final outcomes, in particularly some routes involving Miami can be irksome to complete.

My favourite map I've played so far is India, as the shorter train sections make route completion a bigger part of the game, and the multiple ways of completing routes means that the game is more balanced. Very much enjoy India map (moreso than USA or Europe mainstream options). 

Despite the clear 'casual' elements of the base game, it also gets points for implementing a decent degree of strategy into a gateway game, and also the theme and intuitive ruleset which makes TtR a very easy sell for nascent gamers. 

Overall, the "why-didn't-I-think-of-that" game design speaks volumes to the accessibility and plain enjoyability of TtR and earns a solid 8 out of 10 from me for the series.

textfield_comment_value:
Basically, you draw cards and lay tracks.  You can't foil anyone as there are virtually a million paths to every destination.  So then it comes down to drawing cards and placing trains.  This has to be the most over-hyped game ever.  

If you are looking for a game where you drink beer and occasionally pay attention to what's going on, this is it.


I once saw a guy draw a circle on his white board then toss small sticky balls (about an inch is size) at it for hours.  I thought he would grow tired of this painfully dull act after a day or so.  A year later he still does it as he finds it most relaxing and fun.  I realized that this is how some people meditate (whether they know it or not).  They focus on the easy task at hand and clear the mind.  The easier the task, the more euphoria the brain experiences.  This game is popular because satisfies the same requirement.  A very simple, zero strategy game that sends the brain in to an easy mediative state.  This euphoria elevates when the brain discovers that it could complete a route and did not have to work - thus fulfilling one the the laws of physics that states everything seeks is lowest energy level.  

For that, I give it a 10.  But for gaming, I give it a 1.  I have played this 11 or 12 times now.  After the first 4 (trying to find something I may have been missing) I mostly observed the other players - a very interesting experiment (try it sometime!).  They had the same happy look on their faces as the guy with the sticky balls.  Don't think me negative, I too now like the sticky balls (heh heh).  But for this type of game, I prefer Risk or Monopoly - a tad more excitement with the dice.

I was and still am dissappointed with this game. It should/could be a 9 for me. Let me explain why. I feel very strongly that the bonuses for completing your rail links between cities is too small. In game play terms I'd add about a 25-50% to the value of the bonus to every city card. You could do this by adding 5 to every card or use a percentage as above. If you added say 30% a 10 would be worth 13. As the game sits its mainly about getting a east to west rail line using as many 5 or 6 link sections as you can. There is virtually no way you can win without using large links. I played a game where I drew mainly north south runs in the east. I completed 7 of 8 but as it turns out even if I'd completed 8 of 8 I still would have lost. This just doesn't seem right. A train game should primarily reward you for building clever rail lines not just a big sections where ever. If you wish you can overlook this completely and play it as a pure strategy game and have fun but I think it still limits the strategic options to one rather than two.

New Idea: I might try a strategy which is to keep two small runs which you can complete easily and focus on playing a mainly defensive strategy to stop others from connecting their big runs. If you get help from one or two other players who may also try this strategy, then completing a big run becomes difficult. This should nicely balance things out. If you really mess with one guy early he will have no choice but to join you in stopping someone else when he is not going to make his big runs. Then this can landslide to 3 or 4 people stopping the last one or two people trying for the big connection.
