Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Has become a staple in our family since we got it in December 2011. Very simple to teach but surprisingly difficult to master, as you need to adjust your strategy based on the tickets you get - do you go for longest cross country routes or do you have bad tickets for that which forces you to do blocking and going for random 6 car routes? Do you start completing your tickets early to seize critical routes or do you hoard cards so as not to tip your hand before you have all the needed cards? When do you force the game to end? The optimal answers to these questions differ with each game and better players will win the vast majority of the time, despite the randomness associated with drawing tickets, drawing cards, and whether you end up competing heavily for certain routes.

Another fun aspect to this game is aesthetic as routes criss cross the board. One game ended with such a beautiful pattern that I literally snapped a picture and made it my phone's lock screen for a couple months.

My only complaint is the variability associated with drawing tickets - it is possible to be at a huge disadvantage out of the gate if you draw poor initial tickets. So we've been experimenting with variants like starting with 6 tickets and keeping at least 3, or starting with 4 tickets and keeping at least 2, etc.

Our family loves gateway games that are light-to medium rules complexity with medium depth to them, and this game fits the bill perfectly, right along with Pandemic and Settlers of Catan. This game's terrific reputation as an awesome gateway game is well deserved.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
I remember learning about this game from SU&SD in my early days of gaming and hearing Paul say that Ticket to Ride is fun and he'd have a good time with it, but given the opportunity to play a board game with friends, he'd rather play about any other SU&SD recommended game. While I think that is a bit harsh on TTR, there is some truth to that. 

I really do like TTR. It's a safe choice that you never really forget how to play even if you only pull it out once or twice a year. Building out your routes and placing your trains is bound to be hailed as clean fun by everyone at the table. As a family game and a gateway game, this is a classic. Really! I genuinely like this game. However, as my tastes have adjusted and my preferences have emerged, there are just other games that fit this same family/gateway niche that I find more compelling. And that's the main problem with TTR. It's not compelling enough to make me suggest it for a game night. Of course there's the trade off between accessibility and compelling gameplay. The more intertwined and obtuse the gameplay, the less accessible it becomes. TTR errs on the side of "uncontroversial" and wants to be a crowd pleaser. For what it aims to do, it is great! I would say it's excellent, but in my opinion the game is a bit too long for the decision space it provides. Although the pace of the game is perfect, I wish it ended about 15 minutes sooner each time we play. Still such a great game but I just don't need it on my shelf. There are other "snappier" and more compelling family games that I prefer over this.

textfield_comment_value:
(Play it digital)

Ticket to Ride is one of the "you have to play it at least once" game, the kind that introduced many people to the modern board game.
It's very easy to explain the rules and to start to play. No need for a previous experience at this game or at any game to know what you want to do. You take cards from the color you need, or try to be lucky with the top deck card. That's very easy. 
The game is quite fast-paced, as each player can play in a few seconds, but from the start to the end it can last quite long, for a "medium-light" game. And most of the time, you just take cards, take cards, take cards, and from time to time, you spend them to claim the railway. And then again, take cards... It lacks variety in action, and you need to do a lot of the same action A before doing action B. For example, in Takenoko, which is also a gateway medium-light game, each turn can be different, as you have to choose between 5 different actions.
Overall, Ticket to Ride has good and bad points. Everybody can play it and understand what's going on. You can plan a """strategy""". The turns are quick, but the game is long, and during your endless journey to victory, you will draw cards over and over again, hoping that nobody else is gonna steal your railway... but what can you do ? You need 3 more blue cards, and they aren't showing up ! Also, the negative points for uncompleted objectives can really hit hard, especially when you just needed one or two more cards. And it's ridiculous that the player who finished first can play again after everybody else...

textfield_comment_value:
I have played this game with my niece at least 6 or 7 times just this past week. I have also played it with a few adults who aren't very interested in games and it has gone down quite well. Some people might think that it is boring because it isn't a "proper" train game, whatever that may be. There isn't a lot of heavy strategy going on in this game which is nice. Sure there are a lot of ways to connect the different routes, which adds a little to the strategy. Do you try to play in an obvious manner and claim routes in a line, or are you a little sneaky, and try to hope that it all coalesces towards the end of the game? I can imagine that with more players it would become quite intense as there are more players potentially competing for the same routes. 
Sure there is a little downtime while everyone is just taking two (or one if you get the up facing locomotive!) cards. However, in this game you can really crush someones dream. I had to laugh at my niece because she would always celebrate when she got certain cards, and I would think that was funny. If you lose friends over playing a game like this, then maybe you should look at the type of company that you keep? Seriously, if your friends cannot take losing in a game as simple and light as this, then maybe that does say more about you than the game. Overall, I really like this series of games. I think it would appeal mostly to children and non-gamers. I would consider this game as a great gateway game for kids who have only played Cluedo and Monopoly.

textfield_comment_value:
When I tell people I play board games for a hobby, there's always the stigma that they think I spend hours and hours playing games like Monopoly and Candy Land. Not so. And if you're on this site reading this review, you probably know what I mean. So, in an effort to share our wonderful hobby we sometimes need those games that bridge the gap between the hardcore enthusiast, and the person who thinks Clue is a brain burner.

Enter Ticket to Ride! This is one of my go-to gateway games. You can teach it in about 5 minutes, and the game can be played within an hour...depending on your players of course.

And it's a pretty easy sell to. A train game of building railroads across the country. Connecting cities from one coast to another. There are all sorts of different sizes of tracks, that when claimed, give you victory points. This is a set collection game (i.e. you collect different sets of different colored train cars to claim routes). But the key to victory is in each players specific "tickets." These tickets are hidden information, for your eyes only. On them are two cities that you need to connect with a continuous railroad. At the end of the game, you score more points for completing these tickets. But beware, you will also go back that many points for NOT completing them!
This game is perfect for families. And the last few rounds always provide nail-biting tension that just seems to make the game enjoyable as you're all desperately trying to finish routes. Oh, and route blocking is perfectly legal!
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
I honestly don't understand the popularity of this game. at all. It is such a boring mediocre game. I would never recommend it as a gateway game either, because if I were new to boardgameing and got introduced this game, I will not come back to boardgaming again.

The game is essentially rummy variant. You spend many turns drawing two cards - oh dear. There is very little player-interaction in this game. It costs too much to block your opponents. So blocking happens rather randomly. This sort of random personal attack is my least favorite aspects in the player-interaction. You can, but don't need to care about other people's hand in this game because blocking is rare as the map has many alternative routes.

Destination cards have too much luck and huge swing between completion or incompletion - positive or negative. This is too rough and seems very unbalanced. Also tickets are valued merely by the length and, needless to say, they are quite unbalanced.

I must mention that the scoring scheme is extremely artificial. 1,2,4,7,10,15? What kind of sequence is that?
http://www.research.att.com/~njas/sequences/A027384
Long segments (5 or 6) clearly has huge advantage because they are far more economical. So of course everyone just keeps drawing cards until they get a set of 5 or 6.

I prefer Santa Fe for Moon's railroad game. As a train game (connection game), Trans America is much better than this. Something similar to Ticket to Ride that I much prefer will be Looting London and Marco Polo.

textfield_comment_value:
{ P - 2 3 [4] 5 }

You have to give Mr. Moon some credit here. Of the big four gateway games (Ticket, Settlers, Ra, Carcassonne), his wins out. After dissecting every materially different starting draw (base set only - with a larger, expansion-inundated deck of Tickets the game is much worse because players can never infer if certain tickets remain in the deck as well as the probability and necessity of getting them) and how players would thus begin the game, one should figure out that a spinal route is usually optimum. (The route extends from Calgary to L.A. to Pitt to Miami, with endpoints truncated if necessary, e.g. tickets in New York or Montreal. A secondary route folds back on itself slightly to encompass Duluth, and requires the black six to coexist with the aforementioned.) The only other possibilities include central tendencies of geography in either the west or east (these players need to acquire some strategic routes to pinch the spinal folks) or two "big" tickets that are almost exactly the same route. (Lucky contestants here can simply come on down, there's not much you can do to prevent SEA-NY + VAN-MON and the brevity with which they can be completed.) I even mapped out the optimum routes for all west/east as well as basic countermeasures against traditional players and break points where routes can be shortened given the absence of tickets to cities like Santa Fe or Chicago. As you may have expected, this game has lost its luster for me, but hey - at least it's not Ra.

textfield_comment_value:
I put off buying or playing this game for several years because it looked like something I'd have played with my kids (except they were too old when I found it). I kept reading how grownups were playing, but the look still put me off. When out of town (non-gamer) relatives came in for a visit, we finally picked this up. We were amazed at how much fun it was and it remains a go-to favorite years later.

I only have the base game listed here because I consider TTR to be one game, with several variations. We own nearly all of the boards and all of the maps now. The ones we don't have do not interest us.

We got rid of the card version because it was horrible. We never dared buy the dice version because the card version sucked so much.

Rules to TTR can be learned quickly and easily, by anyone from an 80-year-old great grandma to a pre-teen. (Don't start with Rails and Sails or the England map.) The underlying strategy, however, is another story. Turns move quickly because you can only do one thing during your turn and you usually know what you want to do by the time your turn rolls around, except Dave.

This game is truly fun to play. Everyone we've ever taught to play LOVES the game and most people end up buying their own copy. I recommend the 1910 expansion because the cards are bigger and I'm old and blind. If you play a lot, I'd recommend some of the extra maps. Alvin & Dexter make for an interesting variant too.

Overall, this is probably the most played game in our collection.

textfield_comment_value:
Well, it's ok.  The theme works, the art is appealing, and the gameplay is engaging enough to get you about 2/3rds of the way through the game (if you can get past the lack of interaction).  The problem is that it really comes down to a luck of the draw endgame.  

There are really two ways to win in the game, going for connecting cities, and drafting cards to make long connections. Either way works well and is nicely balanced, but my issue is that the endgame devolves around waiting for the right cards to come up.  After you have connected routes, there is a desire to get more routes as there is nothing left for you to do in the game--no objective.  Well, near the end game, in a desire to continue to get points you are given the decision to draw new routes again and hope that the cards come up that will allow you to connect.  If you can get them you will probably win, if you don't you will probably lose.  

Ultimately, I just can't love a game that relies that heavily on the luck of the draw.  Clippers is more my speed. 

I was coerced into playing Phase 10 at a party and realised that this is really just a variant on that with a board and more to choose from.  Can't see myself ever playing this again. 

Draw, Draw, Draw, Draw, Draw, Draw, Draw, Draw, Draw, Play, Draw, Draw, Draw, Play, Draw, Draw, Draw, Play, Zzzz, Draw, Draw, Draw, Play.

Update: I played it again, thought I should downgrade my rating to a 4, then saw that it was already a 4.  I was right the first time.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
*I've revisited TtR because I love connection games and the geography lesson they throw in. Now that the hype has gone, I've warmed to the design though it will never surpass the charm of the distilled and less confrontational TransAmerica. 

The race to place trains on prime routes, enforced by the tickets, is a source of most of the tension in the minds of some, though the set collecting (coupled with the 3 wild discard rule) and risk taking in drawing additional tickets ratchets up the stress as well, (though I find the US map for 2 player is too 'open' so not as exciting). Yet I can see that such an adrenaline rich experience can also be a source of frustration, especially with more players. 

I appreciate there is alot more decision making involved here than in TransAmerica, such as when to wait and draw or when to lay track, or when to switch from picking tickets to getting all your trains on the board.

But the main reason TtR falls short for me is that it is too 'score' heavy, with the summing up of the tickets making the end too anticlimatic unless I can enforced the "reveal rule". 

Update: Recently played 7 games in 3 days, which included 3 newbies who play Rummikub. Definitely a good intro to the new breed of boardgames (as well as the series) which initially induces alot of tension, but this soon evaporates when played with 2 or 3 as there doesn't seem to be enough conflict for cities (will have to try the expansion). Rating for at least 4 players.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Ticket to Ride is simply the best game I've used for introducing people to gaming.

It is quickly picked up, it is fun for most, it does involve some thought, tension in timing, and risk in gambling (the destination tickets). The other important aspect of the game is the bonding and socializing of the players. That is true gaming interaction betwixt the gamers. Socializing is also the main lure to draw the new people back to gaming.

If you have a great night, even a relaxing night, with laughs and some gaming...well, you're going to get repeat players.
As long as I have people to play with, people to share my life with, people who will play my games I will be happy; and I will find (or create) deeper game groups too.

It's all about balance, and that's something that Ticket to Ride has. It's why the game works. It's why people learn it quick, it's why people come back to it. You can talk. You can laugh. You can block others. You can take risks. You can plan. 
Ticket to Ride has a very important element in its design; it's got the basics most gamers (even extremely casual ones) grew up with and it's close to card games they played. It doesn't hurt the head when playing (though I've seen lots of pained faces brooding over their cards and the board) and it allows for people to relax and talk. It removes the "chess" fear (think of math anxiety and you'll know what I'm talking about) from new players.

Is it the best gateway game? Yep.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
With 2 players..."blah". After so many plays a 2 player game holds little appeal pre-game and provides little fun during the game.

With 4-5 players...more fun, though still not something I enjoy or appreciate. I can deal with the lack of theme and themeless mechanics with more grace when I play with 4-5 players than with 2 players. The game is much more competitive & the board is so much tighter. Highly recommended as a 4-5 player game for new gamers, light Euro gamer types, and Ameritrashers who can suspend their need for theme and blowing things up (which means you're likely not an Ameritrasher!).

Caveats: 
(1) This game is a great game for gateway gamers and gamers who like lighter fare.
(2) This game has no theme, in my opinion. That really drags down its rating. If being immersed in theme or an excellent integration of theme & mechanics is important, proceed cautiously or don't proceed at all.
(3) The 2 player game is competitive but lacks important tension, as the map is generally so wide open. I would rate the 2 player game very low, say a "4".
(4) Played with 4-5 players, the competitive nature of the game more than makes up for most of its shortfalls.

Final verdict: It will not be my first choice, even with 4-5 players, unless there are no other sensible options. But if someone else suggests a 4-5 player game of TTR, I probably won't have a problem playing and will likely enjoy the experience. As a 2 player game..."blah".
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
It is so hard to describe my relationship with Ticket to Ride. I got it for Christmas from my girlfriend because I really wanted it. At this point I had begun to play games such as Puerto Rico and El Grande. I had also been branching out to try other games as well. The first time I played Ticket to Ride it didn't seem to have the spark or staying power that El Grande (my current favorite) had. My family enjoyed it and that was great so it got played at home, but when I brought it to school there was a lukewarm reaction to it.

It sat shelved for months until the summer when I tried to get together a weekly gaming group. Ticket to Ride was my game of choice for indoctrinating new gamers because it supported a larger group of players better than Carcassonne. At first I did not see how there was a lot of strategy in the game. All of the meaningful decisions seemed to be made when you picked your tickets (before you even start the game); however, the more I played the more I realized that board position was important. Long routes are better than short routes, regardless of what type of ticket to you have. You have to balance your important priorities now vs. your long term goals.

I came back to school with a renewed sense of how to play and love this game and I was lucky enough to find a lot of people who share my love for it. It is one of the games that gets pulled out the most often now which is great, because it is truly a great game.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
A fairly average set collecting / drafting card game with an often unessential board. In theory, the routes on the board add tension and uncertainty, but unless you have a full table there is little room for defensive play, which made this strangely feel like a solitaire game in that any time a player thwarted another, except in extremely rare circumstances, it was circumstantial. 

A bit of room for good play: drawing cards to prevent changing the face up pile, and getting a huge hand and then creating a huge run of 6 links, and it seems the choice between short and long tickets, and long runs vs. quantity of tickets is decently balanced. 

Very little tension most of the time though, pick up a card, pick up a card, lay out several cards, accidentally screw someone along the way. Note that I am more fond of the later Nordic variant that has few enough routes to make this actually competitive in many situations, even with only 2, and especially with 3. This original version of the game really requires a fullish table to have any sense of competition.

(Note that Elfengold has many of the good things about TtR while adding many more gamer friendly aspects such as auctions and opportunities to screw with your opponents. I suggest it by a wide margin over this lighter implementation of a 'route planning' game...and if you really want something light in this vein on the cheap I recommend Canasta, all it takes is two Bicycle decks!)
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Cutthroat and quick... I like it! With higher player counts it can feel sort of repetitive though. NEEDS fast players, or else it feels like you're constantly just waiting to draw cards... again. Also 1910 expansion is pretty much a must because screw small cards. Globetrotter bonus makes things more fun too.

This is a great map because it handles all player counts 2-5 well. At any given player count there's probably a map that does it marginally better, but here is your versatile map that can handle cutthroat 2 player games just as well as it can handle looser 4 player games or crowded 5 player games

[b]Criticisms:[/b] 

*The 1910 expansion really should have been rolled into the base game by now in a second edition, since it's essentially a minor "fix" or update for the base game, balancing short routes vs long ones and adding the Globetrotter bonus

* This game is often hailed as a great gateway game, and I can see it working for some (and it must have worked for many people to get that reputation in the first place) but honestly the player interaction is subtle and sophisticated, and so it can feel a bit cold and non-inclusive for many people I think. The quiet and tense interaction is very real when everyone already "gets" the game, but as a gateway option that's more interesting to social-types, I'd rather do something with more table talk and inter-person interaction.

(5 Design + 3 Enjoyment)

textfield_comment_value:
There are things I will always value high in a game. One of them (perhaps the one I value the most) is the beauty that arises from simplicity of rules, components and mechanisms that are nontheless capable of delivering considerable depth in gameplay, enjoyment and engagement. "Ticket to Ride" has all that, and that's basically why I needed it to be in my collection.  Just bought it today and played it with my nieces who have happened to love it!

My only possible critic to this game is that I wish it costed (and I believe it COULD cost) around 10€ less (yes, I'm the kind of person who wouldn't mind at all the 225 plastic train wagons being just plain cheap painted wooden sticks or tiles if it helps lowering the final price!). It's ok if the game tells me that what we are building is the train line itself, instead of the wagons.

It's a clever, gorgeous game design that does exactly what you expect it to do and it does it well. It's simple to learn, simple (and fast!) to play (you don't need to spend a day learning and understanding super-complicated rules or ever visiting the rules during gameplay!) and it just WORKS! Your kids will love it and so will their grandparents! Perfect family game, clearly among the best ones I've tried in the category.

I believe this is my first euro style game ever (actually owned by me), and it won't be my last one.

textfield_comment_value:
Ask yourself this question, why is this better than Monopoly? Honestly think about it and you realize how overrated this game is...36??????????. (I am not a big fan of Monopoly BTW)

This is probably more random, same amount of luck (card draw vs. dice), same amount of strategy (very very little)although Monopoly probably has more, they are both set collection, the only bonus is this is over faster but most of the game all you do is draw cards like "GO FISH"? This is fun? Almost no choices to make here, pull a ticket, pull some more cards or build a route.

Monopoly at least has trading & negotiation, building up properties and an economic factor that makes it fun getting rich. The first 2 games of this I thought it wasn't bad and could see why people liked it but then it became very uninteresting and repetitive after that, this would have been somewhat better off being shorter and therefore not a bad filler, as it is it plays like a LONG filler but can still be used as a 'gateway game'. 

This gets rated one fraction below Monopoly and Europe is only a tad better but then its a tad longer which is not good for these kind of games. 

If you are looking for a very light gateway game that kids could play this certainly fits the bill. If you want a good gateway game that also has some substance and meaningful decisions to make keep looking.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: Ticket to Ride sowed in me the early seeds of board game enthusiasm, namely because it did something I was unaware could be done - made it just as fun and tense with two players as with higher players counts.  I’m certain it was not the first game to achieve this feat, but it was my introduction to effective scaling.  As of my writing this, I have yet to play a round that I didn’t thoroughly enjoy.  Timing is everything in Ticket to Ride.  You will have tipped your hand when you claim your first leg, so how long can you hold out before doing so?  Another player is nosing around in your territory and they just started picking up a lot of yellow train cards - should you use your precious locomotives to claim that four-yellow leg, just in case that’s what she’s after?  An opponent’s supply of plastic train tokens is quite depleted - should you abandon picking up cards and start claiming legs before the game ends, possibly forsaking your master plan?  Yes, I have seen players miss out on a crucial leg and end up getting hosed, but I have not witnessed anyone overly upset about it.  Failure in this game makes one introspective, appreciating that there had been other options available and that, in all likelihood, one’s plight might have been avoided.  I feel a nervous empowerment when I play, like navigating a big city alone for the first time.

[q="Past me"]Bought in April 2013. I don't get to play this game enough. Ridiculously accessible, tense without being stressful, quick and fun. Note - I've never played this without [thing=24439][/thing].[/q]

But even after I've had to keep upping my dose of gaming again and again just to relive the initial thrill, this game still packs the same old punch.

It tends to go unplayed for a while in favour of more novel games, but whenever I come back to it I have so much fun I rarely stop after just one game.

Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
I like a game that has very simple rules but a lot of depth, and Ticket to Ride fits that bill. The goal is to get the most points, and these are obtained by completing short routes, completing service between two assigned cities, and by having the most longest line of continuous routes. On any given turn you're drawing train cards, playing train cards to complete a route, or drawing new assignments for service between two cities. There are a few exceptions to these rules, but overall it's a very easy game to learn. 

UPDATE: Dropping from 9 to an 8. Still very good, but after repeated playings I feel like I want "more to do" in the game. I've begun to see the same strategies repeated, so it's taken a hit on replay value. But still a great game, and really one of the best "full-strength" gateway games to recruit new gamers. I'm very much enjoying the Swiss map variant as included in the PC computer game version of the board game.

UPDATE: Dropping from an 8 to a 7. After numerous plays, the game wears on me. It's still good as a gateway game, though, and I am willing to play. I would prefer to play a TTR variant, and I'm quite likely to bring up a counter-suggestion rather than go ahead with another TTR. Because of this, my rating could drop to a 6.5. I hate to do it though, because it's a great game, I've just played it to death.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Probably one of the most overrated games I have seen yet.

You draw cards to cover train routes.  Different cards have different colors, and so do the routes.  The bigger the route you take, the more points you receive.  In addition, semi-random "tickets" can be chosen that give you a bonus for finishing the route or a decrement if you do not cover the route.

The good thing about this game is that it is easy to learn.  Most people (including a 6 year old) figured it out in 3 minutes and could play it.

So why is this game a fail?  It's entire design revolves around card counting, deck memorization, and knowing the shape of the map.  You had better keep track of how many red cards (and blue, purple, white, etc) have been played or you will never know what % chance you have of finishing one route over another (quickly that is).  Knowing what cards are left in the "tickets" deck is crucial.  Drawing another ticket can win or lose a game for you, if you know that it is highly unlikely that anything left is going to help you, you had better skip pulling another card.  And finally, knowing which sides of the map are easy or hard depending on your ticket selection is crucial.  

Basically that means you need to memorize a lot.  The person who owns it will probably destroy everyone else.  That doesn't lead to many replays in some groups.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
This used to be my go-to introductory Eurogame, but that position has been completely supplanted by [i]Century: Spice Road[/i].

Why's that?  Well, for one, I think that [i]CSR[/i] is actually slightly easier to teach (which is saying something, given how easy [i]TtR[/i] is to explain).  But the big reason is that the starting tickets can be capricious, and negative points at the end of the game can feel bad for first-time modern gamers.  Those of us who have been in the hobby longer likely don't mind so much, but it can feel rough to work hard during a game, fail at the end, and be penalized for your efforts.  It's also very opaque in early games when (or if) you should go diving for additional tickets, unless you get extraordinarily lucky with your starting group, in which case you're likely to win the game anyway.

None of this is to say that [i]Ticket to Ride[/i] is a bad game.  It's not, although why the hell are they still selling this game with the tiny cards, forcing you to buy the expansion for the full-sized ones?  ...I digress.  I'm always happy to play this, and I'm happy to pull it out if someone requests it.  But it's not something that [i]I[/i] am likely to pick when it comes to game time, and I feel that that's the deciding factor between a 7 and an 8.

I'll probably always hold an element of nostalgia towards this game. Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
[Initial Impression: 7]
This train-themed game is simple enough to be enjoyed by the whole family, but introduces newer players to multiple options on each turn and multiple scoring possibilities.  This makes it a very good introductory game (although TtR: Europe may be even better for this because the stations mitigate some possible cutthroat blocking moves).  However, with only one action per turn, the game can really bog down with high player counts (4-5), as each player will typically draw cards, wait for everyone else to take a turn, and then draw more cards.  This makes it feel like you aren't doing anything but drawing cards for much of the game.  In fact, some players will hoard cards by simply drawing for the first half of the game, only laying track when their needed routes appear threatened by other players.  Such hoarding can be a very good strategy, because it increases your ability to claim longer (and high-scoring) routes later, while also limiting which color routes your opponents will be able to claim.  Good players will usually also block some routes that they don't need, making it more difficult for opponents to complete their destination tickets.  Such play can sometimes put off new gamers, so it is important to know your group before employing such cutthroat tactics.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Extremely easy to teach. Whenever I want to introduce the archetypical "non-gamer" to the hobby, chances are I'll start with this one. Turns moves fast and a full game can be finished within an hour, even with total newbies.

The amount of conflict can be adjusted by the players, so it has the potential of offering two different experiences without throwing balance out of the window, which is nice. Want a friendly game where each player tries to mind their own business, yet competing with others when they have similar objectives? You can have that. Or maybe you prefer a super cutthroat game where players are constantly blocking each other? That's possible too.

Funny enough, this is the opposite of Settlers in terms of luck impact: while luck can have a tremendous impact in determining the winner, its mechanisms give the illusion of a larger degree of control.

In any case, I'm raising its mark to a perfect ten. Over the year it's been my most successful introductory game, by far. A game that's this good in getting people into the hobby deserves all the recognition it can get.

It's simple and accessible, but there's not much more to it - overall I find Ticket to Ride (USA) to be pretty underwhelming (considering its almost legendary status). There's just not enough interesting decisions here (even by the gateway game standards). You just draw cards, slowly build your hand and hope that others won't block your routes (and trust me - the game can get pretty cutthroat in this regard). 

The starting hand of bad tickets can really hinder your entire game. Not only that -  experienced players who know the highest scoring ticket cards inside-out have a huge advantage over novices as they can predict what you are doing and block you accordingly (as a novice you are put at a disadvantage just because you don't know what to expect from the tickets - this game rewards "experience and memory" over skillful play and I'm not a big fan of that).

I would rather play Quadropolis or Splendor if I were to suggest a great looking gateway game. Even Catan is more interesting and involving due to negotiations and trading aspect. 

I don't hate it, but I'm far from being amazed by it.  I understand it has its fans though, it's just not my cup of tea.

textfield_comment_value:
Designer: Alan Moon

If you can accept this game for what it is (a largely luck-driven game) then you should enjoy it. If you do not like randomness, look elsewhere.

Pros: 
-Easy to learn
-Easy to teach
-Great gateway game for new gamers and fun to play with non-gamers as well
-Most people seem to enjoy it
-Limited AP
-Expandability seems endless

Cons:
-Considering its price tag, the components should be better (I had to upgrade to wooden trains).
-Minimal strategy involved. Mostly luck-driven--cards are usually drawn randomly
-Multiplayer solitaire--if you like high player interaction, then this is not the game for you. Direct confrontation is rare

Overall, I really enjoy this game. It has grown on me quite a bit thanks to the exceptional iPad implementation. For 2 players though, definitely check out Switzerland/India map or Big Cites under the 1910 expansion. I have played Nordic Countries and did not enjoy it. I would recommend TTR to most people. In particular, I think children 12 and under would enjoy this game. For serious gamers, it can certainly be frustrating. Though, if you can accept it for what it is--a light, fun game, and don't take it too seriously, I think even the most hardcore gamers can find a gem here.

Il suffit d’une partie des Aventuriers du rail pour comprendre qu’il ait remporté toutes les récompenses ludiques les plus prestigieuses en 2004/2005. Extrêmement accessible avec ses principes expliqués clairement en quelques minutes, il reste remarquablement fluide grâce à son unique action à chaque tour de jeu, y compris à quatre ou cinq joueurs, pour des parties rapides offrant pourtant ce qu’il faut de questionnements tactiques, sur les missions que l’on accepte, le blocage de ses adversaires au détriment de ses propres trajets, l’accumulation de petits segments ou la préférence pour de longs segments, plus rentables mais plus longs à construire…

Cela en fait un excellent jeu familial, satisfaisant encore parfaitement aux standards contemporains, et dont je ne suis pas étonné que d’autres titres s’inspirent directement de l’élégance.

Sa dimension pédagogique (on y apprend la localisation de nombreuses villes) ajoute encore à son charme, et est renforcée par la présence de multiples extensions, promettant mille voyages et découvertes.

Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Awesome game- I'll push my luck, a bit further, a bit further, yes, AAARRGHH I need that route, but now I don't even have enough trains to even complete my tickets... I'm so screwed!

Needs 1910. It's still good without it, but to be truly excellent T2R needs the expansion. 

The tension comes from the press your luck element. The more you build the more you empty your hand. If you have a big hand, you are threatening your opponents to potentially build anywhere. Hence you want to maintain a large hand for most of the game, keeping Jokers in reserve and using them last (I typically hoard them until either I'm desperate or to do a random 15 point build just before the end). Also draw face down cards early, and face up cards late. Most games I never take a face up loco.

It is best to go in cycles of "pick up, pick up, pick up, build, build, build" rather than "pick up, build, pick up, build, pick up, build" i.e. do as much building as possible in a short time frame. This reduces the window of opportunity for others to react to what you're doing in a way that harms you. However, this is where we reach the core problem of the game. The longer you wait before building, the more chance someone builds a key link before you.

textfield_comment_value:
One of those games that just screams "instant classic". I remember seeing it on the table of the game shop I would frequent when I lived in Seattle, being played consistently. Anybody can sink their teeth into this one and enjoy themselves.

While I find Ticket to Ride to maybe be a little too simple in execution, it gets serious points for being intuitive and easy to teach. There's really no reason not to own this game, since it's a bulls-eye for introducing new people to the hobby. The component quality is rock-solid and the pace of the game is a quick clip, giving just the right amount of time to plan out your next move before it's your turn again. 

And, considering how straightforward the game is, it has a decent amount of freedom in strategy. Depending on how things are playing out, it may be best to just try for all of the six train routes, or maybe you're feeling cutthroat and just want to prevent other players from completing their routes. I've even seen a player do a mad grab for more route tickets at the end of the game, in order to hopefully have fulfilled them already. Which worked!

Ticket to Ride may seem like a bit of a relic at this point, but it's status as a go-to gateway game or simple competition isn't a question in my mind.

In summary of this game, you score points based on how many carts and/or how long your carts are on your train. It's quite simple, but I can see this a great game for euro players to start playing board games.

Some people say this is the "gateway" game for board gamers, and it is the favorite for many. I have to say the game is built well and finishes in a short time. However... I did not like "style" of this game, and I do not think it will be the only "gateway" game for new players to play board games. I recommend new players try to find a game that matches a similar style of a game they have played in the past or to experiment different types of games that are short and popular. I wish I played this game first as one my first euro games, but I don't t hink I would stayed playing board games if I didn't play fun thematic games like Dead of Winter, Shadows of Camelot, and Coup.

 I feel like a much shorter game like Coup or Codenames would be better "gateway" games. For more hardcore RPG players, the I suggest Jaws of the Lion (Gloomhaven franchise) or 5 minute dungeon are great "gateway" games. For MTG (Magic the gathering) or Yu-Gi-Oh! players I suggest decking games like Dominion, Marvel Legendary, or Wingspan are great "gateway" games.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Ticket to Ride is a modern-day classic, deserves to be in most collections as a good intro set-collection game.

Ticket to Ride is a classic along the level of Catan, and I definitely enjoy its simplicity and elegance. It's a very simple mechanic, but the player competition and the unknown aspect of the cards makes it different every time. 

Basically, players are competing to build train routes along different colored tracks throughout the United States. They accomplish this by drawing cards of the correct color, then claiming routes by placing their own trains along the route. 

You earn points by completing Tickets (preset routes that you draw from the ticket deck), placing routes, and winning the longest connected route, which is similar to the Longest Road in Settlers of Catan. 

Overall, I enjoy Ticket to Ride, but I don't feel the need to have it in my collection. It's definitely worth some plays even if you're a hardcore gamer, and the rules can be gone over in about fifteen minutes. This makes Ticket to Ride a great choice for new or reluctant gamers, since it's really easy to have a fun time with it.
Update: I've since re-acquired this game, I will personally never play it, but it's a good one for the non-gamers, so back it goes.

textfield_comment_value:
5/9/17 - A great game! I think in 20 years this game will be what Monopoly is/was - the "classic" game that everyone has and everyone likes. 

I just wish there was some mechanic to help fix the "stale board" near the end of the game - when the face-up cards are not needed by any particular player, so they never get taken and thus never get refreshed. The players who are looking for a specific color just draw random cards hoping to hit what they are looking for, which takes away some of the fun for me (it's annoying to lose just because you couldn't find that last orange card you were trying to get for 6 turns in a row).

2/16/22 - I've downgraded to a 7. They have improved on this original version in the later games and going back to this really makes those issues stand out. For example, Rails & Sails has both kinds of cards to choose from, so if the train color you want isn't there, a ship that you need probably is, or vice versa. I just can't emphasize enough how much I hate the "stale deck" aspect and it seems to happen way more often in this version than most of the others. So if someone wants to play TTR, I would always suggest one of the other ones instead of this. But I would play this if someone really wanted to.

textfield_comment_value:
Finally played the much talked about and highly rated TtR, bringing it home for a weekend with the family. Was surprised how enjoyable it was (having read the rules before, it appeared a bit too simple and "flat" for me.)  Turns out it has alot of appeal, and a very good set of critical choices per turn.

I must confess, there's just something deeply entertaining about laying out your lines of train cars. In my opinion the Destination Tickets really help define the game, as I prefer games with some hidden element to them, and the surprise win from filling out your DT's while also building high-scoring routes turns TtR from a thought exercise into a true pleasure of a game.  

Another very important point for me is that the game flows along very smoothly, with very little downtime between turns, as the "analysis paralysis" seems to stay at a low rate with only mild peaks every so often.

Finally, it appears this weekend was yet another definite confirmation that this game works fabulously as an introduction to the bigger world of board games for non-heavy-gamers.  My brother was frothing at the mouth to play it again and again all weekend, and even my mom was eager to play another game right after the first.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Like it or not, Ticket to Ride is just a little more complex version of the extremely simplistic Transamerica: you still have to connect cities with your railways, even though now you need to play with a more subtle strategy in order to get points for completing routes and avoid point losses for missing tickets.

Anyhow, I find Ticket to Ride is the perfect gateway game for non-gamers, since it’s easy to learn, plays smoothly and in the end it even feels like playing a bigger or harder game as it constantly requires the players to make relevant decisions and overcome new obstacles: its mix of simplicity and complexity is enough for me to make it one of the best games to play with anyone, no matter how much «gamers» they are. [i](September 2011)[/i]

[b]Update I[/b] - In light of the very comment above, in July 2013 I found it proper to raise my rating from 6.5 to 8, which feels better fitting.

[b]Update II[/b] - So many years after my original comment, Ticket to Ride is still both a favorite of the several groups I play with and one of the best games to choose when non-gaming players drop by: hence during my Fall 2015 rating revise I raised my rating from 8 to 9. I still can’t see it reaching 10 though.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Ticket to Ride offers quite a bit of bang for your buck, where I measure bucks in terms of time required to explain the game, ability to play without referring to the rules, and to play comfortably without too much familiarity with the game, or with gaming in general; and bang in terms of giving you different things to think about (timing, long routes vs. completing lots of tickets...) and different possible approaches. First time, Carl made a spider, which I thought was an intriguing borrowing of strategy from Havannah, which he's never played... 

Lighter than I'd imagined, but a very simple set of rules, which I appreciate. In theory, as people get more experienced and learn the cards, the game could turn overly defensive for something so light, although I haven't actually experienced this, and it seems to be addressed by the 1910 expansion. 

I had to drop my rating a bit due to the endgame problem. (That is, "luck into" a win by drawing the right tickets near the end, when you've nothing else to do.) I also have a problem with some details like the Duluth-to-Houston route being so useless. But (unlike Carcassonne) I'm still playing it, and it seems to have legs. Better with three than with two.

textfield_comment_value:
I really don't know why this is ranked at a 7.5. I would say that is low. 

We have several games and we always end up bringing this out every few weeks. 

Here is our lowdown:

1. Fun for everyone. We will play this with our kids and adults of any age. 

2. Easy to learn. Just find the color ticket you want and off you go. 

3. Great transition over to modern gaming. As you see there is a whole new generation of games coming out. For someone new to board gaming, this could be a challenge. This game kind of takes you away from the Hasbro stuff and into the new world. 

4. Decent Strategy. You need to find a way to maximize points. Will you complete your routes? Will you go for longer trains? You need to think a lot to find the way to victory. 

5. There are 2 flaws I see with the game that prevent me from scoring 10. The first one is that the cards are small. We bought the 1910 expansion to get larger cards. The second flaw is that the 2 player mode is boring. With 3 - 5 players, you can intercept routes and make it hard for your opponent to win. In 2 player mode, you pretty much just build your route and don't need to worry about anyone. 

Overall a wonderful game. We take it out all the time.

textfield_comment_value:
[i][u]Disclaimer:[/u][/i] This is a [color=#000099][b]standalone game[/b][/color]. Its rating is based on [color=#000099][b]desire to play[/b][/color].

The perfect gateway game. I have very few bad things to say about [b]Ticket to Ride[/b]. The one issue I would have with the base game is the limited number of tickets, which both allows for easy blocking if you commit to learning them all, and also makes the outcome of the game very dependant on the ones you draw at the start. But apart from that, it plays well at all player counts, doesn’t trigger analysis paralysis, is easy to teach and hard to optimize. Luck plays a factor but I rarely lose versus my family which means there is some skill expression as well. It’s a different story versus my friends, where the game gets meaner with a lot more blocking going on : that’s the sign of a great design to me.

In the end though, while I will never refuse a game of [b]Ticket to Ride[/b] if it comes up, I generally prefer to play more complex games. I'm also pretty sure that I would find more enjoyment playing on the European map, just because I have no emotional attachment to cities like "Duluth" or "Helena" that I never heard about in my life.

textfield_comment_value:
I have come to really appreciate the game for the addictive joy that it is. It is a great gateway because it's simple, beautiful, and has a very positive first play experience. But please stop saying this is "just" a gateway game. Yes, it is an amazing game to introduce people to the hobby, but it is more than a simple game when experienced players sit down to play. Deep? Maybe not, but fully engaging to a player choosing to track every detail.  

I do think in every way that it is a landmark for the hobby and that was clear from the very beginning. My first set of cards are nearly ragged. And sharing it with my students was a great joy. 

The tension can be palpable with some groups, and yet I can play loose with others. I love that range of experience based on my fellow players. Those who say it is all luck fail to regard how you can play your way out of any hand by knowing the game and watching the other players. The best players win much, much more often---but not so much that a new player can't pull a game out. The group I play this with make me proud to play games because anyone can win and people can still play with a personal style. That's a very high compliment in my book!

Letter Grade: A.  A modern classic family game.  [05-08-09]

So elegant and simple it's ridiculous no one had thought of it before Mr Moon.  Looks like it's fairly nonconfrontational with two, but at the very end of the game, when tension is heating up as players are attempting to make their final connections, the map gets crowded and can make for some last-second nail-biting offensive and defensive moves.  I could see experienced players having a bit of an edge in that familiarity with destination tickets could clue them in on what other players are attempting to connect. Holds up with any group or number of players, though the end-game tension increases markedly with more players, as the opportunities to make those last few destination tickets dwindles rapidly. 

9-2-08: From 8.5 to 7.  I'm still attracted to this game, partially because of the scale of the map, partially because of the components, but I can't see myself suggesting it with anyone but new or less-experienced board gamers.

12-24-07: Reflecting on Tatsu's comments, would be willing to try this again with really experienced TTR players to see how it changes things.  Perhaps too easy to pigeon-hole this game?

It is ticket to ride, a game which for some reason is one of the "mainstream" games in Norway.

textfield_comment_value:
This review covers several variants of Ticket to Ride, including 2004, Europe, USA 1910, Europa 1912, Asia, and India.  It is a gateway game. I use Ticket to Ride as a baseline to measure other games that could be easily taught to a wide range of new players. The map and components are very friendly and welcoming, and helps to bring players into the game. The rules can be taught quickly and there aren’t too many special cases to worry about. Players have satisfactory moves on most of their turns and as they lay track, they feel a sense of accomplishment. Because scores are mostly unknown until the end of the game, players don’t feel like they are too far behind to have a hope of winning. Interaction between the players is mostly gentle. Normally being blocked on your route is the result of another player trying to complete their routes more often than just them wasting a move to hamper you. 

For the other versions of the game, they add new rules (ferries, tunnels, etc.) that are simple enough to not over complicate the game for the target audience, and the different maps are diverting.

The IOS app is well done and play is very quick.

It seems that you can’t go wrong with a Ticket to Ride board game. I’ve yet to find a person who doesn’t enjoy them and I've played them with nephews, nieces, in-laws, parents, friends, gamers, and non-gamers. Plus I still get a kick out of them after many plays. For all of the games in the series the rules are easy to learn, turns go quickly, and the basic strategy is apparent but the competition for links and the risk of getting blocked keeps things interesting for everyone.

textfield_comment_value:
Ticket To Ride is a good, yet childishly simple game. Its simplicity isn't a bad thing though; it is easy to teach. Play can be very fast if players don't overthink each turn as only one action is possible.

On our first playthrough a friend came up with a strategy that seems to circumvent the games intent: If a player does nothing but go for all the 6-car routes he'll make more points on average then someone completing tickets. If everyone were to play in this fashion then the tickets deck seems superfluous after the initial draw. After several games of testing, this method is a gamble: If other players haven't been snatching up the 6-car routes to complete their tickets, this strategy can pay off big. If the others have done so, then a player using this plan will have nothing more than a bunch of disconnected routes. If 2 people try the same method they will wind up with the lowest overall scores.

Oh, and everyone is right about the cards being way too small. The train deck as a whole is almost impossible to shuffle conventionally. Can't wait to get my hands on the Anniversary Edition!
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Gin Rummy on steroids. I actually like the train theme and the twist on gin rummy is awesome. You have to make matched sets of cards, but you have to make the right set and you've got goals you're trying to complete...oh yeah and you can probably figure out what everyone else's goal is too and you can either work towards your own goals or screw someone elses' up.

The best way I can describe the emotional impact of this game is: mounting tension.

Each turn you have to decide between:
* Do I try and get more cards to make more/better sets or claim what I can now?
* Do I claim that route before someone else does?
* If I claim that route, will it give me away?
* Do I claim a route that I don't need because I believe that someone else does and it will screw them up?
* Do I risk going for more destination cards or not?

No matter what you choose, you're worried about what you're opponents are thinking and what they're going to do next and if you chose the right thing or not. Great fun! The only down side I can think of is the setup and cleanup take a smidgen longer than a normal game.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Ticket to Ride does a great many things well. It has simple rules: easy to learn, and easy to teach. Games are quick, taking about an hour to play. The game lets individuals build train networks (and building things is inherently fun), but it forces players to interact as players will place their trains in each other's way. There are genuine strategic choices, but there is enough luck to keep the game winnable for a wide range of players: the most strategic players will tend to do better but will not dominate every game.

All this makes it a game that appeals to a wide audience. I love playing this game, but I absolutely adore how I can play this game with anyone.

However, the original USA game is not my favorite. The cards are small. A few cities (like St. Louis and Charleston) do not have destination cards. Players dealt long east-west routes hold a distinct advantage over players trying to connect multiple short north-south routes. I strongly advise you to buy the USA 1910 expansion. It gives you larger cards, adds more destinations, and adds the most completed routes bonus.

textfield_comment_value:
15 plays: 

A light game, accessible to kids, able to be cutthroat and intense with skilled players. 

What's great is that it's quick to learn and to set up, and the turn to turn play is satisfying and flows nicely. There is little analysis paralysis. 

My complaint is that the whole thing doesn't quite add up to more than the sum of its parts. The many colors have no ultimate meaning; they are interchangeable abstractions that have no consistent role on the board. The destinations are arbitrary. Scoring seems almost like an afterthought. 

Also, it just runs a bit long. Playing with a group of 5 can take 90 minutes, and it's kind of a long 90 minutes because there are sooooo many turns, most of which are just drawing more train cards.

I think part of why the gameplay feels so flat to me is that you don't change over the course of the game; your capabilities are the same at the end as the beginning.

But it's one of the most widely flexible games for various ages and skill levels, and visually appealing.

==2018/06/15==
A little concerned that I've found a close-to-optimal strategy.  I don't think I've fully solved it, but it'll be a while before I play with people who min-max the game like I do.


==2018/12/22==
Possibly the best family game that I know of.  It's very, very engaging, but simple enough that my mom and brother can play it.

The game moves pretty fast around the table with interested, dialed-in players, even at 5p.  The puzzle is also really good; I like that you have to adapt your route planning based on what cards show up in the market, and top-decking is a brilliant way to fix the moments when the market has nothing that you want.

Scoring is also tense.  You already have quite a lot of points from the bulk of the game, but the secret routes and longest route bonus can still upturn the order of the game.

Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Modern classic game of train routes in which players try to play out combos of cards of a single colour from their hands to build railway tracks between cities in the US (these tracks are several spaces long in one colour: one card must be played per space in the track). These cards are drafted from a line of cards open to all players, or drawn blindly from the stock. 

While the game is neither the most tactically rich of its kind (the only slightly more modern Thurn & Taxis allows more elaborate planning) nor the most elegant (the earlier Trans America is even more concise), Ticket to Ride is more urgent (and addictive) than either of these two games due to two clever strokes: each railway track can only be taken by one player (first come, first served) and players are given several goals at the beginning of the game, from which they can choose which they want to commit to. 

It's no wonder that Ticket to Ride has become such a success: its concept is crystal clear, it balances luck and skill wondrously and its presentation is exquisite.

textfield_comment_value:
A great game, very popular and enjoyed by a large range of people. Noticeably men and women like it equally, that's a big plus to play it in a mixed group of friends.

The gameplay is actually about risk management, how much are you willing to wait to stock enough same colour cards, increasing the risk that somebody else will block your path, and if there is a reasonable alternative path. The risk to reward ratio is extremely well balanced, possibly a valuable reason for its success. It's also the reason you can play it with kids, as there is always a simple way to play, as well as with highly competitive players: A bit like in poker, I think you can get some advanced guessing whenever somebody else is trying to collect the same colour, and then you can guess which path he's trying to get built.

The illustration, graphics and thematic inclusion is very well done, you can completely dive in the new train world.

I like that the production is not too skimpy and provide additional train pieces just in case you loose some.

textfield_comment_value:
Ticket to Ride shows how a few simple rules can be combined to make an exceptionally rich and deep playing experience.  When played quickly, this feels like a wild race of the wits - it is fast, exciting, suspenseful and challenging.

EUROPE:  This is such a big map that there is no competition for routes.  Competition is further lessened by the station rules.  I guess this is good for folks who like a less aggressive style of play, but other maps support both play styles whereas this one does not allow for the aggressive, "dynamite joe" style of play.

ASIA: One side is a large map meant to be played with teams.  I haven't played the team game, but it's otherwise a big open map.  The smaller modern Asia map is a good map with some tough routes.

UK:  The board is a bit hard to read.  The technologies divide your attention away from the card-play and route-building.  It's a different feeling experience.

PENN:  The stock buying is somewhat neat, but not great at 2-players.

(Includes 1910, Europe, Asia, UK expansions)

A big hit in my circle. Fantastic thematically, great fun to play. turns are short so its always quick to come back to you so not too much down time. trying to create intricate routes to connect cities, and gambling on taking more mission cards as the game goes on are all fun mechanics. Super fun any everyone is always happy to play when we have a group, even the non gamers. Fun saving up cards of different colors and then building that one big track. Not too much strategic depth to be found, but for a game to relax and play with friends its a sure success.  

Cons:
-Can sometimes feel really bad if you get blocked from completing a big route and then you know you have lost the game but have to continue to play anyway. Has the potential for some really nasty plays made just to screw people over which leaves a sour taste. And losing a 21 point mission isnt just missing out on 21 points, its also getting -21 so its a 42 point swing which will single handedly decide a game. Many games decided in one turn/move.

textfield_comment_value:
Beautiful components. New players enjoy the setup and play of this game a lot, making it a great intro game. After playing a number of times, I find it lacks much "Take That". There also appears to be a winning strategy of connecting long paths between cities. 
I would perhaps recommend TTR Europe even to new Euro collectors above TTR as it appears to have a bit more strategy, though I haven't played it myself. 
UPDATE: 7.0 I cant help it but I must raise the rating. New players are all over this game, and it is pretty satisfying to tell them - "look just make sure you get your tickets done", then on the second turn slap down a three route like its the end of the world and see the pressure  hit the roof on thier faces. I mean it doesn't even have to be near their routes! The moment they feel that tension they are hooked, and its pretty fun to be the one to get the kettle boiling. 3-4 players only please.

Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: Ticket to Ride is a push your luck game that takes rummy inspired set collection and combines it with a race-like tension to lay tracks and connect cities. "Pushing your luck" is the most engaging mechanism board games can offer, and everything here rewards players based on how successful they are. This is a easy to play game that keeps the focus between the players. The board is a catalyst to figure out what an opponent is trying to accomplish. Interactions remain directly between players with everything else become an indirect hint at what may happen. The feel of Ticket to Ride is nearly perfect. The only slight mar on an otherwise fantastic experience is that it is tedious to consistently refill the card market after each draw. Each player's decision is immediate and meaningful. It doesn't hurt that the pieces and board are wonderfully bright, colorful, and fun to place. Ticket to Ride does what it sets out to do very well, and rightfully earns its place as the poster-child for hobby gaming.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Great game with the family. Never introduced it to someone that didn't like it, although it can wear out its welcome after a while.

Quite tense when you are trying to get those last few routes done. Usually in my group there is high demand for routes and the person that gets all the long routes that line up ends up winning.

Doesn't get played much recently except for 2 player, since my sister burned out on it. She too much enjoyed blocking people and she got a bit twisted when she was on the receiving end a couple times.

So far enjoy USA, Europe, and Nordic Countries. Looking to pick up a couple more maps but haven't yet, as the cost seems a bit high. Mostly play 2 player anymore.

1910 expansion is mandatory. Death to the baby cards!

Great at all player counts.

UPDATE: Finally played with the boys (10 & 9). No problem whatsoever. Until this the only one we played was the junior or kids version. The accidental blocking almost brought on some tears, but it was also late and they were tired.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
2-5(4)

It's a great, great, great gateway. Probably the best I've encountered. (A good metric is what my "I've got two kids, I'm playing a game, I don't want to work" sister thinks of it, and she would play this one again). It's incidentally, and non-confrontationally, interactive (until you get more advanced, in which case you start to tactically block).

There are some "more dominant" strategies: I can see accumulating lots of cards, getting long routes and then, after your network is established, cycling tickets being really hard to beat. But it's Ticket to Ride! If you're playing that way against people you're trying to introduce to gaming, you're not doing "gateway" very well. Not saying that you should try to lose, but don't break the game.

People (correctly) say that it's basically set collection. Sure, but it's easy to get, attractive, and all of it feels thematic enough (and not tacked on) to really engage players. Not something I'll always play, but a go-to gateway, easily.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Ticket to Ride is everything I wanted it to be.  At the time of reviewing this, I have been playing modern board games for about 7 years yet I only just played Ticket to Ride.  

Ticket to Ride is special because it has something for everyone.  It is simple enough for anyone to play (kids, elderly, drunk people, etc.) yet has some complexity that it will engage your local min-maxers at least enough to convince them to play.  The game also has some meat to it, it lasts long enough to plan far into the future and feels like a filling game, despite its very simple and short set of rules.

Too many games are either too short and simple or too long and complex, few are simple and long, and I think that is just what Ticket to Ride achieves.  And while for some they may hate it for that very reason, that is the exact reason I love it.

Ultimately the biggest downfall of ticket to ride is its boring theme and status as a mass-market product which turns off many players from wanting to play it.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: While treated like a gateway game, I rather firmly argue it most absolutely is not; it's a casual game. It has very little strategic depth to it, and what little there is consists almost entirely of counterplay elements. While none of it is quite aggressive enough to constitute "Take that" mechanics, and there's an adaptive element to tactical planning, there's very little to intuiting what your best move is unless you're actively trying to undercut people rather than merely read/react to them. This means the game is essentially painfully straightforward and dull unless you're playing aggressively, putting in a place where it's either boringly simple and unpleasantly hostile, or peaceful but so utterly boring it's agonizing. There are much better "Take that" games that are simple enough to teach casuals, while there's an endless number of gateway games that are easy enough for new players to learn while being far more interesting to experienced gamers if that's all you're looking for.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Based on the North American map, Ticket to Ride is the original. (Many board gamers erroneously call this game's map, the US map, but the game board does include Canadian cities, so they are only partially correct.) Although TtR does lack some of the more interesting features of its newer cousins (a la 'Ticket to Ride Europe' and 'Ticket to Ride Märklin Edition'), it is still a fun game to play. Be forewarned that luck is required (because of the card and ticket draws). However, the game plays quickly since there are only three possible actions to choose from during any particular turn. Some tactical play is possible (by blocking your opponent's key routes), but only if you have protected your own destination routes. All-in-all it's a good game to try out and play, if you've never done so before. If you are thinking of permanently adding one of the TtR games to your collection, one of the newer games in this series might be a better choice. {7}

Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Not much interaction or fun, and highly derivative of other pick-up-and-deliver games. It dragged with five players, and no one tried blocking anyone else; it just seemed to be a case of "collect cards and play them."  (Same thing in my second play, with four players -- no one really focuses on anything except his own goals. The small amount of blocking that occurred was unwitting.) A step above Transamerica, but that's not saying much. Don't understand why people rate it so highly. The only real strategy here is to try to make long chains; shorter ones are almost worthless. I'm sure this game -- and its offspring -- made Mr. Moon a millionaire, but I just don't see it.

Whoever wrote this nailed it: "The merit of good light games is they have some sort of dynamic fun factor. I don't consider draw-draw-draw-draw-draw-draw- play route -draw-draw-draw- play route (screw someone blindly)- draw-draw-draw-draw-draw-draw-draw-draw- play route - to be a very fun gaming experience."
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: This game is not really about connecting cities with your trains: is about getting the most possible cards of the same color in your hand so that you can score more points when you play them. The fact that you are putting trains on a map in the process is kinda secondary. It's really all about that: trying to zero in on your objectives by building lot of short paths while neglecting the longest ones will simply make you lose, because the longest paths are way much more lucrative, no matter if you need to pass through them to fulfill your objectives or not. In a sense, this must be one of the few games i played that got a quite flavorful and very precise objective...that you have to put aside because, if you want to play to win, you have to focus on the deeper math of the game instead. And why i would want to do that while playing a "light" game that is completely about pushing your luck with cards? To say that this game is a letdown still kinda makes it better than it is.

Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: Light set collection game with a railway theme. Players are attempting to collect sets of different coloured cards, which in turn allow them to place their carriages onto the tracks linking different American cities. The longer the track, the more points are awarded (one point for a one length track, 15 for a six length). Players can also earn point by having the longest continual track at the end of the game and from completing tickets, whereby two cities on the map have to be linked together and the further they are apart, the more points are available. This can have a downside as incomplete tickets lead to a deduction of points. The game flows well, it is a simple concept and players new to board gaming seem to grasp it. There is a bit of luck involved when acquiring the tickets as some of them are very similar to one another thereby making them a lot easier to complete, but overall this is a tried and tested gateway game, useful for introducing people to the hobby.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
My wife would probably give this game an 11/10. Honestly, this game is like a drug to her. She's addicted beyond belief, going as far as to get the digital copy on her phone and play it whenever she can. For me? It's more of an 8, so hence the official score of 9. It's not that I don't like the game, but rather I'm burned out on it. It hits the table at EVERY game night. We're constantly asked to bring it when we visit family, and I've yet to find someone who turns their nose up at it when it hits the table. 

In a way, that's a good thing. It truly is the perfect stepping stone into a realm beyond most of the Milton Bradley and Hasbro fare everyone knows. It's simple enough that it's quick to pick up, but offers enough in the way of management and strategy to keep things fresh. Something about it seems to stick in the minds of most who come across it which is just praise to the designers of it. 

Definitely a game that should be in everyone's collection.

Update 08/14/07: Reduced rating from 7.5 to 7.2. Because of the insufficient number of destination cards, particularly the long ones, after several plays the long destination cards become well known and it can become easy to guess an opponent's routes, thus blocking tends to distract from the game. TtR 1910 fixes this issue for the most part, although it introduces its own luck factor. A player may end up with several overlapping routes, giving him a big advantage.

Other than that:
Ttr is highly entertaining, fun, and full of tension. Offers the player lots of play choices, tactical and strategical moves, and risk taking. Great balance for such a multi-player game. Some compare this to TransAmerica, but this is a much better and deeper game with a much higher replayability factor than the one dimentional TransAmerica.
