Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: I have two main problems with TtR.  First of all, it's too easy to score points strictly by taking only the longest routes, despite the tickets you start with.  Just snag as many six-spot routes as you can and you'll almost always win - you can usually pick up a ticket or two along the way with only a couple of other routes.  Second, I despise the way that on the last turn or two of the game, someone who's losing can shoot the moon - they just grab three tickets, hoping that they'll either already have one completed, or be able to easily complete one by slapping down a quick one or two train route.  It's risky enough that someone in the lead should not try it, but not so risky that it doesn't work a good portion of the time.  It just irritates me.  A good gateway game, though, and we've used it successfully to bring a few gamers into the "Euro-Gamer" fold, and then we can move them along to something I like better.  (And it's all about me, of course...)
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: A real fun game, Ticket to Ride is simple to play and games are pretty quick. The route system (and rather, how it's randomly handed out at the start of the game) can put players at a disadvantage, but the real point winners in this game are the six-length train routes. Games between experienced players can be pretty fun, because you start to get a good feel for what routes the other guy has, so it's easier to be a bit more cutthroat.The 'resource' system of drawing cards is very well done; Even if you draw resources you can't use, the ability to 'cash' them in for five and 6 length train routes (and big points) makes sure that the player isn't frustrated by his bad 'luck.' In fact, building a giant hand of cards is a pretty good strategy, allowing you to pick and choose the routes you take.The game is extremely easy to teach to new players, and while a great game with only two players, is still a lot of fun with 3 to 5. A game you can't go wrong with!
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Beginner level of serious boardgaming (I suppose basic Catan is, too, but I like Catan more). Some tatctics and strategy are involved, but it is light — not the nail-biting agony of making a decision in other games, and as I play more games of higher strategy and complexity I find myself less and less inclined to play Ticket to Ride. That being said, if you want a fun, lightly complex game to pass some time with friends over a pint, then this would be an excellent choice.

Oh, funny story… there is no hand limit in Ticket to Ride. This simple fact popped in my head one evening as I began a game of the electronic version. I spent the first many rounds of the game only collecting cards. Eventually there were no cards for the computer opponents to take! I then spent my rounds filling in the longest route segments on the board, which gave the opponents a choice of my same-color cards. Rinse, repeat. I did not win the game, but it was funny in the process.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
I have both the app version as well as the physical board game. The app is great - it doesn't feel old and you can get a game out in 20mins. It only suffers from my fat fingers but I suspect the issue is mitigated when you play it on a larger screen. 

As for the board game, it is a winner - a welcoming entry level game for new gamers, limited actions, the tension between getting another card vs whether your opponents are going to take your route, the push your luck element in the ticket draws, and the timing in which the final round is being played. If this map is boring there are a ton of other map packs which tweaks the game a bit. It doesn't get a lot of play but with new gamers I will play this game without hesitation.

Apr 2024: first game with 5yo son. He won! We focused on reading location names, basic math, route connection, focusing on objectives (how to connect, what coloured cards required). Son got longest road through his own decisions!
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: Personally, I think this game is broken, but still fun to play in spite of its flaws.  I generally love Days of Wonder games, but this one falls short because I have found that the best way to win is by going for the biggest railroad pieces and not worrying about the tickets.  That's right, build all the six piece lengths for an amazing 15 points each turn instead of taking a ton of turns to connect cities by building in the 1 or 2 slot spots.  Those smallers slots burn up turns without producing much bang at the end when completing the ticket.  Some might argue with me, but I have won the last few games easily by employing this strategy.  And even when players think they can beat me when they know that I am using this strategy by collecting and filling out tickets still come up short in the end and lose.  Like I said, this game is broken.  Maybe the other expansions fixed this issue - I don't know because I have never played them.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
VERY EASY TO PLAY. I'm talking about 1 page of rules here. Yet the possibilities of the route goals are amazing. I want to play this again and with more people. One thing I'm afraid of is that the cards are so small, which makes finding cases impossible. Also, due to the large amount of cards in one stack, it is hard to shuffle.

It's got a lot of good things going for it. It's really easy to learn, the artwork is bright and interesting, America is easily recognizable and it fits up to 5. It's just that I realized that 90% of the game is just drawing 2 cards. It just takes so long to get little done in this game. It's not particularly good with 2 players as well. I mean you will only get to use 1 of the 2-sided routes, but there just isn't too much blockage there. If they could have made the game end quicker, I'd be happy for it, but as it is... it's too long to be doing something not interesting such as drawing 2 cards each turn.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: I was playing with 5 relatives who were all somewhat new to the game.  The game got complicated quickly but everyone had fun because the rules are easy to follow and intuitive and its a nice visual/tactile method of play.  I was feeling pretty good about things then one of the other players ran out of trains which means we all only had 1 turn left.  This was OK because I only needed to connect Las Vegas to Los Angeles, an easy 2 train connection.  I had the trains ready to go and when I made this connection I would get an extra 20 points and probably in the game.  My sister in law who was in maybe 2nd to last place, put a train right on the route I needed, blocking me.  She knew exactly what she was doing and just wanted to see the world burn.  Now I was 20 points to the negative for not finishing that route.  The ecstatic highs and lows this game can present is a testament to it being a good game.  It does make you feel things.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: Though I modestly enjoy the game, my high rating is really due to the enthusiasm it has generated amongst my non-gaming peers.  Ticket to ride has been very well received by almost everyone to whom I have introduced it.  The best is watching everyone tap their fingers nervously, biting their nails, trying to hide their disappointment when they are getting blocked.  There are a number of ways to win the game, and you can play a very defensive, interactive game if you like.  I probably have the same level of enjoyment from this as from carcassonne, though the emotions ticket to ride generates in others have been more fun to watch.  EDIT:  never mind about being able to play a 'defensive' game.  Even if you have a very good guess as to what your opponents are doing, hurting someone else hurts yourself nearly as much, as time is ticking for you to complete your task!  Still a good, tense game, though strategically a little limited.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Wow!  My opinion of this game has changed a lot from when I entered the hobby.  First, it remains a great gateway game.  However, after being in the hobby for almost 10 years, I find this game much better than most.  First off, there are simple rules so the "how do you play" gets out of the way almost immediately.  However, experienced players will almost always win because knowing the tickets is a huge advantage.  Second off, it's not a multi-player solitaire game like so many modern euros.  To play well, player need to manage risk (choke points, single routes) and pay attention to what other players are collecting.  There's never downtime.  Turns on quick and even when it's someone else's turn, you need to be paying attention.  Third off, with all that said, it's still a great game to play with company over a beer.  

I do like the expansions better (Switzerland, Nordic Countries, and India) but I'd never say no to base game.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
After 3 plays, not as excited as I thought I'd be. Midway through the first play the long route strategy became obvious to all of us. Perhaps there's a way around that, but right now it seems near-unstoppable. 

12/25: one play of this today convinced me to lower from 8 to 7. It's not the long-route strategy that annoys me. It's the solo feeling it gives. There is very little interaction, because screwing with others ALWAYS will hurt YOU more in the end, so you don't bother screwing with others. The decisions (lay down track now? or draw and lay down more track another turn?) *feel* important but now I see it matters very very little, and therefore is a pseudo-decision, which kinda pisses me off. Maaaaaybe I was spoiled this evening by playing a few games of Ingenious first, whose strategies began unfurling their petals like a flower. TtR felt incredibly flat in comparison.

3-1-08: Lowering to 6. I don't hate it, I guess.

One of my first gateway games, its good for beginners...and not much else. It quickly gets boring.

Plays: 4+?

On a replay of one of the later ones, I'm finding this still to be enjoyable despite its age and repetitive formula. I guess it's an evergreen for a reason. Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
This game is hovering between a 5 or 6 for me. It’s the least favorite of the big 3 game way euros with Carcassonne and Settlers taking the top 2 spots. 

The reason for the rating is because the game seems rather boring just collecting cards for much of the time. Yes, I know it’s a simple game but other simple gateway euros had more interesting and varied decisions that this one. 

That said, I do like the tightness and meanness that this game can bring when routes are taken ahead of someone else. Because of this, the game is very fun for me. I still need to be in a certain mood to play it however. 

The most redeeming quality is that it is really perfect for families with young kids who can deal with not winning.

2/17/24: Realizing that this game is so much more fun when played with the right kind of players. That is, you want to play with players who are all trying to win. It's pretty interactive and cutthroat.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: The word 'angst' is often used as a compliment for a game. We all want hard and crucial decisions to make each turn in our games. But for me Ticket to Ride has too much angst! You get to do so little per turn compared to what you'd like/need to do that it often feels very frustrating. The worst thing is playing a connection that is less than 4 trains. It is such an obviously inefficient move that it is literally painful to do. I don%u2019t think a game should punish a player so harshly for doing what is the central mechanic of the game %u2013 connecting two cities with trains. ****UPDATE**** After several more plays I've raised my rating a point. The funny thing is I still agree with all my criticisms above, but there's no denying that the game has a certain spark. And it's such a great introductory game for newbies that it deserves some credit for that. Overall I think it's a fine game that I don't mind playing.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
This holds a spot in my heart as the first game that I played over and over. There was absolutely nothing like it at the time, and it had all the fun and interactive board game elements that kept me wanting more and getting more interested in board gaming as a hobby. Having a hand of cards and quests to complete, a big shared board space, your own miniatures to play... yet it was about trains, and I couldn't care less. I'll still play it now, but I prefer TTR Europe over the USA board present in this version.

I find this best at 3 or 5. Five is long, but there's a sense of urgency at both 3 or 5 that you don't get at 2 or 4. This is because TTR balances gameplay with the 'double route' mechanic when you play with more than 4 players, reducing the effect that route blocking has and improving the ability for players to realistically complete tickets.

In reality, I won't turn down a play at any count between 2-5.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: 3rd boardgame I have bought since started my hobby, but it was the first Euro game I have played. I bought this for to play at party with my relatives, who do like games, like Pit, Pictionary, etc but aren't familar with Euro games. It was ver easy to teach and it went over well everything but the session was a little long with 5 new players, like 2 hours, but since it was our first time, that was understandable. While I thought it was a little light, as compared with my experience with playing Last Night On Earth, which I loved, I did like it as I could see the strategies in the game. My cousins especially really liked the game and wanted to play in the future so it was a successful hit with my relatives, and I got them excited to play other games I think, just like a good gateway game should do. If I had a choice, I'd play Downfall of Pompeii as the first gateway game, as it's quicker, and has a better theme.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
UPDATE II - My now 8- and 10-year-olds both prefer TTR: Europe, and so do my wife and I.

UPDATE - I have upped my rating since I found out how much fun this game is to play with my 7- and 5-year-olds.  They crave the game, and with a minor handicap (they can play on both routes at any time, while I have to play by the standard three-player rules) it is challenging for all of us.

This is a good game, and it fits my taste, but I'm not sure it's perfect or a SDJ lock.  One issue I have is that the game tension, while strong, isn't strategic.  Luck plays a large factor in the game, as card arrival is the main component of TWO game factors - resources and goals.  I will play this often, but likely not for more than 6 months or so.  As for SDJ... well, Alhambra won, so I guess this one could win and still be a better choice than 2003.  Days of Wonder bits and boxes are still the top of the heap in production.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
An evolution of Union Pacific that makes things fun, instead of tedious bean-counting. It's not well balanced for gamers, but it's amazing how well this works for casual players, they get super invested. I don't know if it started here, but I see the popular eurogame trend of players too busy with their own tasks to even look at each other, unless they accidentally block each other. But it's just tight enough that I don't mind it too much.

It's still dumb how nobody wants to take wilds from the card market, and the way routes are rewarded (smugly showing off your progress at the end, the only time anyone bothers to pay attention to each other), but the game has to reward difficult paths with extra points or else nobody will bother doing them. Alright, I guess it's intended for children (the artwork and all) and it succeeds at that. I still think TtR Switzerland is a better design, but this is acceptable.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Draft and play sets of cards to build train routes and connect tickets for most points.

Plays: More than 100.
Type: VP race = a game where you race to collect victory points (fastest/most).
Complexity: Family game = a game that is easy to teach and play.
# of players: 3-5.
Playing time: 10 mins per player.
Player interaction: Competition for routes.
Randomness: Medium - card draw (lower with USA 1910 expansion).

Replayability: Very high, often everyone wants to play again immediately.
Fun: The fun lies in the decision making of hand and board management.
Memorability: Low, it's a VP engine that doesn't create stories.

Thematic integration: Weak.
Components: Nice.
Expansions: Definitely get USA 1910.

Who will like this: Everyone. No kidding. This is a must-have in every game collection. I have yet to encounter anyone who doesn't enjoy TTR. Even non-gamers often buy their own copy after playing.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Keeping mainly because it's such a good gateway, although I find it a bit repetitive for my taste. 

15/01/'17: Decided that in spite of its new-player friendliness it isn't worth keeping for us because I don't ever feel like playing it. The main reason for this is the limited play - draw cards to collect a set and play a set to lay trains, with a bit of route building on the side. I always felt like there was something off in the tickets mechanic since they seem really important but actually aren't, and short tickets are not worth it - like they don't score enough or something. Playing with the expansion helps because you can use just the big tickets, but essentially the game is uninteresting because of the limited decision making round to round. Hand-management and tempo (do I build before you) are really the only ongoing gameplay and while it was fun for a bunch of plays I think I am played out.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
One of THE go to game when you are introducing people to tabletop board gaming. It is easy to learn, hard to master. It has a decent amount of luck involved, while not seeming unfair. If you failed a ticket, it's most often because you were off with your timing. You feel responsible.

+ Setup is easy. Grab your bag of trains, set out the board, shuffle the two decks and go.
+ Easy to learn, just 3 options. Everyone can count to six and recognize colors (or you are probably too young for games anyway)
+ The plastic trains are great game pieces and well made

- The tiny cards are just stupid. Days of Wonder, just put the big cards in the big box instead of shoving them into an expansion. It is really annoying and it makes me not want to buy that expansion.   

One third of my 'Introduction Trinity', games I'd play to introduce players to tabletop gaming, with Pandemic and Settlers of Catan
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
It's better than some of the terrible classic board games, but this gateway game was still too close to them for me to enjoy.

You look at the board and identify some cities to connect.  Even this is going to be heavily influenced by the city connection bonus cards you are randomly dealt.  And then you draw cards that have the color you need.  And you draw and draw and draw.  

Decision making time is over.  Now you sit and take turns drawing cards to see who's plan is going to work out best.

It's not quite that terrible.  You can sometimes spot an opening and slightly modify your plan or take advantage of an opening to block an opponent, but it really isn't that interesting.

Ultimately, the meaningful decision making offered by the game doesn't come close to the amount of time you spend trying to collect matching sets of colored cards in your hand.  It's just a fancy Rummy variant.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Good - usually willing to play.

My favorite thing about this game is how small the rule book is.  It's funny how the rule book is smaller than the amount of advertisements that came with it.  

It's also thrilling when someone grabs their little train pieces and slowly moves them to the track you have been planning on using.  Then when you are just about to curse them out for placing it on your spot, they place their trains on an adjacent track.

However the game could get boring.  Most turns are just picking up cards and usually they are not the ones you need.  So you just keep picking up cards on every turn until you can finally do something.

For some reason the base game comes with these extra small cards.  These are a big inconvenience and you have to buy an expansion just to get the bigger set.

The game is a little expensive and I don't recommend to buy the game at full price.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: This is a great game for new and old gamers.  I'm not sure how to rate this game because it should be 10 based on it's gateway potential alone.  In my situation it helped turn family and friends into a weekly gaming group.  That's worth a lot!  I recommend this before Settlers of Catan as a gateway game for new folks.  I think it plays faster and has more eye candy than Settlers.  On a personal level I find the US map kind of boring and the small cards in this game are really a pain to hold and shuffle.  For those reasons I rate Marklin higher and prefer it of the two.  I have not played Europe yet.  I have to admit that I was put off by the Choo-Choo look of the box and bought it as a sacrifice to family gaming with the kids. Turns out I love the gameplay and I'm hooked!   The game has tension and decision making delivered with a minimum of rules.  I'm always happy to play it.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
had to downgrade the rating to 4 cause I just dont like to play this even though its a decent intro game. 9.5.23

Has this ever happend to you? you're with your favorite gaming group and you dont now what to play. "That one's too complex, the newbie doesnt know that one, that one doesn't play good with four..." Then someone brings up TTR. "It's for beginners and a good introduction to german wargames." 12.8.29

It's like a Budweiser it meets all the general requirements of a generic game without offending anyone and has no character, no edge, to speak of. 

It’s not really a bad game at all it’s biggest fault is probably that it takes too long for what it is. It’s not very deep and there’s not a whole of excitement to it either. This might be fine for ½ hour but 2 hours is way too long. We can get it down to just under 2 hrs but not by much. If it was shorter I would up the mark.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: I got this for my wife and for my non-gamer friends and family members. For playing with them it's absolutely a ten. There is a lot more game hidden in this than is advertised by those who would reductively call it a rummy game. While there is that element, it also includes strategic and tactical play, as well as press-your-luck and bluffing mechanics. I feel this a much better gateway game than Settlers or Carcassonne. It is perfect for anyone who wants to play a game with depth and engage others resistant to "designer games." Gamers like myself who usually like a litte more mystery about what is under the hood will find themselves reaching for other games. However, the engine of this game is without a doubt so elegant that you won't find yourself leaving a game of Ticket to Ride unsatisfied. Note: the USA 1910 expansion is probably a required purchase along with the base game.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Le boss du chemin de fer sera moi !
Carte USA :
Jeu de connexion où l'on va devoir collecter des cartes de wagons de couleurs pour ensuite les jouer pour poser nos wagons sur une liaison de même couleur sur la carte.
Le but est de remplir les contrats de connexion que l'on possède au risque qu'ils nous apportent des points négatifs en fin de partie si ils ne sont pas réalisés.
La partie s'arrête un tour après qu'il reste moins de 4 wagons à un joueur.

+ Mécanique simple
+ Interaction sur la carte où l'on peut gêner ses adversaires.

- Un peu long ? Réduire le nombre de wagons
- Pas de limite de carte en main ce qui encourage à ne pas montrer tout de suite les connexions que l'on va avoir besoin ( mettre une limite de 10-12 cartes )

Classique parmi les classiques de jeu de connexions. Le 1er de la gamme est toujours au top.
A conseiller pour jouer en famille/ non-initiés.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
A fairly decent family game, in which you are collecting sets of cards in order to claim train routes. 

Works well as a a gateway game, very simple rules and quick to get into.  I like any game that has missions of some description and as such I like the ticket mechanic here, you are always trying to connect two towns in order to score maximum points.

Only thing I don't like is the fact that seem cities can be blocked entirely from all directions quite quickly, this can mean that when drawing a new ticket all the options are impossible, meaning that by simply trying to draw new tickets you are guaranteed to lose points at the end of the game.  This is unlikely but can certainly happen, I believe that some of the expansions address this issue.

Overall, a nice game to introduce to non gamers and children, not much to keep a seasoned gamer interested though unfortunately.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Prior to 2020: 3 plays

While many people encounter this as one of their first Ticket to Ride experiences, this came as one of the later maps to which I was exposed.  Overall, there's not much more that I can say than I imagine many will say here - it's an interesting, tense game of rummy with spatial play.  The USA board incentivizes fighting for some of the longer routes, and being cut off can be more devastating in this version than many of the others that followed and allow players to redirect more efficiently / quickly.  Even still, it's an excellent map and one that's quite fun to play regardless.  There's a reason TtR will be around long after we're gone: it's that good of a game and manages to create an experience where players can plan, interfere with each other's plans, and make interesting, approachable choices.  A great game and certainly a modern classic.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
This is one of those games--like monopoly--that I played before I got into boardgames and made me think that I hated boardgames. Nonetheless, it's possible that I just got a crappy introduction to it. 

Update: Got this in a humble bundle some time ago. Finally got around to trying it 2-player with my wife. It is ok, I guess. Base game map seems too roomy for two. After more careful reflection, I think I don't like this game because of the mean-hearted nature of the interaction. Of course, you don't have to play mean, but in that case it's just boring all around.

Update 2: Played a 3-player game with wife and sister. The app is really irritating when used for pass-and-play, since there is hidden information. I think it works a lot better with 3 than with 2, but it's still either nasty or boring. I did have more fun, though, being on the other end of nasty this time.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
cant say enough about this game. fantastic game. can play with non gamers and gamers and have just as much fun and challenging. if i was to say anything negative about this game, it would be that an experienced player will blow a new player out of the water.

Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: Very light.  Good intro to gaming, but the USA board is way too big for two players.  Have played with 4 and the group had fun, which is a big part of gaming, but I'm always left with a slightly underwhelmed feeling at the end.  My boyfriend enjoys this more than me because he sometimes likes the light games that require a little strategy/thinking but not too much, but I really feel (even as a relatively new gamer) that there aren't enough decisions to make here.  And as with many Euros, there's not enough interaction.  Yes, there's blocking, but sometimes you're guessing as to whether you're even accomplishing a successful "block" and that's still a pretty limited form of interaction.  I think this would be a good game for families with kids.  I've also played the Swiss map with 2 players -- definitely an improvement for 2, but most of my complaints still remain.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Fun, but can get a bit long at times.  The planning and strategy is fun, and occasionally you are forced to improvise when you get beat to the punch on claiming certain tracks.  It's also interesting how you can play friendly or agressive depending on the group you are gaming with.  My biggest beef is with the claiming of route cards.  For some reason it seems to take players way too long to decide, and if you don't wait they may change their decisions based on what other players do while they're choosing.

I have found that the game has a very wide appeal and many non-gamers will jump right on board for this game.  The rules are simple and the strategies aren't too deep so almost anyone can play.  I should mention that I find the 1910 expansion to be almost a requirement.  Still this game, even without the expansion, is fun and can be played by almost anyone.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
One of the most quintessential games that can appeal to the widest audience, from families to more serious settings. 

The rules are simple, it is easy to teach, inoffensive in theme and playstyle, straightforward and fast-paced. While each player acts independently, there is a modest amount of interaction from blocking and changing trajectories. 

A lot of it is about taking risks and deciding when and how many tickets to draw. If you go too far or are unlucky, you will have bitter consequences. If you play it safe and make do with the starting tickets, you will end up with a mediocre score and will be at a disadvantage compared to those who took a little more risk. 

I don't think Ticket to Ride will ever be my favorite game, especially because the game has a certain softness to it and it feels a bit lifeless, but as an accessible family game it's rock solid.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Overall, TtR is a good entry-level game, particularly for younger kids (taking turns, logic of routes). Yes, it can be played on a high level, and there are various threads on BGG about that, but if you want a high-level play experience, you should look to deeper games. TtR feels very repetitive, particularly among the large number of modern games.

• Europe - 2 to 5 players. I like it better than the base game because the map doesn't sprawl out as much. There's more strategic blocking here. 
• Nordic Countries - tight, vicious map for 2 to 3 players. The snowy theme on the board and train cards makes this the most eye-catching edition. 
• India & Switzerland - Switzerland is consistently named the best 2/3-player map (although I'm partial to Nordic Countries). India is for 2 to 4 and I've played it the least.
• Pink cars - some players like to play with pink.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Played two player a couple of times.  Interesting concept, but I had two problems with it.  The main problem is the insane amount of card shuffling necessary to start the game and/or reshuffle the discard deck.  Since you play cards in sets of the same color, if you don't shuffle 10+ times, you will see these same sets show up again.  I can't count how many times we had the same card color show up four draws in a row.

The other problem was that there wasn't really any competition to get the tracks; I laid the ones to get my destination, and the other guy laid the ones to get his--there didn't seem to be much overlap in what we wanted.  This could easily be a problem with the two player game that doesn't show up with more players.

I could see this being a good game with more players and therefore more competition, but as a two player game, it's just ok.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: Based on my limited experience, TtR is a solid, fun game. I think it is likely the best gateway game I have ever played. If I needed a game for a group of gamers and non-gamers, or ALL non-gamers, TtR would be at the top of my list. The set-collecting mechanic works well as a means of developing your routes, and the route cards add a timing element to the strategy of that enriches what would otherwise be a more tedious affair. Best of all, my 5 year old can play it and has fun, even if she doesn't always make the best decisions. Unfortunately, Ticket to Ride takes just a *little* it too long for what it offers: which is a light, social gaming experience. I wouldn't want to play it with more than four players again, and I don't think I would ever request it, but I wouldn't mind playing it as light entertainment while having a discussion about something else.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
fun game that is short, fast, and slightly addictive. easy to teach and learn. worth some of the hype for its accessibility and playability. not the greatest game ever, but potentially will be regarded as a classic. i've enjoyed every game of this i've played so far. hopefully this game’s success will spur bigger game companies to produce better games.

update:nah, the game is still pretty fun. the only thing is i have so many other games i haven't played as much as this one, so i've been trying to get those on the table and ticket to ride kinda fell on the back burner. busted it out and it was pretty fun. i wish the route ticket distribution wasn't so random, but whatever.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: My husband and I really love this game. We played it many times (sometimes 3 per day) during my pregnancy. Now that our baby requires us to be more at home we find us playing this board game so happy as if we were dining out. Now we play it with more people and there is a sense of a party, mostly because of the game. I think that its best side is that you do not know if you may win or not until the end. I do not like Risk precisely for the opposite: Risk is designed for smashing others in a predatory way, so at the middle of the game a guy feels "dictatorial" and the others are just looking at their watches... I love Ticket to Ride exactly for being the opposite. TR has a little share of luck but no dice, so it is more strategical; almost all the players feel, throughout the game, that they can win. It is very easy to play, addictive and fun, really fun.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
TTR is a good game with a light ruleset. It's not light enough to play with the in-laws, but not far off. The components are lovely and the overall theme is engaging, simply because the geography is interesting. 

The actualy gameplay is as tense as a wrestler's bicep. I constantly find myself praying that someone else won't build a line where I want to build. Not only that, the smaller maps (like India) enhance this tension and the game can feel like a knifefight in a phonebooth. This can lead to players complaining that they were 'screwed by the cards' (myself included), but I think that with careful planning the game usually offers enough room for strategic planning, keeping it from feeling random.

We don't get this to the table that often because it's a bit too take-that-y for our tastes, but it's proven to be a good game to have for certain groups.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Ticket to Ride (w/ USA 1910 expansion) is fairly light, medium length, and easy to learn.  Overall, I think the game could be a touch shorter, to balance the degree of luck with drawing tickets.  I don't really mind the tickets and their push-your-luck effect since I like a degree of managing probabilities in a game, and I do enjoy games with spatial contention.

I liked the USA 1910 expansion, and was told that it helps fix some design problems TtR (Ticket to Ride).

OVERALL: I've enjoyed playing TtR and will play again, though preferably w/ the USA 1910 expansion.

RECOMMENDATIONS: TtR fans interested in a shorter game with a bit more push-your-luck should certainly check out Ra (http://www.boardgamegeek.com/boardgame/12).  For fans of the spatial aspects of TtR, Through the Desert (http://www.boardgamegeek.com/game/503) is an absolute gem of a game.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
[b]Includes 1910 expansion[/b]

My first "gateway game" purchase... in Dec. 2008.

This is the ultimate gateway game. I have not yet found a person that did not like this game at least a little bit. I still enjoy it, even though I'm increasingly attracted to more difficult games.

This is a definite keeper and a great means for introducing new people to board games.

Update: Just played this game with three other "gamers" familiar with TTR, and it was still very enjoyable... possibly even more so with the increased competition. Yes, this is a "gateway" game, but that's not to suggest that the game's limit is for introducing newbies. TTR can stand on its own. I've dropped the rating to a "7", but only because I've played this many more times prior to my official effort to log games. I'm not actively suggesting it, but I certainly won't turn down a game.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Perhaps the perfect gateway game, I have yet to play this with a non-gamer who wasn't at least partially intrigued.  A brilliant design that deserves every award and accolade it has received.  Most games don't give you much of a clue as to any overarching strategy - your first couple plays might solely consist of fumbling through, trying different things out and seeing what works.  TTR obviates this through the destination tickets - right off the bat you have a few long term goals, and you can see each turn how much progress you have made toward them.  This makes things a lot easier for new players, and also leads to a nice balance between strategy and tactics.  

And yet... the more games I add to my collection, the less enthusiasm I have to get this one to the table.  A victim of its own success perhaps?  

approximate number of plays (pre-2017):  15
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Far more enjoyable than TransAmerica. Almost an 8 in 4 4-player game. Rating went up with four-players but the game wasn't played too cutthroat. Longer track segments are the way to go. Penalty for failure to complete routes is too severe (one idea is to segregate the long routes from the shorter so in the initial deal each player will receive only one long route as in TtR Europe).

I haven't won a single game; I think I'm so worried about making my connections that I don't have the patience to go for long segments and non-branching routes. I think the longest route bonus is too large, often decides the game by a difference of only 1 or 2 trains, maybe go 10-5-3-1.

Up 1 more point with new Destination Card rule: Any of the initial cards will pay FULL points MINUS 2 points per unfinished route spaces. Any Additional cards are under the original rules.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
My sister-in-law got this game for Christmas, so at 5pm on Xmas day we sat down to play. Playing one game after another, we finished at 1am! The next day, the calls started early afternoon:
'You busy this evening? Maybe you want to play Ticket to Ride again?'
'Actually, I was gonna call you and suggest it, but I didn't want to sound like I've been thinking about it all morning.'
We played again on the 26th, 27th and New Year's Day. It's truly addictive.
There's a great cocktail of emotions when you play Ticket to Ride: Hope that you'll build your lines and complete tickets, fear that others will block your routes, relief at securing key connections and frustration when your plans are thwarted. Playing at a fast tempo with practically no downtime, you rollercoaster between these positive and negative emotions for 45 minutes and finish wanting more!
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
This is one of my personal favorite games. It is one of those games that has more then one component going on, is easy to learn, and requires some strategy to win. 

Pros:
-uses simple, yet thought out strategy
-each turn you need to make 1 of 3 decisions
-great for tweens and teens
-nice board game design

Cons:
-nothing I can think of

Education:
-learning about mapping
-familiarizing us cities

Tip:
As you play add some questions through the board like say something interesting about the city you are in. You can also ask what direction children are going. So many ways to bring the education into this already great game. 

Overall: 
We like this game. It requires us to think, strategize, and only make one move per turn. 

There are a few ways to tally up the points which means you never know who will be the ultimate winner at the end of the game.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
A nearly flawless game. Extremely simple rules, with a great mix of luck and strategy. Can get tense since players have the opportunity to be mean by blocking each other, but they won't be able to do so constantly, preventing the game from becoming unpleasant.

Only reason I'm not giving this a 10 is that the cards it comes with are extremely small and unpleasant to use. Also, the designer/publisher have long since determined that the ticket cards needed to be rebalanced. Thankfully, both of these issues have been resolved in the 1910 expansion, which comes with full-sized train cards and full-size, rebalanced ticket cards. So as long as you get the 1910 expansion as well, it solves all my issues - but it still loses a point for making me buy that, and fit it awkwardly into the insert, instead of just including it by default in newer versions.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
A great gateway game. Compared to Marklin, it is lighter, quicker, and less strategic. There is also more potential for getting hosed and having some intense competition without passengers to bring in extra points. We like this version because it is much easier to finish in a short amount of time, compared to Marklin.

Over time, this game has become a drag for me. I still like playing, but I don't like that every game feels like a game of "who will get the luckiest ticket draws?" The game seems to lack player control, offering little payback for good decisions. This has taken the rating down to 7.5 for me.

The other reason this game has worn on me is that it gets requested so often. As a result, all of the other good games in my collection receive less love. I do like this version more than TTR: Europe, but I'd rather play Marklin anytime.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Played 20+ Played with 3,4 and 5. This is a great game for the family. We played 3 times over the Easter break. Like with Elfenland, sensitive family members can get upset when a route they have been planning for an hour is maliciously messed up by another player in the last 5 minutes of play. The story about traveling around America in 7 days makes little sense. A more believable tale could have been thought up by Alan Moon which would have made the rules seem less abstract. Was enjoyed by a group who normally only play Trivial Pursuit. *UPDATE* This game is getting a lot of play and my respect is increasing. It stands up to competetive play online which is a good test. Oct 04

*UPDATE* I have now played this game face to face over 30 times mostly with none gaming relatives. It is the perfect Christmas game. I'll promote it to a 9. Dec 11
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: Okay, okay, I'm a convert, but the rating is still a 5.  This one is a keeper, will probably be played for years to come, and has an accessibility that makes it a good non-gamer-introduction-to-european-style-gaming game.  However. . . it is somewhat fiddly with the bits.  The train metaphor is a thinly camouflaged Gin Rummy variant.  The game can have good player interaction, with both offensive and defensive plays to block other people, but most of the time each player is playing soley for themselves and pays less attention to other player's actions.  This can cause player interaction to become significantly low.  And for a more family-oriented light game, TTR inspires very little table talk.  On the whole, the choices and decisions you make in TTR don't seem as important as they feel in other games.  Still, it's more than a diversion.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Just mindless fun.  You could say there's not enough interaction and you'd be right.  You could say there's too much randomness and you'd be right.  It's just fun. (2007-12-06)

Updated:  OK, this has gotten much less fun over the course of maybe six or eight total plays.  The flaws are really starting to show for me.  The fun part of the game is placing the little trains, but most of the game is just drawing cards and then waiting while others draw cards.  Because of the randomness of the cards and the ability of others to block your plans, the best strategy seems to be holding back from playing cards for the first half of the game.  That means that good players spend the first 20 minutes of the game just drawing cards and claiming a few key routes.  Why would I do a boring thing for 20 minutes when the whole game only takes 45 minutes?
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
To many players this is the ultimate gateway game. And I have to agree, this has many qualities to lure in people how don’t know that they are gamers. For me personally though, the game has faded a bit from its initial shine as it feels like rinse and repeat. However, there is a tension in when you are going to reveal your plan and when to build the most crucial parts of your network. If you start too early, it becomes easy to block you when people know where you want to build. If you are too late the good connections are taken. There is also a tension when you draw tickets, but other than that the game consists mostly of drawing cards. Personally I prefer the other games in the Ticket to Ride line more, but nothing beats the simplicity of the first game.

The game works well with any number of players.

textfield_comment_value: Very fun, light-ish game with a "getting in each other's way" layer of strategy which I love.  4 player is best.  2 player is fun. My wife & I play this often.  3 player gets tricky because the double routes do not become available unless you have 4 or more players.  The 1910 expansion to this is essential since I believe it fixes a flaw in the original game.  There were too few routes in the original and its easy for people to determine a route that you have if they see you laying track toward a specific city. (since it may be a critical segment that you need to get before everyone else)  For example, I believe there are only one Portland and one Nashville route in the original game and they are on the same card.  Generally, I don't like expansions to games in that the "muddy the waters" of the original.  This is the exception.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: This game would be a lot more fun if you had to start in one city and arrive at another before the end of the game, circumventing various obstacles and other players along the way. Instead, despite the theme of a turn of the century "Around the World in 80 Days" re-enactment you can, in fact, grab any route on the board you have the cards for at any time. Scoring has been rigged to encourage you to try to connect up everything by the end of the game but it plays like an afterthought... actually, at best, it plays like you're *flying* from one city to the next, then taking short train trips. In the end the game is fun enough, but with a little extra attention to theme this game could have been so much better. Addendum: And what's the deal with all the card accumulating at the start? The more I play the less this appeals to me...
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Despite all the hype, all the awards, and all the love, Ticket to Ride is merely an ok set collection game.  In it, you are attempting to collect cards of the same colour to complete train routes across North America.  Whomever completes the routes totalling the greatest number of points wins.

No doubt the components are top notch.  The overly large board is a nice map, and the cards are very good quality. The best component is the plastic train pieces that are put out on the board to complete routes.

When I discovered Airlines Europe, by the same designer, it killed any lingering desire I had for continued ownership of Ticket to Ride.  That game is also about making routes, but with much more interesting decisions.  I can not, in good conscience, ever recommend Ticket to Ride knowing the far superior Airlines Europe exists.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Having recently gotten into gaming with 'heavier' games such as Scythe and Gaia Project, I decided to buy Ticket to Ride as a lighter shorter 'entry' level board game to play more casually with my friends and partner. 

The game itself has a simple premise, construct routes between various cities to score points. Longer routes gain you more points (with some level of inbuilt multiplier - doubling length of route more than doubles points gained). You also have destination tickets, for which if you can construct a route between two specific cities, you gain a heap of points. The player with the most points at the end of the game wins.

A very simple enjoyable game, approximate duration was around 30-40 minutes, but it went very quickly. 

Definitely a game to get you into board gaming, alongside games like Carcassone and Pandemic
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Ticket to Ride is a pretty decent game. At the heart of it, it is a resource acquisition/placement game. But it does have a fun amount of strategy that goes along with it.

Depending on the amount of players, early turns can be dull. I rarely see any better strategy than stocking up on random cards for a number of turns. This can change a little when playing with 4 players - if other players start playing on Central European routes. Denial is a HUGE strategy in this game! 

The game is really designed for 4 players. 2 players gives too much space so there is little competition for routes. 3 players can, likewise, be a quiet game. 4 players is where this game is experienced best.

This is also a great game to introduce to non-gamers, as it is very easy to pick up and learn.

All in all, a very solid game that I do like to play!
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
After multiple playings this game is fun and I would play again but probably wouldn't be the one to suggest playing it. I fear that the same simplicity that makes this a great starter game in the eyes of many will equal shallowness and boredom upon too many repeat playings. However, it hasn't happened yet.  (Update: now it has)

Most annoying of all is the choice of components.  I hate the fact that many euros use non-standard card sizes.  The small cards in many euros are annoying, but often forgivable because the cards are usually only a small part of the game.  However, ANY game which focuses primarily on card play including BLUE MOON and Ticket to Ride should most definitely stick with standard sized cards.  They are what we are all used to holding comfortably and can be protected from wear by sleeves if heavily played.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: I've heard many places that this is a good beginner game, and I agree--the gameplay is simple, so much so that at first you wouldn't expect this game to offer so much. Turns go quickly, which generally makes this game much more bearable, time-wise, than Settlers or the like can be. I've discovered the most enjoyable way to play this (without squabbling with other players) is to play with three or four players; at five, this game really turns into fighting over a few key paths. I've also discovered that an effective strategy is to save cards and build up for your biggest paths first, rather than placing down the small tracks first, as it becomes harder and harder to claim certain routes later in the game. Still, I've not managed to ever win this one, which perhaps makes me a little more hesitant to play this than previously.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: Review – I would place Ticket to Ride as the second best game (Catan being the first) for bridging the gap between your typical board games and more intensive strategy games. What Ticket to Ride lacks in variety it makes up for in simplicity, solid mechanics, and scale-ability (great for all applicable player counts). The game is very consistent (though occasionally bad ticket draws can lead to a less satisfying experience) and the difference between great and mediocre players shouldn’t be so great as to absolutely destroy the experience, because of that it really is an incredible gateway game. I do think the longevity is a little low, but it’s certainly one you can go back to from time to time. The expansions do a good job of mixing things up and adding new mechanics while still maintaining the strengths of the original.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
The perfect gateway game, while still being fun for experienced gamers -- TTR changed how I thought about board games, and taught me a lot about what I liked. I'd been sticking with games like Carcassonne despite fading interest, and playing TTR for the first time was like a breath of fresh air. I've gone on to really enjoy a lot of other lighter Euros, particularly Zooloretto.

TTR was also the first game my entire group was always in the mood to play -- a rarity! I prefer both Marklin and Europe to vanilla TTR, but I'll still happily play it anytime.

The only problem I've run into is that (at least the way my group plays it) whoever lucks into the best long route tends to win. I'm told that if you play TTR more aggressively -- blocking at every opportunity -- an entirely different game emerges; I'd like to try that.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Swiss map & 1910 expansion add a fair amount to the base game. Good, clean, simple all-American* fun for everyone I've played with, too - a hit with all that touch it. - seriously, even people who aren't really into games - and a lot of my enjoyment comes from introducing it to others.

Bumping the score up another 0.5 for that (already bumped from 8 to 9) - it's the only game on this list that friends and family are clamouring to play again and again.
EDIT: Apart from Pandemic, but even so, TTR is the one which family and friends are picking up - to date, Dad, sister, school mate, wife's friends have all picked it up.

"Whoooo - whoooo! I'm laying track baby"

EDIT - score was 9.5 in Jun 2012. Taking it down a bit to 8.5 as it's not really hitting the table in the last 3 years or so...


* except for the Swiss map
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
I am not so sure why this game is rated that high.  

Production: great quality, sturdy box, nice illustrations, not very realistic geography wise. 

Rules and mechanic: not much, the whole game is about three or four rules. you exchange cards for trains and claim so-called "routes." Very, very abstract. And while abstract, no big strategy either. Emotion wise it is overally a negative game.  All you need to do is to cut the other person, that'd be the basically the major strategy.   

I am not a uber-board gamer; however, this game is far too dry for any kind of taste.  We have tried with 2-3 people, no difference. As boring as it gets.  I am looking other RR games, such as Railways of the World, or Steam, even a crayon game, Empire Builder "awesome map!."  Maybe my mistake was to think this as a RR game. 

Avoid.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Do not heed the snobby geeks who turn up their noses at the proletariat of board games, Ticket To Ride. Listen not as they tell you how this game, or that, accomplishes everything TTR accomplishes but with more "depth". Ticket to Ride is one of the best games every designed. Simple and fast with real decisions. I can't think of a single game that can be as cutthroat and gamey (when played with real gamers) and as light hearted and fun with grandma at Thanksgiving.

Ticket to Ride is a modern masterpiece worthy of every accolade it has garnered. Also, I suck at it. My wife beats me every game without fail. I haven't won a game in years. But damn, if I don't try. Get TTR and ignore the snobs. They're probably playing some dull Euro or that ugly Terraforming Mars. I'll play trains with grandma, thank you very much.

textfield_comment_value:
Can't believe they're STILL putting out the original with such tiny cards... hard to shuffle, hard to hold a big hand. Get a clue, Days of Wonder... it's a MUCH too obvious expansion sales scam. Makes you look slimy in an industry that cares.

Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
This game saved me! It helped me break my friends out of the never ending Monopoly/Risk/Stratego nights that were the bane of my existence! (Although covid quarantine kind of helped too..)

The rules are fairly simple, but there is still enough strategic depth and risk/reward decisions to add tension and keep everyone interested. 

But my favorite part about this game is the built in time limit! No more endless grinds to finish a Monopoly or Risk “campaign”! Our first game might have run a little long, but the second game was much faster, and we whipped through the third game in under 45 minutes! With 5 players! And everyone wanted to play again!

No matter if I still want to play this game in three months or three years, it will always hold a special place in my heart for helping me escape Monopoly and Risk.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: The 1st time I played this game... I was open in my expectations yet still anticipating that it would be very good as it has a lot of supporters on BGG. I didn't get an immediate vibe of... "yes this is very good". Upon playing a 2nd and 3rd time it has improved as I see the strategies and tactics that can be explored in the game. The game is dead simple to play  and learn yet there are enough points where you need to make interesting and meaningful decisions that the game is not just a spiraling luck fest. While I don't think the game is extremely deep... there are several interesting strategies that can be pursued and I think we will get our money's worth out of this one as replayability looks good at this point. I have basically played only 2 player so far but 3-5 player looks to be even more interesting.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Other games take the TtR formula and take it leaps and bounds above what this game offers, but this still stands as one of the great gateway games to turn newcomers on to resource management/territory control games.

This game will have every turn ending with players lamenting over their singular action and worrying about another player ruining their well-laid plans. From that comes my only real gripe with the game - it can be easy to dogpile a player in the lead, especially if you're a veteran who knows the route values and destinations more so than a newbie. With that in mind, it's generally best to minimize table talk and pseudo-quarterbacking between players.

If you're a veteran to the genre, you probably already have this game or can skip it, but it's a solid game to have in the collection otherwise.

Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
I enjoy Ticket to Ride. I'm not madly in love with it. In fact I like the app more than the actual board game, mostly because dealing with the trains and the scoring is so fiddly. The original is also not my favorite. It favors those who snag the 6-train routes, and those are the routes that you can only get via luck. Too many tickets overlap, which encourages ticket-fishing, which I absolutely hate because, once again, it favors the lucky. And it has too many choke points (the optimal number would be zero). 

Furthermore, I still hate that they sell this and Europe without the expansion decks. The expansion decks are far too expensive for what you are getting. Considering both this and Europe now routinely sell for under $40, they need to be done with the expansions and sell Deluxe versions of both.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
The third game in the gateway "Holy Trimurti" (Settlers of Catan and Carcassonne being the other two), it's simple and funny and well worth a play or three when you have some non-gamer friend and you want to give him his first dose of eurogaming drugs...
Ticket to Ride can be just a very simple set collection game, but the competition on the map contributes to a tense gameplay: mr. Moon delivered a home run (as far as you want a gateway game) and did deserve his Spiel des Jahres!

Update august 30th, 2012: after I bought the iOS version of TTR Europe, physical versions of the game had seen play again, and I must admit the light fare is quite enjoyable... vote raised to 6.5!

Update january 1st, 2015: the game sees the table quite often, thanks to the in-laws and the iOS version. Vote raised to 7.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: Very mindless game. The game boils down to planning your train routes based on your cards to optimize your train sets placed on the board, and then spending 95% of the game mindlessly drawing train cards until you can fill your route. This is one of those games where you can see what your first and last turn will be and everything in between but the game moves too slowly to compensate for that lack of tactics. At a 5-player count, the game was a slog, but at least it was more likely for the game state to change on the board between turns from opponents placing trains. At a 2-player count, the game moved faster but there's little to virtually no interaction between players because the board is so big, and the special 2-player variant rule that turns double railways into single doesn't help much.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
I do not own a physical copy of Targi and I played it 10 times on BGA. It is a medium-lenght game best played with 3-4 players (about 15 min per player). The game is based on connecting points (cities) on the board (map) by efficiently managing cards in your hand. VPs are scored bbased on the lenght of the connection made and on the personal objectives.
The rules are simple, and the gameplay flows well. The theme fits very well the game.
The balance of the game is good, though there is in my opinion a strong luck element related to both objective selection and availability of cards needed to build connections. The variability is good and the replayability is high.
Personally, I will not probably buy a physical copy since I do not particular enjoy the mechanism nor the luck element in this game.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
An easy "euro" type game (no dice).  Players draw cards and attempt to build railroad segments between cities to score points.  These segments are built using color coded cards.  As an example, one needs to hand in a set of colored cards equal to the lenght and color of the track one wants to build/own between two cities.

Tickets are double edged, in that they provide you with extra points if you complete the route listed on the ticket, else you loose the points.

Once a player's markers (45) are reduced to less than 3, the last turn of the game is played, then the points are counted and compared to find a winner.

Player interaction is limited, although one may block another player by building a segment of track which he/she thinks the other player needs in order to complete a ticket.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
This generation's Monopoly.

1. Card / Set Collecting - Check.
2. Competition on getting limited resources (Properties vs. Routes) - Check.
3. Luck Element (Dice Rolling vs. Card Drawing) - Check
4. Limited supply of components to utilize the resources (Train miniatures vs. House / Hotels) - Check
5. Low Learning Curve - Check

Ticket to Ride has a better process to end the game vs. Monopoly. The worst case with Monopoly is when nobody owns a Monopoly AND the players refuse to negotiate. The game goes on an on with people paying anywhere from $ 2 to $ 50 rentals. The only way to mitigate this is via time limit, but if time limit was not set this lends to a long and boring game. Ticket to Ride addresses this by having either the board filled out or the depletion of train supply by any player.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: This game is mildly entertaining when the group plays quickly, and mind-numbingly boring when the group plays slowly. If my entire turn is to draw two cards, and then I have to wait five minutes until my next turn, I'd simply rather not play the game. But if people play quickly enough to keep me engaged, I'm willing to play a game now and then. Additionally, I think Carcassonne, Settlers of Catan, Fjords, Through the Desert, and a host of other games are more interesting 'gateway games' than Ticket to Ride, further reducing its appeal to me. On iOS, the game is more enjoyable (less upkeep, faster pace), but still doesn't offer much in the way of interesting decisions or a particularly enjoyable experience -- perhaps a 5 or 6 rather than a 4. (2011-11; updated 2012-03; minor text edits after)
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
So, I recently played the original TtR (with Mystery Train edition). We ended up playing a variant that I made up - I separated the 17-22 pt long routes and distributed them as one of the route cards at the beginning of the game. All discards are still returned to the bottom of the deck, so if someone ends up picking a long route later (even with the Engineer card), that's fine. I only wanted to even out the beginning routes so that everyone has an opportunity to keep a long route ticket. 

With 5 players, TtR becomes too chaotic and less strategic - it's more of a frantic scramble to complete the first route. Perhaps TtR makes a better 4 player game. Played Ticket to Ride several times before I started tracking my games played (approx. 2-5 times). Tracked on family game list (grooven).
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: My first play of Ticket to Ride did not go well. I was stuck with only cross-country tickets and quickly blocked off from easily achieving any of them. I think Alvin & Dexter might give this game some much needed confrontation, though my main problem with the game might be the way Tickets are handled. There seems to be a problem with a runaway leader as the person who gets the best tracks seems to be able to draw tickets that instantly score. It doesn't help that those who are blocked from completing their goals must also suffer negative points as extra punishment. It's not a bad game, it just supports the worst kind of luck. Though I must say, even after getting thoroughly walloped, I had some fun with Ticket to Ride. It's fast and colorful with a sort of charm I can't really define.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Update: After 30 games (base and expansions), I have grown to appreciate this game more than I once did. It works with almost any group. I have never played with anyone who really hated it. I do think they should have included some variants to account for the fact that the base game does not play very well with 2 or 3. Instead you have to buy an expansion to fix this problem. An alternate board side or built in mechanism using routes would have been nice.

Regardless the mechanic is good, and the theme is nice. This is one of the few games that everyone I have introduced it to has requested again --- all non gamers and including my wife who is notoriously picky. If you only play 2 or 3 you could skip this entirely and go straight for Nordic Countries, it is designed for a small group.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
If you didn't already know, Ticket to Ride is a light network building game that serves great as a gateway for new gamers. I wish hoarding train cards until you laid them all down in one fell swoop wasn't as good as it was (aside for the occasional choke point route), but that seems to be the most solid strategy in this game.

EDIT: I lowered my rating because I realized stockpiling cards before splurging in large bursts or just making aimless long connections can be quite good, and that really abstracts the theme of the game, focusing more on the set collection rummy part rather than the route building that implements up the train theme.

EDIT 2: The game simultaneously is so stressful with the routes while also the routes not mattering enough given the theme. Lowered down to a 5.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
:thumbsup: I get why this is popular as a gateway game. It's easy to explain but doesn't feel like a brainless waste of time once you're playing.
:thumbsup: A fun blend of different 'push your luck'-factors. [i]"Am I going to draw cards or play cards? And if I'm drawing cards, will I draw from the deck or from the open cards? What are my opponents up to?"[/i]

Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Bought to be the easiest game I own, and it delivered on that goal. Accomplishes a fair amount with few rules. Where the "game" is is obvious, but you can't ask for much at this weight. I like that there is a push your luck mechanism that busts depending on other players' actions rather than the game itself (like in Quacks of Quedlinburg). Probably best with 4 or 5. I see why people call it dull, but this one is not about me, it is about being able to play with anyone. 

Compared to other light family games:
Easier to teach than Carcassonne.
Much less frustrating than Catan, and wraps up quicker.
Azul is a much better game, but it can eek a bit above comfortable weight for the least experienced folks out there. This might be too easy, but better than than someone feeling lost.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: Awesome game that is great for beginners just getting into more complex board games. This is a favorite at my house and I usually won't turn down a game when it's suggested. Works great as a two player game as well as with more plays (just note that the game can get really long if you have a lot of people playing). The train theme is very interesting and the little train figures are modelled well (and they give you a few extras in case you lose some!). I like how the cards are miniature so they don't take up as much room on the table (however, you still need a pretty big area to play this game properly). The only annoyance is that it's kind of annoying to be the person viewing the map from above (i.e. backwards, or to the south), as you're looking at everything upside-down.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
This year I've played some vanilla Ticket to Ride after being accustomed to TTR:E version. And the more I played this version the more I hated it. 

First reason - distribution of tickets. TTR:E and following editions have long tickets separated. 
Second reason and the main reason: this version does not promote drawing more tickets. Instead it awards card counting and doing long relations even if not a part of one's tickets. This turns a game which was for me more of a laid back fun with some risk taking into a calculating game of optimisation. :yuk:
In short: what takes one to be good at this game is what I like the least in TTR:E
Third reason: you call this geography... Heh. Well I live in Europe so I'm kinda more connected to European map. 

Currently I rate TTR:E a 7.0
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: Quite possibly the perfect game for our group.  Very simple, elegant rules means non-gamers can learn it very quickly and you don't have to spend a lot of time explaining special cases.  Strategically, you have to balance getting your own work done vs sacrificing yourself to hinder the leader.  In building your lines, you must combine deception with backup plans to prevent getting blocked, but on the other hand must construct efficiently.  Risk taking plays a role as well, as you can grab for points which are essential to victory but costs time and is catastrophic if you miss.  The board scales elegantly to fewer or more players with the double line option, and I noticed this game is gender neutral, as women seem just as interested as men and have little trouble winning.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Pros:
* Easy to teach and it's usually very popular with non-gamers
* Components are both nice to look at and color/symbol coded to facilitate gameplay.
* Every turn has a nice tense feeling where you hope that your opponents don't see what you're up to and mess things up for you.

Cons:
* Too many long tracks and an incentive to just build a long consecutive track (because of the longest track bonus) leads to people just drawing massive amounts of cards and not really interacting with each other.
* Extra destination tickets are rarely drawn because of the above problem
* Too few destination tickets
* The cards are too small

The USA 1910 expansion solves much of the problems I have with this game. If you are going to play Ticket to Ride: USA, get the 1910 expansion.

textfield_comment_value:
There can’t possibly be anything new to say about Ticket to Ride. It’s reputation, endless top sales and evergreen status are more than well deserved. I ignored it for a long time, thinking a game about making train routes couldn’t possibly be fun, thinking the drab board couldn’t be engaging and thinking that something so simple couldn’t be compelling.

And I was wrong on every level. It’s just about a perfect board game. It’s so simple a 3 day old baby could play it. It’s smart enough that you could play it until you were elderly and still enjoy it. It’s great for dumb people, it’s great for smart people. Really it’s great for just about anyone except the kind of people no one really wants to play games with. You know who they are, unless you don’t and it’s you.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Yes, I have never played TTR until this game. I had the app years ago (Iphone 4) and played a few dozen games there.

Flo and I had a really fun experience with this one. I had a feeling she would enjoy it and she did. I did beat her, 146-89. But I can tell she will get better with more plays. 

I went heavy into card drawing early (got up to 16 cards in my hand and had 5 open Destination tickets) while Flo went for shorter routes trying to connect her initial Destination draws. I was able to add track 5 turns in a row connecting 2 of my initial tickets.

I see us playing this one many more times in the future. I will pick up the USA 1910 expansion at some point as I really don't like the hobbit sized cards. I might also get a map expansion or 2 down the line.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
I always found this game a little bit boring. It might be because I didn't play it until after I had my fair share of other gateway games: Carcassonne, Catan, 7 Wonders, Small World, Dominion. By the time I reached it, I was looking for something a bit more.

Even today, I would probably just go to Irish Gauge or Paris Connection as a choo-choo gateway. Or go to Lanterns if I want a light set collection game.

Update: TTR is excellently paced and with light rules, makes for a fantastic family game. With a limitation on how many 6-length tracks, as well as optimal path from destination to destination, there's a bit of a push your luck aspect as you need to decide when to cash in your cards for points, or watch someone beat you to it and get left holding the bag.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
I bought it as a way of bringing my wife and me into "real" gaming.  Folks suggested it as a "gateway game" and those folks where right on the money.  Great game for us, including my 8 year-old daughter.  And defintely a hit with non-game playing friends.  So easy to learn and beautiful to look at as well.

Update (Feb.'09): No doubt this is the best gateway game.  We've had it for 3 or 4 years now and it never fails.  A favorite of my study hall and h.s. boardgaming club.  Got students who play a bunch online now too.
