Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: A unique playstyle, Ticket to Ride is pretty easy to understand and catch onto. I imagine even a fairly young audience could understand it without the "First Journey" edition. Reminds me of Catan in the sense of resources and building to connect certain places to others. A few mechanics were a bit weird to start, and I would have done things differently had I understood from the get-go. Not the first game I reach for, but one to keep for sure. I love that it goes up to five players, as our group has five people and often makes playing board games together difficult. I also find the "Alexa mode" intriguing, while we haven't tried it yet, I like the idea of having a narrator walk you through the set up. Worth checking out, if I can ever get my Alexa to work.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
2012 tax return splurge for Zack and Julia

This is THE gateway game that I can recommend to anyone curious about 21st century tabletop games.  It is a milestone in modern gaming history and is proof that good introductory strategy games can be both educational, well-designed, simple to teach, and still appeal to both Euro gamers as well as thematic gamers. It never feels like a dumbed down game, rather its simplicity in set-collecting and route-building is what makes the game quite tactical and replayable especially with so many available expansion maps.  The only reason we don't play this board game more often is because it has become available to us to play online locally via our iOS devices. This is a great gift for non-gamer friends and family too!
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
A game which is OK, but not great. I do like that it's a connection game where you're competing to make connections, and there's skill in choosing the tickets you need to achieve. However I don't like that invariably everybody else is taking the cards you need so you're frustrated from making the connections anyway.

I like games where you can make a great move that sets you up. That just doesn't happen in Ticket to Ride - you have to lay down your tracks one at a time and it becomes very obvious which direction you're heading in. Your opponents are never surprised by your brilliant move. There's a lot of tension in the game, but it's just "I hope I don't get screwed over". I much prefer games where the tension is "I hope nobody sees my brilliant plan".
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: This game is truly a 10. It may not be the game that I want to play all of the time anymore, but this game rivals or may even best Catan at this point for the most converts into gaming. It's not even in my top 10 games of all time, but I can't discount it's genius. If you are just getting into the hobby, do yourself a favor and go buy this game right now. Accessible, fun, hidden objectives, set collection, board play, take that, long term strategy, quick tactical decisions, expandable, great art, easy to teach, short game time, addictive and not the nerdiest thing on the block (all due respect to all of us nerds). Must have in any gamers collection. Parents will love it around holidays and my wife surely loves it so all I can say is, GAMING PERFECTION!

textfield_comment_value:
When I go to my parents' house, this is THE most played game they have. Due to its simplicity, I wholeheartedly recommend it as a smooth and enjoyable experience that is very easy to learn.

I recommend playing it with 4-5 players because if you go lower than that, routes get less competitive and the game loses some of its strategic, competitive, and intense elements. The game is built upon balancing the number of cards you have to spend and how fast you should put down your tracks to show your potential plans to other players. For that reason,  4 to 5 is where it's at its best, though I can see why some strictly prefer 4, as the game becomes less random when all players have a little more control, which enables them to make more calculated decisions.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: Wow! When I first played this one, early in my boardgaming career in January 2005, I couldn't understand what the fuss was about. Was this really the game that drew so many to the hobby, that some people played dozens and dozens and dozens of times and couldn't get enough? Bah. Fast forward to two years later: Thurn und Taxis & the Marklin edition of Ticket to Ride had recently won my heart, so I decided it was time to give the original TtR another chance. Although the simpler mechanics seemed somewhat bland after having playing TtR Marklin, guess what, I liked this one best! The passenger mechanics make Marklin a more complex game, sure, but they don't add all that much fun in return for making the game more difficult to manage and harder to absorb.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: Hra s jednoduchými pravidly, která nový hráč pochopí během několika málo minut, přenese hráče na začátek 20. století do Severní Ameriky. Cílem je vybudovat železniční síť mezi dvojicemi měst, které každému hráči určí tajný los na začátku hry (hráči si mohou v průběhu hry vzít další karty určující dvojice měst k propojení). Na konci hry je vítězem vyhlášen hráč s největším počtem bodů. Ty je možné získávat již v průběhu hry budováním tratí různých délek (čím delší trať, tím více bodů). Na konci hry je navíc ještě vyhodnoceno, zda se povedlo každému z hráčů spojit města, která mu byla určena. Pokud uspěl, získává další body dle vzdálenosti těchto měst. Ale pozor, pokud přecenil své síly a některou z dvojice určených měst propojit nestihl, body ztrácí.

[Original comment] Excellent game. Our adult family group really enjoys this (as of August 2005, February 2006). Is played almost weekly. Good challenges, requires much planning and analysis, and some luck.

Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: A colourful set collection and route building game with universal appeal. There are a couple of fairly minor downsides: luck of the draw can't be eliminated from the initial tickets that you get, and once you've completed your first 2/3 tickets the game's nearly over, so taking more is a high risk play. The key to winning is to save your cards to build the longer links and not get rushed into building the shortest route to your destination. The US map is a bit bland when compared with later versions, but it's the balance between most of the scoring methods that makes this game, imbalance would make it half as good. The 1910 update goes a long way to solving the ticket problem, so I rarely play without it, but the base game is fine for casual play.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: What a good game!  It works well with any number of players from 2-5, but plays very differently with each.  I use different tactics accordingly.  It's light, colourful, well made, simple to play, but with plenty to make you think.  It's not as deep as some German-style games, but it's elegant and fun and much better than Santa Fe and several other rail games.  Tactically, it's hard to tie down.  I've won by going for a few long tickets, lots of shorter tickets, playing for long (5 and 6) routes, dominating the middle of the board, dominating a side, going North to South, East to West.  And of course, most often I lose, anyway!  It's this hard to tie down quality added to the fun factor that makes me return to it so often.  I'll play this anytime.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
I prefer playing this game online against bots as a simple diversion -- with other people, I find there's too much analysis paralysis for such a straightforward game.  A little too much solitaire masquerading as a group boardgame, though there is some interaction and screw-your-buddy involved.  Fantastic game for getting newbies into boardgaming, however, and it'll always be one of my first recommendations for new gamers to get into the hobby.  There's just something about trains!

Edit 08/08/09:  Revised down to a 6 from 6.5 after playing TTR:E for the first time (which I gave a 7).  I guess I'd play regular TTR if someone asked, but TTR:E really is the better game and there's no reason not to play it instead (other than not having it on hand).

textfield_comment_value:
The destination card being a private information takes away all the interaction element from this game. If you are going for completing the destination, you can only hope that the other players do not claim the necessary route before you do. Since you don’t know what destination card they have and players can claim routes which are not adjacent to existing route, it is impossible for you to counteract their strategy.

If you are going for claiming a long route in order to gain points, the market will become dead at some point when nobody wants the ticket in the market, although this problem is alleviated at a high player count.  I guess the number of colours is too much in this game, or there should be ways to refresh the tickets in the market.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
I hate this game. Everybody has that reserved one time game where they can say "I hate this game, and you can't take that opinion away from me." I hate it like the Grinch hates Christmas, and I hate to see other people enjoy it even.

Still, I'll be a good sport and play it to the best of my ability, but don't mind me if I want to yawn my face off.

The game aims to be a gateway game and it is successful in that respect. There aren't a lot of options, and the depth you have is....well, you can potentially make a ton of decisions, but the decisions are extremely straightforward. Build your ticket.

I am giving this a 6 because it is a good gateway game, but I don't want to play it. No interaction with fellow players stops it from receiving a 7.

Update (7/2014) - in reviewing my ratings I noticed that I unjustly had this at a 7. It is a wonderful game, my favorite map. Those that think that this is a luck game are simply wrong. In fact, I often hesitate to introduce this to new game players because they would lose so badly. With all experienced players, Ticket to Ride always guarantees a good time. Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Horrible luck-dependend - it happens by far too often that you sit there for  ten turns or more just drawing cards and getting no color you need - neither for your "ticket to ride" nor for an alternative route. Games swing just by the loss of one ticket done or not done. 

(Example: You have two 10-point-tickets; if you happen to make them both, then you score 20 points; of one not just by random bad lack, then 0 points, because you have to subtract 10 from the other 10 - and this totally decides a game).

Sometimes funny as an entry-game for family-evenings with little children. Or maybe you really love totally luck-driven games. For me it is just a "throw a coin at the start of the game" - would decide the winner with the same randomness.

I hadn't played the original Ticket to Ride until it appeared on Board Game Arena recently, having only played Europe, which seems the more common version in... Europe.

I like the original version a lot more than Europe. Every time I introduced Europe to inexperienced board game players, I always taught the base game's rules and only introduced tunnels, ferries, and stations after a few turns. I guess the luck of the draw with regards to destination tickets is a lot more impactful, but I don't really mind, it's not like we're playing 18XX here.

It's one of the classic gateways for a reason.

Played only on X-Box 360.  I can see why TTR is considered a great gateway game.  It's easy to learn and play. textfield_comment_value: Ticket to Ride gets loads of praise for being a great gateway game and it's easy to see why. The rules can be explained in minutes, yet there is enough decision making to keep even serious gamers interested. Another nice feature is that it can be played either casually (just score points) or aggressively (by blocking routes), so it's great for playing with non-gamers and younger children. Although no one in my group owns a copy of Ticket to Ride, I get to play all the time thanks to X-box live. Indeed, I think I like Ticket to Ride better as an electronic game, since all of the tedious card shuffling and display refreshing are taken care of by the CPU, not to mention there are always a bevy of online opponents to play. Solid game.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: Ticket to Ride is not a highbrow, grimly game. It is easy to handle and serves the pleasure that many feel in planning and building something. The subject of railways does the rest. The tension arises because others thwart your own plans if you build an important route too late. A little skill in collecting cards is required. So far the game is attractive even with children. The only catch is that in the end, luck in drawing the order cards decides whether you win or lose, which includes a certain ruthlessness, accepting scoring minus points in the worst case. Since children usually lack such a gambling mentality, they only win if the others have bad luck. The small cards are annoying, which can be turned off by expansion USA 1910.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Random thoughts:

Without USA 1910 expansion - 6/10.
With USA 1910 expansion - 7/10.
This is annoying because USA 1910 is overpriced at $30 - it’s only a handful of cards (that 100% should have been included in newer versions of Ticket to Ride by default).

Ticket to Ride would greatly benefit from a more optimized newer edition/version, but I’m not confident that will ever happen. For instance, the Nashville-Atlanta connection really needs to be a double track. I wish there was a second board for 2 player games - the alternative 2 player ruleset simply isn't enough.

Ticket to Ride is simply ok. It doesn’t ever really impress anybody besides ultra-normies. It’s just too basic.

I’m confident I’ll donate this game away eventually.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: Ticket to Ride is the BEST gateway game out there.  I don't even think it's close.  Newbies are going to be able to pick this one up in a heartbeat but will probably get destroyed by board game veterans...the reason being is this game has so much hidden depth.  There is little to no luck in this game and it's highly strategic (aside from starting destination tickets).  Every route you connect matters.  There's also a great dash of tactical play with taking cards you know your opponent needs and laying routes that block your opponents.  There's a great amount of tension in between your turns where you are sweating if someone is going to take the card you want or lay a route that you needed.  Highly recommend this game to everyone!
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
I feel this game is a little overrated. I never beg to play this game, but lots of other people rave about it. Only would play if a group of friends asked me to. It's an easy to learn, straightforward game. The plastic trains are poor quality for the cost. The only benefit is the quick refresh rate on game rules and the fact that you can play it with a bunch of inexperienced friends who don't know any better.

Maybe the game mechanics just don't appeal to me, such as the hand management... Ticket to Ride feels too similar to Uno. It can be fun with a group of drunk friends in a party mood cause it's simple and a 'classic', but that's about the only reason you own it. Or maybe you own it cause it's also your wife's favorite. ; )
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
path building game on graph
already a classic
really good concept (!)
tense
works well as family or gateway game but also interesting and somewhat challenging for experienced players
quite abstract

I like the America map a lot more than other maps (although I'm from Europe). It's something about the relatively rectangular shape even distribution and the normal connections. No weird special rules. Also, it's the original.


I don't quite get why you put chains of wagons on the board in this game. It's not a train (without a locomotive) and it's just to symbolize that you control that link. It feels wrong not to use something more abstract like colored wooden bars (e.g. like the old wooden road pieces from "Settlers of Catan").
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
What I liked
* Easy to teach and play
* Appeals to gamers and non gamers
* Thought the theme would be dry, but enjoyed it
* Plays fast, little downtime
* The map just feels less interesting than the Europe map.
* Pieces come baged and with spare carrages!

What I didn't like
* Need to make sure the deck is VERY shuffled before starting each game.
* Game is all about efficiency, unfortunately luck plays a fairly big part in how efficiant you can be.

If experienced players are playing against beginners, they really should give some helpful advice about what to go for and strategy before the game starts otherwise there is a very big advantage to the experienced player.

* Some of the printing on the cards on my copy was dodgy
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Comments based on: 1 recent play and several plays pre-BGG logging; owned.

Things I like:
• Easy to learn (my 9-yr-old picked it up pretty quickly)
• A nice mix of luck (determines which cards are available on your turn) and strategy (deciding which routes to claim and when to claim routes vs pick up train cards, etc.)
• Accommodates up to 5 players (too many games only accommodate 4)
• Fun theme (I like to travel)
• Quality components

Things I dislike:
• Not quite enough strategy (Ticket to Ride: Europe is better in this sense)
• The mess when someone bumps the board after lots of trains have been placed
• Moves a little slower than I'd prefer (our games never seem to fall into the 30-60 minute window listed on the box)
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
"EXCELLENT"
This rating includes the expansion "USA 1910" (see comments below)
Very nice light card drafting, theme and artwork.

I´d like to get it to the table more often, to enjoy and test the longevity / replayability, but there have been so many other games lately that are more favourable to play with kids. Still to ponder if the USA 1910 expansion would really make sense to us.

Update: 1910 expansion acquired. The rating of the base game was at risk of decreasing to 8.5, or maybe 8.25, on account of limited replay value (only 30 destinations tickets in the base game), but the expansion seems to have solved the issue with the three new ways of playing and a flood of new destination tickets, which warrant the upgrade.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: Now this game is one that I find really interesting. The concept and gameplay and scoring of the game is so simple, yet never once does a play through feel like one that has happened before. It is beautifully dynamic within its basic construction, while also always a fun table presence. The way that the strategy changes as the board develops is something that always has me on my toes, and there are some simple mechanics in this game that I think were absolutely critical in my own understanding of game design. I don't think that I consider this a game that I would play frequently (just to avoid letting it feel boring), but I absolutely will always enjoy having this one on the shelf for when the right rainy day comes along!
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Now that I own and have played Ticket to Ride I am amazed by comparisons I have read regarding this and TransAmerica.  Aside from both being about trains and situated in North America, they are nothing alike.

In Ticket to Ride hand management plays a key role in winning or losing.  I enjoy how different strategies regarding route cards come into play after mulitple playings.  For anyone who enjoys rummy and it's variants, this game is for you.  I also feel that the game scales very well from two to five players.  

I believe, and it's been proven, that this is an excellent gateway game for non-gamers.   I wouldn't mind a variant with trading of route cards or train cards, but then again, I could do it on my own.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: Excellent game for beginners and game enthusiasts. The concept is simple enough-select tickets/routes to connect cities together, collect train cards, and build routes to connect the cities. It's simple enough for anyone to play, but there is a lot of strategy involved when selecting which tickets to pursue because there may be several shorter routes to build along the way to building one long one. Don't worry though, I have found that there is enough random chance and luck of the draw involved for a beginner to legitimately challenge an intermediate to advanced player. If you are just starting out, I highly recommend the standard USA version as it is the simplest version. I have played every variant and enjoy them all.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
I think this game doesn't deserve this much excitement around it. It's just drawing cards and waiting to get what you need to build some railway routes. There is not much tactic around it, mostly just luck and you can't improve much in playing (except knowing the route by heart, better than other newer players). Also in the last round some players will lose their turn just because they're not on their turn prior to someone who remains without trains, while other players will have that turn just because their turn is prior to that person, why is that even a rule? 

So if you (like me) don't enjoy so much games based mostly on luck and prefer more tactical games - just go on and play something more balanced and strategic.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
A decent light-weight route building game, where you draft cards hoping to form sets that allow you to place routes.  You have a hand of ticket cards showing connections you need to make with those routes you're placing.  Make the connection to score points, but if you don't you'll lose the points!

Lots of fun with lots of very tense moments as the board gets crowded and potential routes are cut off by your opponents.  You can also gamble on taking extra tickets, but if you draw poorly, you might really get screwed into getting tickets you can't complete!  So, overall, the tension here is very good.

Overall, a light game that is still very enjoyable despite the simplicity.  Great for introducing people to the hobby.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: Newbies love this game.  I don't think it's the bee's knees (I greatly prefer Union Pacific), but it's got some strategic merit.  I prefer playing with 3 players than with 5 -- strategy is worth more than luck with fewer players.  One key to the game is to play as many 6-links as you can, even if they don't help your routes that much.  In fact, if you're really daring, take the two cheapest routes, then ignore them completely, and try to screw with the other people's routes... that can lead to some pretty big negative scores all around, but less for you, because you're just going for the most points in links.  And don't take new tickets -- they don't help, as far as I can tell.  A 6-link is better than most tickets.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
It's a good as a light game and a gateway game.  That's all it tries to be, and all it is.  

Each player start with different route card.  Most points in the game come from connecting the pairs of cities on your card.  Then on most turns, you either draw 1-2 train cards, or spent train cards to lay tracks.  It's simple, there's some push-your-luck strategy, there's strategy from guess at the opponents intentions, and there's backstabbing but without being a king maker game.  That's enough for a good lightweight game.

The biggest thing holding it back is that the routes are very unequal in value.  If you draw all North-South routes on turn 1, and your opponents get East-West routes, you've pretty much already lost.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Core + 1910 ; First Impression (2plyr game).

A streamlined set collection game that appeals to the widest audience.

Now I've been playing board games for 6+ years now and I can say that this is definitely a "gateway" game. The rules are ~2pgs long and the IP of trains offends no one. But its strengths are also its biggest weaknesses. The streamlined rules means I don't have to think hardly at all and the IP isn't something I can get attached to. I can see how playing with 3+ players would add some spice to the game by cutting off certain routes, but honestly if you're a long time board gamer I would say skip this one for something else that has some more "meat" to it or at the very least try to get it on sale.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: I initially played this w/ a larger group when I first moved to Portland and really enjoyed it.  Then I discovered the wild world of gaming and forgot about this because I thought it was simplistic.  Now I've come back to it and appreciate it for what it is.  There is definitely a big component of luck with the card draw but the decision of where and when to play your trains can feel very strategic and I find myself in anxious anticipation of everyone's moves.  I have yet to play using the 1910 expansion (outside of just using the larger cards) nor any other expansions and am really looking forward to getting plays of this in again.  This will also play well with newbies/family which gives it an extra plus.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Classic.  This is the first game I break out when I meet people who haven't played a board game since monopoly in childhood.  

TTR USA is better at higher player counts.  If I am going to play 2P or 3P, I prefer to play Nordic TTR to make it more competitive.  But if "direct competition" is daunting to a new gamer, then I definitely stick to this one (even before trying to introduce them to co-op games).  I would even pick this over Sushi Go for the completely uninitiated because this rule set is much easier to understand and quicker to explain.  Being able to explain ALL the rules in under 2 minutes is a great selling point when approaching people who are not sure about "Board gaming" in the first place...
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
From a gateway-accessibility angle, it is easy to recommend TtR for American non-gamers. [b]One of the best (if not THE best) gateway boardgames.[/b] Stay away from TtR:Europe for American beginners, due to the weirdness of the European cities for Americans.
I can't decide which is the better game, between TtR and TtR:Europe. Each has strengths. I'd rather have TtR:Europe with more hardcore gamers, and TtR with family/non-gamers, I guess. And since family/non-gamers is where this series is aimed at (IMO), I conclude that TtR is the better game at succeeding with its target demographic.
TtR is a hard game to 'play down' on, and unfortunately usually leads to 1st-time players getting blown out, points-wise.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: After one playing, I can say that I really enjoyed it, but I am a little disappointed.  I was expecting the "be-all-end-all" of middleweights, and I don't think that this is it.  Maybe I'm missing something, but it doesn't have that "oomph" that I look for when playing a game.  This could conceivably change with more playings and/or playing with different numbers of people.  I can certainly see the multiple paths to victory here... Update: I can take this game or leave it; if someone suggests it, I'll play...but I won't be the one suggesting it. Update: I seem to be going through a love/hate relationship with TtR.  Rating increased from a 5.5 to a 7.  I've been wanting to play this one recently.  Why? :)
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
An average game at best... not one of Mr. Moon's better efforts.  Another SdJ winner that failed to grab my interest.  If you want an Alan Moon train game, you are far better off with either Union Pacific or Freight Train.  I really don't understand what all the fuss is about... I've played the game a few times now and, while I did enjoy the game, did not find it much fun.  According to the ratings here at the 'Geek a 6, "Ok game, some fun or challenge at least, will play sporadically if in the right mood," hits the nail on the head for me.

Since I've added this to my Steam account (along with the 1910 expansion), I've played hundreds of games.  My opinion has gone up, but not enough to rate it higher.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
2009/09
Easy to teach, fun to play. This is the best game for all audiences. The reason I don't own this anymore is, that I substituted the base game for Märklin Edition.


2013/01
To be honest, I'll turn down a game on certain occasions. TtR has grown slightly old.
8->7 

2014/10
Original = Best for families with 4-5 players, elegant rules, suffers from card hoarding strategy

Märklin = Most satisfactory for gamers, strong incentive to make early plays mitigating the hoarding problem, a bit fiddly

Nordic = Best for families with 2-3 players, slight hoarding problems which are mitigated by the tight map, random take that aspects due to the tunnel mechanics

Europe = worst of the bunch in all aspects
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Ticket to Ride was hip when I was on a long boardgaming hiatus and today, many years later, it's hard for me to grasp its insane success. It's very accessible for sure, easygoing and mildly entertaining, but also rather unexciting and repetitive with all the card draws. 

Recently I literally found the game as a giveaway free on the street, complete and in perfect condition, so it will get more plays until maybe it will click.

Update. I know some of my OG buddies are very high on the game or one of its iterations. I'm not. With some more plays I'm appreciating TTR's qualities more, still it's swinging somewhere between "ok" and "boring" for me. There are many "gateway" games out there I like better.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: This is my favorite strategy game, bar none, especially the US version.  It is light, family friendly, can be played with any number of people (no easy solitaire mode, however), and expansions (with other maps) provide good variation.  Can be played by both adults and young kids without losing strategic interest.  The US map is my favorite, and for expansions, and other versions, I really like Italy (Expansion, with Japan), Nordic Countries (self-contained, not expansion), and the Old West (Expansion, with France) in that order (I have all expansions and versions).  Highly recommended.  If you get only one family strategy board game, I would get this one and I would get the original, US map version.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
TTR has earned the right to be called a classic, just as it has earned the right to be made into an acronym. While luck in the initial draw (and to a lesser degree, later draws) of tickets can have a game-long impact on fortunes, once people begin competing for routes, the gloves come off.

Pick up colored cards that help you lay cars that complete routes that connect cities on your tickets. There are precious few other rules, so it works well either as a family game or for late-night backstabbing revelry. Usually it comes off as someplace between the two (though it leans toward backstabbing).

Setup and re-boxing are both relatively simple, but taking it down is certainly the longer process.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
DEREK

Finally purchased it and played it with my family. Was worried that it wouldn't live up to all the hype. Family enjoyed it, but didn't love it. Fun game. Held everyone's attention. Lots of planning and strategizing and yelling (jokingly?) at each other for taking cards or routes. Lots of strategy without being too difficult. Components are eye-catching and high quality. While not the first game we have played with a sort of "get you" mechanism, is probably the one that has it the strongest. I think this game may not be pulled off the shelf very often - there are many games my family loves that they would rather play and some of the scoring mechanisms get a bit confusing for the family.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
This is a fun game, more on the casual side, and fairly easy to learn.  It's a great game for socializing and casual play because it doesn't require a lot of deep strategy to do well.

The components are well-made and the board, cards, & pieces are colorful.  The printing of locations is large and clear, easy to read from various spots around the table (although reading upside-down is naturally more difficult).  

You can definitely play the game more cutthroat or more relaxed.  We have always played pretty laidback, not trying to block others from routes.  Fortunately, each player can only claim one route on a particular destination path, which helps prevent monopolies of particular regions.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
I enjoyed this a lot more than Europe. The lack of stations gave it a bit more tension, as I genuinely worried at times that other players may 'steal my routes'.

Of course, if that threat had become reality, I may have hated it...

Rules are simple to teach and it works as a gateway game, yet there's a good few choices to make. Choosing cards to take, a route to claim or pushing your luck with more tickets - these 3 possible moves each involve their own set of choices and whilst it never gets particularly heavy, there is potential for trying out varying strategies.

Pushing your luck by getting more routes is probably the most interesting part of the game, as well as the potential screwage.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
I really USED to love this game. It was one of the first strategy games I learned. Very simple rules- collect cards and use cards of the same color to build routes connecting cities. Non-gamers can easily learn the rules in 5 minutes and play it in 30 minutes.

Some resource management in terms of deciding what cards to collect and when/where/how to build the routes.

However, after playing it online for a year, I have burnt out on the game big time. I do bring it every week to my games group as it's very popular among the lighter gamers and they can easily teach others to play. I think it's a good starter game but lacks the challenges, variety, and strategy to keep gamers interested in it.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: Fun, quick, and easy to learn. Ticket to Ride builds on classics like Monopoly where you are essentially owning real estate and trying to build the most cohesive train across the country. This game is a little too luck-based for my liking. There is some strategy, but if you don't draw the cards that others gather, you can still be competitive… but it's hard to win consistently. Even with the best strategy, card pulls control the game. Sometimes there are 4-6 turns in a row where the color you want doesn't show up so you are trying to find other plays elsewhere that don't align with your goals just to get points. But overall this game would be easy to pull out with newbie board game players.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: Nice and quite fast. There's a high possibility of positive stress to be found in the endgame when you need to draw some crucial card to win a huge amount of points. It's, however, a little sad that the early game is just about drawing more and more cards because putting wagons on the board too early offers your opponents quite an easy chance to screw your game. Scoring system also benefits longer tracks too much which also encourages drawing cards early. With new maps and mechanical additions the basic TtR is turning more and more into a mere platform, for better, newer stuff. Also, I consider the original US map to be one of the weaker ones and most of my plays come on expansion maps.

textfield_comment_value:
Honestly, I didn't think I would enjoy this game based on what I had read. Just seemed too tame and boring. Boy was I wrong.

While it is certainly not a deep game, it has enough light strategy going on to hold a players interest. It's universal appeal is a big upside here as it makes it easy to teach new players and get them interested in the game...and it can and will hit the table very often.

Any game I can teach to my parents, wife, and friends and that they actually request playing is certainly a win in my eyes.

Make routes, get points, block opponents, and make sure everything is well timed. A very enjoyable game.

Components are excellent too!

(extra copy *** at the lake ***)
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: It's an awesome gateway game and I put it into the same category as say "Settlers of Catan" but maybe a notch or two below in complexity and a notch or two above in theme. This will always be in my collection and in my opinion most of the newer versions or spin-offs from this series simply add complexity without adding much more "fun" so the base game is what remains timeless on my shelf. This game fires games like Monopoly, Life, and most other classic board game titles. While the novelty of the title has long since faded for me, it still hits the table when I want to introduce newcomers to the board gaming space. It is an essential component of a well-rounded board game education.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: I loved this when I first played it, and it really hooked me in. I played it over and over for a few days but quickly became fatigued. It's an interesting and different experience when not used to connection games but I don't think there is much of a game here. I particularly don't like the ticket system, where you are pigeon holed into building a certain way and then you are penalised for drawing more choices of tickets. I understand from a gameplay perspective but it really drives the player with limited choice, and the game is so quick the tickets do little but that. A little random but not too bad, bit of strategy in what cards to pick and when to play them, I like that about it.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Ticket to Ride (Zug um Zug) is easily one of the greatest games ever produced. The mechanics are simple, the playing time is moderate, the interaction with other players is plentiful and while you compete continuously for winning the game, each player has a chance to grab the victory at the very end of the game - depending on the success on the hidden missions. 

We love the game because it is easy, fast paced and works well as a family game. Due to the complex interaction of the missions and the ahead planning, I recommend this game for age 9+.

With its large collection of expansions, new boards and more complex building rules, the ticket-to-ride-family brings very long playing fun.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: I think it's an okay game, and I can absolutely understand the appeal. However, I think it is far too dependent on the luck of the draw when it comes to routes, and to a lesser extent train cards. I get that it's a light experience, but it's definitely one of my least favorite of the "classic" examples of modern gateway games. I far prefer Carcassonne, 7 Wonders, and Settlers of Catan, among others. There's too much luck and not enough player interaction (although there is tension when it comes to the race to build, so there is some interaction). Ultimately it just doesn't do it for me. I do think overall it is a nice, solid design, though. And I generally could be convinced to play.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: This game for me never gets tiring it always seems fresh. It's like and not like elfenland, there are  simalarities and differences and here they are,  in both games you travel to cites and collect points,  and the differnce os in ticket to ride you get "destination cards" which if you travel from A to point B while building track (or using some of your old track) you earn a certain amount of points And in elfenland you get animal cards are boats that each one has different amount ofmovement they can move in each distinct area. I would recommend it to people  who are already fans of Alan R. Moon  are interested in it ( which should be everyone or your missing  out on fantastic game!
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Played physically and on Boardgamearena.

Full acknowledgment that this is one of the games that brought a lot of people into the modern board-games. Also, many other games have surpassed it. Also, with the game having been explored in depth, it is no longer new player friendly.

The player interaction in this game is either:
a) forced (Las Vegas as a location without any destinations leading to it) 
or, 
b) if players go for the plan of collecting big decks in hand, limited

Replay is limited by both limited number of destinations (30) and the way the game plays. With experienced players, the starting moves go in limited number of ways.

1910 expansion moved this up to a solid 6.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: This has been called the greatest gateway game ever, and I'd have to agree with that assessment.  This game has beautiful pieces and artwork, plus it's simple to explain, simple to understand, and simple to play.  It's so easy to get new players excited about this game, and the strategy is simple enough that everyone has a good time playing it.  The really tough strategy comes through meta-gaming as you try to outsmart your opponents and block their success, but none of that is required for simply having an enjoyable game.  While I'd generally prefer to play a more strategic middle-weight game with more experienced players, I love playing this game with a group of casual gamers.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Ok, so it's not the DEEPEST game.  A lot depends on luck - which destination cards you draw and which your opponent(s) draw.  Two player games are over faster than my wife would like, but she's always ready to go again.  The more you play, though, the more strategies open up.  Blocking becomes enjoyable to try and accomplish, though it's not very apparent WHO you should block.  It also becomes important to watch how many trains your opponent(s) have left - in that it reminds me of Lost Cities (among others) where you have to be aware of when the game will end.

Most of all, though, this game is FUN.  And I've enjoyed every time I've played it - and how often can you say that?
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
This game gets better the more you play.  Playing it online made me appreciate the subtle tension in the game.  Sometimes it is a little dry for me, but with the right group (mainly, a fast-playing one) this game shines.

The main tension is simple really.  It comes in deciding whether to take more cards or spend the cards you have to grab routes.  If you draw too many cards you might lose a key route, but if you move too fast to grab a route you'll find it hard to grab the longer, more valuable routes.  It's a simple game with simple decisions, but these simple decisions make for some interesting and challenging decisions.  The game's challenging simplicity makes it a classic.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
This one is a no-brainer.  It has a great feel to it, is very easy to teach, and I imagine it will be considered a classic 10 years from now.  One of the best family/group of friends board games out there.  

Update February 2013: Have finally gotten back into gaming after a sort of break, and this game is still a ton of fun. I keep expecting it to get old, but it really doesn't. There's a reason it's so popular.  

Update feb 2016: Ticket to ride is a modern classic without equal for playing with ANYONE. The only thing keeping me from giving it a 10 is I can't decide which version is my favorite, but you cannot go wrong with original Ticket to ride and the 1910 expansion.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
One of the first games I got.  I believe this is the game that actually broke the mold for my wife and I.  It opened our horizons and left us wanting more.  I consider this game to be my groups original gateway game and I owe it a lot more than I give it credit for.

Players take destination cards that tell them what cities they need to connect by collecting train cards and matching sets of the proper colors to claim routes.  In the end players score points on the destination cards they finished, and the amount of trains they have on the board.

Fun game that is easy to teach and does not last too long.  Allows players to make some tough decisions without hurting the brain.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
I've got to admit, that although I was skeptical, I actually enjoyed this game.  Could be because I won in my first game (against 3 other players)!  But, after playing Thurn & Taxis, I didn't think TTR would be as entertaining.  

Well, it isn't quite as fun, but it was still pretty good.  The game offers enough options to keep it from being completely out of the players' control.  And, being a light game, it doesn't drag on too long.  The hidden VPs in the route cards really make it a good game, rather than a decent one.

Like other light, gateway games, this one will be fun to play once in a while.  Being the gamer that I am, I will want to play meatier games more often.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
The game that should be a household keeper instead of Monopoly. 

+ Easy to learn.
+ Quite competitive with some strategy involved. Do you play your pieces or block your opponent's route?
+ Doesn't feel too long or short. 
+ Turns are quick as there is only so much you can do on it (draw cards, new routes or place train cars). 
+ Push-your-luck element as you can only score your ticket route if you complete it - not completing it will deduct from your overall score. 

- Takes up a fair bit of room on the table. 
- While blocking routes can be a strategy, you would have to know the cards and there's a lot of them!
- Sometimes the winner is obvious way before the game ends.

textfield_comment_value:
Wow, for such a simple game, it creates a surprisingly exciting atmosphere. Every decision in the game is tense because of the anticipation of what might happen before your next turn. My wife does not like this game anymore because it stresses her out. It's not a game I can play over and over, but it's one that will never lose its appeal to me. Our house rule is that all your trains have to be gone before the game ends. It lengthens the game slightly, but I think it requires better planning. 

On a side note, I recently played a game where one card (or the lack thereof) made a difference of -166 points in my score. I had bet it all on the big routes and came up short.

Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: TTR is a great gateway or middle ground game that anyone can play.  The game mechanics work perfectly and make for some tense moments as you hope to not get cut off by your opponents.  Easy enough to teach to kids and non-gamers, although the heavy amount of luck could be a turn off to those who like more brain burning games.  Nastier players can go on an all out defensive by simply cutting off all the important routes.  Once you complete your routes you can take new route cards.  This is a dangerous lottery as you will usually get either easy points, or instantly get stuck with impossible routes that will end your would-be victory.  All in all though, a good game.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Another highly overrated, outdated game.
It has such high ratings everywhere that new-ish players always pick this up at stores:
Why would you play this instead of Brass? Or at least powergrid?
I don't get why this gets a low complexity rating. The good moves are all hard (you need to predict what the state of the board will be couple of turns ahead) which causes  that a more experienced player will always crush newer. Brass is equally complex in my opinion, it's just that it's more obvious in punishing bad plays - but the point % difference between a good and new player is the same.

No point playing this anymore, I can barely remember the days where I liked this.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value: Fun gateway game. Who doesn't love playing with trains? Seems overly simple at first, but the strategy becomes more complicated and compelling over time as you find the most lucrative routes to complete your ticket, guess and sabotage your opponent's routes, and keep them guessing about your own routes so you don't become vulnerable to sabotage. I've heard some people say they play "nice" in this game, but doing that is actually what initially turned me off to it--if you're not trying to screw over your opponent, you're just picking up cards and setting down trains. Even with it, it can get a bit repetitive if played too often, but it's still a great game overall.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
This game is so boring.  You pick up colors that you want and play routes.  You hope that other players don't pick the same routes.  That's it. It boils down to luck and knowledge of the game. If you know what routes are available, it is easier to guess what players are trying to achieve and block them from getting it. That's about the only strategy I can see in it. 

The routes I picked up had colors that were not getting pulled from the deck.  My wife got all of her colors and consequently got to lay down all of her routes.  Neither of us enjoyed the game as it felt like none of our decisions made any difference. The build quality of the game isn't great either.

This rating is for the overall series.  Some maps are better than others, but the overall system is gaming perfection.


The more games I see where you jump through hoops to collect milk or cheese or cloth or wood or stone on and on and on, the more I realize how few games there are that measure up to Ticket to Ride.  Turns are quick and there is significant tension as routes start disappearing. But I will say, game days with a round of Ticket to Ride are much better than game days without.

textfield_comment_value:
This is a light weight competitive hand management and network building game where players are seeking to build networks of trains across America. 

Players will collect sets of train cards in order to build up networks across America, playing a set of train cards to claim a route. The longer the route, the more points. 

Players also have destination cards which have specific routes that players are seeking to claim. If players complete the route they get end game victory points, if they don't the lose points. 

The game ends when a player uses their last carriage to claim a route. The final scores are tallied and the player with the most points wins.

textfield_comment_value: An excellent game with only a slight superficial resemblance (in appearance) to Union Pacific, also designed by Mr. Moon.  T2R has universal appeal to the casual/non-gamer crowd and gamer fans alike, so it makes a great "gateway" game to introduce boardgaming to newbies.  The game's central challenges are card-set collections and tactical board strategy by laying train links.  It's nerve-wracking from turn to turn, in a delightful way, watching to see if others lay track where you want your tracks to be, or taking the train cards you covet.  The production quality is outstanding (as you come to expect from Days of Wonder).

Just doesn't grab me.  I can see its gateway potential, but the rules seem to me to cry out for the thing to be played with spoiler-style nastiness.  For some reason, we just don't do it that way, and as a result it's pretty blah.

Update: I think the problem is that the disincentive for spoiling play is so great - you miss a turn.  But what if there was a rule allowing you to lay down n-1 cards instead of the required n as long as the rails you were claiming shared an endpoint town with the last player's move?

textfield_comment_value:
A really nice game. The art and the concept are great. 

Ticket to Ride is really easy to play and to learn. The goal is to connect all the routes you have, to score more points than the other players. The routes are kept in secret, and only at the end of the game are revealed to score (+) or (-) points depending if you did the connection between the two places of the route or not. 

There are 3 options to do, but only 1 per turn. You can go for train tickets (the trains are colored), claim a route (discarding many train tickets according to the route path) and draw extra route tickets (to try to make more routes).

textfield_comment_value: FAVOURITE GAME - Ticket to Ride is a cross-country train adventure game. Players collect train cards that enable them to claim railway routes connecting cities throughout North America. The longer the routes, the more points they earn. Additional points come to those who can fulfill their Destination Tickets by connecting two distant cities, and to the player who builds the longest continuous railway. It is one of the best family games I have tried until now. With the simple rules and relatively fast playing time it catches on very quickly.

textfield_comment_value:
TTR got me into what I think of as modern boardgaming. simply collecting resources and marking territory by spending the correct resources allows you to complete goals. Resources are train cars of certain color,  territory is defined by rail paths, and goals are to two cities via paths. The real fun is trying to determine the path your opponent may be completing and claim those path segments to force your opponent to spend more resources.

Points are awarded based on all path segments and goals.

textfield_comment_value:
One of the standard gateway games that I play with non-gamers or if people want a shorter game.  It serves this purpose very well.

What I like:
- Very easy to teach.  Only 3 fairly simple actions to explain
- It is a fairly short game (45-60 minutes) and there is not much downtime between turns.
- There is some tension in being able to complete your routes without being blocked (4-5 players)

What I don't like:
- You can get screwed right from the beginning with a poor starting ticket hand
- Luck of the draw (both from the deck and the face up pile) largely determines if you can collect all the sets you need
- There is not much tension with 2 players

textfield_comment_value: This is a great game for several reasons. First, the mechanics are simple and it's easy to learn. Second, it moves along at a very good pace. Third, the excitement is there because at multiple points in the game you are forced to make critical decisions that could make or break you. Will another player take that critical route before I am able to get it? Should I gamble and take more tickets? It's just a lot of fun and easy enough that you can probably play with your kids. My 10 year-old has no problem handling this game.

textfield_comment_value:
For our 2 player games we use the "Mega" card set with the following variant:

-2 Sets of trains for each player
-Separate destination tickets for each set (color)
-1 set of train cards for both colors

You decide on each of your turns which set to use your cards on.

When you pull new destination tickets you must declare which set they are for BEFORE looking at them.

The game does not end until the player has reduced both of his sets to 2 trains or less.

Score each player's lowest color x2, highest x1
Example: Player A has the Red and Blue sets. 
Blue scores 80. Red scores 110.
Player A's total score would be 80 X 2 + 110 = 270

Solo Player Value = Excellent. Playing solo with a single character is rough. I like to use two characters. A single player can manage two character easily.

Two Player Value = Excellent. Pandemic scales flawlessly.


Pandemic is a very well designed cooperative game that scales nicely from being played solo to being played with many. With a single player the game is absolutely fantastic. The single player can play as a single roll or as multiple rolls allowing for more choices.

Essentially Pandemic has been built as a solo solitaire game that has a strong win or lose victory condition with the player fighting against the game itself. More players can play the game because the game is solitaire based and the players are cooperatively fighting against the game. 

This multi-player solitaire against the game works well in Pandemic and actually changes the games difficulty. The game gets more difficult with more players as each player then gets fewer turn. In the solo game this is the player playing multiple rolls.

Playing against the game is accomplished by a player taking a turn for himself, followed by taking a turn as the game; after which it is the next players turn to follow the same pattern. The game's turn is fairly scripted and pre-set making it easy and clean to run the game.

Since Pandemic is designed to be played as the players versus the game the players can strategically work together for victory. This leads to some wonderfully tight strategic choices for the players that can truly make the difference in victory or defeat. Every choice feels like it is important.


Pros - 
- Great design
- Scales well
- Excellent strategic choices for the players
- Suits many players from solo to four

Cons - None

[b]-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------[/b]


Here I will discuss the Pandemic expansion [thing=40849][/thing].

This is truly a wonderful expansion.  If only all expansions could be this good.

This is the first expansion that I can remember which offers multiple expansion components inside the single expansion.  Basically, in this expansion are three separate and individual expansions that can be added to the base game in any combination.  This is a great idea and goes a long way to improve the game longevity.

Due to that I will discuss each piece of this expansion separately.  

------------------

The Virulent Strain is the first piece of this expansion.

With this piece a single disease becomes more powerful and deadly.  That particular disease then has extra rules to govern it which are somewhat random and unpredictable.  This does a lot to increase the difficulty of the game.  

This new difficulty makes the players re-think the games strategy.  The players must now come up with a way to keep the Virulent Strain from quickly spinning of control, while maintaining control over the other three diseases.  This is often much harder than it sounds as the Virulent Strain is designed to cause the players problems.

------------------

The Mutation is the second piece of the expansion.

With this piece a fifth disease is added to the game, called the Mutant Strain.  The Mutant Strain has half as many cubes as regular diseases which make it twice as deadly.  This really cranks up the games difficulty.

The Mutant Strain is governed by special cards which are in both the player draw deck and the disease deck.  This makes the Mutant Strain spread quickly.  Dealing with the Mutant Strain often take precedence due to its lethality, but players must still contend with the other four diseases as well.

------------------

For a real challenge players might want to play with both the Virulent Strain and the Mutant Strain together.

Dealing with both of these disease at the same time is both fun and challenging and offers a huge step up in difficulty.

------------------

The third piece of this expansion is the Bio Terrorist.

This is the first game I can remember that takes a cooperative base game and turns it in a competitive game.  Many games now offer this ability with expansions and I think Pandemic was ahead of its time in this manner.

In this expansion one player becomes a Bio Terrorist and works against the other players.  The Bio Terrorist controls the Mutant Strain and decides how and where the Mutant Strain moves and grows.  The Bio Terrorist gets a turn like normal players but has actions geared toward spreading the Mutant Strain and damaging the players.

While this is a fantastic idea, I think this fails in practice.  The actions the Bio Terrorist can take are limited and weak and somewhat diminish the potency of the Mutant Strain.

Also, this expansion has an element of Scotland Yard to it.  The Bio Terrorist remains, and plays his turns, hidden.  Finding and capturing the Bio Terrorist greatly slows him down.  I don't think this adds anything fun to the game and even confuses the other mechanics.  

-----------------

I think two out of the three new pieces are absolutely fantastic.  The third piece I simply do not like.

Because this expansion so greatly changes the base game I think I should re-score the game.

textfield_comment_value:
Longtemps, les jeux de coopération sont restés un genre mineur, généralement destiné aux enfants. En 2000, avec son grand jeu du Seigneur des Anneaux, Reiner Knizia a entièrement renouvelé le genre et pratiquement inventé le jeu de société coopératif pour adultes. Nombre d’auteurs s’en sont ensuite inspirés, et le jeu de société coopératif est devenu un genre à part entière. La plupart de ces jeux utilisent le même mécanisme de base – une pioche d’événements néfastes – les « cartes noires » - arrivant dans un ordre plus ou moins aléatoire, une pioche de « cartes blanches » permettant aux joueurs de régler les problèmes. Les jeux les plus réussis, comme Les Chevaliers de la Table Ronde, sont ceux qui parviennent à créer une réelle interaction entre les joueurs et à faire sans cesse remonter la tension, maintenant le petit univers du jeu sur le fil du rasoir. Ce sont aussi ceux dont les mécanismes sont suffisamment variés et aléatoires pour permettre un renouvellement des parties et éviter les automatismes. Les jeux de coopération semblent devoir être l’une des grandes tendances des mois à venir, et j’en ai d’ailleurs moi-même un dans les tuyaux.

Pandemic est donc un pur jeu de coopération, dans la lignée du Seigneur des Anneaux. Comme de coutume, le but est de sauver le monde menacé, cette fois, par quatre terribles virus se répandant rapidement sur la planète. Les joueurs sont des scientifiques, bénéficiant chacun d’un petit avantage particulier, qui parcourent le globe tentant tout à la fois de ralentir l’épidémie dans les cités touchées et d’avancer dans la recherche de vaccins ou de remèdes. À la fin de chaque tour d’un joueur, des cartes d’infection sont piochée indiquant dans quelles villes les virus encore actifs se répandent, parfois très rapidement. Les joueurs l’emportent s’ils parviennent à éradiquer les quatre maladies, et perdent si elles échappent entièrement à leur contrôle.

Le thème, sans doute l’un des plus sombres jamais vu dans un jeu de société, pourra certainement choquer. Traité au premier degré, avec un graphisme sombre et sans humour apparent, il parvient cependant à échapper au mauvais goût et à créer une réelle tension, ce qui est la clef du succès pour un jeu de coopération. Les discussions entre joueurs sont tendues, et les choix difficiles. Vaut-il mieux se concentrer sur la recherche ou sur les soins ? Doit-on négliger l’Amérique quelque temps pour tenter tous ensemble d’éradiquer le virus qui s’est répandu en Asie, ou au contraire se répartir sur les différents continents pour pouvoir réagir facilement aux crises ? Peut-on prendre le temps de se rencontrer pour échanger des informations, c’est à dire des cartes, ou doit on compter sur la chance de la pioche ? Ne me demandez pas la bonne réponse, j’ai à ce jour perdu mes trois parties de Pandemic.

Comparé aux autres jeux de coopération parus ces derniers temps, Pandemic est certainement le plus rapide, une partie durant à peine plus d’une demi-heure. C’est aussi l’un des plus simples à jouer, avec des règles logiques et fort bien présentées, mais qui risquent peut-être de manquer de variété après une dizaine de parties. Mais attention, ce n’est certainement pas le plus facile !
---
Cooperative games have long been a minor genre, mostly aimed at young kids. With his big box Lord of the Rings game, Reiner Knizia has reinvented the genre and designed the first modern adult cooperative boardgame. Many authors have followed since, and cooperative game has become a noticeable genre these last years. Most of these games use the same kind of “game engine”, with a drawing deck of bad events – the “black cards” - arriving in a more or less random order, and a drawing deck of “white cards” used by the players to solve the critical situations. The most successful such games, like Shadows over Camelot, have a strong player interaction and a high tension, the small game world always standing on the edge. They also have enough variety and randomness to make every new game different. Cooperative game seem to be a strong trend at the moment, with several scheduled to hit the shelves. I also have one in the pipe.

Pandemic is a pure cooperative game, in the Lord of the Rings style. As usual, the goal is to save the world, this time from four viruses threatening to spread all over the planet. Players are scientists, each one with a specific ability, travelling across the globe trying to treat and slow the infection, and if possible to find cures for the four diseases. At the end of a player’s turn, infection cards are drawn to know in which town the active viruses will multiply, and sometimes spread to neighbouring cities. The players win if they manage to eradicate the four diseases, and lose if they get out of control and overtake the world.

The theme, probably the darkest one ever used in a boardgame, can feel disturbing. It is treated very seriously, with dark and realistic graphics and no apparent hum or, but avoiding bad taste. It also create a strong and always renewed tension, which is the critical point in a cooperative game. The debate between players is always very lively, and the decisions hard to make. Better focus on searching a cure or on treating the infected cities? Better ignore America for a while and all together try to eradicate the Asian disease, or scatter through the world and be ready to jump on any crisis situation? Is it worth taking time and movement to share knowledge, meaning giving or taking a card, or just rely on the luck of the draw ? Don’t ask me what the right answers are – so far, I’ve lost all my games of Pandemic.

Pandemic plays much faster than all other cooperative games, a game lasting little more than half an hour. It also has the simplest and clearest rules, and I’m a bit weary that it can become repetitive after a dozen games. This doesn’t mean, however, that the game is easy.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
"Pandemie" hat schon einige Jahre auf dem Buckel und es brachte schon viele erfolgreiche Ableger hervor. Die bekanntesten unter ihnen werden wohl die drei Legacy Teile "Pandemic Season 1", 2 und 0 sein.
Das Spiel begleitet mich seit nahezu Beginn meiner Spielerkarriere und ich glaube sogar, dass ich damit meine erste kooperative Erfahrung gemacht hatte.
Damals noch im Vertrieb von 'Pegasus Spiele', in einer größeren Schachtel verpackt und mit viel Holzmaterial steht es heute von 'Z-Man Games' mit Plastikpöppeln und -würfeln im Regal. Ich muss schon sagen, dass ich der alten Variante etwas nachtrauere, doch die war mit der zweiten und dritten Erweiterung nicht mehr kompatibel und so habe ich bereits vor Jahren entschieden, auf die neuste Version des Spiels 'upzugraden'.

In "Pandemie" schlüpfen die Spieler in die Rollen von Wissenschaftlern, Ärzten, Krisenmanagern und Co., mit dem Ziel, die Erde, bzw. dessen Bewohner vor vier kursierenden Krankheiten zu schützen.
Die Spieler agieren mit jeweils vier Aktionen pro Zug gegen das Spielsystem, das überwiegend durch Karten getrieben ist.
Mit Aktionen können die Spielfiguren auf dem Globus bewegt, Krankheiten in Form kleiner Würfel aus den Städten entfernt, wissenschaftliche Forschungszentren errichtet und schlussendlich die rettenden Heilmittel erforscht werden.
Einige der Aktionen erfordern zusätzliche Handkarten, deren Kartenfarbe oder sogar Standort wichtig ist. So kann beispielsweise ein Forschungszentrum in der Stadt 'Essen' nur mit der entsprechenden Karte errichtet werden und jede Stadtkarte gibt es im Deck nur ein einziges Mal! Um ein Heilmittel zu erforschen sind sogar fünf Karten der gleichen Farbe nötig! Das ist alles gar nicht so leicht zu bewerkstelligen.

Zu Hilfe kommen die eigenen, individuellen Charaktereigenschaften der Rollenkarten jedes Spielers. So kann beispielsweise die Wissenschaftlerin ein Heilmittel bereits mit vier gleichfarbigen Karten herstellen, was die Sache deutlich vereinfacht. Der Logistiker hingegen darf Spielfiguren der anderen Spieler bewegen, als wären es die eigenen. Und der Sanitäter kann mit nur einer Aktion alle Krankheitswürfel aus seiner Stadt entfernen, statt nur einem.
Am Ende des Zuges zieht der aktive Spieler zwei neue Handkarten vom Spielerdeck und muss danach welche vom Infektionsdeck aufdecken. Die auf diesen Karten angegebenen Städte erhalten jeweils einen (weiteren) Krankheitswürfel. Liegen bereits drei Würfel einer Art dort, geschieht ein Ausbruch und ALLE angrenzenden Städte erhalten je einen Krankheitswürfel!
Dies kann zu Kaskaden führen, die überhaupt nicht gesund sind!
Immer mal wieder tauchen Epidemiekarten auf. Dann muss der Ablagestapel der Infektionskarten gemischt und oben auf deren Nachzugstapel gelegt werden. Nun kommen alle bereits betroffenen Städte wieder an die Reihe!
Das Spiel kann auf unterschiedliche Weise verloren gehen: Beim achten Ausbruch, sobald der Spielerkarten-Nachzugstapel leer ist oder sobald zu viele Würfel einer Krankheit auf dem Brett liegen, also deren Reserve erschöpft ist.
Gewonnen ist es hingegen nur auf eine einzige Weise: Alle vier Heilmittel sind gefunden!

Das Spiel ist großartig. Obwohl es schon so alt ist, hat sich der Mechanismus mit dem Infektionskartenstapel nicht abgenutzt. Dieser fühlt sich immer noch sehr gut an und passt thematisch super zum Spiel. Krankheiten breiten sich vorwiegend in Städten aus, die bereits betroffene Einwohner haben. Doch auch andere Städte kann es hier und da mal treffen. Kümmern sich die Spieler nicht schnell genug um Eindämmung oder Behandlung, kommt es zu unkontrollierbaren Ausbrüchen.
Auch die Charaktere und deren Eigenschaften sind super für das Setting ausgedacht. Sogar die Sondereigenschaften sind stimmig und wirken je nach Spielsituation in etwa gleich stark.
Leider gibt es dennoch sehr starke und sehr schwache Konstellationen.
Ein Beispiel für ein überpowertes Duo:
- Forscherin: kann jede beliebige Handkarte an einen Mitspieler abgeben.
- Wissenschaftlerin: benötigt für die Heilmittelforschung nur vier statt fünf Karten.
Beide Spieler bleiben in der Anfangsstadt Atlanta stehen, der einzigen Stadt, die von Beginn an ein kostenloses Forschungszentrum hat. Alle Aktionspunkte der beiden Spieler werden allein dafür genutzt, Karten von der Forscherin zur Wissenschaftlerin zu geben, um dann mit ihr Heilmittel um Heilmittel zu entdecken.
Was derweil auf der Welt passiert, ist nicht wichtig. Ein paar Ausbrüche vielleicht, doch bevor es wirklich brenzlig wird, wurden alle Heilmittel erforscht und das Spiel ist damit gewonnen, ohne auch nur einen Fuß vor die Tür gesetzt zu haben.
Wer schon einige Partien gespielt hat, weiß um solche Konstellationen und vermeidet sie beim Spielaufbau.

Ich spiele "Pandemie" noch immer sehr gerne.
Auch meine Tochter liebt das Spiel, sodass wir mittlerweile alle Module aus allen Erweiterungen Stück für Stück dem Grundspiel hinzugefügt und ausprobiert haben.
Uns hat das 'Labormodul' sowie das 'Supervirus' sehr gut gefallen. Auch die 'Quarantäne' sowie die neuen Charaktere und Ereignisse sind leicht zu integrieren und spielen zukünftig in jeder Partie mit.

:thumbsup: [b]POSITIVE POINTS:[/b]

++ Very good medium-light weight coop gateway game that is usually really tense until the end.
++ The use of the infection deck that reuse the cities' cards in which infection has already occurred to propagate diseases in a thematically and mechanically sound manner that still include a bit of randomness (by shuffling the discard pile and putting it back on top of the deck).
++ The game user-chosen variable difficulty depending on the number of "Epidemic" cards uses (and can range from easy to nearly impossible).
++ Good replayability because of the randomness of the setup (both for the disease cubes placement but also the "Special cards" used for the game and the variable players' roles.
++ Variable players' power (role) assigned randomly at each game.
++ Great game insert which hold everything in an orderly fashion (base game and expansion, and you can use the OtB expansion insert to store everything in just one box).
++ The "On the Brink" expansion adds a lot of replayability and also challenge as the game difficulty can be enhanced greatly with more "Epidemic" cards, the "Virulent Strain" and the new Purple Virus.
++ There are expansions available for this game (which is useful to refresh the game when we have overplayed it).


:thumbsdown: [b]NEGATIVE POINTS:[/b]

-- A bit long to set up at the beginning of the game.
-- Being a coop game, it is prone to the Alpha Player Syndrome (where an experienced player can dictate other players everything to do to ensure a win).
