textfield_comment_value:
I like Pandemic but I think that it fails as a cooperative game. There are two important reasons for this: abstraction and necessity.

The game of Chess is an abstraction. The players are representative of two noble parties in feud as they compete over a given plot of land. The land itself is represented by a logical map and not a physical one. The individual pieces move in accordance with abstract rules, only loosely in keeping with the roles for which they are named - while it is true that a King relies greatly on his subjects or a mounted Knight might be afforded greater mobility, the nature of a Bishop's movement speaks more to play mechanics than it does any interplay between theology and monarchy. Similarly, games like Go and Checkers and even Tic-Tac-Toe are abstractions; they are oppositional games of strategy and tactics. Theme in these sorts of games is superfluous because the players are primarily engaged in left-brain activity.

Despite its dressing, Pandemic is also an abstraction. The theme of epidemiology might easily be substituted with one of farmers faced with the spread of weeds among their crops. The map, while seemingly more realistic than a chess board, remains a logical representation governed by arbitrary rules. Each player, assigned an appropriately themed identity, is granted unique abilities - and these abilities are incorporated to facilitate (or force) player interaction, not because they engender a personal relationship between each player and his or her given role.

The appeal of Chess is not diminished by its abstraction for two reasons: it pits players against one another and, further, it does not necessitate communication among players on the same team.

When you eliminate the opposing player, an abstract game is more akin to a puzzle. There remains no emotional investment of pride. The incentive of winning is reduced to the exercise of skill; and the challenge becomes merely a question of comprehension and complexity.

When you take an abstract puzzle - such as I characterize Pandemic to be - and you introduce the pretense of teamwork, you're going to run into trouble. People don't rally under abstraction. It takes necessity, language and sometimes even symbolism for people to unite.

Simply put: Pandemic allows for two-to-four players, but it only requires one. In fact, the aphorism that two heads are better than one doesn't even apply. Each additional player only introduces additional frustration.

The mechanics of Pandemic are not exceedingly complex. Many have already attested to the fact that on any given turn there exist only a few - sometimes as few as one - reasonable actions of play. Because of the manner in which played cards are reshuffled, a careful player can very easily anticipate and preempt imminent obstacles. The more you understand the mechanics, the easier the game becomes; and by extrapolation, a general solution can be devised and applied.

I approach Pandemic the same way I might approach Sudoku. Both are abstract puzzles, though they initially appear to be otherwise (beginners often mistake Sudoku for a math problem, however, the numbers could just as easily be substituted with the first nine sequential letters of the alphabet).

I suppose you could attempt to solve a Sudoku puzzle with a partner. Having identified the right number for a particular cell you might then explain to your partner why it is so. But your ability to communicate why it is the right number and, further, your partner's ability to understand you has no bearing on the solution itself. The number is either right or it is wrong, and the deciding factor is not dependent on a consensus of the players. What's more, to communicate this way for each cell would become exceedingly tedious.

Pandemic is cooperative in the same sense that Sudoku might be cooperative if you and your partner took turns with the pencil. A given player is no more or less empowered with respect to whose turn it might happen to be; the game is simply played by whomever identifies the next best action.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Pandemic is the newest in the recent fad of cooperative games, and seems to be one of the more promising entries for fans of straight Euro games.

Pandemic presents a deceptively simple concept: the board is seeded with disease cubes, and after each player's turn, more cards are drawn which create or amplify the disease issues. When an area would have more than 3 cubes placed into it, an outbreak occurs, spreading disease to the surrounding areas and generally causing chaos. The game is based on cooperation, and each player has a special ability that can allow them to combat the diseases in a slightly more efficient way: for instance, the medic allows a player to completely clear a city of disease for 1 action rather tha the 1 cube rate of the other characters.

Over the course of the game, players are also collecting city cards in the 4 coloured suits of the game. When someone has 5 of a colour, they can cash them in at a research station to cure the disease, and then it's just a matter of stamping it out on the board. If that is done successfully, then any cards representing that disease are ignored.

The thing that makes this game insidious is the epidemic mechanic. When an epidemic card is drawn from the "good deck" (which each player receives 2 cards out of each round) then all hell breaks loose on the board: a card is drawn from the bottom of the deck, and that place becomes triple diseased, and then the discard deck and that card are reshuffled and placed ON TOP of the negative deck. What this means is that the same cities keep reappearing, and when you combine that with the negative impact of having more than 3 cubes in a given city, the game can get ugly quickly.

So in terms of concept, this is an interesting game, certainly one of the best coops that I've played. The game is essentially one long puzzle game where each player has 4 action points to spend, and in-depth strategy discussions tend to break out as regularly as the diseases. The game is challenging enough to be interesting as well, which is a key for long-term interest.

The downsides, however, primarily do relate to the difficulty of the game. Though difficulty is partially dictated by the number of epidemic cards that are seeded into the positive deck, the game's difficulty also hinges heavily on how the negative deck ends up stacked. If one area's cards are all clustered at the top of the deck, a single early epidemic card can absolutely ream the players before they can even get going. Conversely, a very dispersed card distribution in the negative deck, or a run of the same colour early in the positive deck can make the game fairly relaxed, as a run of the same colour from the positive deck will result in an easy early cure or two, and dispersed diseases, when they occur, rarely will lead to outbreak chains. This isn't to say that the game is easy to win even given these circumstances, because the end can sneak up on you, but the ideal game experience seems to be somewhere in-between, and I'm not sure if there's a way to artificially manufacture that while still keeping the uncertainty that makes this game interesting.

I think my final feelings on this are pretty positive though. It's a short game with some interesting decisions, and some funny moments. If I'm in the mood for a game in this style (hourish co-op), it would probably be my first pick pretty easily but it's not exactly sitting in a crowded niche, and in a longer time frame I would prefer Knizia's LotR or (with 2) Arkham. 

As of 2016 I'd have to say this is great as a couple's co-op title, but that the Legacy version makes it a pale a bit by comparison.

As an aside: nice component quality: big cubes, thick, weighty cards, a sturdy but not overly glossy board. Kudos to Z Man for the job that was done on this one.

textfield_comment_value:
[2023] I tried Pandemic at the start of the pandemic with some friends on Tabletop Simulator. We played one game and won - frankly, it was barely even much of a challenge. What I recall about our experience was that there was a fair bit of quarterbacking which was not even necessarily our fault - the puzzle we were tasked with solving just felt painfully obvious given some of the luck that went our way. We were left with a bit of a "That's it?" impression. 

I never gave Pandemic much of a second look, largely because I came to learn that I would never be able to get Legacy games to the table despite all of the praise I have heard for it. As I have been revisiting a lot of games I had previously played on Board Game Arena, I decided to give it a try. Something I was immediately reminded of was how much I hate the visual design of the rulebook; personally, I believe there is a reason why there is both a "Commonly Overlooked Rules" section of the rulebook and a pinned thread titled "Common Mistakes" on Board Game Geek.

In my first game, someone lamented that I had set "Closed hands" in the settings. The two people with 600+ score proposed we concede during my third teammate's second turn, who had 50 ELO. Friendly reminder that Board Game Arena is not always beginner-friendly, and maybe will not match your expectations (Saboteur flashbacks...). We probably would have lost a few turns later regardless.

I gave it a few more chances playing Solo 2-handed to get more intimate with the mechanics. On my 3rd try, I got a win using Researcher and Scientist - with few exceptions, I barely had to move off my starting research facility. I cured the Black diseases near-instantly off lucky draws before curing Red a few turns later, so I largely dodged the first two epidemics. I cannot say I ever necessarily felt threatened, especially since the rules state that players can cure a disease at any research station; likewise, despite my fumbling, I cannot say I ever really had much of a chance at winning my first two games based on the epidemic triggers that occurred. Those two games went downhill too fast, and the epidemic spread everywhere too quickly to manage.

Sure, I went into Pandemic not expecting much, and here is a wall-of-text just reiterating that I did not feel much while playing. This disinterest is not surprising for me as I recently played Marvel United and was bored through most of it. At the same time, I would much rather be playing Marvel United compared to Pandemic. I own Spirit Island with a few expansions, but I have been struggling to get it to the table (despite keeping up on expansions...). There is no denying that Pandemic was a hugely-important game for modern boardgaming, but I'm willing to completely skip this one. Whether On The Brink!, Legacy Season 1, or Star Wars: Clone Wars would make me have a change of mind, I will probably never know - existence of strategy or not (card-counting will not make Pandemic more fun for me, sorry!), 

My opinion doesn't particularly change - the original Pandemic was woefully underwhelming. Chances are, most Pandemic games will feel particularly prone to 'alpha gaming' for me - with how difficult Pandemic is paired with how restrictive a player's turn is, my feeling is that players need to all be at roughly the same skill level for Pandemic to work. I laughed at someone else's comment describing their miserable experience with Pandemic where they described their experience when playing as the Researcher with experienced players as: "I was basically a doormat" (rating: 2, May 2023).
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Overall, my cooperative game crown still goes to Knizia's Lord of the Rings. But while Lord of the Rings is a co-op game that really requires a group of "gamers", Pandemic is a go-to game for any group of people.

The tension around the table is just palpable playing Pandemic, and the game plays in under an hour, so it's really perfect for a weeknight get together with friends. To succeed, team members must really plan things out together. If each player simply pursues his or her own "plan", then the group is sure to lose the game, especially on Normal or (god forbid) Heroic settings. Pandemic is an ultra-cooperative game. This is its greatest asset, but also the thing about it which I foresee will put me off a bit over time. There is little room for autonomy and self-determination. Success requires the closest sort of collaboration. So be warned: play this only with people you like! If you play it with someone you don't have a lot of patience with, you *will* want to throttle them. Pandemic throws very difficult situations right in the face of the players, and good brainstorming is required to win the game. If someone is being boorish and trying to "quarterback" the whole game, you will be driven to distraction. Likewise if someone is being an utter dolt and failing to grasp the plan that the group came up with.

Again, VERY tense. VERY exciting. LOADS of fun. But play it with the right people. Otherwise Pandemic possesses the potential to devolve into an exercise in frustration. It also shines with 3-4 players, but the tension is significantly less with only 2. This is because 2 players can tightly coordinate their actions, working as a team and moving more or less together around the world in order to cure the diseases. With 3 and 4 players, it's harder to get ahead of the intensity curve - the point where, after a few epidemics, you start infecting new cities without any disease (and hence a lesser chance of outbreaks). Because of this, I think 3-4 player games are actually slightly more challenging than 2 player games.

Components: the board is crap. The disease cubes, pawns, research stations, and cards are all just fine. But I'd shell out another $10 for a decent board. This one warps, wrinkles, smells funny, and peels up from the edge. I like the size of it, I like the art and design. It's the physical quality which is just dismal. That's a shame when it affects such a super game.

Update: this one has settled at a perpetual 7 for me. When I like it, I love it. But it's not really something I'm in the mood for any time, in plenty of situations I'd just rather not play it. You have to be in the mood to do the group-think thing, communicating extensively with the other players at every turn, in order to win. And sometimes, I feel that players can make all the right choices (optimal ones) and still lose due to luck and game balance. If this weren't so, it is true that Pandemic would lose some tension, as it would become a puzzle - solvable by an experienced group of players. That would be a shame, and a downfall. Yet the game falls down anyway, as once you ARE very experienced, it is frustrating to lose a perfectly played game. For some reason, this complaint doesn't arise for me when playing Lord of the Rings. The balance of choices in LotR maintains at least the illusion that your success depends only on your choices.

Anyway, despite my gripes I rate Pandemic a "strong buy" for its accessibility, tension, and short play-time.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
[2009-11-25 Rating: n.a. -> 7.5]

Overview:
--------------
Pandemic is a cooperative game where 2 to 4 players try to save the world by curing four deadly diseases. The map of Pandemic depicts the world with various cities. After each players turn, some of these cities are infected by placing cubes in it. If the infection rate of one of the four diseases reaches a cube limit of three in one city and this city gets infected again, an outbreak will occur and the disease will spread.
On their turn, a player can take up to four actions. These actions include:
- Travelling to another city.
- Building a Research Station (these are needed to find the cure for a disease and to travel faster)
- Lowering the infection rate of a city by being in it and removing some of the infection cubes.
- Exchanging city cards with other players.
- Finding a cure by being in a city with a research station and discarding a set number of city cards in the diseases colour.
After their turn, the player draws two new city cards and infects some new cities. After this, the play continues with the next player until one of the game endings conditions is met. These are:
1. Players run out of cubes representing one disease.
2. Players have 8 outbreaks happen.
3. Players run out of cities cards to draw.
4. Players find the cures for all four diseases.
Since Pandemic is a cooperative game, all players win the game when the fourth ending condition is met. If one of the other game ending conditions is met, all players lose and the game wins.

Comments:
---------------
* The card mechanism to infect new cities is really clever and well thought out. Because of its implementation, the same cities get infected again and again. While this puts some pressure on you, this also keeps the game from being too random or too deterministic (and thereby solvable). While you don’t exactly know when an infected city will be infected again, you do know that it will happen for sure. So there is some risk management and push your luck built into the game. I like this.

* The cooperative aspect has it pros and cons. What I like is the fact that I can easily get my non gamer friends to join in for a game of Pandemic. Since all players act together, there is no competition and this is quite appealing to them. The drawback of the missing competition is that some of them are not really involved in the game since they do rely completely on the evaluation of the other participating players. An often heard comment in this regard is: "I like this game because I don’t have to think that much. You can tell me what to do". This kills the fun a little for me.

* After playing my first few games I would have rated this game 9. After more plays with some of my gaming friends my desire to play this game cooled down a little bit. I still enjoy the theme immensely, but with experienced players I discovered the puzzle aspect of the game more and more. Basically the game is won if you manage to optimize your action selection. With experience, it is often times quite easy to see the best play and the discussions about the actions to be taken are replaced by a mutual agreement. I have to see if this issue is addressed in the expansion.

* Great replayability thanks to the different role cards and the great infection mechanism.

* I love the theme and it really helps to get new players to join in for a game of Pandemic.

Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
(Using BGG star rating system)

What it is
- Herofest - play as a group of everyday heroes taking on a not-so-everyday challenge of saving the world from a pandemic
- Quality - the components are great quality and really help sell the theme for what would otherwise be an abstract probability cruncher 
- Co-op - work together to beat the game

What it isn't
- Easy - variable settings means you can change the difficulty but our group has always struggled even on medium. About 50/50 win ratio at this level
- Nice - this is a mean puzzle and be prepared for strong disagreements around the table on how to beat the virus
- Long - games run true to time and feels fast

Liked
- Saviourism - I feel like I am really trying to save the world. There is enough theme to give an air of seriousness about the endeavour
- Delicate balancing act - so many ways to fail and only one way to succeed
- AI - a simple deck of cards cause terror when reshuffled replacing all of the previous infected destinations at the top of the deck after all of the work you did to clear the virus. Did you manage to clear enough infection cubes to prevent an outbreak?

Disliked
- Disputes - some sour moments when a disagreement on strategy leaves some players feeling marginalised, especially when you lose.
- Replayability - It is somewhat replayable as the destinations which come up mean the puzzle changes every time, but the puzzle is still the same. If you like this game definitely recommend getting an expansion or two to revamp the experience

Play if
- Solid game group - this would not be a great team builder. Rather more of a team tester
- Thrill-seeker - games, win or lose, come down to the wire. So well balanced that way
- Covid revenge - take on the virus and see if you can do it better than the real world leaders

Don't play if
- Looking for a quiet night - it's an exciting, tense experience 
- Trauma-warning - it is a game about viruses killing millions of people. Be cautious about which audience to bring this out with

Evaluation
A fun, tense and quick beat-the-game puzzle dressed in a compelling theme with high quality components. Just be sensitive about the theme with some audiences. This game was released long before the covid pandemic was a thing. I wonder if they would of handled the subject matter differently if it was made today>#? Nothing explicit or disrespectful built-in. 

Why missing out on the 10/10 spot?
Quarterbacking - experienced players will end up calling the shots rather than letting less experienced payers learn the puzzle for themselves. This limits player agency slightly. However, it is more of a nit-pick. A 10/10 would have given some way to have an equal role such as giving players hidden information. 

Similar games
- Risk - but pandemic is way better 
- Diplomacy - for negotiations and strategising 
- Plague Inc - but this time you play as the virus

Gateway Games
- Snakes and ladders - for young children as it trains them in the piece  movement 
- Dam it - teaches asymmetric starting point, dynamic board states and set collection

Recommendation
This is a staple of any board game collection. This was the game that got me into gaming in the first place so take that for what it is. Looking for an exciting co-op puzzle? This game is the best in the business.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Fun Factor: 1 
Components: 7
Theme: 8
Mechanics: 9 
Theme + Mechanics: 9
Replay Value: 9 (This thing wants you to replay it, nay, dares you.  Problem is, is it really worth it?)
Scaling/Players: 8
Subjective:  -0.50  As cooperative games go, I find this to be more of a multi player logic puzzle than a game.  Arkham Horror on the other hand, is unquestionably a game.  Perhaps great coops fall between this spectrum?

I will go down as a martyr here, but Pandemic just doesn't seem like a game to me. Granted, there are decisions to be made and player interactions to be had-- but really it just feels like one big logic puzzle to me. A puzzle does not a game make. Before somebody charges me with co-op rage, I love cooperative games. The active word being "games"  Cooperative puzzles, not so much.

Games differ from puzzles through:
Player interaction.
Dynamism.
No predetermined outcome.
Superior involvement of skill and chance.
A more active agent of antagonism.

I consider Pandemic to have little player interaction, be very static, and have a relatively predetermined framework within which the players muddle about believing that they can control the outcome. Chance and skill are severely muted within the context of Pandemic, and the agent of antagonism doesn't impress me, because after all it is just a sequence of shuffled cards that regurgitate. Sounds more and more like a puzzle.

Read this quote from Wikipedia on "Jigsaw Puzzle Strategy"...
Quote:
The most common approach to building a puzzle is to start by separating the edges from the inside pieces. Once the edges are built it can become easier to move inward. For those new to puzzles, it is recommended to choose one consisting of multiple areas with contrasting designs and colors. This enables the narrowing down of potential portions of the puzzle where a particular piece will fit.

Some people like to use the picture on the box to help solve the puzzle. Once you have completed the edge, if you can find the location of a particular piece on the picture, you can place it down inside of the overall puzzle at approximately the place it belongs. If you do this enough times, you find pieces eventually will start fitting together.

Another approach is to sort the pieces by color, and work on one color at a time. When you get to large areas with the same color (such as the sky in many landscape puzzles), you can go by shape, or you can place all the pieces in a grid and approach the problem by taking a piece that already has an anchor (such as an edge piece) and trying it against all the pieces laid out.
Strange, but this sounds an awful lot like a game of Pandemic.

The worst part is that you might even be working on a puzzle that cannot be won, so Pandemic probably does not fit the standard for even the most sadistic of puzzles. It is like a jigsaw puzzle that you are working on, and when you are looking the other way, the dog comes in and scarfs down a few pieces. Am I going to keep working the puzzle, or am I astute enough to sit up and take notice that some of my pieces are missing at this point so I might as well chuck this whole "Pandemic" thing in the trash and go play a thoroughly enlivened game of Twilight Struggle?

Also:  HOW IS THIS GAME RANKED SO HIGHLY ON BGG?  FOR SHAME.

textfield_comment_value:
I WANT to love this game, but I just don't. I keep trying and trying, I play it every now and again, but my issues with the game just never get resolved. 1) I hate how it scales...if you play at 4 players, you may not get a 3rd turn...no fun. 2) thematically, and mechanically, running out of resource cards is about the stupidest, contrived, and wholly arbitrary way to end a game as you can get, it's right up there with roll and move if you ask me, why not reshuffle the discards and keep on playing? Hate that. No game should end because you can't draw a freaking card. 3) 9 out of 10 games can basically be scripted as winning or losing simply by how the initial random layout goes (in combo with the first few turns) and/or the distribution of cards at the beginning of the game. If a player lucks into drawing their 3rd and 4th card of one color on their first turn...or the initial distribution is particularly nice...the game can be a breeze...and equally impossible to win, if everyone struggles to get a pair of same color cards turn after turn...and don't get me started on how annoying it is you have to be on the actual city to trade the city card...my god that's stupid. You should be able to at LEAST trade cards of the same color in the region of that color. For me, the game is WAY to dependent on random draws, random distribution of cubes, which means you can basically get easy games and impossible to beat games without any actual game play. 

I love the theme of the game, and the mechanics are great, the outbreaks, the moving around the board...I just think they created arbitrary limitations to gameplay which just jacks up the difficulty of an already difficult game to win. I've played the game dozens of times, won my first game, like 10 games in, solely by lucky draws, and though I have played games where it was fun right up to the end (win or lose), I still found myself frustrated by the dozens of losses that I never felt were a result of my gameplay...they were either unwinnable to begin with, or just one frustration piled upon another. Like when the initial cluster of cubes are all centered around central and eastern asia, and the first outbreak in the region causes a chain reaction that ends the game before the 3rd player in a 3 player game, gets a 2nd turn...that's no fun. There are just too many "no fun" outcomes to this game. I shouldn't have to house rule this game to make it fun. I don't know, maybe it's just the nature of the cooperative beast. I guess I'd just rather play a competitive game where every game there is at least one winner...than a coop game where 90% of the games end up with everyone losing. And again, it's not the winning or losing that make a game fun, I realize that, if I lose the game by the skin of my teeth and was THIS close to winning...that's great. It's losing game after game simply by chance and luck where it doesn't matter how well you play...that's just frustrating and not fun. That's where I am with this game.

Pandemic to dla mnie gra problematyczna.

Jest bardzo prosta, a więc odpowiednia dla początkujących. To plus. Równocześnie jednak jest za mało wszystkiego - to minus. I nie wynika to tylko z mojego zafiksowania na punkcie masy elementów (im więcej, tym lepiej!). Po prostu często mam wrażenie, że Pandemic jest... pusty. Sterylny. Za mało gracz ma możliwości, za mało jest interakcji między graczami jak na grę kooperacyjną, za mało się dzieje (bo tylko pojawiają się kolejne choroby, a mogłoby się zdarzać coś jeszcze, komplikacje związane z badaniami, reakcje opinii publicznej, cokolwiek). Nawet wrzucenie większej liczby kart losowych rozruszałoby rozgrywkę- jest ich za mało, a szkoda, bo naprawdę coś się dzieje, gdy rzucisz zdarzeniem i przerywasz nudę żmudnego leczenia chorób. Często myślę sobie - "ach, nudna ta gra, nie sięgnę po nią". I choć na początku intrygował mnie nieco klimat, pomysł z zespołem badawczym i chorobami, to jednak szybko się przekonałem, że brakuje tutaj tego, na co tak naprawdę liczyłem (kombinowanie z lekarstwami, jakieś poważniejsze działania laboratoryjne), a zamiast tego dostałem symulator pasażera linii lotniczych, który ma zbyt dużo wolnego czasu. Trochę kicha.

Równocześnie jednak jej prostota sprawia, że mogę sobie strzelić partyjkę niemal w każdym momencie (czego nie da się zrobić z Arkham Horrorem). Rozgrywka jest szybka i pełna napięcia, bo pandemia nie ogląda się na graczy, choróbsk pojawia się dużo i wirusy mnożą się jak króliki, toteż trzeba reagować prędko. Często nawet wkrada się panika do gry, kiedy to dochodzi do intensyfikacji i trzeba lecieć tu i tam, bo zaraz stracimy kompletnie kontrolę. A skoro nie masz za wiele możliwości działania, to odpada dylemat z Arkham Horrora (chciałbym robić coś ciekawszego, eksplorować dom wiedźmy, ale otwierają się kolejne bramy, więc nic z tego) - trzeba się skupić na jednym zadaniu i tyle. I jest to o dziwo dla mnie odświeżające. Rozgrywka jest elegancka, ma cel, jest - że się tak wyrażę - skupiona, nie ma tu miejsca na radosny chaos.

Czasami więc mam ochotę Pandemicowi obniżyć ocenę, bo rozgrywka nie sprawia mi radości. Kiedy indziej natomiast mam wrażenie, że moje szare komórki działają na pełnych obrotach i, uwijając się jak w ukropie, by świat nie został zalany przez zarazę, realizuję mozolnie swoją strategię, równocześnie reagując na najnowsze zwroty akcji. I wtedy gra jest piękna, wtedy uważam, że 7 jest zasłużona, a może nawet dałoby się 8. Być może zależy to od zestawu postaci biorących udział w grze. Być może niektóre zestawy serwują mi nudę, inne świetną rozgrywkę. Nie wiem. Jestem jednak pewien, że lepiej się ta gra sprawdza jako solówa niż kooperacja, bo kooperacji jest dość mało - zazwyczaj jeden gracz przejmuje inicjatywę i rozstawia innych po kątach, a pozostali potulnie realizują jego master plan i czasami się wręcz nudzą, bo są pionkami w grze alfa gracza. A może tak właśnie miało być? Może właśnie tak działają prawdziwe zespoły naukowców?

[i]Posted: 4/6/10, Rated: 9[/i]
{2P: 9, 3P: 10, 4: 8}

[i]Pandemic[/i] is one of those games that gets a tremendous amount of "buzz" here on the Geek.  It is a cooperative title, which means players are working together to beat the game instead of each other.  In this case, it means they are trying to find cures to four globally-threatening diseases.  The subject matter of global epidemics isn't sexy in the slightest, but it very quickly grows on you all the same.

The amazing feature of [i]Pandemic[/i] is how refined it is.  It embodies Albert Einstein's quote, "Make things as simple as possible, but not simpler."  Each player gets four action points per turn, and can choose from a list of basic and advanced actions.  Reference cards are provided, which is always a nice touch.  She can also use her role's special power; there are five roles provided in the game.  You would think that this recipe is bland enough for the game to feel "solved," but that's not the case.  After having played over 50 games online and in person, I am still surprised by the creativity of some players.

The method of spreading disease has been perfectly implemented.  Reshuffling the discard pile onto the top of the Infection Deck after an epidemic does a wonderful job of making sick places...sicker.  You dread the "Draw 2 Player Cards" phase of your turn as you feel an epidemic lurking around the corner.  There is a sense of urgency to do as much as you can to knock down the "hot spots" before the next one strikes.  Two epidemics in rapid succession can be fatal.

The difficulty of the game can easily scale by adjusting the number of "Epidemic" cards in the Infection Deck.  Player-wise, the game doesn't scale as well: the 2 player game is almost too easy (even at "Hard" difficulty), the 3 player game is perfection, and the 4 player game is very difficult.  Hand management is the differentiator: in a 2p game, it is easier for one player to find a "cure" by collecting five cards of the same color, only four cards if you have the "Researcher" role.  In a 4p game the cards are spread out, and players have to use turns trying to pass cards between each other instead of treating infected cities.  Minus one point for this lack of scalability.  Interestingly, [thing=40849]the expansion's[/thing] introduction of a "Legendary" difficulty provides a solution.

Cooperative games resonate with me, because they offer me a chance to teach a game, and also try to win at the same time.  [i]Pandemic[/i] has a theme which allows for a streamlined rule set which also provides a compelling challenge.  You can even [url=http://www.brettspielwelt.de/Spiele/Pandemie/]play it online for free[/url].  Don't be inoculated by all of the hype: [i]Pandemic[/i] really is a game you should try.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
A couple comments on the components. The cubes and research stations are a little large. The cubes are easier to manage because there will never be more than three of one color at one city. However, if you get three cubes and three pawns and a research facility all in one city, spillover will occur. It isn't that big of a deal, but makes it kind of fiddly. The infection cards are black and I worry about them standing up to repeated playing. They certainly do look sharp though.

The infection / epidemic mechanic is interesting. There are a couple of threads discussing the details. By reading the rules, it does seem counter-intuitive, i.e. drawing off of the bottom during an epidemic. However, through playing it does make sense as this introduces a completely new city to contend with, along with intensifying the need to control the cities currently that have been infected.

A couple of thoughts.  First, this game is accessible to all. The rules are well-written, well-illustrated and don't leave many questions. For some, it may initially appear intimidating, but the system is very elegant. I also believe that being a cooperative game makes it less intimidating - everyone is working together. Second, I am wondering if three people is an optimum number. This gives three roles available in the game and doesn't dilute the player deck too much. Third, I can't see how you can win this game without the researcher. Every game I have played has included the researcher and that player has been the key to getting information to the right players. The medic is nice, but without the medic the strategy becomes controlling the cubes rather than eliminating them. The scientist can be helpful, but usually there are enough cards to pass around that one less isn't a deal breaker. The dispatcher, in my opinion, would be the second most important role. The operations expert is the weakest, and needs a secondary power such as immediately being able to move to any research station from any other city. Finally, the game isn't over until the final cure is reached. Games go from being won in two turns to being lost due to having no more cubes in stock due to outbreaks.

After a couple more plays I have increased my rating of this game. It is fun, and I enjoy playing it. In addition, my wife is already trying to figure out when the next time we will have people over so we can play. I reminded her that we can play with two, and she was ready to set the game up right then.

textfield_comment_value:
Pandemic is the only coop game I've ever played.  I never really saw the appeal of coop games until somebody brought this in to work.  After my first play through I knew I needed to buy it.

In Pandemic you and the other players are all trying to cure 4 diseases before they outbreak too much and just become unmanageable.  You will start with 9 random cities with disease cubes on them, the first 3 get 3 cubes, the next 3 get 2 cubes and the last 3 get 1 cube.  The world is grouped into 4 regions (denoted by colors) for each of the 4 diseases.  The starting cities get the color of disease cube for the color of city they are.

Each player now takes a special role that will help them specialize in things that will help out in the game.  Now the players need to build research stations, remove disease cubes, share knowledge, and eventually cure all 4 diseases.

The difficulty comes from the constant onslaught of disease cubes.  After each players' turn the next cities are flipped over and receive disease cubes.  If a city gets flipped over and it is already at 3 cubes it then outbreaks giving one cube to each city attached to it.  Throughout the player deck epidemics are included, as these come up you get a brand new city with 3 cubes.  In addition all those cities you've already been adding cubes to, yes those ones you've been removing cubes from as well, get shuffled and thrown right back on top to add even more cubes.

This is a rewarding game.  It is fun to work together and not have to come up with the strategy all by yourself.  It might be good to play the first few times with open hands, but I wouldn't do that for long.  It might be easier, but it seems like it turns into 1 or 2 people running the whole game.

I gave this a 7 because it is quick to play and offers a lot of tough decisions in that short amount of time.  If you lose, at least it was only 15 or 20 minutes so you can easily get in another game to try and win.  If playing with only 4 epidemics becomes to easy, just add one.  Once you get up to 6, which is the most for the base game, things get really tough, so you will never feel like this game is too easy.  I love this game and I am really looking forward to the expansion On the Brink.

textfield_comment_value:
This is an extremely well-designed game with a unique and clever theme that I just don't enjoy all that much.  It's absolutely worth playing if you like co-ops though, just because it's so dang smart.  

The best example of cleverness in this game is that, unlike in so many other co-ops, the bad stuff that happens to you is not [i]completely[/i] random.  After each epidemic, the cities that were infected last round get shuffled and placed on top of the deck.  This means that the same cities will be infected over and over again.  This not only makes the situation more desperate (building tension), but also means that you can really strategize around the cities that you [i]know[/i] will come up (just not exactly when).  Everything seems to be designed around these basic tenets of controlled randomness, building tension, and partial information.

Clearly, I respect this game a lot.  I just don't love it.  The biggest problem for me is an extremely petty one: I hate preparing the deck before each game--shuffling the cards, dealing out the hands, dividing the rest into little stacks, shuffling an epidemic card into each stack, and stacking them all on top of each other. Blah!  If someone else would take this job off my hands, I would like Pandemic much more.  This is evidenced by my greater like for Forbidden Island, which is very similar without the deck building business.

The second problem is that the game just feels "samey" after a while.  Everyone I've introduced it to loves this game, so we play it fairly often, and it just always feels very similar.  The consistency of the game is part of what makes the design so smart, but ultimately it hurts it a bit in my eyes.  You never play a game of Pandemic and say, HOLY CRAP THAT HAS NEVER HAPPENED BEFORE!!!  I'm hesitant to say this is because the game isn't random enough because it's true that you get fluky situations like 5-6 of your first cards all of one color (leading to a quick loss).  I think it has more to do with how constraining the game is in general, leaving not many opportunities for truly creative play by the players.

The expansion does help mix things up quite a bit, and it breathed a bit more life into Pandemic for me.  And of course, as I've already stressed (and is reflected in my score), I think Pandemic is a very smart game in a lot of ways.  I just don't have enough fun while playing it.

---

Update over a decade later: BGA has totally rejuvenated this for me. I play with a group that did two seasons of Pandemic Legacy together, and the vanilla game is still challenging and great fun. We play both async (strategizing in the chat) and occasionally synchronously with Zoom. Not having to prep the decks is also really nice!

textfield_comment_value:
3/10/09
-----------------------------

[i]Pandemic[/i] is a co-operative game where the players are researchers from the Centre for Disease Control in Atlanta, and are attempting to contain the global outbreak of four deadly diseases before the world succumbs to the plague. The game supports 2-4 players, though there is a variant available for a Solitaire game. This game uses networks and a few new ingenious mechanisms to simulate the spread of disease across the globe.

In order to cure the diseases, the players need to collect sets of cards from a deck, and then turn these sets of cards in at research centres around the world. The caveat is that within the deck the players draw cards from, there are special epidemic cards, which intensify the situation on Earth, bringing the players one step closer to their destruction, of which there are three ways that it can happen. These are the players running out of cards to draw from, more than 8 outbreaks occurring, or if there is more disease on the globe than they can cope with, simulated by running out of cubes to put on the board for a specific colour of disease.

[i]Pandemic[/i] is a fun game because of the interaction between the players, and the ideas and discussion that is generated as each person decides what to do on their turn. There have been accusations of [i]Pandemic[/i] being a ‘puzzle’ rather than a game, and I agree, but it is seeing whether you can beat the puzzle with your wits that forms the heart of the game, rather than anything else.  [i]Pandemic[/i] can suffer from one person dominating the game, telling everyone what they should do, and this is a big problem, in fact, one of the main reasons why I do not rate it higher, as it can ruin the discussion that makes this game what it is. It is hard to enjoy yourself when someone, who is usually right, is dictating your every move.

In conclusion, [i]Pandemic[/i] is a game that includes many unique decisions and mechanisms within it, which give it a feel unlike any other game I have played. It is this that keeps me coming back to the game, as well as the immense replayability resulting from the different difficulty settings and variable player amounts. The only problem is the possible domination of the game by a single player, most often occurring with players of varied experience levels.

[b]Pros[/b]
- Variable difficulty levels
- Good interaction and discussion
- Requires good planning and co-ordination

[b]Cons[/b]
- Can be dominated by a single player
- Difficult to play with different expereince levels

textfield_comment_value:
Visual Appeal: (4)
The board and pieces look really nice and streamlined. I have the older version, and from what I have seen, the newer one looks a tad better. One pet peeve is that the map has cities in some odd places. I suppose it is just to fit the words and other graphics comfortably, so I can get over it.
 
Components: (5)
I am playing every game with the first expansion now, and it really enhances some of the components. I love the petri dishes and the smaller pawns are a sensible touch. Cards all feel nice and they aren't wearing too quickly. I like the tracks on the board because they're easy to read and access for all players.

Theme: (5)
Best part of the game is theme. Unlike other games whose theme could be considered nerdy or boring, this one stands out as a player magnet. I can also dig the more-equal-than-usual gender representation in the game. Welcome to the modern age, boardgames, where women do sciencey things too; they don't just pose in futile chain-mail bikinis! Getting back to the topic at hand, the game does a great job making you feel like you are cooperating to save the world from certain doom. Even the likelihood of failure is well simulated. In case you haven't played the game, that is a very HIGH likelihood on harder settings.

Learning: (4)
This is on the list of many people's gateway games. I believe it is rightly on that list because it is easy to learn and fairly low pressure. I mean, the game is hard, but you don't have to worry about experienced players laying the smackdown on you. In fact they will be helping you. Which means, only a short intro is needed before you can jump right in and learn through experiencing the game. Difficulty settings are really well balanced for the casual and hardcore players alike. 

Gameplay: (4)
I only say 4 due to the ever present Alpha Gamer problem in co-op games. Really if you feel the need to control everyone's actions, you shouldn't be playing this type of game, but it happens. Sharing cards is a challenge and provides players with good points of discussion on how to use their actions the most efficiently.

Overall Fun: (5)
This game has been a huge hit with even my non-gamer or casual gamer friends. It is low pressure enough that everyone feels comfortable jumping in. I always enjoy teaching it and watching the horror on new players' faces as the realize how tough some decisions actually can be and what sacrifices need to be made to save the world! This is my go-to Co-operative game without a doubt.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Don't even start with the Alpha-Player argument! 

As an Alpha,having played this game enough times to buy a replacement, don't be a schmuck-ask players questions,include players, and let players play.  By the 3rd game, most players have found their voice and have caught on to the game.  The only times I have ended up grossly Alpha-Playing is when I teach the game to a whole group of new players.  Don't do that.

The great thing about this coop game is that the randomness is predictable and risk assessment good.  At first, it seems like the cards are stacked against you; but as you master the game, you can make calculated risks and weigh your choices.  This means that your choice has value.  When we loose a game, I can generally point to a choice we made that didn't pan out during the game.  That makes me feel in-control; unlike Robinson Crusoe. Additionally, it is that weight and calculated risk that keeps good-players guessing, there is no standard tactic, obvious choice, or methodological mechanics that makes the game rote for good-players; unlike Castle Panic.  This means that every game is different enough so your choice has meaning and your decision will shape the game.  That is a difficult balance in coop games.

Suggestions for Alphas: 
1) Don't teach a whole group of newbies-they will all look to you for decisions, letting you play the game for them.
2) Introduce the game to a group with another player who has played the game.  Let that player go Alpha, you get to be the Obi-wan of the game and be a mentor.  Hint-Ask questions of the new players.
3) If you are introducing Pandemic, then just introduce to a single newbie.  Play the two player game, it will be quick and you can play again, and again, and again, until they really start grasping the game.
4) Don't be the Scientist, Researcher, or Medic; make the newbies be those characters.  These characters abilities directly affect the game and bring a sense of glory during a loosing game.  Contingency Planner is always a good character to take when teaching the game.  
5) Throw the first game.  If the group easily wins the game, then most players will dismiss Pandemic; probably because someone Alpha-played.  If you loose, those competitive players' aggression starts to come out, and then they want to beat the game.  With a bit wise mentoring, these players can encourage other players' voice.  By the end of the night, you got a group of coop gamers talking over each other. Just lovely.

Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Pandemic pits the players against four diseases (blue, red, black and yellow) spreading over the world. The goal is to find cures for all four before time runs out, the diseases become too widely spread or too many outbreaks occur.

Players need to collect and discard sets of five cards of each different color, one set for each disease. Given that there are twelve cards of each color, a hand limit of seven cards and limitations of trading cards accumulating those cards can be tricky. The cards can also be discarded for faster travel and to build research stations which further reduces the available cards. Players start with four cards each in hand and draw another two from the player deck at the end of their turn. If a player has to draw cards and the player deck is empty, players lose.

The diseases spread each turn by drawing from an infection deck, placing more disease cubes on the map. If the infection cubes of any disease runs out, players lose. Infections can also lead to outbreaks, when a city that is already at three infection cubes is hit. No cube is added to the city, but all cities connected to is are infected, which can lead to chain reactions. If eight total outbreaks occur, players lose.

Apart from the city cards, the player deck also contains event cards that provide benefits to the players and epidemics (5 for a standard game). If an epidemic is drawn, the infection rate is increased, leading to more infection cards being drawn each round. Then an infection card is pulled from the bottom of the deck and infected with the maximum of three infection cubes. Lastly the infection discard pile is shuffled and placed back on top of the infection deck. This means cities already infected will be drawn again.

If the players on the other hand manages to clear all infection cubes of a cured disease, that disease is eradicated and cannot infect again.

The players have to weigh multiple priorities over the course of the game. Treating infected is important, but so is trading city cards between players. Should a player hold on to a card or use it to build a research station or travel by plane to a city threatening to outbreak? What color to hold on to?

Despite being a fairly simple game, it has enormous replay value. At the time of writing I have 77 logged plays and I'm still not tired of it.

Make sure to try it as soon as possible!

textfield_comment_value:
Well we ended up playing this game 9 times in one setting!  There were four of us for the first 4 games or so then we ended up adding a fifth for the remaining games.  None of us had ever played it before.  The game overall is pretty easy to pick up...think I read the manual twice and had about 90% of the game down (looked over some subtle nuances).  Probably took the rest of the group 10-15 minutes to get a good grasp of the rules and I'd say by the end of the second or thrid game anyone at the table could have taught the game with ease.  

In terms of playing we went 0-9.  I think the first three maybe four tries everyone was really into it and having a good time.  After that though I think some of the guys started to get a little pissed off at the fact that they were getting their asses handed to them by the board game and insisted on playing another game to try and save a little pride.  In the end though our efforts were fruitless and the game prevailed everytime.

For me though overall I had a great time playing in all 9 games.  The game played out quick and rules were simple enough and you really believe the first few rounds that everything is good...or that you have a fighting chance.  But I will say things sprial out of control real quick.  

I strongly recommend that people new to the game play out the introductory lvl at least once if not a couple of times before progressing.  Part of our problem was that we progressed to the heroic after the first game and of course the heroic lvl is as advertised...quite diffcult!

On a final note this game probably won't make our weekly gaming rotation mostly due to the fact that it is a co-op game.  It provides a nice change of pace for the group but we tend to be more competative with each other (I guess I mean to say that we get to much satisfaction out of kicking each others' asses).  That said though I'm sure we'll sneak it in a time or two a month!  

**Edit** Played this with the wife and she seemed intrigued with it...got multiple plays in...also the gaming group was interested in playing again...going to bump this up a little to an 8

***Edit***  Has grown a bit stale.  Suffers from a dominant person or two suggesting all the moves.  Haven't played with the expansion yet so would like to try it. Bumped down to a 6 which is probably were it will stay.

textfield_comment_value:
Kurz: "Pandemie" soll ein kooperatives Spiel sein? Ist das überhaupt Thematisch?  ->Ich erinnere nur an 1,5m-Abstandsregeln, max. 2 Haushalte und Co.  ^^  ...Scherz beiseite. Die Mechaniken mit Epedemie, Ausbrüchen und Forschung funktioniert super und erzeugen u.A. eine gute Vorstellung von Krankheitsausbreitung. Und wir, als Forschungsteam, müssen eng  zusammenarbeiten um die Gegenmittel zu erforschen.

Langform:
Ich würde behaupten, dass es eines der wenigen kooperativen Spiele ist, dass eine durchgängig hohe Spannungskurve bietet. Außerdem ist es eines der ersten Spiele, die ich kennenlernen durfte. Es hat mich damals in den Bann gerissen und gezeigt was so möglich ist. (Allg. Brettspielbezogen, Thematisch, wie auch Mechanisch) Insgesamt sehr empfehlenswert.
Pro:
-Es gibt mehrere Möglichkeiten das Spiel zu verlieren -> Das macht es erst so spannend.
-Thematische Umsetzung (z.B. wie sich die Krankheiten ausbreiten, erforscht wird oder wie man in Krisenregionen gelangt)
-schnell gespielt für ein (gehobenes) Kennerspiel
-Karten können für unterschiedliche Aktionen genutzt werden, ohne dass diese mehrere Karten-Bereiche haben. (wie es bei anderen Multi-Use-Karten üblich ist)
-Grafische Gestaltung mag ich sehr (kenne nur 3. Edition)
-klare, kompakte Regeln (3. Edition)
-miteinander Absprechen, was als nächstes getan werden sollte.
-Anpassung Schwierigkeitsgrad (durch Anzahl Epedemie-Karten)
-Charackterboni (variable Spielerpower, bisschen Varianz)
Neutral:
-Hat paralelen zur realen Pandemie mit Corona, der letzten 3 Jahre
Kontra:
-Glück/Pech: Einmal hatten wir die Partie verloren, ohne das der 4. Spieler überhaupt einen Zug hatte. (in höchster Schwierigkeit)
-"Alpha-Leader-Problem": Wenn jmd. durch mehrere Partien Erfahrungen sammeln konnte und die anderen nicht, wird meist das gemacht, was der Erfahrene Spieler "empfiehlt" (/bestimmt)
-Es fehlt etwas Varianz und ist daher kein Spiel was regelmäßig innerhalb kurzer Abstände gespielt wird, sondern immer mal wieder

Edit:
Habe nun die alte, als auch die neue Version gespielt. Die Verbindungen auf dem Spielbrett der alter Edition sehen so gedrungen aus. Und auch wenn ich Holz eigentlich besser finde, machen die halbdurchsichtigen Plastik-Würfel in den neueren Versionen schon was her. Ansonsten scheint es mir das sich zumindest spielerisch nichts geändert hat.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
I love the theme. I really feels like a race against time to eradicate nasty, flesh-eating, puking death before it consumes the world around you.
However- this game is a puzzle, and you have to play it cooperatively. That means it has two big strikes against it: 
1. Dominating players will end up telling you what to do.

2. They are frequently right.

There is usually "one best option" to take, and if you don't do it, or maybe you didn't see it at first, the game is OVER. 
It's just OVER, and it's suddenly your fault that Aunt Minnie in Chicago died on the toilet along with half the population of North America.

Similar to Castle Panic, Forbidden Desert, Defenders of the Realm, and other cooperative games -if you don't do the "next right thing," you're toast. Or in this case, a quivering, feces soiled, vomit-covered invalid who just lost the game for everyone because you wanted to take that flight to Buenos Aries to cure the black plague. Who knew the red Captain Tripps virus was about to break out in Moscow?
We knew, you moron. 
And you didn't listen to us.

Get out.

Okay, maybe we were harsh with you, but this game does create a real sense of tension, and when outbreaks occur you almost can hear the screaming humanity.
It's difficult to win, but early on, you will win a few times - mostly because you were playing it wrong.
That happens a lot. 
There are so many house rules for Pandemic, I'm sure Z-Man games is trying to come up with a vaccine for them. It can get a little "fiddly" especially if you forget your characters power, or don't follow the outbreak rules just right. Since it is very hard to win, I think that's where all the house rules pop up. This is often the first co-op game many new players experience, and the concept of losing as a team with the game lurching to sudden halt realy surprises them. Look at everyone's reaction on Will Wheaton's table top when they loose Pandemic. Look at Morgan Webb.  
Yes, let's do that for a while.
Mmmmm. Morgan Webb.

I'd like to buy the On the Brink expansion, but I just don't get to play this game enough to justify the expense. If this is the first game you use to expose your friends to co-operatives, then explain to them about the fun of playing without actually winning. 
It may go down as less of a bitter pill when they loose.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
(Since On the Brink feels basically mandatory, this review is for Pandemic with On the Brink within reach)

My opinion as a gamer:
Pandemic on easy (4 epidemics) and open hands feels very average -- the correct course of action seems obvious at all times. But the premise and art are solid, and it picks up dramatically with the variety that the On the Brink modules add. It's a lightweight gamer's game and serves as a decent gateway. It's easy to teach; it makes sense by the time everyone is done their first turn. It's got a compelling theme and nice pieces. The difficulty is adjustable. Since it's co-op, people with poor sportsmanship won't be sore losers. The game also (usually) runs less than 90 minutes no matter the player count. It's alright.

My opinion as a host:
Although I would rather play Pandemic than Ticket to Ride, I feel something is missing for the more casual audience this is geared towards. On the Brink modules never seem to be a hit with more casual groups. Pandemic in general also seems to take a long time to set up due to the sheer amount of shuffling and dealing and re-shuffling involved. The stock insert sucks and does almost nothing to aid setup. Casual players get easily disappointed by losing, which seems to keep happening at any difficulty above vanilla with four epidemics -- I will start introducing expansions on a Very Easy difficulty to avoid scaring people if this ever hits the table again. It's very easy for inexperienced people, on easy, not to cure enough diseases even if this is my singleminded focus of the group from minute 1 (without alpha-ing the group). The game also has way too much downtime as people repeatedly fumble around with cards and wait for others to move and optimize their turns.

I think that this is a good intro gamer game for gamers, but seems to be missing something that it needs to be a good gateway game for normal people.

As an aside: Pandemic's biggest problem for normal gamers is the alpha gamer (me, usually) who has to fight the urge to coordinate everyone, and On The Brink just lets you slam that player in the bio-terrorist bin where they can have fun being the villain in their own corner. This is a hilariously effective solution.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
The basic story for the game is that you are scientists working for the CDC trying to cure four deadly diseases sweeping across the world. Failure results in global eradication of human population... so try not to fail.

At it's base it's a cooperative strategy game which plays out more as group puzzle solving. If you don't play well with others then you are going to want to keep moving. 

In Pandemic each player takes their own turn, what they do is ultimately their decision, but the nice part is that anyone can talk about what actions should be taken during each turn. It makes every turn a group discussion which adds a little length to the game but makes it a team effort. If you have a team working well you can knock out a game in about 45 minutes, but on the flip side it can take a full hour and a half if things aren't going smoothly within the group.

This game is difficult, no sugar coating, but it just makes the actual victories that much sweeter. The game does scale to player skill level so less experienced players can play an intro game and people well versed can play at settings that give the same feeling as the waiting room at your proctologist.

A downsides to the game is that it can lead to someone taking over as table captain. Occasionally someone will feel, for one reason or another, that they are the smartest and therefore their suggestions should be exactly what the entire group should do. My response to this is that the meek should speak up! Just about every school I've been to the teacher always said "There is no such thing as a stupid question" and in Pandemic that is absolutely applicable. Your idea might not be the greatest for the situation, but part of your idea might be useful. I've had many games where I thought A+B=C, then someone suggests A+D=F, to which we then come up with D+B=W... W for winning! Bottom line is you should voice your opinions. If you are a quiet talker then use your legs to kick people until you are heard out. 

Personally I love co-op games. I really enjoy seeing how other people are working on the same puzzle as opposed to how I am working it out. Pandemic scratches that itch to the point my leg involuntarily shakes.

Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
It’s a solid cooperative game, and with an extremely simple set of rules it is a phenomenal gateway into more complex cooperative games.

Though, I feel, it suffers one of the many pitfalls of deck games - it is extremely swingy. Not even that it is too random per se, but rather the cards can literally be stacked against your favor. I found that most play throughs feel like a loss was predetermined, or a win was suspiciously ‘too easy.’ This is a difficult problem to come across in a game, because losses can feel unwarranted and wins do not feel victorious. It’s a tough critique for me to flesh out too - I don’t necessarily think the game’s best actions are too obvious (e.g. Forbidden Island), or that the best actions are too obscured, but rather that you feel like you can never do enough. 4 actions is surprisingly limiting, and pulling bad City cards is brutal, not to mention trading them is a nightmare.

Margins are thin in this game, and it makes the cooperative element less about ‘what can we do by coming together’ and more ‘what can we decide is best together’ - turns taken one at a time become a discussion of what’s the best course of action for a character, instead of a player coming to a conclusion on how to best help the team. This exacerbates the prior critique, that losses feel collectively unjustified, and wins feel collectively undignified.

That is the thrust of my critiques about the game - now for the positives. This game creates, holds, and builds tension excellently. Flipping over cards to reveal Epidemics is ominous and captures everyone’s attention. Reshuffling the infection deck and pulling and outbreak takes the game up a notch. Every game I have played, everyone is always zeroed in on the home stretch. The game is extremely collaborative, and the simplistic rules allow for all players to be engaged and involved in discussion without ever having to pull out a rulebook to better understand what’s going on.

The simplicity really is a marvel - just a glance at the board is all it takes to understand what’s going on. How to go about doing it is an entire other task, and is what makes the game a joy to play with friends.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
““Disease is the retribution of outraged nature.” -Hosea Ballou

I found it on the interweb (not verified). I had to look Hosea up but the quote captures the moment.

GAMEPLAY
A co-operative game where the players try to stop the spread of 4 deadly diseases across the globe in the largest cities in the world. On a player’s turn, you may move around the world, halt the spread of a disease or with gathered resources cure a disease. The game works against the players, but each has a special ability to help slow the spread of the disease, move around the board faster, or more quickly find cures. A common issue with co-op games is that they can really be played by a single person. This is a fair comment and I have played it solo several times, its tons of fun. If you are playing in a group make sure that there is not a single player directing everyone, try to allow each player to have space to decide how to play so that everyone stays engaged.
COMPONENTS
The most important game pieces are the infection cubes in four different colors. I was thinking that it would be cool to have microbes of different shapes but the cubes simplicity keeps the board well organized and a quick visual sweep of the board gives a clear understanding of the crisis. The cards and board are of good quality and the art is clear but not remarkable.
THEME
An excellent unique vision for a game. Cinematic gameplay. The first time I played with my brother it felt as though we were flying around the world to hold off the infectious threat. The tension builds throughout the game as outbreaks build. Every time I have played the outcome has been extremely close. This building tension is a credit to the game mechanics and how the theme integrates extremely well with the rules.
WHO IS IT FOR?
Casual, non-competitive play is found here. With the game rushing the players towards the inevitable doom of mankind, its fairly simple gameplay will be entertaining for most. I have played solo and its fun but its designed for 2 to 4 players. Games last about an hour. This game is not heavy and there is a small amount of determinism as the card stack can prevent victory but not too often.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Generally, I’m not a fan of cooperative games.  They strike me as less of a game and more of just an ‘activity’ to engage in with friends/co-players.  Its a case of, ‘let’s all get together to play a game of solitaire’ and Pandemic is no different.  I guess what makes Pandemic better than most cooperatives is that: it is, what it is, in its purist form with rules and mechanics that are fast, clean, straight-forward, intuitive and very streamlined.  
With an average game length of about one hour, I feel that’s about the right amount of time for a this game (as long as it doesn’t go over 60 minutes).  The game is essentially a puzzle, but even to the most experienced player, whether you win or lose is randomly pre-determined based on how the cards are, literally, stacked-against-you or for-you before the game begins.  
There are several options every round, but really there is always ONE option that is undeniably best and inevitably it’s the most experienced player that sees it (I’m sure even if he actively choose to hold back, it would be frustrating from his perspective and truthfully not really beneficial to winning the game in the end).  And thus, like most cooperative games, I don’t really feel I have any personal vested interest in the game and just want to sit back and let the alpha-player do his magic.  Thus the nature of cooperatives makes us ask, ‘do we fundamentally play games to win, or is it the game-play that is solely fun.’  If we play to win, then let the alpha-player take the lead.  If we play to enjoy the brain-burning aspect of figuring out a puzzle to best of our abilities, then best to play as a solitaire game (I’m sure it would be a frustrating time for the alpha-player to sit back and let players engage in less-efficient options).  
Perhaps this game really works best as a solitaire game (a field that I have zero interest in).  
Among cooperative games, I currently like 2010’s “Forbidden Island” best.  That game’s 30 minutes game time hits a perfect sweet-spot for these types of games/activities and the theme there is a bit more flavourful and imaginative to hold one’s attention.
Title: Pandemic

Includes:

[u]06-Feb-2013[/u]: I think this was the fist co-op game I played after getting into the hobby, and it has spiraled from there.  First, I do enjoy working together with the other players to defeat the game.  I don't have trouble with the "alpha player problem" since I only play with my family and, on the rare occasion, my two buddies.  Second, I enjoy the puzzle aspect of most co-op games.  That is something that attracts me in games.  And finally, and probably most importantly, I can play them solo controlling any number of players.

So, what about this one in particular?  I think it's fantastic.  I like the theme of fighting against ever spreading diseases around the world.  I like all of the various roles (especially when you include the On The Brink expansion).  The "AI deck" is a fantastic, and brutal, mechanism to play against as it continues to add more and more trouble on the map.  The replayability is very high, in my opinion, as the set up varies from game to game, roles mix and match in interesting ways, the difficulty level can be adjusted, and with On The Brink, three additional options can be added to the base set of rules to really liven things up.

I really can't say anything negative about this game.  However, I think you can give yourself help if you "count cards."  Personally, I don't do that.  Of course, I'll have a general idea of what may be coming up next, but I try not to memorize everything that has happened with the AI deck and what is still to come.  I like being surprised and that tension of not exactly knowing what will happen next.  Maybe that's just me.

[u]24-Jan-2014[/u]:  Man, I can't believe it's been six months since I've played this...what is wrong with me?  Such a great co-op game.  I still hold this one in high regard even though so many co-ops have arrived...and landed in my collection...since.  I would easily recommend this one to any gamer, new or otherwise, interested in a solid, challenging co-op experience.  Oh, and definitely pick up the first expansion for additional options and even more replayability.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
After all these years I'm still torn on my opinion of Pandemic.  On one hand I cannot like it that much as I've sought out many a replacement be it Defenders of the Realm or even something like Zombie State.  In the end though I've lost interest in those alternatives while still not disliking Pandemic.  I think perhaps my issue is in not having liked Pandemic quite enough to have explored the expansions to which I hear the On the Brink one can be considered quite essential.  Perhaps it didn't exist back when I played it with others who were far bigger fans (and perhaps we suffered too much from Alpha Gamers bossing us around at the time!).

I do know that the base game by itself I don't really prefer vs. Forbidden Desert which also has similar role cards and cooperative mechanics.  My wife also finds the theme of Pandemic very morbid while our son tolerates it when I explain it differently.  I do prefer certain things about Pandemic in the way outbreaks occur and are managed but, at least in the 3 player game, we've found it hard to eradicate a cured virus altogether such that it almost seems not worth the effort.

Overall I think there is now a permanent place for it in our collection though, along with Pandemic Lite (Forbidden Desert) and a Pandemic Thematic (Currently looking at Defenders of the Last Stand).  So I'm hoping to think more highly of Pandemic once I acquire some expansions and view it as more of an Advanced Game version.

Odd to find a place for 3 different versions of the same game in a collection when none of them are particularly my favorite but I guess over time the pandemic sort of gameplay has become not unlike worker placement or deck building or something like that which is easily something you'd have a few different versions of even if not quite your favorite thing.

I really like the new box cover art for the entire Pandemic series.  Nice job there.  The current editions bits looks really great as well and the card quality is perfect.  I think that might have helped my opinion of the game a little bit.

I've not really lost yet, so I don't know how true that is.Pandemic is a very slick attempt at a cooperative game. The main problem with it isn't a problem with the game perse, it's a problem with the Genre. One domineering, loud, or stubborn player basically plays everyone's hand. In fact, in order to maximize the chances of winning this is really the optimal strategy. Ideally, everyone collaborates to determine the best course for everyone, but that one loud guy can ruin the fun for the other players by saying "you do this, you do this, and you do this!" Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Pandemic is an excellent game that is worthy of shelf space for several reasons:
1) It's very different from the usual Euro.  Co-op play is such a different dynamic.  It is not one that I want all the time, but it offers a nice change of pace, and is also highly suitable for gaming with "non-gamers".
2) The theme is really, really well done.  And it's not set in Renaissance Europe.  Again, a nice change of pace.
3) Plays well with 2, and is, again, a great change from games in which you or your spouse have been a little bit dominant in recent times, leading to a blacklisting of said game.  Hypothetically speaking.
4) The game mechanics that you are playing against offer scaleable difficulty, and give a real challenge.  I think it's probably very difficult to design a game which will give a satisfying challenge to players of all skill levels, but Pandemic accomplishes this admirably.

Bottom line: It's Co-op.  This is good, and bad, but mainly, it's very different.  Pandemic is a really, really well done Co-op game.  If you never want to play cooperatively, this is not for you.  But, for most of us, Pandemic is a great option in many situations, and provides a welcome change of pace.

Expect games to go 30-45 minutes, with time decreasing with experience (and also when you get a brutal draw, and lose in the first three turns).  Replayability is very good.  Suitability for 2 players is high. 

Update: after 10 plays, I've upgraded my rating from 8 to 9: Always want to play.  This comes with something of an asterisk - I think there are many games I would pick over this, if it was just up to me, because I like competition more than co-op, and I prefer deeper games.  But, there are many situations where Pandemic is just the best game for the situation, because of the other players.  And, so far, this one has not worn out it's welcome.  So it's fair to say that, in those situations that call for a gateway game, or a co-op game, or a lighter game, I will always want to play Pandemic.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Jogo bastante imersivo, onde as mecânicas casam perfeitamente bem com o tema. Doenças surgem inicialmente em algumas cidades pelo mundo e vão se espalhando pelas cidades vizinhas, e todos os jogadores, interpretando profissionais úteis de áreas diversas, precisam unir esforços para conter esse crescimento das doenças, que pode avançar de forma incrivelmente rápida, causando desespero, horror e caos em toda a humanidade. E se isso acontecer, seus esforços foram em vão e o jogo acabou para vocês. Lindo!

O tempo de partida respeita o que está escrito na caixa (45 min) e, contra intuitivamente ao que se espera dos jogos de tabuleiro, este jogo tende a ser ligeiramente mais longo com menos jogadores, De mesa cheia ficará dentro dos 45 min ou menos, e em dois jogadores pode chegar a 1h (máximo). Tudo isso independentemente de ganhar ou perder. O que também é incomum em jogos cooperativos.

Também é um jogo mais difícil de ganhar de mesa cheia. Não consigo ganhar nem com apenas quatro cartas de epidemia. Parece ser impossível ganhar esse jogo, mas adoro! E jogo sempre com rigor máximo nas regras, pois creio que isso é indispensável em um cooperativo. Possui bastante minúcias de regra: se você ganhou fácil uma partida de Pandemic, releia o manual, pois provavelmente errou alguma regra importante. Já jogo ele há quatro anos e até hoje nunca consegui ganhar em mais de dois jogadores.
