textfield_comment_value:
My favorite board game of all time, not including one-time games like Pandemic Legacy or escape-room games.

The more you play, the more you realize how tight the game mechanics are.  All mechanics are very tightly intermeshed:  there's not an ounce of fat in there.  What gives the game so much replayability are all the different roles and events that you can randomly place into the game.  Therefore, I recommend getting all the expansions, including On the Brink, In the Lab, and State of Emergency, which all add new roles and events to the base game and give endless variety.

I've never played any of the expansion games except for In the Lab's "Lab Challenge" game, which is also excellent.

My favorite mode is solo, with three roles.  Since I like winning, I play "Intro" difficulty.  I feel adding more epidemic cards to the deck simply increases the randomness of the game.  I add my own goals to add spice to the game:  a favorite is attempting to eradicate all four diseases.

The Dispatcher role is hands-down the best; it may actually be a bit overpowered.  It synergizes extremely well with many other roles in the game, though my favorite is Dispatcher-Medic.

The app is also fantastic...I play it all the time, perhaps over 1000 times.  Sadly it doesn't include all the expansions, so you don't get access to all the roles and events.  Tip:  to speed up game setup in the app, tap the screen repeatedly.

A note on bling:
I love the Meeple Source meeples, including the "character germ set" and the character meeples.

Broken Token's "Biohazard Containment Unit" is very nice, but I wish they'd made the card area 1-2 mm wider to accommodate FFG-sleeved cards; FFG's sleeves are pretty large.

Update (2021):  They broke the mobile app, so to me it's basically unplayable.  Wish I could go back to the original version of the app.  The PC version is awful.

The physical board game is still just as good, though I got all the expansions just to get max variety of roles and events.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
The first co-op I truly, truly loved. The base game is a little easy unless you're playing on Hero (where luck is obviously the determining factor), but goddamn if this isn't a well-designed game.

First off, SAVING THE WORLD FROM DISEASE! is a fun theme that feels appropriately epic and heroic. Watching the board get overrun by disease and losing feels uniquely disappointing (I mean this as a positive).

Pandemic perfects the "randomized puzzle" style of co-ops for me. Sometimes I just want to try and solve a puzzle with my friends. Trying to figure out the best way to optimize your turns as a team is fun. There's heaps of tension, and the way Epidemics (specifically the Intensify step) works is just downright genius - allowing you to see how the game mitigates some luck and makes things even more scary in the process is just fantastic.

Some people hate on co-ops because they play with jerks who like to dictate everyone's turns for them. Pandemic is a game that certainly would allow you to do that, so if you play with jerks stay away. BUT even if you don't play with jerks... it is true that it is very, very difficult for someone new to the game/genre to play with an otherwise super experienced group. Even if your group allows everyone to vocalize their opinions, etc., it's hard for a newbie to contribute anything meaningful in a group of seasoned players and that can ruin the experience for them. For that reason, it's really best played with people of equal skill level.

Update: Upgraded this + OtB both for aesthetic purposes (I think we can all agree these blow the original out of the water under THAT criteria) but mostly to be compatible with In the Lab. Worth it!

Update: Years later, this is still my favorite co-op. Ghost Stories is pretty equally fun to base game Pandemic, but I have to give Pandemic the edge just on the basis of expansions - so far they've managed to release universally excellent expansions that only improve the base game.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
For how popular it is, I expected a little bit more, but Pandemic is an okay game that's worth owning if you don't have other co-op titles. 

Working together to figure out the best moves can be a lot of fun, but often leads to one person ordering the others around - not out of malice or anything, but whoever understands games the best naturally takes over and, even for them, it can feel tedious. So 3 of the party feel like they don't have agency, and the final person feels like they're doing all the work.

The admin is also legit over half the game. As in: you will spend more time flipping infection cards and placing cubes than you will spend actually taking your turn, which isn't a super big deal, but it does make the game feel like it's playing itself.

My final point of contention is this game is really hard to play consistently. What I mean is even after you understand the game and its strategies, you'll still feel helpless against the random system from time to time. Such as the bad luck of going to 1 place to stop the spread and then, while you're there, somewhere on the other side of the world gets dumped on by the infection deck and leads to a nearly unstoppable outbreak that you can't do much about. You simultaneously want everyone to spread out to deal with that stuff and all stay together so you can share knowledge and which is better to do at any point is totally up to chance.

I know I only said negative stuff, but that's because there is so much positive about the game I felt like it was more useful to point out its flaws. I do think Pandemic is a good game. It's good for family game nights since it's pretty simple to teach and play - it's rather lightweight. Playing something that won't leave anyone feeling sour with each other after a loss is also a plus. The flexible action system is fun to puzzle around as you try and optimize your turns to be as effective as possible. So while it may have some big flaws, it's still fun to play.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
[b] Logged plays split between base game and On the Brink expansion[/b]

Rated "8" after one solo play. Curious to see how this rating changes when playing with others. I lost first time through... this is harder than I expected! And, I found myself getting a little angry--in a good way. There's a pressure that develops to "beat the clock." As a true collaborative or solo game, it's more about puzzle solving than playing other players, but at the same time it's a pretty darn intriguing puzzle.

I like the challenge. But, if I keep losing and never win, I'll get angry--in a bad way!

Update: Yay! I finally beat it as a solo game. I can safely like this game now. The strategies are becoming more apparent. I'll be curious to see how many plays this game offers before it becomes a bit repetitive. That's certainly not the case yet.

Update after 25 plays: every play has been solo so far, and I still enjoy this. At some point, I might pick up the expansion to breathe more life into this, but this is much more mileage out of the game than I expected. If only every game held up for 25 plays!

Update: My 50th play, and it was the first time playing with other people. That's a bit tricky, as a pure cooperative game is hard to play if there is great disparity in people's familiarity with the game. I still had a good time, but 49 solo plays means that I have to restrain from bossing others around. Still, Pandemic is easily the only game I've enjoyed playing solo, and for that reason alone, I'm happy to own it.

Update: traded it away along with the expansion for Thebes. After 50 plays, I called it quits. This for me was a great solo game, but I never wanted to play it with a group because of the risk of the "bossing others" factor. It's still a solid game, and I certainly don't regret the purchase! If only every gamed yielded 50 quality plays. But now, I think it's time to "pay it forward."
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Played once.

This is a pretty interesting co-op game which, like most co-op games, has a nice narrative.  The board is a map of the world with regions delineated by color (East Asia is red, for example).  The presence of disease is noted by placing cubes into a city, and the placements are based on a somewhat random card draw at the end of each player's turn.  If a city ever gets more than three cubes, there is an outbreak, and all connecting cities get cubes of that color.  The game is over when players either cure all four diseases or there are more than nine outbreaks.  

On a player's turn, there are eight possible actions, some of which are made easier by the roles that are selected at the start of the game.  You need to move quickly around the board and clear cubes out in anticipation of the next outbreak.  There's also trading of cards between players to achieve a cure.  So the fun part of the game is working together to figure out the most efficient way for each player to spend their turn.

That said, most of the decisions in that regard are fairly obvious.  You do have some idea of what cities are likely to experience repeated infections, and which are less likely, so you can anticipate outbreaks.  It's also fairly plain that you can't afford to have two connected cities with three cubes each, since that would trigger a double outbreak, which cuts way down on the time you have to get cures.  

In short, this is a really straightforward game with a great narrative, about a 70:30 strategy to luck ratio, that can be taught and played in about 45 minutes.  It looks good and was pretty fun for my one play.  I'm a little unsure of its long-term replayability, but I can see some potential for expansions.  I'd particularly like to see some random event cards that were conditionally helpful or hindering, so you had more of a decision than to automatically use them.

Played 20+ times with 1-4 players.
Ratings history: 6|8|8|8|8........|10......

[b]Sharp looking co-op about saving the world from deadly diseases. It presents a challenging, ever-shifting puzzle to the players. I own this and expect to keep the game in my collection.
PROS:[/b]
- easy to learn, tricky to master
- variable, shifting puzzle
- variety of player roles (special abilities)
- well-designed modular expansions are available for purchase
- very attractive graphic design (I even prefer the plastic cubes)
[b]CONS:[/b]
- as much of a puzzle as a game (but I like this)
- could feel samey from play to play for some people (but I enjoy the shifting challenge)
- most gamers will probably need an expansion to keep this fresh (but game + expansion ~=~ $ of good strategy game)
- has "alpha" problem common to co-ops (but I let newbs do their thing)

:star::star::star::star::star: - My rating. 
:star::star::star::star::nostar: - Partner's rating.

1st play: Huh. Well, it is a good piece of design, but I didn't find it that fun. It was just a puzzle with shifting parts. I wasn't at all impressed by it. I prefer Shadows Over Camelot a bit more, and Terra and Lord of the Rings co-op a LOT more.

5 plays in: I like this a lot more than I used to. Really want the expansion.

12 plays in: I bought an expansion and am enjoying this game more than ever before, even without having added the expansion.

15 plays in: Good official solitaire variant.

20 plays in, and I have to say how impressed I am with the skeleton of the game. It is just so clever. The Infecting and Intensifying mechanics are brilliant, the asymmetrical links on the map (Santiago...grrrr). The outbreak mechanics, the decisions to make card passing difficult (and more thematic!). Multi-use cards, a variety of player roles... All of this for an incredibly reasonable price.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Pandemic is currently the only co-op game in my collection. I don't particularly like the genre because I have been indoctrinated that gaming is about beating someone - and that someone is not the game (I came to boardgames through trick-taking card games such as Whist, rather than RPGs, the latter genre would probably have made me more open to co-ops). This means I will never be completely sold on Pandemic, it's not my perfect game. BUT it is a good game nonetheless as there's plenty working for it. It is a short, clever game that has an engaging theme that seems to entice beginners, and it plays very well with two players. I love the short set-up time and the mechanism of how the outbreaks spawn. The downside is that it feels more like a puzzle than a game for me;  it's mostly about tactics with quite little strategy; and after a while it feels a bit gimmicky.

textfield_comment_value:
I understand why this game is a strong gateway game, but I've noticed that both Zee Garcia and Rahdo have this as their favorite game, despite the thousands of games that they have played, and that rather mystifies me.

The general complaint with many games is that they are insufficiently play tested and unbalanced by certain cards/dice rolls/etc. Pandemic, I would argue, is a game that suffers by being too well play tested. It feels, as you play it, like everything was carefully measured out so that the game play would happen exactly like this every time you play it:

1. The players act freely, doing the obvious thing, without really needing to put much effort into coordination or thinking.
2. Until the very last round, when *gasp* we can't win!
3. And then everyone puts their heads together, and *gasp* exactly 50% of the time, there is a special card or special power which allows them to solve the problem. And they win if there is, and lose if there isn't.

I enjoy stage 3, and would play a game that is stage 3 throughout the whole game. But 95% of the game is stage 1. The whole game ends up being an elaborate randomizer to determine the state of the game on the last round, and it has been so finely tuned to be this way that I don't feel like there will ever be a game which doesn't play out exactly as said. You could set your clock to the thing.

From a mechanical, perfectly crafted "thrill the non-gamers with a well-themed coop" sense, it's a great game. It knows what it needs to do to appeal to the average person and will do it every single time. But I'm not part of that audience. If I'm playing a co-op, I want to have to coordinate with my team and come up with solutions through the whole thing, not just once.

textfield_comment_value:
This can be a very enjoyable game. It scales well from 1-5, though you need to increase the difficulty for fewer players. It's easy to learn, easy to teach, and doesn't take long to play. It's an excellent game to play with non-gamers. When you are in the middle of the game and things are getting out of control, it can be a wonderfully intense and immersive game to play. Unfortunately, those aspects peter out as you approach the end since you can usually see whether or not you will be able to win 3-5 turns too soon. At that point, you're just going through the motions to bring the game to it's inevitable conclusion. Win or lose, it's very anti-climactic. The only truly exciting ending is getting too many outbreaks, as that is an ending whose certainty cannot be calculated beforehand.  As a house-rule, I think it would be more enjoyable to remove the losing conditions for running out of cubes (the more cubes you have, the more likely you are to get outbreaks) and for exhausting the player deck (just reset the deck, re-seeded with Epidemic cards, and continue playing). I'm not sure how to make winning more enjoyable... maybe if the person who goes to the research station and plays the cards to cure a disease, and only that person, had to take an action to roll a die (I know, I know...) and get a 5 or 6 to succeed in producing the cure. Yeah, it adds luck to the game, but at least the ending would be exciting.... Honestly, if the anti-climatic end game could be remedied, this game would easily be a 10. As it is, I'm not sure how long it will hold out at a 9 rating.... 

Oh, and while the game does look good, the board tends to warp and the player pawns, research stations, and disease cubes are all far too large.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Co-op:hand management:crisis management:gateway

Very thematic fast playing co-op game, maybe the quickest playtime (45 min) for a co-op to date which is one of it's biggest strengths. Group think is definitey the game, yes a domineering person can spoil this AND that can be said for any co-op, don't play co-ops with those people!  

Decisions being fairly obvious is maybe the biggest flaw, there might be a few ways to skin the cat but the overall "puzzle" really has no depth to it, there is a little planning but its more of a tactical excerise of staying on top of things and it does that very well. It is going to feel very 'samey' fast but will still be worth pulling out once in awhile, especially with non-gamers. More characters or powers could have really helped with this, maybe even a double-sided map, mini expansion to come I suppose but these should have been included.

Great tension, easy to learn and fun are all more strengths, these really make it an excellent game for gateway to hook non-gamers on games, extra points for this. The difficulty level being scalable was sure an excellent inclusion and another strength.  Of course luck of the draw plays a big factor but we are not playing this for the high strategy element anyway, we are playing for the fun aspect which is definitely here in a short game so complaints about luck aren't as big as the others. Will scale well 2 to 4 so extra points for this. 

I would seem due to the missing roles and decreased mobility less players could be harder but the cards in hand when starting are different so I'm not sure yet and have only played two 4 player games to date. 5 Epidemic cards for 2 players is a good challenge at any rate.

textfield_comment_value:
Solitaire multiplayer. Too easy for one or two veteran players to make the decisions for the other players in the game. At least with, say, Arkham Horror, a player gets to draw an Encounter card and play it out. Thematically, I find it annoying that the cards function like one part disease research solution and other part like... airline tickets. I *do* like how the gameplay changes depending on which roles are *not* in play. If you like solitaire games, this one's for you. I'd probably play this game when I'm in a mood to watch a game unfold, rather than meaningfully play it.

****

What I liked about Pandemic is that all five roles are critical to solving winning the game. And you only have four of them!

But that's about all I liked. Pandemic also reminds me of AH -- except that there's none of the Encounter card chrome (aka. "randomness") that puts a player in that amusing position of making a possibly human "sacrifice" for the team.

Arkham Horror:
"Hey, Beaver! Go into that Witch's House and get the Clue token!"
"No, way Whitey! There's a Gug there, and all I have is this crappy Dagger! I might get Injured, and Mom would be upset!"
"Oh, alright, Beaver. We'll meet in the street and I'll give you my Curse of Azathoth. But you'll have to give me $2 for it, because I'm low on Sanity and need to go to the Sanitarium."
"I told you, you shouldn't have read the Livre De Lion."
"Shut up Beaver, and sneak past that Gug!"

Pandemic:
"Okay, Beaver will remove two cubes in Mexico City, Dad will build a research center, and Mom will dispatch me to Beijing."
"Hey, Wally. You should let Beaver make a decision."
"No way, Dad! Last time he did that, there was an outbreak in Tehran!"
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Rated a 10 with 25+ plays (12/23/08). This is the only co-op game that allows for real teamwork, has almost zero downtime, provides lots of tough choices, and has enough built-in variability to be played again and again. An initial double-header of this is almost mandatory. Pandemic also affords some of the best two-player gaming with experienced players. 

One of the things the rulebook sort of glosses over is that player-number impacts the difficulty nearly as much as epidemic number (with 2-players being easiest). Lately my girlfriend and I have moved onto 2P6E (2-player, 6 Epidemics). We're doing fairly well. I still think my favorite way to play Pandemic is 3P5E. I've tried 3P6E, and even with clear boons of luck from the deck, it usually ends in disaster. It's been 40 or so games since I last tried though. I rarely play with four (I'd much rather play Space Alert if there are four of us), but if I do I usually keep it to 4 epidemics. More often than not, the major threat in 4P4E is running out of time. Because the cards are split four ways, I feel like the luck of the draw (cure sets) has a somewhat higher impact. Every now and then it's fun to play 5P5E (not actually "allowed" in the rules). You need that extra epidemic to make up for the fact that you have every advantage at your disposal.  

Update: An incredible game, but it's so playable and accessible and innovative and fun that it is possible to eventually 'play it out.' I'm still a big fan, but play rarely. I can't imagine downgrading it below a 9, though, having played 150 times. I'm not the one suggesting this anymore, but if an enthusiastic new player wanted me on the team, I'd be there in a heartbeat.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
(+) marvelous door-opener/gatewaygame, it captivates variouse beginners and casual players
(+-) alpha leader problem, it is hard to be quite for a sophisticated mate and allow some failures
(+) aha moments and reactions without challenging each other or feel inferior 

Sollen wir mit der Lagebesprechung beginnen? Wir müssen uns etwas Zeit verschaffen, um die Welt weiter von infizierten "Männchen" zu befreien. Wir wissen, dass bald die nächste Epedemie ausbricht, da ca. 5 Epedemie-Karten im Infektionsstapel gleichmäßig verteilt sind. Außerdem sind wir besorgt über die Pandemie und wir möchten gerne wissen, ob es neue Spreader gibt und wir über den Atlantik fliegt müssen? Ihr überlegt, ob ihr Städte in Quarantäne stellt oder die Spreader-Städte vor der nächsten Epedemie behandelt. Jedes Mitglied eures Teams hat eine besondere Fähigkeit, mit denen ihr eure wenigen Aktionspunkte verstärken könnt. Dies kann auch in Kooperation und mit Synergien erfolgen.

Ich finde das Spiel thematisch sehr stimmig. Jeder der an der Reihe ist hat grundsätzlich 4 Aktionspunkte für Bewegung oder Heilung oder den Laborbau oder den Wissenstausch oder die Heilmittel-Entdeckung. Das Spielkonzept ist einfach wie genial. Dadurch ist es ein wunderbares Einstiegsspiel. Es fesselt diverse Anfänger und Gelegenheitsspieler. Zu beachten ist jedoch das Alpha-Leader-Problem. Es fällt schwer, für einen anspruchsvollen Mitspieler ruhig zu sein und einige Fehlschläge zuzulassen. Im Team erlebt man Aha-Momente und Reaktionen, ohne sich gegenseitig herauszufordern oder minderwertig zu fühlen. Auch wenn es nur ein Spiel ist, ist es doch "mehr", weil man etwas über sich und die Mitspieler lernt.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Having played the Pandemic "system" (including Legacy) nearly 40 times now, I'm never excited to reach for vanilla Pandemic anymore. I'm just not that interested in the puzzle-solving underlying the game as a whole, especially when it's hard to know when you've "really" won or lost due to the randomness of the system. To play truly well, you have to be more committed to solving the puzzle than I typically am. Pandemic Legacy did a great job of using the underlying system to drive an experience, but when you're back to the original, it feels too much like an exercise.

As a result, I had Pandemic at a 4 for a while, but a couple aspects of the game are bringing it back onto my radar. First, it remains as solid a gateway game as ever. We probably prefer Through the Desert, but that game isn't quite as eye-opening as Pandemic's interactive, cooperative nature. It's fun seeing others get excited about "saving the world" and puzzling their way through their turns the way we did when we were first starting out. Second, the underlying system has proven to be remarkably customizable, which opens up not more variety through expansions but also opportunities for my own design tweaks. (This is an advantage Pandemic has over its simpler siblings like Forbidden Desert or variants like Pandemic: Realm of Cthulhu.) I've started [url=http://mulrah.droppages.com/Customization/Pandemic]thinking through some of these possibilities elsewhere[/url], and if I really get into any of them, the rating here could actually go up. But for now, a 6 seems fair: we're fine with this as an introduction to the hobby, but aren't going to be busting it out all that often beyond that.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Just got this, played through a 2p game tonight to familiarize myself with the rules.  Wow!  The sheer amount of replayability and variety and choice in game setup is incredible.  I bought it with On the Brink for this very reason and I'm blown away at the quality and design of this game.  I can't wait to dig in.

UPDATE: played it 10 times now with 2p and 4p.  Great game.  Lots of variety between each game due to the randomized board layout, shuffle of the deck, etc.  Crumby roles combined with a crumby shuffle tend to result in a loss, but I'm willing to chalk that up to inexperience utilizing all of the roles effectively. Very happy with this purchase.

UPDATE: Haven't really added much from On the Brink.  Just roles and events.  And only attempted In the Lab once, but found it too much and decided there's still plenty of fun to be had in the base game for now, so we shelved that expansion and have been plugging away at more or less base Pandemic.  It's a great game and we'll be playing it for years and years.  There's no rush.  And it's nice to know that there's plenty of room to grow as we get used to the game.

UPDATE: We've added Virulent Strain Epidemics and it's adding some nice flavor to the game.  We win consistently with 5 epidemics but can't seem to win with 6 very often.  

The game is still fantastic and the perfect sweet spot for weight / duration on the nights when we want to play something but we don't have the energy left to do a multi-hour brain burner.  This is concentrated middle-weight thought in a 45 minute package.  Awesome in that regard. I upped it in points to reflect just how much we've been playing it lately.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
The whole concept of cooperative games was completely new to us, so when I first heard of [GAMEID=30549], I know I had to give it a try.  I was also motivated because in general, she beats me in most games.  This way, I wouldn't have to lose to her again.

The theme was cool (save the world instead of conquering it!), and the mechanism for the spread of the diseases is a very slick design.  Despite having only colored cubes, they took on an ominous feeling as they began to cover the world.  However, she didn't really like it.  For her, the core gameplay seemed too dry and mathematical.  Plus, she's also pretty competitive and the cooperative aspect didn't sit right with her.  On the other hand, I enjoyed it a lot.  Luckily, [GAMEID=30549] is a good solo game (probably due to being cooperative in nature).  This is one of the few games where our responses were very different.

However, when we brought this home for Christmas, we got the family playing and we all had a blast trying to save the world.  Even my girlfriend got into it---we ended up playing over and over again until we finally won.  I have to agree that cooperative games like this shine with more people---there's more discussion and more people to get involved.  It's adding a key social aspect to it that you just don't get with two players.  It's become one of my go to games for new players---I've had good luck introducing the game to new players who've liked it.  However, while it does work, I would hesitate recommending it for just two until you've tried it first.

textfield_comment_value:
A great game for gamers who like to table talk, because here you can plan and plot together against the plagues all you want. This game brings non-confrontational gaming to a whole new level. Missing the outright winner of Lord of the Rings, or the secret traitor of Shadows over Camelot, the game is all about beating the cards. Good co-operation, deduction, guesswork and (card seeding) luck will carry you along to ultimate victory or failure - everyone either wins or loses together.

Meanwhile... back at the ranch... well... I guess it'd appeal to gamers who like the social interaction and banter that goes together with a game like this. I feel it's more like some sort of corporate training course where the course instructor will give us a summary at the end of his/her observations of the behavioural traits of the participants - the aggressive, the passive-aggressive, the follower and all the other personalities a game like this can bring out.

My wife complained that it's not actually a game and could I please pack it away so as to make room on the table for a real game. I think that's a tad harsh - there's some fun to be had here - it's not always obvious what the best choice is, but it feels like it doesn't really matter if you're there or not - the whole thing can be played solo and it'd be much easier to agree on what to do in your turn(s). Ultimately, in the words of a wise friend - "I don't mind it." That said, couldn't we play a game instead?

I might be inclined to bump the rating up a notch when playing with the terrorist variant - a little human interaction to mess with the best laid plans goes a long way to making fun.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
First time I played I walked away thinking winning was all based on luck. Too many car draws to get lucky or unlucky draws with. After reading some tips, I can see how some of this can be planned for, but I still think that luck is going to have a big impact on if you win or lose.

I think the my main issue with the game is that you don't have have many options for actions. Most of the actions are just ways to move. Then there's building research stations, healing people, finding a cure and trading knowledge. Cure is not an option for an action. If you can do it then you do, there's no reason to put it off. Healing people isn't really a decision because there's usually a few cities at 3 that need to be taken care of. So you move and then heal those areas that need it. It's mostly a forced action. Research stations waste cards, so you're really only looking to do that if the role that build them is out of the game. So the only real decision in the game is trading knowledge and IMO that's such an action waster that I would argue that it's best just to heal and draw cards and get the cures if someone gets lucky. We had to waste 3 people's turns to trade enough cards for a cure and that was with efficient planning. One of them was usually the medic so we were losing out on taking a lot of cubes off the board to get the cures. In the meantime we added 6 cubes to the board putting us closer to outbreaks which is how we lost in the end.

I'm wondering how many times people have won this have been either lucky card draws at the beginning of the game or people missing rules that restrict the researcher or sharing knowledge in general.

Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
I don't think Pandemic is a great game, and would not recommend it for experienced gamers. However, i think it is a great gateway game for the sole reason that it breaks a lot of misconceptions about what board games are.

-Contrary to many classic abstract games, it has a strong theme
-Contrary to Monopoly, it requires a fair bit of strategy to win on the hard mode
-The theme is not geeky, which is off-putting for some people. The theme also isn't macho. The theme is family friendly. The theme puts everyone as a good samaritan/hero. 
-The game is good for non-confrontational people
-The game is more complicated than most classic games, but it is not out of reach to learn for a beginner.
-This game has good representation of different genders and races. This is especially important for children, who are still forming their opinion about their role could be in society. 

I think that Pandemic is not that fun when a more experienced player bosses the newbies around, which is it's biggest weakness and why I can't give it any higher than a 6. It can get more confrontational than a competitive game with people who just want to win. My favorite easy Co-op game is The Crew, which circumvents this problem, by not allowing players to communicate verbally. The Crew is also simpler to teach to newbies. I would only teach Pandemic to a really dedicated beginner, because I think it is a good first "big" game. It's barely even medium heavy, but it sure does feel big to a new gamer. I've played some of the expansions, but they don't really interest me. People do seem to like Iberia though.

textfield_comment_value:
This is my revised comments on Pandemic:  The co-op genre has changed quite a bit over the year. If there is one place that I would recommend someone to start, it's here.  Pandemic is probably one of the best games for couples out there being a co-op, as regular life with a significant other can sometimes be confrontational enough as it is without adding 'take that'/competitive games to heat things up.  In addition to that, this game is very easy to learn and not overly long which makes it a perfect gateway game.  Co-ops of the modern day need a way to scale the difficulty levels and Pandemic is one of the best in this regard.  I had initially rated this game a 6 because it lacked the variety to hold my interest and while I still feel this way about the base game, On the Brink has transformed the game to something much more enjoyable and variable.  In addition to that, after having played some other co-ops, I have a much deeper appreciation for the game, even in it's base form. textfield_comment_value:
I always love a good co-op game, but unfortunately a lot of them usually take way too long for my liking (i.e. Shadow Over Camelot and Arkham Horror), so Pandemic's promise of a 45 minutes play time is definitely something to look forward to.  I will however admit that I was unimpressed with the mechanics when I first read the rules.

Many of the reviews and session reports claimed that Pandemic was brutally tough on the players.  Some even went as far as to warn people not to expect to win in their first few games, so imagine my surprise when we claimed our victory with a comfortable margin (the city draw deck was still half full and the outbreak was only at 4), so much so that my reaction was a "is that it?"  Granted we didn't play with the advance rule, which I think is an addition of two more epidemic cards, but we did beat the game without the use of a medic, and that was a pretty big accomplishment if I do say so myself.

Ultimately, I did appreciate the tension and urgency one felt periodically throughout the game, especially during an outbreak.  Yet there were still lulls during the session in which I'm just going through the motion while waiting for something interesting to happen; would it be weird if I said I wanted epidemic to occur more often?  I like Pandemic, especially how quick it is, but my fear is that it won't stand up to heavy replays.  Considering there are only 5 roles available, I imagine that each game would be very similar to another outside of the combination of the roles randomly selected.  So the jury is still out for me on this one.

textfield_comment_value:
When this was first released I wasn't a big fan.  I played several games that were either terrible losses or easy wins.  Now that I own Pandemic Legacy I went back and played several more of this base game in preparation and had a different experience.  It's still possible to get those swingy games, but player actions have more of an impact than they seem at first.

I think there are some tricky considerations.  1) Some characters play better as teams, e.g., Dispatcher and Medic vs Generalist and anyone.  2) For all players to have fun, they all need to be approximately the same experience level and be about the same amount engaged (which means they all need to be able to contribute equally to this sort of logic puzzle). Otherwise, one player is probably going to dominate everyone's actions in the interest of efficiency/victory.  3) The game's apparent randomness decreases significantly once everyone understands how the infection deck works and specifically how that interacts with epidemics.  4) The game will always be random...if you get two epidemic cards back-to-back, or if every epidemic city outbreaks immediately.

So this is in no way my favorite cooperative game...that might be Lord of the Rings, even though it's so much longer.  There's also Forbidden Island/Desert, which have re-used these mechanics in a much more entertaining fashion.  And if you like the traitor mechanic then those games (e.g., Battlestar Galactica) neatly solve the problem of one player controlling all the characters.  With all that said, I am having a blast with Pandemic Legacy.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value: This game is widely praised for good reason. It's beautifully designed with respect to its themes. There are so many genius mechanics that ties well into the thematic elements, such as epidemics and outbreaks. The game is not too complicated and it fosters a good sense of teamwork without any secret agendas. If I were to point to problems, finding the right challenge is tricky with regards to number of players, number of epidemic cards and roles. Speaking of which, some roles are flat out better than others (the researcher for example makes the game far too easy). That being said, all the roles are well thought-out when it comes to approaching the narrative of trying to cure diseases and makes each player feel unique. The other slight issue is that luck can unfortunately be a bigger deciding factor than I would have hoped for some games depending on which cities get infected at a particular point. One note on the players' hands being open for all to see: while I like that players can really help each other out and formulate strategies together, it can make so that more experienced players (or who owns the game) tells others what to do on their turn. I don't think too much is lost by making hands closed, as players can still say what cards they have (such as how many of a certain colour) but there is an extra barrier in place so it is harder for players to dictate what others do on their turn. All that said, Pandemic is amazingly designed, very tense and its theme is so well executed that players really can get invested in trying to save the world.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Prior to 2020: 100 plays (est)

If Catan, Carcassonne, and Ticket to Ride introduced me to modern hobby gaming, Pandemic is the game that officially made me take the deep plunge (shortly followed by another masterpiece I discovered, Race for the Galaxy) into its sweet, sweet bliss.  Pandemic is, and will probably always be, the cooperative game by which all others are compared and, ultimately, judged, and I feel this way primarily because of how well Pandemic streamlines the depth-to-complexity ratio as well as how well the difficulty can be scaled based on group and player count.  Additionally, the mechanisms of the game remain intuitive and simplistic, yet come together in a way that's deeply thematic and puzzly, rewarding both the new and experienced players at the table. There's such a brilliant blend of luck and skill as well as tactics and strategy here, and the epidemic system just works so well at keeping escalating pressure on the players throughout the game.  The base game is still compelling after all these years (especially with 6 epidemic cards shuffled in), and the system works so perfectly with all of its expansions, each which further develop out one portion of the game to be more rich and, often, challenging. Pandemic just is a modern classic in every regard and should be played by anyone seriously interested in the hobby.  While some might suspect I've played the game to death, this actually isn't the case, and I'd happily revisit this one (especially with expansions) just about any time.  An absolute masterpiece. Keeper!

textfield_comment_value:
Co-operative game where you and the other players try to save the world from four diseases ravaging it.  For bonus fun, name the diseases!  Scramble to find cures for Bronchial Marmosets, Bloatyhead, Splatterlung, or Zombieism!

When playing co-op, you sometimes wind up with a player the owner of my favorite games shop refers to as "The Colonel."  The Colonel knows the game better than anybody else (or at least thinks he does [and yeah, it's usually a "he"]) and does his level best to turn the game into a solitaire exercise where you're just along for the ride and there to bask in his glory.

Some co-op games have mechanisms that thwart The Colonel.  Pandemic, unfortunately, is very nearly The Colonel's ideal environment.

If you can avoid having that ass at your table -- and avoid the temptation to BE that ass -- this game will easily rate a 9 or 10.  Despite very simple mechanics, it's tense as hell.  Every decision means something, and the next card drawn could be victory or disaster.  It manages to be challenging without feeling unfair, and can make for a great experience.

But if you've got The Colonel at your table ... seriously.  Give him one warning that he needs to stop ramming unsolicited advice down everybody else's throats.  Then when he gets pissy with you for not doing exactly what he told you to do, get up and go play something else, and make a mental note to never play a co-op with this jagoff again.  (And fer Chrissake, don't actually BE that guy.)  Because, seriously.  Fuck The Colonel, man.  Fuck 'im.

textfield_comment_value:
I haven't played Pandemic since the beginning of 2013 and I believe that there are a number of reasons for it. The first being that this is a brutal coop. I know that there are people that say that it's "easy" and that they have expansions to make it more difficult but I believe that my win percentage is well below 50%... and that's just the base game. I recall playing a few games with my wife where we were just destroyed and having her say that she "played games for fun and this just wasn't fun". While I don't agree with that statement 100%, I do understand where she was coming from. The game sets you up for failure and, depending on the card draws, and beat you down to a pulp. If you're not in to that style of game where the game itself is trying to destroy you, I can see how it wouldn't be "fun".

The next knock against it is that you really need to play with a full compliment of people and/or play with two people using two roles each. It seems like the game was designed to work this way as certain combinations of roles seem vastly superior to others.

And the final knock against it is that it can suffer from the alpha-player syndrome (as many coops can). I don't know how you can negate that concern other than trying not to be the alpha-player, but it's a concern and something that needs to be taken into account.

While I think that it's a great game to introduce people to newer types of board games as you're working together to beat the game, it isn't something that I'm chomping at the bit to play again soon.

Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
When I think of Pandemic, I think that it's the perfect game.  It's a co-op, and it brings people together to complete the noblest of tasks: save the world population from extinction by disease.  It does it in such a great way, where mechanics and theme come together seamlessly to immerse players in the narrative.

In Pandemic players take on various roles, each with its own unique powers.  Using these powers wisely in conjunction with other players' roles is the the best chance you have to win the game.  On a player's turn they will move around the board, which is a global map.  They will try to treat diseased populations, build research facilities where cures can be found, gather cards to be used for curing disease, and then actually cure those diseases.  Watch out though, every turn more cities become infected with one of four deadly viruses, which are colour coded. 

To win, players must cure all four diseases.  However, there are many ways to lose.  If any one disease has gotten so out of control that there are no more cubes left in its colour, players lose.  Players will also lose if there are too many outbreaks triggered.  Finally, if the draw deck runs out before all four diseases are cured, that also counts as a loss for the players.

Pandemic is tense right from the beginning, and it only gets worse as the game progresses.  You're immediately thinking, "How can we possibly put out all these 'fires' all over the globe?".  It will take teamwork, skill, and luck to save the world from the Pandemic!
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Purchased 3/1/2008 $33.10 - Rated after one play (2-player, introductory game).  The game was pretty easy to win as we had only one outbreak during the three epidemics that came up.  Red (SARS) was eradicated, Black (plague) was rampant in Europe, Bird Flu was taking over the US, and we almost eradicated AIDS in Africa and South America, but couldn't get the last cube off and it reemerged strong.  We had the Scientist and Medic, which seems to be a great pair for two players.  Will need to play with 6 epidemics soon (or weaker characters).  2 Bogata Player cards, 2 Scientists, no Dispatcher, so yes there are assembly problems.  Update: Have now played with 5 epidemics and twice with 6.  With the exception of a game that no one could win (just bad card sequencing, using up all black cubes in the second turn when the first epidemic card was turned), we have won all games and only one got close to using all the cards in the deck.  It plays much like a baseball simulation--you set it up and make the "right" decisions during play and watch it all unfold.

For those who say it's straightforward, I believe that's only true after a couple of plays.  There aren't many options, but remembering the details (must play card of city to build a research center; cured diseases get the Medic privelege; etc) isn't perfect.  Those rules should be on a cheat sheet card as well.  Personally, I'm not sure I like the "variable powers" mechanic.  I wouldn't mind if you could pick your character trait to use every turn.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Game in a Nutshell: Co-op game fighting disease outbreaks around the world. Take on a role, collect cards, and travel the globe fighting the spread one action at a time.

Played as: solo (w/ 2 characters), 2,3,4 player

Played with: On the Brink: Roles and Events (3 player)

Pros: Easy game to learn and play fast. The scaling difficulty makes a good intro game up to a tense challenge for experienced players. Simple enough that it should encourage talking and planning rather then individual situational analysis. The infections work in a way that balances the complete randomness with just enough info to help focus your efforts while still remaining tense with each card flip. This game begs to be played until it's beaten. 

Cons: The game can lead to frustration when played with mixed personality types who are forced to cooperate. After a while, the cooperative discussion becomes straight forward and things boil down to how well the cards play out with the theme seemingly faded away. The base game should have included more roles.  

Other: My advice is play this ALWAYS on the most difficult level. The hooks of this game is in the losses; so don't let newbies win. I'm typically a expansion hater, but this game is one that basically needs it to add the necessary variety for anything more then 5-10 interesting plays (especially if in high rotation)... if only for the additional roles alone.  

Best Use: The friendliest of Gateway games for loud-mouths who don't think they're smarter then everyone else.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Love this game!  Co-operative strategy game in which the players are characters with different abilities, and they have to work together in order to prevent four diseases from doing some significant damage to humanity, and causing a pandemic.

As with many co-operative games, experienced players need to be willing to step back and not take over inexperienced player's characters by only providing options during the player's turn that they would do.  It is not going to interest players if they are basically just going to have to sit back and watch the other players manage their character.  Experienced players need to allow the new players to make mistakes and possibly not end up winning the game.  Also, because there is an app for this game which allows one person to control as many characters as they want to play (up to player max) this is a tendancy that is made worse because in that situation, they really CAN do just that, and those players need to work even harder at stepping back because they often have played MANY times with MANY of the different characters and will be controlling right from the start.

That said, it is a really fun game with the right group of people, and if you have people that are experienced with it and can read others, it is an easy one to get a new player involved in since the group is working co-operatively with no betrayer and can offer up suggestions about what the person can do with their character during their turn and what the impact will be on the other players.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
[Z-man 2008 edition] {Pathology; variable-player-power, cooperative; scalable}  {4/5-Epidemic: 7; 6-Epidemic: 7.5} Pandemic is a thematic cooperative game.  The mechanic is familiar - players play cards for their own good and cards for the 'evil'.  It's not ground-breaking but it is very fun to play.

The game is engaging, esp. with more epidemic cards.  I prefer the 6-Epidemic setup.  It is just so exciting that epidemics happen again and again and players are busily cure the disease and yet finding cure in the same time.  However, it is anti-climax at late game when the result is almost determined.  There are nearly no surprise.  Essentially, it's a card collection game.  Players have the shared goal to collect 4 sets of cards with limited time and resources.  The challenge is how players can optimize their moves together to achieve the goal.  Comparatively short playing time and scalable with few players (2-3 players) are its selling point.

It is too easy to have a player (or leader) dominating the game.  This leader will instruct every other player to follow the best plan in order to win. That won't be fun at all!

Thematically, I think it can be expanded to include some hidden elements for the cure that the players have to hunt for in the game.

The components are quite nice.  The board is sturdy.  The cardstock is thick enough.  The card illustration is nice and effective, even though there are pieces of wrong information.  The pawns are too large but the cure markers are too small.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value: Pandemic is een uitstekend spel om de eerste stappen in het coöperatieve genre mee te zetten. De regels zijn eenvoudig, dus je pakt het spel zo op. Ondanks de eenvoudige regels is het spel soms lastig te winnen, een goede samenwerking en tactiek is dan echt nodig. Dit maakt het spel ook zo leuk en uitdagend. Pandemic is niet een spel dat je achter elkaar door blijft spelen, op een gegeven moment ken je het ‘trucje’ wel een beetje of wil je ook eens tégen anderen spelen, in plaats van mét. Maar als je het dan eens in de zoveel tijd er weer bij pakt of met nieuwe mensen speelt, is het direct weer leuk. Gelukkig zijn er wel meerdere uitbreidingen voor het spel verkrijgbaar om het spel meer diepgang te geven. Dit gebrek aan diepgang zorgt er voor dat het voor casual spelers een toegankelijk spel is. En een uitstekende opstap naar de uitbreidingen en andere coöperatieve spellen zoals De Legenden van Andor, Paleo of zelfs Gloomhaven. Maar de ervaren spelers van coöperatieve spellen raken waarschijnlijk snel op het basisspel van Pandemic uitgekeken. Al blijft het ook voor hen leuk om eens in de zoveel tijd met casual spelers mee te doen. Omdat het thema goed in het spel verwerkt is, Pandemic leuk en toegankelijk is voor een brede doelgroep, er meerdere uitbreidingen verkrijgbaar zijn en Pandemic het ideale startspel is voor het coöperatieve genre, noem ik Pandemic met recht een klassieker en heeft Pandemic het label BRDGMZ Essentials. Oftewel, Pandemic mag echt niet in je spellenkast ontbreken!
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
tl;dr: a huge success with good reason

I remember this game being announced. There was NO buzz. I was working for a distributor or Z-Man titles at the time, so I ordered just a couple of cases. I had requested pre-orders from shops, there were very few. The day the games arrived though, the game was sold out. So I contacted Zev to order more. He had sold out. He told me he had printed 3000, a very normal print run at the time. So this game went from no buzz to THE hype of the moment in no time. And it seems to still be growing, with all these variations and expansions coming out.
In any case... I've never been a fan of co-ops. And I probably never will be. I don't hate them, but I just prefer some healthy competition. That being said, I think this is still my favorite co-op (of the ones I've played, duh!). I think it has the perfect balance of amount of rules, play time and complexity for all experience levels. Most co-ops have some variation of the if-this-happens-resolve-this-random-event-card-mechanism. Pandemic kind of has that with the epidemic cards, but other games like [thing=121921][/thing] have way more of that. If feels kind of like a lame way to throw problems at the players to me. But the (sparce) way it is implemented in Pandemic is perfect. There's only a little bit of it, but the tension it creates is great.
Also, this game is pretty streamlined and usually takes less than an hour.
All in all, very good, though not my favorite.

Rating: 7.5/10
BGG scale: 7/10
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
We played this at UCON 2012

I am sure people have complaints about Pandemic, such as quaterbacking and damage control (which honestly you get tired of both after playing a few co-op board games these days).

This is my take: Pandemic is a more interesting version of Forbidden Island with a Risk-like element to it :)

I love Forbidden Island, and so also loved Pandemic.

It was hard to tell before playing it if I would like it or not- some reviews made me wary and others made me curious.

I think now that none of those people had played Forbidden Island or else they would have been forced to mention it. Pandemic IS Forbidden Island, stolen, re-imagined (slightly) and re-themed, and made bigger and a bit more board-gamey and relevant.

That is, a global virus spreading is more topical and relevant to us than... a magical island... sinking... which we can stop how? And we care because? Yea, I think you get the point.

So. Just like Forbidden Island, damage control, flood management, hand-size management, character placement management, set collection and timed tracks.

Also, the really cool over-flow mechanic which can set off chain reactions (which ended the world in our game). I liked the flight-by-cards and control-center-building mechanics too.

There is even an option for one player to be a bad guy bio terrorist and a 5th virus expansion. 

I liked Pandemic. Oddly, enough. It is now at the top of my to-get co-op game list. Can't wait till we can afford to buy it, oi :P
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Pandemic used to be my favourite game when I first started getting into board gaming but I've cooled on it a little bit over the years, possibly just because I'm simply not as enthusiastic about cooperative games in general these days. It is still a great game though and I really love the puzzle in Pandemic of trying to plan your actions together to pull off a win. The game also has a very nice pace to it, since unlike some other co-ops which feel like you're constantly up against overwhelming difficulties, it occasionally gives you a bit of breathing room... until everything suddenly ramps up again. 

Also while there is randomness in the game with the card draws, it never feels luck-based or unfair. Since you're always able to look through the discard pile and the previously revealed infection cards get shuffled to the top of the deck, you sort of have an idea of what might be happening and know how to plan for the worst, or take a calculated risk. The unique player powers are also a great plus as depending on the composition of your team the experience can be quite different each time, and (most of) the powers are really cool and let each player feel like they're doing something fun and unique that's helping the whole team. It also has some very good expansions, especially In the Lab is absolutely fantastic. I would always choose to play with it but rarely get the chance since it adds a fair bunch of complexity which makes the game difficult to introduce to newcomers.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
I enjoy this game a bit more every time I play. That means about a dozen times, mostly two-player games and a few four-player ones.

This is a great game for casual players. It is one of the very few games where you don't have to explain the rules in detail and the others can catch up while you're playing. The theme is awesome, the mechanics are simple but fit very well.

The replayability seems to be pretty good so far as well. I was worried that I will lose interest in a few games. But the games and our overall strategies were pretty different so far, depending on our characters, player count and the cube distribution. Sure, there is a lot of randomness, but not so much that you don't have any real control over it. Or if it is actually the case, then the game hides that pretty well. However, I am a bit worried that maybe there are some general patterns I have not discovered yet and things could get really repetitive if I do.

One negative remark: The colors of the 2013 version are really dark for my taste. The cubes are nice, but I would prefer wooden components, sturdier cards and brighter colors.

But either way. This game is tough to win but easy to understand, is super interactive in a friendly way, and has an awesome theme with fitting mechanics. It's an incredible design.

Update: We have gotten really good at the game. So we tried it with the OTB expansion, but it has lost some of its charm even so. But anyway, it took us a far amount of plays to get here.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
The best part of this game is that it's co-operative.  The theme is wonderful, the gameplay is challenging, but it's the interaction and working with the other players that really makes this game fun to play.  

This game could be played Solo, however this makes it too easy.  It's more interesting with more people, as it gets harder to communicate, and explain the best possible route of action, much like the real world, where there are many truths and solutions that are independent of what people know, but it's much more beneficial for everyone to understand than for just one person to understand.  

If you understand exactly what to do in this game all the time, or are more experienced than those you play with, it's better to hang back a little, and learn to communicate without manipulating others turns.  Allowing others to discover the right action without explicitly telling them will actually help them have a better experience.  

I find it interesting because self absorbed people who may be impatient and really smart will feel like they are playing a solo game, and don't need anyone else around, which is true, but that's part of the challenge and appeal... to have to work with others..  and if they play with others who are self absorbed/controlling but smarter, they will feel like they aren't making decisions.. or being pushed around... This game has led me to a lot of personality analysis, and led me to understanding co-operative leadership a little more.

Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value: Pandemic is an innovative, cooperative game about the spread of disease across our planet. Each player is given a character with a different set of abilities. Cards are flipped and disease bits, of four different types, are placed on corresponding cities on the world map. When a city reaches critical mass, there will be an outbreak that spreads to all of its neighboring cities, potentially triggering a chain of outbreaks. Players win the game by curing each of the disease types and ridding the world of disease entirely. It's a pretty interesting and exciting game, the first few times, working with your team to figure out the best order of operations as plague is breaking out everywhere. I've played a few games, and my only concerns so far are that the space that seperates "We're doing great!" from..."Holy sh*t, my eyes are bleeding and the world will implode in a mass of ebola monkies!" seems far too narrow on the gauge of effectiveness. Replay value may also become limited, when playing with the same group. For a four player game, I wish there would have been like 8 different random character roles, so the game would be different every time. With that said, it plays very quickly (particularly if you get your arse handed to you), it's innovative, and it's a fun cooperative experience. The production is great too. I will recommend it to all my friends, particularly those that like co-op games, and for me, it is a must-buy.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
[q="Past me"]Bought from Barnardo's charity shop in Brixton for £3.99, in November 2012. (Although we'd played my brother-in-law's copy plenty of times before that.)

One of my wife's favourite games, which helps me love it even more. This and [thing=98778][/thing] fill the co-op niche in my collection and I don't feel any desire to get more.

Pandemic creates tension like nothing else I've played. It plays fast, escalates fast, and if you start getting good at it you can always make it harder...

And you know what? As much as I love abstract games, theme [i]matters[/i]. Saving the world from a series of horrific disease outbreaks? Yes! Makes heroes of all of us![/q]

I don't generally enjoy co-operative games, but that's at least partly because I've never played one that comes close to matching Pandemic's bang-for-your-buck. With relatively easy rules and a thrilling theme, this delivers a fantastic experience in just 40 minutes.

The number of times we have been just "one turn away" from winning (or losing) is a testament to the quality of [person=378][/person]'s design. I've played [thing=161936][/thing], and enjoyed it, but still prefer the beautiful simplicity of the base game.

[b]PROS:[/b]
- Plays fast, often with a wonderfully tense ending.
- Lots of ways of making it harder (including expansions).

[b]CONS:[/b]
- An "alpha player" will be tempted to take over everyone else's moves.
- More of a puzzle than a game.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Super solid foundation and a truly fundamental go to to teach people how to play a cooperative board game.

However, the deck randomness in this game is absolutely abysmal. I know some people can find this thematic, but to me there is nothing fun whatsoever in being destroyed in a game with none of it being the players fault. 

In theory, the epidemic mechanic makes sense as an interesting mechanic. Keeps a subset of the world in constant threat of infection, simulating a try pandemic. However, due to the likely minimal testing that must have been done with this game prior to release, they seemed to have missed that the math can just leave the players wrecked with no way to come back. 

In a single game, the likelihood of this happening is not extremely high, but by no means whatsoever extremely low. Due to the game heavily relying of not one, but two shuffled decks that need to continuously interact, one of them being top deck shuffled multiple time, you can end of getting epidemic-ed less than 2 turns apart, which means that the same 3-4 cities are going to get an outbreak with nothing the players could have possibly done in order to properly prepare for such a strong assault. 

This game can be very chill to play with fresh people, and it always deserves space at the table for that reason. But I will never go reaching for this game when I want an actually stimulating and fair cooperative board gaming experience.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value: great real-life concept for a cooperative game...great game mechanic & flow of play...and since it's not easy to win...it encourages/rewards out-of-the-box thinking...have enjoyed customizing it slightly to add a Role & Health Protocols & Meta-Rules...the new Role being "Resource Contractor" who can bring unused roles into the game for one round of play or bring a discarded city card back into the game...the Health Protocols being derived from the 2015 Promo Roles expansion which chips away at the health of a Role if they're in a city when an infection occurs there + a new Epidemic-like card to activate said Health Protocols...three Meta-Rules are (1) another way to win is that any diseases which haven't been cured are not present in any cities when it's a player's turn to draw 2 cards...this rule addresses the randomness with which the cards enter gameplay...sometimes requiring that city cards be used more for travel/building at the expense of using them for cures & (2) only 6 research centers can be built...this rule promotes thought-out & long-range gameplay over just doing an action because it's available & (3) turning in a cure for a disease at a research station in a city the same color as the disease...also removes all cubes of the same color as the just cured disease in all cities the same color as the disease...this rule rewards more complex & time-consuming gameplay...anyway...thanks for reading this far!
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Love the game, but it really depends on who you play with. Since this is a cooperative game, control freaks who essentially try to play solitaire and boss you around, and on the other side of the coin, players who don't put much effort in and refuse to discuss moves, can ruin your game completely. With people you know well and at your skill level though, the game's really fun! A game between experts creates discussions that really make you feel like a brainy doctor as you calculate possibilities to do the most good with those preciously few 4 actions each turn. I love the mechanism of spending 4 action points per turn, the theme is popular, original, intense and immersive, and the rulebook is amazing. Wish it had cool figurines like those in Fury of Dracula, Shadows Over Camelot, Tannhauser etc, or even have the pawns labeled 'M', 'S' etc because I often have trouble distinguishing them from each other when I glance at the board, since the colors of each role are arbitrary. 

What I really love about this game is that if time is tight and 2-4 of us want a game, Pandemic will definitely finish within 45-60 minutes, even if there are new players. What I'm leery about is that there is a definite shelf-life to the game before things get much less intense and interesting (after you internalize all of the mechanisms and strategy), and I currently estimate this at 10 plays. But those first few plays are a BLAST.

5+2
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Wow! Pandemic is really really good.  My group played for the first time last night and was just blown away.  It's the first new game that we've played in a long while that we've decided to play the game again after playing it once... and then we played it a third time, and were it not so late, would have played it a fourth time.

I'm not usually one for co-op games, but this has a great feel to it where all of the players are working together to use their respective abilities to best quell the infection and outbreaks.  

On our second game, we nearly lost because of our hubris of thinking we had the entire thing sewn up -- I was holding the cure for the last disease, I was within range of a research station, and there had only been two outbreaks for the entire game.  But, we didn't notice that I could only reach the station, and that I would be out of actions to cure... we thought all was well, except that an epidemic hit, which caused the hot zone in South America to have an outbreak... that caused another outbreak... that caused another outbreak... suddenly we were in a crisis situation because we were down to the last yellow cube... any further activity in that area would lose the game for us (not to mention that we had just kicked the outbreak counter up by 3-4).  We did end up winning, but it was so interesting that the game could turn on us so quickly.

I look forward to playing this one again soon.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
I resisted play Pandemic for a long time--probably because the theme doesn't exactly appeal to me.  I get nervous and clammy just thinking about those medical shows on TV.  One time I passed out in class when a teacher was telling an anecdote about a trip to the hospital.  However, there is too much strategic goodness to resist Pandemic.  I especially enjoy the different roles that each player can take because it means that different players have different mini goals even if the overall goal is the same.  

I can see that it would be possible to have one experienced player boss the other players around to the extent that the other players would just be pawns that might as well be painted pink, green or white, but that didn't happen in my game, and I would say that as long as all of the player were of similar skill levels, that this shouldn't be a problem.


***Update after playing with my boyfriend who likes almost none of the games I like***

I think I've finally found the holy grail game!  This is a game that has strategy, but doesn't leave us hating each other at the end.  Pandemic is a game that my boyfriend actually likes!  And I like it too.  A lot.  In the two or three player games that I'm likely to play at home, Pandemic is not going to suffer from dominate personality problems because we are all introverts and great at listening to each other!  Hooray!

My rating is raised from an 8 to a 9.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
This may displace Lord of the Rings as the best cooperative game (of course, in my opinion) and I still really like LOTR.

The theme here works extremely well. The rules are tight and not complicated. The graphical representations are very intuitive. I really felt like we were fighting epidemics. Nicely done!

You'd think that being able to tell people pretty much exactly what you have in your hand would distill the game down to a puzzle that any lone person could solve. The danger with a coop game is always that one dominant personality (or person with more experience) is going to start dictating to others what to do...and then, why are the others playing?  I thought that might be an issue here, but it was not. There was enough dynamic stuff going on that each player could contribute to the overall plan.

But what really makes Pandemic shine is the variable player powers. Firstly, you KNOW one of the powers is not going to be in the game. Secondly, there are natural activities each person can do better than the others. Finding a way to work as a team was a very enjoyable challenge. It also gives a sense of ownership to the actions, even if someone else suggested the move...it was ONLY your character who could do it.

Finally, the whole package fits easily under an hour. And its not easy to win. I'd like to add this one to my collection....and I think it will appeal broadly to casual gamers.

Pandemic – Your team of experts combats four diseases: cure them all before they take over the world.

Idea for a new role

Pioneer
When you use a city card to build a research station or take a flight, you may  place a disease cube of that city's colour on the city and deposit the card in its respective city, instead of discarding the card. In the same turn, you can use the deposited card to build a research station or take a flight, placing an additional disease cube each time. 

Create a separate pile of deposited city cards; players may freely examine them at any time. Any player in a city with a deposited card can Share Knowledge to take it or can Discover a Cure using it instead of one of the needed cards.

Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value: Just finished my second play of this game, and unfortunately, I think of this game in relation to Eldritch Horror (which I love). How does it stack up? Both games build tension marvelously. However, where eldritch revolves on dice rolls, Pandemic's gameplay is elegant and streamlined. This makes the game somewhat more methodical, and less of a romp, but still feels thematic as the game is simply very well designed. It is also 1/4 to 1/5 the length of Eldritch horror, and so even though the potential for memorable narratives in this game is far lower, and it manages to generate at most frustration as opposed to dread, I have to give this game the better score. This is also a difficult game. I have played Edlritch Horror 11 times and have triumphed over the warped machinations of the old gods 7 times. Of my two plays of this game I have twice been thwarted by the the lowest and most primordial of earthly life forms. Those looking for a challenge will not be disappointed. The one theme breaking element I encountered in this somewhat abstracted game, is at the end of my most recent play (2 player) all diseases were cured, 2 were eradicated, and there was one disease cube of both of the other colors left and we lost because we ran out of cards to draw. I say, give us more character cards to draw (with more interesting resources and events) even if it means also adding more epidemic cards.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
After a bunch of plays, I have to conclude I don't like Pandemic. It was OK at first when both myself and my partner were getting to know it, but it was all downhill after we both decided we knew best what the next move was. 

I listened to Tom Vasel's podcast extolling this sort of game last year, in which he suggested that players who don't like take orders should just develop a stronger personality, but you can't win this without extensive discussion and strategy sessions. And in those, you're going to take orders a lot of the time, or issue them. You might talk and talk and talk everything out, but that gets boring and eventually someone has to make a call. Simple as that. 

I think I just hate games that have subordinates built into the rules. I don't play games so that I can outsource my already meagre decision-making capacity to others. 

This is ingenious and fun and an innovative, interesting design - but only insofar as everyone agrees, and as soon as that stops happening, prepare to be either bored or angry.

The board is about a 3, though. The cards are substantial, which helps, but the colors of the pieces don't really match those of the roles. Plus, that sunburst graphic, and the silly looking Hairy Virus around the title? If you're going to put out board games, spend more than half an hour learning how to handle photoshop, eh?

But hey, it set me back £24.99. Not bad.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
classic cooperative game fighting epidemics on a world map
I like the theme.
surprisingly good production (Z-MAN version), even the box feels more sturdy

It's said to have a big alpha player / quarterbacking problem. So, it's best to play solo with 3-4 characters. (!)
But you can also play with hidden hand cards and communicate. Just be careful that one player makes too many decisions alone. In my experience the difficulty could be too high for playing with mulitple players when playing with standard rules and more than 4 epidemic cards. Although it depends a bit which characters are played. And luck is always a factor.

The simplified finding of a cure by turning in a number of cards of the appropriate color seems a bit silly to me. This really wants the "In the Lab" expansion to make it more interesting and thematic and less clunky (when exchanging the cards with small hand limit).

I'm not sure. I like the basic idea of a cooperative game, but in practice it is odd to play against the game.
If a single turn of a card decides the outcome of a game, why not just throw a coin instead? Isn't it too often just a gamble of where the one city card that mustn't come up at that moment is placed in the stack when put on top during the last epidemic?

I'm very displeased and disappointed that they discontinued (selling) the app on Steam. Sometimes publishers are dumb like bread.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
The mechanics are very similar to Shadows Over Camelot. Each turn, you do good stuff, and draw cards that produce bad stuff. The game is a race to complete some good tasks, while constantly being distracted having to prevent imminent disaster. Every player has a special ability.

Two aspects make it an improvement over Shadows Over Camelot. One, the board has geography. In Shadows Over Camelot, there is a cost to move from place to place, which means you have to plan ahead before you go somewhere, to be sure you can stay there for long enough to be efficient. However you can move from anywhere to anywhere. In Pandemic, there is a connection graph, so some places are more costly to move between. You have to consider what you need to do in a whole region.

I also think the roles complement each other better than in Shadows. In Shadows, each role has interesting uses on its own, but there are not so many interactions. It seems like in Pandemic, every pair of roles will have some critical interaction.

Follow up:

I've played a lot more of this. All of the things I said above remain true. In addition, I think this game is a lot more tactically challenging than other cooperative games I've played. A really good tactical plan can really save the day. In the cooperative setting, this is great, as the group can brainstorm and come up with the tactical plan together.
