There is also Healing Blade:

https://www.boardgamegeek.com/boardgame/179322/healing-blade-defenders-soma

Pandemic is a perfect example of what unfettered capitalism and mob mentality inflicts on all of us - there are many ways to make a game about the same subject matter (I live not much more than walking distance from the CDC and count many epidemiologists there as close friends) morally and in a way that respects life - in the case of Pandemic, simply changing fatalities to number of infections would be a start. Infectious diseases do not exist outside the context of global politics and society and Pandemic's crass and banal approach to the inequalities of our world is simply repugnant. 

It's also a poor game as pointed out by many other reviewers. Barnes and Noble, how I loathe thee for popularizing such thoughtless "games".
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Great, elegant and crunchy coop game.
-Explanation is about 10 minutes. Game is really straightforward even for non-gamers.
-The theme and mechanics marry beautifully in this game. The components and the board look great, and the game is packaged brilliantly.
-Elegant way to teach action point selection, cooperative gaming, and variable player powers.
-Game is perfectly scalable from 2 (or even one) to 4 players. The game feels surprising and is consistently difficult with each play.
-Only minor flaws. It is possible for some games to be super difficult (if not impossible) or too easy based on card draws. This is rare, but makes it somewhat worrisome to introduce the game to new-players, only to find the system doesn't work normally. It is also very easy for someone to take over (ie. alpha gamers). Normally we try to mitigate this by asking others what we should do (often there's at least a couple viable options, so you can present the options and let newcomers decide). The game's simplicity, while a strength, can also be a weakness. You get to the point where you can quickly narrow down the couple best options, making the puzzle a little less thought provoking and a little less conservation provoking.
-Even with the flaws, this game does an amazing job as a simple, fun, tactical game that is great for teaching newcomers into the possibilities of gaming.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
[March 2015 - 6.6]
My wife and I recently played Pandemic again (after awhile of not playing it) and it left me thinking I was a bit harsh with my initial review. It was a fun game, fairly quick, challenging and exciting. Then, we played it again with some friends soon after ... and my misgivings about this game began to return. That day, we played it twice in a row, and it brought me back to my initial thoughts. People take control, those with the best roles do most of the actions and the rest of the players are left pushing pieces across the board on command. At least the games are fairly fast. I think playing this game two-player every once in a while will keep my interest in it. 

[August 2014 - 6.5]
I'm surprised that Pandemic was No.1 on the Dice Tower's 2014 People's Choice. I'm wondering how many times the voters played the game. From my perspective, the game is pretty good the first few times you play it, but then it begins to lose its luster, especially if you have someone who wants to control the game. That could be said about many co-ops, but I think Pandemic is one or two mechanics away from being a more interesting game. And it would seem that there's an onslaught of new games (eg. Dead of Winter) attempting to take co-ops to the next level. It's good that this one is spreading to the general market though -- I've seen it even in Target.

textfield_comment_value:
An excellent co-operative that doesn't feel like the more traditional games of this genre (notably LoTR and Shadows Over Camelot) because of the swift pace and less need for players to confer. Tidy, simple but effective mechanics keep the disease cubes spreading and means that players can't afford to stagnate. Surprisingly tense stuff too as you reach the final stages. It looks like the expansion will help to customise this a dozen different ways for all levels of difficulty and enjoyment.

Further Thoughts: Lacking in longevity, it would seem. We've done all we can with the game, and it looks like we might be going back to Shadows Over Camelot. Downgraded from 9 to 7.

textfield_comment_value:
[b]Well established as the essential co-op game, and for good reason[/b]
- - - - - - - - - -
If you've played this game, it's very apparent why this game is so lauded. It's simple enough to not intimidate newcomers and strategic enough to keep them playing. This includes me. Pandemic was the second game I bought and it hasn't faded on me yet. Underneath the hood of this gateway co-op game is a smooth system of mechanisms that is balanced as hell - never too easy, never too hard. At least for me. It's a well oiled engine that makes you think your safe, then explodes in your face. And by explodes in your face, I mean a deadly infection that frankly, you thought wasn't going to be a problem. While there are certain things that, after playing a few times, you know you have to do; I don't feel like this game is "solved". And this is because of the way the epidemic and infection deck work. The way the shuffling of cards after an epidemic means you know what's in the deck, just not when it'll come up; means it's a struggle of risk and reward. If I ignore that, i can trade cards and get closer to the cure... When you have a great idea in this game, it's likely at the risk of something else collapsing. But you've gotta play those odds. And deciding which odds to play, together with a group of friends, is exactly why I love this game.

***
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
A moderately fun co-op. Since I just adore cooperative games in general, I have to give thanks to Pandemic for doing so much to popularize the genre.

I personally don't find the medical theme super interesting, but it does come across pretty well. I really like the world map, which looks great and gives the game a surprisingly epic feel. Another nice thing is that the game is pretty short--four people can easily get it done in under an hour. Setup is a little awkward with the need to seed the Epidemic cards into the draw deck, but still pretty fast.

On the minus side, I don't find the actual gameplay to be super interesting. There is some strategy but the luck of the draw unquestionably predominates. And really, I just don't find the game's mechanic for finding cures (collect a bunch of cards of the same color, then discard them at a research station) all that compelling.

However, Pandemic's simplicity, brevity, and strong theme may make it a good choice for introducing people to the world of co-op gaming (particularly someone interested in medicine or public health). I myself would rather just play Eldritch Horror (a game that obviously owes much to Pandemic, but is much more interesting).

I should note that Pandemic Legacy, by all accounts, fixes my complaints about Pandemic's uninspired gameplay. I hope to try it someday.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value: When this game first came out I followed it closely.  I even listened to a Google Talk that the designer of the game gave.  Honestly, I didn't get it.  I couldn't tell if it was just another one of these co-ops that ends up being *essentially* "Go Fish" (e.g., Lord of the Rings, Shadows over Camelot).  Also, there were reviewers who were writing that every play was obvious and mechanical.  Well, I played this for the first time at GenCon '09.  Z-Man had sold out by the end of Saturday, so I bought a copy as soon as I got home.  It's that kind of game.  In ease of rules to interesting outcomes, I'd rate it similarly to Ticket to Ride.  The rules are incredibly simple, and very, very tight.  What the rules don't capture, though is that ambiguous dimension of tension.  Some games are able to produce it, some aren't.  Pandemic's the latter.  This was true of a bunch of adults (at GenCon), and has been true with my two daughters (11 and 14).  It's a similar feeling to Twilight Struggle: you never have control over the board, and things can deteriorate very, very quickly.  Me, I like that kind of game, and I'd rank this as the best pure co-op that I've played so far.  Finally, it is simple enough that my daughters have pulled it out on their own when their friends have come over.  I think Z-Man has got a "classic" on its hands here.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
There are some very clever mechanics here which inspire panic and dread as well as any you'll find. There is a real sense of accomplishment when you can solve the puzzle - which had no guarantee of a solution at any time. The theme makes perfect sense with the mechanics though it can make for a bit of a "downer" when another loss occurs. I'm probably in the minority, but however silly it is, it's just more fun to conceive of diabolical, Lovecraftian doom than real doom being visited upon the world population. This is a classic game for a reason and it deserves to be tried by everyone, but I might find myself playing the considerably lighter Forbidden Island when I want to play with the same mechanics.

Update: I've raised this to a 7 after getting some experience with the iPad app. It really is very clean and sometimes I want that. I still feel it's probably best as a solo game because the alpha gamer factor is very high here (a factor addressed well in more recent co-op games)...maybe expansions will mitigate that somewhat in this title; I will have to see.

Update: Yep - an 8 now. A modern classic. Playing Pandemic Legacy (a stone cold 10) helped me see more theme in the original game in addition to its cleanness and elegance. The alpha-gaming issue is still there, but that issue isn't enough to have it less than an 8.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value: “Clear!” (Bu-Bump!) That’s the sound of Pandemic paddles bringing the stale, crusty heart of board gaming apathy back to life. If you, like many people, are under the impression that board games can be categorized into Monopoly, Scrabble and Clue… than let me suggest a double dose of Pandemic. It has a board, cards and pawns, but it plays nothing like its predecessors. This is a game about saving humanity from the ever growing threat of infection and life threatening outbreaks. The mechanics provide a constant drip of impending doom as players race cooperatively around the world to save humanity from extinction. This is a great game for couples and for introducing people to the hobby. The cooperative play is a unique element to new gamers, and the theme of saving the planet from disease is something most people can get behind.  A player’s turn will see them traveling to all parts of the world, beating back outbreaks and establishing research stations to cure diseases before they reach a Pandemic state. In addition, your team will activate crucial events like air lifts, government grants and sanitation that add an often needed shot of moral as you battle outbreaks in the most remote parts of the world. Like many other games, prescribing individualized roles for each player is what truly what gives this game a heart.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
PROS: 
- A simple and yet entertaining game system. 
- The games are exciting and fast-paced. The game length is moving at around 25-45 minutes. 
- Very cleverly elaborated topic. 
- Variable difficulty. 
- It is necessary to cooperate. 
- Fun and playable in even 2 or more players. Solo play is also possible (the player will play several characters).  
- Entertaining even after many games. 
- It can take a rare players as well as experienced players. Quickly explaination of rules. 
- Some game material is somewhat minimalist (wooden cubes and classic wooden figures), but for this game it fits.
- Sympathetic size of box and the board (game does not need much space). 
- The influence of chance is adequate for gameplay, fun and thrill of the game. 
- Set up of the game is quite fast. 

CONS:
- Dominant players can theoretically take the reins of the game (but it never happened in our case). 
- Some cities on the map are shown somewhat confusingly (mainly in Asia), so sometimes the site is looking a while. 
- Some of characters are more powerful than the others.

CONCLUSION:
Best cooperative boardgame I've ever played. A brisk, exciting (sometimes it's really adrenalin), fun... and yet rules can be explained in a few minutes. Pandemic clearly belongs to our most popular games. And I highly recommend the expansion.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
As a dissenting voice, let me say that I guess I just don't get this one. I was looking forward to it but, having played it a few times, it just doesn't excite. Leaves me very cold. Girlfriend finds the theme depressing. I read session reports and reviews, each raving about the innovation and tension, but it doesn't work for me, nor for anyone I've so far played with. It's really frustrating to play a game with varied groups in the hope that one of them will say: "Yeah, man. It really works for us." 

Basically, it's a co-operative game with a "ticking-bomb" type of mechanism determined by the turn of a card. Its innovation is that when the "bomb" goes off, infections escalate and the cards that have caused the epidemic are placed back on top of the stack to increase the threat. Wooo. Somebody wake me up.

To explain my problem with the game, here it is: you are reliant on all the other idiots around the table to succeed, and even then it's likely the system will screw you. I think it's because I'm excited by competing against the other players. I've never liked solo games - they're too dry. This is essentially a solo game where you don't get to make all the decisions that lose you the game. Lots of people like this kind of guff. I'm not one of them.

Not my worst game ever, but my biggest disappointment.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
I know this game is very popular and I can understand how that is.
I on the other hand find it punishingly hard and for no good reason.  What comes across as a strategy game in which players work together to cure the world of 4 spreading diseases, is in fact a luck-based game in which the order of cards in the draw deck pretty much dictates whether you will win or lose.
Furthermore, a well-thought-out theme of research centers, players with specialized roles, and an efficient system where disease spreads across borders falls apart with an awkward mechanic of "playing 5 cards" to cure a disease.  With such detail put in to creating methods to lose, the only method to win is the least thematic of them all.
In the end, it feels like a game that was simply written to be hard.  Change one number in the rule book (such as number of cards needed to cure a disease) and you'd have a completely different game on your hands.
Lastly, realize that Pandemic is a solitary game.  The number of players you have is completely irrelevant.  You can take each turn yourself, or share with a friend - there's really no difference.
I've played several times, and had the same challenges each time.  The game doesn't change much, play after play - it just comes down to which cards are drawn when to determine if you'll win.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value: Solid cooperative game that works well with theme of the CDC basically seeking to contain epidemics and find cures as you travel the globe.  Each person has a special ability which can aid in carrying out actions of your character or another in some cases.  Its definitely difficult to contain the different diseases and easy to get distracted from what you really need to do at times.  Considering that you will often need to use 1/3 of the cards towards finding cures, that leaves you with the last 2/3 of the cards to fend off epidemics long enough to find the four cures and win.  10-2 record with 4 epidemic cards thus far and 16-5 record with 5 epidemic cards and 5-10 record with 6 epidemic cards!  I can see where you might need to start adding the 5th or 6th epidemic card after a few plays to boost the challenge level as people learn to use their roles efficiently.  You can definitely play with 5 players as well.  I must admit that I have no desire to play with only 4 epidemics any more as it is too easy (after losing my first two games with 4 epidemics, I have not been part of a losing effort since).  Even five is starting to become easy.  I do appreciate that this game plays very quickly and I usually find myself playing twice in a row (often able to get both games completed in under an hour!)
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Best with 4, but almost as playable with 2 or solo , this co-op game took BGG by storm and rightly so. The mechanics behind the game increase tension as time goes on. There's a card limit - if they run out, you lose. There's an infection cube limit - if you can't place a cube when required, you lose. There's an outbreak limit - too many outbreaks and you lose. There are also epidemic cards which not only cause an instant batch of cubes to hit the board in a new city, but also force all the places already infected to get put back on top of the infection pile, so they'll all be coming at you again from then on. These mechanisms link and compound each other too. The option to vary the difficulty by amending the number of epidemic cards in the deck is clever also. 

My first solo game (with 4 epidemic cards - the easiest setting) saw my 2 players win by curing the 4th disease with 1 black cube left unplayed, 1 outbreak remaining until I lost and only 3 cards left in the draw pile. Pretty close on all counts and quite dramatic at the end!

There was a buzz about this game everywhere and even the people who usually announce "I never play co-op, I'm too competitive" wanted a go at this one.

I've found this to be an immensely enjoyable game, there's plenty of theme here, it just drags you in.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value: First played March 11th, 2008. Taught in ~10min, played in ~45min with 5 payers. Great co-opertive game with good tension. It has great luck/strategy ratio. Player work together to beat the virus'. Each player draws a role: operations expert(build a research station in current city); dispatcher(mover others pawns as your own or to another pawn); scientist(cure a disease with 4 cards instead of 5); medic(remove all cubes in one city for 1AP; administer known cure free) and researcher(may give others a card for 1AP if in same city). There are two decks in the game. 1) Infector city cards and 2) player city, special, and epedemic cards. Each players starts with a certain number of cards. On your turn you have 4APs to: move(adjacent city), flight(to/from city card in hand; discard), move from and to research station, or special actions(build research station(need card for the city you are in; discard), discover cure(discard 5 like color cards @ research station), treat disease(remove 1 cube), share knowlege(take/pass one card matching city both pawns are in). After 4APs, draw two player cards then draw two infector cards(place cubes in those cities). Players win if you treat 4 diseases, lose if you run out of player cards or 8 epedemics. I'd strongly recommend giving this purchase consideration.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
If you've played this game then you probably don't need to read this.  If you haven't played then I hope you're comfortable losing because that's what will happen when you play this game.  Pandemic is a very tightly balanced game that will bring you right up to the edge of either winning or losing near the end.  And it really does feel good to win.  But it isn't the worst thing to lose either because the game is easy to setup and reasonably quick to play.  So if you lose, play it again.  A game group could easily play this a couple times in a night if they'd like. 

The re-playability of Pandemic is pretty good since each player gets to pick a special role with a special ability unique to them.  Some of the roles are almost a must have to win, while other roles pretty much guarantee a loss in a two player game.

I'm on the fence between a 7 and 8 for this game.  I'd give the game an 8 without hesitation IF the game came with better viruses components rather than colored cubes and better containers to hold the cards and cubes. And if the player miniatures actually looked like the card in design and color that would be nice.  I opted to buy the more life-like ones.  The game play is great enough that I'll err on the side of an 8/10, but the components could improve as well as the storage.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value: There's no doubt that in the couple of co-operative board games I have played, players seem to be very much at the mercy of the cards that come up.  But the thing is, co-operative games are all about the experience, and that's what I love about them.  Pandemic definitely shines in this regard.  It is fun to strategize as a team, come up with a plan of attack, and sweat it out together as the odds seem to build against you.  It's theme is unique and very well-implemented, and while I would have preferred if they had named the diseases, I can see why they chose not to.  The components are basic and the board is a little small, but it all comes in a very compact and very portable box.  The game itself is remarkably easy to learn and is well-suited to playing with non-gamers.  I don't know how it will hold up with repeat plays, but so far I've played with 2, 3, 4, and 5 players, and we've had a lot of fun every time.  [Edit: I now know that, for myself at least, it doesn't hold up really well with repeat plays, and my rating has dropped.  I find myself fairly bored with this board game, yet it remains one of my wife's all-time favourites.  Go figure.  I'm interested to see if an expansion will revitalize my interest.]  Game design: 3.5/5  Personal enjoyment: 3/5  Total: 6.5/10

textfield_comment_value:
Fundamentally flawed as a coop game. The only way to win if you're playing at a reasonable difficulty is to coordinate several players' turns in advance to meet up in specific cities to exchange cards. This requires every player to play their part to a tee without agency, since player order is fixed and you have to live with what you draw. As a solo multi-hand puzzle, it's a quite interesting challenge, but if you pretend like you are actually making your own choices you're not engaging with the game in good faith. You can't just refuse to meet up in Jakarta and use the card to fly to Paris and pick up a cube next to the medic instead, what should everyone else that spent their last few turns expecting you to do your part do then? How are we going to cure the black disease, why did Alice build that research station over there if we're not going to use it? 

That's why this game has such a big quarterbacking problem, it's not that players can't shut up and let people have fun, it's that a single player can't actually accomplish anything in this game on their own and the ways you can help each other is extremely restrictive. If we all play our own game, then we may as well draw at random from a deck of cards and see if we all get four of a kind before the deck runs out.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Pandemic is a fun co-op game that everyone (at least that I've introduced it to) loves. I definitely enjoyed it a lot the first couple times I played it too.

Thinking about it currently though, I don't really have a desire to play. Maybe I've just been in a weird mood recently, but it has definitely dropped off my radar. The in-game chaos is definitely great, but I think that the progression gets a bit old (at least to me). I really enjoy games that throw me unpredictable twists and, while the placement of the "Outbreak!" cards are somewhat unpredictable, the "Outbreak!" system is really the only bit of randomness you find.

Objectively, I can recognize that I may end up revisiting this game in a year or so, praising it for the exact reason I'm currently knocking it. However, I'm currently looking for a really expansive, complex experience (definitely not the point of Pandemic), and I think it's making me unnecessarily hard on Pandemic since I'm holding it to the standards of this yet undiscovered game.

Sorry for the ramble there though. Pandemic is a great game for just about anyone, I can recognize that for sure. It's also why I rated it an 8 and am sitting here getting frustrated with it. If you don't own it, get it. It's absolutely worth having on hand.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Pandemic was the first co-operative game after the venerable Lord of the Rings by Reiner Knizia, and when I first played there was some unexplicable 'click' between me and the design. It took me a few years and horrendous encounters with other co-ops to realise what the reason for this strange alchemy was: the fact that all actions you do as player [i]succeed[/i], with utmost certainty. The game obviously throws quite a lot of random shit at you... but players are always sure about what they are doing. This has since become an absolute necessity for me to like a co-op, and so Pandemic has stayed with me throughout the years.

That said, it took me a while to learn how to play to win, and when I finally did something of the magic vanished. Making the game harder would be tantamout to 'merely' optimising the various semi-strategical paths built into the combination of various roles. While not easy, it amounts to working out the solution to a puzzle rather than creatively gaming oneself out of a tight spot. For this reason I've decided to lower the rate I've given it all those years ago. Perhaps that with the expansions (especially the Bioterrorist one which endows the spread of diseases with actual intelligence, we hope...) the actual game can be redeemed.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
A landmark game that kick-started the cooperative game genre. Sure, I know there were some big names out there before this one came along, but this is the one that created a sensation and started a flurry of other designs. I played the game dozens of times (on table & online) and enjoyed it as a group puzzle, but I think other designs have surpassed it. For example, despite coming out several years before Pandemic, Knizia’s LOTR coop game gives players much more interesting decisions with their cards -- and thus a chance for individually creative contributions. 

Flash Point: Fire Rescue, in particular, offers a similar experience but with many maps to choose from and the ability to swap roles during the game. Other cooperative games give players more individual decisions than the group puzzle laid bare on the board here. 

At this point, I can’t say I’ve much interest in revisiting Pandemic but I’m happy to have played it as much as I did. I’d rather play Flash Point or some other type of cooperative game, preferably one that gives players more individual decisions such as LOTR TCG or Gears of War.

And then comes along Pandemic: Legacy and shoots up to #1 on BGG with raves from all my friends who’ve played it. Looks like I need to try that one.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
The rules are simple, concise and clear, with few if any ambiguities. Game play is fluid, and there is considerable interaction between the players with the right group. There is one way to win and there are 3 ways to lose the game, and each of the 3 seems to occur with roughly equal frequency, which means that players must pay attention to three different countdowns. It's agreeably hard to beat, and the level of difficulty is easily adjusted to the level of experience of the players. 

The mechanics - in particular the mechanism for intensifying threat - are familiar from Forbidden Island, but better implemented with a cascade mechanism that adds a little piquancy to the game.

The game is vulnerable to the alpha gamer, and there are no individual goals that might have mitigated that. In the groups I've played with this has not been an issue, so it may be more theoretical than real. 

While the cards and the jewel-like viruses are excellent, I'm less keen on the bland anonymous pawns, some of whose colours are difficult to distinguish in low light. I've replaced mine with small figurines that make it easier for players to find their avatar easily on the board. 

I would recommend this game without reservation to anyone new to boardgames.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Played it first with 4 players, and enjoyed it.  It uses various mechanics that are different from other games, which makes it fun to play for a change.  Reshuffling just the discard pile of the infector deck is a nice touch -- you have to watch out for what cities were already infected, because they'll be on the diseases' hit list again soon!  Also, player cards are gone forever once played, so it's not good to discard them due to hand limits.

I've played with 2 players and with 3, and it works quite well in both cases.  2 is probably hardest, because you have the least special abilities, and you can't fan out to cover the board.

I've even played with 5 players, and it can be quite hard.  There's a lot of down-time; you may have just drawn enough cards for a cure, but you have to wait for 5 Infector phases (including your own) before you can even attempt a cure.  A lot can happen in 4 draw phases and 5 Infector phases!  Outbreaks are the thing to worry about here.

I tried playing with the Epidemics just randomly shuffled into the deck instead of roughly equally spaced, and it's too easy -- if the first Epidemic shows up after half the deck is gone, then the re-infection risk for any city (and hence the risk of Outbreaks) isn't as big.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value: Pandemic is simply the greatest board game ever. There isn't one thing that this game doesn't do perfectly. The only thing I could possibly say that this game does "wrong" is that its coop, so if you actually enjoy screwing your friends over, then this game doesn't really allow you to do that. I like the concept of the game, and I'm a scientist myself, so its good to see a game depart from the fantasy/sci fi genre and excel. I love that there is no "bad guy" in the game. I have play lots of other coop games, but I always end up having to be the GM or DM or BAD GUYS or whatever. In this game each person takes their turn, then takes a turn for the viruses. This actually works out great, and makes the game even harder for more players, which is how a game should be. The game is very customizable, allowing for easy rule changes, and differing levels of difficulty that should give you a very pleasing game experience. Where I don't LIKE losing a game, sometimes its actually nice to know that you can indeed, lose even in a coop setting. Really easy to learn for non-gamers as well. I also bought the expansion, and although I like some of it, the game really didnt NEED an expansion in my opinion. Although, Bioterrorist game is quite interesting.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
I played this once way back '07, then didn't play it again until seven years later. I wish I hadn't wasted those 7 years. I think this game does nearly everything right.

1) It looks good.
2) It accepts a pretty wide number of players and scales well through them all. Including solo!
3) The game is infinitely tweak-able to suit the challenge your looking for. The expansions only enhance this.
4) The theme is both unique and engaging.
5) It is accessible to many levels of gamers and non-gamers. Some of this is due to the theme. Some due to the tweakability mentioned above. Some due to a fairly simple rules set. Some is due to it being a co-op (it is less scary for some than competitive and you more experienced players can help you learn to play while you play).
6) It is well supported by quality expansions.
7) It has fun gameplay that is well integrated with its theme.




Suitability for Travel:

I have a 1 to 5 scale for four categories (1 is worst, 5 is best) in order of importance:

Portability (the less luggage space the better) - 1
Footprint (the less table space when playing the better) - 1
Scalability (the wider range of player counts the better) - 3
Learnability (the easier to teach non-gamers the better) - 3


Overall - 1.25

My girlfriend and I love playing this together. It's usually pretty intense throughout the game, a lot of interaction with each other, very satisfying to win, but still fun if you lose. Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
I truly do not understand how people actually enjoy this game! First off its main game driving mechanism are two separate decks both of which need to be aligned in just the right way or you lose period. Yeah that's fun. When a games main mechanic can be so in favor of losing because a bad shuffle ruins the game it ceases being fun! I am not saying you should win every time or even half the time. Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Hey! I can finally rate this game I've been playtesting on and off for a couple years. I really like Pandemic, it's the best cooperative game I've played since Lord of the Rings. The key is in the pacing; the game successfully ratchets up the tension as infections spread and outbreaks pop up all over the place, and the players fight a race against time to conquer the various diseases. The game is just a perfect length, about 45 minutes, and the endgame tension is just right - the game doesn't end before it's over. The different roles give the players significantly different prisms through which to look at the game, which is helpful in cleanly driving table-talk and discussion without phony artificial restrictions like Shadows over Camelot had. All in all, this is finally another good cooperative game that gamers can enjoy. It's not as deep as Lord of the Rings, but it's also simpler and shorter and should be accessible to a wide variety of players.

Gamers should probably bypass the "easy" game and go straight to the standard game.

If you'd like to tweak the difficulty a little bit without going straight to Heroic level (which can be pretty tough) try starting the infection rate marker on the second or third space.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Pandemic was one of the earlier members of the co-op trend, and by now has become a little stale.  There's not much I find wrong with it, but it's almost as much puzzle as game.  That leads to people feeling like it can be solved, which leads to playing the turns collectively and analysis paralysis.  I'm at least as much guilty of this as anyone else, but that's how I usually want to play it.  The main thing keeping it back is how much it's been played up to now.
My sole serious dislike is the scaling. With 3, it's harder to cover the globe and more difficult to exchange cards if everyone's widely separated.  But that's preferable to 5, where your coverage really isn't any better, since it takes longer to get back to anyone's turn.  It doesn't do much good to have the medic over in Asia where the black cubes are piling up if 2 more people have to go before him and the cities will outbreak before then.  Worse, the deck is diluted and it's less likely people are going to get sets, so you have to burn more time trading.  The number of turns each player gets is less, since the deck is a timer.  Most of the games I've lost with 5 have been on time, so I feel like it's just a little unbalanced there.

Plays: dozens
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
It's okay and I'm engaged the whole time. I usually play with 4. I just worry that the outcome may be determined more by the draw of the cards than by smart play or teamwork.

It's more of a multi-player puzzle than a true game. Another thing to note is that with true games, as you get better, your opponents also tend to get better. When you are playing against a random number generator (like Pandemic), it takes the same approach every time (random), it doesn't think and it sometimes coughs up easy combos, sometimes impossible draws. 

This is more akin to playing "solitaire" or "spider solitaire" on a PC. There are different situations you can be in (without knowing it at the start): sometimes you win with no trouble, sometimes the setup is impossible due to the shuffle of the initial cards. You don't know which situation you are in until you play it through. The activity of playing it through can be fun (I occasionally play solitaire on PC while waiting for other things to load), but it doesn't change the fact that whether you win or not is almost completely random- it was based on the cards, not your decisions.

Bought Jan 2009, Sold Feb 2011 after realising I don't like pure co-ops or the randomness.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Played a half dozen solitaire games and absolutely love it. Every game that I have played with five infection cards has come down to the wire, and I lost my first attempt at six infections with four characters by running out of yellow cubes during a chain reaction outbreak. Waiting to add On the Brink until I get 20 or 30 rounds in. This is a bit too deep for my kids, but great for solitaire and I will play with my wife and gaming group as well. I like this better than Forbidden Island as it has more interesting decisions and deeper strategy, however Forbidden Island is a good primer for this, and I will probably stick with that for play with my kids. The theme in this game is also great. It doesn't feel pasted on at all. 

Update: 20 plays in and this has become my favorite game. I love solving the basic puzzle every time - how to cure the virus with a limited number of actions. It is very basic, but depending on how it sets up and your characters it is always different. 6 epidemic cards has become the norm and I can usually win with 2-4 characters over half of the time. Also, get the On the Brink expansion if you like the base game. It adds some really cool tweaks, and the extra characters are nice.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
In terms of sheer brilliant mechanics, playability, replay value, and theme, Pandemic is the grandaddy of all co-ops. I do like Ghost Stories a bit better (you can read why in my Ghost Stories comment), but Pandemic is in a league all its own. I can't think of another game that so beautifully and perfectly integrates a game mechanism with the theme of the game. The cards being reintroduced into the deck when the epidemic card is drawn is such a perfect mechanic to represent an illness spreading.

The game itself looks great, the graphic presentation perfectly fits the theme. Mind you, I have the original version which significantly differs from what I consider to be an inferior graphic presentation overhaul. 

I've played loads of games of Pandemic and my wife and I are quite good at it. We can routinely beat heroic level, which leads me to my one issue with this game. In time, it becomes too easy. I know there are expansion to fix this, but I would have to buy a NEW version of Pandemic, or find an old copy of the expansion. It's all kind of a bummer. Pandemic worked perfectly, I'm not sure why companies keep changing and reworking games that don't need it. Anyway, Pandemic is great, buy it.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Unfortunately I have to admit this is no longer a perfect 10 for me, even though it would be in the top 10 games that have inspired me as a designer. The feelings of tension and teamwork this game produces is unmatched. Like many other co-op games that strive to accomplish the same thing, it pulls you in too many directions to handle at once. Unlike those other co-ops, the Epidemic reshuffle-and-put-on-top mechanism both gives you the ability to plan far into the future (but not too far) and adds a zing of dread - equivalent moments in other co-ops are typically too weak to be engaging or too strong to make you want to keep playing. Pandemic hit the goldilocks on the first try and now the only co-ops that excite me don't steal the good-turn bad-event structure. 

The reasons this isn't a 10 almost aren't it's fault. Pandemic Legacy was so good that it was difficult to go back to the OG. Quarterbacking is definitely a player problem but also other games actually prevent it. The only problem that's Pandemic's fault is that some setups on the same difficulty are stupid easy and some are impossible to solve - the range there is a little too wide, but at least 95% of games are just right.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
You are specialists at the CDC/Atlanta where you watch several virulent diseases break out simultaneously all over the world. The team mission is to prevent a world-wide pandemic outbreak, treating hotspots while researching cures for each of the four plagues before they get out of hand.
\13\\13\
Players must plan their strategy to mesh their specialist's strengths before the diseases overwhelm the world. For example, the Operations Specialist can build research stations which are needed to find cures for the diseases. The Scientist needs only 4 cards of a particular disease to cure it instead of the normal 5. But the diseases are breaking out fast and time is running out: the team must try to stem the tide of infection in diseased areas while developing cures. If disease spreads uncontrolled, the players all lose. If they can cure all four diseases, they win.
\13\\13\
The board shows earth with some big population centres. On each turn a player can use four actions to travel, cure, discover and build. Cards are used for this but the deck also contains Epidemics...
\13\\13\
Note: Pandemic: On the Brink expansion is store in the base game box. The expansion allows a 5th player.

I have played this twice solo to get the feel of the game.  I absolutely love the ramp up mechanism that creates an escalating tension in the game from start to finish.  I won the first, but lost the second, as the Black Death took over in the Middle East (ran out of cubes).

The group included what I consider non-gamer types, including my wife.  She likes Hive, but not enough to suggest it during off hours.  The others have played Settlers, but absolutely disliked PR.  They all have biology interests so the theme intrigued them.  We played the introductory game and by the end, were getting the turn rhythm down.  But we lost by one turn!  We ran out of cards.  Everyone wants to play again (especially me!).

Why this is not a 10:

Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value: I enjoy Pandemic, and I love how co-operative it is. The roles are enjoyable and none are really that horrible to have. That being said one of our cards ripped our first play before we ran out and purchased protectors. Also the art is decent and everything makes sense. Players need to strategize  or else they will end up not being able to travel or build a required research station. That being said the game can be a blowout either direction far too easily, and sometimes the directions are fuzzy. (for instance how many cards one can have pre-epidemic or what to do with an outbreak that causes a second outbreak) I was super excited to play after watching TableTop. After five or six plays I really enjoy this game with the following in mind: the art is kinda boring, the pieces are just cubes, and a few scenarios or further objectives would be nice, especially with a shuffle of the player deck to continue the game. 7/12/2018 - After 1.5 years, I still love Pandemic and I will still play it, but this is no longer my favorite version. I now believe Pandemic Iberia is the best bang-for-the-buck as it combines Pandemic with several expansions in a beautiful package of lovely artwork. Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Cooperative games often suffer from issues like alpha players, scripted gameplay and luck feasts and I seldom see the point in playing against a game instead of playing against humans. However, Pandemic turned out to be a pleasant surprise.

The mechanisms are simple but with many interesting applications: the game board consists of connected cities and cards are used both for actions and for telling which cities are hit by diseases. So far nothing interesting - gather cards and use them to move and fight diseases.

But once epidemics erupt, previously drawn disease cards are returned to the top of the stack, giving all players (even newbies) a fair chance to predict the next wave. If left unchecked, chain reactions will spread diseases to nearby cities with sometimes dramatic results.

The players must constantly balance short-term disease treating (to avoid letting the situation go out of hand) against long term cure researching (to fulfill the victory conditions) and the tension and engagement is high throughout the game. Even lost games are fun and the quick and short gameplay invites repeated plays.

Finally a cooperative game I can appreciate!

textfield_comment_value: The best coaprative game, great job matt leacock, I dont usually give high rating such 7.8 to boardgames, the stunning map, all the ways that you could loose, all the discussion you make while playing, the price tag, and the moment you win it you just have the greatest feeling, are all the reason I give it 7.8, but the reasons I give it 7.8 (which is still excellent) is because of that when you become an expert at it, you tell everyone else what to do, taking out the enjoyment of the game for others, you always win when you are an expert at it, but thanks again to matt leacock, he made two great expansions (The Lab) which solves the always winning problem, by making you not to radicate and of the deadly viruses immediately, (on the brink) makes the expert in the game to play against all the others, which no longer makes it boring for the others because the expert no longer tells them what to do, I love those to expansion because of how the solve the problems,the only epansions I have ever seen that solves a boardgame problem, but here we are rating the boardgame not the expansions that is why i give it 7.8. with the expansions I would give it 8.4.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
The de facto coop game now, and well deserved. This is still a really great game and very smart, but I just don't love it as much as I once did partially because Pandemic Legacy is simply so much more fun, and partially because Pandemic no longer offers our group interesting decisions as it is basically a solved game as well--the turn by turn choices are pretty easy after many plays. 

Update May 2021: Upping this rating to an 8. Everything above still applies, and yet the magic of Pandemic continues to make this a game that sees the table and everyone has fun playing. Yes, I'm to the point where the strategic choices no longer offer much to consider, yet it still can be a bit of a fun romp to execute. Plus part of Pandemic's brilliance is how it manages to have a delightful arc to the game, it does drama well for you always feel there is a bit of danger somewhere, and the epidemics ensure the board at least threatens to go a bit out of control. Even if you know the strategy, just riding that wave of drama and watching it all unfold is a good time. Any game that continues to provide joyful gaming experiences year after year is a great game.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
+1.5 collaborative mechanics work wonderfully and the PvE elements, feel like a real threat without seeming hollow or like we're playing against ourselves. 
+1 sense of building pressure and impending danger is worked into the mechanics fantastically
+1 difficulty is really well balanced
+1 if you have one player who knows the rules well, it's actually very quick to teach a new player just what they need to know

- .5 sometimes strong personalities can take over. While mostly a player problem, some of the mechanics/characters encourage that rather than prevent it

-.5 luck does play a bigger factor than I'd like

-1 Can feel like you're solving the same optimization puzzle every turn (researcher collects cards, medic moves/cures, operations builds stations etc). characters are specialized enough that it almost hinders choices so it feels like you're just prioritizing different severities of the same task over and over... There's still engaging choices balanced well to create tension - but choices can often seem limited. 

A great collaborative puzzle for 4 people to enjoy, with lots of tension and drama woven in. Not for powergamers though.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Pandemic is about players combined their efforts to save the world from 4 diseases.  Players can be one of the 5 characters which has their own individual abilites.  Players may draw epidemic cards which will hasten the spread of the diseases.

It is a race against time to save the world.  Players have to find the cure of 4 diseases before 8 outbreaks of diseases, depletion of city cards or one of the disease cubes has been depleted.  

Good points:  It is a easy game and players can learn the game easily.  Players can increase the difficulty of the game by adding more epidemic cards among the city cards.  The game can be exciting when players draw epidemic cards and hasten the spread of the diseases while players frantically tries to treat the diseases.

Bad points: The game can be exciting, but it can also be boring.  The excitment of the game really depends on the time, the epidemic cards appear and the appearance of which infection cards that affects the cities.  Sometimes, from the start of the game, players are able to determine the outcome of the game.  Only at times, the game is an even match and entertaining to the players.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Alisha loves this one, so I finally caved and bought it. What do you want me to say about it, it's Pandemic? I won't play 2-player with her, though. 

I am finding Pandemic Legacy to be a whole lot more interesting, because your decisions carry over from game to game, and it communicates the tension of the theme more effectively. Base Pandemic is just absolutely boring. I think that the base game needs a random deck of 'objective' cards (similar to how you face different objectives in Pandemic Legacy) to spruce it up and keep it fresh. 

Beyond that, something that I dislike in all of Matt Leacock's games is the alpha player tendency. I know I can be this kind of player myself, and I hate that the game doesn't do anything to smack me down and keep the collaboration even among players. While it is intensely satisfying to dream up a last-ditch effort to save the world and win the game, it's frustrating that the game doesn't force you to come up with that plan together. 

It's Pandemic. I have problems with the alpha-player tendency (which the game does nothing to curb) and the repetitiveness, but it's everyone's favorite co-op for a reason.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Found it on sale on Amazon for $25, and since my four boys (ages 10-16) and I enjoy playing games I figured it was worth a shot.  One of the best game investments I've ever made, no question - to the point that when I found Pandemic: On the Brink on sale I purchased it for the point in time when we're ready to expand.

My 13 year-old is very particular about what games he likes to play, so he's usually my litmus test.  The only one who didn't like it was my 16 year-old, but he's at the age of not wanting to spend time with me anyway, so I take that with a grain of salt. :)

The first game took about an hour as we figured out the dynamics and game play.  Needless to say the outcome was not in our favor - despite an early eradication we quickly lost ground.  After that we were able to sort through the best way to leverage the various roles' strengths.

This is one of the few games that, even after a rocky start, my boys kept asking me to play - THAT is a win.

The only downside thus far (and it's a stretch) is that role combination can swing things pretty substantially.  But it's a small downside, and if anything makes it more challenging.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
