textfield_comment_value:
[2023] I played Splendor years ago and I remember strongly disliking it. Even still, having replayed it on Board Game Arena, I can say I still do not enjoy playing Splendor. 

Gather cards and collect spices to generate an engine capable of racing other people toward scoring cards? I love it (Century: Spice Road). Race for cards to establish rail roads along a track, connecting different points and denying opponents of different scoring opportunities of long railroad tracks? Enjoy it (Ticket to Ride). Establish colonies in sectors using cards to advance your gold and victory point production engines based on probabilities and dice rolls? I get it, but I just don't seem to generally enjoy dice games (Space Base). Forge dice to directly change the odds of your resource generation? I get it, but I'm not a dice person (Dice Forge). 

I seem to understand the flow of Splendor and I can recognize why, for example, reserving cards is actually incredibly beneficial. I can tell that strategies need to remain malleable for players to remain competitive. I can also tell that there exists a solid amount of luck, but *generally* that luck is, at least, manageable. At the same time, playing Splendor like an engine-builder will likely make you regret making certain choices when the cards necessary to put your engine to use suddenly vanish from the shop, or the game will be over by the time you're done setting up. 

The review titled "Splendor after 70 plays: observations and strategic tidbits" notes a few things to which I wish to pull from:
(1) "Splendor is not an engine-building game, nor is it about doggedly pursuing that one Moby Dick of a 5 VP card. It’s a game of getting to 15 VP before your opponent(s), and 15 VP is an intentionally awkward number."
(2) "The fun is in responding, not (or at least not wholly) in scheming";
(3) "Neither the game nor your opponents will let you pursue your agenda unchallenged, and it often feels like a puzzle with a time limit and no definite solution. You either embrace this feeling or you don’t."

The 'situational enjoyment' (as Kurt described it 8 years ago) was clearly not to my liking. It reminds me of some older dexterity games that require players to spontaneously react to things in front of them instead of a deep, strategic experience. Sure, maybe Splendor is not random and not anti-strategic, but I cannot look past the dry exterior of Splendor to find that fun, spontaneous game play. This is not a game that I can relish in the chaos of ever-changing dynamics - and, part of it I think is that nothing ever feels in control. Whether I win or I lose, there's something bothering me about the experience; like, the best I get out of Splendor is a sigh of relief that it is over. I don't get to say "So close - maybe if I took that red thingimajig sooner to duplicate my blue doohickey to produce my yellow thingummywhat sooner, then maybe I could have scored enough to secure the final whatchamacallum" like after playing many engine builders. I don't find myself holding my head out of sheer exasperation that something like the end-game arcs of Ticket to Ride or Castles of Burgundy would induce. I don't go jumping out of my chair in the final stages of a close point salad game like Barenpark where victory is usually only a couple of points apart. Part of that may be because 15 victory points is completely arbitrary - not only is it awkward, it's a lot less easily identifiable compared to something like Century's 5 victory point cards, to which perhaps scoring only 3 high-value cards might be better than racing to fulfill the end-game condition. There are little tidbits that playing Splendor with better opponents will steadily teach you about the flow of the game at a higher-level, but I'm not sure I care enough to ever find out.

To me, it just feels as over as it started - it's like you're making progress in solving some complex calculus problem and the teacher yells "pencils down!" because Timmy finished the test first and Timmy remembered the solution to half of the questions from the homework questions he reviewed 5 minutes prior. Do not ask me why I thought this example makes any sense - perhaps mild PTSD from my years in school. I would be probably be looking at Timmy calling him a lucky weasel ruining it for the rest of us.

For example, in one game: all 4 nobles consisted of Black/Red/White, and but my dumb brain decided to heavily invest in Blue for... no reason. I just did not properly recognize what the cards I was gathering were working me toward until at least the mid-game, where I realized my two opponents were likely in a fierce battle for those three aforementioned colors (before one just started securing Green cards for no apparent reason). On the top row was a 7 Blue card and a 7 Blue 3 Green card that I realized my opponents were never going to work toward; eventually, a 5 Blue and a 6 Blue showed up in the middle row granting... more Blue. I won the game in what felt like 5 back-to-back turns just by being at the right place at the right time. Hooray, I guess? The game crawled its way past the early-game setup, and right as people started making moves, the game was over.

In the end, Splendor just made me want to play a game like Jaipur or Lost Cities instead - simple, streamlined hand management set collection games. Or, it just made me want to play an engine builder - Century: Spice Road and Gizmos come to mind. Somehow, Splendor even made me just want to play Ticket to Ride, which is not a comparison I was ever expecting to make. My love for 7 Wonders: Duel and my enjoyment of Jaipur and Lost Cities is actually tempting me to give Splendor: Duel a shot, as I'm hoping it'll be a tighter experience really highlighting the uniqueness of Splendor. 

Splendor, itself? Easy skip for me.

:star: [b] Samo's worst game ever played.[/b] :star:
[i]The game that is pure EEVIL[/i]

I hate this one for political reasons. [i]No ... I don't mean ... look ... [/i] political in the sense that I read Splendour to be a [i]counterrevolutionary game[/i]. By the end of 2000s casual games realised eurogames hate them. Euros became arcane mechanical gizmos that pretty much all played the same way. Thus, casual gamers turned to games more in line with what normal people want from boardgames: light social fun. There were microgames, new party games and the entire social deduction genre returned from obscurity (courtesy of The Resistance). Suddenly there were many new beer and pretzel games, German family games became a factor. And this meant that "gateway" game as an idea was dead. Suddenly there were no light accessible games which would double as a introduction to the mechanistic MPS complex clockworks the euros have become. Casual players were happy playing casual games, not "progressing" towards the eurogaming nerdvana. This was not good. Something had to be done.

Enter Splendour. 
Eurogaming equivalent of Empire Strikes Back.

Splendour is accessible, Splendour is simple, Splendour as is asocial as it gets. It's taking your generic euro engine building and removing from it anything remotely interesting to the point that it looks like an early prototype version. Suddenly you have a MPS engine gizmo you can drop on innocent nongamers and there's a high 0.5% chance they'll turn into gamerz! And then there are CHITs. [i]Ahhh! It's PLASTIC! I needz! [/i]Spledour is a hobbyist wet dream: combining plastic bits with the hope of turning nongamers into gamers. This combo also justifies putting a simple deck of cards in a relatively huge box and charging a premium for it.

From my original rating notes. 

[i]Somewhere in the middle I looked at my tableau, plateau thingy and went "whee, I'm snowballing". What joy.

So, firstly, there's no game in here, it's just a puzzle exercise. Secondly the game plays itself. Thirdly no theme, no dramaturgy (apart from whee snowballing), they didn't even try getting some theme that would make sense. Fourthly the graphics are terribly uninspired - like somebody just drew over photographs.

About Knizian adjective this game gets and undeservedly so. While it's simple and sorta kinda has tension, there's no tension arriving from the players, no shared space, it's a MPS. Tension is there, but what kind of tension? It's a tension you get from withdrawal symptom. Your engine is snowballing and you want just more and more and one more gem and one more card, and why did you take that, it's mine, mine, mine, precious! A friend (Martin) made a really clever comparison to game apps played on phones and tablets and such which makes sense both in what this game is and why is it liked. The tension of the game doesn't come from tense choices or risk taking, it comes from addiction. And addiction is not social, there's no common space players share here, it's just people tring to get their fix. 

t felt to me like somebody took your average MPS engine buiding euro and streamlined it by cutting off anything remotely interesting. It even feels to me like a prototype, something than would need to be properly developed. [/i]

textfield_comment_value:
[thing=148228][/thing] is a light set collection type of game. In your turn you have a small set of options:
- take two chips of the same color (if there are at least 4 chips in the stack);
- take 3 chips, all of different colors;
- take one card from the rows and one gold chip (maximum of three cards separated - you must always pay the cost of these cards, you can't just put them back in the rows);
- pay the cost of one card and put it in front of you.

The cards are divided in three rows, accordingly to the amount of chips necessarry to build them. The less chips, the easier to pay its costs. Every card will have the kind of chips necessary to pay for it, and also will have a type of precious stone - once you take it, the cost of that type of color will reduce in one. So, for example, if the card you took has 1 green gem on it, the next time you will pay for some card that needs green, you will pay one less (up to zero).

Some of the cards are worth victory points, and also there are nobles, which are worth 3 points and require a set of colors to "visit" the first player that complete the set. The game ends when someone reaches 15 points, when this happen, the players will finish the round of play so that everyone has had the same number of turns. The winner will be the player with the most points.

As one can see, [thing=148228][/thing] is a game that can be explained in few minutes and played by anyone that grasped games like [thing=9209][/thing], beign as light as this one. And it plays even faster: usually you will have your turn figure out way before the game returns to you. When we played, one AP player was always surprise to see that the play had already returned to him. Even with this, we played the whole game in around 40 minutes. I won't be surprise at all if the plays, once everyone has the flow of the game set in, will last around only 30 minutes.

It is an easy going game, with some indirect confrontation (I can take a card I see you want to take, or I can hold chips of one color in order to prevent, for some time, other to build cards of that color), nothing major, so, even if you play with family or players that dislike confront, they will probably still enjoy [thing=148228][/thing].

The game has some luck in its play: for instance, if you take several cards that lower the cost one, say white (diamonds) cards, and the ones that are worth points requiring a high number of white don't show up, well... So it is best, as far as I can see, the spread your options, taking, at least in the beginning, cards of almost every color, in order to be somewhat prepare for everything that shows up later. Even with luck, usually the player that played the best will win - something that is always great.

As it was said many time, [thing=148228][/thing] has some [b]awesome[/b] chips - they are sturdy, heavy - a friend of mine thought they were made of metal (but no). Yes, the box is huge for what comes inside, but everything stay in its place, the cards fit even when sleeved (a major plus for me) - so I can't complain about the box. The cards are OK and the noble tiles are thick. Overall, an excellent production value - it makes well worth the price of it (which isn't cheap, considering the game doesn't came with a big lot of components).

So, [thing=148228][/thing] has proven itself as a great option of filler, giving several things to consider in every turn, but none of them overwhelmingly hard nor requiring several minutes of ponderation. It isn't as portable as, say, [thing=172][/thing], nor it accepts as many players as [thing=37759][/thing], but it is a heavier than both, and it will probably be a good choice for players that want more meat in their fillers.

Recommended!

textfield_comment_value:
Kurzrezension:
"Splendor" baut mit gutem Spielmaterial auf das haptische Spielgefühl von Kennerspielern.

Spielablauf:
Eine Partie ist schnell aufgebaut. Lediglich drei verschiedene Kartenstapel sind zu mischen und jeweils vier Karten von ihnen aufzudecken. Daneben werden die Ressourcen in Form von Pokerchips und eine Reihe von Adligen in Form von Plättchen daneben gelegt.
Wer an der Reihe ist, nimmt sich entweder Ressourcen aus dem Spielbereich oder bezahlt mit ihnen eine Karte aus der Auslage.
Die erwirtschaftete Karte gewährt zum einen Siegpunkte, zum anderen eine dauerhafte Ressource, die beim Kauf zukünftiger Karten nicht mehr mit Chips bezahlt werden muss. Zudem stellen Adlige Bedingungen an Kartenfarben und gewähren demjenigen Bonuspunkte, der sie zuerst erfüllt.
Sobald ein Spieler 15 Punkte erreicht, endet das Spiel nach der aktuellen Runde und derjenige mit den meisten Punkten gewinnt.

Erweiterung:
Die Erweiterung "Städte von Splendor" enthält fünf Module, die einzeln oder zusammen hinzugenommen werden können.
Die 'Städte' ersetzen die Adligen aus dem Grundspiel. Sie geben eine Punktzahl und eine Kartenauslage vor, die ein Spieler vorweisen muss, um sich eine Stadt zu sichern. Das Spiel endet mit diesem Modul erst, wenn mindestens ein Spieler eine Stadt für sich beansprucht hat.
Die 'Handelsposten' gewähren denjenigen Spielern Vorteile im Spiel, die eine bestimmte Kartenauslage vorweisen können. So dürfen beispielsweise zusätzliche Ressourcen aus der Mitte genommen oder Karten günstiger gekauft werden
Der 'Orient' fügt zusätzliche Karten der mittleren Auslage hinzu, die wie alle anderen mit Edelsteinen gekauft werden können. Mit ihren Effekten können Dauerressourcen kopiert oder Adlige reserviert werden
Das letzte Modul sind die 'Festungen', von denen jeder Spieler drei erhält. Sie können am Ende des Spielzugs auf die Karten der Auslage gesetzt werden. Diese können dann nur vom entsprechenden Spieler beansprucht werden und gewähren obendrein einen Rabatt. Alternativ zum Setzen kann auch eine Festung eines Gegners abgerissen werden.
Die Module fügen nicht viel Regeln hinzu, sorgen aber dafür, dass sich "Splendor" ganz anders spielt, wie gewohnt. Vor allem im Zweispielerspiel, sind die 'Städte' sehr zu empfehlen, da sie den Fokus wieder auf die Karten in der Spielfeldmitte lenken. Aber auch die anderen Module sorgen dafür, dass so mancher mechanische Knick des Grundspiels ausgebügelt wird.

Meinung:
"Splendor" ist super schnell erklärt, was schon an der zweiseitigen Anleitung zu sehen ist. Das Spielmaterial ist überdurchschnittlich gut und die Mechanik sehr einfach und Spielzüge schnell durchgeführt, was dazu führt, dass kaum Downtime entsteht. Manchmal kommt es vor, dass einem Spieler eine begehrte Karte vor der Nase weggeschnappt wurde, aber auch dann ist schnell neu gedacht und ein neuer Plan ersonnen.
Im Zweipersonenspiel entsteht das Problem, dass das Spiel oft mit einer schnellen Vergabe der Adligen endet. Die ungleichmäßige Verteilung in Kombination mit den verhältnismäßig vielen Punkten sorgt oft dazu, dass nur die billigsten Karten aus der Auslage gekauft werden, um schlicht mit den Adligen zu gewinnen.
Zu dritt und zu viert kommt zusätzlich Bewegung in die Kartenauslage und die Spieler müssen auf die Punkte der Karten spielen.
Mir gefällt "Splendor" trotz des alters noch heute sehr gut. Es macht nichts verkehrt, begeistert dagegen aber auch nicht sonderlich. Es ist ein Spiel, welches von Zeit zu Zeit gerne auf den Tisch gebracht werden darf, ich aber auch nicht traurig wäre, wenn es im Schrank bleibt.

(I've only played a single 2-player game of Splendor so far. This is just my notes-to-self)

= 2015-06-04

Almost a year later and I've only played the game twice now. Just wasn't that exciting. Putting it on the trade pile.

= 2014-05-22

I picked up Splendor because it was described as having "Fired" Jaipur. In some ways, however, it's the opposite of Jaipur. In Splendor, you're building up a points engine. The precious gems you collect are used to collect cards which then reduce the price of future card purchases. The game ramps up from multiple turns per victory point to multiple victory points per turn fairly quickly.

In Jaipur, you're taking cards to collect precious commodities. The most valuable scoring tokens are available early in the game and towards the end you're either fighting for one last high scoring bonus token or going back and forth on a few low scoring turns trying to end the game while you're ahead. Jaipur has a rather significant push-your-luck component. You might chose (or almost be forced) to take a large number of camel cards all at once and then have to draw a bunch of new cards for your opponent to chose from. Jaipur allows for a better calculation of risk. For each type of item (gold, diamonds, leather, etc), there is one more card than there are scoring tokens. If there's only one gold scoring token left, then there are two gold cards left. Do you risk letting your opponent take the 2nd to last gold card so you can focus on building up five leather cards? Is the "Most Camels" bonus worth the risk of turning up good cards for your opponent? Jaipur feels very interactive and it allows just enough calucation to feel like skill played a part in your win.

I haven't figured out Splendor yet. There's no penalty for reserving a card so if you're both (2 player game) getting close to earning a particular card, there's not a ton of risk in just grabbing it.

Once you collect your tokens in Jaipur, you're done with them. There's no reason to ever look back at the things you've earned (except to add up points at the end). In Splendor, you're constantly counting up how many of each token (real and virtual) the other player(s) has and evaluating that against the cards and nobles currently on the table.

Jaipur ends when three piles are exhausted and then the person with the most points wins. Splendor ends when someone gets to a certain number of points so the end game condition is also the win condition (I can't remember for certain, but I think the game continues until everyone has had the same number of turns).

We've only played one 2p game of Splendor, but I think I'll disagree at this point that it fired Jaipur if only because I don't think the games really scratch a similar itch.

Incidentally, I've seen a few people comment on how spectacular the components are in this game. It's true that the poker chips feel good and certainly give the game some heft but wouldn't little acrylic gems have been more thematic and cost less? If ever there was a game that would have benefited from oodles of shiny plastic gems, this is it.

Like this game quite a bit, but I do have some issues though:

1) If you compress it, it takes up about 1/4th of the box...I really wish they hadn't made it so extravagant/obnoxiously big. I know it goes with the Splendor theme of rich extravagance, but I wouldn't have minded slightly smaller gems in a much smaller box.

2) At least at 4P, it switches to a more tactical game than strategic one, and its harder to plan long term - there's not much you can do if your plan happens to overlap with the two players next to you and the fourth takes advantage. Once you're behind, you stay behind but fortunately the game ends pretty shortly and skill will prevail more often than not.

There are some ways I think this game could've been improved (personally at least): more variant rules and objective/bonus cards to spice up the game some more (ex: set number of turns variant, most greens gets a bonus, fewest cards gets a bonus, etc - these are just ideas, I'm sure the designer could come up with better if he had time), player mats to track the chips and cards (not necessary but its a nice touch as players may miscount the number of chips they have and the box has a lot of space), and I wouldn't have minded more nobles.

As far as similarities, I think this game feels extremely similar to both Ticket to Ride and Dominion, but I prefer Splendor. Light ish theme, engine building, card generation...I do like that its easier to set up though and no shuffling, so I do prefer it, though there's no special or cool effects (which is part of the allure, its simplicity). Its selections are similar to TTR's and its close simplicity wise too, though its time is much faster and more consistent than both. Interaction wise, its mostly blocking, which I don't mind.

One small issue is how gunning for VPs can get you the 15 VPs really quick, which changes this from the engine game I thought it was originally. Not sure how I feel about this, but I could always play to more points if I want a longer game.

textfield_comment_value:
40 plays, all on the app:

A simple game with depth and rhythm, that plays in about half an hour. An engine/tableau builder built around a market rhythm game similar to Jaipur.

The core drafting mechanism, where cards show both a price and a value that they yield towards buying new cards, is elegant and addictive. And the layout of the "store" of cards you can buy is perfectly calibrated: enough expensive options to make you yearn to save up, and few enough total options that you can occasionally snatch up a card an opponent needs.

There are several mechanisms for pacing and balance. Buying a card (good for you) also replenishes the various colors of coin (good for others) and also reveals a new card (others have the chance to buy it until your next turn). You often want several more of a particular color; you can be patient and collect these one at a time, or take two of them but sacrifice the third coin--and signal your intentions to others. There is a fine-tuned quality to so many of these mechanics: the game is long enough to reward a deep engine, but short enough to allow sprinters to edge by you right before you would be stronger; the 10-coin limit gives you enough room to be flexible, but imposes pressure to act, and makes hoarding gold coins restrict your room to maneuver. The limited number of cards introduces uncertainty that any color will appear, while the variety of cards showing allows for making diverse plans for chains of purchases. The fact that some cards are bargains while others are expensive introduces an elegant mechanism where you want to snatch up bargains to keep them out of others' hands even if that isn't the right move purely from the perspective of your own points.

Each turn presents a small, satisfying decision, though a close game presents analysis paralysis because there's so much useful information to consider. For such a short and easily teachable game there is plenty of depth, but it opens itself organically; you could constantly reassess the market and adjust tactics, or you could stick to a simple strategy and do OK.

That said, I wish there were a rhyme or reason to the card costs. In other builders, you might have a sense of, say, using the ore that your land produced to invest in another city, which will increase your production. Here, I've used 3 red coins and 5 black to buy a green card that gives me 2 points. Why these colors? There is absolutely no reason. 

This makes it feel dry, compared to the clearer theme of 7 Wonders or the deck-building, play-chaining satisfaction of Dominion. Like those, there is player interaction, but it's hard to make deliberate tactical use of it. The endgame is anticlimactic if you're behind. And the gold coin makes it much harder to be clear about which cards you can afford to buy, and at what cost.

textfield_comment_value:
[i][u]Disclaimer:[/u][/i] This is a [color=#000099][b]standalone game[/b][/color]. Its rating is based on [color=#000099][b]desire to play[/b][/color].

[b]Splendor[/b] is the favorite game of my father. As a result, I have played quite a bit of it and for the longest time I felt it was a good game, worthy of a 7/10 rating. The game was smooth and the poker chips feel amazing (worth a rating point by themselves) but it was just too automatic for me. I was going through the motions: building the economy, and slowing going up in the prices, with maybe a blocking move or two at the end.

Then one day I decided to wander in the strategy section of the BGG forum dedicated to the game, and a whole new world opened to me. I discovered there were alternative ways to play [b]Splendor[/b], which were actually better ways to play if nobody's stopping you.

The mistake most people (including me, of course) make in [b]Splendor[/b] is to believe that you have to building your economy before going for the most expensive tiles. When you play with this mindset, the nobles play a crucial role and the game becomes quite a luckfest where small advantages will be built upon revealing a 3-cost card or a 5-cost card after you're forced to buy something at 10 chips.

What I discovered was that a much more efficient way to play [b]Splendor[/b] is to go for the expensive cards right from the start, ignoring the economy engine and the noble tiles. This has two huge benefits : it makes the game more interactive, since you can see what people are accumulating chips for, which means you can block them by reserving cards or hoarding chips of the color they need. And it makes some of the game options more relevant: reserving a card, taking 2 chips of the same color, going over 10 chips and giving the excess back to the bank ; they all become more relevant after you learn of this "high-tier" buildings strategy.

And now the best part: while a player that goes for expensive cards unimpeded will easily crush his opposition, the same isn't true once the table becomes aware of it and starts playing in a more reactive way. This strategy is not unbeatable, instead it gives the game more player interaction, less reliance on luck and less automatic plays: all positives in my book. And once it is figured out by the players, if people block each other well enough, you're left buying small cards again... which means it becomes interesting again to aim for the noble tiles! The game has now gone full circle with every strategy being viable.

And that's the story of how [b]Splendor[/b], a much deeper game that it looked at first, went from 7/10 to 8/10.

textfield_comment_value:
Having played it three times the first day I got it and four times the next day, which is highly unusual for me, I definitely understand why Splendor has been nominated for Spiel des Jahres! It’s such a good, light family game with a decent amount of strategy. People who say that there isn’t much strategy don’t understand the deeper layers in this game! You can block your opponents and at the start of the game you need to have a plan in order to get at least one of the bonus cards (which is a great feature of the game by the way), otherwise it’s going to be difficult to win.

The simplicity of the gameplay is what makes the game shine: you can do one action on your turn out of four possible actions which are extremely basic and easy to understand. Basically you collect gems to build cards which give you points and a discount on future cards. The first player to 15 (sort of) wins the game; the round is played to the end, but it usually doesn’t matter, though most games seem to be somewhat tight. The game starts out fairly slowly with players grabbing chips, but as you get more cards you also get bigger discounts, so the game speeds up and I think it ends exactly when it should after about half an hour. It’s not exactly a snow-balling effect as the more expensive cards are, well, expensive, so even though you get a discount you still need to pay a lot of chips. But some points give you 4 or 5 points, so the game can end suddenly and you can surprise your opponents - although everything is open information, so they can still try to block you from getting the cards you want. And this is actually a big part of the game, especially in a 2p-game as you really need to watch out for what your opponent can do. One of my plays against my wife was really awesome as we both played extremely well and blocked/reserved the cards the other player needed.

The components are nice, but the box is oversized which I hate due to limited shelf space. My siblings don’t dislike this game which is something that says a lot… Sure, it’s not a heavy gamer’s game, but I think it is suited for gamers too in between bigger games. Definitely take a look, it’s a splendid game (sorry, I had to do it)! It’s so simple yet strangely addicting – I know I am going to play it a lot more! It won’t be for anybody, but it was a hit for me.

textfield_comment_value:
Splendor Review
Rating: 7/10

Splendor is a well-designed and accessible game that offers a blend of strategy and simplicity, making it a great choice for introducing new players to the hobby. The game revolves around collecting gems, acquiring development cards, and ultimately earning points to win the favor of nobles.

Components and Art One of Splendor's standout features is the quality of its components. The game includes heavy, poker-style chips representing different types of gems, which provide a satisfying tactile experience as you collect and stack them. The development cards are well-designed, with clear iconography and elegant artwork that enhances the game's theme without overwhelming it.

Gameplay Splendor is easy to teach, with straightforward rules that allow new players to grasp the basics quickly. The game’s mechanics revolve around collecting gem tokens, using them to purchase development cards, and strategically planning your moves to maximize points. It’s a game of gradual buildup, where each decision contributes to your overall strategy.

Player Interaction While Splendor is primarily a game of personal strategy, there’s a subtle layer of interaction as players compete for the same resources and cards. The game encourages you to keep an eye on your opponents' moves, adding a strategic element to the otherwise calm and methodical gameplay.

Replayability and Strategy Splendor offers a good balance of strategy and replayability. While the core mechanics remain consistent, the variety of development cards and the evolving board state keep each game fresh. Players often find themselves wanting to play multiple games in a row, exploring different strategies and enjoying the satisfying flow of the game.

Final Thoughts Splendor is a fun and engaging game that’s easy to introduce to new players, making it a great addition to any gaming collection. The high-quality components, particularly the real chips, add to the overall experience, making each game enjoyable from start to finish. While it may not be the most complex game out there, it’s consistently fun and has a broad appeal, which is why I rate it a 7 out of 10. Whether you’re playing with seasoned gamers or newcomers, Splendor is a game that everyone can enjoy and will likely want to play again and again.

textfield_comment_value:
While I enjoyed my first game, it soon became clear in our second game that the runaway leader / snowball effect meant that luck was a dominating factor.

Perhaps it was just very unlucky, but our second game resulted in one person getting 6 or 7 cards in a row early on (i.e. without having to pick up any tokens), most for free and the rest for one token. Prior to that lucky streak the game had been quite close (everybody had 1 point, and 5 +/- 1 development cards), but in the end that person reached 15 points while the other three of us each had 3 points (IIRC they had ~13 development cards while we each had ~7)!! Furthermore, the other three of us did try to gang up on that person for the last couple rounds (e.g. using gold coins in a vain attempt to block a winning move, discussing all possibilities openly), but it didn't matter... every card we took revealed another one they could grab outright, or could just reserve with a gold coin and claim for victory in the next round. Just to elaborate how bad this was: the leader could grab multiple cards in the third row, while none of us other three could buy even a single card in the second row (first row was empty at this time).

It's hard to explain just how bad this game was... two of the people involved will never play again (including the purchaser of the game!). I'm personally willing to play once more just to see if I'm missing anything (how in the world is this ranked 97?!?). I also re-read the rules to ensure we didn't miss anything (the rulebook is very clearly written, and the rules are simple to learn and understand). The only rules I hadn't known were a limit on 3 reserved (but not yet purchased) cards, and picking one noble if two are triggered at the same time; but neither of these had any relevance to the 'game' we'd just played.

Update: Played a few more games on boardgamearena. Won against 250-rated players. The game we played above was definitely bad, but others are not so dominating (although the timing of the appearance of a key colour still matters a lot). Moved into the meh category. Maybe I was just expecting a lot more depth (bgg complexity is accurate).

textfield_comment_value:
RE-ACQIURED. Was on sale, and my mother and brother used to like it when I still had it. 

~

SOLD because Jenny doesn't like it, so it was not getting any 2-player play. In addition, I was not playing with casual gamers nearly enough to keep it. Last it got played was March 2020, when I was abroad with work and I brought it along... Will play Port Royal instead as the theme and art are nicer, and it has more excitement (of course, it is also more luck dependent).

~

1) Acquire various gems in order to purchase mines, transportation devices, artisans, and shops - to procure and sell more gems.
2) A very light, very accessible, and very fast engine-builder. Using gems you acquire as an action, buy cards in one of three tiers in order to gain permanent discounts or points. 
3) I loved: How clean and fast the game is, how easy it is to teach, that it goes well with non-gamers, that while there is no direct interaction, there are boatloads of player interaction by hoarding gems your opponents need and via reserving cards your opponents need.
4) Could be improved: Can run long with skilled players (where everyone also maintains some resources in their hand that are not useful for them but serve to block their opponents only).
5) One of the first games we’ve got, at this time we rarely ever play it. My wife doesn’t like it, so we don’t play it 2-player. When we have other people, I prefer to play something meatier (Especially with 3-4 players - this game does not go beyond that and it might get played more if it did). The thing with Splendor is: when you first get into it, you start off by attempting to build an engine. However, you soon realize that is the way to lose, so you start racing for the big cards. Then, if you play with the same players, a meta develops where people block each other by hoarding the types of gems necessary for others to fulfill their big cards, so people have to revert to building engines and trying to get nobles, and games become like mexican standoffs where players are waiting for someone to blink first and “spend” the blocked resource... which can make games run longer than what is ideal for Splendor.

textfield_comment_value:
I've played this now three or four times and, each time, I find myself simply not caring. Star Realms is just as easy to teach, just as portable, and is basically the same game with a little bit of added flavor and more player interaction. Minus all that, and you're just playing Klondike. I'd gladly play Klondike by myself, but I can't think of any reason to play it in a variant where you have to wait for other people to play a move before you're allowed to play your next move.

I think that my other issue with the game is that I would like it to be an engine building game. I want to create something that's able to churn out gems and power my way through whatever might come. It presents itself like it should be that sort of game. But at the official game length (and, granted, I don't play Star Realms to its official hit point count), winning in Splendor seems to be more of a puzzle rather than a build. It's purely down to looking at the highest valued card on the table when the game starts and finding the shortest path to it.

I like puzzle games. I've exhausted Simon Tatham's Portable Puzzle Collection. But those are solitary games. Splendor is also a solitary game, where other players act as a randomizing element to obscure the path to the target. And played solitary, on a cell phone, I might become very good at the puzzle and be able to dominate in live play, but meh.

Star Realms doesn't have that same, definable target, the high card. There is some flavor to the different strategies one can take to defeat his opponent. When you lose, you have to figure out what tricks your opponent pulled, and see if you can pull it off as well, or find a way to defeat it. While subtle, there is some jostling around in there. In Splendor, there is only one real strategy: The shortest path. And once you've gotten good at that, success against your opponents becomes luck of the draw.

textfield_comment_value:
A game which boils down the pattern of snowballing to its utmost basics, stripping everything away that could possibly be interpreted as a distraction. It's even more basic in this approach than is ageing St. Petersburg; and probably attracts the same people too. Do not believe people who claim that the game is empty and without skill: they are wrong, and they know it. There is definitely skill in managing the turn order cycles, and whether or not to go for a blocking move instead of furthering your own position. These may be simple deliberations, but [i]simple[/i] is not the same as [i]absent[/i], which happened to be the point of the naysayers. 

However, I do also feel that once players begin to get a feeling for the various paths and options, that luck of the draw will [i]worsen[/i]. Someone who accidentally uncovers a 'free' card for his left neighbour for example puts himself in [i]gote[/i] through no fault of his own. It was just luck which caused the card to appear as it did. So between experienced players more lookahead is a must. This isn't difficult to accomplish, of course, but the absense of such a rule still dents Splendor's gleaming exterior.

In the end I think I like the game for what it is. It shouldn't be compared to much more difficult and complex snowballs, as it won't survive that comparison. This is not meant to be a gamer's game; I even think that a serious gamer will be done with it after a handful of attempts because it all boils down to discovering not-all-that-hot relations in the upgrade paths with ever lessening upgrade efficiencies. Nevertheless, given its strong limitations it actually accomplishes what it sets out to do rather well. This is an easy game to explain to families, and the artwork and solid gem execution aid this process tremendously. Consequently I'm generous with my rate.

Owned by Matt & Kailin and Noah.

==2018/12/15==
When I'm losing at Splendor, it's a 4.  When I'm winning at Splendor, it's an 8.  I'm going to split the difference and call it a 6?

I normally make decisions by quick rules of thumb (intuitive) rather than take in the full spread of information needed to calculate the future.  That gave me two victories tonight, but not last time we played.  It was frustrating that intuitive play seemed unviable last time.


==2018/11/29==
I don't like it.

The game is just about finding a balance between rushdown and economy.  But you have to find a path through the cards on the table that lets you build your engine at the speed you want.

There is SO MUCH INFORMATION on the table that, in order to play the game well, you have to look several steps ahead at future purchases beyond just what you want right now.  I was trying to play the game quickly using intuitive rules of thumb rather than calculating for future purchases, but that probably hurt me.

Also, you have to keep an eye on other players in order to make optimal calculations about your own choices.  It's just too much information, and I don't want to process any of it.

Euros have a selling point that everyone participates equally in a game's mechanism, and at the end of the game everyone compares points.  Because every player gets to play the game equally, every player should be satisfied.  But somehow, I never felt like I got to make clever plays in Splendor.  I didn't feel satisfied at the end of the game.  I was just doing some math next to my friends, and they did the math better than me.

Also, the game felt like I was staring at a system on a table that just happened to have other people around it.  I might have been impatient during play because other players' turns didn't actually affect my play.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
I really enjoy Splendor, as I've always enjoyed engine building games, and this one does it very simply and very well.  Basically, players are acquiring and spending colored chips in order to obtain cards.  All of the cards you acquire will give you a permanent chip of a color to spend toward future cards, and some cards also give you points.  First to 15 points wins.

The game strikes a nice balance of needing to build your engine, but also needing to race for points at the same time.  The cheap cards in the game allow you to build that engine more rapidly, but the expensive cards are the ones that also give you points.  So, a balance has to be struck.

Splendor is a great example of a game that is fun for gamers, yet super accessible for non-gamers, as the game can be taught in about a minute.  But, while the rules are simple, the decisions are not always so straight forward.

The only drawback with this game is the theme, which makes it seem as if they didn't even try to think of something reasonable.  Players could have been fighters recruiting heroes to slay monsters, CEOs assembling a work force to finish jobs, star travelers assembling a star fleet to complete missions, or any number of fun themes.  Instead, you get a generic renaissance theme that is really poorly done even as renaissance themes go, and the graphic design is quite uninspired to top it off.  It's really a shame, since the yawn inducing theme and art work may turn people off to what is a really fun game, especially when it comes to the non-gamer crowd which will easily be able to pick up on this game.

None the less, despite the missed opportunity for a good theme that could have added to the fun of playing, Splendor is a great, simple, mechanically fun game that I'd likely never turn down a game of.  Good stuff!
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: Very high quality components and quick play times are great. Since I consider this to be an engine building, I want to emphasize that the player turns don't get long and bloated as the game goes on. As an engine building, I would describe Splendor as idealized. Player actions center around buying cards to add to your engine. The engine of cards enables the buying of better cards. Scoring is from specific cards or combinations of cards. There aren't any unique/confusing rules that can be misread (Terraforming Mars), or specific combinations that can be balance breaking (Space Base). The trickiest mechanic is managing scarcities in the gem/chip market. It's an interesting aspect of player interaction, and the number of chips available is well balanced for the player counts. The four player limit is the biggest flaw for me, but one good thing about the player count is that it limits changes to the buy market between turns. The card buying market is another thing that sets Splendor apart. The three tiers ensure that cards relevant to the current game stage are always present. It also makes more cards available at all times so there is always something you want in the market (something Wingspan could benefit from). Usually there is more than one thing you want in the market, which makes for interesting strategy decisions between taking cheap cards for small gains or saving up for an expensive card to make big gains. The ability to reserve cards is also great because you can sacrifice some chip income for a more flexible wild gold piece while also securing a card you want from being bought out before you can afford it. The ten chip limit is another great point as it limits your buying power while keeping the market circulating. Every rule in Splendor feels purposeful and significant.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
This game is a long-time favorite because of how easy it is to learn, and even compete within the first play or two. It became very popular for a hobby game and for several years supported a competitive following. There are many games modeled after Splendor, but I prefer its simple ruleset, quality components and consistently engaging decision space.

Splendor is a fast-playing tableau-building game where players draft gem tokens and, in subsequent turns, trade them in for cards. The more expensive cards are worth points, but every card grants a permanent bonus of exactly one gem to its owner. Tokens are very limited, and players are aware of how spending them often opens and opportunity for their opponents. Once someone accumulates enough purchasing power, they can chase points with more expensive cards or the bonus "noble" tiles, which are awarded for tableaus of qualifying size.

The small ruleset and modest "board" (a 3 x 4 grid of cards) can lead people to underestimate the depth of Splendor, but it has supported competitions and tournaments for a number of years. Players can opt to build a broadly-based tableau of low-cost cards and decouple themselves from the struggle for chips,  getting a lead on multiple noble tiles in the process. Others will quickly reserve top-tier cards worth 5 or more points and hoard resources on their way to big scores. My favorite approach lies in between: aim for certain middle tier cards that give bonus gems in the same color as the gems required to buy them, in order to quickly turn over significant milestones in a strategic direction. I'm sure there are still other approaches, which will emerge as you get exposed to different game situations.

Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
This is an extremely simple and quick filler.  At the start of the game there are 3 rows of gems of increasing cost.  Some give you points (more at higher cost) and they all give you gem production.  Each turn a player selects three different colored gems (or 2 of one color if none are claimed yet), stores a card to be built later and acquires a wild gem, or pays the cost to build a card.  There are also goal tiles worth 3 points each that are acquired when a player builds a certain number of cards of specific gem colors.  This continues until one player gets 15+ points, then the other player gets one final turn to match or beat that score.

For what it is, this game's simplicity doesn't bother me.  It is easy to teach to almost anyone, plays quickly, and is somewhat intriguing.  What really hurts it for me though is the extreme amount of luck that can just ruin a play for someone.  When a card is bought another is flipped over immediately and after the first couple turns those may be automatically acquired by a player if it flips over at the start of their turn.  This way one player may never see the gems they need while the other acquires all the ones they do potentially for free.  I've played this game twice and this happened to me both times, once to an extremely bad degree as each row of 4 cards had 3 of one particular unneeded gem color in them and my opponent constantly got the needed missing colors at the start of his turn free of charge.

If it weren't for that this would be an extremely charming and easy filler.  But I just can't abide being beat by luck every time no matter how well I play.  I wouldn't get much enjoyment out of winning that way either.  The poker chips that come in the game are nice though.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
I'm embarrassed to admit I avoided this one like the plague when it was the nu hotness, partly because I didn't like the abstractness, and partly because its reputation as a gateway game made me assume (quite wrongly!) that there would be little to interest me. Fortunately, our town recently opened up a game cafe, and Monse and I could try before we bought--by the end of the first match, we agreed we'd be leaving with it. Now, we're living it up like everyone else was in 2015, playing several matches a week, and often 2-4 matches in a session.

Given the short playtime and tight action economy, it surprisingly rewards strategic planning and long-term reading of the market--although since there's a pretty strict horizon on how much of the market you can see up front, early strategic commitments can be speculative and somewhat risk-prone. (As weird as this may sound, I feel like some of my enjoyment of this game, and perhaps some of my skill at it, are related to my recent love of High Frontier, which, while at the opposite end of the spectrum complexity wise, explores some similar dynamics in its early game.) Though some players have apparently been put off by its seemingly inconsistent identity as an almost-engine-builder, I think that's where most of its interesting competitive qualities lie...certainly it's a game of efficient synergies, but some of that efficiency can come from using as few cards for discounts as you can get away with...and how lean of a tableau you can get away with is partially a function of the market flops, but also of how the other player(s) are pushing their own tempo and squeezing you out of your preferred choices.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: This game is a great bite-sized activity that is highly accessible for players of varied backgrounds in board game experience while also creating depth that can satisfy serious board game strategists. The random elements in this game are central to both the theme as well as the mechanics and, while they can be infuriating at times when you cannot find the gem you need from the market, planning for what you can see as well as what might be drawn to replace purchased cards is what makes this game interesting. This game favors those who can prepare for a breadth of different scenarios. It feels like each action has a meaningful effect on what you can do on future turns, the state of the game for the other players, and your overall success. There are many different ways to put together a win, and I feel like I never approach the game the same way each game. I have very few criticisms of this game, but the most prevalent is the “people” tiles at the top of the board. Because they are randomized each game, it is very possible that one player is able to meet the criteria for several cards that have some overlap, leading to a crushing one-sided game. It adds heavier emphasis to early turns that can snowball into complete control over the important color(s) right at the beginning of the game. There are ways to interrupt that strategy, but depending on which cards get drawn when, there is only so much agency that players can have over the opportunities for other players. With that being said, I highly recommend this game as a staple in any collection. It is relatively easy to teach, set up and clean up and can be played in usually about 30 minutes.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
We've played this a lot and I still don't know what to think about it.

I guess the main thing that holds it back for me is the circular nature of it. Even if I have a clear end goal, it's never obvious how to actually achieve that goal.

Like let's say I really want this white card that is worth 5 points, and it costs several blue and green gems to get it. Ok, so I need to acquire blue and green gems, great, how do I do that? Oh, there are a few that need lots of black gems, so how do I get black gems? Oh, I need some green and white gems. So how do I get green and white gems? Wait, I need green for the other thing though. But right now I need blue and red to get the green. Or whatever. 

You can never get to a "starting point" where it's like "ok, from here I have a clear path to my goal". Every turn is, more or less, "uhm... I guess I will take this one" and then hopefully that one will be useful to buy future ones.

So I don't know, I just don't like that you can't clearly plan on what you want to do, you're just basically taking whatever you can afford at any given time and hoping that the next cards available cost what you've already acquired, which isn't as fun to me as it would be if I could know for certain "yes, I will need exactly 4 red cards for my goal" because no, I might not. It's hard to say until the actual turn I try to accomplish that goal, and only then will I know how many cards I actually needed vs how many gems I could just have saved up instead, and I don't like "not knowing" what is going to be useful or not.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Splendor is a 20-30 minute engine building game in which players have only 3 options on their turns - take gems (the currency, in five colors), buy a card, or reserve a card and take a wild gem.  Cards give purchasing power in one of the 5 colors, and possibly points, and come in 3 levels, with higher levels costing more but worth more points.  

I like that Splendor strongly constrains the players options to essentially a single decision each turn.  This makes it very easy to teach.  Turns are short, and the game moves very quickly.  Players' engines build up quickly, which gives a noticeable feeling of progress.  The game usually finishes before it becomes tedious - my wife and I can play a 2 player game in 10-15 minutes.  It plays well from 2 to 4 players, although 4 players gets a little long, and can feel a little more random as well - which cards flip can decide the game.

However, I have found that with experienced players, Splendor can easily be decided by how the cards turn up.  This is a game with essentially a single mechanism and a single strategy (I may be exaggerating a little here, but this is clearly not a "many paths to victory" kind of game).  It is a quick, simple game - a filler - and will disappoint if it is expected to be more than a diversion.  

For me, this is my go-to filler game.  It is great for playing with those with AP, and with non-gamers.  At the price, I consider it an excellent buy, worthy of being in most collections, the exception being "serious" gamers who never play light games with non-gamers.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Having played it a few times I’d say that:
1.	The theme is abandoned as soon as you open the box, since it has no relationship with the mechanics.
2.	The aim is to snowball by buying stuff of identical worth until you can buy stuff that’s worth a bit more.
3.	The game consists of a pair of double steps: wait for your turn, pick up chips, wait for your turn, buy a card …
4.	… until you have so many cards that you don’t need to pick up chips any more and your turn now consists of wait for your turn, buy a card.
5.	Each player obsessively wants the same thing: the right card to build a set. If you share that ambition this gives the game the same addictive feel as solitaire. If you don't, you might get the same enjoyment from punching and sorting out the counters from a new box of Eclipse.   
6.	The main tactical decision you can make is to block another player. 
7.	You can make no other significant decisions.
8.	You can take no risks.
9.	There is no tension, only mild frustration (I wanted that card. Oh, well.). 
10.	The analysis, if you can be bothered, amounts to a dreary mathematical problem.
11.	The snowball effect and the luck of the draw determine who wins.
12. The end feels like oh, you (or I) won. Gosh. 
13.	The replayability is close to zero unless you like games of obsession governed by chance.
14.	It’s not so much a socially entertaining game as a tedious, obsessive slog. 
15. This is solitare in which you can be frustrated by other players.
16.	It has the merit of being over quickly.
17.	Perhaps not quickly enough.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Probably a 7.5* game for me, it is a good easy game to learn, fairly fun to play and it is pretty quick.  Although definitely addictive for a while, it can get old quickly and I up the victory points to win so the game at least goes for long enough to build up some pretty good engines.

"REVIEW THE REVIEW" - 1 YEAR LATER:  Still a 7.5.  It is a great gateway game and have pulled it out several times to introduce others to board games.  Although I have gone through stages of not playing Splendor, after a period of time I will go back and play it again and enjoy it as much as I used to again.  A keeper.

FOOTNOTE:  Splendor Marvel is the better of the two, introduces a new mechanic to add to the game.

PROS:
+ Love the artwork
+ Love the plastic poker pieces for gems
+ Fairly quick to set up
+ Gateway game
+ Quick games - 20-30 mins
+ Doesn't require lots of brain power to learn, function or play
+ Game ends at the end of the round
+ Standard sized footprint on the table
+ High replayability and Noble tiles adds in an extra decision making variety each game

CONS:
- Although it is quite replayable the games themselves are the same (collect gems, score 15 points first)
- Only one linear strategy in that you only win by getting 15 pts first
- Tiebreaker being whoever is higher than 15 pts does not always reward the first player to reach 15 pts
- It loses its novelty after a while
- There is only three actions you can do for the whole game
- Very abstract, no theme.  Could be collecting different car badges than gems
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
There are 3 main drawbacks:
1. Cards are too imbalanced. Low efficiency cards are almost never picked (can only be picked when a strong engine is built to be precise, but the game usually ends before this is achieved), making the tier 3 market dead throughout the game once all the tier 3 cards are of low efficiency
2. Noble strategy is too unreliable: it is not only slow but is too reliant on the cards unfolded during the course of the game. If the cards unfolded later do not match the noble's requirement, then efficient strategy would just win the game. Unfortunately, the player going for noble strategy has no idea whether the cards unfolded later match the noble or not, making noble strategy inferior to efficiency strategy
3. The above worsens the problem of first player advantage because only the first player is able to reserve the most valuable cards on the board. In a 2p game, if there is only 1 such cards and all the other tier 3 cards are of low efficiency, then the whole tier 3 market is dead after the first player reserves the only valuable card as his first move. The second player has no choice but to go for the unreliable noble strategy because there is no effective cards on the board anymore. He is forced to buy many low tier cards in order to counter the strategy adopted by the first player, but buying many cards could unfold many useful or high efficiency cards for the first player (for example, cards that match noble's requirement or cards that help to develop the high efficiency cards).
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Splendor, not a game I own. I did manage to try it at the 2018 UK Games Expo. A couple who liked the game alot sat down to teach us the gameplay, which was much appreciated. Honestly though I did not like it. Considering the hype and endlessly hearing about it, the game dissapointed me.

Pros - The game is not very complicated, the art is ok and its a reasonable length. Nice solid poker chip pieces to represent the resources - (however more on this below). There's a little strategy in planning ahead for what cards you plan to buy to help get you the most points.

Cons - Although the art is ok personally I found it pretty boring, the theme was not very interesting to me. The box cover was ok but didn't grab my attention. The gameplay was basic, not very engaging and theme lackluster.

So I'm not a fan, the hype helped in my dissapointment and I did not like the game at all but I also had a gripe with it. Why Poker chips? Surely coloured gem pieces would have made more sense in this game and made it look more aesthetically pleasing plus inkeeping with the theme, he's even holding one on the cover! It may have increased the cost a little but it would have been a much better choice in my eyes. Try this one if your interested or want a simple game but sadly its not a game I plan to own or ever sit down and play again.

textfield_comment_value: And suddenly there was Splendor. We were walking around a convention, and noticed a couple of players that were very enthusiastic. A bit too enthusiastic if you would asked me, but it got us curious to this game we’ve never heard of. In one way, that wasn’t strange, because the official release date was March 26, 2014, three days after we walked at the convention. I did some research on the internet, and the game ended on our wishlist. Just three days after it’s official release, we went to a board game store in Essen. And there it was. Brand new, only one copy left, like it was just waiting for us. We grabbed the copy and when we arrived back home, we started playing it. Wow, this game is a little gem. The enthusiasm of the players at the convention was a bit over the top, but on the other hand, not all people express their feelings like we do. We can be very enthusiastic about a game, and nobody would notice it. So, this was such kind of a game. The rules a very easy to understand and explain. Picking up playing the game, will take less then 5 minutes. The end of the game is most of the time very close with two players. Often it only differs one turn in who is winning the game. If we would have to give a point of criticism to this game, then it will be the short playing time. This makes it not suitable as a game. It’s too long for a filler game. It’s too short to give you the feeling that you’ve played a game. And the theme? Well, it’s a Eurogame. It’s pasted on.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
This game lives up to its fast-earned reputation. First thing I noticed when I opened the box, after the great organization design? Amazing artwork! Every inch of this game is beautifully rendered, and the gem chips are so satisfying to hold and clack against one another, with the heft of thick poker chips. Completes the theme very well, highly pleasant to look at, and makes the overall game much more fun to play.

Splendor reminds me of the best part of the real time strategy games we all love: the engine-building phase - the central mechanic in this game of spending gems to purchase developments which, in effect, yield more gems, which build the engine to yield more developments, etc. The system is simple and elegant, flows naturally and seamlessly, and is very satisfying with immediately apparent benefits.

The game moves quickly, while there is a good amount of strategy, balancing between collecting gems, reserving and buying developments, and blazing a path to prestige points and acquiring favor from nobles, which takes careful planning with each step, with a view toward the final goals. Don't save up gems too long, or your fellow greedy merchants will steal your prize before you can get to it!

Great fun with lots of player interaction, a short, addictive game with good decisions that doesn't require a ton of brain power on a Friday eve - fantastic for families or any group who enjoys the thrill of a well-themed game of fortunes.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
It takes a while to move on and get past the quality of the chips in this game. When you do the game is just as good.

A real thinky, planning and efficiency reward game set in the world of jewels. Where nobels are inexplicably drawn to you when you have enough gems (and I thought it was my personality that drew all the nobels to our door)! Needless to say I am not that great at it. My family do enjoy playing it, but not the youngest daughter and my son. They don't like it when you reserve a card they were planning to buy on there next go. A Mexican stand off with my youngest daughter resulted after I attempted (an attempt was as far as I got) to reserve a card she was planning to buy.

"I'm so angry I could just ... just ... rip this card in half!" she said as she held out the card between us, gripping it with a Chinese burn ready to tear it in two.

"Don't!" I yelled in blind panic having never faced anything like this before in gaming (I didn't ever think of Splendor as a legacy game). I held out my arms with palms pacifyingly upwards unsure what to do or how to react to this small bundle of terrifying wildness. "I ... I ... I don't actually have to reserve that card. I have just had a better idea."

"You have! Well that's good then" She said sitting back down.

She eventually relented and I now have a sturdily premium sleeved game of Splendor.

Great for the family but not so great with younger kids! Keeper.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Splendor was the 17th hobby game I purchased.  I fell in love with it, and I have never really fallen out of love, even though better games have come and gone.  There have been two chief rivals to this game in my opinion.  One was by Marc Andre, and it was called Majesty.  I never ended up getting this one because it looked too similar to Splendor.  The other was Century: Spice Road, which I thought was ok, but not great.  So, I traded it.  

Splendor is a competitive, set-collection, racing game in which the players are cast as merchants in the medieval age who are literally trading in the Mediterranean.  The premise is cliche, but the execution is tightly paced and very well designed, with a number of paths to victory that emerge over the course of getting to know the game.  There is just enough randomness to make the game competitive between players of different levels even if the best player typically wins.  I also appreciate that it is important to try avoid telegraphing your plan so your opponents can't block you.  Somehow it usually comes down to the last couple of plays with relatively few blowouts.  

I love the heavy poker chips.

I ended up 3d printing a new box for it, which was a mistake because without the name of the game on the box, I don't even notice it anymore.  Also, the directions don't fit in the box.  

I'll have to print a label and a smaller version of the rules.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
[b]9/16/2015 Comment[/b]: Dry and unexciting. I think this is a concession game, as Carcassonne was before it. Meaning it plays quickly and people can agree on it because it's mostly inoffensive, and it'll have staying power because it's the second choice for loads of people. There's a longevity in that. 

[b]1/2/2020 update[/b]: I still think this is pretty dry, but my son loves it and I'm likely to play it many more times over the coming months or even years. While I've softened on it with repeated exposure (there's an immune system joke in here somewhere), it's still not a favorite and unlikely to ever be. Having said that, it does have a few things going for it: 

1.) Simple and stripped-down. I don't need to consult the rules for edge cases, and I don't need to refresh myself on anything if a long time passes between plays. 

2.) Doesn't take up a ton of table space. 

3.) Plays sub-30 minutes, which is where I want engine building games to be because I think that's a genre of game that wears out its welcome awfully quick. 

So where we are in our season of life, this currently fits. I still don't think it's that exciting (interaction is minimal), and I stand by my "it's an inoffensive concession game" remark from 5 years ago. I am not conceding as much by agreeing to play it now, but it's missing a spark. It works, it's fast, and it's simple, but it's not that exciting.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Game in a Nutshell: Collect chips to buy cards which give permanent discounts on buying more cards. Buy enough cards that are worth points and win!

Played as: 2,3,4 player

Pros: Very clean game. I don't know if engine building games get much more simple than this without losing interest. Seems to be different twists on viable strategy to winning while remaining at its heart a race of efficiency. The game does offer a sense of satisfaction having built something in a relatively short amount of time.

Cons: I think there are a few key strategic rules that once you understand, you could play most of this game on autopilot.  There's still some reliance on luck with your engine usually directed down a certain path, and if the random cards don't fit into that path, you can start to stall out.  I've had the opposite where everything randomly falls into place and I cross the finish line with 3 times more points than anyone else.

Other: Some games seem to strip down an idea or mechanic to it's most basic form. After that, the trick becomes if the game is still interesting enough to stand out. Splendor is exactly that kind of game for engine building.  Engine builders aren't necessarily my thing, but I can appreciate what this game accomplishes despite my personal taste such that I would absolutely say it stands out. 

Best Use: When you need a quick "I built something" fix.
Title: Splendor

Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
A easy to learn, easy to teach, strategy game that's difficulty is based by the players at the table. Play is fast as each turn you have three options; Take gems, reserve card, buy card(it could be considered four as "take gems" actually has two different ways.) Cards have victory points along with Noble tiles which are acquired if you have the right cards. When a player reaches 15 the game is in it's final round, allowing all players equal turns. Highest score wins.

Up until recently I thought this game was underrated and should be played more. It's simple, yet has teeth in the game play by blocking opponents plays. After a few plays this month it's been brought back down to earth. Much like Race for the Galaxy, this is probably best played at two player, but can be played at a higher player count. 

The problem is, a weaker player at the table can screw the balance of the game up. If they aren't blocking somebody at the table is going to be having their way. If you are lucky it's you and you win. Unlucky, well enjoy losing a game simply by seating arrangement. It's mightily frustrating to sit at a table and watch someone give somebody else the win as you are too polite or defeated to scream "FOR THE LOVE OF GOD STOP THEM!"

At two players, with evenly matched competition, it's a pretty fun. At more players... you better be really evenly matched.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
2 player variant:
In an attempt to keep our games closer to the feel of 3 & 4 player games, we’ve been using a 2 player variant(suggested in the games forum https://www.boardgamegeek.com/article/17132785#17132785 that removes half of the level one cards.
In 2 player games, there tends to be an abundance of level one gem cards. Players tableaus turn into a frantic back and forth of - I take a card - You take card - I take card - etc.  Having an excess of Level 1 cards in play diminishes the chips value much too quickly from the game.  The game often turns into a race for the nobles with victory going to the player that gets 2 of the 3 first.

Simply remove half of the level one gem cards by dividing them into two equal cost/valued sets. This assures an even split of colors and creates two “half level one gem decks” that can be used for consecutive games.

Taking out half of the level one cards with 2 players gives a similar feel to a 3 or 4 player game by bringing back the risk that the cards may/will run out part way the through the game. The reduction of the level one cards ensures that the chips are in demand throughout the game.  As a result, the level 2 and 3 cards are purchased more often as well as an added attention for the need to reserve cards. 

YMMV; but also suggest increasing to 20 victory points instead of 15 for 2 player games.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: Very good game, looks fantastic if a bit repetitive. Same art work is recycled on many cards. Doesn't take away the fact though that art itself looks good and fits the theme really well. Components are high quality and I appreciate that all the gems are weighty pieces of metal and plastic, giving more authentic feel of touching something with value, instead of doing that part just with cards (which would have been even easier but a lot more boring decision). Game is very simple, on your turn there's only a few things that you can do. Victory conditions are very clear too. In a very slight way this is like building an engine (even though this is not officially an engine-building game at all), because you have to build yourself a bonus-system that you can utilize in order to start collecting victory points as soon and efficiently as possible. This is once again one of those games that is easy to recommend as a gateway game for basically anyone who's even remotely interested about boardgames. It won't offer anything too extensive and for hobbyists it is something more casual and filler-like. Still, all said and done, as a family game or for more casual gaming, it's a perfect choice. Please do keep in mind that with Cities of Splendor you can considerably improve the experience. Must have for anyone who keep playing Splendor on regular basis.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Favorite game: 2018-2020

As of 2019, still my favorite game of all time.
As of Q1 & Q2 2020, still my favorite game of all time.
As of Q3 2020, this has been dethroned by Merlin but it is still ne of my favorite games.

Update: August 2021, no longer one of my favorite games, but it is still a solid one.

This is not good, not great, but a phenomenal game, made greater by its simplicity.  I have played this a ton and it continues be a favorite among not just me, but everyone I play it with.  I played it once with someone who bought it on their phone while we were playing.  

The simple rules, variability every-time you play it, and yet complex strategy is an elegance not matched by any other board game.  This is one of those games that you can explain while playing the first few rounds and yet is incredibly deep without being too prone to over-analysis, though admittedly those players will do pretty well in this game. 

The best thing about this game, though, and what really sends it over the top for me is the pure-engine building experience that snowballs out of control.  It is like pushing a snowball down a hill and it lightly glides just to suddenly gain incredible size and speed and smash against a mountain wall.  When you are 50% way to victory, the game is probably 90% over, and as a result, every game feels close.
