textfield_comment_value:
Splendor is a game that I won't veto if asked to play, but it doesn't really "do it" for me.

On the plus side, the components are well done.  I love the poker chip feel and heft.  They are fun to play with on their own..... Don't look at me like that - that's not weird and I doting cause a distraction at the table :).  The cars are just a tiny bit flimsy for my taste, but they are fine for the amount you use them.  I like that the game time is pretty quick, so the game doesn't over stay it's welcome so to speak.  Lastly I like simplicity of the rules - they are easy to teach to newbies.

On the minus side, the noble goals seem "off" to me.  They are tough to get, but only worth three points.  Even with a lot of overlap of card desires, I would think it would be pretty tough to obtain multiple nobles and still win the game.  Also, some of the card costs don't seem balanced to me.  I'll be the first to admit that maybe it's me that's at fault here.  I don't claim to be a veteran player of Splendor so maybe I don't understand the reasons behind some of the choices.  That being said, some cards just seem pretty much all around better to me - you get the same effect for an easier to get combo of tiles in my opinion.  Again, maybe that's by design and there's something I'm. Not seeing, but it bugs me currently.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: This is an easy to teach, fast-paced, exceptionally fun game that works as well for 2 as it does for 4 players. It's a great intro game for new gamers, yet has enough strategy and replayability to keep sophisticated gamers engaged. As others have pointed out the game components are quite high quality especially the heavy weight poker chip style gem tokens. Nonetheless I prefer to play my custom version with upgraded acrylic gems in the correct colors with gold coins replacing the wild tokens. This adds realism to the already fun and well illustrated jeweler theme. I've also added metal Brass coins from Eagle Gryphon Games in 1 and 5 denominations to use as scoring tokens to more easily keep track of everyone's score on the way to 15 prestige points. It makes it much easier to glance over at your opponents coins as opposed to counting card points every turn. Finally, I added the Spendor play mat to provide a logical place for all the cards and nobles, looks great and keeps the cards from sliding around on the tabletop. It's a great stand alone game you can easily complete in 20 mins, but I'd love so see some expansions for Splendor to further augment strategic options. Who's to say the noble that comes to visit your shop couldn't be enticed over to the jeweler across the street who just acquired better gems?
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
The rules are simple and can easily be explained in a very short time. Splendor is an engine building puzzle with incomplete information: every time a card is purchased, a new random card of the same level takes its place; not having complete information reduces downtime as there isn't too much to analyze, but is also an unwanted source of randomness. This is one of the game's problems: not knowing which card is going to appear, it's not possible to plan effectively, as the game is shaped by cards that aren't known and will reveal themselves only in the future. The lack of mitigating factors and a suspect balance (how can cards like 3 [0p], 2-1 [0p], 1-1-1-1 [0p] and 2-1-1-1 [0p] be worth the same?) mean that the luck of the draw has too much influence on the outcome. The game is not devoid of tactics, as players can try blocking the opponents, but this has an opportunity cost and is not guaranteed to succeed due to the luck of the draw. The theme has fundamentally no connection to the game mechanics and I have nothing good to say about the art.

To summarize: gameplay is lackluster at best. This is a very simple game where the most thrilling moment is the turn of a new card when one gets purchased: will it help you or someone else? At least the game is short, but it's still too long to be a decent filler.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
An exceptionally polished and mathematically perfect engine-building gameplay loop laid so bare that you might start wondering how Sisyphus is doing. Devoid of the satisfaction of your engine actually producing anything, Splendor instead opts for a continual loop of making things cheaper, but infuriatingly never cheap enough that you feel like your work paid off. This is the central tension of the game--knowing when to hoard and when to spend so that you don't have to do as much hoarding later. Luckily, this question isn't too difficult to parse, since the resources boil down to tokens of a few functionally identical colors. This is elegant, but it also means that Splendor doesn't allow for any sense of meaningful differentiation between your tableau and your friends'. Having the right amount of the right color at the right time is all you care about; it'll feel roughly the same every game outside of slightly different answers to that question.

Its saving graces are that engine building is an intrinsically fun core loop, and that it's over in a half hour at most. Another might be that it's so simple it can work as a gateway game. But I think I only appreciate this as a pared-back iteration on more exciting designs. If I were introduced to Eurogames with this, I would wonder if they were all this boring.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: This is game is an exercise in mathematics. Not the kind of difficult mathematics that are obnoxious if you try to mess with them or makes you feel stupid if you refuse to, but still, if you are not onto almost pure mathematic games, you should steer clear of this. Occasionally, there are variations: you will recognize at some step the need to not clog your hand with reserved cards too early, so that you can always grab a vital one if it suddenly appears on the table, or likewise you will be wary to not buy a card when you may live without it, to avoid offering a possibly much more powerful one to the next player, but otherwise that's that. Also, even if the relative short duration of the game kinda mitigates it,  i'm afraid there's a heavily runaway leader problem at work here, mostly because it's almost impossible to get in the way of one player's lead with such limited options at your disposal. But the overall biggest problem of this game, at the least for my tastes, it's again the fact that it's so cold and so mathy, and despite the gorgeous art you gonna see while playing, you will never feel not even one bit like doing the work of a jeweler. However whoever can go over the absence of a theme and appreciate the puzzle and the race aspects behind it, may possibly like Splendor way more than me.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
2 plays.

This is a fun little filler with some gem-related theme pasted on. Basically, though, it's a game of set collection where you're racing to score 15 VP to trigger the end of the game (equal turns) and likely win the game. 

The 3 decks of cards have gems with various costs in other gems. On your turn, either collect poker chips (3 different ones, or 2 of one color as long as you leave at least 2 behind) or claim a card from the display by paying it's cost in gems. Cards you collect remain face up in your display, and act as discounts (essentially, virtual poker chips). OR, you can reserve a card from the display, adding it to your hand and taking one gold chip (acts as a wild color chip). At the start of the game, several bonus tiles were randomly selected; these show particular card combinations. At the end of your turn, if you have any of these combos, you may claim 1 tile. These tiles, and many of the cards, are worth VP; if anyone gets to 15+ VP, finish the current round (even turns): the player with the most VP wins.

It's kind of a cool little game that plays quickly (30-45 minutes) and has some decisions to make without taxing your brain too much. You have to pay attention to what other people are collecting towards, so you can snake those cards/tiles away from them!
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
"Good, but overrated, abstract engine-building game. It's OK, but unexciting. Rating went from 6 to 7 with more plays. I won't ask to play it, but won't resist either. "

What I like:
- Easy to teach and learn
- The chips have a nice heft
- Plays quickly (45 minute 3p learning game)
- I like engine-building
- A "sprint for points" strategy can beat a solid engine

What I don't like:
- Abstract
- Relies heavily on denial (including hoarding)
- Excessively large box

This is a decent little game. Thinkier than it appears, although it can be played (poorly) without much strategy. I think it's awfully dry (and thinky) for an SdJ, but abstracts have won before. I have trouble seeing why so many people are going gaga over it, but I suppose it does have a bit of Knizia-like minimalist charm.

Although there are no attacks (yay), I really dislike the form of interaction. If I reserve a card, I might get denied the chips I need, plus I'm falling behind in getting resources. but if I collect the resources first, the card I'm saving for might get taken before I get to it. For some reason, I just don't enjoy that form of "damned if you do, damned if you don't" dilemma in games. 

I guess the BGG-voted weight of 1.8 is reasonable. It's simpler than that rules-wise, but has more depth.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
[b]Thoughts after first play[/b] [BGCOLOR=#66ff99] [b]8[/b] [/BGCOLOR]
Excellent, Excellent game. Replaces tons of card based fillers.

[b]Thoughts after tenth play[/b] [BGCOLOR=#66ff99] [b]8[/b] [/BGCOLOR]
Splendor is a gem of a game. Lu and I love it. On the surface, Splendor appears to be a simple card game. On your turn you can do one of four actions. Of those four, two will acquire you chips, and the other two gain you cards and the coveted wild chip.

Splendor plays quickly, but in a agonizing way. It’s fun, however the simplicity is a veneer that covers the hidden complexity and depth that only repeated plays start to chip away at. A game that by all accounts defines the term “filler game”, but in reality hides a complex economic game under it’s many layers.

Don’t let Splendor’s short rule book, and simple mechanisms lull you into a belief that this is a casual game. This game will have you quietly mulling over what to do from turn to turn, while carefully tracking your opponents card tableau trying to determine exactly how many turns you have left to amass the greatest fortune.

I recommend this game for any collection. Splendor is fun, small, easy to teach, hard to master, and has that certain quality of addictiveness that is oh so hard to capture in a game.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Played twice : Once 2p and once 3p.

Liked it a lot both times. Easy to set up, great components (had to cut the box to a third of its original side) and rule book.

Engine-building Jaipur-style (I played Jaipur hundreds of time with my gf and got quite tired of it) game in the sense that with limited resources (max 3 cards and 10 chips), you need to get point and try slowing down other players growth.

I preferred it slightly at 2 players, as there seem to be more interactions (could come from our inexperience though).

Would play anytime at any player count!

Several more plays at 2p

Strategy becomes clearer. Like it more every game. Balance between clear plan and path (a useless turn can make you lose) and flexibility (you might need to change plan 180º). Would like to play more games with >2p.

Dropped to 7,5 as we reach replayability issue after 20 2p games.

2 more 4p games. Strategy is similar. Reserve when gold is available, take colors when available and buy high value cards. Won both games, last one with only 7 cards. Important to reserve good cards and then play around these cards.

Moved rating back to 8. Always a pleasure to play even though the experience is a bit dry. Player interaction is needed not to let lucky players win.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Really interesting little set collection/tablaeu building game.
Gems come is 5 different colours and a wild colour and are used to but cards from the selection on board or one you 'reserved' earlier.

Cards have a free gem on them that you can spend each round and some have points upon them. First to 15 points wins.

Its not particularly strategic as it is dependent upon the gems available on your turn and what buildings are available but it is quite tactical as you can 'reserve' take to your hand cards which you know your opponent was about to be able to play.

I was initially concerned there would be a win more mechanic as the lower cost buildings are quick and easy to play and each card gives you a free gem a turn however this is not the case as the cost balance has been done very cleverly as whilst the free gems from previously claimed cards are needed to purchase the higher cost cards you also need a fistful of the correct colour gems.

Components are very nice and the poker chip gems are very good and have a good weight to them. There is a slight issue with the green/blue/black gems being very similar in colour and shape however the background pictures are different and so you can tell them apart.

Sold with Nobles promo in 2017.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
This is a relatively quick game.  It has lots of little decisions that make it slow to start, but then when it gets rolling, people start picking up cards for free or for 1 good, and the game can end in a big rush.

It reminds me of one of the things I dislike about Alhambra -- you plan to buy a card and save goods accordingly, but then the player to your left gets the card, and a new card shows up that you could also buy, but the next player picks that one up, and so on.  So there's a lot of luck-of-the-draw that seems unfair to me.  But I guess that's to be expected for a quick filler game like this.

It's very important to pay attention to what Nobles are available to be won, since it's a race to get them.  You could focus on getting cards with colours that could be used for more than one of those nobles.  For example, if there is a noble to be won for having 3 white, 3 blue, and 3 red, and another to be won for having 3 white, 3 blue, and 3 green, it would be good to pick up 3 white and 3 blue!

It might be a good idea to pick a couple of easy cards from the face-down pile at the beginning, so that you have a chance to go for something that nobody else knows about, and pick up a couple of gold coins (wildcards) as a side benefit.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
I've only played 3 games of this so far, but my wife and I enjoyed it so much it seemed worth giving it the 10 out of 10. Each turn you take gems (the currency of the game), buy a development card, or reserve a development card. Most of the development cards have a point value, and they also help you buy more development cards. Whomever accumulates 15 points first winds. (There are more details, but that's the gist of it). For such a simple premise, it is surprisingly engaging, and even though you only do one thing per turn, there are many factors to consider in making those decisions. So it's easy to get going and start doing things, but takes a good amount of thought to figure out how to play optimally.

If you're given the chance, definitely play a demo or check it out at your local game store if they do rentals. When a store clerk explained it to me, I wasn't necessarily sold on it. But the cards and the "gems" (plastic coins, really) are really well made. The gems have a poker chip like quality to them that's very satisfying. A game isn't all about the physical components, of course, but the easy to learn/difficult to master nature of the game, combined with the build quality make it a really satisfying game to own and play.

textfield_comment_value: The perfect mix of balance in what cards cost and different ways to gain significant points from controlling nobles or going for tier 3 cards.  This game never plays out quite the same way and while some "strategies" might appear to be dominant (I have heard players at gaming clubs talking about this) they are absolutely not dominant their opponents just do not know how to adjust to what other players are doing.  I have general tactics for my early game that rarely change very much depending on the options but I never play the end game one specific way "because it is the dominant strategy".  I have an absurd win rate for a game like this by tactically keeping track of everything each player is doing and the mathematical value of all my turn options.  To achieve this win rate I have to constantly be willing to change my planned turn and to not be relying on no one trying to stop my best visible options by reserving a card or two.  Even when everyone at the table is aware I am the biggest threat and try to conspire against me this game rewards careful decision making.  Luck can occasionally dominate an entire game and make a win "nearly impossible" but 80% of games will go to the player who made the best decisions.

textfield_comment_value:
Lo de este juego fue amor a primera vista XD. Es verdad que uno de los aciertos y razones de su éxito es la producción, pero no únicamente. Muchos otros juegos poseen una producción de alto nivel y, sin embargo, fracasan estrepitosamente.

Splendor es una carrera en provocar un efecto de bola de nieve. Partiendo de cero, se van desarrollando cartas de cara a lograr 15 puntos. Se pueden conseguir directamente con las cartas de tu zona de juego más las bonificaciones que sumes, por las que hay una feroz competencia. 

Con una reglas muy sencillas, propone partidas muy interactivas y emocionantes. Nada de juegos en piloto automático, ya que no estar atento a tus contrarios supone perder. Como todo juego de cartas, hay un pequeño factor de azar, que yo afirmaría que forma parte de la estrategia: obligar a robar a tu contrario para ver si así sale la carta que estás esperando.

¿A quién se parece? 
- Por el efecto bola de nieve, me recuerda al Dominión, pero menos farragoso. De hecho, apenas jugamos al Dominion, mientras que Splendor frecuenta la mesa.
- Por tener que contemporizar cuando conviene robar o aguantar, lo compararía con el Jaipur o con el 7 wonders duel.

En definitiva, una juego muy satisfactorio.

textfield_comment_value:
A solid game, a better designed game there has never been.  It really boils down the essence of quite a few other engine/take-that games into a really good little package.

That said, there are three itches this scratches:
1) Getting stuff that wins you the game
2) Screwing-over someone else who wants your stuff
3) Building some semblance of an engine

And I found myself thinking that Cargo Noir was actually pretty good at 1 & 2, and I feel like there's a huge thrill-fest in engine building that makes this either better or worse depending on your situation. 

I'm not much for being an engine guy, but over repeated plays, engine stuff is where it's at.

For all the design, and everything that's good about it...  still kind of 'meh' on all of it.   No 'wow' factor in it for me other than this - It would definitely be the first thing I reached for in the more advanced games.  Not that it's more advanced, but a lot of the theory is expanded in advanced games.  If you love the engine building stuff....hooo boy are there a lot of games to see.  If you hate the engine building stuff....well, lots of options.

On an aside, the iOS app...  go for bonus tiles every time, and you'll do no worse than 2nd place.

textfield_comment_value:
Based on 1 play with 4 players:

This is a compelling, solidly designed system. The turns are quick and decisions are interesting. It's just not the sort of game I would play twice in a night.

It's not that Splendor does anything wrong. It just lacks some kind of hook for me. It is a game that is all about Scoring Points. I enjoy a great deal of these kinds of games, but generally they have either one killer mechanic going for them (even No Thanks, possibly the simplest game ever made, has a more tough and juicy mechanical hook) OR have a sense of progression and accomplishment - games where you're building something you can enjoy on an emotional/aesthetic level.

This game lacks both, and so is a game I would not turn down if offered, but will never be one of my great gaming loves.

Update: It is worth pointing out though that there REALLY aren't any other solidly designed economic games that play in this timeframe, so if you've got your heart set on a quick economic game this is IT. And this is still one of the meatiest games you can get in 20 minutes in general so if you don't already have something quick ' meaty (your Biblioses, your Eight-Minute Empires) this'll definitely fit the bill.

textfield_comment_value:
This is such a great game.

It's juuuust barely not an abstract, in a way that reminds me a lot of classic Knizia (Battle Line, Lost Cities, and the like), and everything under the hood is amazingly tight -- also just like a Knizia design.

Every game opens up a new layer of things to notice, learn from, react to, figure out, assess, plan around, build, play with, or try out. It walks and talks like an engine builder, but it doesn't have to be played that way.

I love the mix of strategy and tactics, which is right in my sweet spot for a shorter game like this one. (Short, but meaty!) You can go in with a plan, but it might change once you see what comes out in the initial spread. And everything that happens after that will require further adjustments, from "Oooh, that card is great!" to "Shit, he's going to get that noble first unless I..."

And all of that is wrapped up in one of the best inserts I've ever seen! With, to top it all off, amazing components. The cards are beautiful, but also clear from every angle and across the table. The choice of poker chips (nice heavy ones, too) was inspired.

I love this game. Instant classic.
---
Bumped from a 9 to a 10. Always a delight.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Solid and very compact set-collecting game in which players pick up coins with different jewels from a common reservoir to draft tiles arranged in a matrix on the table. These tiles bring both points and "virtual jewels" to purchase more expensive tiles (or cheaper tiles faster). Gaining different combinations of these "virtual jewels" brings extra points by means of three extra tiles with "patrons"  beside the matrix with jewel tiles. The first player to score 15 points wins the game.

Splendor is not the most original game there is, but it condenses its relatively well-known ingredients delightfully: it's short, simple to explain, simple to set up and extremely varied through the myriad of combinations of jewels and patrons that can appear in every game. Players can develop tactical awareness straight from the first play, but the game doesn't run dry after repeated play: the way the matrix gets replenished with random tiles guarantees the right amount of luck to add risk management to the game, and having a common reservoir of coins for all players means that every turn brings its own challenges regarding resources and timing.

To put it short, Splendor is a joy to play.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
This game has elements that I love (like resource gathering) but really lacks player interaction. The only way you really interact with other players is to see what gems they have - then aim to take something that you knew they probably wanted. It's funny how silent games of Splendor are - there is very little game related to talk about beyond "oooh, i wanted that". Mechanics of the game are simple enough and a new player will have no problem getting stuck in after only a little explanation time.

The other thing is that three of the gem types are very similar colours for colour-blind people. While I can get around this issue by focusing on the shapes of the gems - it's either a bit of an oversight by the game developers, or the usual "we don't care about 10% of people being colour blind". My girlfriend took our set and marked every single card/piece to make the game easier for me to recognise the different gems and play.

While it is a reasonable game, mechanics wise. I'm afraid that the lack of player interaction means it would never be a go-to game for me or one I'd ever suggest playing, though I could be talked into playing if someone else really wanted to play it.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
There are some tactically interesting plays, and a little bit of strategic planning.  It was a clean and pleasing game, but ultimately pretty forgettable.  My biggest complain is that it didn't feel like there was any interaction -- the other players were just pseudo-random number generators affecting my solitaire game.  I could spend a lot of time figuring out the details of their positions in order to gain a small advantage, but that doesn't seem interesting.  Also, there is a lot of luck in what gets flipped up just before your turn -- that may average out, but it is frustrating and unsatisfying.

update: on more plays, I find the nobles to be problematic -- they over-reward infrastructure and undermine the strategic planning of aiming for high up cards.  Especially in 2p, they seem to create a dominant strategy which in turn becomes a lot about luck of the draw.

update 2:  with larger player counts and skilled opponents, the nobles get distributed and other sources of points matter more.   As a result, reserving actually makes sense, and sometimes taking 2 tokens does too.  But with 2 players or with casual players, the nobles dominate in a boring way.
Title: Splendor

-Really needs an expansion

Overall:
This is likely the best gateway game on the market.  Almost always a hit and, due to its simple rules, players can quickly into the game without feeling overwhelmed.  After the first few turns, you will start to hear new players have their epiphanies when they start to see the bigger strategy.  This is the perfect litmus to determine if the people you coerced into playing one game with you are interested in playing more strategy games.  The game teeters on being a filler game because of its length but is too deep for that label.  The reserve mechanic allows this game to have significant strategic depth that is often missed by its critics.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: This game is a lot of fun for people who are not really into games. The idea is very simple and not complicated to play. I really like the concept of how early game there's no way to afford the expensive cards but, by the late game you can buy all sorts of things as you build up your collection. There is an interesting aspect in the game of taking the free ones (using only cards) early on and timing it right for when you step onto buying cards that require using a lot of your gems rather than cards. Then you can maximize reaching the highest victory points as early as possible. If you start too soon though you will get passed by people going the safe and consistent route. Overall, the game is exciting and I would never say no to playing unless I just finished playing a round. Great game for kids and adults alike. The only thing to dislike about the game is it is quite similar after playing the game for a lot of plays. Nothing really mechanically changes from play to play and I think for me that makes the game a little stale. Again still very happy to play if someone else picks it, I'm just not the one reaching for it on game night.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Prior to 2020: 3 plays

Splendor is a game that I can't honestly seem to make up my mind about.  For one, it's certainly a dry, calculating game whose theme is about as far divorced from its mechanisms as games can get.  On the other hand, however, the game presents players with intricate puzzles to solve, in which they must be continually planning and adapting those plans to the decisions of their opponents.  It's a game that felt too shallow in my first play, but was a game in which further plays revealed to me just how tight this engine-building, optimization game was.  Furthermore, it's a game that provides a surprising amount of strategic paths to victory, a real feat for such a fast filler game, and it's a game that rewards skillful play significantly.  It's fast, smooth, and easy to get lost in the puzzle of it all, which makes for an intensely satisfying game.  Even still, the game is certainly repetitive, and the optimization puzzle doesn't even try to hide itself, which is certainly a deterrent for many people.  Personally, I really like this one, and I definitely look forward to many more plays of it moving forwards.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: Das größte Plus von SPLENDOR ist die Großzügigkeit im Spielmaterial: dicke, fette, pfundschwere Chips, die jedem Ocean Eleven-Casino in Las Vegas zu Ehre reichen würden. Die Dinger liegen in der Hand wie Münzen aus dem Schatz der 40 Räuber. Das Klappern beim Stapeln ist ein nervöses Wohlgeräusch vom Pokertisch. Auch die Personenplättchen hätten mit dünnerer Pappe den gleichen Zweck erfüllt, aber auch hier gilt Prosperität. So 1a das Materialbewusstsein, so konventionell das Spiel selbst: mit den Chips, die verschiedene Arten von Edelsteinen verkörpern, bezahlt man Karten, die Dauer-Edelsteine oder Punkte bringen und wer zuerst 15 Punkte hat, gewinnt den Bazar. Das haben andere auch schon 1001x gemacht im Orient. In seinem solitären Charakter dürfte SPENDOR zu zweit am Besten kommen, weil am Taktischsten, weil man hier Chips blocken kann. Unter Berücksichtigung der Zielgruppe Familienmitglied steht SPLENDOR als gute, solide Dutzendware im Regal von Karstadt, den die attraktive, aber ahnungslose Verkaufsberaterin auch ohne Wissen von Brett- und Gesellschaftsspielen vorbehaltlos empfehlen kann. Ihre Telefonnummer wäre mir lieber.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
This is an all-around fun game: it has a lot of luck, but just enough strategy to make it interesting, such as wasting a move to reserve a key card at the right time. It's short (20-30 minutes); the cards and chips have a beautiful design and feel to them; and the game is simple and has only a few rules. I'd say it's my very favorite short game, but it's just robust enough to not really be a filler game. The rules can be taught quickly and the game can be mostly understood on the first try playing the game. And it works just as well with only 2 players as it does with 3 or 4, which makes it double as a challenging 2 player game as well, which is rare for multi-player board games.

Official game description: As a wealthy Renaissance merchant, acquire mines and transportation, hire artisans and woo the nobility. Create the most fantastic jewelry to become the best-known merchant of them all! Acquire precious stones to trade them for development cards. Use development cards to acquire more gem stones. Use your gems and gold to create the most fantastic jewelry, and appeal to the nobles to gain the prestige you need to win.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Honestly a great game. It stands out as a fun game to let non-board gamers get into. There's enough complexity that it stands as one of my most played board games. 

You'll find that it's almost impossible to just play 1 round. You start to build up general strategies over the course of the first 5 games or so, and then you might start calculating avg outcomes for each type of move you can make. I mean, yeah you can get real math-y here and 'count cards'. 

There's a great deal of luck involved with what strategies will work best with each game, but I think that's just a given for this type of game. Never would I say that it isn't fair, or fun. But because moves are equally weighted in some senses, how fun this game ultimately is will depend heavily on the level of your competition. Because the idea of 'first to 15 points' doesn't necessarily jive with how the overall early game play works, they won't know how bad they're losing until the game is practically over already. 

But yeah, playing with the same crowd the 2nd time while be a much better experience than the first.

9.5/10 for the casual board game experience.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
I'm really not sure what the fuss is about with this game. Don't get me wrong, it's a good game - I rated it a 6 after my first play, but upped it to a 7 after my second, seeing a bit more strategy to it that time. And we've played it fairly frequently since then. But, while I'm usually happy to play it, I don't think I'd ever request to do so. There is nothing at all original, it's just an economic snowball-type game of collecting gems to buy cards which give you more gems... 

This is a primarily tactical game, which is quick but with plenty of decisions, and which will play at least a little differently each time. Yet it feels like there's nothing here that hasn't been done before.

It's a good game, very playable - but also quite forgettable as modern releases go. I am puzzled by all the acclaim it seems to have received. (Yet at the same time I enjoy playing it, which of course is ultimately what matters.)

I realise that this is a very confusing, even schizophrenic, kind of judgement on the game - but that's genuinely how I feel. I see almost nothing here to really like - and yet I do enjoy playing it.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Splendor is a game of chip-collecting and card development. Players are merchants of the Renaissance trying to buy gem mines, means of transportation, shops—all in order to acquire the most prestige points. If you're wealthy enough, you might even receive a visit from a noble at some point, which of course will further increase your prestige.

On your turn, you may (1) collect chips (gems), or (2) buy and build a card, or (3) reserve one card. If you collect chips, you take either three different kinds of chips or two chips of the same kind. If you buy a card, you pay its price in chips and add it to your playing area. To reserve a card—in order to make sure you get it, or, why not, your opponents don't get it—you place it in front of you face down for later building; this costs you a round, but you also get gold in the form of a joker chip, which you can use as any gem.

All of the cards you buy increase your wealth as they give you a permanent gem bonus for later buys; some of the cards also give you prestige points. In order to win the game, you must reach 15 prestige points before your opponents do.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Splendor is a fast and easy game, especially recommended to casual players. It's a good way to introduce resource management/engine building to players that are new to it. It's a great game to play between sessions or introduce people to boardgaming. The components themselves are really great, especially the resource chips. The art is decent, perhaps a bit to generic but it's still a pleasant game to look at.

On each round, you have 3 different actions at your disposal where you earn resource chips, these are used to buy resource cards to increase your output. The goal is to build up an engine in order to gain the more expensive ones which net the player victory points. It's all very streamlined.

My biggest gripes is that after playing many games, there is just not much choice in terms of strategy. It's a limited system but still enjoyable to play, just not suited for extended sessions. Also the theme itself is rather bland, there is not much flavor nor does it evoke the feeling of being a merchant that purchases properties. Overall, it's pretty abstract in that regard.

Would recommend it though.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Poorly balanced and not developed.

Could be interesting with better numbers/balancing. The early cards are particularly egregious in that one player building a relatively expensive 2/1/1/1 [0 pts] card can flip over a 2/1 [0 pts] card for their opponents to enjoy.  Fifteen points does not feel like the right number; it is probably closest to correct in a 4-player game, but 2-player it should probably go to 20/21.  

All this is moot because the points themselves should be refactored to provide less swing-y endgame results (basically double all existing point cards and fine-tune for difficulty (e.g. all the early cards with points become 2 points and the more difficult 0 point cards become 1 point cards).

Couple all of this with stupidly interacting color schemes (study the cards of each suit relative to one another to discover what I mean), and...well, this game needed some more work.  A few quick changes could make this a much more enjoyable filler game, but as-is it feels like they just called it good enough to sell to the masses of idiots who will never investigate what they are playing.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: I found Splendor before ever having heard of it on a clearance rack at Walmart.  Its box art bored me so I did a quick search on my phone to see if it was well received.  Since it was unanimously praised I brought it home.  Serendipitous.  Many plays later this is still a game I look forward to putting on the table.  The components are excellent, especially those meaty poker chips.  Everyone starts with nothing and has an equal shot at victory since luck is virtually nonexistent.  Games progress quickly and usually end with multiple players crossing 15 victory points in the same round.  It’s a simple game to teach and learn, and even a rookie can stumble into a win.  Splendor sets up quickly and scales well.  Unfortunately, the theme is pretty dull and the art is as boring as it is beautiful.  This is a major drag on the game.  Its lack of a strong, evocative theme makes this at times feel like a stodgy old card game, especially when you find yourself mired in a hopeless losing effort.  Plus, my mother keeps calling the black gems brown because there’s some pigment ambiguity there.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
The first time that I played Splendor I felt that it was just an "OK" game. It was fairly light and quick to play but nothing overly impressive. Time passed by and I saw it shooting up the BGG ranks but didn't think much about it. It wasn't until I started playing more games during my lunch hour and realizing that I didn't have many games that were suitable to fit in that time slot that Splendor came back on my radar. Yes... it was "OK" but, if found at a decent price, I would pick it up.

Well... I'm happy that I did. Yes... it is a simple and quick playing game but it's a lot of fun, looks great and, who doesn't like weighty custom poker chips? The game feels like a tactical deck builder to me, where you're trying to improve your own economic engine while ensuring that your opponents can't maximize theirs. The games generally end up being fairly close and it always seems to be a race at the end. Very fun.

I can comfortably play 1 -2 games in under 60 minutes. Given that this has gone over well at lunch and that my wife enjoys it as well... this could see quite a bit of action.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Yes, Splendor is a simple exercise in resource management. You buy A to give you X, You buy B to give you Y, etc. Then use X and Y to buy C. That is it. There aren't even many ways to win prestige points. Just those that are being printed on the resource cards as well as nobles. First player to reach 15 prestige points triggers the last round and the game ends. Most points win. Simple, straightforward, no chrome.

Yet, after a few plays, the game stands out for its simplicity distilled down to the bare essence that is resource management. In a way, I find this refreshing. The resource generation in Splendor is not unlike 7 wonders minus the drafting. But think of 7 wonders and I shudder at explaining all the ways points are accumulated in the game. It is just so much chrome tacked on the basic game play. Splendor is almost the antithesis of 7 wonders. 

Still, this game will find only a smaller audience. Folks who eschew lengthy rules, want a simple game without messy explanations and fast game play. When those folks are around, I shall reach for Splendor and....Caveman Curling.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Straight up engine building filler game goodness.

This game benefits from being played often against the same person. When you get to know how your opponent thinks and you become familiar with the game & cards & strategy, there's a bit of a boxing / fencing vibe as you jockey back and forth for scarce resources to build a balanced hand that can win you the royals and then catapult you into a position to buy higher value cards and cross the finish line first. Such a smooth mechanic. Tough decisions beginning to end and very seldom does the deck favor one opponent over the other in a way that can't be overcome by good strategy. They must have play-tested it a lot before releasing it as this game plays like a Swiss watch and the component quality is first class and so is the artwork. 

Downsides / Caveats: Well, the theme is of secondary importance, though it is a nice theme and the artwork is beautiful. The box is big for what the game is. I put the game in a reproduction medieval coin-purse which not only looks cool but now the game travels well in a suitcase / purse / backpack.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
A game with multiple paths to victory, but only one of those paths is the right one.  There are 2 problems with this game: 
1) There is little interaction because everyone is quiet while they are concentrating. 
2) There is a dominant winning strategy in this game that makes any other strategy seem like playing the sucker bets in craps. 

After many, many games of this.  The balance issues reared their ugly head.  The winning strategy is to go for the high value point cards every time.  You can reserve the points you need to win, and no one can stop you, they can only hope to reach 15 points faster than you.  This works almost every time; the exception is when all but one player is playing this strategy and the remaining player is free to collect the nobles without interference and no need to block anyone.  Otherwise, it is very hard to win by going for nobles because it is almost impossible to both block someone and go for your noble cards at the same time.  A better balanced game would make both strategies - high value cards and nobles - viable every time during every game.

textfield_comment_value: Splendor is a great starter game. It has nice clicky-clack poker chip jewels, a simple, straightforward premise, and not quite enough depth to hold my interest. This is probably among the top 10 games I would suggest to get new people into gaming, but it would be my last recommendation, because while it offers a satisfying, quick, pretty engine-building experience, it doesn't have the enjoyable longevity of things like Codenames, Sheriff of Nottingham, Carcassonne, or Quest for El Dorado. Among evenly matched players, going first provides a small advantage that snowballs round after round. Nobles are a bit too easy to claim for the massive point advantage they grant and they make the game feel less balanced. They also make the top-tier cards, which it seems you should be working toward all game, feel less relevant. I like showing this off to new people for whom it still has all its glittery glory, but I don't really like playing it myself. The expansion adds some considerable improvements including fixing the Nobles system, but it's still far from a favorite for me.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
What a fantastic game. We love it both in the Base form and using the Cities module. At a higher level this is a game about pure optimization. Most games I lose, is because I made a mistake and let those vultures pick me apart. Also, like most card games you can’t win every game but if, you win more than you lose, you’re doing great. (I hate when Pancakes gets on a hot streak.) 

Base Game: It’s a race to 15, nothing more and nothing less. You could call this game “Row 2” because that where you be spending the majority of your time. This game has amazing player interaction but you don’t have to be into “take that” to win (although it doesn’t hurt.) 

Cities: This changes everything. You are no longer racing for 15 points. You have to earn a city making the game a lot like when you first started playing the Base Game and thought you needed a Nobel. Playing like this utilizes much more of the cards. 

We always play at least one Base and one Cities game in every siting. Always fun and always a good time. One of the few games that Pancakes will ask to play.

Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Very simple and abstract card game. You get gems to buy cards that provide permanent gems, and over time you increase your ability to buy more expensive and valuable cards. There is also some set collection that may give you bonus points in the form of nobles' tiles.

It works, but there really isn't much to the simplistic gameplay. My only game had a strange arc, very slow for the most part and then suddenly moving fast to the end, but it seems that it's very dependent on how the cards come out. There is obviously a significant amount of randomness, aggravated by the lack of any perceivable logic in the cost of different cards in the same deck. It may be a good fit for non-gamers and I wouldn't mind to play it once in a while, but it left me with the general impression that it isn't more than an oversized, overpriced, overlong (and seriously overhyped) filler.

The art is pretty and the sturdy tokens are nice, but in a game about precious stones, it's a real shame that the publisher missed the obvious opportunity to include some beautiful plastic gems.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
It's a game in the euro/optimization style, seemingly simple on the surface but it has some depth actually. It plays quickly too, I'd rather play this than Azul, it lasts about 20 minutes without AP-prone players, but perhaps could go 45 minutes with 4. If it were a 10-minute game I'd like it even better. For me a lot of the fun comes from how to evaluate card buys through the game similar to buying shares in stock holding games, and it lends itself to some nerdy analysis, surely each action could be quantified by opportunity costs, I'd like to see some stats on it.

On BGA, on average the winner is x2 more likely to take 3 actions each turn than to reserve a card, usually holds around 6 tokens per turn, and will claim one noble per game. Winning point composition (rounded up) is about 7 pts from rank 2 cards 9 (so about 3 of these), 6 points from rank 3 cards (about 2 of these), 3 points from nobles, and 1 point from row 1 cards. Winner average action selection rate is 1/2.5 buy a card, 1/3 take 3 tokens, 1/6 reserve a card, 1/25 take 2 tokens.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
I understand the general love of Splendor. I have played it over 10 times now and only now feel like I understand its full potential. It is as simple or complex as the player would like it to be. By that I mean, you can really just focus on your own little engine and try to get a well rounded flow of gems. But in order to really ascend you have to consider what your opponent is doing also. If you can delay an aquisition for a turn in order to swipe an important card for them you might set them back a few turns. This game always seems to end out of nowhere. The moment you think you're about to get your engine going, someone has won. This is the first board game I have ever seen my 60+ mother like. She picked up the rules quickly and wanted to buy it after we finished our first and only game. I have to comment on the absurdly large box. This game could fit in a large deck box but instead takes as much space up as Mage Knight.

Got expansions as a gift and made an insert that fits everything in one half of the box. Thinking of chopping it down.

Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
While there is a tension between making plans and watching what other players are attempting to be able to preempt them by reserving cards, it comes down so fast to the luck of the draw being able to keep a color of gem away from a player or not (and as with many games of this preempting nature, there is a lot of left-right binding with which to contend).
Even ignoring the luck and downstream-malice, the biggest problem is a total lack of texture. Every color of development is of the exact same value with the exact same distribution and the exact same abilities. There is no unique strength or value to building particular developments or particular levels of developments, which makes players' tables basically the same and also makes the game feel the same every time it is played.

The heart of the game however boils down to a struggle between a blanket Nobles-rush strategy or a faster and more challenging Market (3rd tier) strategy that functionally ignores the Nobles.  For this reason, 3 player games struggle, but 2 and 4 work.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
09-04-2015. Rated after 1 play. Wow, I took a long time trying to play Splendor. And now I've played it, I really like it too.

Basically, Splendor is a race. You try to buy cards, in order to get up to 15 VPs ASAP. There are always 12 open cards, 4 easy, 4 intermediate and 4 difficult (ie. expensive) ones. There are 2 basic ways to score those VPs. You can get them on the cards you buy, and you can get them from having a certain number of cards of colors depending on the tiles that are out there. There are 5 colors (blue, red, white, black, green) and yellow (wild) of resources and cards, and each bought card gives you a subsequent discount based on the jewel in the top corner. 

During your turn, you can take 3 chips of any 3 different colors, except yellow. Or you can take 2 chips of a single color if there are 4 minimum present. You can also take a yellow (wild) chip, and reserve a card you want to buy later. Reserving is possible from the of the deck, or from the display.

I like it. There is not much to it, but it's fun.

textfield_comment_value: One of those games where you can play it as a light filler and let it play itself, taking the obvious chips for cards you can buy before the other players will have the requisite chips, and therefore buying cards as they present themselves. Or you can study exactly what chips all the other players have at all times, what cards they're intending to go for next and alter your plans accordingly. Put me in the former bucket. With new cards coming out all the time, taking the extra time is probably worthwhile results-wise, but just not worth it given the luck and the slowing down of the game for the other players. Take chips, buy cheap cards that allow you to build with less chips later, build an engine accordingly, buy bigger cards worth VPs, hope cards come out that you can buy cheaply and that the same doesn't happen to the other players - then you'll enjoy the win. Take chips or take a card. Every turn. Not that interesting. Ok for what it is, but too decision-light and theme-light and fun-light to warrant a lot of replay.

textfield_comment_value:
Splendor is another awesome filler game that will appeal to pretty much everyone. I'm so glad that I have this game because my wife loves it and even though it is a light game I still feel pleased as I'm playing it because you're constantly making choices in the game. I find that I love games that offer you opportunities to make different choices. Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
finally sat and played this with my daughter.  Not bad.  Its not quite our style game but I can see it being much better with 4 players.  Rules are simple to read and learn.
Game play is quick with each turn being only an option of doing 4-5 actions, then on to the next.  gem tokens are the base of the game and each player can take some of various colors as an action, save them up (limit 10), to buy a card from a replenishing bed of cards, cards have gem values also, and influence which can merit a visit from a noble-which in turn provides more influence.  The player to get 15 influence first, wins.  The game starts off a bit slow but as you build your card inventory, you soon rely less on taking gems for your single action, and can now use the cards.  thus, the game points add up exponentially.  Its a fast game, and fast paced game where it can be easy to lose focus on a goal.  Again, its good, and I would rate it higher with the right set of pals.  A few drinks would make it especially entertaining!
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: (17 year old boy here) I bought this game just this summer and man this game addicted me from the first time I tried it..the heavy tokens OHHH the game is just prestigiously RICH but sadly a bit underplayed in our household. My brother likes the game, wins much more frequently than me but says the game sometimes gets boring when people decide on what they want to do during their turn (which may take 2+ minutes) bec my gamer group is competitive. My dad which adores Catan quite a lot actually loved this game and would be happy to play some more but he's busy most of the time and yeah..now you see why this game gets underplayed in our house. Would have been an easy 10 stars if only I had a gamer group that would enjoy such a well-made game and would play it often with me and only if turns were somewhat quicker during the course of the game. Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Splendor is everything I both love and despise about modern board games. It is a simple design that is easy to teach, keeps runaway leaders to a minimum, plays equally well with 2-4 players, plays quickly and quietly in about 30-45min depending on AP... and it is SO dry.  You can hear the math in your head as you plot out your turns, and it gets very repetitive very quickly.  Also, the theme is nonsense; you are solving a math puzzle, and the game never lets you forget that.  The buy-in rate for non-gamers on this game, which is its target audience, is nearly zero.

The shine wore off Splendor in record time.  It occupies a space along with Kingdom Builder and will probably win awards like crazy, but yeah, I'm done.

UPDATED: Stop asking me to play this game.  Especially if you're going to analyze every single move to the point where it becomes a 45min game.  Here's how you win: Go for the Royals.  Don't do anything that isn't going to help you eventually win 1+ Royals.  It's literally that simple.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
I'm convinced the success of this game is directly connected to its components. When I ask people what they like about splendor, too many people have told me they love the poker chips before they mention anything about the game play. 

To me, it's a dry theme-less engine builder that takes too long to play. There's not enough substance here to hate let alone like. Splendor feel like the epitome of gaming 'meh'. I keep it in my collection only because it's easy to teach to non-gamers (and because it doesn't take up much room after I threw away the ridiculously large box). 

Easily one of the most anti-social gaming experiences I've had was playing a game of Splendor at Gencon, where my opponents insisted on sitting in total silence throughout so they could concentrate on their moves. And this was in a casual pick-up game. None of these people had ever met before, but all of them expressed a love for Splendor before we began. If these are the type of people who love Splendor, I'm glad I don't.

Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: Splendor is a relatively quick race to 15 points. It's an engine-building card game where the players are collecting coloured chips to match various cards on a three-tier display of cards. The tiers increase in cost and points value. When taking chips, you either take three different colours or two of the same (assuming it has at least so many (it's more than two but I can't recall the exact number). When you complete a card, it goes into your tableau and gives you a virtual chip of a specific colour. You can also reserve a card which you want to build or your opponent wants to build and are given a consolation wild chip. Beyond the three-tiered display, there are some noble tiles which require sets of  specific-coloured cards to be complete to claim them. All of this drives a quaint, but relatively ho-hum system. It's quick and easy to play and explain, it's attractive, and probably a good gateway or family game. There are just other games that fit this category that I'd rather play.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
This game is fine, but I find that for my best games the game plays itself.  You just take what it gives you.  There is sometimes some end game decisions, but in general you're at the mercy of the cards and the slight whims of who's able to grab something first.

.... playing it more now i have realized there is more strategy especially depending if you're playing against hard core gamers that are counting and paying attention to your color strengths, people can steal cards you badly need if you fail to reserve them.  also there is the strategy of grabbing the last gems of certain colors to put the next player in a bad way.  it's a very reactive game, one has to be nimble and adjust, whether it's going for the end bonuses or grabbing prestige points from the board, it's a balance while building your engine to finish just a turn ahead of your nearest competitor.  i've played with 4 which seems quite fun on the app... fairly addictive as it plays at about 20 minutes online.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Great pieces, particularly the poker chips that are really nice to manipulate ! Splendor is a relatively short game with easy to learn mechanics.

Basically, you can take resources - 3 different ones or two of the same type - or buy a card which'll give you one virtual resource each turn. Doing so,you score victory points and begin to build your engine to buy cards granting more points, as they are more expensive resource-wise to get...

There are also noble guests to invite to your house, those VIPs only granting 3 victory points each. They'll come to visit you if you manage to get a certain number of cards giving you particular resources... Whenever a player reaches 15 points, the other players have one more turn to play. The player with the most victory points total wins the game.

The game is fluid, quick, tensed, but feels really different if you play with 2 or 4 players, the former being less chaotic than the later. I'll never turnaway from a Splendor game.

textfield_comment_value: Initial rating after 1 play = 8.8 , need to play more. Seems fun, slick and clever. 1/1/15: Am raising to 9.4, played a few more games and top notch. Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Splendor takes an old-school Euro design approach (with more than a passing resemblance to [thing=9217][/thing]) and strips the gameplay down to its barest mechanisms. The engine here is simple – gems will get you cards, which in turn provide more gems to buy more cards.

However, many subtleties and nuances seem to have been lost in midst of streamlining the gameplay. Decisions here are procedural as players routinely count their number of gems, compare them to the costs of cards in the market and take the necessary gems. Sure, players have to keep an eye out for what their opponents are building up towards, but there are very limited opportunities for clever play here.

Other minor drawbacks include the potential for minor downtime as the number of purchasable cards increase towards the midgame, and luck of the draw can allow cards to fall straight into players' laps. Splendor is a solid design overall, but its calculative gameplay simply lacks verve.

Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: It's way too clinical, too basic, and too dry, the whole gameplay is just extremely boring contract fulfillment with nothing providing a mechanical hook otherwise, offering very little satisfaction or pay-off. The theme really doesn't do it any favours either, I don't mind pasted-on themes, but this one could really use a more interesting pasted-on theme or at least better artwork. It's also falsely hailed as an engine-builder, when the game is actually a race. If you're focusing on building up your tableau instead of really optimizing the way you're taking gems and fulfilling contracts, you will absolutely lose, as the game will be over before you're able to build up anything that feels satisfying. The strategy of hoarding chips of certain colour and reserving cards you don't want just to deny other players does provide some interaction, but not sure how much I enjoy a game where the only interaction dynamic is to hate-draft and spite your opponents.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
*Rating based on one play.

Splendor is the definition of a game with a pasted-on theme.  The game is simple and has decent decision points, but also a fairly high degree of luck.  It's short enough that it doesn't overstay its welcome, so it has that going for it.  As a light filler goes, you could do worse.

Having said that, I would not pay the $40 MSRP for this game.  The game has clay chips that are very nice, but there aren't that many (40), and the rest of the game is some cards and a handful of chipboard tiles.  There are quite a few unique illustrations on the cards, which probably contributed to the cost, but not all 90 cards have their own illustration.  I would put this at a $30 value.  On top of that, the box has an excessive amount of unused space (probably to justify the price of the game), making it take up far more room than I would like for a light filler.  It takes up more space on the shelf and in the game bag than it deserves.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
It's good? It's good, it's good. But it's not amazing, and I played it half to death with my friends and family. Naturally, I'm quite tired of it. I'll gladly play it when asked, and I wouldn't ever turn a game of Splendor down, but it's not a game I truly love. It was, once, one of my favorites, but that time has passed. 

Splendor is a sharp, fast (competent players can end the game in 15 minutes in a two-player game), clever engine builder that is magnificently accessible. Playing it for the first time really was a major turning point in my life, setting the road to Catan and beyond. Thus you can say it was my gateway game, and I wouldn't deny that it has a special place in my heart. My close friends and family all know how to play this game, and they all enjoyed it.

However, while Splendor can endure good dozens of plays, it lacks variety and I am no longer excited about it enough to suggest it in favor of other great games in my collection.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
In Splendor players are jewel merchants that are collecting different gemstones to attract the attention of nobles.  The theme is pretty much pasted on and it plays very much like an abstract game. 

During a turn, players choose certain gem chips or use collected chips to purchase cards that provide a certain type of gem and possibly score certain points.  The game play is very straightforward and easy to teach/learn.  The game plays like an engine builder and the strategy is different every game depending on what cards and nobles are in play.

Player interaction is limited to taking cards/chips that someone else might need.  Of all the games I own, this one plays the most silently as everyone is staring intently at the field and contemplating their moves.  Even Blokus has more trash talking!  

This is a fun game for those that dislike direct player conflict and want a short, strategic game that is simple and very elegant.  

Recommended!
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
This is the least thematic game I've ever played. It's mechanics don't marry the theme in any way. It's art doesn't give any hints as to how the theme makes sense. Why are we buying coal mines and boats and jewellery stores and men in funny hats with funny moustaches? 

However that aside, this game is fantastic. You're constantly trying to think three moves ahead, while also trying to read your opponent's plays and predict those as well. It works just as well with two players as it does three or four. The poker chips used in the game feel fantastic to pick up and slam down for payment. And the length of the game is perfect, going on just long enough to see your engine work in all its glory, without ever feeling like it's dragging on for too long. 

This is one of my favourite strategy games around, and one that sees the table time and time again. It's just a shame that trying to explain what the game is to other players is so difficult!

Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
In this game, there are five different colors of gems, plus a 6th color, gold, which acts as a joker. Players use gems to buy development cards (which provide more gems or give VPs) and they may be able to attract nobles for more VPs. The mechanics are very simple (collect gems, reserve card and gain a gold or buy a card). 

There is a lot of angst waiting to see if the card you want is going to get snapped up by an opponent, and you have to decide if you want to reserve a card. There is a race element to be the first one to 15 VPs, and also a race to see who can get the nobles first. It's a lot of fun, and I'd like to get in more plays. 

I can see the strategy progression in this game. First we tried to buy row 1 cards for cheap and get the nobles, now we have progressed to reserving row 2 cards (6 gems for 3 VP as it is the most economical). I can hardly wait to see how the next games go and looking forward to more plays.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Combines the two worst feelings in gaming: waiting while other players take forever deciding whether or not to take the option you wanted and getting screwed over by large point value swings from random draws at the end of the game. 

At first glance, it seems like it could've been a fun game about being flexible and making lemonade out of the cards presented to you. However, higher level play becomes more on more focused on the "reserve" action---it's actually cut-throat brutality about sniping away what your opponent needs before they can do so to you. Purely negative play with reservations is often rewarded, as the right top level card that gives an opponent a noble can be worth 7-8pts to them. This is not so bad with two players, but with more it suddenly becomes everyone's duty to not give away too much to the player after them leading to all sorts of obnoxious dynamics with player order, kingmaking, manipulation, etc.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Okay, I have to say I honestly don't get it. Why the raving reviews? Why the accolades? It's a very, VERY average game. And extremely basic at that - a single mechanic plus a bit of chrome (some pretty cards and nice, thick tokens). Thing is, I don't really think the game has anything new to offer in second, third or tenth play - and it didn't grab me during the first. Tried to understand what's the excitement about and failed miserably. 

For instance, building your little engine is not exciting at all. Okay, so I'll get a discount, so I can get more cards, to get even more discount, to get even more cards. Oh, look, somebody has 15 points already! And that's it. Well, sorry, but there are better light, gateway eurogames out there. Like Kingdom Builder, that game has so much more to offer! Or Dominion, or Carcassonne, or whatever. 

I will try it again, no doubt, maybe I missed something, but it was a huge "meh" for me.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Drops in as an instant 10 I don't think this is the best game every made, but for me it is the best game that I can easily setup and play in 30 minutes or less. The amount of interesting dilemmas squeezed in to that tiny time frame are really a treat. Also, props to the publisher for using nice thick tokens. They are a joy to handle and could have easily cheaped out and used cardboard. One of my criteria for rating a game is how much will it hit the table, and how many different types of people can I play it with. This is basically anytime and almost anyone. Big, big thumbs up.

After 20 plays it holds up. The design of the game lends itself to very close contests. I recently played Arboretum and I actually like it better for a short game, but it is really best at 2 when you go back and forth against one opponent. Therefore this is still my favorite 30 or less game since it plays equally well with any available count.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Splendor is my go-to game to recommend to pretty much anyone. I’ve played with my 6 and 8 year old (with nobles removed), with my mom (who doesn’t like board games but wanted to play multiple sessions), and with my board game group that enjoys dungeon crawlers and strategy games.

Splendor can be taught in under 5 minutes, is a perfect duration of ~30 minutes, and is both simple and deeply strategic for those that want it to be. 

You naturally get “stronger” overtime, so even new players feel like they’re progressing and doing well against seasoned players. Multiple strategies are viable, which adds variety to each gameplay. 

I’ve had games where I focused on nobles nearly 100% and won, games where I got 0 nobles and won, and a “just for kicks” game where I didn’t buy a single card that wasn’t worth a victory point (and won). There is a ton of replayability, and I haven’t met someone who hasn’t enjoyed playing it.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
This game is so great! It lasts just long enough, you can plan decisions far in advance, and you can really mess up your opponents while also benefitting yourself. Most of your information is on the board, but there is so much going on that it helps to obscure your face-up strategy from your opponent. They could think they have you figured out, but the options that are available to you every turn allow you to pivot in another direction quite easily if required. The components are also excellent quality. 

I wish there was so more variety with the nobles, or perhaps reduce their reward because it feels like whoever is turned up at the beginning of the game determines your entire strategy. 

I always love playing this game. It's a great blend of strategy, time investment, planning, and reward. There's also so much going on that luck and variance don't feel like a burden and the randomness of the cards is quite fun.
Title: Splendor

Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
I like games with very simple, clear rules, so this hits the spot. That said, it's a really dry game that doesn't encourage interesting interaction with other players--the games I've played have been quiet, and your only interaction with other players is blocking them (nabbing cards before they do or starving them of the colour tokens they want). I'll play this game occasionally but it lacks flavour.

UPDATE: Having played this and Century: Spice Road, I can't decide which is duller. C:SR has the major plus of being able to use a card for multiple conversions at once, though in my experience players often grab way more cards than they need and the game drags on interminably. Splendor has the virtue of a more fluid card market than C:SR (where things can badly stall if the cards come out in the wrong order).

Neither is in my "refuse to play" list but they are both in my "only play to humour other people" list.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
That's it? The box is only "slightly" large for what's in it:
[imageid=1991004 medium]

That was my initial reaction, not just when opening the game, but also when reading the rules and playing. Admittedly I didn't do much research (I rarely do), but given the box size and hype (from trusted sources), I expected this to be a bit more complex. At least like St. Petersberg or Carcassonne level. But this is a very very very simple card game. It's is clearly a filler. There's a ton of luck, but enough decisions that it's still fun. Something on par with like Biblios or something. 

This has to be one of the worst recent offenders for percentage of space that is air in the box. Put this game in a box half the size and I'd raise my rating a full point. I like the chunky tokens (perhaps the chunkiest of any game I own), but they could be laid flat in one cylinder with the cards next them. Ridiculous waste of space.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: Splendor might be one of the most streamlined engine-building games out there, and it is a strong game design.  I am always a fan of games where you just make one small decision on your turn, but that can balloon out into a lot of complex strategies over the course of a game.  I like the somewhat slow-paced start, and how it grows into a game where you can do so much.  I also think it's interesting the different paths you can take to victory, and how much you have to think about when to switch from cheap cards that make it easier to complete cards, over to the big point cards.  There's really no theme here, so it doesn't surprise me that they re-skinned it as a Marvel game.  While I would happily play Splendor any time, I am thinking about letting it go from my collection merely because there are other engine-building games that I find more interesting, so I rarely reach to pull this one off the shelf.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
I've played this game dozens of times via the mobile app.  The physical game is much better, imo.  The social aspect (not play and pass) makes this game really shine.

This game is so smart.  The rules are so simple and the depth of strategy is amazing.  You feel so satisfied gaining a card to help your engine get you better cards later.

I honestly can't think of a single point of criticism.  This game plays fantastically with 2, 3 (best) and 4 players.
