Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
I had the unfortunate experience the first time I played this of playing against someone who knew the top strategy and handily won by ignoring the entire engine building premise of this game. You shouldn't buy any tier one gems (they're a trap) and don't care about the discounts or the nobles at all. Just rush the 3 point cards for 6 gems of one color, 4 points for 7 of one color or 5 points for 7 and 3. If you don't believe me, watch any World Series of Board Gaming plays of Splendor. All the pros do the exact same thing. 

If the main strategy of an engine building game is to completely ignore the engine building, then sorry it's just a bad game. Most people though wouldn't play this way because they follow the intended design of the game. It also has a very simple rules teach and works great as a gateway game. So treat it as a gateway and never play this with anyone more serious than that.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
The gams is fascinating, because it is so simple. There are just a few rules, however plenty of decisions to make. You have to choose, which cards to save for and which cards to take into you hand so that others won't steel them from you. Do you need three different chips or two of the same sort? By the way, the opportunity to take two of the same occurs not that often. Finally, it is important to pay attention to what nobles are available. To sum up, it is not that easy to find the best way to victory.

Žaidimas žavi savo paprastumu. Taisyklių tikrai nedaug, tačiau sprendimų pakankamai. Kurioms kortelėms taupyti, o kurias pasiimti į ranką, kad kiti nenukniauktų. Ar imti tris skirtingus, ar du vienodus žetonus. Beje, du vienodus paimti ne taip dažnai ir pavyksta. Galiausiai, svarbu atkreipti dėmesį į tai, kokie didikai yra prieinami. Žodžiu ne taip paprasta rasti tiesiausią kelią į pergalę.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
8.4.15. While I do the elegance in the design of this game, to me, the flaws outweigh the fun I have when I play this game. First the game is almost too simple for my tastes. While I don't mind simple games in general, if you couple this with an AP person, this games becomes almost unbearable. The other real issues I have is with serious vs casual players. I all my games, I got to the left of a person who watched the board and took what I needed when able. I did my best to go with what I had. The person across had a person who just kinda took what looked good. Each game that person across just killed us all. I like a game where my decisions matter to help me build up my game and are not heavily dependent on what the person before me does.

1/11/18 After more plays, this has turned out to be a better 2 player game than 4. We can both watch each other and the blocking is much better served.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Fast & light. Fun although far from 'addicting' as others have claimed. A clear strategy is needed to avoid just being 1 or 2 turns short of your own victory when the game ends. I think 15 VP is too little; extending the game to 20-25 VP would mitigate the 'luck-of-the-draw' for the highest point cards (that may never change before the final round). 

The 'claiming' of cards adds a small amount of nastiness that may be misplaced in such a light game (more experienced gamers will more easily see what others need for their strategy), as there is no penalty (other than a lost turn which is often more than made up for with the utility of the gold chip) in keeping cards out of play at the end of the game. I believe that any card held at the end of the game should cost 1 VP each, or better yet, no cards can be held in order to win.

Update: It looks nice and plays easily but isn't a favorite.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
I love this game for two reasons, first it's a great warm-up to a "main feature" game. It's easy to set up, teach if necessary, and play. The game takes up little time and works the brain up to whatever the next game will be, usually something more time consuming and difficult. Second, it's amazing all on its own! Great one-on-one for a best-of-three/five over a beer or two with the SO. 

Classic game. 

If I must complain I would point out that the box is very large compared to the actual components, definitely would fit into something 1/4th the size. The plastic insert that holds the components is also a problem, if the box is stored on its edge the "pogs" will fly and be all over the place when you open it again. Not huge, just annoying!

Sometimes I want this game to be more complex but at the same time I love its simplicity. I am definitely hesitant on adding expansions... for now!
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
A basic efficiency/engine builder, stripped of any parts that aren't essential to the core mechanisms.  More interesting to view as a design exercise than to play as a game. Sort of like a piece of modern art in that regard -- I can be interested for a time analyzing it but wouldn't necessarily hang it in my living room (or with Splendor, actually own it to bring it out on my game table).  Another analogy would be a training exercise for a sport -- it might make you better at that aspect but it in no way compares to the satisfaction of actually playing the full sport. 
 And with board games, I'm not looking to "train" myself on simple engine building.
Maybe all this is a bit harsh -- I don't hate playing it, it just doesn’t hold my interest after 4-5 games. Both strategy and tactics seem painfully obvious after a few games, at which point luck of the card flips start to weigh heavily.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
I really can not understand the hype around this game and the high ratings. I think so many people could have come up with this game but thinking it was so dull and cheap they threw that idea away. 

It's like a deckbuilding game engine but without deckbuilding ... It's like dominion (already non-thematic), take away the best aspect of dominion (deck building), add more type of coins and you get this residu. This is the pinnacle of non-creativity of boardgaming and it saddens me deeply so many people actually like it, it's a real demotivation for aspirant game designers like me. I don't want to make garbage, but apparantly garbage sells. 

The boredom is supported by the runaway nature of the 'design'. How a runaway leader game sells anno 2014 is beyond me. I guess poker chips is the way to design games today.

I rather play a 24h Monopoly marathon than one more game of this torture.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
[March 2020 - 7.7]
Inches up as I've had good success introducing it to non-boardgamers and it's kept my attention.

[April 2015 - 7.5]
I was skeptical of Splendor despite all the high praise. It just didn't seem like my type of game. Then I played it at a game night and really enjoyed it. To me, this games kills 7 Wonders (minus its lackluster theme) because there's that same aspect of building up and taking other cards that people really want, but in a much more public and interactive way. I also really like the simple supply-and-demand economic system of the chips and the checks and balances it provides. Even the chip play is interactive in that you either need people to play their chips to free them up or grab chips before the other players do. In all, it fosters some of those great game moments when it isn't about your movement as much as it is guessing what the others will do.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
After 9 plays, my wife and I (mid 30s part-time Eurogamers w/young kids) love this game!!

It is quick to understand, easy to play, and leaves you with that "Let's just play one more time" feeling.

We love engine building games, but our lifestyle allows us to play mostly just quick games.  Splendor satisfies both of these criteria.   Sometimes we each wish that the we had a couple more turns in the game to better realize the output of our engines (and it would be easy to allow this, simply raising the number of victory points required to trigger the last round).  However, doing this would clash with criteria #2.

As a side note, our 2-year old twins love to play with the gem chips!!  They just sort them by color/gem into the pockets in the box insert and then declare "all done."  They actually request this game more than some of the kids games we have purchased to play with them.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
An okay and fairly fast set set collection engine game that is easy to pull off the shelf and play with little or no rules reading.  That said, the gameplay is so simplistic and tactical (low strategy) that I'm not sure if Splendor brings enough fun and repeatability to the table.

Additional thoughts: Better with 3p, more strategic, chips run out quickly and chips don't cycle as rapidly as in the 4p game where someone is buying a card and thus returning chips to the supply almost every turn.

UPDATE 2016: I'd like to try without the bonus tiles; they might balance the game for players that buy a bunch of low-end gem cards, but it bugs me that only a few high-end (3rd row) cards get bought in most games.  Perhaps this has more to do with groupthink (in my game groups) than imbalanced design.  I'd like to see if high-end card strategies can work and how to execute these strategies.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
My nephew was having trouble with his 14 year old son. He is a single father (divorced from a woman who is in and out of jail/prison for drug use), so we advised him that he do something that they could share in as a family. We suggested to the nephew to try playing board games. The son said he did not like board games, but we convinced him to try one he had never played (Ticket to Ride). They both enjoyed it. The second game we tried was Splendor. The nephew really enjoyed it...but the son LOVED it.

They borrowed our old copy of the game and wore it out over the summer of 2021. (My wife happily replaced it with a new copy.) The son even taught it to his high school buddies. They have played it over and over and over. They now have a friendship that they have never had, and board games in general (and this game specifically) are responsible for it.

This game gets a 10 from me.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Purchased after developing an affection for Jaipur, and on the grounds of it being a minimalist distillation of the engine building style. 

After a single play, I found it a touch lack luster with two. The play experience felt relatively dry. Unlike Jaipur, it doesn't feel like the game space is tight enough for two; the game would have more tension if you were vying over a tighter selection of cards. As it stands now, it is unlikely you'll both value the same card, so play becomes little more than a race to grab to see who can optimize their chosen path quickest. 

Will try it again. Perhaps my provisional rating will increase. 

For what it is worth, my partner enjoyed the experience faaaaar more, and we enjoyed its fast playtime as well. 

Oct. 22nd update: Yes, I raised the score from 5 to 6.5. It is a fun, very thinky game. Sadly, the ending is abrupt and anticlimactic.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
A race type game with style. Very well made components.  Fun and light.  Stands up to repeated play.  I appreciate the effort that went into the design but the theme does feel "pasted" on.

Big discussion about pasted on themes but still like the mechanics in this game. Played three with Brian, won two.  I also got lucky.  We both noticed how the game speeds up somewhere in the fourth or fifth round. 

Played a very good game last night.  I made the mistake of not tracking my opponent's stockpile which would have been a tipoff of his strategy and averted a huge comeback victory for him. Do not treat this game like solitaire. It has more depth than that for sure. 

Played several online games.  A few bugs that I'm sure will be fixed.  But' gameplay was smooth and pace was excellent.  Not handling the chips has some getting used to but overall an excellent gaming experience.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
The slim rulebook makes this game easy to teach and the activation energy required to get it to the table is low because it's a relatively short, fast-paced game.

The engine-building element of the game is very fun.

The strategy is there and pretty deep; the cleverer you are, the better you will do. A friend of mine, in his first game, completely dominated others of us who had experience with the game by adopting a strategy where he completely ignored engine-building and calculated the least resource-intensive route to purchase the cards on the top row to get to 15 -- it was a strategy that seemed so non-intuitive to me. We could have probably stopped this strategy if we'd understood what he was doing earlier and taken active steps to block him and force him to adopt an engine-building approach in order to have more general buying power, but it was still amazing!
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
A great game with simple, polished mechanics. The strategy of the game is mostly linear, but will change each game based on the cards revealed. normally a game with "random chance" can hinder or block players, but in this case the element of chance gives a different game play each time with minimal or negligible hindrance. There are some play-throughs that just by chance might give everyone the short end of the stick, but this can add to the strategy of trying to get new cards out without taking too many turns. 

The game play time is fairly accurate and can be shortened with people who plan their turns/strategy ahead of time.

Also important to note, I once accidentally played this game with five players and it worked, but was much slower as the chips became a finite/sparse resource.

Update:
After dozens of plays over 2019, I increased my rating from 8.25 to 8.5
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Nice quick game, the haptic sensation (and most of all, the weight) of the gem-chips makes this game in my opinion. Not liking it all that much, one can get easily locked out of chips in a 1v1 and can't really plan much in a 4 player game - generally, I don't feel like there is that much choice involved.

It just doesn't excite me to be frank. It's a nice little game (in a box much too big for it which I hate) but will never be much more than an easy filler. Which is fine, there's just enough games out there that do what splendor does, but better. I can see the appeal and realize I am in the minority here, considering how popular this game is.

Edit: Sold. As the fanciness of a new game, in this case splendor, declined there was little (read: NO) interest from me or my friends in playing this, and the box takes much, MUCH more space on the shelf than it should.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
I played this game once, so take this score with a grain of salt. But, as I have no intention to play it ever again, I feel like sharing my score and impressions.

Interestingly enough, I kind of liked my time with Splendor - just pleasure of brain working on figuring out one another optimization puzzle. And yet, more time passed, less satisfied I feel with my experience with this game. So, what I dislike in this game:
- The biggest issue is that I don't see any sense to play it with other people. Our table was unusually silent, while everybody was trying to look at their cards 20th time and find out the best tactics. I understand the nature of MPS game, but it felt almost discouraging interactions.
- It as no theme. It's not a big issue, but still somewhat lessen experience.
- It is too easy to activate analysis paralysis in this game, making it way too long.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Splendor is a nice and good game, but at least for me, it has its issues. For one the late game feels way too rushed and automatic (every player just seems to grab whatever he can afford for free and what gives the most points - the amount of decisions is very limited towards the end) and - at least with 2 players - one player can - by luck of the card draw - completly shut the other player out of one of the colors - which makes it nearly impossible for the other player to win. This can be very frustrating as it has nothing to do with skill but just with knwoing about this denial strategy and having the luck of the right cards showing up at the right times.

It plays super fast (10-15min), setup and teardown are minimal and the quality of the components is perfect, but for a really "great" game a bit more emphasizeon skill vs. luck would have been required.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Splendor is a very engaging, very quick, economic-engine game that provides a moderate amount of brain-burn. It's a game that I really enjoy playing and something that has received nothing but positive remarks from other gamers. That being said, the speed/engaging-feel might be making the game feel more deep than it actually is. Don't get me wrong, your decisions matter in this game and you need to focus on the board and other players. But after 9-plays, I'm starting to feel how the random elements can impact the game.

But being such a quick game, it is essentially a filler... and has a remarkable number of meaningful decisions for that. Component quality is amazing but I am actually starting to dislike the heavy-weight poker chips; if you carry your game around, they tend to fly everywhere. Perhaps lighter wooden chips would have been a better decision.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: Belle découverte, un jeu avec règles simples et décisions intéressantes comme je les aime. L'interaction vient du fait qu'il faut surveiller les possibilités des autres pour leur subtiliser les cartes avant qu'ils ne le fasse. Un peu trop de cartes accumulées à mon goût (on a complètement vidé la pile 1, je ne sais pas si c'est fréquent). À la fin, nous avions tellement de cartes que le jeu se jouait presque tout seul (on pouvait aisément prendre des cartes gratuites ou presque). Thème absent, froid pour ceux qui ont besoin de se sentir un marchand, un entrepreneur, un architecte ou quoique ce soit - on fait seulement acheter des cartes sans signification. Pour ma part la simplicité, la mécanique, la qualités des décisions et la durée relativement courte font en sorte qu'il est définitivement à rejouer, avec un achat possible si concluant. 8/10. (04-2014)
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Everyone likes to doodoo on Splendor for having a pasted-on theme, but it's a card game, most of which have pasted-on themes. Century Spice Road is a very similar game to Splendor, and nobody whines about its pasted-on theme. (To be honest, I have Century Golem Edition and it's just as pasted on, but those Golems sure are adorable!)

That said, the game deserves to be put to the fire a little bit because it's far too expensive for what it is: cards and poker chips. Maybe people are reacting more to this, the theme just coming off as the game thinks it's more important than it really is. It is a good game, though. It's also extremely hard to teach and it's a bit fiddly. Because of this, I got the app, which I enjoy way more than the physical version, so it rarely hits the table. It'd probably be an 8.5, but I'm dropping it .5 for not being worth the price.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Extremely elegant, tableau-building euro-game.
-Explanation is about 10 minutes, and players usually understand the game after a couple rounds of their first game. No fiddliness or rules exceptions that murk-up the explanation.
-Components are beautiful. The gems genuinely feel good to handle (they are nice, weighted poker chips).
-Great entry-point into eurogaming, the idea of engine-building is straightforward.
-In my experience, games of splendor are quiet, and you can be quite mean if you intend to be.
-Definitely a luck factor, and the first few games can be misleading -- making you feel like you need to be getting a noble, even though it's completely viable to just shoot for the high-point cards, as well as making you think you need to have the best engine to win, when often you can win with even a mediocre engine and just gun the high-point cards.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
We were introduced to this game by friends of ours and I loved it so much! Every game night with them includes at least 1 round of Splendor. It's been a few years now and it's still my favorite game!

Dad's review: "The best part of this game is that no strategy will always work which keeps it interesting. Sometimes saving up for the higher level cards help you take the game but the next match you may just stock up on a ton of lower level cards. 5 stars."

Mom's review: "There is a lot of strategy involved with this game and you have to keep an eye on what your opponents are doing to make sure you stay a step ahead or pivot your plans before it's too late to pivot. I don't ever get bored with this game because the way you play will always change depending on who you're playing with and what their strategies are. All the stars!!"

Final rating: 5/5 stars
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
This game was the surprise of the game night. I didn't expect a lot from this one, however after playing it i changed my mind. The game is an abstract strategy game without a strong theme so what is insteresting about it? Well it is kinda an engine building game just like Fleet but in this one you can take the limited resourced before your opponents manage to take them. It has one of the easiest rules but the strategy is deeper than it first appears. After that i no longer wonder why this game is so popular. The playtime is around 40 minutes.

Pros / Cons:
-This game gives you an opportunity to kick ouf your opponents from the valuable resources to force them to buy from a more expensive one (golden).
-The rules are quite simple yet the strategy is deeper than that.

-Well it is hard to say bad about it, but im not sure if it has enough replayability.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: Great example of a set collection mechanic streamlined to the maximum and I like it. The rules are so simple that my 6 year old son is playing with me and my wife without any issues. I dare the say that the game could be streamlined even more with the removal of nobles, but I guess that this would be an exaggeration. I even wondered a bit how the design looked like for this game. Did they remove rules until almost nothing was left? This may be the case if one looks at the available expansions, especially the orient one and the market one which all have more "gamy" things in them. I still love the game. During my two week holidays I played it at least once a day which says a lot how my family likes it. I think I am falling in love with games with small amount of rules, almost minimalistic ones. Splendor will definitely have a place in my collection.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
It's simple and, despite what I have seen others say, I don't find the randomness is a problem here. Hell, I don't even think player interference is much of a problem either once you have a solid strategy paradigm in place.

Which might be a problem in itself?
I mean that there's a way to basically win every time. It requires the right balance of flexibility, with a fixed and solid end goal plan.
Now, I usually dislike games for which, once you find the winning strategy, you just play along that dumbly and win every time. But here, the strategy is just that, a strategy, and you still require flexible and adaptable tactics along the way to drive it all to fruition. As a result, using the robustness of the strategy I am referring to does not feel like coasting brainlessly along, with a sort of cheat code in hand. It feels damn satisfying, actually!
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
The description for a "3" reads "Likely won't play this again, although could be convinced.  Bad."  The pretty much sums up how I felt about this game.  I didn't have very much fun playing it.  Your mileage may vary.

It's nothing more than a mechanism.  You build an engine by buying stuff that allows you to buy more stuff more efficiently.  Eventually one player has fine-tuned their array to the point where they win.  There's nothing inherently wrong with that idea, but I'm frankly tired of "building an engine" when I should be playing a game.  I would rather be interacting rather than reacting.  This game felt like a lot of reacting: "Fred bought the card I thought I wanted.  Now what do I do?"  

Not my idea of fun, but I'd play it again with the right group.  It's 20 minutes of activity with the opportunity to cuss Fred out once in a while.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
SOLOABLE!! (See Hans Solo's guide on Youtube)

KING OF THE GATEWAY GAMES!!
An EXCELLENT GAME and my go-to for introducing non-gamers to the hobby gently. The mechanics are on-par with Century however Splendor is ever so slightly easier to teach and learn thus making it the better gateway game in my opinion.

The theme is boring so for ages I avoided buying it. Then one board game night at my FLGS, nobody brought any games. Someone grabbed this from the in-store library and within minutes we knew how to play and were having fun.

Then I saw the solo variant and was sold!

I introduced it to some non-gamer friends and I just heard they bought a copy for their home haha

+ Quality components
+ Fantastic insert
+ Easy to teach
+ Easy to learn

- Theme is 'meh' (but better rare gems than collecting spices. Not as cool as collecting Golems, though :D)
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
"VERY GOOD"
Exceptional artwork and components. Easy to teach and really fun.
This game can be played casually or in a thinkier way, counting cards, etc. , which means it has a good chance to please a wide range of players´ tastes.

My 9 y.o. boy just beat me in the last turn: I was the first player, made 15 points (win !), and then, on his last legal turn (to end the round and finish the game), he said: "Dad, just see my master move !": he took a 3rd row 4-point-card, which was his fourth emerald, and, instantly, attracted the last noble card (3 points), leaping from 10 to 17 points - and beating me "in the last minute". 
I´ve always been competitive, and use to do my best when playing with kids after the age of 8 or 9. Being beaten by a son is an ambiguous event ! "That´s what you get when you marry a clever woman...", is all I can say 
:-D
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
This double-drafting game seemed fairly clever and entertaining. Players draft from limited resource pools, then use these to draft cards which may or may not be worth victory points but which always give card discounts and contribute to bonus objectives. A good overall strategy is to not have the same overall strategy as the player on your right, since this heavily influences your rate of freebies. Now, both of our games had runaway victories decided several rounds before we actually stopped playing: whoever comes out of the first age with a few more freebies and claims the first noble is most likely to get a second and seal the deal. Also the age three cards might as well not have existed. If this pattern holds it would put a dent in the game's elegance. Well-deserved poster child for ridiculously oversized boxes.

Thrifted on 4/9 2021.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
You slowly accrue gems to buy cards which become permanent gems, and once you have enough permanent gems you can buy patricians, who simply give victory points, and whoever gets to 15 victory points typically is the winner (other players still get one more turn).

So, my takeaway was frankly the game wasn't nearly as bad as I thought it would be. It's very much a Euro, it plays fairly quick, and it just lacks any real meat. I felt like if maybe the patricians were then used to do something, as an additional layer to the game, it'd be REALLY good, but without that, it feels like it's missing a piece. The quality of the gem chips is very nice, some sort of ceramic-acrylic mix I'd bet, and that certainly adds some quality to the game, but overall a very underwhelming experience. I don't think it deserves any of the praise it's received.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Simple engine-building.  Easy to teach and learn, with nice presentation and components.

Take a resource chip or two, spend to buy a card.  Use said card plus more resource chips to buy more cards that give points and more resources...  repeat until target point threshold has been reached by one player.

This game did not excite me at all. Has minimal interaction, none of which is "direct", which lands it outside of my particular tastes. The amount of praise that it often receives just doesn't align with my opinions of it.  I don't find that it has any real "meat" and after half a dozen or so plays, I had no desire to play it again.  

Certainly not a bad game, as it's ease of understanding offers a nice introduction for some common mechanisms within the hobby. For this reason, it'll remain in my collection for a while longer.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
At first, it feels like just some simple set collection game with Luck being the major factor to win the game. But after the second game, third game, and so on, I realized that it's definitely not luck. You need a good strategy, hand management, pay attention to your enemies' step and cover your own to win the game. And the more I play, the more I'm excited about this game. 

The first 2 or 3 games, we played splendor in silence. But as we keep playing, it's getting noisier as each of us trying to redirect and distract our own movement by pointing other player's movement possibilities, especially when they're approaching 15 pts. 

When that happened, we usually try to convince other players into joining our cause and collectively taking steps to hinder the winning player's step (and silently delivering our own steps to victory).
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Jan 22 - Rating 10.0: After almost 200 plays, unsurpassed. Excellent art, excellent components and has not been equaled by either Majesty, Spice Road or Marvel Splendour. Using the nobles, the coin pieces and even varying the amount of columns adds a lot of variability to the game. I don't get the criticsm about lack of theme. It a puzzle, not Ameritrash and I think you are playing as gem dealers, from source to market. It is always a fantastic puzzle, a game yes. Easy to set-up & take-down and best at 2 player. At 3-4 players I'd knock it back to an 8.5.

Aug 17 - Rating 9.0: Excellent art & components, always tough choices and elements of both tactics and strategy.  Although it is abstract, it's easy to teach and set-up and this game is worthy of all its accolades and I have no doubt will remain in-print for decades to come.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Splendor is a game I'm always willing to play, but I never leave satisfied... Even when I win.

I think the issue with Splendor is the way it ramps up. Everybody spends 80% of the game with no points, fighting for resources to play the early cards and pursuing their strategy, only for the game to end abruptly in just a few turns when somebody hit the right combination of cards to get points.

The points cap for winning should be much higher than 15. The game drags slowly, then ends abruptly before anybody can really pursue any long-term strategy.

The only strategy that works with this game is pursuing the cards that grant you points early. Forget about the nobility cards, forget about developing your production pool, just go straight for money and then cards with points and you'll win far before anybody can finish a strategy.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
سبلندير(الفخامة او العظمة) لعبة من تصميم مارك اندرو الفرنسي والفنان باسكال كويدلت انت تلعب بصفتك تاجر من عصر النهضة الاوربية في القرن الرابع عشر إلى القرن الخامس عشر حيث تقوم بالتنقيب عن المناجم للحصول على الموارد وهي الذهب بالإضافة إلى الأحجار الكريمة وهي الزمرد والعقيق اليماني والألماس والياقوت الأزرق والياقوت وهذا المتواجدة في اللعبة ونقلها وجعل بعض الحرفيين يصنع من هذه المجوهرات زينة وحلي ومن خلال ذلك تحاول التوسع في التجارة والحصول على السمعة والنفوذ وجذبه من خلال النبلاء في ذلك العصر ومنهم سليمان القانوني وشارل الخامس وفرانسوا الأول وهنري الثامن وماري انطوانيت وغيرهم 

اللعبة لا تحتاج لغة ويلعبها من 2 إلى 4 وتأخذ 30 دقيقة إلى ساعة، وتصميم اللعبة يجعل اللعبة اكثر جمالاً ومتعة وهي من النوع الاستراتيجي الذي يقوم على الاقتصاد واستخدام الأموال المنقولة او الثابتة لبسط النفوذ على السوق فتستطيع ان تحتكر بعض الموارد من السوق
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Poker style tokens are the biggest magnet to the game ;) just kidding. Splendor is great. It doesn't have strong theme, box is too big and too pretty compared to what's inside. In the box You will find some cardboard tiles, cards and heavy tokens. It is so great to hold them in hand ;) It is a game of chip-collecting and card development. All of the cards you buy increase your wealth as they give you a permanent bonus in the future  buys. Some of the cards also give you prestige points. STRONG RECOMMENDATION.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: Fura kis játék ez. Rendkívül addaktív "engine builder" a "gateway" kategóriában. A furaság csak annyiból áll, hogy az első játék alkalmával, mindenki csak tapogatózik, hogyan is kellene játszani a játékot jól, a második játéknál már van fogalmunk arról, hogy miről is szól a játék, de még csak a kezdeti stratégiánkat csiszolgatjuk, majd egy méretes zakó után (amit a feleségemtől kaptam :)), át kellett gondolnom, hogy mi lehet a nyerő stratégia és a harmadik játéknál már taroltam is vele, a negyedik játék után elárultam a számomra nyerő stratégiát a többieknek és az ötödik játékot már csak szoros küzdelemben sikerült megnyernem és akkor a játék megcsillantotta a következő mélységét, amit még csak ezután fogunk felfedezni. Ha mindenképp összehasonlítanom kellene a Fűszerúttal, akkor százszor is ezt választanám. (2018.12.29.)
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: I really wanted to like this game a lot. Of course ultimately, this game is seriously very light. However several factors keep it from being "good". Number one and foremost is the fact that the game ends at 15 points. It feels way too soon for most of the strategies in the game, as you feel like it's barely half over by that point. Also the component quality is really poor. Really, poker chips for gems when you can buy actual acrylic gem pieces much cheaper? Really guys? And a box that's 4 times larger than the components all assembled together. The game is also very swingy based on what nobles are in play and when certain gems come up. If the deck(s) clump together, it throws off the entire game's balance forever which I see as a fatal flaw. Otherwise the game has a ton of potential and I can be talked into playing it.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
A great game, all-around. Splendor is an engine-building game. It's thin on theme, but rich in gameplay. It's easy to learn, but difficult to master. The game components are excellent-quality. The turns are short. Everyone at the table stays involved as the board and resources keep changing. The games are short enough that you're likely to play more than one game in a sitting. I foresee this being a regular at the gaming table.

Get this: If you like Dominion. If you like engine-building games (like Dominion). If you like your strategy games with a bit of luck. If you're looking to a "gateway game" other than Ticket to Ride.

Avoid this: If you hate strategy games. If you only like games with complex rules. If you play games for their themes (you could paste any number of themes onto this game and it wouldn't matter).
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
It's a perfect game. First of all: it's elegant and easy to get into: The theme is pleasing, but barely there, but it's not needed anyway: the abstract skill-rewarding gameplay stands on its own. The player interaction is indirect but, especially with more experienced players, stronger than it appears at first glance.

First I found it too streamlined and mechanic that it didn't excite me at all. After more plays, a deeper dive into the strategy, and my first wins, I realize that Splendor may be *the* benchmark for this kind of game: streamlined light/mid-weight filler that appeals to a *wide* audience and comes with great components.  My early verdict (in 2014) was: “Next year, next perfect game.” — now, mid-2016, I still don't see any game taking Splendor's place.

Rating history:
2014: 6.5
2015: 6.85
2016: 7.5
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
This is about as light as I think you could make a pure engine building game. You collect gemstones so that you can collect even more gemstones, and all the while it's a race to 15 points.
I really like this game. It's simple to teach and to set up. Games are 15-30 minutes. I think it really shines at 2 players; 3 players is good, and 4 players can sometimes drag as you wait for your turn.
I think the box is unnecessarily large for the sake of accommodating the page-size of the (very short) rulebook. Easily could have fit everything into a box the size of Patchwork or Kingdomino to make it more portable.
There is an expansion (I think it's actually 4 expansions in one box), but I don't think the game needs it and I don't plan to buy it. Splendor is great just how it is and I'd recommend it to just about anyone.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Such simple rules disguising a rather tense engine building game.  The tension is from the race itself, which always seems to be close no matter what you do, and the choices you have to make.  The forfeiting of a turn to reserve a card is a particularly interesting dynamic which presents tough decisions.

In some respects I feel that this is a fairly basic single mechanic which has been made into an entire game, and perhaps it would benefit in being as part of a greater game.  But then on the other hand this essential simplicity and short game-play is what makes the game so attractive.  So on balance I'm sold and have since purchased a copy.  It may tire after a few plays but until that time I am looking forward to investigating it some more.

UPDATE: the game is too processional and dry.  I have sold my copy.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: 5 plays under my belt and really enjoying it. The theme seems pasted on, but the artwork is great and the gem chips are awesome and weighty and definitely meant to be fidgeted with. Haven't been able to find a good strategy yet as witnessed by my 12 yr old beating me the first time he played. I tend to grab low cost cards to build an engine to get high cost cards but it seems like other players often skip this step and go right for the big points by amassing many gems and supplementing with the wild card golds to nab big points. The nobles haven't seemed to play a big part in the game as someone usually wins before there are enough cards out to be deemed worthy of a visit. This game is a definite family night hit and the stragey is deep enough to keep heavy gamers thinking and interested. A definite keeper!
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Engine building/set collection game. Simple to introduce players to.

Scratches the same itch as dominion while being a much simpler game. Good amount of strategic decision making where you have to chose between a number of simple to comprehend choices. Depending upon the tiles and cards that come up there are a number of viable strategies - going for an engine that allows you to build up to inexpensive victory points or just rushing straight for the 5VP card. The 15VP goal is low enough that you can just rush points but high enough that sometimes an efficient engine is better.

Strategy varies depending upon the number of players playing because of the changing ratio of money/player, pursuing sets that nobody is going for and having more/less players to block.

The poker chips are a very satisfying weight.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
We play on iOS.  My wife loves this game, and for the past few years we have played it at a rate of nearly one game a day.  (We often use the Cities expansion, which we like.  I have not tried the others yet.)  So we have a 1000+ games under out belt.  My daughter sometimes joins us.  I think -- contrary to the BGG player # poll -- that my favorite player count is two players.  There is offense and defense in Splendor, and with two players it is crystal clear who must play defense against an opponent doing well, namely, YOU.

Now that we are used to digital play, where the app does the bookkeeping for you and shows you what cards you can afford to buy, I think we would find playing the physical game too slow for our tastes, alas.  Sad but probably true.  In fact we have never once played the physical game.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
This game is really good.  In under 5 minutes you can explain it and be playing it.  Sometimes, that's just important, and some people are only going to play a game where that is the case.

I've played 3 player, 2 player, and 4 player.  All games were tight, and moved quickly.

I haven't played enough to see a clear strategy as others seem to claim and refute.  It's certainly tactical vs strategic.  I can see this game popping out in a variety of groups and looking forward to getting it on the table a bunch coming up here. 

The components are great, and I think really help out a lot - you sort of just want to play with the poker chips.  In terms of value....I don't know.  I picked it up for 20 on a sale - I think for 30, it feels a little light.  But hey, if you like the game, it probably doesn't matter.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
ANOTHER UPDATE: This one is a solid 6. With more play, I've gotten quite good at the game, but it's just too dry. I've basically circled 'round to my original opinion. Oh well!

---

UPDATE: Yes, it's a snowball, but after playing the game with another new player (my first few plays were with experienced and well practiced players), I enjoy it much, much more. I had a little extra breathing room to figure out what to do and how to do it. I now gladly play, and I can see my rating moving up to an 8. Time will tell.

Interesting. Lovely components. But ultimately a bit too straightforward. It's a race to create an economic snowball. The card reservation mechanic saves the game from being too chaotic in a multi-player setting, but, to be honest, I'm worried Splendor is just a bit, well, boring.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
You would think that a game with instructions this simple just wouldn't be any fun, especially when one turn is similar to the next.  But in fact, it's quite enjoyable and plays very fast.

Players can take a few different types of gems, eventually "buying" a card which will give a discount in the future.  You keep acquiring those and then have a number of turns where you can afford anything - but which ones to choose in order to get you the most points?  Or the favor of a visiting noble?  You also need to think about the endgame - once someone hits 15 points, the round plays out and it's over.  You have to be careful not to end things prematurely if someone can beat you on their last turn.

Super fast, super easy, thick tokens and nicely illustrated cards.  This is a great filler for gamers.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Nice concept, but feels unbalanced. It's plays best with 3 people. With 2 it's a bit too simple. You build up your machine that generates gems to buy more gem mines. But once you feel you're engine is really running and you start to pick 1 or 2 level 3 cards, all the royals have visited and the game ends. It's lacking just that one mechanic or layer of depth to make it really interesting. It needs to be a bit more puzzlely. The royals should be a little harder to get i guess. Or need to be more specific vs the general cards. (i.e. 8 black, instead of 3 red/green/blue for instance. So you really have to pick a strategypuzz. 

Great artwork & components though! (But in a too big box)

Update: "Century: Spice road" is the "Splendor game killer" for us that solves the issues I had with this game.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Probably my most played game in my collection. So easy to pull out and surprisingly deep.

I entirely do NOT understand complaints of multiplayer solitaire on this game. All player states are completely visible and very easy to parse at a glance.  You can guess opponent strategy fairly seamlessly and move in to block by reserving something they want or see they will beat you to a card and move toward another one.

The only negative on this game is that giving away your strategies can be so damaging to your play that we find ourselves closely guarding our plans, making this a fairly quiet game of people staring at the table and quietly making their moves.  This type of behavior is NOT multiplayer solitaire, quite the reverse, but I can see that this is not what some are looking for in a game.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Really enjoyed this. Played twice in succession, very fast to play. Really liked the progression and tension in timing of your actions. No direct inter-action but the obvious direction other players go in makes it clear if you can pick a card they were aiming for. So there is indirect play and you need to either keep your options open or try to hide your intentions. The balance of benefits was always interesting too. Nice artwork, although it's strictly an abstract.

+++

Played again today, as a 2p game, lost and then won. Still really enjoyed the game. With fewer chips out, it's still a contest to get the cards you want. There was more direct competition for cards and my opponent got into the 2nd row faster than me. I'm not quite reading the tactics yet, but really enjoying the challenge.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
This game is so simple and lean, I don't understand why I enjoy it so much. I believe I'm most competitive with my wife (she beats me all the time), to the point we played a round at the hospital post delivery of our second child....she won....she deserved it. I often ask people if they would like this game as much as they do without the chips. Pretty much the unanimous answer is "No". Let's be real. Components don't make the game, but they do definitely improve it. The components in this game add so much fun to the game that had this used cardboard chits, I don't think it would have been on my radar. This is a perfect blend of game play & component quality. 

Artwork 4-4
Component Quality 3-3
Variability between games 1-2
Strategy over Luck 2-2
Easy to teach 4-4
Will my wife play it 5-5
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: Huh.  Maybe I should give more credit to the board game popularity awards, 'cause this is actually a really good little game.  This is basically the most stripped-down version of an "economic engine building" game that one could possibly create, yet it works (it works really well, in fact!).  And though it is a simple game, it moves along at a good clip and doesn't overstay its welcome.  The physical components are top notch: besides the obviously satisfying chunky chips, all the cards are lavishly illustrated, helping the players to remember what the completely unimportant theme of the game is.  The game box should have been much smaller, but that's the only real complaint I can drum up.  So I will just say that this is a splendidly fun and clever game, and leave off with that groaner.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: Splendor es un juego que sirve para introducir a personas no jugonas al mundo de los juegos de mesa y particularmente en los engine building, ya que ofrece mecánicas sencillas, una duración de partida moderada (40 min) y la dosis de interacción mínima que requiere un juego de mesa, el problema con Splendor, es que tiene un inicio lento, es decir habrán pasado 2-3 rondas completas y es muy probable que nadie haya comprado una carta o que tenga 0 puntos de victoria acumulados, por lo cual, si no existe un buen clima de partida o buena disposición por parte de los jugadores, estos terminarán aburriéndose. Por mucho cariño que le tenga, ya que gracias a él me introduje en los juegos de mesa, debo decir que es un juego que cumple y me parece bien, pero que hay mejores juegos en su categoría.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: I'm appreciating Splendor more in hindsight.  The game starts at the granular level.  You start picking up chips in different colors, value 1 each, to be used for buying cards.  Cards come out from shuffled decks into a public array, each one a little contract to fulfill -- maybe 3 reds and a white to get a cheap card, but something like 7 blues and 3 blacks to get a card worth 4 or 5 victory points.  Credit alert, though, because even the cheapest cards count as value 1 of a particular color, for unlimited reuse on all further buys!  So you start with the cheapest cards to improve your buying power, but the game is really pretty short so you don't want to wait too long to transition to buying the cards worth VP.  The flow is very smooth and I believe the game will repay repeated play.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Nice little engine-building game. Works also with non-gamers. Love the components! (28.3.2016)

I still like Splendor. With gamers it turns into a thinky and deep game with difficult decisions turn after turn. It rewards skill which has affected negatively my win %. It just shows there's more than meets the eye and room for improvement! I'm eager to try the expansion. (15.9.17)

Splendor is still good times. I own the expansion (got as a gift). It's not necessary by any means. I like the Cities and the Strongholds modules most. Cities alters the winning conditions but keeps the core gameplay same. Strongholds adds nice player interaction: should I block a card opponent might want or reserve one for myself? The other two are fine. I'm always happy to just play the base game. (1.5.2019)

Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
[Space Cowboys 14 edition] {Medieval; set-collection, card-drafting; scalable} Splendor is a very popular family game among my friends.  I am not fond of it; however, my elder daughter likes this game very much. For a 2p game, luck of draw is more significant; esp. when all new cards contains the largest set of a single color of your opponent.

Splendor is indeed a solid game with good player action and meaningful tactical move.  Its abstract nature doesn’t attract me.

It is easy to explain and learn this game.  Tactical moves are obvious.  The mechanic is nice and smooth.

The game is over-produced.  The box his horribly larger than necesssary. I would rather some plastic gems than the plastic tokens even though the tokens are heavy and nice.  The card illustration is so so.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: A well-made product, nice illustrations on the cards, heavy and pleasant to the touch plastic tokens, interesting card selection and scoring mechanics. We set our strategy depending on what is on the card market. At the beginning, the game is slow, but once we expand our table - it gains momentum. To win, at the right time, you need to start collecting higher scoring cards and noble tokens. The game is relatively quick (30-40 minutes) and easy to learn - you can already play with 6-8 year old children, but - as it happens with kids, sometimes it is hard for them to swallow the bitterness of defeat. Advanced players who have already played many titles, after 2-3 games they can start to get bored. A good game when we don't have time for longer titles or as a warm-up before them.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: I really liked the look, feel, gameplay, and elegance of this game. It has a huge amount of replay value and a quick set up and take down for the layers of strategy it offers in what is essentially an elegant and simple card drafting and resource management game. I actually prefer this game over 7 wonders--not that they're incredibly similar but I do like it. That being said, it is fundamentally an abstract game and mistakes you make early can really hold you back throughout but I can see this being incredibly fun between several players who are all seasoned and played multiple times. Luckily, because it's simple and easy to teach and fast, it's quick to get people to become seasoned. Definitely a winner despite being largely abstract which is usually quite a negative for me.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Play splendor once and you're hooked. The container box is ridiculously large, the poker pieces are too heavy to take it with you on holiday, and the rules could be explained more clearly.

But what an amazing game (you'd never expect that from Ravensburger, the logo equivalent to 70's housewives doing 1000 piece puzzles of a yacht scene).

In essence, splendor has a certain Soul, or call it personality, in it, that seems to come alive when you play. After 1 game everyone wants another, and another and so on. There is nothing like it. Great building system, great interaction, stuff to go for that makes a difference...

Play this game with gamers and it becomes very deep. Awesome, a keeper. 

A slight minor is the box size, mostly air, but easily fixed by cutting up the board.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
4 - Could be talked into it on occasion.

This game just doesn't tick any boxes for me. It's not terrible, just not good enough to play it again unless someone asks. 

- No Depth: There are many other games which are interesting even on the 50th play. After playing 20 games of Splendor, the depth of strategy does not expand past 5 or so plays. I've even read strategy articles on this game from tournament winners to see if I was wrong. Nope. 
- No Interaction: It feels like a solo game in the sense that your actions do not affect others to a significant degree. 
- No Theme: The theme is pasted on. It could be about anything.

It's offensively bland. I don't need a game to be strategic, interactive, and thematic, but I need one of those. A game can't just be easy and balanced.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Splendor is a great gateway game. It comes with easy rules, an engine building, and a race to victory. Perfect to introduce new players to the great world of modern boardgames. Also, the components are great, in particular the poker chips which feel so good in hand.

However, the game is just "that". The game doesn't change when you play only with experienced gamers. There is no "hidden" complexity levels. Basically, you'll deny other people the cards they can buy, and you'll deny the gems they need for the cards the took, and that's just a stalemate. Nothing exciting here.

So I wouldn't recommand it for experienced gamer, unless you want to try it once to know what you are talking about. But for new players, hell yeah, it should be in the "10 games to start playing" list.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: Ik vind dit echt een leuk en verslavend spel! De regels zijn simpel, maar toch ben je vanaf moment 1 al tactisch bezig. Hiervoor moet je het spel wel een keertje gespeeld hebben, maar vanaf het eerste moment is duidelijk wat je moet doen. Het duurt even voordat je echt punten kan gaan verzamelen waardoor je het gevoel hebt dat het spel wat langzaam op gang komt. Ook duurt het spel wat langer dan de aangegeven 30 minuten. Ik ben er toch vaak wel 45 minuten mee zoet (en dan speel ik met 3 a 4 personen). Het spel is verder wat aan de prijzige kant in vergelijking met de inhoud. Desalniettemin vind ik dit spel een aanrader voor iedereen die eens een ander spel wil spelen. Ik kende het spel tot voor kort niet, maar heb het inmiddels al een aantal keer met veel plezier gespeeld!
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Laura's Rank (3/15) – 3.5 out of 5. Pros: Super easy to learn. Quick play, which is good in certain situations. Every game is somewhat different based on what cards come out. It is high strategy. Can get exciting towards the end as players are getting close. Cons: Low player interaction. The theme falls flat. It's much more about the mechanic (which is good), so there is not really any theme. Jewels instead of money is good, but not a strong theme at all.

Ryan's Rank (3/15) – 4 out of 5. This is a great filler. Short, a good balance of strategy. Great components. Our last few games where we both understood the strategy well was really fun. Even though I lost, I enjoyed the game and didn't feel like I'd sunk hours into something I was terrible at. I'll bring it out often.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
This has quickly become one of my favourite games and friends are always requesting it on game nights. It plays very smoothly for 2, 3 and 4 players and has a surprisingly amount of depth for a game that is very easy to teach new players. I love it for it's easy learning curve because I can use it as a gateway game but it still retains depth and challenge even after dozens of games. My group routinely plays 3 or 4 games of Splendor in a row before moving to another game. It's very well balanced and it's rare that any one player has a runaway victory.

If there is one criticism, the box is way to big for the size of the components, but I just put all the components in an Ultra Pro deck box and it travels amazingly well, I take this to the park all the time in the summer.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
enjoyable light "filler"-kind game, part engine building and part scoring-race; to me it is very similar to the recent Builders:Middle-Age that offers the same feel, same difficulty level/decision ratio, same playing time in a MUCH smaller box and more attractive theme (that feels less pasted on).

[+] very nice components and box insert, fast paced & short game with a good amount of decisions to make, easy to teach, not easy to master (you have to get the timing right of when to stop building an engine and start scoring)
[-] theme or no theme, that is the question... abrupt end game (Builders:Midddle-Age has that as well), seems weird that the "cost" of similar cards can be very different (a level 1 card with no point value costs between 3 and 5-6 gems, why?)
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
A nice game that plays quickly and easily and flows nicely with mellow decision-making that nicely focuses your attention on wanting certain cards.  I can see it's appeal and accessibility, and it does have noteworthy art and nice chips.  

On the other hand, it seems to me to be wholly lacking in theme which really diminishes my desire to play it again, and for me, it lacks particularly compelling, interesting or original mechanics.  Bottom line:  there is a pleasing, mellow, short sweetness to Splendor, but it doesn't grab my heart or desire much. 

June 2014:  7 of 10.

Playing this game for a fourth time, I simply have no desire to play this simplistic, borderline annoying, theme-free game ever again, so going to have to drop my rating to a 5.  March 2018.
Title: Splendor

Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: It is a great game, well polished, great components (e.g., the heavy chips) with a good length (short enough) and good replayability.  Easy to teach, I can see this as a good introductory and gateway game.  I am not a fan of purely abstract games and therefore will not prefer it over other choices, but for what it is, it is excellent.  Also, it is somewhat MPS but has enough interaction, especially for a Euro.  Players tend to focus on their own tableaus but the tableaus are simple enough that after a while you pay attention to the drafting and denials and interact with other players.  One of the games that is good to have in one's collection, it fills a good niche and sometimes it is just the game you want to bring out.  Sustains repeated back to back plays.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Simple to teach, simple to play but with a decent amount of strategy. I like the engine building aspect of the game coupled with the set collection mechanic and there is something about making the decision of when to start going for the more expensive cards over the freebies in the mid to late game that I enjoy. Wait too long and it's too late. Go too early and you'll struggle to buy the more expensive cards. The ability to reserve cards is a nice touch though. 

The game doesn't outstay its welcome which a huge selling point but the size of the box is a big negative as it makes it very unfriendly for travel. I ended up making my own custom box for it which while not as pretty as the actual box it's now at least far more portable.

Joe and Phil also own this.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Splendor is a set collection game where players collect gems and exchange them for resources that subsequently grant the player permanently available gems that count towards the exchange requirements of additional resources.  As a player accumulates permanent resources, he or she can better afford new, more valuable resources.  This mechanism results in a thrilling snowball effect.  

I've found that I pay very little attention to my opponents progress, so I wish that the game encouraged a bit more player interaction.  Otherwise, Splendor is an simple and enjoyable "filler" game.  The components are top notch. 

Rating: 6.7 (Fun 6; Gameplay 6; Components 10; Theme 5)

Formula:
[Weighted rating = (((Fun*4) + (Gameplay*3) + (Components *2) + (Theme *1))/10)]

Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: Management of five different currencies on two levels. There's a variable form of currency with limited total quantity for you to have and you use this form to generate the permanent form of currency that isn't spent when you use it. The latter form also contains the main bunch of your points. You have to have an engine in the permanent form of currency to do well, but while building your engine you shouldn't forget making points by acquiring more expensive and harder to get pieces of the permanent currency. There's also some neat outguessing and very nice components included. After several plays I've formed a stern opinion that if you focus on blue, white and big buildings and forget red, green, engine building and nobles you're likely going to do well.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Very, very simple rules, makes this an excellent gateway game and for the more experienced gamer it has some good depth. Lotsa of fun!

This has easily been my most successful gateway game.:

I have one co-worker who played it, loved it. Bought it and then back in North Dakota, he played it with two other friends who subsequently bought it.
I played this with our marketing guy who doesn't particularly care for board games and he's told me twice how much he's liked it, as well as the salesman who really enjoyed it, too.
My brother-in-law and his wife (and my in-laws are NOT board gamers) played it and ended up buying it.

I've never had this kind of response to a game, and to me, this is more of a filler game, but people really just seem to grab on to it!
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
The simplest possible engine-builder. Get gems, spend them for discounts on gems (some of which come with points). There's a reasonable amount of jockeying for in-demand gem colors, blocking in the form of reservation capability (which also gives wild gems that can ease pressure on particular colors). All of this is added to the conventional switching problem -at what point do I shift from infrastructure to points?

I appreciate simplicity, so this game is right in my wheelhouse, but I'm not sure the game is mean enough for me. Blocking can be more costly for you than for your opponents, as the gems they build up can be used to get alternate infrastructure/points. While this doesn't fit my tastes, it works well with newer or more conflict-averse players
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
A solid little set collection/engine building game. Nothing super special here and the theme is pasted on despite the good artwork, but very clean execution. Works pretty well as a family/gateway game. 

Besides chaining your cards to spend the fewest gems as possible, there is strategy in prioritizing colors that are required for a lot of  goals, hoarding gems until a card everyone shows up, and tactics of reserving cards you want and taking gems that are low in quantity. 

The cons of this game is the engine building snowballs easily, which can create runaway leader if someone just plays super poorly, and there isn't a good way to mill for cards you want, so sometimes you will have e.g. 4 cards completed with diamond bonuses but nothing to use it on.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
I absolutely love this game. Easy to teach, accessible to those new to gaming and still interesting for more experienced gamers. 

The theme is completely irrelevant, and it's rather like an abstract strategy card game. Not a game that is high in interaction, and can feel a bit like multi-player solitaire with players that don't actively work to thwart each other. Which makes this a really great game for me to play with my kids when I want a more focused and (somewhat) quiet experience. 

I think this is a really great family game to include even very young players. The game play is not at all complicated, so a 4 yr old could play this easily. My 6 yr old says this is one of her favourite games, and she definitely holds her own against the rest of us.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: Let me be clear: there's nothing wrong with Splendor. It works, it's fine, it does a thing. But that's as far as it goes, or even seems to aim for. It's another item on the list of recent games that seem to be happy eliciting a response of, "Yep, that's a game, all right." We played two games in pretty much silence, doing the things you do in the game until someone won. Occasionally someone called someone else a jerk for taking a card the former person wanted. There's nothing here aggressively bad enough to make one dislike it, nor captivating enough to demand further play. It seems designed specifically to sit on a shelf as part of a "collection". If it wins the prize it's up for, that will be the only way anyone will be thinking about it next year.
Title: Splendor

Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
The best board game ever. Easy to learn yet difficult to master. It won 2014 Golden Geek Awards for a reason.

PROS:
- Easy to learn

- Veterans can still lose to beginners due to randomness of cards especially >3 players

- Fun for 2-4 people

- Merit game time, usually around 20-35 minutes depending on number of players

- Can be highly addictive after playing a few rounds (maybe a CON)

CONS:
- 15 points to win, concentrating on Nobles (the special cards at the top) can be pointless

- 4 players max

- Lacks starting person indicator/token (the expansion has a blue token)

- No game board or mat considering the massive box but small contents inside

Overall: A splendid board game without having to memorize complex rules or instructions. Must buy.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
One of the best introduction games to board gaming. I have taught this to my parents, my siblings, their kids, tons of friends. It no one's favorite game but not a single person dislikes it. It is so easy to pick up on the rules and so enjoyable to build your engine.
This game deserves the awards it's won and probably more. I have played the base game dozens of times. I own the cities of splendor expansion and would like to say that combing some of the expansions together breaks the game and leads to extremely fast wins. But individually each expansion is enjoyable, strongholds being my least favorite, and the orient being my most played.
Each expansion is simple to learn and adds to your potential strategy. Will always keep this in my collection.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
I only played this game once, but it was not fun at all. My biggest gripe with the game is the limited resources. It's not inherently bad, but i ended up unintentionally holding onto a color that another player needed. I had picked it up earlier in the game and it just sat in front of me, never being used and i never had any intentions of using it. It ended up costing the other person a lot of points. Yes, i can see how this is a strategy that could be used. But, IMO that is not good game design. I essentially made that person lose and there was nothing they could have done to get the color.

If you enjoy this game, that is fine, i can understand, but overall, it was boring, and the accidental resource shortage possibilities just turned me off.
Title: Splendor

Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Honestly not too sure where all of hour hype is coming from.  It's a fine game, but a bit of a mindless point race.  It's nice for being just that, but nothing hat I would get excited about.

Jaipur feels like a very similar game, perhaps a little more luck based, but also has more depth of strategy having to weigh your odds and manipulate your opponent.  Splendor is simply making efficient choices and hoping it pans out better than your opponents'.

After several more plays, I'm warming up to it a bit more, there is a bit more strategy than I originally thought, but still nothing too exciting.  The excitement really just comes from hoping the other person doesn't buy what you're after first, or the right card is flipped at the right time.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Fantastic game when its all new and shiny and players are having a ball learning how to  best build a winning strategy against one another. Loved it, gave it an 8 rating.

As time wore on my play group has gotten more savvy at the game and honestly, the game has lost all it's shine. Now the games are almost completely quiet, tense, concentration fests. Nerves are on edge and when some players lose they take it kinda hard. What a bummer. I still like the game but I have to rate it a 6.5 now, not willing to play it so much anymore.

Now to be fair, not all play groups will have the same experience as mine, just saying, be warned if you have even semi-competitive people in your groups, this game can start to be a bit of a downer after awhile.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: I feel like there are other games similar to this that have come out since that are better such as Century: Spice Road/Golem but this definitely paved the way for those games. I'm not a big fan of the theme but there are other versions out there to fix that. It's very easy to understand and there are multiple strategies you can use to win. I have won both from quickly acquiring cards to make buying free and also from going to the high point cards early on and getting enough points to win before anyone is able to build up enough. I was very surprised when my grandpa really enjoyed this game. I think that is a good indicator that this is a pretty good game for those who aren't too familiar with board games and you want to get them eased in.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
An accessible engine building game that will appeal to families/casual gamers.  Despite the simplicity, there is some thought and planning involved and there is room for screwage for those who choose to play that way.  Since the SdJ has become geared towards family styles games, this is a perfect fit for the award even though the award went to another title.

UPDATE:  After many plays on BGA, it becomes obvious that this game has some teeth.  The skill ceiling is higher than many give it credit for and it seems to be a near perfect game for organized tournament play.  
But to continue to live on this level, I would suggest adding the orient cards as it balances engine building a little better against the high tier/vertical strategy.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Absolute classic and one of the best gateway games. Everybody loves it. Best at 3 players and best if played fast. Too much of thinking ruins this one. Perfect with kids after a long tiring day.

BTW: Splendor: Marvel is a nice variety. Maybe even better than the original. Hard to say. Marvel is fun but the original is more charming with the nobles. Theme is in both ways very generic, though. So you can be a Marvel fan and still like the original Splendor more because your heroes and villains do not matter, it's just the numbers.

The rule changes in Splendor: Marvel offer some possibilities for "thrilling" the end game but the simplicity of the original actually leads more players to deeper tactics. I am happy owning both games.
Title: Splendor

The components (including the insert) are fantastic, the gameplay is smooth and the playtime is short (30 minutes or so with 2), but it just feels sort of dry. Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Good little resource-management game. Quick-playing and easy to learn. I found it surprisingly tactical for a game that relies heavily on random card flips. The card-reserve mechanic adds a nice bit of tension to the overall game, and makes every turn a tough decisions since you can do it at any time (barring the 3-card hand limit). I recommend this game for families, and groups interested in a light-weight, fast-playing game that looks good and teaches easy.


The tension in game play surfaces after only a few plays. Get through the first two and you'll discover a delightful game. However, my gut tells me it will start to feel a it samey after a dozen or so plays; maybe less. I'll update after a few more plays (currently at 4).
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Played it for the first time tonight.  Played 3 rounds.  Definitely fun.  Has a bit of a slow start and frustration when you're blocked from getting cards you want at the start and everyone's grabbing resources, but once things slowly unfold and the gem stock is replenished it starts to flow better.

I can see this not being a game I'd want to play with people who suffer from Analysis Paralysis.  I think it might lower in rank slightly (maybe to 8.6 or 8.4)after more plays, but for now it's fun. :)

* Played many times since then; I have expansions but never played with. Nobody seems to want to play with them, they enjoy the regular enough.  I think it's a great "feels light and filler" but still more meaty.  Not overly comlpex.

Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
It's interesting, but individual groups seem to go through the same few patterns with this. Everyone starts out with a basic engine-building strategy. Eventually, players figure out they can get an edge on the engine-builders if they go for a high-tier strategy. Other players figure out they can easily derail the high-tier strategists by hoarding the gems they need. And you end up with a well-balanced game with multiple winning approaches... at which point, the game is mostly determined by the random order that the cards turn up in. Well, that's disappointing. This started as an easy favorite, but unfortunately it just bores me at this point.
