Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Quick to teach and play. A shallow game, but quite fun. Best family game of 2014. My middle daughter is a WBC Juniors champ. :)

UPDATE: I guess the "degenerate" strategy of only going after high-value cards does hurt the game. The designers surely meant this to be an engine-building race game. I'm rather good at the degenerate strategy. But I recognize that it kills the fun of those around me (particularly the fun of some of my kids, who initially really loved the game!) and so that is sad. :(

I wonder if there is a clever way to nerf this approach without harming what is a brilliant design. I don't know that even making the Nobles worth 6 points instead of 3 would make a big difference in many of the games I'm in lately!
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
I played this game with Liz and some other guy whose name I forget. It was pretty much a Euro, by which I mean exactly like a Euro, by which I mean you're just taking turns doing a solitaire kinda sorta math problem thingie about nothing in particular and then counting up points.

What is the deal with "engine building?" If this game were a car, it would be [i]just[/i] an engine, sitting by the curb, humming along efficiently under the admiring stares of the unsmiling. An AmeriTrasher would walk up and ask, "What does it do?" And the admirers would just shrug and say, "But look how it hums!"

I'd like to say that at this point--finally--something explodes. But it's not that kind of game.

But hey, two points for Liz.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
It's not... bad. But it's so simple that you can get the same kicks from nearly any other decent Euro game that involves trade-offs or planning of any kind. Somebody who didn't like learning new games but enjoyed that type of thinking might want to pick this up and play it 100 times. But somebody who likes learning new games doesn't have too much reason to play this even 5 times.

Update 2022: I like this even less the more I play it. The mental busywork of remembering a bunch of meaningless costs... do I need two red and four blue or two red and four green, or was it three green? And a black?... hasn't gotten easier with more plays. It's not even easier when playing online with a computer to help. I'm tired.

[31 plays]
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: With new games, I don't normally play them four times (kinda sad) in the first month that I own them, but Splendor has that quality that makes you want to play it again and again. There's not too much to this game: you get chips to buy cards which make it easier to buy other cards which eventually have points and having certain configurations of cards allows you to get more points. It's an efficiency engine much like St. Petersburg. However, this one is a lot more interesting for some reason, nice poker chips maybe?. Another benefit to the game is that it plays in about 30 to 45 minutes with all of the player counts and that time will get much faster with repeat plays. I'm looking forward to playing this one a lot more.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
A resource management game with a surprising richness for how simple the components are. The directions seem complicated at first blush, but there are very few mechanics to teach. It sets up and learns quickly.

I find that this game is a quiet experience. It can be tense, especially if you defensively take a card or a token when you catch on to someone else's strategy, but I generally find that Splendor plays are lower key. A good one for a game night with lower attendance numbers, and/or a mellower crowd.

I like to start typical game nights with the louder, more interactive games, but games like this are good for near the end of the night, when the potluck table is picked over and food comas are beginning to set in.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
A design that epitomizes elegance.  A modicum of rules easily explained in a few minutes, yielding quite a bit of depth for a game that can be played in half an hour.  Set up and break down is also a breeze.  I think this is one of the best gateway games to come out since Ticket to Ride, but one I usually enjoy playing more.  I've had a lot of success introducing it to non-gamers.  Not for everyone, as it is a bit dry and the theme is clearly pasted on.  I call it a "chin stroker" since I find the game lends itself more to silent pondering than to table talk.  Also, can start to feel a bit samey after many plays, but I'm closing in on 50 plays and have yet to tire of it.

approximate number of plays (pre-2017):  50+
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Very quick and light set collection "engine building" game.
It's the king of gateway game, probably the lighter I have in my collection. I think it miss a bit of player interaction, this probably come with a future expansion but anyway it's a fun game to play and it's an excellent one to introduce new player to the hobby.

Un "set collecting / engine building" très léger et vraiment rapide. C'est le roi des jeux d'introduction. Probablement le jeu le plus léger que je possède. Je pense qu'il manque un peu d'intéraction entre les joueurs, ça viendra surement avec une extension future mais c'est quand même un excellent jeu, amusant et c'est un excellent choix pour introduire des nouveaux joueurs dans le passe-temps.
Title: Splendor

Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
I bought this one as something simple to play with my family but it delivered beyond what I expected. This game is so easy to teach but still gives you a bit of the same feeling of building an engine that you get in much meatier games.  Turns go fast and the games are short while still giving you several turns at the end when you feel your engine running at full capacity.  The game is also more interactive than it gets credit for as a well-times reservation can really hurt someone's progress.  

Although this is not something that I really seek out playing all that much anymore it remains one of the best games that I've found for playing with kids and other family members who aren't up for a heavy strategy game.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
It says the game is meant for up to 4 players, but I've played with 5 players and it was pretty interesting! One game played pretty straightforward with 5, and one played very intense. It was a nice change of pace to see two very different games with an extra player. We didn't add any additional tokens or anything, just played with 6 nobles. 

Note for 5 players: Towards the end of the game it did seem like the cards players wanted were constantly being purchased by other players due to less development cards in the field, but if you're okay with a little competition for said cards, then it should be okay! One game we played ended this way, and another ended more laid back. It really just depends on the game.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
I've never seen a game draw people in so easily as Splendor does.  Easy-to-learn, fast-paced, with plenty of tension and well made components.  It reminds me a lot of St. Petersburg, with a lot of the administration (i.e. boring) parts removed.  I personally preferred this over Camel Up to win the 2014 Spiel Des Jahres.  

I thought I'd tire of playing it after a few times.  That hasn't happened.  

At least in four player games, there does appear to be a dominant strategy: reserve and/or buy up only the single color cards in the second and third rows (i.e. the cards that require 5, 6, or 7 of only one color).  With some clever hand management, this strategy seems to win a disproportionate number of games.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Very fun game for anyone to play. Good at 3 or 4 players, but I do not recommend it at 2 players. I've found that there is a strong advantage going to the first player with options to block resources or cards the other player needs. This maybe can be said at higher player counts to a degree, but at 2 players, the first player has more control on the flow of the game. Was a 9, now I'd say an 8 based on the game at 2 player count.

Update:
I'm not excited to play this game unless I use it as a family or gateway game. I enjoy playing this with younger family members. I like that the game is quick, but playing against poker players showed me that generally, the first player has an advantage in a 2 player game.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
this confirms the low esteem i often have for SdJ.
It's not bad because it has a good rhytm and plays fast... and yet... and yet it's an exercise in resources conversion. I'd use it as a gateway game but then leave it in a corner. 
Components, as everyone say, are quite good.
The theme is completely inexistent and in this case it is felt too much.
It is also quite slow at the beginning and it takes quite a long time to start "running". I can't find a lot of interesting decisions to make.

[Edit]: after my second game (that i lost badly) i want to raise the vote of this a bit. Its fast pace and the different ways you can set up your own game make it a fun light game after all and i'll play it again gladly.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: Super fast, super simple, super fun.  Very pure engine-builder game.  Clean quick rules and moves with a constant flow of strategy and thinking ahead.  Stockpile resources for long haul purchasing of big points or hit mid range point/resource combos?  Maybe you use turns to block an opponents future purchase or to hide your own future purchase for yourself.  Play is very fast and games are right in the sweet spot of time.  You might have a plan laid out for a purchase down the road, but every other players plans can make your big idea vanish before it gets to your turn.  Gotta plan ahead but be malleable and making moves in the moment.  Anybody can pick it up and be playing in 5 minutes.  Very, very good.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Edit: Went up from a 7 to an 8.

At first I was afraid that the game gets dull after a couple of plays, but that has not been the case. The games are short enough (only played it 2 players) and the ever changing tableau forces you to adapt your strategy from game to game. The last game played for example, required a lot of white gems, but the tableau did not provide any white gems until two thirds into the game. It was very interesting to see how both players reacted to that situation.

Edit: played it 8 more times. Still enjoy every game. I attribute this to the fact, that the game is a well designed abstract. You love them or you hate them, but they never get old (feel the same about Hive and Qwirkle)
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: Nettes Spiel, das vorallem durch seine einfachen und schnellerklärten Regeln besticht. Dabei fühlt sich Splendor sehr belohnend an- das liegt vorallem daran, dass die Züge locker von der Hand gehen und man im Late-Game beinahe jede Runde eine Karte kaufen kann. Mein erstes Problem: das Spiel ist brutal langweilig, da man auch einfach nicht wirklich interagieren oder sprechen muss. Das wird mit der tollen Erweiterung zumindest so weit ausgemerzt, als dass der Spielflow und die Entscheidungen etwas spannender werden. Mein zweites Problem: wenn ich das Spiel mit irgendwelchen Spackos spiele, die jeden Zug totdenken, macht mir das Spiel einfach keinen Spaß. Leider lädt das Spiel aber gneau dazu ein. Schade!
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: Splendor isn't a game that I knew anything about specifically, other than that it was a light, quick game that "didn't really do much new". And that's all true. But I like this game. You take chips to buy gems which give you discounts on other gems, and eventually you buy gems that are actually worth something and/or attract some person of note who is also worth something. The game is fairly simple, but requires a constant evaluation of what's important and what people are trying to do. You've got to think about what's going on a good bit. It's a lot of thinky in a very small package and it's quick. And despite being thinky, it's a game my family could play and enjoy. That's a fairly rare combination.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: I've gotten a ton of mileage out of this game. The rules are extremely simple/elegant, and it appeals to almost anyone I've introduced it to. Having said that, most people I've played with have quickly caught on to the fact that the level 1 cards are almost completely useless, and going for extra points via a visit from the nobles is rarely a good strategy. I've tried to experiment with alternate strategies but online discussion generally seems to confirm these observations. For me, this kind of taints the game a bit. I think a few balance changes could pave the way for more strategic options and creativity, but as it stands, experienced players mostly just all end up doing the same thing every game.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Easy to learn engine building game, with a optimization puzzle at later depths. But as boring and dry as sand.

It might as well be an abstract game between it's lack of theme and tight mechanics.

Owned digitally: iOS

2022: tried it again on BGA and I still don't enjoy it, the optimization puzzle does not feel fun to me, it feels like I'm trying to race a group to solve a math equation. I also don't like how everyone has access to pretty much the same moveset, where the only asymmetry in the game is the cards you've previously bought for your engine. I also don't like how scoring points and engine building are essentially the same mechanically instead of having scoring be a separate game mechanic.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: Played A LOT.  The students that play board games after school love this game.  I even had on student who read a big ol' pile of books to get a copy with her AR points.  A game is already going and you showed up late?  Sure I'll play a game.  It reminds me of solitaire a bit, but there is definitely interaction (let me buy that card!).  I get that the theme is pasted on, but the components feel nice and look beautiful.  It is also a nice iOS ap to boot.  I only wish the box was a bit smaller.  I have reboxed many games in tiny boxes for shelf space, but I can't bring myself to take it apart.... yet.  I think this is still a great game... but I am tired of it.  My students play the mess out it still.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Very nice. light strategy game that your entire family could play, while not boring you and them at the slightest.  
There are 2 main problems for me.
The first is that it might make players feel stupid in the first couple of times the play, and make them angry and unwilling to play (in my gaming group, this was me)  but that is a problem shared by every strategy game to an extent, and in Splendor, it is not as apparent. 
My second problem is that many times it can feel like the game fucks you over once you are skilled enough, as it strikes an equal balance between strategy and luck. My dad should have won much more than he did.
Still a very solid game and a good entryway to strategic board games.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Can't say enough about this game--though ironically, there also isn't much to say. Its amazingly simple but has plenty of turn-by-turn strategy. Best part of this game is its appeal to a wide audience and how easy it is to teach. I've introduced it to 60+ people at all sorts of events... I can't recall a single negative experience!
Oh, and it's also fast (like 20-30min), no matter who you're playing with. Many of my games can vary significantly in length depending on the players. I greatly appreciate the conciseness of this game.
Overall, I'm shocked it doesn't have a higher rating. I think this fills another perfect slot in my game collection, especially when considering the average time to play.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
классные тяжёлые фишки камней с металлическими вставками. красочное оформление (хоть и отдаёт цыганским шиком на мой вкус). сама игра простая, по ощущениям напомнила Ticket to Ride: тоже собираешь цветные сеты, чтобы потом ими расплатиться за карты. карты же сами по себе "производят" (или дают скидку на) один цветной элемент. в итоге ты довольно быстро выстраиваешь свою микроимперию цвета, которая потом сама бесплатно снабжает тебя картами. 

очень много зависит от того, какая карта придёт следующей из стопки на стол. часто бывает, покупаешь что-то не очень оптимальное, на его место приходит суперкласс, и противник разумеется тут же его покупает себе (после чего снова выходит какая-то вялость).
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: Get rich or die getting slightly less rich!  I think Splendor's mechanics are top notch - letting your opponent take a few turns saving up chips for a card and then nabbing the card under their nose is a great feeling.  There's also enough randomness to make it possible to recover from a few bad investments - squirreling away mines for a gem that isn't well represented NOW might come in handy later when that gem is in high demand.  The theme of the game is pretty thin, which is a complaint that Asmodee seems to have addressed in the app version.  It would also be nice to have variable player powers.  I think its a solid chip collecting/card collecting game.  An imperfect gem that still shines.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Call me blasphemous, but I don't really find it a ton of fun. I like that it's quick, and it's a solid design. But I really dislike the utter dearth of interaction among players. It's 20 - 30 minutes of silently building an engine to pursue your strategy, slightly tweaking plans if someone grabs what you want. Diehards will say I'm playing it wrong probably...

[i]Edit[/i]: Okay, okay, I recently played a couple rounds of this that were actually a lot of fun. Much more interactive than before, due to how we played. So I'm starting to think the lack on interaction in the other rounds I played was more of a player problem and not a game design aspect. I'm coming around on this one a little...
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Splendor... how frustrating you are.

We borrowed this for a week and managed to play 3 games a day. For the first day, maybe two, I quite liked it. Slowly building up your gems so you can get better cards, strategically reserving certain cards at the right time, all stuff I usually like.

Then one of us read a guide on BGG and found out the best way to win was to reserve a high-value card, then just build up chips for it. I would like to say that we were able to block whoever tried to do this but sadly that strategy won every single time.

By the end of the week I'd had enough. I'll never play it again unless there's literally nothing else to play - there's nothing to bring me back to it.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Splendor is a game that has grown on me. My initial impressions weren't great as I wondered what was so novel about its engine building that seemed to end before it could begin to really allow powerful moves. The more I played it, the more I found that it is about building the leanest engine possible, not the most powerful.

It has some issues - namely in the randomness department, especially with more than two players. The trade-off is that is makes a great gateway game as it is simple to explain and gives even first-timers an outside shot of winning.

After some consideration, it's earned a spot in my collection thanks to its simplicity and intricate challenge even for veteran players.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: Review – Splendor is a really solid game. It excels as a gateway game and a filler game, but lacks some variety and depth. I’d certainly recommend it to anyone as a good all-around game, but feel it falls just a little short of the longevity needed to be a great game. With the limited setup and shallow learning curve it works well in most settings. One of its best qualities is its consistency, when you get into a game of Splendor you really know what you’re getting into and rarely have to worry about lulls (aside from potential analysis paralysis) or huge point differentials. It’s a very solid game, but really just doesn’t offer quite enough variety to really shine (don’t mind the pun!).
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
This is our top-ranked welcoming game for those new to the hobby.  It's a relatively simple engine-building and set collection game.  New players can quickly understand how to play, while existing players will still need to be thoughtful about their own strategy.  Adding more players means more cards and/or chips are taken between turns.  This has the effect of making the game feel more tactical than strategic at higher player counts, though it is still enjoyable.  It's still a fun--and more importantly, fast--play at two players.

I will say that I think that Marvel Splendor is a better game.  The few small tweaks in its rules actually make it much more interesting and entertaining.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
This is AMAZING.  It's been years since I've been so excited about a game.  It teaches in two minutes, it plays quickly and smoothly, it's interactive without being vicious, and there are multiple paths to victory.  It's elegant, has good quality components, etc etc etc.  It's just really, really fun to play.

It seems odd that I would like this game as much as I do-- my typical top-10 fare are long civilization or development games (Agricola, Clash of Cultures, Mage Knight).  But this simple little "gem" might be better than the lot.

(Update) After a while with this game, lack of theme is stopping me from coming back with the same enthusiasm, though I would never turn down a game.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: I liked it but I am not sure I would ever love this. It has some things going I am often drawn to in games: not too long, easy to learn and pick up, on the downside I don't think it offers so much hidden depth as some of these "easy" games can do. It was fun but stayed a bit too much on the surface for me. A plus point is though that you can put this literally in front of anybody and they will likely have a decent time with it: gamers will enjoy it as a filler, the rest of the family will also have fun since it is a simple yet fun experience; we just played it with a 6-year old on the team who did just fine. Like it enough to be happy to play, not enough love to consider owning it.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
It is a good game to introduce people to the hobby. Usually our to-go game for this. Easy to play, since the card order of reveal is random, it allows to try different strategies and not have a only clear winning strategy.
Personally I find the game to be a 7-7,5. I give it 8 because it created a system reimplemented later by many other games, so it deserve the credit and the quality of the components is very good.
The box size is puzzling since it is just a deck of cards and about 30 chips. But I advise to get the expansions that add some variety and make it a definite 8, and with a 3rd party box insert it can be fitted all in the original box (or expansion one if you prefer it).
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Splendor is a beautiful game of engine building. The two-currencies system makes it very strategical, and it is always a great fun playing it.  It plays pretty fast, around 20-30 minutes. IDuring this time both you and your opponent/s will stare at the cards on the table, not even realising the time passes.

Most of the reviewers find that the theme tie is too weal. To me, the theme is enough to keep you focused on the logic. Enough, not a bit more not a bit less.

In my experience, the game is really immersive.

The best set up is - by far - with 2 players. To me, Splendor is a 2-players strategical game that can be played in multiplayer, resulting  in a much looser experience.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: Absolutely excellent game. So glad I purchased this. Me and the husband have decided to get into board games to remove ourselves away from our phones and internet devices and have quality time. We have tried a few 2 Player games and this ranks as one of our top faves along with Jaipur,Ticket to Ride Europe, Fungi and The Good Life. Really fun strategy game. Good playability. Simple to understand but strategic. Lots of "how to play" videos on YouTube if needed. After a couple of practice games you soon pick it up. Certainly worth the money. We also as 2 players let ourselves score to 40 and we don't use the noble cards so the game length extend. Buy it you won't be disappointed.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
What a truly enjoyable game this is. 
Rules are very simple to learn (approx. 5-10 min) and game is also easy to play. 
I have played this game now numerous times with my young daughter of 8 years and although I believe her to be smart she has learned this game (10+ years) in no time and really likes it as well.
Also my wife who normally dislikes playing boardgames can appreciate this one and even manages to win some times.

On the other hand, the game is not that easy to master. It takes skill to plan ahead, make the right decisions in buying cards or taking gems and on a higher level to decide when to start gathering points or to reserve a card.

Splendor is a gem of a game!
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
When someone says "here's a new collect resources to buy points game!" I die a little inside and either find an excuse and leave or resign myself to a hour or two of tedium as it seems I've been playing variations on this well-worn theme for 20 years now.

However, against expectations this one felt fresh and fun. 

We may have read something wrong, but 15 points seemed a low total to play to - none of us got anywhere near taking the bonus tiles. It certainly didn't outstay its welcome (which was good, as I find the long resource/points optimisers particularly tedious), indeed it felt like it finished just as we were starting the midgame.

Simple rules, and good looking too.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
An elegant, quick, and simple game that is easy to teach and learn. But, there is also a lot of strategy and depth to the game despite how easy it is. It's a game that is easy to introduce to non-gamers, and everyone will have a good time.

I like how well everything in the game works. Going for a few big point cards, or going for lots of smaller cards to build a stronger engine. Playing for the nobles. Denying cards and/or gems from other players. It all just works so well. 

The game scales excellently from 2-4 players. It's a great game to have - it can be a little bland which means it doesn't get to the table as often as it should, but when it does I'm never disappointed.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
I have a weird opinion about Splendor: I enjoy playing it, but will basically never suggest it.  It's such a pure engine-building game that when it goes off the rails I feel like there's nothing I can do to stop it, which can make the act of playing it feel very frustrating.  I respect the hell out of it, but I'm not always in the mood for that purity of design.

The randomness of the rows can also sometimes be a huge detriment, in that they stymie reasonable attempts to build towards nobles, and punish players who actually attempt to clear cards from the rows. I like to call this the "Ascension" design flaw, and it's weird to see it in what is otherwise such a tight design.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Bokkensprong 17/10/14, met Roy. Kort, vlot spelletje met vrij eenvoudige regels. Doel: 15 punten halen door voldoende kaarten te kopen (sommige zijn punten waard, andere niet). Kaarten worden betaald met edelstenen, meer gekochte kaarten zijn ook edelstenen waard. Per beurt kies je één van vier mogelijke acties: 1) drie verschillende kleuren (edelstenen op pokerfiches) nemen; 2) twee edelstenen van dezelfde kleur nemen (mag enkel als er daarvan vier beschikbaar zijn); 3) een kaart reserveren (je neemt ze op hand en krijgt een gele jokerfiche erbij); 4) een kaart kopen. Best leuk, maar de te volgen strategie is niet zo helder de eerste keer.

6/12/14 gekregen van Sinterklaas!
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: This is one of the most well thought out games to be produced in some time. Sure, it isn't mind-blowingly complex or thought=provoking. You collect resources via some poker-style chips and use them to purchase cards from a central display. Those cards add to a permanent set of resources you control that aid in purchasing more expensive cards from the central display again. It is simple but brings out a complex game that moves along at a steady pace and never wears out its welcome. This game should win the Spiel award it has been nominated for. We don't think there is another game out there that plays as smooth and as seamlessly as this one but still brings out so much fun.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
After my first couple of plays, I knew I wanted to own this game.  So far, it remains a game I will happily play any time.  It's not the main course of a game night, but it's certainly good enough to get the night started or to wrap it up.  On its own, it's a game that hits on an average evening where we just want to relax and play a short, fun game.

Now that I've had this one for about a year, I've begun to wonder if I really like it or not.  I don't carry it to game nights anymore, and I don't pull it out unless requested.

About the only way I enjoy it anymore is with 2 players.  I may enjoy it with 3.  It's merely an exercise in sweat management and frustration with 4.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: Simple and very engaging. Great components - heavy tokens. This game gives me a lot of satisfaction and sort of a thrill even if I loose at the end. I enjoy the process of planning, buying, reacting to other player's actions. My wife is also a huge fan of this game since the first play. The only con IMO is the style of the art, I think it could be a bit better, less sketchy with more class, but that seems to be a problem of many board games. Fotunately it changes for better nowadays with the bar set high by newer games. In case of Splendor, the mechanics are so clever and low-key, that it does not really matter. But I would give it a higher rating if it looked a bit better.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: Splendor has already been praised and dragged through the mud by enough people so I'll spare anyone reading this the pain of doing it again. It's a fine design, but one that ultimately lacks moments of inspiration or satisfaction. You just go along and take the next fairly obvious action until someone wins. The production is good, although the box could easily be a quarter of the size without issue. I tend to get in trouble fidgeting with the chips, clinking them together until the others playing yell at me to stop. The game definitely has a classic feel, but I think the theme and dry experience will ultimately keep this out of the tier of games like Catan or Carcassonne.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: Some games swoop in and become our dominant games for a while. We've played this so many times and with a lot of different people. The components are so satisfyingly solid! The fun artwork and components seem to draw in new gamers. The decisions are pretty straightforward, enough so that most people we've played the game with end up really enjoying it. My wife and I have had some fun battles in the 2 player version of the game. So, even more experienced players can squeeze good strategic value out of it. At the end of the day, without expansions, the replay value has capped out for us and we are far less likely to play Splendor vs other two player games in our collection.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
+ promo Noble tiles

Rating based on 2-4 players, but mostly 2.

Simple to teach and play, but there's a fair amount of depth to it for its length (which is nice and snappy). A good blend between making plans based on the high value cards and nobles available, but having to change those plans quickly depending on what cards are drawn.

Scales well between 2-4 players, but how you play the game will change dramatically depending on player count. I tend to use this as an introductory game.

Expansion comments: I've only played the module with the cities, but I think it's a nice addition to the base game. If I owned that expansion, I'd probably play with it most of the time.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
:d10-3:
Splendor had been off my radar for some time, as it didn't seem to offer anything of interest to me personally. After playing, I can see the appeal.

The resource system feels a bit like Magic's mana system, which makes you feel smart for proper sequencing. The economic snowball makes you feel like you are continually improving, even if other players are improving more efficiently. The character tiles give you a long-term goal to pursue, which provides an ever-so-subtle element of coopetition in the early-to-mid game.

That said, the decisions were not interesting enough for me to want to play again. If I did, I sense that it would be best with exactly 3 players.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: Grab the gems, steal the lands, and gather the nobles in Splendor  It's a very good evergreen greenhorn game to introduce new players or just to play with some experience gamers.  The poker chip gems are fun to play with, because they are a satisfying weight.  The game is fairly compact in which you could minimize it from the box to a case available on Amazon or just a few sandwich sized bags.  Splendor is a fairly quick game that you'll want to play again.  The object is to get to 15 points by collecting gem cards and nobles for points.  It's a quick engine builder that will want you to play a second time after your first.  I'll happily play this when it hits the table.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: Good filler game, lasts around 30-40 minutes and is well thought out and designed with nice artwork. Our edition had good quality cards and chips. Easy to pick up with good replay value. The creators have attempted to incorporate a story line into the game, but I think it's lost. However, the game itself doesn't really lose anything by a slightly weak narrative. We've tried it with 2, 3 and 4 players of different ages and I was concerned there might be a lot of waiting around between shots, but that's not been the case. There is certainly depth and strategy in how you approach collecting resources and prestige points and this provides interest and high addictive value.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Incredibly pure distillation of an infrastructure game. As usual, you want purchasing-power early and points late; the challenge comes from the constraints of what cards are available. (What you have to pay with may not be what the cheaper infrastructure cards require, or the colors they provide may not be what you need for nobles or for more expensive cards you're eyeing for later in the game.)

So you have to flow with the available options, which may sometimes mean breaking that "infrastructure first" heuristic, and *that's* interesting. (As is the potential for sniping out key steps in opponents' buildups, and the counter of reserving cards at a relative cost.)
Title: Splendor

Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
My wife and I played this with another couple. The other couple own it and have been playing it 2 player for a while. They really enjoy it and wanted to see what we thought. I really hated it.

It being the first time I played it I didn't count on winning and I didn't but I didn't do very poorly. But I also knew I wasn't going to win 4 or 5 turns before the game ended. I realized my strategy wasn't going to work by then but didn't have enough time to pivot and go for a different one. I have a similar issue with 7 Wonders except I think there are some opportunities to come back in 7 Wonders.

In the end I came in a close 3rd and never want to play this game again.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: This is a great game for a specific niche.  It's easy to play for people who are not big on table top games, or kids who can't handle a lot of complexity; so when Grandma comes over, everyone can play and still have fun.  It is also short enough but still interesting that we can pull it out for a quick gaming fix.  It's not terribly deep or involved but it stays fun enough to play occasionally when you don't have time for something better or don't have people who will enjoy more complex games.  Basically lite and easy enough for a smart 6, 7, or 8 year old, without getting too boring for the adult game lovers.  But for that specific niche, it's dang near perfect.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Splendor is an engine-building filler, where you collect and spend gems to buy cards that make buying future cards cheaper.  As the game progresses you'll be able to afford more expensive cards, which aren't any better than the cheap cards in-game, but do provide more points.  You can also claim goal tiles if you're the first one to collect a certain assortment of cards.  All the cards to be claimed are public, so sniping is possible, but you can see what everyone is doing, so there's not much surprise.  I don't think I've played a filler that feels like this before, so it gets points for originality, but it still only has a filler's amount of depth.

(5+ plays)
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
I rate this game a 4 out of respect for the praise and enjoyment so many others seem to give and get from it. But honestly, I would be hard-pressed not to flatly refuse to play it again. I hated it that much.

It's just -- it doesn't feel like a "game" to me, it feels like a math problem. There's no luck or randomness really, it's just straight solving the best and most efficient way to score points based on the cards that are out there and how you can lightly interfere with another player by taking the last of a certain gem color. Where is the fun??? The theme is meaningless. The art is well-drawn but has no life to it.

This game is just so cold and soulless.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
The game has a neat idea, but I think it suffers a little bit due to a few mechanisms.  The buying phase of the game is interesting, with the ramp up from being poor to being rich happening swiftly, so it feels like there's a lot of spending, and then the game is over.  It doesn't allow much time for altering plans, but then again, it's so short that it might not be an issue.  I also had problems with the game not penalizing players for reserving cards, since it seemed like it was too easy for players to mess others up just by taking cards.  It's an OK game, and I'd play it if others wanted to, but it doesn't strike me as something special.

3 plays: 3 players
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: A group of us gathered to play this one evening. It took a little bit of time but once we got the gist of it - it became an instant addiction! We've hosted game parties and Splendor has become a popular addition to our household! I need to play when we have lesser than a full complement of players and the only real regret to the game is the fact that it's limited to 4 players -- that's how popular this game is! But we quickly found out that we can form teams to help with strategy as you work your way to winning all the victory points you can! This one was a keeper and one of the first games I bought here locally - I so love supporting our local game store!!!
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Christmas 2014!

Splendor is a beautiful lightweight filler, and a very good family game. It's a race to get 15 points, and you accomplish this by collecting gems of various colors (especially the gems on the cards). Set-up takes about two minutes, and gameplay is quick. Splendor has top notch components, but I'm not sure why they put it in such a large box. The game bits only require a little more room than the bits for Biblios. The only downside for me is that it always feels like the game ends too quickly, but I think giving everyone one more turn would make it too long. Still, I'm happy to have this on the shelf, and looking forward to many more plays.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
This is a fantastic engine building game. Like 7 Wonders, it plays very quickly but it still feels like you get a deep strategy experience. Even with such simple rules, there are many different paths to victory. You can try to build your engine with many cheap Tier 1 cards, or rush to the second and third tier to collect points and hopefully end the game early. But it's also a good idea to try and satisfy the nobles.

I very much recommend it. The only problem is that there is a lot of information on the table which means that sometimes you don't notice some of the possible options, and players may be overwhelmed when looking at all the cards in the offer.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Played a couple of times online.  Simple collection game, light rules with quick game play, and looks like a nice combination of cards & tokens (chips). Light on the theme (which is boring anyway), though I think I would enjoy the Marvel version more.  If I'm going to be collecting cards it might be more fun if the characters were familiar or had a little more depth.
One big difference in the Marvel version is that you need at least one card of each colour (plus the green Time Stone) to meet the victory condition, forcing everyone to diversify slightly - in basic Splendor it is possible to specialize in a few colours and still meet the victory condition.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
A solid family game/gateway game with a tight mechanisms and resource management. 

The theme on here is light, but you can see where they tried to convey the sense of "gaining gems" through the mines. 

Poker chips provide a nice tactile feeling and the game has a nice table presence. 

WHO IS THIS FOR? Casual gamers who are seeking a quick 30-45 minute game with a focus on resource management. Nothing here will really win the hearts of more experienced euro gamers or those who adore a well integrated theme, but it's still serves it's purpose for an introductory/family game. 

Also check out Century: Golem Edition for a similar but IMO, better game.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: Really simple game with beautiful production. Great as gateway game and filler. However, it's rather light on theme and pretty mechanical. While manipulating the pieces is fun (because they are awesome) I don't get great satisfaction at the end of the game. Yes, you start out with nothing and accumulate gems, but they don't lead to much besides points so you don't get the feeling of actually having built something. So while it's probably one of the best gateway games out there at the moment and for some reason really appeals to the lady gamers, I don't feel the urge to play it often or multiple times in a row because it's not enjoyable enough for me.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Simple, yet strategic. Most people I have introduced the game to have taken to the game and like it a lot, usually more so than myself. This is a good game to introduce to a new or casual gamer, as it is easy to teach and get the basic strategy within a game or two. I would rate it an 8 if it wasn't for this game sometimes getting in the way of me introducing a new game to my gaming group, because they want to play this game instead. (LOL)

Positives: Easy to learn. Easy to get on the table. Enough strategy to make the game interesting. Quick to play, set up and take down.

Negatives: Generic copy and paste theme. Not for people who like heavy games.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: This is absolutely more what a game should be.  Spencer taught it incredibly quickly and we got rolling with the mechanics of the game.  Although we didn't get the strategy of when to start trying for point cards, or how to get the bonus point cards we really knew what we wanted to do each turn.  I thoroughly enjoyed this, even if it meant we sat in perfect silence, trying to figure what we wanted to do for ourselves.  I also never seemed to know when to start claiming cards for later, instead trying to just get my stuff together to be able to take them sooner from the tableau.  Simple but fantastically deep game.  I must have this and have it soon.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: The theme is pasted onto this engine builder. But the gameplay is just so smooth and polished that it doesn't matter. This game is pretty and the chips (gems) are SO satisfying to play with! I don't know how many times I have played this with my kids but it's a lot! If you get the expansion, then I recommend springing for the "broken token" box insert and it will all fit into the base box nicely. This one is one you should buy. It's easy to get to the table, quick to setup and teach, plays just as well with 2 as it does with 4, has good length of play, and just does will with so many types of players. Could easily use this as a gateway game as well.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Love this game, though I can see that it might not appeal to everyone since it's rather simple. In this game you collect gems (in the form of cards and poker chips) to purchase more gems, all with the goal of becoming a reputed gem merchant who may attract the attention of noble patrons. Certain gem cards have points, as do the noble cards you can obtain if you fulfill certain card hands, and the first person to 15 points wins. 

This is one of those gateway games that I can teach quickly to anyone and that will be fun to play as a 20-30 minute filler. I taught this to my husband's 70 year old grandma and she raved about how much she enjoyed it.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
After 4 plays, I can appreciate the design of this game a bit better, and have seen different strategies emerge depending on player count (in 4 player games, gold is more available than 3 player games). The sort of game which doesn't outstay its welcome, is readily accessible to new comers and is quite enjoyable overall.  Timing important as is blocking and keeping an eye on what one's opponents are doing.

Initial rating of 7:  Good but not great filler.  Can see why it would get alot of play, but it is pretty themeless.  Just about building an economy and set collection.  With some luck of the draw elements, and timing important for the chips.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
This is not a bad game, but...I am not as enamored with it as others seem to be.  I feel like luck can play quite a bit of a role.  You need personage tiles to win, but snagging the right cards to acquire them can prove to be a tricky endeavor if the right ones come out at the wrong time (i.e. before you even have an opportunity to acquire them).  

This is one of those games where someone else besides the winner was always about to win the game on their next turn.  Unfortunately, that someone else inevitably thinks of at least one instance where they were screwed by the luck of the draw (which, of course, could have made all of the difference).
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Simple build your engine filler. Early game is used to collect chips to obtain cards to make buying future cards easier. Later you will be able to afford more expensive cards which also provides victory points. The first to collect certain assortments of cards will be able to claim Nobles (goal cards), which also provides points. 

All cards are public so you can see what others are doing, and can revise your optimization accordingly. It is a filler so there is little depth but it does play quickly. 

Like the chip components and I've not see this twist before so it get a point for originality. Also gets a point since my wife really likes it.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Rated a 3 after my first play. 3p, took nearly an hour, we all went for the same 'mass cards, get nobles' strat and were relieved when the game ended. 

Decided it needed another shot and have put a few hours into Prestige and now the official app. Upgraded to a 6. I think it's too abstract to be a good gateway for most, but as I find myself thinking more about how chips circulate, reserving cards, when/how to go for the higher tier cards right off the bat... I'm finding it a bit more interesting than I previously thought. 

In terms of the physical game I still think I'd keep it to 3p max, I expect it to be a bit too slow and chaotic at 4p.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
This game... pardon the pun... was a diamond in the rough. I had picked this game up 100 times at the game store and put back down thinking it sounded kind of boring. Cut to Christmas where I am opening it up. My partner and I decided to try it out, and I immediately fell in love. 
It is just tense enough to feel like a good challenge without being so mentally taxing that I don't feel like I can play anything else the rest of the night. I have been able to easily explain the rules to new people without issue. On top of that, 2 and 3 player games are really fun as well (assuming you remember to scale down the chips like you're supposed to).
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: Ever wondered what it'd feel like to be debeers? I am always up for a game of splendor. It is a well designed game involving a little luck but mostly skill. You spend your rounds either acquiring gems or using them to purchase mines that auto produce buying power and sometimes have victory points. You are attempting to obtain enough buying power to purchase enough mines to gain enough victory points to win. If you purchase the right configurations, you also attract nobles worth points and speed along your victory. This game was second place in the spiel to camel up and I believe the first game by space Cowboys. Thankfully not their last.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
~Get gems to buy mines to get more gems and more mines~

This is a light game, but it's still fun.  You take terms either taking gem tokens of 5 colors or buying "developments" with the gems which give you discounts on future development purchases.  But the simple system does have some depth.

It's best at 2 players with reasonable interaction though attempting to deny what you opponent might want.  3 or 4 players tends toward multi-player solitaire, but does move reasonably quickly.

When someone asks for a quick 2-player game, I used to often say "let's just play a round of Splendor", but now I find Azul taking that slot more and more.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
A minimalist engine building/set collection game. While it may seem like there is a decent amount of guessing your opponents' intentions and blocking going on at first, it soon turns out that a lot of it is just for show. Grabbing a tile just before someone else would isn't actually very effective if it is immediately replaced by something even better (usually: cheaper) and that happens a lot more often than you would think.

In the end, turning up the right cards at the right moment is a lot more important than any deliberate player move, a deficit that is amplified by an engine building scheme that rewards quantity instead of quality.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
The component quality and simplicity of rules explanation mask what is at its core an AP inducer without any of the a-ha moments that usually follows when a strategy reveals itself.

In games like Five Tribes, you may think for a while, but you'll eventually come up with something to do and *have reasons for doing it*. In Splendor, every reason you may come up with is ephemeral. How do you weight choices or map decision trees when the actions that you take either accomplish nothing immediately (and rely on the card you are going after not being claimed) or sacrifice a large amount of resources to add a single component to your "engine".
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
First off, the game is fun for what it is. A 20-30 minute soulless, themeless, romp with friends. I give this game a lot of garbage, but it is indeed a good solid game. To me, I consider it too-light, but my gaming group really loves it, hence why I keep it, and is also very easy to teach and can be played really quick, which is probably the main draw this game has. 

Overall, an good game at best. If you're looking for theme, look elsewhere. At a $25 price point, I'd be less critical, but at $40 I will recommend you purchase online instead of locally. Hopefully Cities of Splendor(expansion) add some more variety and life to this game
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
[i]The chips drew me in; the tactical intricacies keep me coming back.[/i]
Played in: [url=https://boardgamegeek.com/geeklist/330164/item/10427909][u]2024[/u][/url], [url=https://boardgamegeek.com/geeklist/10156070/item/9575533][u]2023[/u][/url],  [url=https://boardgamegeek.com/geeklist/301212/item/9432012][u]2022[/u][/url], [url=https://boardgamegeek.com/geeklist/288902/item/8664210][u]2021[/u][/url], [url=https://boardgamegeek.com/geeklist/278184/item/8010395][u]2020[/u][/url], [url=https://boardgamegeek.com/geeklist/268367/item/7643130][u]2019[/u][/url],  [url=https://boardgamegeek.com/geeklist/248145/item/6629651][u]2018[/u][/url]
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Jan 2016: Some of my non-gamer friends have discovered it and can't get enough of it. Downgrade from 5.5 to 2. The game is simply not fun. 

Feb 2015: Minimalist engine building, optimization card drafting game. 

If this game came in a small box with small cardboard tokens instead of big plastic chips, then I would consider buying it. This game is too overproduced for how dry it is. In a way it feels like an abstract strategy game without its geometric elegance... All you are doing is acquiring resources for cards that give you VP and "permanent" resources. It's like an abstract because the game is usually played in pensive silence.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
2015-10-02 : Can't really understand all the hype surrounding this game. It's just a simple engine builder with zero theme and a high luck factor as to what color of gems will come up for purchase. Second play and even more underwhelmed with it this time
2023-10-29 : Got talked into another play of this and executed the only sensible mathematical strategy again. One other player did exactly the same and the end result was I won, he came in second and the other 2 players were way behind us. A game where there's only 1 winning strategy and when multiple players execute it, it comes down to luck who wins is not a game, it's an activity.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
A great little engine builder (in a famously oversized box...) which has been a hit both with my family and with gaming friends.

[i]Splendor[/i] is a game about optimising your route to victory while at the same time staying flexible and changing course as the game demands. It plays like a breeze and does not overstay its welcome. In fact, I am never ready for this game to end when it does – right when your engine begins to pick up speed and you just need those few extra rounds to see it run, it's over... This can be sometimes frustrating (and perhaps even anti-climatic), but I think that it's healthy for the game in the long run.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
This might be my new go-to gateway game.  It appears to be a straight forward engine building game...well it is... but there is more complexity and more strategic options than at first appears.  After 5 games, I'm still looking forward to trying different things.

The real allure here is a very simple rule set with some depth and a short play time that escalates quickly.  Indirect player interaction is enough to keep from being multi-player solitaire, while not turning off confrontation-disliking players.

Components are really amazing.  They're almost over the top, but the components take it from being a good game to a great one.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
As a predominantly medium-heavy Eurogamer, I've now outgrown Splendor. I would still wholeheartedly recommend it as a gateway game and play it every now and then, but I no longer feel the need to keep it in my collection. 7/10.

-------------------------------------------

The gateway game that started it all for me. Still a great game after 20+ plays (even as someone who grows tired of light games after 10-15 plays), and one that I love playing with non-gamers as an introduction to the pure satisfaction and fun of engine-building. There is also just enough interaction through the reserve action to keep things interesting. 8/10.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Splendor is a solid game that got me back into the hobby. I started researching games for a 2-player couple scenario and decided to strike on this one; no regrets. It's simple yet you can be very strategic if you think about it hard enough. It moves at a good pace and feels satisfying when you acquire cards you've been keeping an eye on. 
Actually, it can be a bit more challenging with a 2 player game since you can often think about your opponents next possible moves; makes it interesting. I also brought this to play with my family of 4 and everyone enjoyed playing it for hours that night. I highly recommend giving this a try!
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Splendor is the perfect introduction game to engine building. It is extremely simple, and new players can start playing within 5 minutes of set-up. My only complaints are that the box is WAY too big for the game. I'd take it along with me on trips if it were smaller. The simplicity of the game can mean that after 2 or 3 plays in a row, you're ready for a new experience.

Update: Since I've added other games to my library, I've found Splendor on the table less and less. It is useful as a gateway for new people to get into board games, but if I am playing with an experienced group, Splendor is rarely the game that we reach for.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
What I like:

-It's beautiful! So beautiful! I have no doubt in my mind that this is actually a huge factor in it's success - the chips and card are just a treat to look at. 
-It's so fast and fun. Easy to teach. Hits a great sweet spot where everyone can learn and play this quickly, and even win, but clever thinking is still going to be rewarded. 
-It's just as fun with 2 as 4 players. 

What I dislike:
I guess in the long run the same advantage that the game has could become it's eventual downfall for you - if you play this a ridiculous amoung of times it might become a little repetitive as the game is so simple as it is.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Pro's:

1) Great components and art style.
2) The game just feels very well designed, everything seems to just work really well, with the limit on the gems; creating the card tableau; then having to completely rework your strategy based on what another player does.

Con's:

1) The game is really simple, I feel like I've basically "experienced" it to its max potential even though logically I haven't.
2) It's so obviously designed to be streamlined and easy to grasp that it makes it way more dry then it should be. I love euro games and this somehow manages to feel more like a spreadsheet then most of the others I have played.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
This game is decent but deceptive to experienced gamers. It [i]looks[/i] like you should be able to build an engine by purchasing lower-level cards and eventually work your way into swiftly buying many expensive point cards/nobles for cheap. However, in reality, the game usually ends before the engine actually pays off.

Also, this game suffers from the same kind of randomness exhibited by Power Grid's auctions - you never know when buying a card from the table may just flip over a much better card for your opponents to buy. This is unavoidable and therefore mildly annoying.

An okay game if you don't take it too seriously.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: Annie's first official board game purchase!!!!!! Wow was I surprised at this game. I had passed this by for years and after Annie played it at Shall We Play Night, she really loved it and bought it that night. It's a very simple game to teach and to learn so it's great to pull out for those who don't play games that often. The quality of the chips also largely contributes to my enjoyment playing. I have found that every game has a different strategy and I love how you really can chose a different path each game. I am looking forward to getting the expansions for this as I think it will help add to the longevity of the game.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Beautiful components, simple rules, straightforward gameplay, some tactics, Splendor is a wonderful introductory/filler game.  Be the first person to accrue 15 victory points by either gaining gems/cards or nobles worth victory points and win the game!  It's also VERY easy to teach, to learn, and to play!  Very little downtime!

Chip collecting and engine-building combine to drive the game forward rapidly -- if everyone knows the rules, it's about 30 minutes per game!

A bit dull with two, Splendor ramps well to three and four players.  Be warned:  there is some luck involved in the game.

Not much to speak of theme-wise.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Description: Abstract, family, tableau building, open drafting, set collection, gem management game for 2-4 players. Best with 3 or 4.
KEEPER

Impression: Light, family game about buying cards and collecting gem sets from cheapest to the most expensive until the first player reaches 15 points. There is decent amount of strategy and math involved. 

Likes: Multiple viable strategies. Component quality (heavy gem chips). Quick game play.

Dislikes: First player gets a slight advantage because of the bonus tiles..

The 'Cities of Splendor' expansions definitely improve this game.  My Rating:  7.0  (8.0 with the expansions).
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: The mechanics of the game don't necessarily relate to the theme at all, but to be honest, I don't really care. Splendor is an extremely satisfying engine builder with the added bonus of being themed around gems. Splendor has a lot going for it, it's artistically appealing, is easy to learn, and a quickplay (30-60 mins). I'm not saying Splendor doesn't get more attention then it deserves, but it's definitely an enchanting game that deserves some clout. Of all its clones, I still find myself preferring Splendor. I would recommend Splendor as a solid introductory engine builder to those interested in the genre. (10-15 plays)
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Mindig kétkedve gondoltam a Splendor sikerére, de a Társasjátékok Ünnepén a kíváncsiság leültetett mellé (meg az akció). De jól tette! Ha ez nem addiktív, akkor nem tudom, mi az. Témája nincs, grafikája sem tetszik, de roppant egyszerű, gyors, és rendkívüli sikerélményt ad, mikor a vége felé beindul a gépezet. Aztán persze hirtelen vége. De annyira jó érzés volt a végén, hogy újra szeretném átélni! Aztán újra, és újra és.. Ah, most már értem a sikerét. Világot nem renget meg, de leültet játszani. Kell ennél több?
A kipróbálás miatt az akciós példányokról lecsúsztam, de már berendeltem, szóval nemsokára itthon is bedobom!
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
There are a lot of similar tableau building games nowadays, but Splendor is still in the top. You put some effort on collecting some cards which create an engine so you will be able to do extremely effective actions in the second half of the game...well, this is really delightful. Simplicity in an elegant way regarding mechanics, quick turns, but with meaningful decisions. Absolutely recommended for all player counts.
The "theme" could have been left out in my opinion. Only gems on cards with cool design would be enough, since the game is pretty abstract, but these renaissance merchants and nobles are a bit meh for me..
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
If you need a special thing-in-a-box  just to teach non-gamers the basics of resource management mechanism to use in actual games, buy this one.
For all other occasions, this is overly simple and dull. I get it, gateway games are supposed to be simple, but this is way too trivial even for a gateway game.
No chance to manipulate card order, just a pure abstract chase for victory points... whoever gets his turn in the moment when good cards randomly come to play is likely to win. And I quite like abstract games, I just don't understand why do they need to add a totally non-connected theme. And I am perplexed by the hype.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: Great components, even if the game does have a pointlessly tacked-on theme. However, the game is deceiving in that there are not as many paths to victory as the game would first have you believe. When playing games like "Caverna" or "Blood Rage", there are so many strategies that players can commit to in order to have a chance of winning the game, and these strategies can change from game to game. Even "Sushi Go!" has more viable paths to victory than this game! "Splendor" does not have the mechanics to reward the freedom to choose how to accumulate points, and therefore becomes a very bland (and overhyped) experience.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
One of my favourite games of all time. Fell in love at first sight and that warm fuzzy feeling is still with me every game.

The simplicity of ones turn allows for in depth analysis for what you want to achieve in addition to being able to figure out what your opponents may want to do. This is an important ingredient in making a game go from good to amazing. Because at the end of the day I play boardgames to play with others, and as this game not only telegraphs the intentions of players but also gives time for players to realise what others want, you truly feel like this is an interactive contest to the finish line.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: family favorite, not mine but the family loves it.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: Excellent gateway game to encourage people in our hobby.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: Excellent for what it is: very quick, simple, economic engine builder.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: Really fun, light game that is easy to learn, easy to teach, & usually a big hit with various players of various skill sets. The theme didn't interest me at all, but after a play I downloaded the iPad version and finally bought the actual game because I liked it so much.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Anyone claiming there is any "depth" to this game likely finds objects such as shoelaces and door-handles "challenging"

That being said if you do need something really simple to play with non gamers this is about as harmless and  procedural as it gets.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: Good game. Great components. Easy to teach. Some strategic depth. Seems to really hit the sweet spot at three players. One of the better set collection games.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: well done with nice arts and HQ components. Mechanics and game play is just ok - simple and nothing spectacular. Splendor is a bit overrated in my opinion. It's a fine game but very average and with a lots of randomness.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: Such a neat little economic engine game - so much in such a short game. Love it. Only complaint would be that it is so 'thinky' that there isn't much scope for banter.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: Played this at CoolStuff in Orlando late one night after being at Universal all day. A really fun experience that has a great simple and elegant design. I'd reccomend it to anyone, but I already have  plenty of games that fulfill that same need.
Title: Splendor

Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: This is a fairly simple engine building/set collecting game.  I really do enjoy it, but yet find it lacking a little.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: I am not enjoying it anymore after over 50 plays. However it continually get requested by others especially by new/lighter gamers. I'm glad I sleeved it despite the fact that I'm continually being mocked by non gamers for sleeving. I'm happy to play a game that others request.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: It's missing the U in its name. Other than that, rather forgettable.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: Fun, addictive, fast paced easy game that tends to be very close and plays in 1/2 an hour.  Great filler game!
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value:
Well balanced game, but there is not much to say about it.
The main issue is that there is only one "strategy". Buy the best cards that happen to be available. The definition of what is best is pretty much the same for every player: more points and gem diversity.
The art is nice, but provides the only real theme.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: Abstracto sencillo, accesible, rápido y con pocos componentes. Uno de esos juegos para todos los públicos que puede funcionar de puerta de entrada para profanos. Básicamente, es una carrera en la que se va desarrollando un motor de recursos que va creciendo exponencialmente. La pena es que cuando estás a tope de power el juego se acaba.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: I like it so far.  Might be a little frustrating with more than two players.  It's basically Airships without dice-rolling.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: Easy to learn, hard to master, quick and enjoyable.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: 2/27/2015 - A decent enough game for me to keep around. The design seems a little plain by modern standards. It's effectively an abstract strategy game that will fit right at home next to other 1990s designs in my collection. I'm a bit surprised by the popularity, but it seems well-balanced, even if a bit stodgy and dated in design.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: Quick and easy to teach. What's not to like?
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: I can fully understand that many people find this game overrated, even boring, but I don't. I'm impressed by the minimalistic elegance and astonished that a game with such simple mechanisms can be so entertaining and addictive. An excellent gateway game, no doubt.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: Easy to teach/learn, fun, quick, good with 2-4 players.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: what a great game. it's amazing how simple it is to play but the underlying synergies and decision making is beautifully subtle. this is definitely a keeper!
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: Not too bad, but a very unthemeatic card with a substansual bit of luck. Very easy to learn and teach.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: I mostly play it with my wife, we enjoy it a lot.
Title: Splendor

textfield_comment_value: used to like this game. However this game has dropped a-lot since other games have replaced this game. Still will unwilling play it from time to time but this is not a fav.

An engine-building race to resources that strips away any pretense of theme or even the illusion of meaningful choice, and tasks you with pathing through the simplistic mechanics to squeeze one or two more points more than your opponents. It's boring, frankly.

During my first game of this, my SO at the time got sick and ended up hospitalized for the night. I should have taken it as a sign. Nothing so dramatic has happened in subsequent plays, but it has reinforced that bad memory with a string of uninspired sessions. The lone point in its favor is its short play time.

textfield_comment_value: It took me quite a few plays to figure out where the game is, but there's a lot more going on in this game than might appear when you first try it.  The key to the game is balancing investment (in the form of purchasing no-point cards for future return) vs. simply saving up to buy points.  The calculation will be different each time, and may change based on the actions of other players.  Finding this game more enjoyable over time and not less, which is a surprise.  Bumping the rating up to 8.

textfield_comment_value:
Splendor / Space Cowboys / German edition (2018)
- Increcibly dull and boring. Take chips, use chips to buy cards that help you buy more cards, repeat until it's over.
- After very few rounds the luck of the card draw becomes the dominant factor, especially in a 2 player game.
- No interesting decisions to make, the best move is mostly obvious.
- The theme is completely arbitrary and so vage that I had actually preferred this to be purely abstract.
- Coponents include annoying poker chips and very flimsy cards
- Artwork almost as dull as the gameplay.
+ Explained in less than a minute ("That's it?!")

Splendor is a game of chip-collecting and card development. Players are merchants of the Renaissance trying to buy gem mines, means of transportation, shops—all in order to acquire the most prestige points. If you're wealthy enough, you might even receive a visit from a noble at some point, which of course will further increase your prestige.
