textfield_comment_value:
Azul probably needs no introduction. The game is stacked with accolades and has won numerous awards. What is more impressive to me is that it has won 2 awards: Spiel des Jahres and Deutscher Spiele Preis in 2018. These two awards are quite apart in terms of the crowds they cater to. Spiel des Jahres has inched more toward family gaming and the trend is that the Jury tends to select lighter and easier games. Meanwhile, Duetscher Spiele Preis, or the German Game Prize select games that agree with the lifestyle gamer which are generally more complex. For Azul to win both awards would indicate that the game is light enough to be embraced by the typical German family, yet having enough depth to attract the serious gamer. The most recent game to win both prizes occurred in 2009 when Dominion bagged both awards. Dominion is considered the granddaddy of all deck building games and is actually moderate in complexity. So that award was well-deserved for DSP but a more awkward selection for SdJ. Still, that was a decade ago and a case can be made that the SdJ is skewing more and more toward lighter family games which makes Azul’s win even more impressive. Having now played the game at least half a dozen times, I think both awards are justified and the game is outstanding for not only casual, family style gaming, but also for your heavy Euro gamers.

Azul is an abstract game that is all about drafting tiles and arranging them in specific patterns to score points. What’s unique about the game is how the tiles are drafted, organized and prioritized to maximize scoring. Not surprisingly, the rules are quite simple. On the middle of the table, are several discs known as the factory display and the number of discs in play depends on player count. Each round, 4 tiles are randomly drawn from a bag and placed on each factory display disc. These tiles are brightly colored acrylic tiles that come in five different colors and patterns. During a player’s turn, one can pick up a group of similar tiles from a single disc while pushing the leftover tiles to the center of the table. That means that for each disc, only one player can select from them because any remaining tiles will be pushed into a common pool. In subsequent turns when tiles are also in the common pool, player are free to pick up a group of similar tiles from the common pool. The important point of this tile drafting phase is that all tiles of a similar color or pattern must be selected. So if there are 5 blue tiles in the common pool and if you select blue tiles, you must pick up all 5.

The fun starts when you have to decide what to do with the tiles. Each player will have a personal board to put tiles. Tiles are place in 5 horizontal columns with increasing number of slots starting with 1 on top and 5 at the bottom. Each slot can only contain one tile and that means that row one can only have 1 tile and row 5 must contain 5. When a group of tiles are selected from the factory display or common pool, they must go into one row and one row only. Any excess tiles must be discarded to the factory floor where they will be penalized with negative points. So, if your row 5 already contains 4 blue tiles and you pick up 3 more blue tile, you can place only one tile in this row and the remaining 2 must be discarded to the factory floor. Of course, if your row 3 is empty, you could place all 3 blue tiles there to complete that row.

In this way, tile drafting and placement continues until all tiles are drafted from the factory floor. The round is then over. Players then check their tile placement and for every horizontal row that is completely filled, one representative tile of that type is moved over from the row to a 5×5 grid. The movement of the single tile from each completed row to the grid will score points based on adjacency to other tiles. Any negative points are also tallied during the end of each round. There is one restriction for placement of the representative tile in the 5×5 grid: no line or row can contain tiles of a similar color. So, this is very soduku-esq in that no row or column can have the same number. Your job is to place these tiles so that no two tiles of a similar type or color may touch each other.

The game continues until one person completely fills a horizontal line on the 5×5 grid which then ends the game immediately. In essence, this means Azul can last somewhere between 5-21 rounds, though it probably rarely exceeds 5-10 rounds per game. When the game is completed, players score bonus points for each completed line, column and for each complete set of 5 tiles of a similar type on the 5×5 grid. That’s it.

Like most abstracts, rules do a poor job of describing the actual experience of playing the game. In Azul, this is also true. The game is light and rules are simple, but there is tactical brilliance that is most evident in a 2 player game where each player has full control of their choice and how they can impact their opponent. Ideally, each tile selection must benefit not only your board, but if possible, must also impede your opponent’s choices. It is quite elegant at the two player level when you have this simple back and forth between players. It is immediately clear to me that some of this brilliance is muted or lost at higher player counts where there is less control on what tiles are available when your turns come around and also how many people will be impacted by your choice. Things are just much harder to control and I think you end up playing more to your own board rather than defensively to block others. With two players, it is easier to do both.

The simplest example of a defensive play in Azul is choice denial. You pick up a tile your opponent wants and deny them the opportunity to score points. This denial can be pretty devastating as a single move to deny someone can result in a huge loss in points, particularly end game point and so it is not to be ignored. You can also force your opponent to pick up groups of tiles that they can no longer place on their board. For example, if the horizontal line on the grid already has blue, your opponent cannot pick up blue for that row. If you force them to select blue and there is no legal placement on that horizontal line, then all the tiles are converted into negative points. You can position your selection such that your opponent is forced to pick up multiple tiles that they cannot place. It’s mean, it’s cruel, but it’s also very satisfying when you leave a 5 tile group for your opponent to place in their factory floor! Of course, everything comes at an opportunity cost. So, balance must be struck to ensure that your offensive and defensive plays maximizes your own score too.

Azul is great and Michael Kiesling is deserving of all the praise for his design. There are already 2 spin-offs for Azul that uses the same tile drafting system, but with different scoring methodologies. I have played Sintra, but still greatly prefer the plain vanilla Azul. There is something to be said about simplicity of the original design that already carries considerable depth. Additional complexity in my book is not always necessary. Still, I think the spin-offs are well regarded and I am happy that the entire Azul family is getting its due. This one stays in my collection right alongside Knizia’s Keltis series. Both games in the series have the same flavor, depth, pace and I hope, durability.

Initial impression: Great!

textfield_comment_value:
"Azul" ist ein thematisch-abstraktes Plättchen Legespiel, wobei anstelle der Plättchen hochwertige Keramiksteine genutzt werden.

Zu Rundenbeginn werden je vier Steine auf die Manufaktur-Plättchen in die Tischmitte gelegt. Die Anzahl dieser Plättchen variiert mit der Anzahl der Mitspieler.
Wer an der Reihe ist, nimmt sich alle gleichfarbigen Fliesen einer Manufaktur und legt sie in eine Reihe des eigenen Tableaus. Passen diese nicht vollständig hinein, kommen überzählige auf die Minuspunkteleiste.
Die nicht genommenen, andersfarbigen Steine der Manufaktur, werden in die Spielfeldmitte, zu eventuell anderen nicht gewählten Fliesen geschoben, aus denen ebenfalls - nach den gleichen Regeln - Steine genommen werden dürfen.
Die Runde endet, sobald alle Fliesen genommen wurden. Dann werden vollständige Reihen auf den Spielertableaus aufgelöst und in ein Fliesenmosaik daneben geschoben. Jeder neu eingesetzte Stein wird gewertet. Je mehr angrenzende Fliesen ausliegen, desto mehr Punkte gibt es für die neu gelegte Fliese.
Sobald ein Spieler mindestens eine Reihe vervollständigt hat, endet das Spiel und derjenige mit den meisten Punkten gewinnt.

Das Grundspiel bringt bereits eine Variation des Spielbretts auf dessen Rückseite mit, worauf keine Farbvorgaben zu finden sind. Die Spieler können beim Werten ihre Steine an beliebige Positionen schieben. Allerdings gilt die Regel, dass jede Farbe in jeder Reihe und Spalte nur jeweils einmal vorkommen darf, was das ganze verzwickt macht!
Die Erweiterung "Das gläserne Mosaik" enthält Plastik-Overlays, die ein Verrutschen der Steine auf den Spielertableaus verhindern sollen. Außerdem sind neue Spielbretter mit Sonderregeln beigefügt.
Auf der ersten Seite sind bereits fünf Felder mit Mosaiksteinen vorgegeben. Sobald diese eingebaut werden, gibt es für deren Wertung doppelte Punkte. Alle anderen Felder sind frei belegbar, wobei immer noch gilt, dass in jeder Reihe und Spalte nur eine Farbe vorkommen darf.
Die zweite Seite gibt ebenfalls fünf Felder vor, die mit entsprechenden Fliesen belegt werden müssen. Die Veränderung liegt hier in der Wertung der Reihen, Spalten und Farben, die am Spielende jeweils etwas mehr Punkte geben, als im Grundspiel.
In der Minierweiterung "Die Joker Tiles" gibt es durchsichtige Fliesen, die beim Nehmen und Einsetzen eine beliebige Farbe annehmen können. Leider müssen sie in das Mosaik eingesetzt werden und gelten dort in der Endwertung nicht als wertbare Farbe.

Anfangs war "Azul" für mich total öde! Wie so etwas Bestnoten in der Spielbox Zeitschrift hervorrufen kann, blieb mir ein Rätsel. Nach weiteren Partien konnte ich mir langsam vorstellen, woher der Spaß kommen könnte, doch war ich immer noch der Meinung, dass es wohl nie mein Lieblingsspiel werden wird. Wieder ein paar Partien später habe ich es mir selbst gekauft, denn es funktioniert in der Familie und sogar mit meiner damals 7 Jahre alten Tochter richtig gut! Und obwohl ich es anfangs nicht leiden konnte, war es 2018 das Spiel, welches am häufigsten auf den Tisch kam und ich mag es heute noch sehr, sehr gerne.
"Azul" bedarf nur wenig Regeln und funktioniert als abstraktes Spiel sehr gut. Auch wenn ihm ein Thema übergestülpt wurde, spüre ich es beim Spielen nicht. Aber Thema ist nicht alles. Durch den eleganten Mechanismus, ist das Spiel schnell aufgebaut, erklärt und gespielt. Außerdem macht der Anblick des wunderschönen Spielmaterials, direkt Lust mitzuspielen.
Die Overlays der Erweiterung "Das gläserne Mosaik" habe ich nach einmaligem Ausprobieren direkt entsorgt. Sie verschandeln die schöne Optik des Spiels und machen das Spiel nicht besser. Ich habe mir mit dem 3D-Drucker vier Raster in Spielerfarben gedruckt, sodass der Punktemarker nicht mehr verrutschen kann. Die Steine selbst verrutschen beim Spielen kaum und wenn, sind sie recht einfach wieder eingesetzt, wo sie waren. Die Spielbretter der Erweiterung sind in Ordnung und bringen eine kleine Variation ins Spiel.
Die "Joker Tiles"-Erweiterung sind nett und dessen Spielsteine wunderschön anzusehen. Sie geben den Spielern eine weitere Option beim Nehmen von Steinen, sodass Reihen schneller befüllt werden, machen dafür die Farbwertung am Spielende kaputt. Ein schönes Dilemma für die Spieler. Ich nutze ab und an die durchsichtigen Fliesen, finde das Grundspiel aber besser und kann die Minierweiterung daher nicht empfehlen, um mit "Azul" Spaß zu haben.
Ich mag das Grundspiel mittlerweile sehr gerne, wie man an der stetig steigenden Bewertung bei BoardGameGeek sehen kann. :) Und auch die Spielbretter der "Das gläserne Mosaik"-Erweiterung kommen bei uns gut an.

Ein alter Bekannter lebt auf! Aus meiner Sicht wurde hier der Klassiker Sudoku (Farben oder Zahlen) auf ein moderneres Level gebracht. Der Kenner spürt allerdings noch weiteres Entwicklungspotenzial bezügliche des Sieges, der strategischen Vielfalt und der Spieleranzahl. Meine Plus- und Minuspunkte im Detail:

(+) macht Spaß
(+) für Alleinstellungsmerkmal (unique characteristic): Farbsudoku für zwei Szenarian (front and flip-side), Farbsudoku unterscheidet sich von der Version des Herstellers "think fun"
(+) für Kennervorteil / mittel lang andauernde Lernkurve: Je öfter man Spielt und die Sudoku-Muster kennt, je besser wird man. Nicht unbedingt steigende Highscore, da die Rundenanzahl variabel ist.
(+) for ballancing:  Es gewinnt der, der die Vorteile am besten ausnutzen kann. Man kann den Gegner aufhalten und/oder einholen.
(+-) dominante Siegstrategie: Dominante Siegstrategien mindern generell den Langzeitspaß, wenn die Züge repetetiv werden. Es wurde noch keine derartige übergewichtige Strategie erkannt. Wer im kurzen Spiel vorn liegt, kann versuchen frühzeitig zu beenden. Jedoch kann dies jeder und es ist unabhängig von den wichtigeren Legestrategien. Die Kurzzeitstrategie gewinnt jedoch vor dem Langzeit-Plan, mit dem man alles vollpuzzeln möchte.
(-) für mehrere Siegpfade / mehrere Siegstrategien: Es gibt nur Punktsiege. Grundsätzlich gibt es keine gleichwertigen unterschiedlichen Siegpfade, wenige verschiedene Strategien
(+) für Abwechslung ohne Erweiterung: In jeder Runde liegen Fliesen unterschiedlich verteilt aus. Freie Varianz besteht für eine Vielzahl an Farbmustern auf dem leeren Puzzelplan. 
(+) für Strategieentwicklung: Man kann Strategien (Farbmuster, Wertungen) entwickeln und timen, ohne das der Glücksfaktor zu viel Planung zunichte macht. Je weniger Spieler, desto besser.
(+) für flexible Entscheidungen: Man kann/muss seine Strategie ändern und auf den Gegner reagieren.
(+-) für Spieleranzahl: Die optimale Spieleranzahl liegt bei 2. Anpassungen in der Auslage für 2-4 Spieler sind vorhanden. Jedoch wird die Vorausplanung mit mehr Spielern schwierig bis unmöglich.
(+) für die Kompensation des Startspielervorteils: Startspielervorteil kaum vorhanden, da man in jeder Runde selbst Startspieler werden kann. Die Kompensation erfolgt über einen Minuspunkt und einen Kompromiss. Startspieler wird, wer zuerst aus der Mitte nimmt.
(-) für Siegmöglichkeit aufgrund unterschiedlicher  Zielbedingungen: profanes Siegpunkte sammeln (Siegpunkte), kein Mehrheiten, kein Wissenschafts- oder Forschungssieg ...
(-) für den Aufbaumechanismus: Verstärkung der Aktionen ist durch verschiedene Elemente/Gebäude/Regeln nicht möglich
(+-) für Konterstrategien / Aufholmechanismen: Kontern durch das wegnehmen oder verschieben in die Mitte möglich. Kontern nimmt aber mit der Spieleranzahl effektiv ab. Es wird erst kurz vor Ende klar wer gewinnt, obwohl man ggf. schon abgeschlagen war. Die Aufholstrategie übernimmt das Spiel, da es immer mehr Punkte zum Ende hin gibt. (Die Anzahl der Steine, die je neuem Stein gewertet werden, nimmt zu.) Kurzes Spiel, was kaum eine Aufholstrategie benötigt.
(+) für Glücksausgleich: Für jede zufällige Auslage lassen sich gewinnbringende Strategien entwickeln.
(+) für Spannung bis zum Ende, Ballancing: Es gibt bei gleich erfahrenen Spielern keine große Siegpunkte-Schere am Ende.
(+) Nahezu alle Entscheidungen sind vom Gegenspieler abhängig.

textfield_comment_value:
I'd heard a lot of good things about Azul, so I really wanted to try it. It's a very abstract tile drafting game.

In the game you have a 5x5 grid you're trying to fill. There are five different colors of tiles and each row on your grid can only have each color one time. The way you get tiles onto your grid is by drafting tiles and putting them into slots next to each row.

There are something like 9 different areas (it differs by player count) where tiles are placed at the beginning of the round. Each area holds four random tiles. When you draft you tiles from an area you take all the matching color tiles from that area and put them in the slots next to a row on your player board. The tiles of a non-matching color go into the center of the drafting area, making an additional area that can be drafted from.

The top row of your player board has one open slot in which you can place drafted tiles, the second row has two open slots, third has three, etc. Each slot must continue a color that has already been started in those slots. If you draft more tiles than will fit in a row's slot then the extra tiles must be put into your waste area (which will score negative points). If you draft fewer tiles than you have slots, you can later on add more tiles to that area.

If at the end of the round, all the slots for a row are filled, you move one of those tiles to your grid (in the matching color area for that row) and the rest go into a used pile. Any unfinished rows where not all the slots have been filled persist (which means you have fewer available areas to place drafted tiles... making it more likely you'll end up with waste and negative vp's).

At round end, when a tile moves from the slots next to a row to a spot in the grid, you score points for that tile, and all the contiguous tiles in that row and column. So placing next to existing things is very good. Additionally at game end, each completed row is 2 points, each completed column is 7 points and if you complete all tiles of a color that's 10 points. The game ends in the round whenever someone completes a row.

There's a lot to think about in this game. Because drafting tiles dumps things into the center, you can set someone up or screw them, by the things you're not choosing but sending into the center. You have to be careful because really bad things can happen... like you can be the person forced to take the 7 red tiles left in the center at round end, only have room for 1 of them, and be forced to take 6 waste (which is a huge penalty!).

The person who taught this game talked through some of their strategy as they played, and you can go deep if you really think things through. I later played with all new players and it was a much lighter game. I enjoyed the game a lot.

Nagyon kedvelem Michael Kiesling munkáit. Nagyon kedvelem (évtizedek óta) az absztrakt stratégiai játékokat. Az AGON: The Lost Sword of Toledo munkálatai óta vonzódom az azulea csempékhez. Valamint azt is el kell ismerni, hogy emberek tízezrei (inkluzíve a Spiel Des Jahres zsűrije) nem véletlenül szeretnek bele egy játékba. És nekem mégsem tetszik az Azul.

Azonnal nem szembeszökő az ok, amiért egyszerűen nem kedvelem, ezért megpróbálom részleteiben összeszedni. 

Nyilvánvalóan zavar a design. Amíg a doboz kifejezetten szép és felidézi a spanyol/portugál csempék és járólapok mintáit és színeit, addig maguk a játékcsempék nem teszik ezt. Talán a kezdőjátékos jelző tile az egyetlen kivétel. Értem én, hogy igyekeztek a tervezők minél jobban megkülönböztethetővé tenni az egyes elemeket, és vélhetően beletört a bicskájuk (a teszteken) a hitelesebb mintákba, de nekem - főleg a sima piros és kék csempék jelenléte - teljes csalódás. (Miközben mindenki áradozik a kivitelezésről.)

Zavar a tematikátlanság. Tudom, hogy a játék absztrakt, de valahogy mégis mintha igyekezne másként eladni magát, miközben igazán még az az alapelem sem stimmel a sztoriban, hogy egy falra pakolunk fel csempéket. Honnan? A mellette lévő falról? Valahogy sem térben, sem logikában nem áll a lábán a játék tematikai része. Pedig nyilvánvalóan csak nagyon kicsi kellett volna ahhoz, hogy itt (akár nem is csempékkel) egy egyszerű mintakirakós játékot játsszunk.

De zavar a mechanizmus erőltetettsége is. A "választok egy színt és betolom a többit középre" ötlet zseniális. Az egyik legeredetibb draftoló megoldás, amivel találkoztam. Még az "aki középről először választ, ő kapja meg a kezdés jogát, de cserébe 1 mínusz pontot ír" is valami olyasmi, ami felett csettintek: ad valamit, de közben elvesz attól, aki a könnyebbik végét fogja meg. Viszont onnantól kezdve, amint a személyes táblára kerülnek a csempék, semmi sem történik magától értetődően, és ezt más sem mutatja jobban, hogy már többedszerre kell a játék (igaz: ritka) előkerülése kapcsán végigolvasni a szabályt: hogy is van az? Erőltetettnek tartom a pontozást is, logikátlannak a pontozómezőt, valamint maga a feladat is nélkülöz minden izgalmat azzal, hogy egy megadott mintának kell megfelelni (pedig tudom, ez a lényeg, és valóban nem egyszerű).

Botlik, döcög, valahogy nem áll kézre és közben irtó álmosító. Nem képes magával rántani. Természetesen a választás szabadsága, nehézsége, a másik építkezésének a megfigyelése, az ebből következő óhatatlan "betartás", valamint a "padlóra eső" csempék büntetőpontjai döntések sorozatát adják, és ezek sokszor nehéz döntések, de valahogy még sem köt le annyira, hogy bármikor is azt mondjam, akkor most játsszunk még egyet! Ez van...
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
[i][u]Disclaimer:[/u][/i] This is a [color=#000099][b]standalone game[/b][/color]. Its rating is based on [color=#000099][b]desire to play[/b][/color].

A friend perfectly encapsulated my problem with [b]Azul[/b] after our first game. There's a huge discrepancy between the visual aspect of the game and its underlying mechanics, he said.

I will try to expand on that now. [b]Azul[/b] components are beautiful, there's no denying that. But behind this appealing product hides a very, VERY math-y game, that just isn't fun for me (and I'm a maths teacher !). The game is very abstract and to me it feels like a maths problem that was reskinned as azuleros decorations, but ultimately doesn't fool anyone.

Now I will concede that "fun" is a very subjective concept, and I'm sure that a lot of people enjoy playing [b]Azul[/b]. Here's the weird part, though : I'm usually not against calculations and planification. Some of my best rated games contain a good deal of it. In [b]Azul[/b], though, it faces two problems.

First of all, the game is just too dry. It makes a world of difference to me when the calculations involve transforming resources to plant a forest to raise the oxygen level to raise the temperature to get a free ocean... versus taking this tile to get 4 points which means I get 3 more points from this next tile, and 7 points for the completed column.

But most importantly I find that in [b]Azul[/b], the course of events is too random for me to invest the energy in boring calculations ("he takes this - she takes this - i take this - etc etc ... so that means HE gets the 50 red tiles and not me"). More than once I have gotten screwed over, not by a perfidious alliance between my opponents to put me down, but instead a suboptimal move by them because they failed to count tiles or points correctly (and admitted so afterwards).

I am aware this sounds very whiny, and as a former poker player I've heard my fair share of lame excuses to the tune of "I only lost because you played badly. A good player would fold here" or whatever. But if you've studied a little bit of game theory, you know that in a game with more than 2 players, mistakes by an opponent are not guaranteed to help you. In fact, they may very well punish you, and it happens A LOT in [b]Azul[/b].

I will say though, it gets much better as a 2-player game, where the situation above doesn't apply (a mistake by your opponent is always going to profit you), which means putting the effort to calculate how the draft will unfold with precision gets more consistently rewarded.

My final rating is the average of the 5/10 I would give for 3 or 4 players, and 7/10 as a two-player game.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
[thing=230802][/thing] is a truly simple game: just collect pieces and use them to assemble a pattern on the personal boards. That is it. Has been quite a while since I see a game like those of the old days, when a game had only one main mechanic that counted for 90% of everything you would do - today, is more usual to find an auction mixed with deck building with area control with mancala with worker placement.

The ideia of [thing=230802][/thing] is to take tiles from the suppliers, at the same time going for what is best for you, and what will make the life of your opponents tougher. Pieces taken are put on the personal board - if they fit, good; if not, they fall and break, giving a penalty in points at the end of the round. Also at this point, after all the tiles were taken, each line filled with tiles will be discarded and one piece of it will enter in the corresponding pattern besides that line. Then players score 1 point for each piece in the same line and column, if they have an unbroken line towards the newly placed tile. Also, at the end of the game, which happens when a line of the pattern is filled, players will score bonus points for each filled line, each filled column and for each color they have all the pieces. Whoever has the most points will be the winner!

To [thing=230802][/thing] fits that term that we often see tossed around in a frivolous or simply wrong way: elegant. Its rules are minimal, its time to set up and explain tiny; with a clever gameplay, giving a lot for players to think about, even if not about something too complex, obscure or that demands deep planning. Its a tatical play, seeking for the best opportunities. Is functional and fits perfectly for the playing time and weight of it.

However, I played with 2, which is the best number accordingly to BGG, and was amazed by how boring and lifeless it is at this numer. Sure, you have much more control, but is very easy to get what you want and, even with the possibility of some mean strikes, these only truly come near the end, when we often found that it was better to play to our advantage than to be agressive. So dull was the experience, that my overall view of the game, from very positive, went to mild excitment, specially since the luck aspect was so prominent in 2 players in the final rounds.

Still, [thing=230802][/thing] quickly became a hit in our group, for the reasons mentioned, and I predict it will remain a regular in our tables. Recommended, but, for me, after a few more games, it remained just an OK game.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
This game is lovely. The first-player token being a negative point is a brilliant choice. There may be a slight early-player advantage beyond that, though, since there's no mitigation to randomly going first in the first round, or going second in 3+ player games. I doubt it's substantial, but it's technically there. That's the closest I can come up with to a flaw so far. One other might be that it doesn't hold up over many repeated plays, but I haven't yet gotten to that point. So far, it just does. Excited to try some of the alternate successors once the pandemic blows over. Sintra wins on aesthetics, but Summer Pavilion looks to have some of the juiciest mechanics yet. Still, I'll happily return to this original any time.

Edit: I've played this game more and more over the years. It definitely holds up, at least at the mostly casual level of play I'm used to. This is one of the most decisive modern classics in recent memory. I have never had a bad game of Azul, and I don't think I've played with anyone who didn't end up loving it. I still haven't gotten to try any of the derivative versions, but I'm not in any rush. It's hard to imagine that they're better than this.

That aside, I find its placement in the "Abstract" category on BGG interesting. The theme is certainly abstract--at least as abstract as chess--but it's not a combinatorial/perfect information game. Does an abstract game have to be? Well, maybe not necessarily, but it certainly makes the distinction fuzzier. The simplicity, accessibility, and classic appeal of its grid boards and bakelite squares also help it feel like an abstract (like this game could be a hidden treasure you discover in your grandparents' cupboard), but Azul's point-crunching gameplay feels a bit more mathy than I expect from an abstract. Again, this isn't necessarily contrary to any definition of an abstract that I'm aware of, but perhaps it's a case of connotation versus denotation. Azul feels so classic that it could have come out 100 years ago, yet it plays so smoothly and has such a pleasant, polished design that there's no question it's more modern than that. I guess my point isn't about semantics or genre labels at all; my point is that Azul is an unassuming game that nonetheless smashes boundaries with ease and defies conventional categorization. It doesn't feel like a game which imitates or reflects industry trends. It's Azul, and it has earned its pedigree.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
My wife bought this for me for Father's day.  We are always on the hunt for anything good below the designer level of board game as our children are too young to take on the heavier board games and she has no interest.  This one came highly recommended by ProZD and many others, so I was eager to diver into this.

Suffice to say, I was not disappointed in any way.  

Right away you notice that despite the simple nature of the game, the components are very good quality.  The tiles are simple but aesthetically pleasing, the player boards are good, everything lends to a relaxing, easy to learn board game.

The rules are likewise simple and clean, with the game divided into a number of rounds broken down into two phases each.  The first phase as the first player populate the "factories" with four tiles each, determind by the number of players.  Players then take turn selecting their tiles of choice to populate the staging side of their board.  Herein lies the deceptive depth of strategy in Azul, where you can't merely select these at random, nor can you fully rely on a plan that may well fall apart merely by bad luck on tile draws.  

Points are scored by tiles being successfully moved from the staging side of the board into the tile wall.  This is done in the second phase for any staging row that has been completely filled up.  These rows grow successively larger, with the first row being a single tile, all the way up to five tiles by column five.  You need all tiles on a row to match in order for it to be completed, so you may or may not be able to complete your plans based on the amount of available tiles, much less what other players are trying to accomplish on their own boards.

The combinations of the order of operations of each turn, tiling, and scoring both allows and necessitates equal parts planning and flexibility on players' parts.  The order of operations is extremely important as two players with very similar end results on their tile wall may have wildly different scores depending on what order those tiles were laid in.

All in all, the game is a great mixture of easy to learn rules (My 7 year old picked it up very quickly), with a good depth of strategy to learn and master.  Azul is a great addition to the collection of anyone looking for a more lightweight board game.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
I think Kiesling really nailed this one. Just by description, it might sound like a pretty standard themeless Euro with an Action Restriction gimmick. It certainly feels like more than that in practice to me -- yes, it's themeless, and yes, it has an Action Selection restriction gimmick; but at 2p it also insists you focus on the other player, a quality I find sorely lacking in modern Eurodom. So this is an abstracted game where you create color-coded rows and columns, not unlike his earlier game Sanssouci (or even Vikings, for that matter). But at 2p it can be vicious. And I think what I enjoy about it the most is that it really shouldn't be played as an "optimize your own tile area" game. You aren't trying to get the most points you can, you're trying to get more than your opponent, and there's a difference: consider options A and B. Option A gives you 8 points and your opponent 8. Option B gives you 5 points and your opponent 2. This isn't the only game to ever do that, but to me it's one of the clearest and cleanest. 

Having said that, the game becomes an "optimize your own tile area" game the more players you add, so this is likely a 2p game for me, period. At the time of this writing I have not played it with more than 2p so I cannot report via experience, but all indications point to the game losing its bite with more players. You cannot force other choices as easily, and you cannot force others to make moves that benefit you as easily -- at 3p you influence on player, s/he influences another, and that player influences you. Add a fourth and all of a sudden you can't influence the player who has the most influence over you and I think the game would cease to be as interesting to me. 

But the game has range: if you want to play it as a breezy 4p family game where everyone simply tinkers with their tile area, go for it. It can scale by Player Intent pretty nicely (like Carcassonne, frankly). But I like it at 2p, where the game feels completely different. I personally love games that allow me to orchestrate a move (or set of moves) where I give my opponent no choice but to benefit me on their turn. Azul lets me do that, and it lets me fight against that.

==2021/04/10==
Nope.  Asmodee games get 2s.  Won't buy unless I can get for massive, massive discount.

==2020/12/08==
This is such an elegant design.

The rules are so easy to remember.  Your turn is so fast and simple to resolve -- draft a color from a group, then add it to a row on your player board's queue.  Scoring is (almost) completely intuitive.

And yet-- Despite how simply turns resolve, and despite how quickly play passes around the table, there is *so much* to think about.  It's a deep game that I can play with anyone.

Azul is the kind of design that deserves to be mentioned in the same breath as Ticket to Ride, definitely.  The design elegance, graphic design, and production are all top-notch.  But I think that Azul is by *far* the better design.

I personally don't consider Azul an abstract.  In my head, abstract games don't have drafting elements.  Because of this, I consider Azul a direct competitor to Splendor and Century: Spice Road.  I think I'll always prefer Azul to Splendor (but I haven't played anything from Century).

My geekbuddies tell me that the game is very cutthroat at 2p, and that sounds right to me.  My first play just now was at 4p, and I was playing quickly with just my own tableau in mind.  I would probably avoid playing this at 2p.

My initial reaction to LAMA was likewise absolutely ecstatic (rating it also a 10), and then I later cooled on the design (bringing it down to an 8).  I will probably experience that same kind of arc here with Azul, if I get enough plays with it.

I'll likely take the same kind of stance on owning Azul as I did with Ticket to Ride -- not worth owning because everyone else around me will have a copy.

Also, regarding the insert:  Ticket to Ride is secretly an extra $25 more expensive than the sticker price, because I had to replace the insert, buy an expansion for the regular-sized cards, and get custom tuckboxes for the deck.  Azul... maybe... needs the plastic overlays from the expansion?  (The scoring track on the top of the player boards was my biggest hesitation with Azul for the longest time)  But otherwise, Azul is a complete product even off-the-shelf.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
My comments refer to the game at two players. This is distilled strategy and psychology in a box. When you first grasp the rules and objectives of the game, it looks straightforward, boring, and arbitrarily constrained. However, as you play a few rounds it quickly becomes clear that there are layers upon layers of strategy which are not totally unlike Chess - except you're looking at two separate boards and a common pool instead of one shared board. In order to stand a chance of winning you have to predict your opponent's drafts (often 2, 3, or 4 turns ahead). Then you need to try to bait him into bad moves, hoping he hasn't detected how you plan to take advantage. You should also try to scupper his plans at every opportunity, all the while trying to play your own board as cleanly as possible. Sometimes the best choice is to hurt yourself when by doing so you can hurt your opponent more. And you need to analyse the board carefully to try to engineer the correct moment to end the game by completing a row so that you'll come out on top. This is one of those games which can look from a distance like multiplayer solitaire, but is in fact viciously competitive when played intelligently.

Scores are tallied up as you play. There are two punishment mechanics (one which directly subtracts points from your score as you go along, and the other which restricts your options and makes you more likely to fall prey to the first) which make sloppy play a dangerous business. One poorly thought-out round can wipe out a huge portion of the points you'd gained up to that point.

Unfortunately, much of this breaks down at higher player counts. Sometimes you can just about analyse the next turn at 3 players, but not the turns beyond that and at 4 players it's probably impossible. The deep tactical analysis is the real core and beauty of the game and at higher player counts you are largely relegated to playing your own board and ignoring everyone, except when someone has made an obvious blunder and it's clear to everyone else which tiles he wants or doesn't want. With two players, it's brilliant. With more, it's fairly mundane unfortunately.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
A very enjoyable lightweight tile placement game. Played it for the first time a few days ago after hearing a lot of recommendations about it so I thought I'd finally give it a try.

[b]Pros:[/b]
[u]Simple rules[/u] - Didn't take too long to learn the game, every step of the gameplay was explained clearly and was accompanied by examples, which made retaining information easier

[u]Easy to set up[/u] - Took literally 1-2 minutes to set up the whole game. Nothing better than a game which has a short setup.

[u]Short play time[/u] - Takes around 30-40 minutes even if you're playing with AP-prone players. The game isn't so strategical as it is tactical

[u]Nice production value[/u] - I absolutely love the resin tiles and it's very satisfying when you reach into the bag and shuffle them.

[u]Accessible[/u] - The tiles don't rely solely on colors but some of them are marked with a certain pattern, which not only makes the game more accessible, but also more thematical and prettier.

[b]Cons:[/b]
[u]Inconvenient score tracker[/u] - Accidental movements might make you move your score marker and lose track of your current points easily. Happened constantly while playing and could've easily been avoided if 1) the player boards are dual layered, or even better 2) the score is tracked by score dials

[u]Tile patterns can easily wear out[/u] - I might be nit-picking here, but I played Azul in a board game club and the printed patterns were nearly unrecognizable. Again, this could be prevented by having them engraved for more durability and for an even better look.

[u]Some rules need to be better emphasized[/u] - For example that the starting player marker must always be placed on each round in the center and that you can have the same color in multiple rows. Even if some of these rules are explicitly shown in an example, without being addressed directly, people will overlook them unless they're specified in written form.

Azul is a fantastic intro game which can be played in-between heavier games, has great replayability and is overall pretty. Felt very engaging and I'll definitely play it again.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Ah, Azul. A beautiful tile-drafting, abstract strategy game. There are many things I love about Azul. I love the pieces and the clink of them in the bag when you are setting up the round by drawing them out. I love the colors, the theme (even though it really doesn't matter), and the length of play (games don't typically take longer than 25-30 minutes). I also like the dual-sided playboards. I vastly prefer the open playspaces rather than the fixed ones, but the fixed side definitely has its place when you are teaching someone the game. I prefer the two player game, personally, but there is also fun to be had in a larger gathering. The game, for me anyway, is more tactical than strategic, and I tend to prefer that. Should I take a chance an take this pair of tiles, understanding that by doing so, I'll dump in some others into the middle that will make it less likely (though not certain!) that my opponent will take them from me when it's my turn again? Should I go ahead and take something from the middle because I want to ensure that I get to go first next time? If I do that, am I sure that I won't get stuck with a bunch of unwanted tiles that I'll have to add to the floor? These kinds of decisions start pretty much from the opening selection and continue all the way through to the very end. Very cool. 

What do I not like about Azul? Not much, actually. Some people dislike how the game sometimes compels you to "hate draft" but that doesn't really bother me too much. My only complaint -- and it's a minor one -- is that some games can just feel unlucky. You've made a good, statistically based gamble that at least two blue tiles are going to come out next time, but they don't. So you've filled up your 5-row with 3 blues in the previous round -- and you can't clear that row this round and it haunts you (in so many ways) for three rounds in a row. Yuck. But that's the game, and you win some and lose some, even when you play well. I have not played any of Azul's offspring, so I will be eager give some of those a try as well.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
:( The game description doesn't describe it well. 

I love this game! There are so many different ways to strategize. Each round starts with small circles, each holding four tiles. Going around to each player, you will decide a single color to pick up from a circle while discarding the rest to the center, you are able to draw from the center as well but the first person has to also pick up a -1 penalty, but this can be an advantage since this person goes first the next round. With each color you pick up those tiles are placed in lanes. The round ends once all the tiles have been picked up. These lanes if filled slide over at the end of the round to the board you are trying to fill. The more tiles you slide that touch each other, the better because the points stack. It is important to place the tiles and get as many touching as you can a single tile is worth one point but if it slides and touches 2 that will be 3 points, if those 2 tiles also touch tiles on a vertical or horizontal axes from the placed tile you can get all the way up to 10 points for a single placement. There are bonus points to be scored at the end of the game if you have all 5 of a color or finish a veryicle or horozontal row. Once everyone has scored for the round 4 more tiles are put out on all the circles. When a player fills one of their horizontal rows that ends the game. The player with the most points at the end wins. Simple strategy comes in with the bonus points or having another player left with tiles they have to pick up but no lanes to go it they have to take negative points. More difficult is to anticipate what the other players need and thwart their attempts. Most difficult is to count tiles and play to your advantage, how many tiles are out on the circles, how many tiles are tied up on the boards which colors and patterns can you take advantage of? I really love how this game can be sinple or take advantage of the many layers possible in this game.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Buen juego abstracto. Funciona genial y tanto diseño como componentes son perfectos.

La idea del juego es sencilla: cada jugador ha de rellenar un tablero individual de las losetas de los cinco colores, con dos objetivos distintos: puntuaciones intermedias a lo largo de la partida que generan puntos según el patrón que se va dibujando en el tablero así como un segundo objetivo final qué es el de completar columnas, filas o colores. El jugador que más puntos obtenga al final, se llevará la victoria en la partida.

Juego abstracto, sin tema, precioso de componentes, corto en tiempo, y agradecido de jugar porque es satisfactorio ver cómo puedes intentar generar tus puntos mientras no quitas de vista a tus oponentes para interactuar y fastidiarles sus jugadas. Se agradece la rapidez del setup del propio juego y la satisfacción que deja tanto si ganas como si pierdes siempre pensando en una siguiente partida. 

Me gusta jugarlo y los componentes son deliciosos. Su único handicap (para mí) reside en su propio ADN: la falta de tema, precisamente por ser un abstracto, pero de los que merece tener en una buena ludoteca.

Y quiero destacar un pequeño detalle: el de que todas las losetas se meten en la bolsa y acaban saliendo todas al final de la partida, limitando el componente azar a el orden en el que van a salir en cada partida, ya que siempre va a ser distinto (este detalle de jugar todas las losetas me recuerda a juegos tan importantes como el Through the Ages, dónde también salen todas las cartas en cada partida y lo que diferencia una partida de otra es el orden en el que lo hacen). Y destaco esto para compararlo con un muy buen juego, el Sagrada (juego con el que se puede comparar en algunos aspectos), donde no todos los dados salen en partidas de menos de cuatro jugadores y de hecho muchos se quedan en la bolsa aumentando así el componente azar que ya presenta el juego.

Lo dicho, juegazo, abstracto y precioso.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
[ImageID=6973671small]
It's the perfect family weight game. 

[b]Pros:[/b]
The puzzle is interesting, the rules are simple and there's just enough interaction that you can play it the way you like, either aggressively or passively. The scoring is great, the first player token is a wonderful balance and I like that while the draft is random, you're guaranteed to see all of the tiles in the bag at least once, so you can plan ahead and weigh some risk vs reward.

My favorite part is how badly you can get punished in this game. It allows for some brutal denials and some welcome interaction. Tempo and adaptability are key to winning the game and it means that this simple rule set allows for some deeper level play.

After playing this game over 20 times I keep liking it more and more. There's a lot of hidden depth and whenever I play it with experienced players, it's anything but multiplayer solitaire. It's so smart, so smooth playing and so fast that I'll never turn down a game.

It's also my go-to recommendation for anyone that asks me for game purchasing advice. It's simple and malleable enough to work for families and it's still deep enough to be engaging for gamers. It also looks great and is tactile!

[b]Cons:[/b]
I can be frustrating to get a bad pull from the bag and the game can feel a bit multiplayer solitaire at times, but most of this should go away once you get better at the game. Bad pulls only really happen when you set yourself up for them in an earlier round by being too greedy and the game is a lot more fun when you try to keep tabs on what your opponents desperately need and plan accordingly.

The production is a bit annoying, at least in that the sequels with much lesser gameplay has some quality of life improvements in terms of production. I want a shared scoreboard (to alleviate bumping) and a tile tower (to simplify filling the bag up again).

textfield_comment_value:
? Game explanation:
Azul is an abstract, tactical tile placement game in which you are going to tile a wall as nicely as possible. Depending on the number of players, a number of factory tiles are placed on which 4 tiles each are placed. On your turn, you take tiles from one of these factory tiles. You must always take all stones of the same colour or symbol that are on that factory tile. Move the rest to the centre of the table. You can also choose to take stones from the centre. If you do this first, you get the starting player stone, which is placed on the minus points field. The round continues like this until all stones are taken. The stones you take are placed in the rows in front of the wall. Stones that no longer fit must be placed at the bottom of the board and count as minus points. All tiles you take must be placed in the same row. When all tiles are taken, phase 2 starts. All players place 1 tile from each full row on their wall. Each tile scores 1 point, but if they are adjacent, they score more points. Once a player has a full horizontal row on his wall, the game ends. At the end of the game, you score additional bonus points for each full row and column, and you get additional points if you managed to collect all stones of 1 colour. The player with the most points wins the game!

⭐ Our review:
We think Azul is a very fun and accessible game. You can also bully each other by leaving stones that the other does not need, giving your opponent the minus points. This small version is ideal for holidays. The game is lightweight, has nice plastic player boards and the stones have a notch, making it easy for them to stay on the plastic boards. In addition, it comes with a nice cloth bag in which you can put everything.

Curious about reviewing other Azul variants? Check our website, link in bio!
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Azul is similar to Dragon Castle in many ways. It's an abstract game using gorgeous bakelite tiles. It has a great sense of player interaction and excellent decision points.

In Azul you are attempting to score points by filling in your carpet/fresco/player mat with tiles in a certain order. You get points when placing tiles next to already placed tiles, and for completing columns and rows. The trick is that you want certain colours in certain quantities and other players will do their best to help themselves while hurting you.

At the start of each round there are a number of small piles of tiles, each pile has 4 tiles at random. On your turn you must choose one pile and take all the tiles of one colour present there. The rest of the tiles are pushed in to the center of the table. You can take all the tiles of one colour from the center but the first person to do that each round gets -1VP. 

You do not get to place the tiles you take directly on your carpet, instead you assign them to the waiting area of a row (on the left). Each waiting area needs some number of tiles of the same colour in it before one of those tiles is promoted into the carpet on the right and the rest are discarded.

It's an elegant game with relatively deep gameplay. Your decisions are influenced by what your opponents are collecting, what moves you leave them, and what you think they will do. You often have a plan to acquire certain tiles but need to manufacture the opportunity to do so. Attempting to predict and manipulate your opponents' moves is where this game shines.

If it weren't for Dragon Castle I would definitely be adding this to my collection. I probably still will because I think Azul will work better as a 4 player game, and it is a bit shorter with less set up time so it works better as a quick filler.

textfield_comment_value:
Pros:
* Simple rules
* Fantastic components which look beautiful
* Good interaction between players
* Scales very well to two players.

Neutral:
* It has been rare for the game to go more than five rounds, which means we can be pretty confident that every tile will come out exactly once. This makes tile-counting more viable as a strategy, but means we rarely get surprise twist endings.

Cons:
* Score track is easy to bump. Would have preferred a central score board.

= 2018-12-27 - R:8.5

Great game. I love the player interaction. As with Carcassonne and Kingdom Builder, Azul can be played nice or cut throat. The game has a high degree of clarity and while each round starts with random tiles, there is no randomness within a round. This allows some of the strong player interaction that combinatorial abstracts enjoy where you can attack and parry and it creates so many delicious tense decisions.

Compared to Sagrada:
[q]I recently picked up Sagrada after enjoying my first two plays of it. Unfortunately, after a few more plays I found that my opponents' choices had too little impact on how the game played out so it started to feel repetitive and dull after only a few plays. I so much prefer Azul where a good chunk of the game is playing hot potato with that group of 7 blue tiles in the middle. It feels just the right level of "mean" where you're almost always doing things to help yourself, but if you help yourself in the right order you also hurt your opponent(s).[/q]

The replayability of Azul comes not from the components but from the way your play [i]style[/i] is directly impacted by that of your opponent.

I very much prefer Azul to Sagrada, there's really not much similarity between them. I also suspect I'll prefer the original Azul to the new Stained Glass version.

textfield_comment_value: Difficult to grade objectively since I disliked it quite a bit but that may be mostly due to personal tastes... what I will say objectively is that the game "swings" entirely too much... singular choices can make a difference of a dozen points at all, and these sorts of "swings" in scoring may occur due to misplays, counterplay, malignant plays (manuvers that don't help the player win but ruins your chances), or just sheer dumb luck. Games where a routine thing is for a single play out of around a hundred over the course of of a game create windfall of points or harsh penalities that more or less decide the game on the spot are huge red flags in terms of poor design, in my mind. The game also has the potential for heavy elements of counterplay and probability calculation ("card counting", as it were) but the game's nature as an abstract title makes it hard to closely watch board states (or at least that's what I found). The result is that there's a very "high cieling" for how much of an advantage can be gained from a high level of awareness of board state, which is difficult to maintain... the result is that this is a game where player skill creates a huge gap in scoring... while most people dislike excessive RNG (for obvious reasons) the problem with a game loaning itself so deeply to "the most skilled player wins" is the results of matches are predictable and less skilled players don't wish to participate. Giving it a couple extras point as a "benefit of the doubt" thing since it clearly is incompatible with what I liked more than it's just objectively awful, but I honestly think there are some pretty objective issues with this game despite it's popularity, outside the fact you'd literally need to pay me to play it again due to how actively unpleasant I found it.

textfield_comment_value:
Got Azul and Sagrada at the same time.  Both are similar games.  Ultimately, I think preference comes down to how much random variation you prefer in your games.  Sagrada has a bit more random variability in that you randomly pick the color of the dice (similar to Azul), but then also have to roll the dice for random numbers.  And then Sagrada also has randomized starting templates to fill out, random private & public goals, and the random "tool" cards.

For me personally, I'll give a slight edge to Sagrada, since I like a bit more variability - it helps with replayability.  But I do really like Azul as well.  I have yet to try the backside of the player boards where the layout is not fixed, so that could be fun.

One final note regarding player counts: I have played Azul with 2, 3 and 4 players.  It is much more cut-throat with 2 players: negative points are more common since there are more tiles per player and harder to place them all.  And giving your opponent negative points is more meaningful in a 2-player game.  So you start actively looking for ways to screw over your opponent and force them to take tiles that will give them negative points.  With 4-players, negative points are much less common.

Edit: we tried out the backside of the boards.  It adds an interesting element in puzzling out how to arrange your tiles, because it is easy to screw yourself in a way where you can't complete rows or columns.  It is definitely for more experienced players.  Also, it may add more thinking than wanted at times from a "lighter" game.  But it is nice to have the option.  I imagine we will primarily use the standard side when playing with others, but we might use the advanced side from time to time when it is just the two of us for a change of pace.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
In Azul, players are drafting tiles from a central area to prepare them to add to a personal tableau. When one player finishes one row of the tableau, the game ends. Basic endgame bonuses (completed rows and columns as well as all tiles of a type covered) are applied and high score wins. Each round, the center of the table is populated with groups of four randomly selected tiles of five types. Players take all of one color from a group and the remainder in the group moves to the center to form another group that the leftover tiles from each group feeds. You can draft from the center group in the same manner you draft from the initial groups. You have to draft all of one color, which can you lead you to drafting tiles you cannot use. Tiles you cannot use are deducted from your score for the round. The tableau you are building is a 5x5 grid with each column and row consisting of 5 different tiles. From top to bottom, the prep area is 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 tiles large. At the end of a round, players move one tile from filled prep areas onto the tableau and discard the rest. Tiles added are immediately scored for columns and rows of adjacent tiles. 

The game can seem overly simple at first, but once you start to understand that adjacent tile types score more points and you prioritize the endgame bonuses, a lot of considerations start to come into play. You can also choose to "hate" draft in a way to block a close competitor or force them to draft tiles they can't use and eat some points. The game is well-produced. The Bakelite tiles are nicely designed and feel good in the hand. I see why this was one of the better received games this year: easy to learn, subtle, beautiful, and satisfying.

textfield_comment_value:
Azul besticht durch seine farbenfrohen und haptischen Plastiksteine. Und auch wenn man sich thematisch als portugiesischer Fliesenleger im Spiel wieder findet, ist es doch ein rein abstraktes Spiel.

Reihum wählen die Spieler in der Vorbereitungsphase von mehreren Plättchen á vier Fliesen alle gleichartigen Fliesen aus, die sie dann bei sich einbauen müssen. Nicht gewählte Fliesen wandern dabei in die Mitte, sodass dort langsam ein größerer Haufen entsteht. Wer zuerst Fliesen aus der Mitte nimmt – natürlich wieder alle gleichartigen – wird auch Startspieler, bekommt dafür aber einen Minuspunkt. Wenn man Fliesen nicht mehr in das eigene Tableau einbauen kann, fallen diese runter und gehen zu Bruch, was ebenfalls Minuspunkte gibt.

In der Wertungsphase baut man nun aus jeder vollständigen Reihe der Planungsphase exakt eine Fliese in den endgültigen Fliesenspiegel ein. Hierfür gibt es Punkte, je nach weiteren, angrenzenden Fliesen in der Reihe und Spalte. Zusätzlich gibt es Punkte für volle Reihen oder Spalten.

Azul ist schnell erklärt und spielt sich auch relativ schnell. Man kann zwar ein bisschen planen, was man bauen will, irgendwann bleiben aber nur noch Fliesen in der Mitte übrig, die man zwingend nehmen muss. Das kann im schlimmsten Fall echt daneben gehen, sodass eine Menge Fliesen zu Bruch gehen. Ebenso kann man einem Spieler natürlich auch die letzte Fliese wegnehmen, die diejenige zum Vervollständigen einer Reihe brauchte. Ansonsten kommt man sich aber eher nicht ins Gehege.

Für mich war das Spiel okay. Auch wenn die Spielsteine recht hübsch gestaltet waren, gibt es bessere, abstrakte Spiele wie z.B. Patchwork.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Azul is an extremely popular abstract game that uses an interesting pool drafting mechanism and scoring that reminds me of Ingenious (I hear it's like Qwirkle, but I haven't played that). People seem to really enjoy this game because it's attractive, it has chunky bakelite game components, has gamer and non-game appeal, plays relatively quickly, and is easy to teach. I mostly agree with this. There is also no luck during the round, but there is in the tiles that come out each round. This means it's not one of those perfect information abstracts. Also, players can be pretty mean in this game and it gets meaner, the less people you play with.

I personally don't like that 3/5 tiles have ornate markings and the other 2/5 are plain red/blue tiles. I also don't like the bumpable scoring tracks on each board. It's not Terraforming Mars bad, but it's annoying. I'd use a scoring app instead. One good thing about this game is that it's easy to mock up and give a try. Some people have used Ticket to Ride trains, [url=https://boardgamegeek.com/thread/1920696/playing-azul-h]while I've used components from another Kiesling game: Heaven and Ale.[/url] It's good, but I don't think it lives up to the hype it currently has at the time of writing this. Maybe further plays will change my mind.

Edit: and now it makes sense why the publisher made the red and blue tiles so boring. The publisher has made a collectors set of red set and blue with ornate markings... you have to pay for each of these collector's set though. It's almost like they planned to make the red/blue tiles lame looking so people would buy these. Poor form Plan B games.

textfield_comment_value:
Very nice and feel-good game that's easy enough to bring all the family together to play it. 

Pros:
- The production quality and the tiles are really nice and brings curious people to your table and even stay and watch a whole game. It brings people together even making them wanting to advice their advocate
- After each round you get immediate feedback regarding points which makes the competition interesting. However it still hides some of your game-end extra points which make for some nice comebacks
- Although it is a solitaire-multiplayer game, there is enough interaction (and even strategy to 'mess' with your opponents) to make it feel that we're really playing a game together
- The theme is masterfully executed to the point that everything you do feels connected like 'messing up' and breaking a precious tile which scores you negative points

Cons:
- It is only an aesthetic thing but I think they went a bit "cheap" with the blue only and red only tiles by not giving them patterns. I would think that you could find 3rd party tiles to replace them on etsy or ebay but haven't found any yet. Maybe a cardboard cutout and spray paint will do the trick
- Limited to 4 players. I have found myself with 2 or 3 people looking on the sidelines wanting to play. Maybe they could work out a 5-6 player expansion and change the way you take tiles (from going around a circle to going back and forth) like Sagrada does. I would really like to play this with more people
- The 'expansion' is not really an expansion, only a plastic 3d cover so tiles and cube don't move and the other versions of Azul are completely different games

textfield_comment_value:
Initial Score: 8
After Azul: Stained Glass of Sintra fell flat for me I was looking at reviews to see what might have gone wrong there and saw that the different flavors of Azul tend to grab the attention of different people. 

This time, I decided to try it digitally first and with an AI so I could learn it / try it out.  I liked it SO MUCH more that I went and grabbed the Mini version.  Felt like it had more strategic choices than Azul: SGoS and like I could better gauge what other players would need and work better with the choices I had.  

Updated Score: 8
The more I learn about this one, the better it clicks with me.  I definitely feel like I can play more strategically and tactically in this one, especially at 2 players.  It also lacks a very glaring flaw that I saw with SGoS.

In SGoS, there was often this HUGE broken glass situation where one player was forced to take catastrophic amounts of negative points because there would be times when there was a lot of a color out that no one could use.  This was due to the randomized board setup and people flipping over their columns at different times.  In regular Azul, this doesn't happen. Even if there is a larger pile of a color people don't want, it never gets catastrophic because there is still a way to use it and mitigate the bad by doing something else with it, even if it isn't ideal for scoring.  You can also, if you are paying attention, see it coming and make your drafting choices such that you can avoid it hitting you.  You can also influence it toward someone else if you want more of a pvp experience.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
In this game, you are a tile laying artist tasked with decorating the palace of King Manuel I of Portugal.  The game is played in rounds with three phases.  The first phase is called the factory offer.  In this phase, players will take turns drafting tiles from a central display and placing them into pattern lines on their player board.  Getting stuck with tiles you can’t use will give you negative points in the next phase.  This next phase is called wall-tiling where players will slide a tile from completed pattern lines onto their wall where they are immediately scored based on adjacency.  The last phase is preparation for the next round.  The game ends immediately after the wall-tiling phase in which at least one player has completed at least one horizontal line of 5 consecutive tiles on their wall.  Bonus points are awarded for every completed horizontal row, vertical column, or set of all 5 of a color.  Most points will win.

The game is beautiful.  I love the tiles.  It is one of my favorite abstract games.  It is easy to teach and plays in about 30 minutes.  I’ve played with 2, 3, and 4 players and it is great with all of them (though maybe feels a little meaner at 2).  I do wish the boards were dual layered, but that’s not too big of a deal.  There are companies that make overlays if I cared enough to go buy them.  Turns are snappy and decision options are constantly changing based on what other players are choosing as they draft.  This keeps me very interested in other players’ turns as I try to mentally will them not to take what I want.  Good game.

textfield_comment_value:
Whatever this does, Qwirkle does it better. And I'm not a big fan of Qwirkle.

It's like all the joy of the engine builder type fiddling plus the joy of engine builder type interaction without the engine building. Yay! Which I guess makes for a lower overhead, more accessible experience. Actually the way how scoring snowballs shows at the traces of engine building still being in there. 

Basically it's a game of glossing over the assembled tiles and player boards and constructing some 5-6 parallel data sequences in your mind and optimise around them. That's it. It's juggling with data that feels exactly like all the engine building games, without the engine building (though, scoring has the same dynamic). It's exactly what's been popular lately in euroblandia, only it's simpler (which is good) and as bland and devoid of any narrative. (Kingomino was better). So you're juggling this data in isolation of your mind, and possible somebody takes and action that makes you need to ditch 3 of the 6 equation sequences and build them anew (the horror! Oh, noes!). What's the point? There's no narrative. No sense of progression. Possibly interaction happens when people get on comparable levels of optimisation proficiency. Possibly. 

Seems similar in interaction and supposed dickery to The Little Prince: Make Me a Planet - and that game looked WAY more charming, had less optimisashun of tedious data sequences,  and had a narrative. A narrative! 

[-]Anyhow, high rating of 2.5 as maybe I would play it once more, with more players. (Above based on one 2 player game).[/-]

textfield_comment_value:
After over one hundred plays on Board Game Arena, this is one of the better games I have played.  However, even though it can handle 4 players, I find the experience to be best as a head-to-head game.

The main thing that stood out to me is how easy the rules are to understand.  As a result, the game can start quickly, even with a complete novice, because everything can be explained in about five minutes. At the same time, because no two games are the same, every game requires a somewhat different strategy, which in turn gives it extra depth.  

Unfortunately, the gameplay experience depends largely on the opponent, as it can be chill, or very competitive.  If the opponent is a try-hard, the game can become tiring and frustrating, since the opponent will try to ruin your board every play, and that person will also likely take a long time on their turns.  Luck becomes a factor too, because there will be rounds when one does not get the required tiles, but it is definitely less than other games.

Overall, this is a good and well-designed game.  Furthermore, since I like games that are more challenging, it scratches the right itch for me.  However, I also have had poor experiences because of the opponents, which I understand is outside of anyone's control, but the game is designed in a way that invite those types of behaviour.  Thus, I give it 7.25/10.  While I I have had more enjoyable experiences than poor ones, those poor ones really stood out in my mind, so even though I enjoy it and have continued to play it, it is one of those good, but not great games.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: Kiesling is such an interesting designer, especially when he is away from Kramer and trying his own thing out.  And he manages to pull out a rather enjoyable abstract that is also beautiful to behold! The game gives you the feeling of tough decisions, though sometimes those decisions are obvious. Playing well is being able to analyze your opponents, which creates a bit of a brainburner and maybe more than I would necessarily like all the time as it's quite a bit to analyze what players have and what they need and the multiple ways they could get those things and how you could stop them and how not stopping them will let them do this or that, etc., etc., If you just avoid that whole aspect and play your own board without care for your opponents, you may do well or you may not and it basically comes down to who didn't screw up and who was luckier. What your opponents do can really affect your opportunities, even if your opponents never planned to help or hinder you. Don't get me wrong: I like Azul and enjoyed playing it the couple of times I did. But this is a game of opportunity and at times these opportunities can create themselves based solely on your opponents. Super seasoned players may be able to analyze their opponents and the supply and play a deeper game. But as a casual game, there's a bit too much luck to keep this in the camp of pure abstract and too much analysis to keep up the enjoyment.  And even though it's a quick game, it can feel a little dry by the end. Still, it's a solid game which I'm glad I've played.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: A fun game to play, suited for 8 year old or + but playable by 5+/6 (my daughter as 5 to 6 and already plays with us and have fun with it). I'd say that it's of simple complexity, game instructions/rules are simple and well defined, the game is most skill than luck, although it presents some kind of strategy. Regarding playing time I believe that it's just right for this type of family game, not too long or too short. As for the graphics, I personally enjoy them, the colours are really beautiful and appealing, the tiles are awesome, and can make a really beautiful board. The materials are also great, the tiles are made of acrylic and the patterns are lovely, the board is nice and thick. The overall game idea is cool, specially cause I’m Portuguese, but it’s a theme of most interest. I’ve really enjoyed the game and, for me, it’s a must have to play since it’s fast to prepare, fun to play and simple enough to explain and put everybody playing. It allows little interaction between players, because we’re trying to play for our own tile wall, but as others choices interfere with our own, it creates an enjoyable environment. In what refers to playing time, has a very cool and relaxed paced time of play and doesn’t create lots of waiting breaks. As for game options, well we’re trying to create a tile wall, so it’s not really that kind of a game, nonetheless, it presents several ways to punctuate defined by the way you’re trying to develop your game, so in the end I would say that it’s just right for this game.

Initial Rating: 6.0 (April 2018)

Last month I played Sagrada and many friends compared both games often so I was expecting similar games, but Azul isn’t very similar to Sagrada, what they have in common is their similar game weight and that both games are abstract.. Azul is a bit heavier, but, paradoxically, I like Sagrada more because it is lighter (and chucking dice is more fun). In general I like my games very heavy or very light, the middle ground isn’t very fun for me and Azul is in that zone.

Azul can be explained under 8 minutes, playtime is around 40 minutes.

The theme is nonexistent, the game is abstract after all.

Azul´s components are gorgeous and they look great on the table.

Gameplay isn’t very obvious but it isn’t very hard either. Players have to carefully choose the better tiles each turn, the catch is that if you take a tile you have to take all the tiles of that color and, if you don´t have space on your board, they will cost you VPs. It is a fun decisions to make and it is more deep than it is initially apparent. There is a variant I haven’t played which I think, increases the difficulty of the game.

Luck of the draw plays a role in the game, but I feel better play is more important. I need more plays to decide the issue.

Bottom line, I was expecting more from Azul, but it is a pleasant game to play and my SO loved it so I will keep it among my game collection. It can be a great family game. It is a gorgeous game.

textfield_comment_value: [2023] Years after its release, the original Azul remains one of my favorite games. The game is relatively easy to teach, requiring only a few sample rounds to demonstrate the turn flow. On any given turn, the decisions can be clear but nonetheless interesting, presenting players with the choice of immediate payoff by seizing a favorable draft, of long-term reward through careful drafting, or of punishing another player by hate-drafting (either denying points or forcing them to suffer penalties through misplays). The game can feel incredibly mean in 3-player games, given my personal experience shows that two players tend to score points where the third receives nothing but penalties due to careful hate-drafting. This makes the 2-player game far more interesting, however, given the risk-reward of drafting tiles to complete a row in the tableau at the cost of perhaps receiving penalties or of being unable to complete other rows before the start of the next round forces Azul to require careful and deliberate planning and risk-taking. Games will always draw to an artificial close but in no fewer than 5 turns; therefore, players may be incentivized to prioritize rushing the end of the game by completing a row before their opponents given their scoring options become fewer and more difficult, assuming the end does not happen naturally before this point (the top row is the usual suspect, requiring only 1 tile of any color to be placed to score on the right side of the tableau).

Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: The so well beloved and popular Azul, a favourite of the masses. Being a Portuguese myself I do get the theme and its historical placement, despite the fact the game should’ve probably been called Azulejo (tile) instead of Azul (colour blue) - I’m sure along the way someone had to make an executive decision on keeping the name short and sweet. Let’s just get this out of the way immediately: it is a great game and you will very likely love it, despite my review. At its heart it’s an abstract pattern building/tile placing game, not hard to teach and get going from the first play. It is a better and more engaging play with more than 2 people, but still perfectly fine if that’s all you have. There are no rough edges here, only a superior distillation of raw gaming elements - everything feels like an elegant minimalist design, function married with form. And still… despite all this and contrary to what is the general opinion, I can’t bring myself to say I love it: it’s just too minimalist and abstract for me - I just don’t fully connect with it. As silly as it may sound, it feels like I’m playing a bit of tiling Soduku. Don’t get me wrong, this is a great little abstract affair, perhaps one of the best around, but me I guess I prefer a bit more meat around the bones of my board game experience. I should always be up for a bit of Azul, but there will probably always be something else around that will connect a little bit more with me.
