textfield_comment_value:
If you ask me for my least favorite genre, I would definitely say "abstract".  Mechanisms and rules make a game, but theme brings out the ~experience~, and I want to have it all.  So Azul, which has the confounding double whammy of a totally pasted on theme that has the most tenuous connection possible to the mechanisms, and a beautiful set of components that comprise about 50% of the games enjoyability, somehow has made me love it.  Why are these coasters factories?  Why do I want to make tiles for the royalty of Portugal?  If I accidentally produce too many tiles, why do I let them cascade to the ground and shatter?  Who cares when the tiles are so fun and the puzzle so satisfying to work out?  

You may be tempted to look down at your board in a round of multiplayer solitaire, but if you do, you'll miss out on the chance to stick it to your friends and family and make them take a big -14 to their score.  But, if you play with too much gleeful vengeance, you will flub the multiplayer solitaire which is the point of the game.  The point is to strike the right management of each.  As mentioned, the components are a joy to hold and lay on the table.  Play it right and you slip into a reflective trance of picking tiles, laying them, and adding up your score at the rounds end.  The second side of the player boards are slightly harder to figure, but more rewarding in the end.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Build a beautiful mural in your palace.  Game is based on blue and white Portuguese tiles known as azulejos.
On your turn collect ALL tiles of the same colour/pattern (your choice) from one of the "tile factories" (discs on table) and then move the remainder to the center discard pile.  Place all your newly collected tiles in a SINGLE row on the left - careful, take too many and they fall to the floor (lower part of the game board) which results in a scoring penalty.  On subsequent rounds, you can also pick from the center discard pile as it grows (not your floor).  In order to install your mural ("wall") in your palace (right side of the board) you must first complete a full row on the left (requirements vary from 1 to 5 of like pieces), at which point you can then move one of said pieces to the matching palace wall/pattern to the immediate right, discarding all remaining in the row you removed it from.  Completing a full row on the right triggers the last round.  Score points each time you wall in a tile on the right (bonus points for vertical/horizontal chains), and again at the end of the game for each complete row/column or set of five like tiles installed.
Game play is quick and takes less-than 5 minutes to learn, though mastering it is another story.  The time required to learn how to play does not reflect the level of strategy involved.  I prefer this to Sagrada.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: good quality components.  i would recommend a third party player board overlay to help hold tiles and score marker (mostly the score marker!).  Fun to play.  Great tactile feel with the tiles. 3 rules that should be highlighted: (1) the #1 player marker that gets put in to the center pool at the game start is only ever there on just this first round.  Afterwards it is maintained by the player that took it (& will have -1 point at the round end).  It does not return there to the center pool at any time thereafter ALTHOUGH a variant to have it return there every other round (once the taker gains its 1st player benefit) to inhibit tile grabbing from the center pool is recommended.  (2) other AZUL versions may charge you -1 point to take the START tile as well as -1 point for any other tiles you took with it---this original AZUL does not do that.  It is just -1 point.  (3) If during a new round you WILL NOT be able to place a tile in your right hand side WALL because it is already filled with a similar color tile from a previous round you CANNOT place any tiles of that color in the left hand side PATTERN LINE (see TOP of Page 4 of RULES).  You still may be forced to take them if you have no other choice and then immediately put them into your negative score row FLOOR LINE but you can't place them in your PATTERN LINE.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Friendly abstract game for families. The idea is that you take small amounts of coloured tiles and arrange them via a 'collector' on your private board into the pattern depicted on the box front. By creating 'blocks' with multiple horizontal and vertical adjacent positions filled you score points. Most points wins.

The overarching pattern here is looking very carefully at what you leave for the player(s) after you, and this wears very thin after a while. There is also the somewhat worrying rule that a player who fills a line in the muster will herald the end of the game. How this combines with the fact that you don't want to leave juicy combos for those after you is not clear. As such its meteoric rise in the ranks surely must be explained by the game bits. Or perhaps simply because this is the level of complexity people can muster. I'll play again, but won't seek it out.

[b]Update[/b] After several repeat plays I noticed that strong players always try to create a staircase of sorts as this maximises VPs for tile placement. At some point the staircase becomes so 'thick' that the end of the game is heralded, at which point they'll be impossible to stop if you too hadn't relied on a staircase. This severely damages the game's long-time outlook for me... assuming there was any to begin with. Downgraded the rate.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Well-designed; well-produced. It's a joy to handle the tiles and arrange them on my board. It's a joy to look at the selections of tiles in the center of the table and think about how they might fit into my grand plan; it's also fun to look at those same tiles and think about how to screw over my opponents by changing what's available to them.

As for strategic depth, it seems like there's basically just one strategy for maximizing points: work from the center outward; try to be the first to complete a column; choose a single pattern and try to collect all tiles of that pattern when you're not busy completing a column. It feels like I'm trying to do basically the same obvious thing every game, and the only interesting decision-making happens when drafting tiles. And even that's only interesting because of how my selection changes what's available to my opponents.

The "advanced" version is even *less* interesting because it's less constrained. The strategy becomes even more obvious: try to collect all tiles of a given pattern, and use them to complete the center column.

Overall, it's an abstract game that's nice to handle and that offers a little bit of decision-making, but it doesn't require nearly as much planning or as many interesting tactics as other abstract games.

Me parece una delicia de juego. Es un abstracto de contruir un mosaico.. con una mecánica sencilla, pero que da para estrujarse los sesos.
En tu turno puedes coger todos los azulejos de un color de una ubicación, y el resto pasa al centro, que a su vez, se convierte en otra ubicación. El primero en coger azulejos del centro se llevará un negativo.
Cuando cojes azulejos los colocas en un pool de colocación, que son filas de 1 a 5 posiciones. Todo lo que pongas va auna fila, y el exceso que no entre, pasa a una zona de puntos negativos.
La partida finaliza cuando alguien llena una fila.
Al final hay bonus por filas completadas (+2), columnas completadas (+7) o haber sido capaz de colocar todas las losetas de un color (+10).

Se explica muy rápido, se juega bastante rápido y es absorvente. Muy recomendable. A mí me encantó, además, el aspecto es preioso. Azulejos pequeños de bakelita.

textfield_comment_value:
I know I am going to get a lot of crap for this but Azul is to me like a mix of backgammon and lost cities  You are tracking what the likelihood of what tiles might come up with what is played and then you have to make a bunch of decisions as to do I help my position or hinder my opponents.  There are always very interesting decisions to be made and enough randomness to not run into the same situations over and over.   

What would I change about this game?   

I think the only thing that is sometimes not rewarding is if you get a column earlier and got a lead and then just push the game as fast as you can to ending.  This doesn't happen often but when those situations arise, the game feels like playing out a forgone conclusion.   

The only other thing that I think could be changed is how it is determined who goes first.  The play who has the very first turn has an advantage in setting themselves up for being first for a number of round. The -1 point penalty is too little, in at least 2 players games.  A bidding mechanism for who goes first would in my opinion balanced out this problem.

The game is best at 2 player since each player is directly impacting each other.  With more players, it gets very hard to track each players motives.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
1/8/2023
Azul is so easy to learn, interact, and play. You can play game after game after game and still enjoy with new players and experienced players. The tactility of those pieces feel good and they are definitely top contenders for game pieces you shouldn't eat.

The double sided boards are much appreciated, since an experienced player can really challenge themselves in the same game as a new player. It adds a puzzle to an already great puzzle game. I'm struggling to add more do to it being so straight forward. The scoring can be a bit challenging when you're trying to get use to it, but it eventually falls into place. This can be a potentially brutal game if you're the last player of a round and have to recruit pieces your board can no longer get. That has happened enough that I would strongly advise that to a new player, since that can be such a demotivation to keep playing the game. After a while, you can try to anticipate that better or you are at least aware that can be a potential hamper to your plans.

This is an easy recommend for about any household. I've only ever played one other version, but the replayability and simplicity in this one has really captured the addictive magic that you want to play over and over again.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Flo and I played back to back games of Azul Saturday night. We split the 2 games. I enjoyed it more than Flo did.

First of all, this is just gorgeous. The tiles, the played boards, the completely superfluous floor tiles to put the tiles on. 

The gameplay is simple and easy to teach and to understand. However, there is some deeper strategy going on here. Knowing how to keep your rows open based on the tiles available and when to start really trying to finish rows can be tricky. It is also extremely tactical as you have to adjust what you are taking and what tiles you are leaving for your opponent constantly. Good stuff.

My only real negative would be the fairly high screwage factor, especially in a 2 player game. You can see what your opponent is going for and what tiles they can add to their rows and therefore really stick it to them with tiles they cannot add. Flo stuck me with 4 tiles that I had to add all of them to my floor for -8 points at the end of the round. I suspect this would be less in 3 and 4 player games.

So, the hype train is there for Azul but maybe not to the same level as it is for other people. I can see Flo and I playing this off and on for many years, and for that I can give this a high recommendation.

textfield_comment_value:
Pros

- Easy to learn and teach.

- Fast to setup and play (less than 30 minutes).

- Doesn't require a huge table.

- Replayable because of the competition among players and the different scoring paths.

- Not multiplayer solitaire. The competition among players makes everyone adapt constantly to make the most out of the current state of the board and always be one step ahead of the opponents. Decisions are divided between best for me or worst for them.

- The game design is brilliantly simple! Just like in the games Reef and Century Eastern Wonders, the rules here are so simple yet very strategic and tactical (though more on tactical).

- I have the Azul mini version. The design of the tiles and the scores wouldn't slide around even when moved. It is also small and can be easily carried around.

Cons

- It is confusing that there are 2 types of blue tiles, they could have chosen another color for more clarity such as green. There is a blue tile and there is also a blue tile with a bit of white, making it confusing to describe.

- I bought the Azul mini version. The box is trash! It is so hard to get the game and also hard to put it back. It isn't the usual "open the lid" type of box but rather like the cereal boxes.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: This is one of the best abstract games. Though it's not a head-to-head battle of wits. No direct player interaction other than choosing to take a set of tiles before another player, or perhaps pushing ones they want into the center to screw up the count they need. But that's enough to be take-that in this game. And while the theme is arbitrary for the mechanics, it does make the game beautiful, and the pieces are nice and chunky. And color-blind friendly. The game has few rules, but is quite interesting. It may not play much different game to game, but I still like it. There is some luck given you don't know what tiles will be drawn from the bag each round, but I just really enjoy reacting to that from round to round. There's also a push your luck aspect as you take tiles hoping that your opponents will let you finish the row in the current round. Or taking a sure thing now, hoping another plan doesn't unravel later. Or you might take something subpar, just to avoid getting hit with negative points at the end of the round. The game moves pretty fast, even at max player count. I've also played with a couple expansions, but really I think the base game is enough. I don't get extra enjoyment out of the expansions.

Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
[b]The theme[/b]: Pff! A theme in an abstract filler game? Why should it be there?

[b]The visuals[/b]: I must admit, I don't like it. I mean, yes, the components are soooo good, big, chunky pieces, high-quality boards...but I don't like this weirdly colorful look. Plus what I simply don't understand - why on earth are there 6 colors of tiles, 4 of them are painted with symbols and 2 are not? Really?

[b]The gameplay[/b]: In [thing=230802][/thing], you collect tiles of one color and place them in one row. In that row, you can't place any other color anymore, until you fill it with tiles of that first color. Then, you move one tile somewhere to your wall and score it, if it connect ortoghonally to other tiles. You can never have the same color twice in the same row OR column. Plus, if you should ever take tiles that you can't place anywhere (which happens almost every round), you lose significant points for them. So you need to carefully navigate through the game, what to take when and where to place it.

[b]The fun[/b]: Although there is no interaction, the game certainly is fun. You solve your own little puzzle but you need to also observe what your opponents could want so you don't help them.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Play (7) 60%
Plays quickly and simply with enough depth to keep you on your toes.  It has elements of push your luck, risk mitigation as well as some long term planning elements.  There is an interesting bit of game state manipulation too especially with 2-3 players where if you can see ahead you can try to skew things in your favor for later turns.  A solid amount of punch is packed into a nice 15 minute game here and the "blank board" can definitely provide some more choices.

Practicality(9) 30%
The rules are a leaflet and extremely easy to remember.  The game plays in about 15 minutes and a new player will understand the mechanics after 1 turn...the strategy will probably take a full play to start to make sense.  For some reason the idea that you fill your depot and then keep 1 tile regardless of which row you filled is hard to grasp initially for some people.

Parts (9) 10%
I really wanted to give the parts a 10 but the scoring track is just suspect enough for me to ding it a point.  I wish the board had a cut outs for the scoring track to avoid knocking the cube around.  Outside of that it is nearly perfect, great insert, attractive art and the pieces really make the game.

Overall: 7.8

textfield_comment_value:
[i]Juin 2021[/i]: [b]6.5[/b]

[i]Edit juin 2024[/i]: [b]6[/b] - Baisse de 0,5 par rapport à son ancienne note, tout comme pour Azul: Maitre chocolatier (6.8 → 6.3). Au même moment, nouvelle note accordée au 3e Azul joué: Pavillons d'été (7).

Je pense qu'Azul peut être considéré mon jeu baromètre pour la note de 6. L'expérience de jeu pas vilaine en soi, le jeu plutôt joli, et sa mise en place et sa durée, rapides toutes les deux, le maintiennent au plancher des jeux "ok" (6).

Néanmoins, j'éprouve certains petits malaises en y jouant. Le type d'interaction que propose Azul me dérange peut-être un peu, ainsi que les points négatifs qui deviennent parfois inévitables dû au nombre de lots (de choix) restants (j'éprouve un peu le même sentiment avec 7 Wonders: Duel).

J'ai étrangement l'impression qu'il est peut-être à son meilleur à deux, alors que paradoxalement, un nombre importants de jeux abstraits (ainsi que d'autres) pour deux joueurs m'apparaissent bien plus stimulants que Azul, tant par rapport aux options que m'offrent ces jeux, mais aussi au type d'analyse, de calculs et d'observation du plan de jeu adverse que requièrent ces autres bons / "meilleurs" jeux à deux (par rapport à Azul.)
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Abstract game in which players have to take one of 5 types of tiles from a number of platters, each filled with 4 tiles randomly drawn from a bag. The tiles not taken end up in the middle. Players can also take all tiles of 1 type from the middle. The first to do so looses 1 point, however. At the same time, this player becomes the start player in the next round.
The tiles taken have to be placed in 1 of 5 rows which can contain 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5 tiles respectively. If too many tiles are taken, so they can't fit in the row, points are lost. At the end of a round the rows which have been completely filled with 1 type of tiles are emptied. 1 tile is placed on a 5 X 5 board on the same row as the one just emptied and on the same type of tile. Each row of course contains the 5 types, and this is also true for each column. When a tile is placed on this 5 x 5 board points are scored: 1 point if not placed orthogonally adjacent to another tile, in the case it is placed next to another tile, the number of tiles in the row and/or the column in which it is placed are counted.
End scoring: 2 points for each row completely filled, 7 points for each column, and 10 points for 5 tiles of the same colour.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
There is usually something about a game that I like, but that's not the case with Azul. I find zero excitement in placing abstractly-patterned tiles into rows and columns for points, and though Azul poses as a light game, it really isn't. It's a sequencer, where you're thinking about possible sequences, over and over and over. 
To calculate the sequences and make informed moves, and not just half-assed ones, you have to take into consideration what is happening on other player boards, and in anything but a drawn-out contest between two players (and there are so many more interesting games for that, chess, for starters), that is just too much information and calculation to process for a "light" game. This just gets worse and worse as the boards fill up, culminating in an endgame that promotes a downtime-inducing orgy of analysis as players calculate ways to avoid ending up with a bunch of negative points, and where one might even calculate final scores, given enough time or room for obstinacy. 
This is a pure abstract calculation game, one I find both painful and completely uninteresting. I'd prefer playing Bingo, or War with 8 decks of cards, over another game of Azul.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Okay, before you get turned off on Azul thinking its a game about tiling a Portuguese bathroom floor, hear me out. This little abstract game leaves me HUNGRY to play more of it. The pieces remind me of starbursts when I hold them in my hand, the game comes with some nice coasters which I've never seen before in a game. It's really well put together, they've thought of everything.

As far as the game itself is concerned, it is an abstract game that provides a lot of chances to mess up other players. The game itself feels amazingly fair, and lends itself strongly to those who can plan ahead in the face of the decisions their friends are going to make. Combos score a lot of points and leave you feeling satisfied. 

Azul plays fairly quickly and doesn't leave you with any kind of fatigue at the end, mostly because the end of the game teeters on a knifes edge as soon as 4 turns into the game. You end up trying to balance ending the game against how many points you and your friends are going to score, always looking at the other people playing and trying to decide if you can go for the next combo or focus on short terms point scoring. Good stuff! Come tile a floor with me!
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
9/5/19 - It's an interesting concept, and usually fun for the first few rounds, where you can go after any color you want, so you can kind of try to play based on what is available.

However, due to the way the game works, where your options become limited based on what you've done in previous rounds, the fun kind of dies out for the last couple of rounds. (like, if you've already played blue tiles in all your rows, you can't ever take blue again... so if you get to the last round and there are blue tiles in the factories that your opponent needs, well you can't really do anything to stop them from taking them)

I don't really know what could be done differently but it just feels like there isn't much to do in the last couple rounds; you're basically just taking the only colors that will fit on your board, regardless of what your opponents are doing, which is a bit anti-climatic.

So, overall it's decent. I'll play it if people want, but if I get asked "what do you want to play?" I'm not going to pick it.


2/16/22 - I've downgraded this from 6 to 5. I put the newer Azul: Summer Pavilion game at 6 and I feel that is better than this one, so I'm bumping this down.

textfield_comment_value:
Very fun game with honestly one of the most beautiful elegant art styles I have seen in a boardgame. The tiles have a wonderful weight to them that makes you want to pick them up and play with them. They also make a great sound when they click together in the mixing bag, weird as that is to say! The boards and the bag is wonderful quality, too.

The game mechanics are good, lends itself to multiple layers of strategy. I have only played this game with two players, and am unsure how the strategy will hold up with more than two, and will come back and edit this post when I have.

All in all, I must be honest that it doesn't see too much play compared to my other boardgames, but that is not because I don't enjoy it, more because it is a particular game that requires people who enjoy the math and one could say, "plain" strategy aspects present in the game. Other games have a narrative or are flashy/humorous in a way that delights people's sense of adventure, whereas this game could be seen as a bit boring compared to those. However, I still enjoy my time playing with those more interested in logicky-slightly mathematical games. They're just harder to find, lol.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Azul is another game that I put in the same "group" with Sagrada and Qwirkle. This group of games require arrangement of playing pieces based on color, number, and/or symbol.

These games are all on the light side , with Complexity Rating (or weight) of under 2, but within the group, I order them from the heaviest to lightest as follows: Sagrada, Azul, and Qwirkle, with Sagrada being the most demanding in terms of longer term planning and more logical thinking . The first two games are essentially multi-player solitaires, with Azul being more so.

Sagrada, by far is the most headache producing of the group since it requires the most concentration to work through all your options to optimize your player board during your turn. Depending on how seriously you want to optimize your score, the process of selecting your dice can be a chore and agonizing, which can reduce the fun factor.

Of the three, I enjoy Azul somewhat more since it's less taxing on the brain than Sagrada, but still offers some decision making challenges. On the other hand, Qwerkle is primarily a party game involving more limited and fewer tough decision making situations.
Reviewed: 05/28/18
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Azul is an interesting but quick abstract strategy game with good looking pieces. It clocks in at about 30 minutes with 4 if everyone has played and is a bit shorter with fewer. It feels a little bit like a less restrictive sagrada, even though there are no dice. You are drafting tiles and then trying to fill out rows in your "production" area so that you can place that color of tile in its spot in your wall. You then score extra points for placing next to tiles you have already placed, and end game points for completed rows, columns, and sets of the same color. 

I have two minor cons that prevent this from being higher. First, with the higher player counts it can be pretty chaotic and much harder to plan/easier to have your plans ruined. Second, there is a bit of luck involved where the colors you need just don't show up how you need them and you end up with one of your bigger rows in limbo until you can get the tiles for them. Also, you can get stuck taking a lot of bad tiles at the end of a round and take enough negative points that you probably won't come back.

Still, the game is so quick and tactful that I would call it a must try for most gamers.

textfield_comment_value:
there is a delicious "i split, you choose" mechanic to the game behind the obvious row/column/set building. it plays as quick as advertised, but can be wonderfully thinky as you try to pick tiles that poison the pool. i can't wait to see how this holds up with four players!! superb with two!

update... okay, years later i find myself walking my fingers past this one when it comes time to pick a game off the shelf. my wife, however, continues to ask for it occasionally. for me it's become a game of managing the last two rows. or rather managing the top three and trying to ignore the siren song of large groups. not to discount my wife's skill at this game, but it really seems like those times where i manage not to get lured into focusing on the bottom two rows i will win by a lot. else i lose by a lot. you'd think i could learn or maybe be intrigued enough to play more and figure out what's happening. instead i'm mostly done. so the rating needs to take a dip.

Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
~Visually appealing abstract mosaic-building with just the right amount of tactics~

There's a lot of interaction here- especially at 2 players.  The tile drafting is all about balancing what you need vs denying your opponent while dancing around who might get stuck with a bunch of unusable tiles (negative points).

My dislike of chess is well-documented, but this is a 2-player abstract that I love.  The sweet spot for tactical planning is 3-to-4 moves ahead in a less complex (but not less satisfying) field.  And it's not a matter of "screw it, I'll just make a move." You *can't* plan ad infinitum since the board resets with new tiles every few turns- which is good.

There's also round-to-round strategic planning.  Since all tiles are eventually drawn from the bag, it's important to pay attention to how much of each type is still out there- but not in an unpleasant way like trying to juggle a dozen different lines of play in your head.

Scaling to 3 or 4 players is likely to create a somewhat more relaxed / less cutthroat game.

Finally, the physical components are compelling.  The tiles have good heft, good color, and are just fun.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Azul for me is the poster child for why sometimes theme doesn't matter.  When I first started this hobby I thought it was the most important thing in a game.  It's not.  

Both Azul and Photosynthesis came out around the same time.  Both have been lauded by serious gamers.  Lots of people say Photosynthesis is an abstract, but it's not.  It's mechanically very thematic.  I suspect the people who say it's not are into flavor text and characters.  What you do in Photosynthesis makes sense thematically.  It's rather easy to teach.  But it's very repetitive and I found it rather boring.  

Azul, on the other hand, has rules that aren't very thematic.  Yes, there's a theme and there are some things that fit.  But at its core it's abstract.  Ah, but the gameplay, that's another matter.  Requires more thought and planning that it first appears.  Screwage is there if you want to play that way.  It's not Chess - not even close - but it's a very good game.  I knew after one play that I liked Azul.  I knew after one play of Photosynthesis that I could never play it again and never care.  Theme didn't play a role in making the better game.

Abstract games, I like them very much and most of the time I am really good at it. textfield_comment_value: I love this game and so does my teen son. We play this game all the time, over and over. We'll play during meals, after meals, randomly during the day - it's just one of those games that's easy to learn how to play, but so much to learn on how to win!  Great things about the game are that it's constantly changing since the tile selection is never the same, there is a grey board side that allows you to choose your own pattern (still following a few rules for tile placement), opportunities to play offensively and defensively, and it's aesthetically pleasing.  The structure of having a negative points board and bonus points adds another level of challenge to the game that can make a big difference on whether you win or lose. I've lost this game a few times simply because the other player ended up with more bonus points than me and stuck me with a few negative points.  I've played with several different people and it's interesting to see how we all think a little differently when it comes to which tiles we take.  I'm still figuring out new strategies each time I play, which makes this game outstanding! Excellent play value!
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: Beautiful tiles. Enjoyable abstract. I like that the game is as much about outthinking your opponents as playing your own board. Definitely keep an eye on what tiles other players need, and factor that into your tile selection. Great tactical strategy about when to select tiles from the middle to change the order of who may get stuck with leftover tiles at the end of the round. Sometimes foisting negative points on other players is just as helpful in terms of end game score outcomes. Also, this game plays well at all player counts. Two-player is great since it's a different strategy than higher player counts due to likely only going through the tile bag once if you stick to 5 rounds. I added an additional bag to my box, so that used tiles go right in the 2nd bag each round. Speeds things up. Also, this game plays great with kids. If needed, you can modify the game for younger players by not having floor tiles count against them. That way they can just focus on the strategy and not get moody about taking negative points. Once the kids start beating you regularly, then you know that they are ready for the regular rules.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Played with correct rules, this was still quite a good game but  it slowed down the game play or at least felt that way from my unintentional variant to game play. Still have opportunity to hose people, particularly late in the game. 

FIRST IMPRESSION:

Played two games, one with the wild tiles and one without and enjoyed both. Appears to be various strategies to pursue while keeping an eye on your opponents to gauge the timing of the end game as well as making life more challenging for them by taking/dumping their desired factory spot. Tiles are pretty but are lighter than I expected. Easily plays in under an hour once everyone knows what they're doing. 

Wild tiles take 10 tiles out of the game (2 of each color) and give you potentially more options in the construction phase.

Okay, played the first 8 games incorrectly with my own variant...;-) We were playing if you took the middle tiles you took everything and floored the ones you didn't use. Instead you only take one color of tiles from the middle and leave the rest so it isn't quite the poison pill as before. Or, perhaps, it is a different type of poison pill.

UPDATE: Played with 4, the scoring seems to be much higher. It's harder to fork other players, so you don't get caught in bad situations as often. There are also more tiles to look at in a turn, so you can usually find what you need in the first couple of passes through the new tiles.

I don't think I'm interested in playing it with 4 again, as the forking is what interests me about the game. But 3 could be very good, giving the right combination of forking, more information than with 2, and no zero-sum outcomes.

11/17: An interesting abstract with shades of Coloretto or Piece o' Cake. My play was with 2 players, which felt a little brain-burny in the same way that Patchwork does. Figure out what you want, what your opponent wants, and how to fork them into doing what you want them to three turns in advance. But I suspect the game is both less brain-burny and potentially more interesting with 3 (or even 4). Players would be able to incentivize others to do things in both of their interest by setting up juicy splits.

Would love to try it with 3, maybe twice in a row, to see if it can become an 8.

textfield_comment_value:
I didn't think I would be saying this, but out of the 13 different board games we got for Christmas in my family, this one might end up being my favorite.  It's so elegant and simple, yet there can be a lot of strategy involved to maximize your score.  I played this Christmas day with two 86 year old women and my 14 year old son and got destroyed by them.  Then I introduced it to my two adult sons and played many games with them and their younger brother.  So simple to teach.  Even the scoring, which I've seen some complain about, was picked up immediately by the older and younger crowd.
My only complaint, which is the case with many games that have come out recently, is the game board.  I'll end up spending half again what the game costs to buy acrylic overlays for it when they come out like I did with Blood Rage, Great Western Trail and Terraforming Mars.  Charge me more and give me a Scythe like game board.  One small bump and you can wipe out everything.  My 26 year old got frustrated with it and started keeping score on a piece of paper.  It's not going to take away from my overall score, but its frustrating.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
tl;dr: solid abstract

This is one of those games that can stand up to [thing=9674][/thing] and [thing=25669][/thing] as a multiplayer abstract that appeals to both families and gamers. Again we have nice chunky bits and easy rules that lead to interesting choices. The main difference is that in this game everyone creates their own tableau, and the interaction comes from competition for tiles from the main pool. When do you take what tiles from the tiles in the middle or the big pool that is created by the left over tiles there?
I do have a couple of thoughts on the bits though. For the most part this has been put together with attention to detail, as one would expect from this publisher. But why does every player have their own scoring track that is easy to screw up when you reach for bits in the center of the table? A separate board with 1 score track for all players would have been better. Also: the red and the blue don't have any pattern printed on them, and it looks a bit like someone forgot to print them. It's a weird choice.
But all in all a solid, enjoyable game!

Initial rating: 7/10

textfield_comment_value: Perfect for in between! Yes, Azul is really simple and yes, there are lots of other fast, simple games. Why is it so easy to find players of any age? First of all there is the constructive aspect. You build something up and measured against the mechanics, the theme is therefore well chosen. Then there's the logical challenge. You have to proceed strategically, otherwise it won't work. Although this can sometimes be quite complex, the way it works remains so comprehensible that children can keep up. Even tactical variations are possible: If you want to score over the columns, it's hard to get full colors, especially if someone else sets on a fast end and therefore primarily on the intermediate instead of the final scores. After all, there is sometimes even an unpleasant amount of interaction when the others make sure that you have to lay your cellars full of stones and the minus points cancel out the nice lead. Not only fast games like to be either one-dimensional or destructive or autistic or show big differences in performance. Azul miraculously succeeds in ensuring that none of this spoils the fun.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
This appeared not long before Christmas 2017 and immediately sold out. It's just about the perfect Christmas gift. It's reasonably compact, but big enough not to seem stingy. It has heft, so it doesn't seem cheap. It's pretty and the pieces are chunky and tactile. It's fairly easy to explain and plays 4. Games are relatively short and don't lead to quarrels. What's not to like?

It's a rather bland puzzle with players only interacting by taking tiles someone else wants. There's not much opportunity to look ahead, because you can't really predict what your opponent(s) might choose to do - there is rarely going to be an obvious best move - so the game is more tactical than strategic. And that makes it shallow. It's sort of thinky, in the sense that every time it comes round to your turn you're solving the same immediate puzzle, but it's not GIPF thinky, and certainly not Hive thinky.

I'd guess that unlike Splendor, which has a enthusiastic following years on down the line (inexplicably, in my view), Azul will almost entirely drop off the voxpop radar within a year.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
1st play didn't grab me. Yes, it is fun trying to puzzle your wall and the drafting is indeed very clever and tense. And yes, the game looks pretty, the tiles feel nice. But I cannot say that there is enough to the game play that you would want to have this in your collection. Expectations were high due to all the hype, but ultimately this fell flat for me: uninteresting theme, no strategic game play whatsoever - this is pure tactics and to top it up, the game gives a strong incentive to screw your fellow players - nothing we fancy in particular.

Edit: Rating adjusted. My wife insisted we play it again - and I am grateful we did, six games in now. Otherwise I might have missed a great game. Trying to maximize your score while minimizing your opponents in this tight and very quick game with no words is a refreshing site after work and at the same time quite addictive

my one caveat remains: this is a very agressive game - where you are encouraged to block your opponent, this stresses me and I am continuing my search for games that are fun without this interaction.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
I really dislikes Azul. I can't understand how it's a family game. I am very much trying to like it but the aspect of blocking, just because you can and therefor terrorise your opponent just doesn't cut me as a family game. It looks good, the idea of placing mosaik tiles sounds nice.. But when it comes down to it I wouldn't show it to my family. A nice day would quickly turn bloody. The game should be labelled "For those who love to make people feel misserable". If you can bow down to the masses and accept that most moves others make feel like a knife in your heart. THEN Azul is it! If you very much enjoy laughing while your opponent is crying, this game is for you. 

If you want to have a nice time and be able to be human after playing a board game.. THIS GAME IS NOT FOR YOU. Try something where you won't get mosaik pieces thrown at you. Like... Engine-building. Mystic Vale could be a suggestion. Welcome too for roll-and-write. Can't stop - to make it even more easy. Still interaction - but it's not something ripping your heart out. Those games are actually fun.

textfield_comment_value:
Wow this game lives up to the Essen hype. Really simple (if slightly intuitive, e.g. odd taking 1st player token gives you negative points and maybe nongamers might be confused about the scorig) yet has quite a bit to think about between balancing how many and what tiles you are placing, and the placement in your grid to maximize points. It also has pretry high interaction for a euro, plays quick, and the graphics and components really highlight how clean the gameplay is. The only negatives are since it is rather deterministic it might lead to AP for some people, and while very solid it is not spectacular. I think almost everyone will like it, but don't fret if you can't play it.

EDIT: Somewhere around my 20th play I really soured on this game. While it is still mechanically very interesting and has a lot of interaction for a euro, it is a lot of brain burning for what isn't particularly rewarding due to the abstract scoring, and compared to full on abstracts it lacks the feeling of creativity of positional play. At the same time, the game feels samey

textfield_comment_value:
As a newbie to the board game hobby I've mostly been playing games that have been tried and true because money is limited and games tend to be better values over time. Despite that, I do love to just browse Barnes and Noble and Target to see what new or clearance board games they have and Azul has caught my eye more than once. When it won the Spiel des Jahres I jumped on it after watching a tutorial on how to play, it looked so beautiful and fun!

The game itself is easy to learn, but I feel that there is a nice amount of depth in strategy to make it a game with longevity. The first game took us slightly over an hour, but the second game took us about 35 minutes now that we have an understanding of how to play.

I'm going to attempt to play a 4 player game very soon to see how that changes things.

Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
1 play

I'm aware I've only scratched the surface, but I think I can see the shape of the depth here. I love that you can play this game light and flowing, or play it deep and thinky. The structure is elegant, and the player interaction feels organic colon looking at other boards can give you a clue as to what is going to be easy and hard to get, and also what might screw up someone else's strategy. I'm usually not a fan of point salad scoring, but The scoring is simple enough here that you can intuitively understand whether a strategy is paying off or not. The game is on the short side, too short to get something very elaborate up and running, but long enough to entice you towards ambitious projects like building verticals or sets of five of a color. 

The instructions do a decent job, though I think there's room for improvement. I can't believe they don't address the question of whether you can build the same color in two different rows at the same time (the consensus I'm seeing online is that you can).

Complexity/weight: 2 out of 5.

"VERY GOOD"

A fun abstract, that makes you smile all the time ! Pleasant to play, and handling such colourful, chunky, tinkling tiles is a real bonus. A game with an inbuilt aesthetic experience !

textfield_comment_value: Absolutely amazing.  Played with my GF last night and after our first game (only 25-30 minutes), we immediately played again... then again.  The pace is excellent, I'm sure with 3 or 4 players it is just as good.  It's an odd thing that we try not to be "mean" to each other and leave a large number of the same tiles on the floor that someone else needs to pick up and lose a bunch of points... it's a game that you don't want to play "confrontational".  At least that's what we are like with it... How it handles the Starting Player round to round is quite brilliant IMO.  And somehow it feels to naturally balance in terms of scoring.  Sometimes the game ends much earlier than you want it too, if you have no choice but to finish a horizontal line before you get to finish more verticals... that or eat a bunch of points to keep going! textfield_comment_value:
1 play, 4p. You can play it from turn to turn like some kind of solitär, but your left neighbor will most likely win. If you want to play it "right", you have to consider the result of your current turn for the options for all players. However, to foresee what impact your turn will have, you have to consider all options and the likelihood that the other players will choose what seems to be the "best" option for them. Only then you can play the game "good". Otherwise it is all just chaos and chance. This applies also if the other players do not choose the option that you decide would be their best one.
The crucial thing is that there seems to be one "best" option for you, and you want to find it considering several dozens or even hundreds variants what the other players may do. This causes downtime and the uncomfortable feeling, that you should have even been thinking more about it, because you have the feeling that there should be a better turn. Kingmaker problem anyway. Poor with 4p, maybe could run with 2 - I will never know.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Azul is a really great abstract drafting game that is pretty easy for non-gamers to pick up in my experience. 

The components (tiles) are fantastic to hold and the unique drafting mechanic really shines in the game. The challenge to pick the right color tiles to try and manipulate the drafting pool to have what you need and not what the other players need is a key part of the game. 

The scoring mechanic has confused some of the people I have played with their first time or two, but I don't think that means it's bad. Rewarding adjacent tile placement is a great way to reward planning, as those who plan well will break away from those who don't in scoring. 

And rewarding the riskier bonus of having all of one color is both a good incentive and allows for people to be competitive with different strategies, which some abstract games fail to do.

One thing that I don't like is that the box lid is part of the game play. I'm likely going to start using something else to put the played tiles in before they are returned to the bag.

textfield_comment_value:
Components: amazing, simply amazing (except the first player tile)
Complex: easy to learn and play
Weight: family
Players: 2 to 4
Length: less than 45 mins
Mechanics: build your pattern scoring as much as you can
Decisions: enough, could seem obvious, but not so much
Opinion: the game is beautiful, really beautiful. You have to build your wall with Portuguese tiles. The tiles are amazing.
There are some factories in the middle producing them, and, in your turn, you pick one color from one of the factories or from the center of the table and place them on your board. If you fill one row, you have built one tile in your wall. And you have to place them like a Sudoku (no same color horizontally or vertically).
It seems pretty easy, but you have enough things to take into account, should I take this one I need, or try to block my opponents, later on they could be too many tiles of that color so I have to place some on my ground floor (and they are minus points).
In a nutshell, amazing family game that can be played by anyone
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Azul is a beautiful game of tile laying and speculation. Or to be exact, early turns in a round are speculative as you are trying to guess what your opponents are up to. As tiles get taken from the offering and after narrowing down the number of possible end game sequences, the nature of the game changes into brutal number crunching exercise for the last few turns of a round. You are just min-maxing the point swings generated through the last moves. This has to be kept in mind when playing with AP prone people, since it can be quite frustrating when the flow of the game is regularly changing. A bit counter-intuitive scoring does not help the matter.

Nevertheless, I liked the game and would like to play again. I also reckon that after a few games under your belt the changes in the pace of the game will become less drastic because you will learn to analyse the situation faster.

I also have to mention that playing the game is also physically quite satisfying since the components are fun to fondle and play with.

Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Probably the most well-known tile placement, abstract puzzle, pattern-building board game out there.

This is one of those games you can easily pull in newcomers and get them addicted to its genius simplicity. The components are well done too. The tiles look like candies and don't get me talking about their Valentine's edition.

I haven't tried the other Azul variants, but this original seems very versatile and long-lasting, like a chess or say a base Mahjong. I'm not exactly good at it, same thing I could say when I'm playing Patchwork. Most of other people I invited to play are very good at it, and they are not even in the hobby. Perhaps, Azul is something that is popular that anyone who doesn't have concrete investment in the hobby can love and keep it for a lifetime.

This is also the game I'm planning to entice my father and mother. It will probably help them exercise their brain given they are aging now.

Given its accessibility and addictive gameplay, I believe Azul, will always stay in my collection.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Components = 4/5
Beautiful components. The only thing missing in my opinion is a layered board to place the tiles for an extra comfort.

Gameplay = 4.5/5
The game is simple to learn but very deep in-play. Cerebral, tactical, and abstract, the game plays very fluidly, with limited down time as observing the decision making process of your opponent(s) is just as important as your own turn.
I would not recommend playing it with more than 3 players. I find dueling very enjoyable too.

Replayability = 4/5
Each finished session calls for a new one. The game has the same replayability as chess.

Fun = 3.5/5
Not everyone will find this game fun, but most people will find it interesting (even non gamers). This game is a great way to introduce people into the hobby.
Games are not too long allowing for rematches. looking at possible plays and reading your opponent is very fun.

A great game with a solid reputation. I find it also make a pretty great birthday present for anyone.
It's pretty, interesting, and fun.

textfield_comment_value:
"Overall, I think Azul is great! It's got a nice blend of luck and strategy, the component quality is excellent (and reminiscent of Splendor and Sagrada, both games that I would say occupy a similar space), and it's a lot of fun to play. The major thing that will draw a lot of people to it is the art, but it's getting lauded by many now for its gameplay. I enjoy the gameplay, sure, but I find the scoring mechanics to be a bit difficult for newer players to get used to, leading to some frustration down the road. It's nothing that can't be overcome, but it may be something worth noting, as I think it's a nontrivial hiccup in an otherwise very smooth and very fun game that may even end up being game of the year. It's still occasionally a bit hard to find new, but if you're looking for a very nicely-produced strategy game that you can play with the whole family, Azul is certainly not a bad choice; it's an excellent one!"

For my full thoughts, check out https://whatsericplaying.com/2018/07/09/azul/

textfield_comment_value: This game is incredibly fun to play and has great replay value!  This is a favorite among my roommates and I.  It’s not too difficult to learn and it doesn’t take too long to set up and play.  The only complaint we had was that getting the square discard tiles out of the box lid and back into the bag can be somewhat tedious.  They get caught up in the corners and the tile bag isn’t with big enough to be able to just dump them straight in.  First world problems you know.  I happened to have a small collapsible pet bowl, you know those silicon ones that fold flat.  It fits perfectly in the box, even when closed and put away.  It’s also just the right size to hold discard tiles and dump them back into the bag without any escaping and doesn’t take up as much space on the table.  So weird as it may sound I highly recommend getting a small collapsible bowl to keep in the box if you play this a lot, it’s a nice quality of experience boost. textfield_comment_value: HEAVEN & ALE, REWORLD, RIVERBOAT und eben AZUL - Kiesling mutiert anno Essen 2017 mengenmässig zum Stefan Feld in seinen produktivsten Phasen. Und dies als Altmeister. Altmeisterschaft merkt man vor allem dem abstrakten AZUL an: retrospektiv in seiner Idee spielt AZUL routiniert seinen eigenen Autor und wird zum Knizia: Steine nehmen, anlegen, werten. Die Steine wurden zwar thematisch zu portugiesischen Kacheln mit wunderhübschen Verzierungen gemacht und sind ein haptisches Vergnügen, AZUL bleibt aber ein reines Wertungsspiel ohne wenn und aber, das sich in 20-30 Minuten runterspielt. Das Spiel hiess in einer früheren Entwicklungsphase EIN STEIN GEHT NOCH und hatte den Einstein als Denkgenie verkappt im Namen, was das Werk besser beschreibt. Für Freunde abstrakter Designs ist AZUL eine sichere Bank ähnlich eines Bausparvertrags. textfield_comment_value: Il migliore astratto degli ultimi anni con quel minimo di ambientazione che serve, grazie alle mattonelle stile andaluso che sono adorabili lo rendono una piccola grande gemma. Il plurisessantenne Michael Kiesling sorprende tutti con un bel gioco semplice ed elegante, facile da apprendere e veloce da eseguire. Appagante e fluido, di media pretesa ma di ottima resa. Con un estetica fantastica e regole semplici si può usare per introdurre i meno avvezzi ai giochi da tavolo, ma ha una profondità che a prima vista non si direbbe, sia per esperti che per giocatori meno esperti. Fattore fortuna lievemente presente, un po conta nell'uscita delle piastrelle dal sacchetto, e fattore sgambetto dell'avversario onnipresente (tenetevi aperti a più strategie). Pertanto vale la pena improvvisarsi, almeno una volta nella vita, piastrellisti intenti a chiudere un mosaico colorato. Invoglia sempre immediatamente a chiedere la rivincita, come le ciliege, una partita tira l'altra. Spiel des Jahres... 2018.

textfield_comment_value:
Might upgrade this to 10 if it stands the test of time or downgrade it to 7 or 8 if it gets repetitive.

Initial impressions after a few games. Quick, tactical game with a sheer elegance, a short playtime, that can appeal to a vast audience of casual and gamers alike. Great production and a fair price.

Plays very differently with 2, 3 and 4 players. The 2-player game has a strategic depth that the 4-player game lacks, but two aspects do not come into play with 2 - set bonus are hard to get and tile penalties are rarely important enough to play a role. I wish the two-player game went a little longer as the player board is half empty when the game ends, but I also wish the 4-player game was more controlled and more strategic. 

I love it right now and it seduces everyone who tries it around me, but I can't say if it will bear repeated play. It feels like the only valid strategy right now is to pick a column and try to fill it, then play vertically and horizontally around it. We'll see.

textfield_comment_value:
This game I can break out with folks that don't really play board games much, and we can all have a good time with it. After so many plays, I still often find myself losing to less experienced players. I make sure to share my strategy ahead of time so they can try it as well.

It's so simple but so satisfying too. Planning out the draft is great. Nailing your rows is great. Missing an important row or taking a bunch of negatives is a heart breaker.

This game would be the perfect coffee table game. It just needs all of its components to be upgraded to display piece quality.

I will say that Azul does get tiring to play on repeat. Doing so makes me yearn for something with a bit more meat. 

In fact now that I think about it, maybe Azul mainly gets its lasting power from how fun it is to play with people you haven't played it with before. I love introducing it to people. After a couple games though, I'd probably want to permanently move on to something else with the same people.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
I really like the idea of this game. A beautiful, nominally abstract game with pleasingly chunky tiles that has a mysterious charm and social capital going for it. However, there's something counterintuitive to the rules. 

When a new player first sees the game components, he just KNOWS he's going to pick up those chunky tiles and put them on the mosaic-pattern board. But then we go through the rules and **actually** you have to put the tiles over here in this step area, and you have to fill up each step before you can put those tiles onto the mosaic area, and anything in excess is going to go to the bottom and penalise you.

There's something unforgivably frustrating about how this game looks very obviously like it's going to do one simple thing, but then it does this other slightly convoluted thing instead.

This is a good game, by the way. Due to its great popularity I feel at liberty to criticise it like this. But it is definitely a good game. Just not an excellent game.

textfield_comment_value:
A relaxing game...until you find the nasty sting in its tail.

[thing=230802][/thing] is an abstract game and one which seems to be becoming one of the hits of Essen.  I found the tile-laying to be a pleasant enough game, with good and interesting simple spatial decisions.  What I was not expecting, and fear may be the undoing of the game with a wider public, is the way a round can end with some real brutal play forcing opponents to take a bunch of negative points.  And with this some kingmaking may be inevitable, as you can be in a position where you decide who takes the negatives that will arise. 

So I started off thinking this is a must-buy game my family can play together, a sort of King Domino, which they love, but with more going on.  But by the end of the game I had changed my mind: the take-that elements presenting themselves at the end of many rounds mean it is too nasty a game for my family. Maybe even so much that it threatens its possible SDJ potential?
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
A game looking so simple, yet beloved by many families and spawning 3 sequel games and a reimplementation…

Azul is a tile placement game in which you draft tiles and place them in rows on your board. When a row is complete you move a tile from that row at the end of the round to score it. The game ends when one player completes a horizontal row. The player with the most victory points wins!

Our thoughts
+ The tiles have a nice look and feel.
+ The rules are easy to teach.
+ Engaging gameplay with high interaction.
+ The game never runs too long, even at a 4-player count.
- Scoring can be a bit confusing the first time.
- The cube to keep your score can be a bit fiddly, don’t bump the table!

We definitely understand how Azul became a well loved game. Neat design along with simple rules and engaging gameplay makes it clear why it can truly be called a “modern day classic”.

Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
The Pitch: Build a bathroom floor.  

The Good: Beautiful art, solid production values.  Simple to teach, and fast games.  Good level of interactivity: easy to say 'fuck you' to another player with only a cursory glance at his boards.  The 'take a tile and throw the rest in the middle' mechanic is novel and easy to understand.

The Bad: Has a slight problem with runaway leaders.  Two variants of blue tiles cause minor communication issues.  Scoring requires a little handholding for new players.  The penalty for taking from the middle seems too light.

The Silly: It's a whole lot of fun for the whole table when one player is forced to eat -10 points because he had to take a whole bunch of tiles he can't use.

The Verdict: Solid filler game.  I liked this game quite a bit but it didn't blow me a way.  It's a gorgeous game, and it has a lot of strategy and will push you to think in different things.  That being said, it's not as good as other short abstract games.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Rating is for the 2 player game, which allows for lots of confrontational interaction. Setup time is zero and it plays in 30 minutes. As you select tiles, you need to balance adjacency scoring, the end-game trigger, the end-game scoring bonuses and the incentive to step all over your opponent's plans. After playing once, you immediately want to play again. Due to my preference for confrontation in games, I find the game best at 2. The directness of the confrontation decreases as you increase in players. The only negative is the game is an abstract. Zero theme, but I'm fine with that due to the setup, play time and level of confrontation at 2 players. Bonus: wife loves the game.

The production is quite nice. The player board and Bakelite tile combination makes it quite easy to glance at your opponents' player board and figure out what they've collected.

Rating for the 3 to 4 player game would be around a 6 as an inoffensive filler.

textfield_comment_value:
Engaging, elegant drafting game.
-Explanation is typically 5-10 minutes. The game is understood well after the first round.
-The game is pretty and the tiles are great to handle.
-The game is rewarding of different strategies, and players can choose how aggressive (eg. hate-drafting), risky (eg. leaving lots of tiles in the middle), or easygoing the game turns out.
-Only very minor set-backs. The point system can be tricky to teach some people. The math may also turn some people off. The theme is not particularly strong (obviously, since it's an abstract) which makes the games a little less immersive. While the game has a nice progression (it gets more crunchy and more rewarding as the game goes on), it can feel a bit repetitive (however, this also makes it relaxing).

Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Azul really shines at 2 players. Its simple mechanics for tile picking, merging tiles, occupied rows, floor line, first player token, combine to produce some very interesting trade offs, leading to an intense, strategic game. The randomness is just enough to force you to adapt to each situation, without swinging the game in either player's favour. This is exactly what I appreciate in a game.
Despite the interaction between players being purely blocking each other, in a two-player game, it becomes absolutely cut-throat. You cannot afford to ignore what your opponent is doing, or what they could do to you.
In conclusion, Azul is a game with a high skill ceiling, and you can really enjoy perfecting your gameplay. Azul teaches you a lesson on every loss and makes you feel like a genius on every win.

P.S. The fact that you can finish a match in under 20 minutes is unusual for a game with so much depth, and makes it much easier to bring it to the table.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
A very solid abstract game where you gather all tiles of a particular color on your turn.  You must take tiles of a particular color if you can.  You place in a 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5 tile location.  If you have any leftover, they go to a negative tile location.  Also, you can go first on the next turn if you are the first to take tiles from the center but you take a -1.  At the end of the turn you move the tiles to corresponding locations.  You get 2 points for completing a row and 7 points for completing a column and you score 1 point for every contiguous tile.  You will play 5-7 rounds.  When someone creates a row of 5 the game is done so it is often over in 5 turns.  

I really like the game.  It is one of the better abstract games.  It is simple, but at the same time, there is a surprisingly high level of interaction as you can really hose your opponents if they don't have room for large numbers of tiles.  I would like to own this game.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Quite enjoyable. I like abstracts :)

Azul presents you with interesting dilemmas between taking the tiles that fit best into your overarching plans and opportunistically taking the tactically best tiles. It also presents you with plenty of brain-burning tactical decisions if you like looking several moves ahead.

If you plan well, placing n tiles should score you something like n² points, or some superlinear function of n in any case. That makes later tiles have greater impact. In a 5-round 2-player game, the random tile drawing at the start of each round becomes increasingly predictable, so where it matters the most the randomness has the fewest opportunities to mess with your plans (because you can predict it well). In particular, in the last round you'll know exactly how many tiles of each color will show up. I like this feature. (You won't know the exact clustering, though, which is fine.)

On the whole a very enjoyable game.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: One of the first games we played. I wish the blue and red squares had some art on them to match the rest of the game without having to buy aftermarket ones. Its definitely simple but I think it could be a good gateway game. Playing it again I forgot how mean it can get. Often times your best moves it to take what your opponent needs to pull off a bit move. That can even happen unintentionally due to his the game is designed with having a dwindling amount of tiles that you can utilize. If you play the friendly version where you don't try to step on each others toes you'll often end up with a ton of negative points at the end. So all the build up after playing is crushing your opponents or getting a ton of negative points. Neither feels very rewarding for someone who doesn't like that feeling. I wish the focus was on how well you built your tiles and rewarded for that without the sort of meanness or punishment that comes at the end.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Azul has grown to become a behemoth in the hobby, and it's easy to see why with its beautiful components, elegant and light ruleset, and decent strategic depth.  Unfortunately, I am often bored by abstracts, and it's not like there are any groundbreaking mechanics here to entice me.  It also feels like it plays the same every time so it gets quite repetitive.  However, I still bring Azul out on occasion because the drafting is done so well.  If you plan ahead a few turns, you can really commit some hateful acts that will inspire rage in your fellow gamers (this is a compliment for the game).  I prefer Azul at 2 players because you have more control in the draft compared to 3 and 4.  This remains preferable to the various Azul spinoffs because the other games seem to have dropped the meaningful player interaction which is Azul's best characteristic.

update [+1.0]:  This has surprisingly grown on me with more plays at 2 player.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
An incredibly difficult spatial game for me, but I am terrible at spatial puzzles.  The components are very nice.  I do wish there were optional implementations to help narrow the point gap between players at different levels.  My husband scored 40 points more than me and neither of us enjoyed that aspect.  But it is a cool-looking game and the strategy and game play is solid.

I definitely appreciate the impact this game has had on the hobby as a whole, and I'm happy so many people enjoy it. It's very abstract, however, and I tend to gravitate toward more thematic games. It also feels "punishing" when you can lose points, which is something I'm not fond of happening in games. I don't mind games where you can lose points to gain benefits, but I do tend to feel like giving up if I lose points because I did something "wrong". I feel like I'm in trouble or something, and so it's just not happy for me to play games like this much.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
At 2P, this game is not for me. I dislike the open-information drafting, being able to see exactly what I want, and knowing that my opponent can see exactly what I want, and knowing they are going to take it and I'm going to be frustrated. Throw in the fact that my wife was too good at it, and I eventually stopped enjoying it. 

But that's just me. A lot of people have described the same scenario for Azul, and it's the exact thing they love about it. So maybe the same goes for you, whoever you are. 

I love the look and mechanics of the game, love how quick and easy it is to pick up, and I liked it a lot at 4P, so my rating could go up with more plays. But very little motivation to play 2P now.

EDIT: I was wrong. Bumped from 8 to 9/10. I have lots of motivation to play this at 2p, and it's a go-to for me and my wife. She had a gnarly win streak in our initial plays of Azul, but now that things have evened out, I love it.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Azul is a very clever abstract tile-drafting/laying game, playing well at any count, but perhaps best at 3 (or 4).
The game involves a draft of tiles from common  pools; as each pool is selected, all similar tiles are taken, and leftover tiles moved to a common pool.
Selected tiles are sorted into rows with 1-5 slots; after a row is complete one tile may be placed in a matching position on the actual player board and scored for orthogonally connected tiles at round end.
But if a tile cannot be played it goes into a penalty queue, also evaluated at round end.
Selecting the common pool penalizes the 1st player to do so as one tile in the queue, but this player will select 1st next round.
The game awards completed columns, rows and sets of 5 similar placed tiles; first to finish a row triggers game end.
This all makes for an attractive, interactive abstract with flexible player counts.
Lives up to all the hype- recommended.

textfield_comment_value:
One of those vanishingly rare games that are just as capable of being a player's introduction to board games as it is to keep seasoned boardgamers at rapt attention. The way each round plays out as a reduction in options leaves players rapidly changing plans or desperately trying to make things work, cursing themselves or their opponents for choosing certain coasters. The strategic depth is precisely as present as individual players want it to be, with more idly interested players able to focus on filling in their particular corner of the board while more advanced ones puzzle over the optimal tiles to take given the strategies chosen by their opponents and the likelihood of tile combinations given the distribution of those left over in the bag. The clackiness of the tiles, the cohesiveness of the art, and the ease of setup and cleanup are just gravy. 

Benefits from playmat organizers and a sand timer to limit turns.

Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
This is a nice and simple tile pattern laying efficiency puzzle somewhat reminiscent of titles like Patchwork or Indian Summer, but with single tiles instead of Tetris-like pieces. However, there's less time matching patterns and it takes more time counting scores. It's visually striking with it's classic Portuguese styled boards and the weighty plastic squares that are thick, hard and shiny to look like ceramic tiles. It's a looker.

I played it with two and four players and cause and effect is much better handled with two. With more players it's difficult to guess what's left for your next turn and it's harder to weigh whether to go for your own success or when to block. You cannot count on other players to block a great move for another player, so the dynamics change with player counts.

Given it's short playing time it is an excellent filler, but it's a bit mathier than the Tetris wannabees that are out there.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: This is a fine little game. Extremely fast (barring playing with people too much prone to AP) and simple. At first, it appears to be a bit random and almost not interactive, but later, all the subtleties (and the mischievousness) of the gameplay becomes apparent. I'm dubious whatever a early rush strategy is feasible: if you want to score the biggest points, you have to take your time covering all the tiles of one (or more) colors and fill columns, which means that you can't cover a row (which ends the game). Sometimes it's easy to think that a early lead is sufficient to win, only for a player to catch up and win because of these additional points. The biggest downside of this game is probably the fact that it's almost impossible to prevent players from screwing up our plans: more often than not a player who is behind will unwittingly help whoever is winning, whick makes for some quite disappointing kingmaking.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
This is recommended as a 2 player game but for me, it just does not work. It requires too much calculating for a game with so much randomness. At the beginning of each round you calculate at least a couple of likely scenarios of which tiles are possible for you to get with maximum points and minimal negative points. This means calculating 6-9ish moves in advance which due to being a simple drafting game is not that difficult but more annoying if you can pretty fast conclude that the round is a disaster. Many times you can sort of see the end result of a round without much calculating by just seeing how many tiles of a specific color is available. At the same time you need to track how many tiles of all colors are still in the bag and try to get the colors that would not block your wall out of options for future turns. The combination of these things is not for me but maybe it is for you.

Probably gets purged.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Nice abstract which is not too heavy and thus plays quick. It also looks nice, has a nice feel to it, especially when handling the very nice components.

It is a well designed, accessible yet 'fresh' game which is a great feat in a well developed genre. Recommended, especially if you like puzzles and tend to game with non-gamers as well. The perfect abstract gateway game to the world of boardgaming.

As for my personal taste: once you 'get' the optimal strategy you tend to quickly grasp that strategy in relation to others as well and hence win the game by a landslide. Thereby eliminating the tension. Also, as with all abstracts, in its core light in theme (though this has a well chosen theme with the mechanics), which leaves me with a taste of: ok this was nice, what shall we play next? Instead of: ok, this was great, I want to play again! Therefore, a 7. If you're into abstracts, up that rating by 2.

Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
A delightful game where your aim is to fill your board with tiles. The center area has little coasters with tiles. On your turn you can take one color of tiles on one coaster, then the other tiles pool into the middle, which becomes a valid place to pull tiles from just like on the coasters. Then you take your new tiles and place them into a preparation row on your board. These rows are all different lengths, and when full will click into place at the end of the round. If you wind up taking too many tiles of a single kind, or tiles you can't place, they will sink to the bottom of your board and hurt your score.

The puzzle is intense, especially watching what other players are aiming for, and trying to both take the tiles you need while not setting up a great move for them. The components are delightful to hold and see. The rules are just the right amount of complicated for a game this length.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
You're gathering tile pieces to help fill in your board. The more you can get directly adjacent when added there, the more points you get. You're required to take all of a color when you do and any excess counts negatively towards you. The tiles are nice, the game is simple to explain and it plays quickly. I'm not sure I was super excited to play it again, but it looks like it'd be a fun and fairly mindless abstract after a day of heavy gaming.

I'd be curious to try the "advanced" side of the board as it doesn't force you into a specific pattern. That might provide a bit more "oopmh" to the game that I felt like was missing from the basic side.

Also, apparently this is much more cutthroat at 2 players, which I could see being more fun.

Edit: After a couple minor rule fixes, I enjoy this one more than I thought I did. Still not in love with it, but I'd be fine playing it again if requested.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
In this game, themed after putting tiles on an Alhambra, there are 100 tiles in the game (20 each of 5 different colors). Each round, a number of tiles are on the 9 market spaces. In player order, you choose one kind of block(s) to put onto your mat. Those not taken on the market go into the middle where everyone can get at them. When all blocks are gone, you move completed rows on your mat to the corresponding symbol on your board. You score points for adjacent blocks when placing them, vertically and horizontally. You also lose points for excess blocks that you cannot place.

This is a tactical game, where you have a certain plan, and you have to watch what other people are collecting, and what blocks might cause you a large penalty. It's a fun game, and takes about 45 minutes or so to play. There are different strategies you can try for collecting. Rating likely to rise after more plays.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
I'm not a big abstract fan, but after seeing a lot of praise for Azul I had to give it a try.  The components are great and are probably the biggest reason to play the game, to be honest.  It's quite satisfying to collect these tiles and arrange them on your board in a nice colorful pattern.

The gameplay itself is also interesting and can be quite cutthroat.  You are trying to collect sets of similar tiles, which you can then transfer to a 5x5 grid on your tableau.  Sets of 1 go to the first row, sets of 2 go to the 2nd row, etc., but you can only make one of each set per round, you can only have one of each color per row, and one of each color per column.  It felt a bit more tactical and less strategic than other abstracts, because the available tiles completely reset from round to round.  Nonetheless, I enjoyed it and this is one of the few abstracts that I would be happy to play again.
