textfield_comment_value:
Introduced by the Moors, azulejos (originally white and blue ceramic tiles) were fully embraced by the Portuguese when their king Manuel I, on a visit to the Alhambra palace in Southern Spain, was mesmerized by the stunning beauty of the Moorish decorative tiles. The king, awestruck by the interior beauty of the Alhambra, immediately ordered that his own palace in Portugal be decorated with similar wall tiles. As a tile-laying artist, you have been challenged to embellish the walls of the Royal Palace of Evora.

In the game Azul, players take turns drafting colored tiles from suppliers to their player board. Later in the round, players score points based on how they've placed their tiles to decorate the palace. Extra points are scored for specific patterns and completing sets; wasted supplies harm the player's score. The player with the most points at the end of the game wins.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
NY
Best @ 2p

WIN: most points (scored at end of each round and at endgame)

Each player gets board with score cube on 0.
5/7/9 coasters for 2/3/4p. 4 tiles per coaster. 

Each turn, players either:
- Take all tiles of 1 color on factory and move rest to center
- Take all tiles of 1 color from center; must take 1P tile if there and place in FLOOR area
Then place tiles in 1 row from right to left. Extras drop to FLOOR
If the WALL already has that color in that row, cannot place in that row

Round scoring:
If row is complete, move 1 tile to WALL. Score by counting all horizontally linked tiles (including itself) + all vertically linked tiles (including itself).
Subtract points based on tiles in FLOOR.
Discard tiles to lid. Refill bag when needed.
Game ends if 1+ player(s) have completed a row.

Endgame scoring (based on WALL):
2 pts/row. 7 pts/column. 10 pts/color with set of 5.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
The game has 20 tiles of every color. In a typical 5-round two player duel, tiles are not shuffled into the bag so that players can count how many tiles are left. A two player game is simple, elegant yet strategic. I could easily rate an 8 or even a 9 for a two-player game

But in a multiplayer game, the game is too chaotic. Players can rarely foresee what tiles he could pick in the coming turn. Contrary to a two-player duel, tiles are shuffled into the bag since round 3. Because of that, some color tiles can be so abundant that every player can get a lot of column bonus or completed color bonus without a struggle. Penalty seems too weak in multiplayer as well. It is hard to see a 4 point penalty in a 4-player game because 3 other players would take up the slack. I could only give a 6 for multiplayer game.

Taking both experience into consideration, I would give a 7 overall
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Azul is the Splendor of drafting games.

Like Splendor, it's intuitiveness and simplicity are it's greatest strength. It's production quality is great, it's price is good, the game play loop is satisfying, and it's length feels just right.

But it also has a similar fault. I believe there's a dominant strategy and I actually think it's harder to stop than Splendor's due to lack of hate drafting incentive and seating order impact.

Therein lies the rub. To lessen that fault, the game would need to expand in some way and while Summer Pavilion and Stained Glass were fine and helped those issues, the simplicity of OG Azul always kept it on top for me over those iterations.

I do think there's room for improvement here and I hope a game can come along at this weight that can deliver what Azul does without that fault. Until then, hail to the king (of light weight drafting games).
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Azul is an excellent game, the rules are simple and the game is very quick. Just choose a set of tiles from plate or the central area and queue them up to be added to the wall. The scoring at the end of every round is reasonably simple, but the end-game bonuses add an enjoyable layer of strategy to the game. It's really simple to play but has a surprising amount of depth. I imagine an experienced player will usually beat a newcomer. The double sided player boards add even more replayability to the game.

A couple of downsides I can see are that turn order matters and that going last in a round can effectively knock a player out of the running in a 4 player game, and there may be also bit bit of a runaway leader issue but it's such a quick game that neither of these issues spoils the game too much. Always enjoy playing this and everyone I've introduced it to has enjoyed it.

Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
After 22 plays, this game has definitely lost its lustre. There’s only 1 winning strategy at 2 players i.e build adjacent columns and rows. Unless your opponent is very inattentive or both of you have been extending the game past 5 rounds (both quite unlikely at 2p), there’s no chance that you’ll get the 5-of-1-colour 10 point bonus. The game then just becomes a matter of who builds their columns/rows more efficiently, which isn’t very fun for me.

This problem is worsened by how there’s no variable setup in the game other than the distribution of tiles. The strategic depth and replayability would’ve been higher if there was variable setup e.g public/private objectives like in Sagrada.

Great gateway game though for newbies though - this was one of my favourites back when I started playing board games (8.5/10) because of the really fun puzzle of drafting tiles.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
I own a physical copy of Azul and I played it 20+ times with my wife. I found it a competitive, short abstract game (10-15' per player) mainly based on drafting and placing tiles to form patterns.
Set-up is fast, ruleset is easily explained and understood, rulebook is well structured, and the gameplay complexity is medium-low (2/5).
The game turns are structured in two part: (1) drafting tiles and placing in your 5 reserve rows; (2) moving the tiles from the reserve rows into the 5x5 board to score points based on the formed patterns.
The gameplay is quite relaxing and the balance is good, though there is a some luck-dependency. Since the game is short at two players, we tipically play until one of us win two games.
Component quality is decent with heavy resin-based tiles and light cardboard boards.
Definitely recommended as a light abstract filler game.

textfield_comment_value:
just downgraded to a 6.5.  it's a lovely game, really.  the drafting and the tallying of points is FUN.  easy fun.  and of course, "hate drafting" is always fun!  But... the first round is a tad boring.  and, worst of all, it has this terribly unfulfilling endgame - you don't get to finish your tiling!  Still and all, i'll keep it around for games nights with non-gamers.  it will always be fun.  but i don't need to play it again, i guess.  Splendour, oddly, lacks the unfulfilling endgame though it is no more thematic.

and while i'm at it:  as a family/non-gamer game, it's non-intuitive that on the top row you place one tile to place one tile and on the bottom you place FIVE to place ALSO A SINGLE TILE.  i try to explain it as "the bottom level is actually a larger tiling project, but you only place one to represent all the tiling you did for REASONS.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: A pleasant tile collection game, but I don't understand why it's so highly rated. The collection mechanic and the way it works into tile placement process on your mat feels fresh and very neat, no doubt. But it's still just a set collection game - observe what other people need, and either get there before them or take other tile sets, judging how long you can take before you need to pick the ones you really want. And work towards completing your sets. It's not a game the family is going to love given how abstract and quiet it is, and how observant you need to be to do well. It's too long for a filler/opener, and not enough theme or oomph to be a game-night centerpiece. I mean, it's an abstract tile collection game. Neat and enjoyable, and I'd happily play it anytime someone requests because it does it well, but it's not something I'd seek out either.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: I went back and forth on this beautiful little abstract strategy game. I am so happy that I made the decision to pick it up after finding it on discount because of VERY minor box damage. I love the drafting of tiles and how the reject tiles build up in the middle until its finally worth the negative point for someone to go there. The game plays fairly differently with 2 than with 3 or 4 in my opinion. You can much more easily manage your needs, denying your opponent their needs, and predicting what is likely to get taken (and therefore left for you in future rounds). I also like going for the goals to get the end game bonus points. In larger player count games, you are having to refill the bag with tiles more often than I'd like. It is a very minor knit pick. It can be taught easily, played quickly, and has fun game play making it a good filler game.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Azul at the moment, here in the Fall of 2017, is getting a fair amount of buzz on BGG.  I find Azul to be a good abstract, but I don't find it to be THAT interesting or fun.  I have played Azul now at a number of player counts, and I believe Azul is at its best as a two player game.  

Played as a two player, Azul does have a nice "zero sum" feeling such that you can really see, studying the limited number of markets in front of you, that the tiles you take, will NOT be available to your opponent.  In this way, you are able to really study the markets/game status quickly and easily and make satisfying, strategic and tactical decisions.  By contrast, when Azul is played at higher player counts, I think this feeling of easy tractability (due to more markets being used) and "zero sum" decision making (who am I trying to defeat by taking this?) is lost.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Azul is a great game, don't get me wrong, but it falls into a strange category for me. 

It's relaxing but can be cut throat at times when people "hate draft" tiles; it mostly runs on autopilot in terms of decisions but there a two or three decisions that are fairly difficult every round; it feels like it would get very samey (I played it exclusively the last two days so around 7 games) but it's also just a fun little puzzle that keeps bringing you back for one more game. 

Interestingly, I think this works best as a 2p game as you get stuck with a lot more tiles that you need to place, whereas in 3p you tend to get clumps of tiles that work out better for your board. So the 2p is thinkier. Haven't played at 4 yet. 

I'd never turn down a game of Azul, and it's definitely nice to have on those nights we want something to play while we watch TV.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
"Abstract. Not many rules, but slightly counter-intuitive. Kind of light but also kind of thinky. Occasionally can feel brutal, at least at 2p. Just not my kind of game. "

What I like:
- Nice production of a bland "theme"
- Plays quickly (30 minutes for 2p learning game)

What I dislike:
- Opportunities to screw your opponent (at 2p)
- Feels brain-burny but chaotic at the same time
- Essentially abstract, which I rarely enjoy
- No sense of escalation throughout the game.

I feel pretty strongly that The Mind was a better SdJ game over Azul. Azul feels more like a kenner to me, plus those penalty points can be really painful, and at 2p it is (or at least can be) quite cutthroat. I really don't see how this would appeal to kids. 

I have never been a fan of Splendor, but at least it had engine-building, so I consider it to be a superior game.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Simple rules and tense gameplay. My main quibble is that it is never going to feel like it presents a very different puzzle from game to game--I finished playing it and felt "well, we could play it again, but it would just be the same thing". -- That said, whenever I have taught it to people they played it once, then immediately played it again. Good sign.

I highly recommend keeping score with a pad of paper or chips/tokens, not with the little black cubes which are very easy to jostle. The player mats on my copy are also not flat and are very easy to move around, shifting tiles. (I believe later editions have better components -- my comments are about the first edition which is what I bought.)

Upped the rating recently as this one keeps gaining in depth the more you play it. Great at 2 players, genuinely chess-like interactions at times.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
It's easy to see why this has been all over the place. It's a beautifully designed game. It presents itself as a quick, light, puzzle game, when in fact there's a good deal of depth there should you wish to explore it. It's a nice social game; you can chit chat and hang out while you play it. (It think the rules, though, are a little bit too fussy to make it appeal to non-gamers, though, but I could be wrong about that.)

For me, though, it just falls short. It's not particularly fun. While there's definitely strategy to be had, and the other players do matter, it didn't really feel like I was doing much of anything interesting. I'm just not into abstracts that much. I like Qwirkle, I like Ingenious, and I like Azul, but neither of the formers are games I own or feel compelled to request, and neither is the latter, as attractive as it is.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Sorry for the cliché, but this is “A modern classic”. It has never failed me and after 20+ plays I have no need to turn the board to the other - grey - side.
So how can an abstract game be so attractive? It all comes down to the indirect player interaction.
See the tiles? They are not eye-candy. They serve a purpose. Being so easy to discern in other player’s boards, these components take a great solo puzzle into an amazing social experience.
The spatial puzzle and the scoring system gives you so many opportunities that are tied to just as many restrictions. Every player will feel both powerful and doomed during the game. And everyone can easily mess with one another. It just takes a glance to see the other player’s board and try to mess with it, while also planning a few turns ahead. You don’t get a ‘simple’ design much richer than this.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Gameplay is not really engaging. The components are nice, but even with that, it is aesthetically unsatisfying not to finish a mosaic during gameplay. 

Somebody else put it well in their comment: to play this best, you need to pay close attention to others' game boards (annoying in multiplayer) and there is a lot of Analysis Paralysis that is entailed in playing best. If you ignore or don't take time to other people's boards, you will often lose and feel you should have played the game better. Negative points is always a downer in true "family" games as well.

#1 abstract and #1 family game?  My family is bored to tears playing this.

As always, don't take BGG ratings at face value as to the quality of a game's play. 

Beautiful components (tiles, minis, etc.) often yield ratings far, far higher than the gameplay would merit on its own.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
We didn't like Azul as much as many other people. The components are fine. I wonder if it is a hype thing here that I expected incredible greatness out of the tokens. Much to our surprise, they are very light and plastic. I expected more weight considering how much people talked about them. The tiles are not colorblind friendly.
For an abstract game, it is ok. The rules are clear and scoring very straightforward.
There is potential for take that. If you like cool and breezy, this may not be it. If you play with equally cool and breezy players, fine. If not, you may have players take a slightly less advantageous type of tiles just to stick you with unplayable tiles. It all depends on the players of course though this may still happen due to the luck of the draw.
I would not refuse to play this game but I don't often think about it either.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
I found Azul to be very pleasant and just had a good table feel. The game is extremely easy to teach but the scoring gives the game a bit of nuance. Timing of your drafts is very important and you want to try to sequence your plays. The game is thinky enough to stay engaging without being so overwhelming you can't have a conversation during it. I've heard from others that they think it's mean at 2 - I can see how you can intentionally spoil a pot for someone, but I didn't think it was that mean really. Another poster put it as "split/choose" for 2, and I think that's an accurate description of the game. Not mind-blowing but well and fun

EDIT: Coming back a year later I think I undersold this. It's really solid. Kiesling's solo designs hit all the right spots when they are good. Azul is one of those. Deserved classic.

Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
A game with simple rules of picking tiles and trying to arrange them to score points but with lots of depth. Every decision needs to be adjusted as each player is going to change the composition of the available tiles left in the center. You may also want to adjust the ordering of your own moves based on the other player's board to deny them points while gaining the most points yourself. As the player counts rise, the game takes longer and the state of the board can change significantly between your turns. For a 30 minute game, this one offers a lot of decisions and enough of a challenge to keep it around for a long time.

textfield_comment_value:
Azul has all the hallmarks of a great design. It has elegance, interesting player interaction, and beautiful production going for it... But something about Azul just fails to excite me. I can see why a lot of people love it. It's an intelligent and original design, and the drafting especially is clever. We did enjoy it for the first 5 plays or so, but the novelty wore off pretty quickly. 

I've played Azul 11 times total at this point and I just don't feel any desire to master this or carry on trying to like it. I wish I could see what others see in it. The only real criticism I even have is that the actual tile laying portion of the game is pretty boring, but that's a really minor criticism since the drafting seems to be the core of the game. I just can't bring myself to feel passion about this game one way or the other.

Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: I bought Azul because of the Spiel de Jahres hype. It looks cool. I like all the components. The gameplay is doesn't strike me as anything particularly special. I'm aiming for tile bonuses while trying to ruin my opponents' options. That can be surprisingly difficult to evaluate leading to a slower game than one might expect. I often don't feel like I'm doing anything amazing, just sort of muddling through the best option I can find in the mess of tiles my opponents' left for me. If I win, I never feel like it was because of some particularly good strategy, but more because of playing the same tactics as everybody else but slightly better, or maybe by playing the same tactics and just chancing into a more favorable tile distribution in a couple more rounds. To the extent that I like Azul, it's mostly tactile and aesthetic enjoyment.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: Azul involves open drafting, tile placement and pattern building. It's similar to Sagrada and Roll Player, but with more player interaction. My family and I played Azul several times with 3p, and we sold it for three reasons. First, we don't love games in which player interaction is limited to drafting because when players hate draft, they tend to focus mostly on the next player in turn order, not other opponents (e.g., to avoid downtime), and this can cause drafting games to feel inadequately interactive with 3p+. Second, my family dislikes scoring negative points. Third, my family prefers games with more post-setup randomness. 60.8% of voters preferred Azul with 2p when I last checked. I played Azul with 2p at BGA, and I think it's a much better game with 2p because hate drafting is less time-consuming and more impactful with 2p.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Nice tile placing game. The game is beautiful, its artistic design really invites you to play.

As for the game, its a relaxing game that I personally enjoy playing in those moments when you want something light and fast. You can actually play it in semi auto pilot  while you talk with your companions or watch a football game in the background... you get the idea. But don't get me wrong, the game offers enough to keep you interested! There is a pleasure in doing this little optimization of tile placement, making combos and winning points!

My girl loves the game and we are usually playing it after lunch or something since the setup is so fast. In summary, if its me thats organizing the games session, I would peak one of my other, more strategic games. If its an espontaneous game session, I would be very willing to play Azul.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Love this game, its a new favorite. Quick playing, with barely any downtime. Puzzly and rewards thinking ahead, but it isn't the end of the world if you don't. Usually very close games for us (2-player). This is always my wife's first suggestion now when we are wondering what to play. Good intro game for people new to the hobby. Looks fantastic on the table, and always gets comments.

textfield_comment_value: Azul might be one of the most effective game designs I've ever seen.  It is simple enough in the rules that almost anyone can play, but at the same time it has a depth of strategy that can keep gamers coming back for more.  It has some slight opportunities to work against your opponents by taking what they want or leaving them with a mess to clean-up, but it's not so devastating that you will ruin their entire game.  I am always excited to play this game because it is fast, so even when things don't go my way, I don't have to wallow in misery for long.  The components are amazing, and there are even 2 different boards to play on in the base game, so you can work on the beginner board, or go to the more complex expert board where you make your own grid.  This game and its sequels are permanent staple in my collection.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
The easiest game recommendation of all time. One of the few games that I think pretty much everyone who likes board games should have. It’s easy to learn, has a good amount of depth, plays great at all player counts, is short, can be as relaxed or as competitive as you want it to, and it’s beautiful. It also has a bit of that “classic game” feel, like something like Rummikub or Scrabble, which makes it easy for anyone not used to modern games to pick up. 

If you’re just getting into board games, this should be one of your first forays - I think it might be a really good litmus test to see if you enjoy the mechanical puzzles that board games offer. It’s not as good of a representation of the fun mind games and above-the-table talk that some modern games present, but the puzzle here is fantastic for how simple it is.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
It's fine. I do like the tension that comes with watching your opponents pick the tiles you wanted, or adding tiles of the color you want to the middle so you now have to decide if its worth the negative points to still take those tiles. Plus the puzzle of which tiles/rows to score this round to maximize your points while also hindering your opponents. And the game looks great on the table.

The problem for me is that there is nothing that really makes one game of Azul feel different from the last. Select tiles, complete rows, slide tiles, repeat. I find the selection mechanics more engaging here than in Sagrada, but Sagrada more than makes up for it with the random scoring goals each game. Azul could have used something similar to make one game of it feel somehow unique when compared to all previous games of it.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Its a OK game, looks good, quality is good. But for me, the more I played it, the less interesting it becomes.
The strategy in where to place the tiles and when to get which tiles is a bit repetetive.

Only have played 2 player games so it might be more fun with more than 2 players.

EDIT:

Gave it more chances but with 4 players. Played it 3 times now with this player count and it definitely increased the fun. 

++ easy to teach, learn, play
++ small set-up
++ short, takes like 40 minutes with 4 players where 2 players have never played it before.
++ with just 2 players you need them of equal strength otherwise the same person (in my case at home that would be me) wins all the time by a mile. But with more players it gets more dynamic and interesting because of the fact other players their win chance increases.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Azul is a modern classic - an abstract game for almost everyone. Interactive, elegantly designed and beautifully produced. It can be pretty cutthroat, though. You can’t avoid messing up other players’ plans - intentionally or otherwise.

For some reason it took me several plays to figure out the right strategy. I was too focused on getting the big lower rows filled, instead of just working my way down from the top. Adjacency is everything in this game, and that is much easier to achieve when you start with the small rows.

My only gripe with this game is the penalty for extra tiles. The possibility of getting 14 negative points in a single round is neither fair or fun. Most times it’s impossible or at least very difficult (and time consuming) to figure out how to avoid ending up with a stack of unwanted tiles.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Excellent game that's perfect for luring people into the hobby. The mechanics are simple enough that learning the game isn't intimidating for new players but at the same time, the decision making is tough enough that people who prefer heavier games can find enjoyment. This game has plenty of interactions, and being able to identify which tiles are sought after by whom is an important skill to learn in order to ensure your own success. At two players the game can become rather mean, as earning points and causing your opponent to lose points is equally good. I'm a fan of this, but beware if you're looking for a friendly two player game (instead I'd look into Sagrada).
The game is beautiful which adds to its welcoming nature that makes it such a wonderful introductory game. Highly recommend.

(played 60+ times)
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: The core gameplay is super solid but I ended up passing it on because it just wasn't getting played. I think there are two main reasons for that which both have to do with scoring. First off, the scoring cubes are way too easy to bump, especially as you are constantly placing, moving and removing tiles from the same player boards. It's strange to have such a disappointing component in the same game as one of the nicest components of all time - the tiles. My second issue is that there is a large amount of slightly fiddly scoring that's all done independently, which I consider a problem in a gateway game. Mistakes were common, and so I either found myself needing to babysit everyone which sucks and kills the vibe, or just accept that the scores might be off to preserve the vibe which sucks for other reasons.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
This is a game that was no surprise to us, once we played, that it won the Spiel des Jahres.  It is a fun, easy to teach game that is full of interesting decisions and strategy while still being easy for new players to grasp what is going on.  Do you let the game go one turn longer to pick up that column bonus? Do you take the three reds and the penalty when you only need two, or hope for a better layout in the next round?  And, most interestingly, what do you take so you don't set up an obvious move for others?

My only knock against the game is that, with more players, it can be hard to keep track of everything that's going on, thus resulting in solely playing offense, or just defending yourself against the next player.  And, the artwork of the tiles didn't do much for me, but I get why people like it.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
I think Azul is a fine game, but I admit I don't understand the mass popularity it received in 2018. Although it has grown on me over the years.

Components are awesome, the rules aren't overly complicated (but aren't as simple as you'd assume going in either). The theme is fairly unique but it's loosely tied in. Scales quite well and plays fast.

It's of course personal preference, but it's not a game I get excited to play. There's depth there but not to the level I love. I think of this game as a gateway +, but for that audience in the couple plays I've had hasn't had them really clamoring for more either.

Overall though, I'm happy for the designer and publisher and believe it's a well executed game. I think the spin-offs have more to explore and that's likely where I'd personally gravitate towards.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
An abstract tile-placement game in which you try to create the best combos to get the most points until you decide (or at least you try) the finish the game at the right moment (by completing two horizontal rows). 

The drafting element at the beginning of each round is really fun and puts a bit of interaction in the game. Everyone tries to get the tiles he needs (you have different plates with tiles on it from which you can chose all tiles from one colour while putting the others in the middle - from which you can also pick up all tiles of a colour if you want).In the other half of the round, everyone is simply putting the tiles onto his wall, trying to complete it and getting the best combos out of it.

Great puzzling game that takes not too much time and is a good way to start the boardgame evening.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: I would have given this a 10 as it is a fantastic abstract game but I dropped it to a 9 due to the fact that I could see one issue.  It will get old after a few plays and I could see it essentially sitting on the shelf collecting dust eventually.  With that said, this game is purely fantastic.  You are a spanish tile layer and you earn victory points by placing tiles on your board.  First one to complete a horizontal row triggers the last round game end.  Looking at this initially I had no interest.  It looked too simplistic in nature.  Over lunch one day a buddy asked if I wanted to play it so I figured I would give it a shot.  I bought it that very night.  It plays well at all player counts (2-4 players) and I couldn't suggest this game more.  If you like abstracts this is a definite must own game.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
I really liked my first 10-20 plays of Azul, mostly 2 player. It is simple and fast and gives enough interaction and feeling of strategy. Well at least for a while. 

I have found that there are some issues with the game however. The flip side of the player boards has a open ended tile. Which, after understanding it's limitations, actually feels too open for me. Player interaction is severely limited playing with this, at least in a 2 player game. However with more plays I find the original set tile slightly solvable. Basically if one or 2 player focuses on the big diagonal line it can lock the other player(s) out of effectively scoring enough to keep up. 

Perhaps decent counter strategies can be found with subsequent plays, but I don't own it and I feel like I have had enough of this for a while.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
1) An abstract tile-drafting/laying to decorate the palace of the king of Portugal.
2) Clever drafting mechanics create an easy-to-pick up game, with a lot of possibilities to screw your opponents starting from the halfway point of the game.
3) I loved: The subtle interactions between players and the depth of the game - people who want could really go to town in counting how many tiles have come out of each of the colors, adjusting their strategy accordingly, and utilizing everything to destroy their opposition.
4) Could be improved: The game begs to be played as a casual filler, but that robs it of its depth and intricacy. On the other hand, if I want to burn my brain while playing a game, I would choose something much meatier.
5) This is one of those rare games that would fit in any collection.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: This is a very difficult game for me to rank.  Rules are simple once you learn them (rulebook could have been just slightly more descriptive of a few rules and turn order).  Gameplay however is COMPLEX.  The level of strategy can range from simple to extraordinary.  Very similar to chess in the complexity of what tiles to choose and when.  The manipulation of the middle is so vital as the player who has to take the final tiles can often take a huge hit in negative points.  The game is very fun but also depends greatly on the amount of experience and also mental effort the players want to put into it.  I've only played 2-player game so far but think this would even be more complex with 3 or 4 players.  This is truly a fascinating game but maybe just a little too intelligent for me to figure out.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
After several plays, I would say the game starts to get samey. The wild side is worst than the front because it's too easy to optimize the early rounds

Still solid but it's a purely tactical experience without that much depth. I would recommend the stained glass version for Gamers
-------------------------
Great gateway game with stellar production. This is exactly what I'm interested in when it comes to lighter/faster games, simple ruleset but has lots of tactical play and some depth.

The set collection elements in this one are simple to understand. But the scoring and the restrictions on how you can build up your board. And there is a bit of denial later on in the game which adds some good indirect player interaction

Probably my go to gateway game now, one that I will be looking to pick up

Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Multiplayer Tetris!

Simple enough to play with the parents-in-law but complex and deep enough to be fun to play. This game is a delicious piece of design. You simply pick tiles you want. But then so does everyone else. And then you end up realising you should have picked those other tiles because now you're getting 5 black tiles and you only needed one. 

Azul is a wolf in granny's clothing. Looking dainty and old fashioned on the outside but don't be fooled, its teeth are sharp and ready to snap at any moment. 

Last night, my wife tried to be nice to everyone at the table, except that she had missed one possibility. Snap! Five broken tiles and hilarious misery as she watched the three adults she loved the most in the world revel in a severe case of schadenfreude.

What a treat this game is.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Good game, with lots of player interaction. The production is gorgeous, but could still be much better. The little black cubes are too easily tossed around by mistake, especially with player mats that tend to spin on the table. I had to put drawer mats under the boards to secure them in place. It would be nice to have a proper place to put discarded tiles too, it is not convenient to put them back in the box lid as the rules suggest. Otherwise, of course the tactility and prettiness of the tiles hugely contribute to the fun of the game. It can be very mean, and seating order is very important. Lots of interesting and tough decisions at every turn, there is more depth here than it first appears.

Edit: Sold in prevision of Azul Pavillion, which on paper seems even better. Looking forward to it!
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
I always explain Azul as the perfect "Sit down, have a cup of tea" kind of game. If I'm in the mood for a board game, Azul is usually going to be too simple to satisfy my desire. However, if I'm not really in the mood for a board game, but my girlfriend asks to play Azul, I'm down. It's her favourite game.

It's a great tile placement game that maintains a lot of risk if you don't actually consider the consequences of your choices. But it's also a nice peaceful game, it just occasionally bites you in the ass and that's a good thing. The more people you play with, the more chaotic it gets. Playing with 4 people requires you to consider every choice you make a lot more.

Overall, I think it's a great game. Unfortunately, not that much of a game for what I like, as I just prefer meatier things.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Relaxing, pretty, tactile game if you don't take it too seriously. 

However, it's yet another game that falls apart when you try hard to win. The point rewards for completing certain patterns are so high that it's usually worth it for the player before you to make purely negative plays just so you can't complete them. This of course degenerates the game into cutthroat brutality where the best way to win is making sure you're going after the worst player at the table. This sort of thing can be rewarding if everyone is of equal skill level, but it's quite stressful.

Unlike something like splendor, at least everyone can agree to not think to hard and just have an easy game playing with nice tiles and making pretty patterns---there's a lot more this game offers than just the abstract strategy.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Excellent gateway game with beautiful artwork. Enough depth to keep you interested for a while.  Unfortunately, it’s gotten a bit stale for me even though I’ve not yet explored the “expert” variant on the back of the player boards. 

Also, it’s yet another example of a game whose audience i fail to identify. It’s likely not deep enough for heavy gamers, and yet it’s way too take-that and cut throat for many families and light gamers.  That said, it seems to sell just fine, so I’ve probably just misjudged it. 

Updated:  I suppose the target audience is actually quite broad.  it works well as a filler for experienced gamers and it can hold up to repeated plays with more casual gamers. The take that isn’t terribly harsh unless players are playing vindictively. quite an enjoyable little gem.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
One play and you'll see why it's considered a classic. Beautiful and thematic for an abstract game. 
The drafting mechanic is the show here, with surprisingly tactical considerations for its simplicity, as you work to defend against devastating hate-drafting opportunities available to your opponents. This is most apparent at two players. Although if you put in the number of plays required to become truly skillful at the game, you're probably the type of player who will want more from the straightforward tile placement and scoring. 
The game can also be played in a lighter fashion at higher player counts with less experience and it provides an aesthetically pleasing family-weight game. 
If you only play one Azul game, or you don't play a lot of games, this is still probably the one to get.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
This is a great game. It has pattern recognition with a great deal of interaction. The game is aesthetically pleasing to look at and the components are good. This is an easy game to teach but there is a lot to think about which keeps you engaged in the game.

The trick of the game is developing your board while trying to prevent your opponents from getting tiles they need to develop their board. Choosing the right factory and placing the titles into the common area is an important choice. Do you take tiles just to block your opponents? Heck yeah! Do you want to see your opponent stuck taking extra tiles and taking negative points? Indubitably. Beware as the tiles become less available. If you do not have an area open for tile placement you can get stuck with taking tiles you cannot use.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
[b]My Collection: Family/New - Abstract Strategy - Beginner[/b]

:thumbsup: Where else other drafting games leave the crumbs as the draft goes longer, Azul's unique public drafting system has the middle sweetened while making it unpredictable is simply genius. Beautiful table presence due to the tactile tiles which is also very pleasant to handle.

:!block: Like most abstract games theme is loose but this is actually pretending to have one. Fiddly individual score tracker. A centralized scoring board would have solved the problem of accidentally knocking the tracker over while allowing players to better draft (aka hate draft) as players can easily see who is leading. No storage for discarded tiles. The game could use more replayability like Azul: The Stained Glass of Sintra (2018) has.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
I normally really dislike abstract strategy games, so when I saw this listed as one, I really wasn't to play, but the bits and presentation of this game still drew me in.

Fortunately, I found this really doesn't feel like an abstract strategy game, despite being pretty void of theme. I don't really know what it does feel like, but it's not really abstract in feel, in the way chess, Go, or the GIPF series is.

The game is about choosing tiles among various lots of tiles, trying to obtain tiles that help you, while leaving poor options for your fellow players. You're trying to guess what you must take this turn vs. what you think your opponents will leave for you until later.

Overall, this is just a really pleasant game. No doubt, the components add a lot to the experience as well!
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
2 plays / 3 players

LIKE: Great choosing mechanism and dropping tiles in the middle, but I would say this is the only mechanism driving the game. The game centered around these choices very well and kept the game cutthroat. Plays quick. Good looking tiles.

DISLIKE: The scoring felt fiddly, I wish there was a way to streamline it, but this was minor. Some of the turns felt repetitive, there's not a lot of progression (compared to say, Splendor). Possible AP turns, because if given enough time, one could see ahead who needs what and figure out what will be left in the middle.

OVERALL: This is a good game, one that has a bite to it. There are some turns that could really mess over someone, which I felt made the game entertaining, but I could see where some people may not enjoy it.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
I was really excited for this game based on the reviews when it came out.  I will say, the production quality is amazing, and there's something soothing about the tactile nature of the tiles.

The game overall is good, however the big problem for me is that it becomes too easy to "math out" what is available/remaining to take.  So instead of just deciding what to take on your turn, it becomes this lengthy "if I take this, then you'll take that, which leaves me with this, forcing you to take that....etc."

I expect this may be exactly why some people love the game (ala thinking 5 moves ahead in chess), but it's not for me.

My gf loves this game, so I'll still play if she wants to.

--
UPDATE: Now that I have Azul Summer Pavilion, I will likely not play the original Azul again.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
One two player game in the books.  One point victory.  Maybe all games will end up being close?  Quick, easy to learn & play.  Suspect we will play many more 2-3 players games.  Max of 4 players though.  Only gripe is that the player boards with all the tokens, are easy to bump and lose track of the tiny scoring marker.  This is significant enough of an issue (occurred like 3 times in the game) to get a Rating Ding.  Guess, though there feels like tons of replay-ability, due to its simplicity, I personally could see myself getting bored of it.

After more plays, wife loves it (and keeps winning)  My alternate strategy attempt horribly failed.  Don't strive to get all the same color filled.  Got two rows on first turn, yet didn't manage to complete the objective by game end.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
I really like the ever-tough decisions, and how that plays into what you leave your opponents, and what you think they might leave for you as a result. Scoring is a bit tedious (but not difficult), begging for either this game to be an app, or for there to be a helper app that lets you photograph your wall and be told your score.

The tiles look cool, but they are too polished with a little too much rounding, resulting in slippery handling on a level with wet bars of soap. Now imagine trying to pick up numerous little wet bars of soap to arrange in a perfect grid on a flat, glossy surface. So, that's a sometimes very destructive downside.

All in all, a nice game I'd probably be happy to play any time; however, for once, perhaps playing with sticky fingers is encouraged?
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Pleasant experience... but why would I choose it from amongst other abstract games (e.g. Ingenious, Through the Desert)? Because of bits (that are cool, but the scoring marker and scoring boards are ridiculous)? Naaaah... the game is cool but it lacks tension or some cool point swings or brainburny moments of for instance - Sanssouci or Vikings from the same designer.
Also I think Azul is just another implementation of Vikings (put tokens in rows), very streamlined implementation and most family-friendly, but it IS NOT the best abstract board game as the BGG ranking would suggest.
I like it, I love how it looks, don't get me wrong, but I don't love it and if I choose between this or any of the GIPF series, then it's nobrainer - I'd rather play Yinsh or Gipf, or whatever.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: This felt like a totally average game. Action selection with restriction and personal board that I optimise. The best part of the game, and I do enjoy this, is that when you perform the action selection, it impacts the board state for the next person. That's cool and makes the decision interesting in the I don't want to be too generous sense. However, the messing with other people to punish them is done through the kind of calculation lookahead thing that I don't particularly enjoy. Fortunately, with four players, there is less of it than with fewer (although still too much for me). I'm more of a heuristic player, application of principles player, intuitive grasp player, rather than a brute force calculate it out player. Love the tiles, mind. They feel nice in my hand.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Azul is one of my few lighter games on the list. It's deserves it's spot as it is a brilliant design. Azul is a tile placement game trying to optimally create a glass-stained window, scoring as much points as possible. Well to be honest, Azul does not require any introduction, as it's a modern classic. Azul is one of the few games I can play with my wife. It helps that it's visually appealing, quick to learn, fast to set-up and that it can be played anywhere (played this while camping). Azul is light but offers enough interesting decisions along the way. Azul is not in directly in my sweet spot of games and it's individual games are fairly forgettable. However, still an amazing joy.

[b]Prefered way to play[/b]: 2-4 player
[b]Status[/b]: Stays in the collection for now
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
A gift from a mate (who has never chosen a wrong game yet!).
Azul gets a play (or three) most weeks (usually on a Saturday morning over  a coffee with my daughter). It is relaxing and fun. Nice theme and design.
Although there is some tension with other players over tile selection,  the lack of game conflict makes it appealing for a relaxing gaming session. However, it is still possible to play for spite if you keep an eye on the board of your opponents and take the tiles they need (as my daughter sometimes, and gleefully, does to me).
The two sided boards adds some variety, and the plastic tiles have some heft to them.
Plays fine with up to 4 players, but we prefer it at 2 players. Games are nice and short (around 15 minutes) and allow for multiple games in a session.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: Azul is een abstract familiespel met een toepasselijk en aantrekkelijk uitziend thema. De spelregels zijn niet moeilijk en het spel is zo uitgelegd aan nieuwe spelers. Je verzamelt gekleurde tegels en probeert deze zo efficiënt mogelijk te plaatsen voor de meeste punten. Zeker mensen die ruimtelijk inzicht hebben en houden van puzzelen gaan Azul leuk vinden, maar voor sommige jonge kinderen kan het spel nog iets te abstract zijn. Ook zal voor de meeste ervaren bordspelers het spel snel eentonig worden omdat er weinig variatie in tactiek zit om het spel te kunnen winnen. Al met al is Azul een leuk spel voor de casual speler die graag een eenvoudig en toegankelijk (familie)spel speelt. Zeker wanneer je een spel zoekt dat ook erg geschikt is om met z’n tweeën te spelen.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Play with Two (2018-07)
Good first play. Some nice limits on lookahead in all but the last round. The drafting is interesting with two.

I like the interaction of forcing people to take tiles they don't want, but not everyone might. The last round is perfectly calculable. That's not ideal, but it's common enough for a Kiesling game.

Play with Four (2018-08-07)
I thought it was far less interesting with four. There was more information to process, more social pressure not to process it, and less ability to interact.

Play with Three (2018-08-19)
It was better with three than four. I think it's by far the best with two, though, because in a three-player game, stopping the next person from drafting what they want could cost you both relation to the uninvolved player.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Review based on 25 plays (08/04/2024)
Including:
- Crystal Mosaic
- Joker Tiles
- Special Factories

From a gameplay point of view, Azul is almost perfectly executed: the tactic choices, the indirect player interaction while choosing tiles, the clean design without fiddly rules,... Yet after having played it now more than 20 times, I don't really come back to it. I think this is due to the fact that it is mostly an abstract tile layer with not that much imagination, and the fact that while being a very streamlined design, I do prefer games that have a little more twists or variability baked into them. So in the end, I think it's fair to say that Azul is a good game, but there is nothing particularly groundbreaking or interesting in it to keep me coming back to it.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
[2019-09-30 Rating: n.a. -> 7]
Azul is an elegant design: Simple, almost minimal rules which leave room for some clever plays. Basically you are doing some set collection in which you should always have an eye on your opponents options. By timing it correctly, you can really screw them or get screwed if you're not careful enough. Quite a lot of fun.

The only thing I'm not quite sure about, and which keeps it from hitting the table more often, is the intended target audience. For a filler or opener, it's a tad too long (and too mean for some). On the other hand, it's not meaty enough to make it the centerpiece of a game night. Somehow it always hovers in this limbo and get's overlooked when it comes to game selection time. But when it hits the table, it delivers.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Fantastic light abstract game, one of the top gateways for sure. Tried it with many different groups and it always works. Gives something to think about, rewards planning, but has also just the right amount of randomness. There is some interaction too, especially in lower player counts - with two, there are opportunities aplenty for some mean moves that result in a lot of negative points for the opponent.

It looks great, it plays smoothly and without any downtime at all. It's also very relaxing - good pick if you want to play with your parents or grandparents. You're spending most of the time building on your pretty player board, which makes it feel less cutthroat that it can sometimes be. All in all, a very solid title to start your adventure with boardgames.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
J'adore les jeux de Kiesling. Celui-ci me fait un peu penser au génial Sanssouci : on y retrouve une mécanique simplicité et astucieuse, ainsi qu'une tension croissante dans les parties. Et en plus, le jeu est super beau avec ces petites pierres en bakélite !

Il n'y a qu'une seule chose à regretter : la règle française est nulle (il y'a des fautes d'orthographe dans tous les sens, des mots anglais qui ont oublié d'être traduits, des points importants qui ne sont pas assez mis en valeur, des termes qui varient d'une page sur l'autre). Malheureusement, le jeu sera difficilement compréhensible en l'état par un public familial qui doit essayer d'analyser les règles.... C'est nul de la part d'un éditeur qui a pourtant de la bouteille dans le domaine de l'édition.

textfield_comment_value:
Smooth, instant-fun and component-wise stunning game.  Bakelite pieces are fantastic.

But the question is: is there enough control?  You need to maximize your score with regard to several objectives.  And many aspects of the game are beyond your control.  Hence, I can see some players, having luck, being able to fulfill somewhat conflicting goals and others, not so lucky, not being able to do so...

The length of the game rises my doubts too.  If at least one player finds it profitable, he will finish the game after just 5 rounds.  Others - with more sophisticated plans - will suffer.  Of course you can always plan short-term, but is it the idea behind the game?
This is the issue to monitor.

EDIT: Meh.  The game is insignificant and generally skippable.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
This is a game that I enjoy playing almost everytime. It works because it's easy to bring to the family and have everyone play it and have a good time. However if I was to host a board game evening, I would like something more heavy and meaty, and Azul in that scenario only works as a filler.

I think the design is really good and the game is really pretty. My wife loves it and we can play regularly which is a great bonus.

Nothing to demerit this game really, except the fact that I like other games better, but I appreciate this for all it brings in a nice package. And the fact that it makes my wife confident that she can win at board games. If it was for that alone it would get a 10 and my heartfelt thanks to the designer. Which he should get anyway! :)
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
2018-01-13 - 9 - What a great, clever game! It reminds me of Ra. It's totally different in terms of gameplay, but the decsisions that you make, must take into consideration what other players do, have, or want to do. The production value speaks for itself, but I'm really glad that with the great looks comes a very, very good game too!

2018-12-30 - 9->8 - after over a dozen of plays it's a very good game, which I will gladly play anytime.

2020-09-06 - 8->9 - I played more. It deserves it's 9! It's a must have in any board game colletion.
And I assure you - in 15-20 years from now it still will be in the stores, while all the Reefs, Sagradas and other epigones will be long forgotten.
Azul is truly a modern classic.

2021-02-15 - 9->8 - a strong 8 it is.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: Genuinely fun, very thinking while also being fairly easy to 'get'. Probably a good SDJ candidate. I haven't played the advance game yet, but I think I'd like it a little more. On the other hand, this game, while great, doesn't scratch that hardcore euro itch for me. It's a game I would buy for others who come over and aren't necessarily into super hard games like I am. I'd rate it right inbetween 'good - I'm usually willing to play' and 'very good - enjoy playing and would suggest it' it's not quite that second one, because in the end, if I'm with people who'd be willing to play a heavier game, I'd always take them up on the heavier game over this one. But if I'm with easier going game people, then this is right up there with the best in that category.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
I usually am very hesitant with hyped games.  Some I've liked, others I haven't.  This was one that lived up to the hype, for me.  The mind-puzzle and spacial intelligence portion elevated this.  I've been enjoying games that have the puzzle feel lately - Roll Player, Sagrada, Barenpark, etc.

I look forward to more plays of this.

textfield_comment_value:
Az egyszerűségéhez képest érdekes döntések vannak benne. Mérlegelni kell, hogy mi ad több pontot, ha valamit elveszek, azzal milyen lehetőségeket nyitok meg, ezekkel ki tud és akar élni, és amit a másik ezután tesz az hogyan hat rám. Sorolhatnám még ezeket a szempontokat, de összefoglalva: nem gondoltam volna, hogy ilyen élményt tud adni egy ennyire könnyen tanulható játék.

For its simplicity, it contains many interesting choices. You have to weigh up what gives you more points, if I take something away, what opportunities I open up, who can and wants to take advantage of it, and how what the other person does next affects me. I could go on and on, but to sum up: I never thought that a game that is so easy to learn could be such an amazing experience.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Abstract game where the theme has been barely integrated, but in this case this is not a big issue. The game is easy to explain and it can ve enjoyed since the first game. Particularly good to be used with casual gamers or people who are not used at all to play board games. For me, the best thing of the game is that you always have the feeling that you were one turn away of completing the board, which I thing is great, because you usually end wanting to start a new game
Positive:
1- easy to explain
2. Easy to play

4- when you end the game you want to start a new game right away
5- more than one strategy can be followed
Negative:
1- regular gamers may find it super basic
2- the optional board doesn’t feel as a huge change
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Good light abstract that hits right on the mark for a light game that is easy to learn but offers enough interesting decisions to be engaging.

A good amount of player interaction as well where you can really set players up to find themselves in a bad spot.

Good look to the game, although the way people raved about this at release was really over the top, production is very good but nothing special.

A fun game I could see being the perfect gift of a family to smash through a tonne of plays over a long period of time.

I would happily play again, but at the same time not something I would race out to play. I have many better light games in my collection and unless an abstract is off the charts in game play, I would rather play something with a theme.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
You may be thinking to yourself, why is this game rated number one in abstract, there is a very good reason. This game takes the abstract genre and turns it on its head. The strategy behind building you different patterns and screwing other people makes this game an instant like for anyone. I’ve introduced this game to one 20 plus people and have yet to find anyone (ranging from nerd to people who aren’t into board games) who didn’t really enjoy this game.

Now as a person who is a fan of the game, I prefer the newest version Azul summer pavilion, it takes the original and takes its core mechanics up to an eleven. If you feel like you’ll love this game just get that one instead. That being said the base azul is a lot more simpler and easy to get into.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: I think a lot of ratings are based on complexity or depth rather than how well a game accomplishes what it sets out to do. For example, should Mage Knight be ranked higher than Azul? Mage Knight is ambitious and actually accomplishes that ambition in a great game. Azul is perhaps not as ambitious but equally, if not more so, accomplished in what it sets out to do. I think this game is perfect for what it attempts to accomplish. Simple rules. Quick (virtually zero) set up time. Very fast gameplay. Great at all player counts. Saturated in crunchy decisions. A great arch of play that ends in a tight narrow finish. And then it ends leaving you wanting another go. And it’s great for gateway gamers or vets. Only complaint…..it could be in a smaller box. :)
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: Actions are a little too simplistic for their own good. That's not in and of itself a bad thing, it's clear that simplicity can create depth and breadth as Splendor and Santorini have shown. The problem is that the game feels loose. There isn't tension for grabbing the big pot first, and since you have more than one chance to grab tiles, there isn't urgency. You can even accidentally fall into a good situation by someone else dumping the right tiles. That being said, it's satisfying in a Carcassonne or Ticket to Ride sort of way. Things aren't stressful, and you can spend a fair chunk of the evening playing this with friends without anyone ending up with hurt feelings. Winning isn't satisfying, but losing doesn't hurt. You're just enjoying the build.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Azul is a quick abstract tile-drafting game. There are a number of different offers containing a mix of tiles, and a player can claim all of a single tile color from one of the offers, putting the rest in the middle. Later, tiles can be claimed from the middle in the same fashion. Claimed tiles go in staging rows of varying size, such that too few of a color won't get placed this turn, and too many will result in penalties. Once actually placed on your tile board, tiles will score for adjacent tiles, with bonuses for completing rows, columns, and all of the same color. The game is actually quite a bit more interesting than it sounds from a description, and there's a fair amount of tension in getting the tiles you need. It's a good filler.

(3 plays)
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
The rules to this game are pretty easy to explain.  The scoring can be handled by young kids who can count.  But planning ahead for the right moves can be tricky.  Some key points:
- try to complete each staging row during this round, otherwise you'll have to wait for another round with few places to hold tiles (potentially leading to big negative points when you have to take unusable tiles).
- focus mostly on making dense rectangles on your tile board (big points for you), but it's sometimes worth it to take a set of tiles to prevent an opponent from filling certain spots on their board (prevent big points for others).
- the game will take at least 5 rounds to end, but not much more than that, so keep an eye on how full other players' boards are.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
The rules are easy to understand, even if they aren't immediately intuitive.

When you take tiles from the display, the remaining tiles gather in the center. This may be compared to the Mancala system. As the game progresses, some tiles become less desirable to take, and even lead to heavy penalties. As tiles merge in the center, the player who is forced to take the last remaining tiles can change. This is similar to the NIM game, which is proven to be fun but can be exhausting.

Contrary to many opinions, I didn't find the visuals satisfying. The rows, columns, and tiles of the same color aren't easily identified at a glance, especially on the opponent's board. Tiles and score markers are difficult to align and can move easily, which is annoying.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Interesting twists from wanting all early to sometimes being cautious mid-game. 

Very nice production.

Serious AP risk in endgame. The game state is very large, all information is open. Several players will be fully blocked in some colours, reducing the game state at a very high cognitive load. The same colours, what rows, what players, how is the distribution on the board. 

The player who thinks the longest in their 3-4 last turns is highly likely to win, as the bonus points at the end are worth so much more than the points you accumulate during the game. This breaks the otherwise nice rythm. Playing fast early is fine, but playing fast in the endgame means the winner to a large part will be random.

Not played on 2, that might work better.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Sold on 1/18/2019. Simply lost its luster. There are so many superior abstracts I'd rather while away time on.

***
(+) Very interesting scoring mechanism in place. It is less so about the draft as it is about setting up your board for a significant scoring bonus.  
(+) Lean ruleset and objectively merciless player blocking and interaction. Meaningful decisions abound.  
(+) Stunning production quality.  

(-) It's not particularly fun. A multiplayer abstract tends to garner a lot of quiet think-time. 
(-) Turn structure is repetitive. Variety is only found in the tile draw, and on that note, a particularly unlucky player can experience in the following:
(-) Agency can feel limited if all the stars misalign and you are left with tile scraps.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
In brief: Zzzzzzzzzzzzz ...
In elaboration, Azul just doesn't make anything I'm doing while playing it feel _fun_.  The production values are genuinely great!  ... But building the board is slow and doesn't really feel rewarding.  You spend more time looking at other players boards than your own.  It doesn't feel good to screw other people or get screwed - it's rarely a clever play and more something you'll see coming a mile away.  There's just nothing here, and I genuinely don't understand the mass appeal beyond "simplewith nice components".  It's the new Splendor, except Splendor was the better game? :S
But hey, if you like Azul, you should look into Sagrada as well.  There's a lot of overlap in how the games go, so you might well like it.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
06.2022

Beyond the beautiful components, what makes Azul is the simple tile selection dynamic: Take a color off a disc and toss the rest in the middle. The first one to grab from the middle, takes a negative. If you have to take tiles that you don’t have spaces for, they count as negative VP. 

In essence, it manages to mesh together an abstract game with personal player boards and yet maintain a decent amount of player interaction – a pretty cool feat! Once past this, however, you’re simply grabbing tiles to fill in rows. The scoring is slightly unintuitive and takes a couple times for new players to get it.
 
Azul is fine but not exciting in the least; I’d play it if someone wanted but would never suggest it. Downgrading from a 6 to a 5.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Azul, on first play, felt lighter than I expected due to the quick game play, but also slightly heavier than expected due to the multiple point scoring strategies. I guess I should have read the point scoring more carefully before I started playing. I was hoping for a light competitive game that would satisfy an audience that isn’t looking for anything even close to a take-that feeling. Azul started to feel like that, but also, it seems that there are some take-that opportunities to force opponents to have penalties from tiles on their floor. I can imagine that being an important consideration in what tiles you leave in the center. 
The box art and typography is beautiful.  The tactile feel and solid look of the tiles is very satisfying.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: Deservedly a modern classic. Visually appealing, approachable, interactive. Though also strategic enough to be an interesting puzzle of trying to collect the right sets for the right spots to score the best points. Drafting a bunch of tiles, placing them on your board, and eventually filling up the pattern is satisfying, and while the game does become more constraining as it goes on, it also starts rewarding you with fun cascading scores. That said though I do find the game infuriating and frustrating when it becomes only about hate drafting and trying to force others to take a bunch of tiles for negative points, especially since this slows the game down considerably. However it's quite enjoyable when played as a casual abstract filler.
