Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
I'm not on board the hype train for this one. It's a fine filler game with stellar components, but the game is not very interesting,

... that was until Christmas, where my sister was gifted this game. I have since then upped my rating of the game from a 6.5 to 7.5.
Turns out, the game excels in a casual/family setting. Prior, I had only played it with experienced gamers (in a setting I suspect to be a bit too competitive for the good of this game), and the game just didn't do anything for me.
With family, the game is easy to pick up and offers more interesting decisions than other games with same weight (such as Splendor).

Though I still won't seek out my own copy of Azul, I just might consider the sister game, with stained glasses.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
One of my favorite drafting games. Fun theme, the game looks great and the component quality is really nice. I like how the drafting component works with simultaneously trying to get the optimal tiles while aiming to stop the plans of your opponent(s). This game really rewards you for outsmarting your opponent (and punishes the player who gets outsmarted in the same way). 1v1 it shares some similarties with chess; Every action has a reaction; You need to think a few steps ahead of your opponent in order to win (and not to end up with all those minus points ;)).
With 4 players it feels less intense and friendlier. All player counts are fun and exciting in their own way and can be played really seriously or with a much breezier mindset.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Looking at this game from a distance, it doesn't seem like something I would like. Take stuff from a central market, put stuff on your player board and score combo's! This type of gameplay usually leads to a lot of heads down play, and I guess Azul *could* be played that way.

Fortunately, player tableaus are easy enough to read so this game turns into a deliciously mean game of hate drafting and trying to stick opponents with as many minus points as possible. Because of this, I think the game works best at two, works fine at three, and I don't think I'd want to play this at four. When playing with three or more I think the game only works if every player is on the same level of hate drafting because of the strong left-right binding.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: A visually attractive drafting abstract the game plays simply and quickly. You can end the game very quickly but by doing that you miss on potentially more lucrative turns. The games a straight shooter in what it wants to do. There are also some fun moments where someone gets screwed up by being forced to take on a lot of one color near the end of the round. A big portion of skill to avoid that would be you ability to calculate players moves in advance and make sure your not the one taking the pot even if it means taking something you might not want. As a host I kind of dread the inventible low that someone will get grabbing the pile but the schadenfreude is usually worth it. If you end up with the pile twice you may just feel dread
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
As gateway games go, this one's a good one. It's easy to learn but difficult to master, the way any great gateway game should be. The beautiful color patterns lend it great table appeal, another bonus for drawing players in. Where it falls short, of course, is theme. If you're with a group that prefers pretending their mighty heroes, this isn't the game for you. Also, it tends to be a somewhat quiet, solitary affair where everyone is absorbed in their personal player board and too wrapped up in their personal decisions to do much talking. These issues keep the game short of greatness for me. They aren't deal-breakers, however, and I do appreciate the game's elegant simplicity and deceptive depth.

Also own wood first player tile
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Widely loved in my friend group, [b]very[/b] visually satisfying and also a very clever feeling game that strikes a nice tone of how much player interaction (interference) it allows.

Game gets just intricate enough one-on-one to feel like it holds up against some of the dedicated abstracts like Onitama and Santorini which I rate similarly, but expands to more players beautifully and is always easy to teach. 

The unsurprising dominant strategy of filling the player board top left to bottom right every time leaves little room for strategic intrigue. You've some some in the form of carrying tiles over round to round and a smidge more if you want to count tiles for some long term planning, but the game is almost entirely tactical.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
3 plays: 3p, 4p, 5p... WOW!  I did NOT understand what this game was until I played it. I should have known better than to doubt Michael Kiesling.  Lesson learned.  This game is incredible. Smooth onramp to the first play, simple ruleset, many-layered puzzle, player interaction IF YOU WANT IT, otherwise, enjoy your personal puzzle and have a good time.  What an accomplishment in game design.... fantastic!

Update after several plays:  been playing incorrectly.  I thought you weren't allowed to work on the same color tile in two different loading rows in a given round.  Allowing me to work on a single-blue and a 3-blue in the same round is just going to loosen the reins and make my scores even higher now.  I really dig this game.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
One of those games that has depth despite a very simple rule set.  It's hard to say if the game would be as popular without the really nice bits, but due to the components, more people are playing it, which is a good thing.  The drafting mechanism is simple, clever, and potentially really mean.  The scoring is loosely related to scrabble/qwirkle and works well here.  I have no doubt that this game will be played years from now.  This will be a classic and will be a staple for many types of groups.

UPDATE: After hundreds and hundreds of plays, I have to move this up to a 10. Insanely addictive even after so many plays. And even after many plays of he sequels, the original is still the best of the series by a significant margin.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: Azul is a fantastic tile drafting game where players aim to complete rows and columns of certain tiles, gaining points for adjacency planning. It is just forgiving enough to the point where decisions are difficult and need to be planned ahead, but if a plan doesn't go through, it is easy enough to shift and aim for another color or row in future rounds. Additionally, there is a table-wide "push your luck" element as the center location fills with appealing pieces, but the first to take it will suffer a negative point. Every decision here feels interesting. Very similar to the in vogue solitary puzzle abstracts, but better integrates open and direct draft planning and most importantly, captures the spark of fun. A great game.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Initial rating (3/2019): 8.5

Smooth, puzzle-like gameplay. Beautiful visual design and tactile experience. Nice tension as you acquire the tiles you need while watching the maneuvers of the other players, reevaluating your plan to try and satisfy your goals.

Playing as two player, a lot of thought goes into predicting what they other player will do and how to influence them so that they do what might benefit you the most or harm their score the most. It is a bit of a mind game in that sense. With more players, it is harder to take into consideration each player's options and probably better to just focus on what's best for you in that moment. I think three players offers enough player interaction without being cut-throat.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
My wife and I played Azul for the first time in a board game cafe and I thought it was fine, but it wasn't until I played on BGA against experienced opponents that I understood the need to optimize your tile placement to maximize points.

Ultimately this game comes down to drafting more strategically than your opponent, and trying to force them to take tiles they don't really want...but then there's the luck factor where no matter how hard you try, things just won't work out in your favour that round.

Ultimately I see this as a great gateway game. I am not sure I will ever buy it, and if I do, I would certainly buy the travel edition. For now, I am perfectly fine pulling this one out at a cafe, or hopping online on BGA.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Difficult to avoid reading about this one on the geek due to mainly positive buzz before it won SdJ 18. I wanted to avoid it because it is an abstract, many years in Euros  has made me realise the importance of narrative, especially listening to my young boys as they grow up. 
But I've reached my tolerance of ignoring the buzz, finally watching half of a Game night video play through just to satisfy what is it about the game that is creating some praise.
It seems the novel and (importantly) variable set drafting and collecting mechanisms is the main appeal, but the abstract, potential draft-hating and downtime as you assess availability and needs of others (since all info is open) has finally turned off the buzz for me.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: Who would've guessed an innocuous game about laying bathroom tiles (or whatever it is you're supposed to be doing) could turn out to be so cruel? Azul is the physical embodiment of hate drafting - a game where tiles are merely a medium through which you express your tyranny. Snatching the last set of blues and gleefully watching as your opponents pile on those negative points is schadenfreude incarnate, and the way the game forces you to consider between tiles you need vs. tiles others need - only to occasionally topple that balance with blissful abandon - is a lovely, brutal thing. Never mind the poor attempts at franchising with window painting and whatnot - nothing beats the original's pure cutthroat tension.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Azul is an abstract game with several elegant and interesting mechanics that fit well together. The objective is to fill rows and columns on your "wall" with tiles of specific colors where each placed tile scores itself AND adjacent rows and columns. 

But the tiles must first be placed in your "shelves" with space for 1-5 tiles and may not be moved further until the shelf is full. Furthermore, the tiles are selected from small "pools" of tiles where you pick all of one color and moves the rest to a larger pool, potentially giving the next player a good pick. Add to this negative points for acquiring more tiles than you can fit on your shelves or move to your wall and you have potential for a very mean game.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: Apparently I am very basic in my board game tastes. But Azul is absolutely incredible upon my first few plays. I love how the scoring builds up throughout. The end game bonuses are also a nice addition. I understand that this game will likely get old after a while but for now I love it very much. That said, I think because this game can get so attacky, it might stand the test of time. If I know my opponent is about to score big, I will take those tiles just so she can't get them. That tactical nature is what will make this game stand the test of time. My family also likes this game which is a plus. The play time is excellent on this with two players. However, with 4 players I felt it get a bit bogged down.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
After 60+ plays it now struggles to get to the table, but for over 50 plays I was totally grabbed by this game! The rating will remain to reflect the enjoyment I've had from the game, rather than how I feel about it now.

I tried picking up Summer Pavilion to inject some freshness back into our Azul plays, but it just didn't have the same charm as the original.

This completely replaced Sagrada for me, which now just seems slow, frustrating and fiddly in comparison.

EDIT: Mandala has now usurped Azul as my favourite in this category, but this will always hold a special place and no game can be expected to last an infinite number of plays!

Definitely best at 2. Plan to pick up the Mini version for travel.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
A must own gateway/family game.  Beautiful and elegant.  My wife's all time favorite game.  We will never tire of Azul.

After further consideration, this version of Azul might just be my favorite of the 3.  More than any other version, vanilla Azul has me reading my opponents’ boards, predicting their moves, and executing tactical drafts to take advantage of their probable behavior.  Later versions elect to reduce this depth of player interaction by expanding options for tile placement.

While the OG Azul is definitely the meanest of the 3 (a downside for some people), it is undoubtedly the most tense and thrilling.  Read my full thoughts of all 3 Azuls here: https://bitewinggames.com/which-azul-is-best/
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
A nice, reasonably weighty game to play with the wife. The colorful and extremely amazing production quality helps to get the wife to try it out. 

The wife likes the game, and I like that the game is fast and easy to setup and to play. 

At 4 players the game is pretty interactive, with players trying to get the tiles they want and also to attempt to deny the other players as well. It gets tense and silent when everyone is thinking hard or observing hard whenever it's a player's turn to pick.

The default side has enough meat to it that it provides us with tough decisions and the usual thinking groans that we like in our game. Not sure when before we attempt the blank advanced side to up the challenge.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Fast, fun, with decisions to make, but easy to implement them (grab some tiles from the centre). 
The only downs are
1) separate scoring tracks on each player's mat: it would be better to have a single track for all players, 
2) the tiny black wooden cubes used to keep score: so easily knocked given the fast furious til grabbing action that involves reaching over the score marker, dragging tiles back onto your mat and plonking them down. 
3) The circular card 'factories cry out to be replaced by orange terracotta mug coasters.
Then you could leave them out on your coffee table as game bait, use them for pretendingly for coffee, and when someone says how pretty they are, you can plonk out the game itself.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: 6.5 initial score but a bit of a pass after 20 plays when I understood it better. The scoring ruins what could have been. I have it at home and while its pretty it definitely doesn't live up to the hype and price. Its kinda hyper mean and the scoring sucks all the fun out of it and creativity it could have had. I would not recommend this one. After playing with more people on boardgame arena it became a drag because there is so much claustrophobic strategy going on that it sucks all the fun out of it. If you like calculating your way to victory in a series of hyper predictable moves its your game. It would be better if the base game had some variability in scoring and tiling. Disappointed in my purchase.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Have many played head to head games. Can be quite nasty, although we aren’t playing very defensively yet and leave ourselves open to getting hip-checked into the rink wall!

Quite smooth game and feels like it had a nice blend of strategy and tactics. We don't normally get this fired up for set collecting drafting games but this one really works for us for some reason? I think part of the special sauce of this game is the big offer of new tiles at several points in the game. Gives a similar rush to a big offer at the beginning of a worker placement round.

It's also a game where it's fun to watch the other player's turn.

I have the Giant Azul version is which epic and ridiculous. It’s amazing looking.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
I purchased this game because I have been it all over. Many people who reviewed Sagrada (our fave) recommended Azul and so when I saw it on sale, I could not pass it up. 

Pros:
-beautiful game
-nice mechanics with some strategy, but not overwhelming

Cons:

Education:

-taking turns
-matching patterns

Overall:

Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
#wifeapproved

Initial thoughts: As a designer, I'm a sucker for games that look nice. The hefty tiles and overall aesthetic of this game caught my eye. I was hesitant after hearing about the possibility of hate drafting and conflict in two player games since I'd largely be playing it with my wife.

After 2 plays: It's a great game and somewhat exceeded my expectations. It's the perfect weight for a relaxing evening. My wife loves tetris and enjoyed the puzzle. She gets her own board to focus on, but the drafting mechanic means your opponents moves also matter. I can see how hate drafting and conflict can enter the game. How much that impacts a gaming table is based on who's sitting around it.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Azul can be fun and light-hearted, or cruel and vicious. And either way, it's real pretty to look at.

As a multiplayer experience, you have a slightly more relaxing experience (unless you're someone who tries to count tiles) that is enjoyable on many levels.

As a two player experience, the game can turn real aggressive, real fast. The level of aggression will of course be dictated by the social contract between players. As long as everyone abides, Azul should be very enjoyable, wether aggressive or relaxed.

Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
P: 2-4, T: 30-45, SdJ-W
Abstract, Family. Laying beautiful clacking tile tokens. Tightly balanced angst based on player decisions. Lightish rules, fast to teach and assemble/put away. Lots of hype but previewing it hasn't really grabbed me. Blocking others (potentially hate drafting) and planning ahead are key to success.
Would like to try at Mox. Compare with Dragon Castle, Sagrada

Now with lots of plays, it's a great accessable game: fast to teach, set up and play. But, it's really gotten stale at 2 players, which is 95% of the way we play; without much variability and the knowledge that colors taken by the other player will eventually come around, there isn't many compelling moments left.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: Fun game that's very easy to learn and teach but hard to master. Definitely takes a lot of thinking ahead to plan out which rows you want to complete or which bonus points you want to target (completed rows, columns, or colors). It can be sort of mean or cut-throat to take tiles someone else needs which can be good or bad depending on the crowd you're playing with. Components are nice and the game board looks nice. Well written rules and easy setup and tear-down. My only very minor complaint is that the floor track doesn't just tell you how many points you need to subtract at certain fill levels, instead it makes you count the negative points yourself. Other than that it's a pretty good game!
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Surprised that this one has captured the attention of so many people and become an award winning design. The game play is very light, the puzzle is rather bland, and the interaction is very limited.  

I feel the same way about this as I did Tokaido a few years back, that the presentation has some how blinded players into believing they are more involved in a game than they actually are.   

I don't see where this game has any legs to stand on against other games.  

I have been impressed by Mr, Kiesling in 2017 but feel the attention to his work has been given to his lesser design.   Heaven & Ale, Riverboat, and even Reworld are more interesting.

This really gives meaning to the term "meh"
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Beautiful tactile game.

Too abstract and scripted to my liking. A person that loves chess would probably love 1v1 games of Azul.

I dislike two things about the game :
* Sometimes, no matter what you take, you'll be stuck with the -14 in one turn making your progress quite useless. Sintra is quite interesting in that regards as you can potentially skip your turn which makes the game maybe less scripted.
* The first player token is too strong for only a penalty of one point. I like what they did in Summer Pavilion and Sintra to fix that.

Overall, it's a good game, simple to learn and teach but not something I enjoy playing as it is too chesslike but I can see why it is so popular and loved.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
This game looks amazing: the art on the player mats and the box/bag and of course the tiles! On top of that the gameplay is equally well done. The different mechanisms (drafting the tiles and managing your production lines) fit together smoothly and are easy to teach. The game is a lot of fun: it plays fast, it's very satisfying to accomplish your plans, and there are ample opportunities to block other players.
In contrast to other raters, I think the game is equally good as a two player or three/four player game. While a four player game is more laid back, a two player game is quite vicious. Also, in the four player game there's enough possibility to predict your opponents and plan ahead.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
If you don't already own Azul I would suggest this over the full sized version. Not only is it cheaper, it's designed with travel in mind and has great plastic overlays to stop tiles moving. It's nearly half the price but has double the functionality.

I have two (very) minor points. 1) Considering how well designed the player board overlays are, the plastic factory insert (while perfectly functional) isn't as nice. 2) The travel bag for all the components only has a small snap button to close it, so if the tiles are loose in the bag and the bag is tipped, the tiles will fall out. I use a small dice bag to hold the tiles inside the travel bag, rather than the little plastic bags provided.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Azul is a reasonably quick abstract tile drafting and placement game.  I really like the game, and it can be played with additional players (I believe there is an expansion that allows for more than 4 players).  We have played with 2, 3, and 4 players.  We purchased crystal mosaic at the same time to get the player board overlays, which are extremely nice.  
The pieces are very nice and have a solid (heavy) feel to them (extremely high quality).  It takes about 5 minutes to setup and learn the game and a two player game will take under 30 minutes which is nice when you want to play a couple games but don’t want have 3-4 hours to invest.
This is an excellent game and it has broad appeal.

textfield_comment_value:
My favourite abstract strategy game. Involves pulling coloured tiles from a bag and placing four on each station in the middle of the table. Players grab from these stations to add to their mosaic, needing either, 1,2,3,4 or 5 tiles to place a tile, depending on the row. Caveat is you can only grab one type of tile from a station and must take all of that tile. Discarded tiles from stations go into the center and form a pool. The first player to grab all of one type from the center takes a -1 token. Points are achieved for making rows, columns, connections and full sets.

update, still love the game, but felt samey after a few plays, and Stained Glass offered more choice and tension.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
A nice game, where you have to draw colored tiles from a common pool, which means you need to be aware of the others need to plan accordingly what you will draw. Regarding what you need, you have to make compromise between the optimal geometrical deployment to maximise your points, and the constraint (one color per line a turn, and more tiles needed to deploy on the bottom line).
It's overall a clever game, with nice component, it's pretty to look at. However, it doesn't appeal more to me than that, I play whenever someone wants to, but I never bring it to the table by myself. Maybe the theme, maybe the fact that the common pool generates only frustration among the people I play with.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: Very pretty mosaic-building game which boasts a lovely production apart from two minor issues:  (1) the game requires a lot of manipulation of heavy resin tiles and the scoring cube is very easy to bump or knock around accidentally; and (2) the boards are warped enough that they spin too easily on the table, and again with all the tile manipulation happening the spinning is a real issue for the players.   The best thing about the game is the scoring system stolen (borrowed) from Qwirkle.   That makes slotting your tiles into the mosaic fun.   The game is not for the AP-prone however...   perfect information and lots to calculate on OTHER player's boards will be an annoyance for some.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Interesting multiplayer abstract. Fairly quick, fairly tactical, not so much strategy. That is to say downstream ramifications are fairly easy to see, but you do have interesting tactical choices that are not often clear cut.

All of that is fine with me. I am a firm believer that abstract games A) should not be rules intensive, easy to teach and B) thinky but not heavy.

I have noted in recent months that this game is available in Walmart. Normally that is a huge, negative red flag about quality of game design. Azul may have a brief life as a mass market game, but probably not too long. It is too good for the mass market. It is an aficionado game.

Quality components are a big plus.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Purchased in Falls Church, VA on a whim around 2018. 

Pro and Con: Winning is dependent on 50% luck, 30% skill and 20% on a player's willingness to fuck someone over.

Pros:
- incredibly easy to bring to the table
- pieces are beautiful and smooth to the touch.
- two board sides with varying difficultly. 
- just enough ways to "fuck over" another player to make for some interesting moments

Cons:
- the main board is more "fun" to play with a group, but also leaves you wanting more out of the game's replayability and mixing/matching of moving parts. 
- Strategy becomes unvaried after multiple games
- patterns and colors are the extent of the theme, which can be unimpressive to some.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: Azul is fine as a simple, abstract game. If you are a fan of abstracts with a decent amount of player interaction in terms of what you select affecting everyone else, especially the next player, then you will probably like Azul. I've heard a good number of gamers singing the praises of this one and I don't dislike this type of game, but it's not what I'm looking for. I do like some abstracts, but this one play didn't set Azul apart in my mind. I can appreciate some of the cleverness in the design, but I don't really desire to play the game again. The only thing that gives me pause is all the positive comments from others I know. The components are very nice... that was a big plus.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Azul is a spiritual successor in the line of simple scoring games like Splendor, Century and Majesty. Even more than those Azul shares similarities to all the roll and write games where you're trying to fill up a bunch of rows. This is why I find it disturbing that the game is often called an "abstract" which has the wrong connotation to abstract strategy games.
It's a clean design that can be teached to just about anyone. My main concern is that in both games I played nearly all players fulfilled all their end game bonuses and were thus left with nothing to discover in the future. Azul is a prime example of a good but once and done game with nothing to offer after your first try.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Secret Santa 2018.  Excellent design--well deserving of all the praise and attention it received coming out of Essen 2017.  

Need to get more plays of this the fully evaluate, but I expect this to continue to shine particularly as our group becomes more familiar with it.  I can see this becoming much more cutthroat after numerous plays (and this is a game where AP-prone players will get more and more trapped as they try to take into account all of their opponents' boards as well as their own), so will have to see if that has a detrimental effect on how frequently it makes it to the table.  Plays quickly enough that I wouldn't expect instances of screwage to totally derail it.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: Stellar abstract game. After about a dozen plays I'm getting to the point that I'm scoring in the 50 to 80 range. This is a 2p for me and as my wife and I understand it more, it's becoming a more face-to-face competition. At first we were just building patterns. Then we began to build multiple patterns and connect them to get large two-vector scores, most recently we've begun playing defensively and trying to anticipate based on which tiles have or haven't already come out in numbers. I think strategy is likely to be limited by luck of the bag-draw, but it's an interesting tactical battle and along with Photosynthesis, is among the best 2p abstracts I've played in quite a while.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
The central puzzle of taking pieces is pretty satisfying, but the challenge of building on your board is, for me, ho-hum. It's a good game, but gets very samey for me personally. Great potential for annoyance if you get up in people's business and try to disrupt their plans.

Regardless, it's a superb gateway game, and since I've gotten rid of Century: Spice Road I kind of feel the obligation to keep this one around as a really nice ease-in to the world of hobby gaming :)

I'd love to see a five-player expansion, because I often have more than four when I'm pitching an easy, gateway-style game.

Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: To me Azul is a 10 if played at 2 players. I'm no longer interested in playing the game on a higher player count. In my opinion it is a perfect two player game. If played over 5 rounds at 2 players the bag doesn't refill which means it's very hard for either player to get a full colour set as you need 15 tiles to complete this and there are only 20 of each. Sometimes you'll want the game to go more than 5 rounds and the bag to refill but usually if you want this your opponent does not so they will likely force the game to end. The strategy at 2 players is 50% about what you lay and 50% controlling what your opponent can lay. It is quite mean but a lot of strategic depth at two.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Absolutelly outstanding. I gotta admit I thought It was just a hype, because the theme is very unusual, but the game is a pure 10/10.

Edit: Woah, easy, Tiger! After 6 months, I drecreased It to 7/10. It's the only game my wife is always in the mood to play, I gotta give 'em that, but to me now It feels like a mandatory massage to warm before you get to what you really want, if you know what I mean. 

You can have a bit of fun, but It's so repetitive, swingy, with a dash of AP, agonizing choices and bad players screwing themselves and draging you and your strategy with them. Beatiful to showcase to non gamers tho, I also give 'em that.

Not fun anymore, but can't get rid of It.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: There's a part of me that wonders if my appreciation for Azul has anything to do with the stellar production values. And another part of me that doesn't care, since the game is great fun regardless. In all honesty, if this was just cardboard chits it would still be a great multiplayer abstract - a niche that was at that time yet unfilled in my collection. That the pieces are so substantial and fun to fiddle with just becomes icing on the cake. Azul works for me whether I'm not in the mood for deep thinking and just want to focus on my own board and its development, or when I'm in the mood to try and math out who best to screw over with that pile of extra tiles in the centre.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
After a good number of plays, I'm now confident in giving this a 10. It's the perfect evergreen. It's super easy to teach and easy to play. Everyone understands the game and is playing very quickly after setting up (which is also quite quick).

The delicious decisions you have in each draft add to the rising tension, as you end up holding your breath to see if a key set of tiles will make it around to you. The unique scoring opportunities start to present themselves as the game evolves, and the ability to minus one point but get first player next round is a fun strategic layer.

Other than some cutthroat moments, I just can't think of much negative about this one. It's great.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: A lovely looking tile laying game, with an old school feel to it.  Players take turns drafting one set of coloured tiles from the available markets, or from the middle of the board.  Tiles from the market not taken are pushed to the middle.  Taken tiles are “prepared” in rows, and when a row is finished, a tile is moved to the “wall” to score points for adjacent tiles.  Bonus points for complete rows and columns on the 5x5 wall, as well as filling in all of one coloured tile on the wall.  Very simple to teach and play, but very subtle and devious - some serious thinking is required here.  Plays very quickly, and has high “one more game” factor.  An instant classic, I suspect.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Really beautiful game. The box calls to you. The pieces reward you for opening it. And the gameplay is quite refreshing and fun. It's a reward splitting game with a neat mechanism that plays along at a brisk clip.

What to choose has to be a balance between what is good for you and how the remaining choices will ripple along through the other players. Often you need to block, so keep your head up. Otherwise someone might run away with all kinds of bonus points.

The four player is fun, but feels a bit chaotic. Haven't played two-player yet, but I worry that it might be a bit brainburny as you try an ply your way through all the back and forth. Three is likely the sweet spot.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: It's a classic tile laying game for a reason. The mechanisms are slick and it leaves a sense of "I could do better" at the end of each game. The potential hate drafting of tiles make for some compelling mind games, too. However, I'm personally not a fan of hate drafting, and in this game it can be very frustrating to need 1 tile, have that one tile appear at the start of a round, and watch your opponent take it just to screw you over. Furthermore, I find the game is a little too limited for my taste. I just feel like I'm doing more or less the same thing every time I play. Although I can see why this is highly regarded, I more often find myself playing Cascadia or Harmonies.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
I know that many don't like games that are open to hate drafting. But I do. And... I love it when someone else does it to me. In an age where most games are about playing nice or limited interaction multiplayer solitaire, there's something satisfying about seeing someone embrace their evil side in a play :)

One of those rare games that plays great from 2-4. Easy learning curve that gets steeper with more plays. Fun watching players waste time going for five of a kind before they clue in that columns are where the big points are.

Top notch production. I just wish all of the cubes had classic azulejo patterns on them. Having both solid red and solid blue tiles feels lazy.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
While certainly in the same family-friendly class as Sagrada (and Blokus, Ingenious, etc.), given that you score your tiles like Qwirkle, I'm surprised more people do not compare it to that.

   It seems the number of tiles is ideal for 2 players, and its play much more cut-throat (if you're playing properly, and keeping an eye on what your opponent needs).  As such, we prefer playing with 2 players.

   I am a bit disappointed that not all tiles have their own design...  I've seen the Alhambra, there's no place for plain tiles (that I remember seeing).  Note, that for those who have difficulties differentiating color, Azul is a better alternative than Sagrada.

141 J
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
I feel ashamed to confess that my first impression with Azul was positive, kind of: it was still light years away from my idea of a fun board game but somehow at first I found it bearable nonetheless.

Then I’ve played it a few times more and each play distanced me further and further from that first impression until I realized it at last: Azul is exactly as dry, puzzly and boring as it looks, if not even worse.
Which also translates into the most annoying activities of board gaming: overplanning, overthinking, analysis paralysis and lack of socialization.

That’s too much to endure for something that should be fun. Hence, you’d better leave Azul in the dump it belongs to
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Really pretty puzzley-type game however it is a bit of a shame the dark blue and the red tiles do not have patterns on them (I kept turning them over expecting a pattern on the other side :blush:) and honestly this could have been half the price tag and had cardboard pieces, but I did enjoy this one.

The selection mechanic for the tiles is really interesting and with each pick you must balance not only what you need but minimise the advantage for your opponents by not leaving anything too tempting for them to take straight after you. 

Scoring is interesting if a little cumbersome and the end game seems to come up pretty fast but overall I really quite enjoyed this one
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
A rhythmic aesthetically appealing tactile board game themed around Portuguese floor tiles. This game is accessible for both gamers and nongamers and its abstract design leads to an elegant gameplay experience. Azul is especially useful for getting non gamers into the hobby. 

Despite my high praise, I have given it a rather middling rating. This may take many by surprise, but should not be misinterpretted. Azul is fundamentally a gateway game, and its lower rating reflects that.  While enjoyable to both seasoned and nonseasoned gamers, the former will not be wowed as easily by pretty, cute components and will become dulled to the gaming experience if played too often.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Pretty . . . forgettable . . . actually, not a bad game, but sometimes struggles to capture my family's imagination . . .

2019 UK Games Expo Best Abstract Game Judges Award Winner (2019): Tric Trac d'Argent (2018); Spiel des Jahres Winner (2018); Origins Awards Best Family Game Winner (2018); Nederlandse Spellenprijs Best Family Game Winner (2018); Mensa Select Winner (2018); Guldbrikken Best Adult Game Winner (2018); Deutscher Spiele Preis Best Family/Adult Game Winner (2018); As d'Or - Jeu de l'Année Winner (2018); Golden Geek Best Family Board Game Winner (2017); Cardboard Republic Architect Laurel Winner (2017).

Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
:thumbsup: As far as gameplay is concerned, they could have just as easily gone with cardboard chits. But they didn't and that gives Azul tremendous visual appeal that's definitely worth its cost.
:thumbsup: The rules are easy to learn, and there's more interaction involved than you'd guess at first glance: "do you pick these tiles to score points, or the other tiles to deny your opponent a good scoring opportunity?"
:thumbsup: Scales very well with different player counts.
:thumbsup: It has built-in revitalization of gameplay: once it starts getting stale, you flip your board to the side without pre-printed patterns.

Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
5/3/2020 | 8 plays | 8/10 | Very enjoyable game. I have played with a wide age range and they've all enjoyed it. The tiles are beautiful and offer a wonderfully tactile experience to the game. Finding the order in which to draft tiles offers an interesting puzzle each time. 

The one negative for me is the scoring. It's a tad convoluted. I understand it, but it's the most difficult thing to explain to new players. Although, it is this scoring system that adds part of the depth of the game. Is what it is.

9/27/2021 | 8 plays | Rating: 7 | Just a negative bump as I haven't played this one in quite some time and had started to tire of it when I last did. A good game.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
This is one of two games my mom (age 70) explicitly asks to play - and we have a 50/50 win streak.

While far from being a favorite of mine, it's super easy to explain and get into. Do you know someone who maybe isn't super into board games, but enjoys an abstract puzzle? This is a good game for you!

A little on the simple side, but satisfying. Brilliant in its simplicity.

I do prefer the Queen's Garden iteration, but this original and basic Azul is more accessible. It's quick and simple to explain, making it rather easy to introduce. Very pretty, tactile tiles which are very satisfying to handle. 

Minor annoyance: the point marker threatens to slide everywhere.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
A top-tier abstract game.  Take tiles according to very specific rules - baroque rules befitting a slightly mad palace owner - line them up in rows of different lengths to prepare them for placement.  When all tiles are taken, shift one tile from a full row over to the actual scoring wall, score points.  Rinse, repeat, until one player completes a single tile row on the scoring wall.  Then score even more points if you've completed rows, columns, or complete color sets.

Perfect for 2, 3, and 4 players.  Drawbacks? Scoring cubes are very fiddly, and the rules for filling the rows are confusing for first time players.  Otherwise, an awesome part of a game collection
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: Azul is the epitome of everything I love about Kiesling's games.  He is my favorite designer.  Kiesling has an incredible ability to design games that have a concise and simple set of rules but have a ton of depth in the strategy and game play.  Azul epitomizes this.  Azul is so simple to remember all the rules, teach the rules, and get to the table.  Yet everytime I play I experience a new moment.  Its a game I can teach someone who has never played a modern board game in their life as well as enjoy playing with the heaviest and most discerning gamers.  I have around 12 plays under my belt and not a single one of those plays did I lose any love for this game.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
[url=https://www.boardgamegeek.com/geeklist/232674/item/5762971]1 play[/url]

Very clever spatial puzzle kind of game. Great production!

Finally tried the back of the board, with no pre-designated spaces. Gah, hated it! I enjoy this game as a quick, light game to play without a lot of thought -- the kind you have to do for deep abstract games, the kind that I find so annoying. This side of the board forces you to think a whole lot more about your play so that you don't inadvertently make some spaces impossible to play into! I'm sure this will be attractive to fans of abstract games, but it's not for me -- I'd be happy to never play this side of the board again!
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Azul packs so many interesting decisions into a really simple rule set. A healthy dose of randomness in the tile distribution keeps experienced players from steamrolling the inexperienced. Definitely a great gateway game, Azul really rewards identifying immediate gains over long term strategy. Mid and end game scoring combos makes the game exciting for everyone, but does so by slightly favouring luck over in-depth analysis. Azul never gets too analytical — a great game for introducing new gamers that is still deep enough for those well steeped in the hobby.

See more of my thoughts at https://www.boardgamegeek.com/blogpost/78860/azul-13-clues-downforce-mainland
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
This game is fantastic. The amount of thinking that the player must muster in order to make a proper move becomes increasingly harder each turn. I love that ramp up of intensity. 

A couple things I'm not a fan of;
The score block is not very secure and I find myself accidentally clipping it and sending it flying while grabbing tiles. Maybe a wheel or some other counting method would work better. The other thing is the scoring method. It takes some effort to count up all your points and leaves my head feeling heavy. 

All in all, this game owns. It's really easy to just sit back, make some tea, and play Azul with my beautiful wife who consistently destroys me.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: I love Azul as a two-player game. I've enjoyed it at more players, but have mostly played it at two. It can be a "take that" game, but often the strategy of focusing on your opponent doesn't work out due to randomness of the tiles. As a result, there's always the threat of meanness, but it's not always a winning strategy to be mean. I do believe paying attention to your opponent is important, but you also should never stop focusing on yourself. At more than two players, the game in my groups becomes very talkative and light. At two, it's tense, quick, and tight. I would like to try the newer Azuls, but I truly have gotten my money's worth out of the original.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: My wife and I were hooked on this game from the moment we first played.  We usually played it multiple times a day, often several times in a row.  It was one of the few games my wife would play at any time (the other being Qwirkle).  She would set it up with morning coffee and would even suggest playing after dinner (which is never usually an option!).  Lately, our interest in it has waned, though.  Have a really cool factory tile holder for it that we got off Etsy:  https://www.etsy.com/listing/833584417/azul-factory-tile-holder?ga_order=most_relevant&ga_search_type=all&ga_view_type=gallery&ga_search_query=azul&ref=sr_gallery-1-7&col=1&variation0=1453692567
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Yes, it's yet another 'get stuff from the middle to arrange on your individual board' game. But it's pretty, the individual board puzzle is interesting and crucially, the 'get stuff' mechanic allows serious interaction (helped by the other players' boards being easily readable at a glance). Some great exclamations of horror as players realise what they're going to get stuck with. So far I've played with 3 and 4; 3p allowed the screwage to become more calculated and I can see it being really nasty with 2.

Edit: it is really nasty with 2, and I like it! Prefer not to play this with 4 now and 3 only when everyone is on the same page regarding the interaction.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: Beautiful Azul is a game to calm your nerves. It is clever, competative, and at the same time it makes you feel happier, even if you lose. It is the prettiness of the design, the colours, the calm way of playing, the clarity and simplicity of the rules, the depth and strategic complexity that makes it a challenge - but in an unexcited and peaceful way - that make this game a gem. Azul also has the tactile element. Handling the pretty pieces, the tiles, simply feels good. It also takes up fairly little tablespace and has a short setup time, so you can just put the box on the table and are ready to play in no tme at all. A must-have! Azul will be a classic.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
[i]Beautifully tessellate with tactically drafted azulejos—an essential for any collection.[/i]
Played in: [url=https://boardgamegeek.com/geeklist/330164/item/10426884][u]2024[/u][/url], [url=https://boardgamegeek.com/geeklist/10156070/item/9670528][u]2023[/u][/url], [url=https://boardgamegeek.com/geeklist/301212/item/9432045][u]2022[/u][/url], [url=https://boardgamegeek.com/geeklist/288902/item/8664246][u]2021[/u][/url], [url=https://boardgamegeek.com/geeklist/278184/item/8010405][u]2020[/u][/url], [url=https://boardgamegeek.com/geeklist/268367/item/7714510][u]2019[/u][/url],  [url=https://boardgamegeek.com/geeklist/248145/item/6629652][u]2018[/u][/url]
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Not my cup of tea in the slightest. I found the premise dull and the tiles weren't as nice as I had thought from product photos. Didn't realize you couldn't create your own patterns until we unboxed the game and had to follow the one given on the board, limiting gameplay options even more. Other side was more open-ended, but you still had to follow a strict set of guidelines. Would not play this game again unless someone really, really wanted to.

Note: My rating is based on my enjoyment level, not the overall gameplay design or production value. I also do not like Euro games in general, or competitive play, so I am not surprised this game wasn't for me.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: I go in ebbs and flows with this one. I think it's really only best at 2, which is fine in our home, since so much of my gaming is at 2, but I've found that the math just becomes the game, and while that's okay in some positional abstracts because the goal is board dominance and necessarily leveraging incremental advantages, I find that for games like this one, I get a bit irked by the zero-sum nature of it, especially when the skill differential between players is even slightly in one player's favor. 3 and 4 players are fine, but more chaotic, which causes unintentional screwage in the late game, which I just don't want in a points optimization puzzle.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: A beautiful abstract with indirect interaction. Color tiles are drawn and placed into lots. On their turn, a player picks all tiles of a color from one lot and adds to storage spaces on their board. Unpicked tiles go into a central lot which can be picked from later. There are some storage restrictions that can lead to negative points. After all tiles are taken, each player moves tiles from storage to scoring area and score based on some rules. Nice components and light rules make for an appealing abstract. Strategy space doesn't appear to be too large and you need to keep track of other players personal boards, which makes this slightly less appealing.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
First and only version we've played and it was a hit. Played two (2 player ) games in a row while learning which is a first. The second game was much more competative and intense which was great. Those last few rounds when you're just taking tiles from the middle and trying to work out how you can force your opponent to take that big bunch of useless so negative scoring tiles .. 

Thinky but not brain burning and with enough shenanigans to be entertaining. A nice abstract game with simple enough rules and mechanics, and quality components. Though not a fan of the thin card factory tiles and plastic holder of the 'mini' version.
Good for non gamers too.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Nachvollziehbar, das Azul zum Spiel des Jahres gekührt wurde. Legespiel, mit echt schönen Steinchen. Total einsteigerfreundlich und trotzdem regt es zum Nachdenken an. Auch die Spielzeit ist optimal. Die Spielermatten hätten besser sein können. Außerdem hoffe ich, dass es eine Reiseversion geben wird. Denn mir ist in der Box zu viel Luft. Oder anders Formuliert: das geht auch kompakter!
(Edit: Bei der Kaufentscheidung, war das Spiel "Codex Naturalis" überzeugender(aufgrund Boxgröße), schlussendlich wurden trotzdem beide gekauft)
(Weiterer Nachtrag: Eine Reise/Mini-Edition gibt es mittlerweile, aber ich finde diese unschön. Auch wenn Sie praktisch ist)
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
I was predisposed to dislike this game since I hate anything popular and good but this has become a favorite of mine (I got Patchwork and Sagrada at the same time and this is the only one I've not only kept, but kept playing).

If you are thinking that this looks like a Separate Board-Common Resource Area-Heads Down Snooze Fest you are mostly WRONG.  The puzzles are separate, yes, but the common resource area is a bloodbath and it is absolutely part of your analysis to consider how best to make your opponent cry.  What else could you want in a game and one that is packaged so beautifully?

Don't eat the pieces no matter how Starburst-like they look.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Core mechanics for acquiring tiles are excellent, and serve as a foundation for all the Azul games thus far. 

Casual game that provides a way to be mean to other players by simply taking tiles out of spite. 

Repeated plays give you more insight into scoring opportunities, and each time it's a great mix of push your luck and meaningful decisions. 

I appreciate the subtle ways to get an advantage by paying attention to probability of remaining tiles in the stock, and what other players are pursuing. Easy to play your own game and ignore everybody else though, if you're going for a family friendly round where you don't want friends to assault you.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
(after three 2p games) 

great theme (love azulejos), great drafting mechanism, fun little game. Abstract but with azulejos so it doesn't matter. In a 2 player game "hate drafting" could be perform pretty easily. But it's also up to you because in this game you have perfect information (nearly no unknown information). So you can prevent it. Generell luck  it's not that relevant in this game. You can follow  your strategy but you have to adapt to the situation and to the other player. The decision at the beginning are not easy but during the game it will be easier. That means you can play more thoughtful.  

I will definitely buy it at Essen Spiel.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Beautifully constructed both in terms of mechanics and the physical build quality of the game, this game's sudden explosion of popularity is definitely not a flash in the pan. It's also great for playing with people who don't really play boardgames usually.

Warning though: the rulebook makes it sounds way harder than it is to play, and it's actually harder than you'd think to explain how to play verbally even once you're confident yourself. With new players it's easier to sort of dive in with the basics and then explain the more nuanced bits of the rules - scoring, placement rules, the floor, basic strategy re end score bonuses, etc - as you go.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
One of the most conflicted games, pretending to be a meditative one.

In Azul, every second of the game you will count the tiles: in the center of the table, your own and your opponents'. Counting and miscalculation — that's what this game is about. Which, by the way, does not make it bad. Simple and clear rules help you focus on the main thing, which is building your field. Pleasant components please the eye and do not let you get bored.

Still, in my opinion, the setting misleads most people who are attracted by theses colorful tiles and imaginary meditativeness. Azul is not a meditative game, but a repetitive one. There will be no relaxation.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: Azul has so many good qualities.  The components are legendary and it has become a cliche to joke about eating the tiles.  Setup is a breeze.  It takes up very little table space but simultaneously makes a big aesthetic statement.  Learning it is simple, teaching it equally so.  It is a puzzle-driven abstract as one sits and works through mathematical options, but there is plenty of social interaction as nearly every decision directly affects other players.  Meanness is a byproduct of the mechanisms and is rarely mistaken for animus.  I only have two complaints:  (1) the game ends if someone bumps the scoring boards and (2) my wife always wins.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: The game is beautiful. And it appeals visually to non-gamers that other games simply don't. My wife, who rarely plays games, loved the look and wanted to learn to play. The rules are simple so any rulebook intimidation is simply not there. As the game progresses it just flows and I've noticed everyone picks up on it within a few minutes. It appears to appeal to folks who love puzzles and patterns. It's definitely one I will bring out with new players or those who've played games for years. And because it so easy to grasp even a new player can easily win so the intimidation of being blown away doesn't tend to exist, at least in our experience.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: Azul is more attractive than it is intuitive and it will unfortunately attract the Ticket to Ride crowd when it is really aimed at the abstract / euro gamer. This makes for a confusing game classification as it is not really a gateway game but looks like it should be. I was ultimately disappointed and had no real urge to play this again but kept wanting to show it to new gamers, none of whom were wowed by it and none ever asked to play it again. I have no idea why this game is ranked this high as it is just not that much fun and the wall mechanics are wonky. Yet, for some reason I keep going back to it months later only to be  underwhelmed.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: The game is an absolute enigma of design.  The rules are incredibly simple, but it yields a thought out tactical game that sinks you into the experience.  It follows a simple drafting mechanic that is as important to you as your opponent.  It may feel like a single player game sometimes as you are fully invested onto your own board with no conflict with the other players, but sometimes you screw yourself over just a little to completely negate another player from acquiring drafts.  The game creates a perfect confluence of draft and pace, where every round matters, and not scoring points could cost you the game if you don't choose carefully!
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Dammit, I wrote a really long comment for this and then it did not save correctly, so let's try again. 

Oh god, I got hammered at this which is fairly rare when I play abstracts with Heather. The game is obviously a lot a fun and I generally really liked it. However, I am not sure it has space in my collection for a few reasons. Firsly, I have a few abstracts already that never get played. Sure this is better but given how impossible it is to get hold of it is not worth trying to track down a copy. Also, not sure how well it players with more than 2 and not sure the theme is that appealing to me sadly (although the tiles are lovely).
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Gifted

Super tight puzzle game with extremely gorgeous and tactile, clackity components. Very easy to teach, and you will often find yourself playing multiple rounds.

Would be a 9/10 but:
- Lay-players can end up getting screwed and taking a bunch of negative points if they play cunning opponents. It's hard to catch up from that.
- Not enough depth or freedom of choice (I'd rather put myself into a crappy constraint than the game putting me into that constraint). The backside I think is my preferred version of the game, but I've never convinced anyone to try that since this game really only gets pulled out with more casual friends.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: Incredibly simple rules, can probably be tought in 5 minutes or less, but the strategy can get incredibly deep. At first you're just thinking about your own wall, but then you start to realize how you can block or mess with the other players, and then you start going deeper into thinking about which pile you want to take from to set up the middle to be a certain way and force or not-force someone else into taking or not taking the pile you might have your eyes on. This really feels like some kind of ancient board game in the vein of mancala or something, but in a really good way where the pure, simple style of it has incredible depth.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Updated when getting rid of it: It's fun! But sometimes with the drafting you can leave a bunch of tiles going on the opponents floor, which isn't much fun and a bit mean for us. 

Original Review: This game is a joy with 2, even with the mean hate drafting. Print paper boards and leave the box at home for an easy holiday game. It just gets better with more players, and is a great game with 3, a tricky player count. Very satisfying puzzle, some may hate the lack of control as you have to respond to other people manipulating the shared tile pool but this isn’t a heavy strategy game, it’s an abstract, competitive puzzle. We love it!
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value: It’s a well thought out game, usually a hit. I got the mini version when I saw it for sale and thought, “Great, Azul in a smaller, convenient package!” Well, no, just no. Stick with the real size version. The little version really is little. The tiny tiles are hard to manipulate and make you feel like you’ve got fat, clumsy fingers. There is a tray instead of the free floating coasters and the spaces are too small. The center space is practically unusable. The tiles sit in spaces on the plastic player boards, but they don’t snap in place and they’re not magnetic, so forget about playing in a moving vehicle. Fiddly, fiddly, fiddly.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Excellent abstract game. Every time I introduce it to someone, they immediately go home and buy their own copy. The mechanics are sleek and well-tuned, but don't be decieved by it's simplicity, there really is a lot going on. Planning your next move, looking for the right tiles at the right time, and keeping your options open really puts you at the edge of your seat and keeps you thinking. 

Azul offers a very rewarding experience from start to finish. The components and artwork really blend into the mechanics of the game well, and offer a dazzling aesthetic that you don't get from a lot of games. Ten out of ten, go buy this one.
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Azul, which won the 2018 Spiel des Jahres, is a 2-4 player game that has players drafting "ceramic tiles" to make a design that'll impress the Portugese king.

4 spinoffs were released since the writing of this review, which goes to show how successful the game has been.

You choose between a design template or make your own, which allows for some freedom.

Once players get settled, everyone will begin drafting tiles.

+ Concurrent turns allow for little to no downtime
+ Starting player marker
+ Simple & advanced game boards
+ Placement restrictions add a puzzle element to the game

- Game components easily slide on player boards
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
Espléndido juego para la familia. Fácil de desplegar y explicar. Muy bien editado (las fichas son bonitas y resistentes). Es un juego que se presta a repetir partida después de la primera. No es largo y siempre genera esa rivalidad que anima a pedir la revancha. 

Se puede jugar con niños pequeños y también funciona muy bien en entornos multiculturales. Es decir, se puede jugar cuando los presentes hablan distintos idiomas porque no exige dominio de ninguna lengua común. No hay cartitas ni cosas que leer durante la partida. 

Es uno de los juegos de mi colección que me cuesta menos poner encima de la mesa con familiares y amigos.

textfield_comment_value: I don't think it's an overstatement to say that by now this is a modern classic. I haven't tried all the new "variations" that have come out since, but I feel there is something beautiful about the simplicity of the original. This is one of those games that I can easily teach to non gamers, and still get a great experience out of it, without feeling I'm playing something I wouldn't have picked otherwise. Beware that it can be very mean, especially at lower player count, but to me it's part of the fun (if you don't take it too seriously of course). It's rare for me to play a title several times, but this is one of the exceptions
Title: Azul

textfield_comment_value:
This is a fairly unique resource gathering, pattern matching game. It's easy to explain, very easy to play, plays quickly - but also has a strong underlying strategy built in. 

At first, any wins will be kind of random until players figure out properly how to play! It's too easy to want to be very cautious in the early game and not take minus points, but a few minus points early build into a lot of plus points later. Plus, it's never a bad idea to take the minus for getting the first player marker.

An interesting little game. Not one I'd immediately suggest playing, but also one that I don't mind being placed in front of me.

Azul should be absolutely 10/10, it is a great game with great looks and great production quality and UX.

The boards teach the game rules with their arrangement, it is very clear how players interact with each other despite the solitaire feeling of having your own board (and it is a strong interaction), you always face dilemmas.

The reason I cannot give 10 is an odd one. This is a game about artisanship. The whole theme is creating something, something pretty.
And you cannot hope to finish it. Ever.
I don't care if I win or not, I want my wall finished. Sorry.

textfield_comment_value: I don't get this game. It's fine. The components are great. But there's not a lot of strategy. Fill spaces next to ones you've already filled for maximum pointage. Also, count out the turns so you don't get stuck with a bunch of tiles you don't need. Once you figure these out, then you can only play with other people who have also figured them out. Multi-player abstracts are hard to pull of well; Azul comes close but it still struggles with the difficulty of an unbalanced play group.

+ Clear layout easy to see opponents' boards
+ Hate drafting exists...

textfield_comment_value: I've decided with a heavy heart to part with this game in favor of Sagrada. The fact is, while I enjoy playing Azul, it's gone the way of Ticket to Ride where they feel like they have to create several new iterations instead of releasing less expensive expansions. Thus, I'm left playing the exact same game every time unless I can convince people to flip their boards to the back (I haven't been able to yet). Sagrada has tons of expansions and promos, so gameplay is always varied and interesting. Since I feel like they both fit the same niche and space is at a premium for me, Azul has to go.

Azul can be very satisfying to play but it also has moments where that satisfaction is frustratingly squashed. I was particularly impressed with the elegance of how the mechanics and components interacted. The components are also great quality. 

There is one big problem which hurts my rating of the game. Fairly regularly, there are moments in Azul where you literally can't avoid taking a devastatingly bad hand, which ruin the otherwise best part of Azul: the chill feel-good pattern-building vibes.

textfield_comment_value: Azul is one of the most cutthroat and aggressive games I've ever played, but it is also very satisfying to execute some of its basic prescribed strategies. The skill cap initially seemed to be a lot higher than I think it actually is, which I guess must be due to the learning curve. Similarly, while I had initially assumed that the game would be very much akin to several concurrent rounds of solitaire, I was stunned by how very exciting of an experience it was, moves being just as much inspired by opponents' boards as my own.
